meta.textbook: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 12th ed.
meta.notes: Exam 2 question bank, rebuilt 2026-11 for concept coverage. Every core concept of every deck objective is tested by at least one application level question; section sizes vary with the content. Regular items are -m01 onward; items marked "difficulty": "difficult" are -x01 onward. Every question stands alone (no case groups). "objective" names the deck objective, "concept" the core concept tested, "coverage" states the source, "note" flags a deck vs textbook conflict. Temperatures are Celsius only.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate absolutes
optionStrategies.cue: always, never, all, none, only, every
optionStrategies.note: Absolutes are usually wrong because medicine rarely deals in certainties.

optionStrategies.name: Favor qualifiers
optionStrategies.cue: usually, generally, often, may, approximately, most
optionStrategies.note: Qualifiers make a statement realistic. Not automatically right, but worth a second look against an absolute.

optionStrategies.name: Opposite pair, look closely
optionStrategies.cue: increase vs decrease, before vs after
optionStrategies.note: Often one of the pair is correct. Sometimes both are distractors, so treat it as a flag for attention.

optionStrategies.name: Global or umbrella option
optionStrategies.cue: one option covers two or more others
optionStrategies.note: If one option encompasses the others it is often the most complete answer.

optionStrategies.name: Patient-centered option
optionStrategies.cue: asks, involves, or respects the patient
optionStrategies.note: Options that involve the patient beat options that decide for them.

optionStrategies.name: Duplicate facts
optionStrategies.cue: a wrong fact shared by two or more options
optionStrategies.note: One shared wrong fact eliminates several options at once.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
optionStrategies.cue: don't worry, it's nothing, most people are fine
optionStrategies.note: Therapeutic communication reflects feelings and invites more.

optionStrategies.name: Odd man wins
optionStrategies.cue: three options share an idea, one stands apart
optionStrategies.note: When most options point one way, the different one is often correct.

optionStrategies.name: Negative polarity
optionStrategies.cue: avoid, except, not, least, contraindicated, requires further teaching
optionStrategies.note: You are hunting the wrong option. Identify polarity before reading the choices.

optionStrategies.name: Priority key word
optionStrategies.cue: priority, immediate, first, best, most, least
optionStrategies.note: More than one option may be true. The key word decides how to choose among them.

optionStrategies.name: Apply the ABCs
optionStrategies.note: In ordering and priority questions, airway, breathing, and circulation come first, then safety, then comfort.

optionStrategies.name: Assessment before intervention
optionStrategies.cue: assess, check, determine versus administer, apply, notify
optionStrategies.note: When the stem asks what comes first and an assessment option is present, assessment usually precedes action.

optionStrategies.name: Treat each option as true or false
optionStrategies.note: Work each option independently. Partial credit means a wrong selection costs you, so only select what the scenario supports.

questions.stem: When a patient returns from radiology, the nurse finds the bed at its highest position with the brakes unlocked. The patient did not fall. After lowering the bed and locking the brakes, what does the nurse do next?

options.text: Take no further action because the patient was not harmed
options.rationale: The hazard is corrected for this patient, but its cause is untouched. Without a report, the same gap can leave the next patient's bed high and unlocked.

options.text: Speak with the transporter privately and keep it between them
options.rationale: Talking with the transporter is reasonable, yet keeping it private hides the event from the system. The agency cannot learn from a hazard it never hears about.

options.text: Report the hazard through the agency's reporting system
options.rationale: A culture of safety encourages reporting hazards and errors, including those that caused no harm. The report lets the agency find the gap in the transport process and fix it for every patient.

options.text: Ask the transport supervisor to discipline the transporter
options.rationale: Discipline aims at one person instead of the process and makes staff afraid to report. A culture of safety is blame free so that hazards come to light.

questions.takeaway: A hazard that caused no harm is still reported, because reporting is how the agency learns and fixes the process behind it.
questions.strategy: No harm makes doing nothing feel acceptable, and discipline feels like accountability. Ask which action lets the system learn without blame.

steps.detail: The bed is fixed, but the cause that produced it is still in place.
Private talks and discipline focus on a person and keep the system from learning.
A report reaches everyone who can change the transport process.

elimination.verdict: Report the hazard through the agency's reporting system.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.objective: Identify patient, environmental, and health care related factors that increase the risk for injury
questions.concept: Culture of safety: report hazards even without harm

questions.stem: At a unit meeting, a nurse reports that she gave a scheduled antibiotic 2 hours late after three infusion pumps alarmed at once during her medication pass. Which response from the charge nurse supports a culture of safety?

options.text: "What about the alarms and workload led to the delay?"
options.rationale: This question looks for contributing factors in the system rather than blaming the nurse. Learning from adverse events in a blame free environment is a core feature of a culture of safety.

options.text: "You will need extra training on managing your time."
options.rationale: Training targets her alone and assumes the cause was personal. Three pumps alarming at once points to a process problem that training one nurse will not fix.

options.text: "Let us keep this out of the meeting so you are not embarrassed."
options.rationale: Protecting her feelings is kind, but hiding the event blocks learning. Discussing adverse events openly and without blame is how the unit prevents the next one.

options.text: "Late doses happen; be more careful next time."
options.rationale: It sounds supportive, yet it treats the event as personal carelessness and changes nothing. A culture of safety studies adverse events instead of brushing them off.

questions.takeaway: A culture of safety responds to an error by asking what in the system allowed it, not by blaming the person who reported it.
questions.strategy: Gentle reassurance and private handling both feel supportive. The response that supports safety is the one that looks for the cause in the process.

steps.detail: Extra training and being more careful both place the cause in the nurse.
Keeping it out of the meeting means nobody learns from it.
Asking about alarms and workload looks for contributing factors.

elimination.verdict: Ask what about the alarms and workload led to the delay.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.objective: Identify patient, environmental, and health care related factors that increase the risk for injury
questions.concept: Culture of safety: blame free learning from adverse events

questions.scenario: Before planning care on a surgical unit, the nurse reviews safety concerns for several patients.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an individual risk factor or a health care environment risk.

rows.text: A bed's side rail latch is broken and the rail drops without warning
rows.rationale: Equipment related injury comes from the tools of care. The bed is taken out of use and reported so that the faulty rail harms no one.

rows.text: A patient with hearing loss nods along but cannot repeat the call light steps
rows.rationale: Sensory and communication impairments are individual risk factors. The patient may agree without understanding, so the nurse checks with teach back and adjusts the approach.

rows.text: A patient's puncture site bleeds after a bedside procedure
rows.rationale: Procedure related injury arises from care itself. Close monitoring after procedures is how the nurse catches this health care environment risk early.

rows.text: A disinfectant splashed onto a patient's arm during room cleaning
rows.rationale: Chemical exposure arises from products used in the care setting. The hazard lives in the environment, so the fix is safe handling of the product.

rows.text: A patient cannot afford the walker the therapist recommended for home
rows.rationale: Limited economic resources belong to the patient and follow the patient home. The nurse addresses them with resources such as a social work referral, not with a change to the unit.

rows.text: A patient plans to keep smoking at home near his home oxygen
rows.rationale: Lifestyle choices are individual risk factors, and oxygen is highly flammable. His habit itself creates the danger, so teaching targets the behavior.

questions.takeaway: Individual risk factors come with the patient, such as economic limits, impairments and lifestyle, while environment risks come from procedures, equipment, chemicals and the workplace.
questions.strategy: Every row involves a patient, so ask where the danger starts: in the person, or in the care setting and its tools.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Money, hearing loss and smoking go home with the patient.
The disinfectant, the broken rail latch and the bleeding procedure site come from the care setting.

elimination.verdict: Individual: walker cost, hearing loss, smoking. Environment: disinfectant, broken rail latch, procedure bleeding.

questions.concept: Individual risk factors and health care environment risks

questions.stem: On a busy medical unit, a nurse with five patients starts a medication pass. The bar code scanner is taking about a minute for each scan, and two patients' doses are due now. Which action best reduces the risk of harm to these patients?

options.text: Scan every wristband and drug, and mention the scanner at shift report
options.rationale: Scanning everything is correct, and reporting the scanner is the right idea. Waiting until shift report leaves the problem in place for hours while other nurses face the same pressure to skip scans.

options.text: Scan every wristband and drug, and report the slow scanner now
options.rationale: Scanning every item keeps the technology check in place instead of trusting memory or a glance. Reporting the slow scanner right away lets the team fix the hazard before it pushes anyone else toward a shortcut.

options.text: Check the drugs by sight against the record until the scanner speeds up
options.rationale: A visual check feels faster under pressure, but it removes the safeguard built to catch a wrong patient or a wrong drug. Slow equipment is reported and fixed, not worked around.

options.text: Scan each drug but skip wristbands of patients the nurse knows by name
options.rationale: Knowing a patient by name relies on memory, which is the weak point that safety skills try to remove. Skipping the wristband scan lets a mixed up room or bed go unnoticed.

questions.takeaway: QSEN safety skills mean using technology and standardized checks instead of memory, and reporting hazards when they are found, even on a busy unit.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option saves time on a heavy day. Keeping every scan and reporting the problem now beats the near miss that waits until shift report.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sight checks and skipped wristbands replace technology with a glance or with memory.
Both keep every scan; only one reports the hazard when it is found.

elimination.verdict: Scan every wristband and drug, and report the slow scanner now.

questions.stem: The day after a knee replacement, a patient is assessed as a fall risk. She says, "I am careful. I never fall at home." Which response by the nurse best identifies her current injury risk?

options.text: "Do you understand why the assessment shows you are at risk?"
options.rationale: This checks her understanding of a score, not her abilities. A yes or no answer reveals nothing about her routines or her new limitations.

options.text: "I will set a bed alarm so that we know when you get up."
options.rationale: A bed alarm may be added later, but it is an intervention chosen before her risk is understood. Assessment comes before intervention.

options.text: "Hospitals are different from home, so call before getting up."
options.rationale: The advice is sound, but it tells instead of asks. It gathers nothing about what she can do now, so the plan cannot be fitted to her.

options.text: "What do you do alone at home, and what feels harder now?"
options.rationale: Asking about her usual abilities and what is new since surgery sees safety through her eyes. The gap between the two shows exactly where she needs help.

questions.takeaway: Seeing safety through the patient's eyes means asking about home routines, normal abilities and new limitations, then planning with the patient.
questions.strategy: Telling her the hospital is different sounds like teaching. The better response gathers the data that shows what changed for her.

steps.detail: Only one response asks about her abilities and limits.
Advice and a bed alarm act before the nurse knows her risk.
A yes or no about a score gives no new data.

elimination.verdict: Ask what she does alone at home and what feels harder now.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient admitted last evening with heart failure who has never fallen. Which finding shows that the hospital stay itself has raised his risk for injury?

options.text: He was woken four times overnight for vital signs
options.rationale: Sleep disruption is one of the ways a hospital stay raises injury risk. Broken sleep dulls his alertness, balance and judgment the next time he gets up to stand or walk.

options.text: He has worn reading glasses for many years
options.rationale: A vision problem can add to fall risk, so it is worth noting. It is long standing and came with him from home, so it is not something the hospital stay has added.

options.text: He presses his call light each time he wants to stand
options.rationale: Using the call light is a protective behavior that lowers his risk. It shows he is accepting help in a setting where his usual habits from home do not fit.

options.text: He bathes and dresses himself without help at home
options.rationale: Independence at home is a strength, not a risk factor. The added risk comes from what changes in the hospital, such as reduced independence and new routines.

questions.takeaway: A hospital stay adds injury risk through unfamiliar surroundings, sleep disruption, changed routines, new medications, tubes and lines, acute illness and reduced independence.
questions.strategy: Reading glasses tempt because poor vision causes falls. The stem asks what the stay has added, so look for the finding that began with admission.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only the overnight vital signs began with admission.
The glasses came from home, and self care and call light use protect him.

elimination.verdict: He was woken four times overnight for vital signs.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with cellulitis of the leg arrives on the unit with an IV line. He has not been shown the room, and he says he will manage on his own. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Begin scheduled toileting with staff every 1 to 2 hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting is an individualized intervention for urgency or frequency. Nothing in his history shows that risk, and the universal precautions come first.

options.text: Tell him where the call light is clipped on the bed rail
options.rationale: Telling him is one step short of the precaution. Without a demonstration, the nurse does not know that he can find and use the call light at night.

options.text: Ask a family member to stay at the bedside through the night
options.rationale: Family presence can help a confused patient, but he is alert and nothing suggests he needs a companion. It also skips the basics every patient needs.

options.text: Show him the room and have him demonstrate the call light
options.rationale: Familiarizing him with the room and having him demonstrate the call light are universal fall precautions every patient receives. A demonstration proves he can use it, which being told cannot.

questions.takeaway: Every patient, regardless of risk, is oriented to the room and demonstrates call light use; individualized measures are added for specific risks.
questions.strategy: Telling him where the call light is sounds complete. The precaution asks the patient to demonstrate it, which closes the gap.

steps.action: Start with what every patient gets
steps.detail: Orientation and call light use are universal precautions.
Scheduled toileting and a companion address risks he has not shown.
Only a demonstration confirms he can use it.

elimination.verdict: Show him the room and have him demonstrate the call light.

questions.stem: After starting a diuretic this morning for leg edema, a patient has twice in 3 hours hurried to the bathroom alone, dragging her IV pole, because she could not wait for help. Which addition to her plan targets this risk?

options.text: Reorientation to the room every hour
options.rationale: Reorientation is the targeted intervention for confusion. She knows where the bathroom is; her problem is that she cannot wait.

options.text: A bed alarm that sounds when she stands
options.rationale: An alarm alerts staff only after she is already up and rushing. It does not remove the urgency that drives the unsafe trip.

options.text: Toileting with staff every 1 to 2 hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting every 1 to 2 hours empties her bladder before urgency builds. It targets the cause of her rushing instead of reacting to it.

options.text: A bedpan so that she stays in bed all day
options.rationale: Keeping her in bed avoids the walk but causes weakness from immobility. Fall prevention aims for safe mobility, not immobility.

questions.takeaway: Urgency and frequency are matched with scheduled toileting every 1 to 2 hours so the patient never has to rush.
questions.strategy: A bed alarm feels protective because it reports her movement. Ask which choice removes the reason she is rushing.

steps.detail: She rushes because the diuretic gives her urgency.
Scheduled toileting heads off urgency before it starts.
An alarm reacts late, a bedpan immobilizes her and reorientation fits confusion.

elimination.verdict: Toileting with staff every 1 to 2 hours.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.objective: Apply individualized fall prevention strategies based on patient specific risk factors and functional status

questions.nursesNote: 0700 Fall risk rounds. Patient is weak in both legs after 5 days of bed rest. Room is cluttered with a chair and an empty meal tray between the bed and the bathroom. Patient reports needing to urinate often since yesterday. Wearing loose cotton socks without treads. Bed is in its highest position after morning care. Oriented to person only this morning. Walker is folded against the far wall. Overhead light is off and the curtains are closed.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that the nurse can correct right away by changing the room or the patient's equipment.

segments.text: weak in both legs after 5 days of bed rest
segments.rationale: Weakness is an intrinsic risk factor that lives in the patient. It is managed with assisted mobility and therapy, not by changing the room.

segments.text: cluttered with a chair and an empty meal tray between the bed and the bathroom
segments.rationale: Clutter is an extrinsic risk factor placed right in her path to the toilet. Keeping care areas uncluttered is a universal fall precaution the nurse can fix now.

segments.text: needing to urinate often since yesterday
segments.rationale: Urinary frequency is an intrinsic risk factor that comes from her body. It calls for scheduled toileting, which targets the patient rather than the room.

segments.text: loose cotton socks without treads
segments.rationale: Improper footwear is an extrinsic risk factor. Nonslip, well fitting footwear is a universal precaution the nurse can provide at once.

segments.text: highest position after morning care
segments.rationale: Bed height is an extrinsic risk factor left over from care. Returning the bed to its low position is a universal fall precaution.

segments.text: Oriented to person only this morning
segments.rationale: Confusion is an intrinsic risk factor arising from her condition. It is managed with reorientation and familiar cues, not with a room change.

segments.text: Walker is folded against the far wall
segments.rationale: An assistive device that is out of reach is an extrinsic risk factor. Placing the walker within reach lets her use it instead of reaching for furniture.

segments.text: Overhead light is off and the curtains are closed
segments.rationale: Poor lighting is an extrinsic risk factor that hides hazards on the floor. Turning on light is a quick environmental fix for the room.

questions.takeaway: Extrinsic factors such as clutter, footwear, bed height, out of reach devices and lighting come from the room and equipment and can be corrected right away.
questions.strategy: Every finding raises fall risk, so the trap is highlighting all of them. Ask whether the nurse fixes the finding by changing the room or must target the patient's body.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weakness, frequency and confusion belong to the patient.
Clutter, socks, bed height, the walker and the light are all items the precautions cover.
Each environmental finding can be corrected before the patient next stands.

elimination.verdict: Clutter, socks without treads, high bed, walker out of reach and poor lighting.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with urinary frequency whose catheter was removed yesterday. He was placed on toileting with staff every 2 hours after rushing to the bathroom alone. Which finding the next day best shows the plan is working?

options.text: He drank less during the day so that he voided less often
options.rationale: Limiting fluids lowers the number of trips but risks dehydration and is not part of the plan. The goal is safe movement, not fewer bathroom needs.

options.text: He walked to the bathroom with staff and never went alone
options.rationale: The goal of scheduled toileting is to reduce urgency driven unsafe movement. Safe, assisted trips with no solo rushing show that the goal was met.

options.text: He pressed the call light once between scheduled rounds
options.rationale: Calling for help is appropriate, but one call does not show the plan works. It is weaker evidence than a full day with no trips alone.

options.text: He used a urinal in bed for the whole shift and had no falls
options.rationale: No falls sounds like success, but staying in bed is not the goal. Immobility weakens him and trades one risk for another.

questions.takeaway: A fall prevention plan is evaluated against its goal; for scheduled toileting, the goal is safe, assisted trips without urgency driven rushing.
questions.strategy: No falls is tempting because falls are what the plan prevents. The plan's goal is safe movement, and staying in bed does not meet it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reduce rushing while keeping him mobile.
Bed rest and drinking less avoid the walk instead of making it safe.
A full day of assisted trips outweighs one call.

elimination.verdict: He walked to the bathroom with staff and never went alone.

questions.stem: A patient with hypertension is dizzy for about 2 hours after her 0800 blood pressure medication. Her walk with staff is scheduled for 0900, and yesterday she nearly fell during it. Which plan does the nurse choose?

options.text: Keep the 0900 walk and add a second staff member
options.rationale: A second helper adds support, but she would still walk at her dizziest. Changing the timing removes the risk instead of bracing for it.

options.text: Hold the 0800 dose on the days she walks with staff
options.rationale: Holding a prescribed medication is not a decision the nurse makes alone. It trades a fall risk for uncontrolled blood pressure.

options.text: Ask the pharmacist about timing and walk her after the dizziness
options.rationale: Adjusting timing and assisting mobility are the targeted interventions for medication dizziness, with the pharmacist as a partner. She still walks, just not at the peak of the side effect.

options.text: Cancel her walks until she goes a full day without dizziness
options.rationale: Canceling walks reduces exposure today but causes weakness from immobility. The goal is safe mobility, so the walk is moved rather than removed.

questions.takeaway: Medication related dizziness is managed by monitoring symptoms, adjusting timing with the pharmacist and assisting with mobility, not by stopping activity.
questions.strategy: A second helper feels like the safest choice. Ask whether the plan changes when she walks or only who walks beside her.

steps.detail: Dizziness peaks for 2 hours after the dose, and the walk falls inside that window.
Holding a dose is outside nursing scope; canceling walks weakens her.
Moving the walk avoids the peak; extra staff only cushions it.

elimination.verdict: Ask the pharmacist about timing and walk her after the dizziness.

questions.stem: On a medical unit, a patient recovering from sepsis has new confusion. He is found in the hall three times in 2 hours, looking for "my kitchen." He walks steadily with his walker, voided 20 minutes before each time and is wearing his glasses. Which intervention targets his risk?

options.text: Staff assistance with every transfer and walk
options.rationale: Hands on assistance fits weakness, yet he walks steadily with his walker. It does not address why he keeps leaving the room.

options.text: Toileting rounds with staff every 1 to 2 hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting fits urgency, but he voided shortly before each trip. His wandering is not driven by bladder needs.

options.text: A night light and his glasses within reach
options.rationale: Lighting and glasses address visual impairment, but he is already wearing his glasses. The cue in this situation is disorientation, not poor vision.

options.text: Frequent reorientation and familiar objects from home
options.rationale: Searching for his kitchen shows disorientation, and confusion leads to unsafe attempts to get up. Reorientation and familiar cues target that cause.

questions.takeaway: Each fall risk factor has its own targeted intervention; confusion calls for frequent reorientation and familiar cues in the environment.
questions.strategy: Every option is a real fall intervention. The stem rules out urgency, weakness and vision one by one, leaving disorientation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He voided before each trip.
He walks steadily and wears his glasses.
Looking for his kitchen points to disorientation.

elimination.verdict: Frequent reorientation and familiar objects from home.

questions.stem: At 0300, a patient admitted with a bleeding stomach ulcer fell while walking to the bathroom. She is uninjured and says she could not see the floor. Her glasses were in a drawer across the dark room. A low bed, locked brakes and nonslip socks were in place. Which change fits her plan?

options.text: A night light on and her glasses within reach
options.rationale: Poor vision increases misjudgment of surroundings, and both her lighting and her glasses were missing. Improving lighting and keeping glasses accessible target that risk directly.

options.text: Toileting with staff every 1 to 2 hours overnight
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting fits urgency, which is not what she described. She fell because she could not see, so the fix must target her vision.

options.text: A move to a room near the nurses' station
options.rationale: Closer observation helps confused patients, but she is oriented and knew where she was going. Being watched more does not help her see the floor.

options.text: All four side rails raised from 2200 to 0600
options.rationale: Four raised rails restrain her and invite a climb over the rails. They do not address the dark room and missing glasses that caused the fall.

questions.takeaway: When a fall points to poor vision, the targeted change is better lighting and glasses kept within reach.
questions.strategy: Side rails feel protective after a night fall. Ask what caused this fall: she could not see.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She could not see, and her glasses were out of reach.
Toileting and closer observation target urgency and confusion.
Four rails restrict her and add a climbing risk.

elimination.verdict: A night light on and her glasses within reach.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.objective: Apply individualized fall prevention strategies based on patient specific risk factors and functional status

questions.stem: After 10 days in bed with pneumonia, a patient now walks with one staff member. Over 2 days she has needed more tries to stand from her chair. She is oriented, denies dizziness and has no new medications. Which change to her plan fits?

options.text: Reorient her to the room and call light before each transfer
options.rationale: Reorientation targets confusion, but she is oriented. Her trouble standing is muscle weakness, which reorientation does not change.

options.text: Continue assisted walks and involve physical therapy for strength
options.rationale: Weakness reduces strength and balance, so the targeted intervention is assisted mobility with physical therapy. Continuing to walk rebuilds the strength that bed rest took.

options.text: Use a wheelchair for all trips until her legs are stronger
options.rationale: A wheelchair avoids the walk but removes the practice that builds strength. Immobility worsens weakness, so this works against the goal.

options.text: Ask the pharmacist to review the timing of her medications
options.rationale: Pharmacist review fits medication dizziness. She denies dizziness and has no new medications, so the cause lies elsewhere.

questions.takeaway: Weakness is matched with assisted transfers and walking, often with physical therapy, because immobility makes weakness worse.
questions.strategy: A wheelchair looks like the safe response to worsening weakness. It removes the activity that would reverse it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: More tries to stand means weakness.
She is oriented, not dizzy and on no new medications.
The wheelchair worsens the weakness it is meant to protect.

elimination.verdict: Continue assisted walks and involve physical therapy for strength.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.objective: Apply individualized fall prevention strategies based on patient specific risk factors and functional status
questions.concept: Weakness: assisted mobility and physical therapy

questions.stem: On a medical unit, the nurse reviews the care of several patients. Which interventions count as a restraint? Select all that apply.

options.text: Having a sitter stay at the bedside overnight
options.rationale: A sitter provides companionship and observation, which are alternatives to restraint. The patient stays free to move while someone watches.

options.text: Using a bed alarm that sounds when a patient stands
options.rationale: An alarm alerts staff but does not stop the patient from moving. Alarms are among the alternatives to restraint.

options.text: Raising all four side rails for a patient who wants to get up
options.rationale: When rails leave no route out of bed, they restrict movement and count as a physical restraint. They also invite the patient to climb over.

options.text: Keeping a patient alone in a room she is not allowed to leave
options.rationale: Involuntary confinement in a room that the patient cannot leave is seclusion. Seclusion counts as a restraint because it restricts where she can move.

options.text: Giving a sedative so that a restless patient stays in bed
options.rationale: A medication used to manage behavior rather than treat a condition is a chemical restraint. It restricts movement as surely as a strap.

options.text: Raising the two upper rails so that a patient can reposition
options.rationale: With the foot of the bed open, the patient has a route out, so these rails are not a restraint. They support turning and stability in bed.

options.text: Tucking sheets tightly so that a patient cannot turn or rise
options.rationale: Any intervention that restricts movement counts, even without a device. Tight sheets hold the patient in place the way a belt would.

questions.takeaway: Restraints include physical devices, chemical restraint, seclusion and any intervention that restricts movement, while alarms and sitters are alternatives.
questions.strategy: Tight sheets and a sedative do not look like restraints. Judge each option by whether it restricts movement, not by whether it is a device.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Does the intervention stop the patient from moving freely?
A behavior sedative, seclusion and tight sheets all restrict movement.
Two upper rails, an alarm and a sitter leave the patient free.

elimination.verdict: The sedative, four side rails, seclusion and tight sheets.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).

questions.stem: A patient's son tells the nurse, "I will keep her in bed so she cannot fall." His mother is recovering from abdominal surgery, is at risk for falls and walks three times a day with one staff member. Which reply by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Thank you. Press the call light if she tries to get up."
options.rationale: This accepts his plan and leaves her in bed. Immobility worsens weakness, so agreeing raises her fall risk over time.

options.text: "Bed rest weakens her; here is how to help her walk."
options.rationale: This explains the reason and specifies the needed assistance while involving the son as a caregiver. The goal of fall prevention is safe mobility, not immobility.

options.text: "Staff handle her walking, so you do not need to watch her."
options.rationale: This dismisses the son instead of involving him. Family caregivers are part of fall education and can reinforce the plan.

options.text: "She can walk whenever she feels steady enough on her own."
options.rationale: This swings to the opposite error and removes the assistance she needs. Her plan calls for one helper, not walking alone.

questions.takeaway: Fall prevention aims for safe mobility, so the nurse explains why bed rest is harmful and teaches family how to assist.
questions.strategy: Thanking the son feels supportive. Ask whether the reply protects her from weakness as well as from falling.

steps.detail: Keeping her in bed and letting her walk alone are both unsafe.
Dismissing the son loses a caregiver who can help.
Explain the reason and specify the help she needs.

elimination.verdict: Explain that bed rest weakens her and show him how to help her walk.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.objective: Apply individualized fall prevention strategies based on patient specific risk factors and functional status
questions.concept: Fall prevention does not mean keeping patients in bed

questions.stem: A patient with left sided weakness after a stroke has a fall prevention plan that calls for a helper at his side for all walking. The nurse teaches his daughter about the plan. Which statement by the daughter shows that the teaching worked?

options.text: "His left leg gives way, so one of us is with him on walks."
options.rationale: She names the reason for his risk and the assistance his plan calls for. Explaining the reason for the risk and specifying the needed help are the goals of fall education.

options.text: "Falls are mostly bad luck, so we will watch him closely at home."
options.rationale: Closer watching is reasonable, but calling falls luck shows she does not understand his risk. Without knowing the reason, she cannot target the help he needs.

options.text: "I will keep all four side rails up at night so he stays safe."
options.rationale: Raising all four rails sounds protective, but it can act as a restraint and tempt him to climb over. It also misses that the goal is safe mobility, not keeping him in bed.

options.text: "He can walk on his own once his walker is in his hand."
options.rationale: A walker adds support, so the idea is not unreasonable. His plan still calls for a helper at his side, and walking alone with the walker skips that assistance.

questions.takeaway: Fall education has worked when the family can state why the risk exists and what assistance is needed, while the plan keeps the patient moving safely.
questions.strategy: Four side rails and close watching both sound protective. Keep the statement that names his risk and the help his plan specifies.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Look for the reason and the help
steps.detail: Only one statement links his weak leg to a helper on every walk.
Four rails restrict him, walking alone skips the helper and luck ignores the cause.

elimination.verdict: "His left leg gives way, so one of us is with him on walks."

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a patient with leg weakness after spinal surgery. Her fall prevention plan: one person assists with walking, and toileting is every 2 hours. Which task does the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: Rescoring her fall risk after her afternoon nap
options.rationale: Assessing fall risk is an RN responsibility. Scoring requires nursing judgment about her condition, so it cannot be handed off.

options.text: Deciding each time she stands whether she needs one helper or two
options.rationale: Choosing the level of assistance is part of determining the prevention plan. That decision stays with the RN.

options.text: Walking her to the toilet every 2 hours and reporting unsafe attempts
options.rationale: Assisting with toileting and mobility according to the plan and reporting concerning behaviors may be delegated. The RN has already set the plan the assistant follows.

options.text: Judging at the end of shift whether the toileting schedule works
options.rationale: Evaluating effectiveness is an RN responsibility. The assistant reports what happened, and the RN decides whether the plan worked.

questions.takeaway: The RN assesses fall risk, sets the plan and evaluates it; assistive personnel carry out toileting and mobility by the plan and report concerns.
questions.strategy: Rescoring after a nap sounds like routine data collection. Assessing, deciding and judging all need RN judgment; carrying out the plan does not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rescoring, deciding and judging are assess, plan and evaluate.
Toileting by the plan and reporting unsafe attempts can be delegated.

elimination.verdict: Walking her to the toilet every 2 hours and reporting unsafe attempts.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).

questions.stem: One hour after receiving a sedating medication for sleep, a patient with chronic lung disease is drowsy and slow to answer. His plan says one person assists him to the toilet. Assistive personnel offer to take him to the toilet. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Let them take him and check his drowsiness once he is back in bed
options.rationale: Reassessing after the trip puts the risky movement before the assessment. Assessment comes before the intervention it guides.

options.text: Let the assistant take him, since toileting by the plan is delegable
options.rationale: Toileting by the plan is delegable, but the plan was written for an alert patient. A new change in his condition calls for RN assessment first.

options.text: Have the assistant bring a second helper if he seems unsteady
options.rationale: A second helper may be the right answer, but the assistant cannot make that judgment. Deciding the level of help requires RN assessment.

options.text: Assess him before he stands and decide what help he needs now
options.rationale: Sedation has changed his risk, and assessing risk and setting the plan belong to the RN. Once the nurse has assessed him, the task can be delegated with clear instructions.

questions.takeaway: A delegated fall task stays delegable only while the patient matches the plan; a change in condition sends the decision back to the RN.
questions.strategy: The plan says toileting is delegable, so letting the assistant go seems correct. The sedation means the plan no longer fits him.

steps.detail: He is drowsy and slow to answer after sedation.
A new risk needs RN assessment before anyone moves him.
Assess first, then delegate with the right level of help.

elimination.verdict: Assess him before he stands and decide what help he needs now.

questions.stem: A patient admitted for blood glucose management scored low risk on the fall risk tool at admission. On day 3 he starts an antidepressant and becomes newly anxious about going home. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Continue the current plan based on the admission score
options.rationale: The admission score was accurate then, but it predates two new risk factors. Acting on an old score leaves his plan behind his condition.

options.text: Ask the assistant to rescore him on the next round
options.rationale: Rescoring is right, but assessing fall risk is an RN responsibility. Assistive personnel can report changes; they do not score the tool.

options.text: Add a bed alarm without changing the rest of the plan
options.rationale: A bed alarm may fit, but choosing it before reassessing skips a step. The plan must match his current risks, which the nurse has not yet measured.

options.text: Rescore his fall risk and update the prevention plan
options.rationale: Antidepressants and psychological changes such as anxiety both raise scores on a fall risk tool. The admission score no longer describes him, so the RN reassesses and adjusts the plan.

questions.takeaway: Fall risk is reassessed whenever the patient's condition or medications change, and the plan is updated to match the new score.
questions.strategy: A bed alarm looks like a quick, sensible response. Ask whether the nurse knows his current risk well enough to choose an intervention yet.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A new antidepressant and new anxiety both count on the tool.
It no longer reflects him.
Rescoring cannot be delegated, and interventions follow it.

elimination.verdict: Rescore his fall risk and update the prevention plan.

questions.concept: Reassessing fall risk when the patient changes

questions.scenario: Four hours after soft wrist restraints were applied, the nurse reassesses a patient with a brain tumor and confusion who had pulled out his urinary catheter.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether the nurse continues current care or intervenes now.

rows.text: He shouts and pulls harder than before the restraints were applied
rows.rationale: Increased agitation and confusion are complications of restraints. The nurse reassesses the cause of the behavior and whether the restraint is still needed.

rows.text: He moves his fingers, wrists and elbows fully when each limb is released
rows.rationale: Full movement on release shows his range of motion is preserved. Loss of mobility is a complication of restraints, and it is not present.

rows.text: Skin under both restraints is intact and its usual color
rows.rationale: Intact skin of normal color shows skin integrity is being maintained. The nurse keeps checking it at each reassessment.

rows.text: His left hand is pale and cool below the restraint
rows.rationale: Pale, cool skin below the restraint means circulation is impaired. Neurovascular injury is a complication of restraints, so the restraint is loosened and the hand assessed now.

rows.text: He has not been offered fluids or the toilet since the restraints went on
rows.rationale: Hydration and elimination are monitoring areas, and 4 hours have passed with neither. He cannot meet these needs himself while restrained.

rows.text: He has slid down so the straps pull his arms above his head
rows.rationale: Positioning is a monitoring area, and this position strains his shoulders and invites escape attempts. He is repositioned and the straps are adjusted.

questions.takeaway: A restrained patient is checked for skin integrity, circulation, positioning, range of motion, hydration, elimination, comfort and mental status, and a problem in any area needs action.
questions.strategy: Rows that sound routine, such as no fluids yet, are easy to pass. Run each row against the monitoring areas and pass it only if that area is intact.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The pale, cool hand fails; intact skin passes.
No fluids or toileting in 4 hours fails.

steps.action: Check position, motion and mental status
steps.detail: Arms pulled overhead fails, full motion passes and rising agitation fails.

elimination.verdict: Intervene for the pale hand, missed needs, poor position and agitation; continue for intact skin and full motion.

questions.stem: The nurse finds a patient with dehydration and new confusion tugging at her IV line and picking at her gown. She last voided 7 hours ago and last had pain medication 6 hours ago. Her husband asks for wrist restraints. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Reassess her orientation to person, place and time
options.rationale: An orientation check confirms confusion, which is already known. It does not uncover why she is pulling at things right now.

options.text: Offer the toilet and assess her for pain
options.rationale: Before using a restraint, the nurse asks why: a full bladder after 7 hours and pain are common causes of picking and pulling. Meeting the need may stop the behavior.

options.text: Apply hand mitts as the least restrictive device
options.rationale: Mitts are less restrictive than wrist restraints, but alternatives come before any restraint. Her behavior may have a cause the nurse has not yet checked.

options.text: Explain to her husband why restraints cause harm
options.rationale: Teaching her husband matters, but it neither protects her IV line nor meets her needs. It can follow once her needs are addressed.

questions.takeaway: Before any restraint, the nurse looks for causes of the behavior such as pain, toileting, hunger, thirst, fear, medication effects and overstimulation.
questions.strategy: Mitts feel like the cautious compromise. The stem gives two unmet needs, and meeting them may make any restraint unnecessary.

steps.detail: 7 hours since voiding and 6 hours since pain medication.
Unmet needs are checked before restraints or alternatives.
Mitts restrain, an orientation check adds nothing new and teaching can wait.

elimination.verdict: Offer the toilet and assess her for pain.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities related to restraint use, restraint alternatives, and ongoing patient monitoring
questions.concept: Before using a restraint: ask why

questions.stem: A patient with a kidney infection and new confusion still reaches for his IV line after he has been toileted and given pain relief. His wife is in the waiting room. Which plan does the nurse try next?

options.text: Bring his wife in, reorient him and offer towels to fold
options.rationale: Family presence, reorientation and diversional activities are restraint alternatives. They engage his hands and attention without restricting his movement.

options.text: Apply hand mitts and remove them every 2 hours for skin care
options.rationale: Mitts are a restraint, and alternatives have not yet been tried. Restraint use comes only after less restrictive options fail.

options.text: Raise all four side rails and check him every 30 minutes
options.rationale: Four raised rails count as a restraint and can lead to a climb over them. Checking every 30 minutes also leaves long gaps with the IV at risk.

options.text: Dim the lights and leave him alone to reduce stimulation
options.rationale: Less stimulation can help, but leaving him alone removes observation. A confused patient reaching for his IV needs more supervision, not less.

questions.takeaway: After unmet needs are addressed, the nurse tries alternatives such as family presence, reorientation, diversion, observation and environmental changes before any restraint.
questions.strategy: Reducing stimulation is a real alternative, which makes the last option tempting. Leaving him alone removes the observation he needs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four side rails and mitts both restrict movement.
Dimming lights helps, but leaving him alone does not.
Family, reorientation and a task for his hands.

elimination.verdict: Bring his wife in, reorient him and offer towels to fold.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).

questions.stem: The nurse reviews four restraint requests from staff on a medical unit during the evening shift. Which request meets restraint guidelines?

options.text: A patient who struck a nurse yesterday and is calm today
options.rationale: Restraining him now would punish past behavior, since there is no immediate harm. Restraints prevent immediate harm and are never punishment.

options.text: A patient who calls often while the unit is short staffed
options.rationale: Frequent calls burden staff, but restraints are never used for staff convenience. The calls signal needs that should be met.

options.text: A confused patient pulling at a new chest tube despite a sitter
options.rationale: Pulling at a critical tube risks immediate harm the patient cannot control, and a sitter has not stopped it. That is a reason restraints may be used when alternatives are not enough.

options.text: A patient at high fall risk, as part of her usual bedtime routine
options.rationale: Restraints are never used for routine fall prevention, and she shows no immediate danger tonight. Her risk calls for targeted fall interventions such as scheduled toileting and a low bed.

questions.takeaway: Restraints are for immediate harm the patient cannot control, such as pulling out tubes, never for staff convenience, punishment or routine fall prevention.
questions.strategy: A high fall risk sounds like a strong safety reason. Restraint as a routine fall measure is one of the three uses the guidelines forbid.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only the chest tube puts the patient in danger right now, and an alternative has already failed.
Fall prevention, staff convenience and punishment.

elimination.verdict: A confused patient pulling at a new chest tube despite a sitter.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities related to restraint use, restraint alternatives, and ongoing patient monitoring
questions.note: Class material says restraints are never used for routine fall prevention. The assigned reading says patients who are confused, repeatedly wander or fall may need temporary restraint, but only after alternatives fail and always in the least restrictive form. On the course exam, key the class rule: a fall risk is never by itself a reason to restrain. On NCLEX, restraint as a routine fall measure is also wrong, but a patient who keeps falling or wandering after alternatives have failed can be a defensible candidate for a temporary, least restrictive restraint.

questions.stem: A patient with dementia has pulled out two IV lines despite family presence, reorientation and close observation, and she needs IV antibiotics. A restraint is prescribed. Which plan follows restraint guidelines?

options.text: Wrist restraints plus a vest so that she cannot slip down in bed
options.rationale: Adding a vest stacks restriction beyond the problem, which is her hands. Least restrictive means the smallest restraint that protects the line.

options.text: Hand mitts with frequent reassessment and early removal
options.rationale: Mitts protect the IV with the least restriction, and reassessing allows removal as soon as the need ends. Both are core restraint guidelines.

options.text: Wrist restraints kept on until the last antibiotic dose
options.rationale: Wrist restraints restrict more than needed, and keeping them on until therapy ends ignores reassessment. Restraints come off as early as possible.

options.text: Hand mitts only on night shift, when fewer staff can watch
options.rationale: Mitts are the right device, but here staffing sets the timing. Restraints are never used for staff convenience.

questions.takeaway: When a restraint is needed, the nurse uses the least restrictive option, keeps reassessing the need and removes it as early as possible.
questions.strategy: Night shift mitts name the right device. The reason given for the timing is staffing, which the guidelines forbid.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mitts restrict less than wrist restraints or a vest.
Staffing is never a reason to restrain.
Restraints are removed as early as possible, not at the end of therapy.

elimination.verdict: Hand mitts with frequent reassessment and early removal.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities related to restraint use, restraint alternatives, and ongoing patient monitoring
questions.concept: Least restrictive restraint and early removal

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a confused patient who was placed in wrist restraints 1 hour ago after pulling out a feeding tube. Since then he shouts and twists against them, and both wrists are red. His last pain medication was 9 hours ago. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Release them with staff present, assess for pain and try alternatives
options.rationale: Rising agitation and red wrists are restraint complications, and untreated pain may be driving the behavior. Releasing safely and asking why addresses both problems.

options.text: Request a sedative so that he stops straining against them
options.rationale: A sedative used to control behavior is a chemical restraint. It adds a second restraint without finding the cause.

options.text: Pad both wrists, loosen each strap a notch and recheck in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Padding protects the skin, but it treats the redness and ignores the agitation. The restraint itself may be causing the escalation.

options.text: Add a vest restraint so that twisting cannot hurt his wrists
options.rationale: More restraint usually increases agitation and the risk of injury from escape attempts. It moves in the wrong direction.

questions.takeaway: Increased agitation, skin and neurovascular injury and escape attempts are restraint complications that call for reassessing the cause and the need for the restraint.
questions.strategy: Padding and loosening look like good restraint care. They protect the skin while the agitation, a complication itself, keeps climbing.

steps.detail: Red wrists and worsening agitation since the restraints went on.
9 hours without pain medication.
A sedative and a vest add restraint instead of reducing it.

elimination.verdict: Release them with staff present, assess for pain and try alternatives.

questions.stem: On entering a room, the nurse finds flames rising from a wastebasket beside the bed of a patient who cannot walk. The fire is small. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Pull the pin and aim low at the base of the fire
options.rationale: Pull and aim are the first two steps of PASS for using an extinguisher. Extinguishing comes after rescue, alarm and containment, and only if the fire is small.

options.text: Close the door to contain the fire and smoke
options.rationale: Containing the fire limits its spread to other rooms and the hallway. The door is closed once the patient is out of the room.

options.text: Activate the alarm and report the exact location
options.rationale: Reporting the exact location brings help and warns others on the unit. It follows rescue because her injury risk is more immediate.

options.text: Move the patient in her bed away from the fire
options.rationale: Protecting patients from immediate injury comes first. The fire may spread before help arrives, and she cannot leave on her own.

options.text: Squeeze the handle and sweep from side to side
options.rationale: Squeeze and sweep finish PASS and coat the burning area evenly. They follow pulling the pin and aiming at the base.

questions.takeaway: In a health care fire, the nurse protects patients first, reports the exact location, contains the fire and then extinguishes it if possible using PASS.
questions.strategy: Grabbing the extinguisher feels fastest for a small fire. Patients near a fire are at risk regardless of its size, so rescue comes first.

steps.detail: She cannot walk and is beside the flames.
Report the location, then close the door.
Pull, aim, squeeze, sweep.

elimination.verdict: Move the patient, activate the alarm, close the door, pull and aim, squeeze and sweep.

questions.stem: A patient with postoperative delirium has worn hand mitts for 6 hours after pulling at her IV line. She is now calm, knows she is in the hospital and left her IV alone during two supervised releases. The prescription runs until morning. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Remove the mitts and raise all four side rails tonight
options.rationale: This trades one restraint for another. Her risk came from her hands on the IV line, which side rails do not address.

options.text: Keep the mitts on overnight, when confusion often worsens
options.rationale: Night confusion is a fair worry, but this restrains her for a risk she is not showing now. Close observation covers that concern.

options.text: Keep the mitts on and reassess at the next scheduled check
options.rationale: Waiting sounds cautious, and the order allows it. The reassessment already shows no need, so keeping the mitts on restrains her without a reason.

options.text: Remove the mitts now and continue close observation
options.rationale: The behavior that justified the mitts has stopped, shown twice with them off. Restraints are removed as early as possible, even when the prescription has time left.

questions.takeaway: Restraints come off as soon as reassessment shows the reason is gone, even if the prescription still has time left.
questions.strategy: Waiting for the next check sounds safe. Ask what that check would add: she is calm, oriented and left the IV alone twice.

steps.detail: Calm, oriented and IV untouched during two releases.
Four side rails are another restraint.
Both waiting options keep a restraint with no current reason.

elimination.verdict: Remove the mitts now and continue close observation.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).

questions.concept: Least restrictive restraint and early removal

questions.stem: A fire alarm sounds, and the charge nurse orders evacuation of the hallway near the fire. The nurse's patients are a man who walks without help and a woman on bed rest with a pelvic fracture. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Keep both patients in their rooms with the doors closed
options.rationale: Closed doors contain a fire, but evacuation has been ordered for patients near it. Patients close to a fire are at risk regardless of its size.

options.text: Carry her to the safe area first, then come back for him
options.rationale: Carrying a patient risks injuring the nurse, which then harms the patient. Her bed moves her safely, and he can walk on his own.

options.text: Send him walking to safety and wheel her out in her bed
options.rationale: Ambulatory patients walk themselves to safety, and patients who cannot get up are moved by bed, stretcher or wheelchair. This moves both quickly without risky lifting.

options.text: Wait at the bedside until fire department staff arrive
options.rationale: Firefighters help evacuate once they arrive, but waiting delays rescue. All personnel evacuate patients when evacuation is ordered.

questions.takeaway: During evacuation, ambulatory patients walk to safety and patients who cannot walk are moved in a bed, stretcher or wheelchair rather than carried.
questions.strategy: Carrying the patient who cannot walk seems the most protective choice. It risks injury to both nurse and patient when the bed can roll.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match each patient to a method
steps.detail: He walks; she rides in her bed.
It risks injury to the nurse and the patient.
Evacuation is ordered now, not when firefighters arrive.

elimination.verdict: Send him walking to safety and wheel her out in her bed.

questions.stem: While plugging in an infusion pump for a patient, the nurse sees a spark at the plug. The pump then powers on and passes its self test. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Remove the pump from use, label it for repair and report it
options.rationale: Equipment that sparks when plugged in is removed, designated for repair and reported to the right staff. A passing self test does not rule out an electrical fault.

options.text: Run the pump on battery until the cord is inspected
options.rationale: Battery use avoids the outlet but keeps faulty equipment at the bedside. Someone may plug it back in later without knowing about the spark.

options.text: Use the pump for now and report the spark at the end of the shift
options.rationale: The pump works, but a spark signals faulty wiring that can cause a shock or a fire. Using it now exposes this patient to that risk.

options.text: Move the plug to another outlet and watch for more sparks
options.rationale: Changing outlets assumes the outlet was at fault. Equipment that sparks when plugged in is removed and repaired regardless of the outlet.

questions.takeaway: Any equipment that sparks or does not work properly is taken out of service, labeled for repair and reported, even if it seems to work.
questions.strategy: The passing self test makes the pump look safe. The spark is the finding that matters, and it does not go away because the screen lights up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A spark at the plug means an electrical fault.
Another outlet or battery power keeps the faulty pump in use.
Remove, label and report.

elimination.verdict: Remove the pump from use, label it for repair and report it.

questions.stem: A bottle of chemical disinfectant breaks on the floor of a patient's room, and the fumes are strong. The nurse has moved the patient to another room. Which resource tells the nurse how to contain and remove the spill?

options.text: The unit's daily room cleaning checklist
options.rationale: A cleaning checklist covers routine tasks, not the hazards of a specific chemical. It lacks the first aid and containment steps the nurse needs now.

options.text: The infection prevention nurse's next unit round
options.rationale: Infection prevention addresses germs, and waiting for a round leaves the spill and fumes in place. The product's own hazard information is needed now.

options.text: The safety data sheet for that product
options.rationale: A safety data sheet lists safe handling, health hazards, first aid and steps for containment and removal after a spill. Every agency is required to keep them available.

options.text: The regional poison control center hotline
options.rationale: Poison control advises on treating a person who has swallowed or touched a poison. It does not give the steps for containing and removing a spilled product in the agency.

questions.takeaway: After a chemical exposure or spill, the nurse uses the product's safety data sheet for hazards, first aid and containment steps.
questions.strategy: Poison control sounds right for anything toxic. It guides treatment of a poisoned person; the steps for a specific product's spill are in its safety data sheet.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Steps to contain and remove a specific chemical.
A checklist and an infection round do not cover chemical hazards.
Poison control guides treatment of a poisoned person, not cleanup of a spill.

elimination.verdict: The safety data sheet for that product.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).

questions.stem: One minute after a tonic clonic seizure in bed ends, a patient with epilepsy is breathing, drowsy and confused about where he is. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Raise all four side rails and dim the room lights
options.rationale: Four raised rails can trap a confused patient and act as a restraint. After a seizure, one rail stays down with the bed in its lowest position for easy exit.

options.text: Let him sleep undisturbed with the room door closed
options.rationale: Rest is reasonable later, but leaving him now skips the injury check after the seizure. Closing the door also removes observation while he is confused.

options.text: Give him water to replace fluid lost during the seizure
options.rationale: A drowsy, confused patient may not swallow safely, so fluids risk aspiration. Nothing about the seizure calls for fluid replacement.

options.text: Reorient him and inspect his mouth and skin for injury
options.rationale: As he regains awareness, the nurse reorients and reassures him, then checks for bites, broken teeth and bruising. The seizure may have caused injuries he cannot yet report.

questions.takeaway: After a seizure, the nurse reorients and reassures the patient, positions the bed low with one rail down and checks the mouth and body for injury.
questions.strategy: Letting him sleep feels kind after a seizure. He is confused and may be injured, so he needs reorientation and an injury check first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Breathing, but drowsy and confused.
Sleeping alone skips the injury check.
Fluids risk aspiration; four rails can trap him.

elimination.verdict: Reorient him and inspect his mouth and skin for injury.

questions.objective: Describe essential safety measures for fire, electrical, chemical, and seizure related emergencies

questions.scenario: A patient admitted after a head injury is sitting in a bedside chair. He gives a sudden cry, loses consciousness, stiffens, then begins rhythmic jerking of all four limbs. He is incontinent of urine, and his teeth are clenched. The nurse notes the time and calls for help.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Turn him to his side and loosen his clothing
options.rationale: Side lying lets secretions drain from his mouth and protects his airway. Loosening clothing eases breathing during the seizure.

options.text: Hold his limbs firmly to stop the jerking
options.rationale: Holding limbs firmly can cause musculoskeletal injury and does not stop a seizure. Limbs are held loosely, if at all.

options.text: Place a tongue depressor between his teeth
options.rationale: Nothing is placed in the mouth when the teeth are clenched. Forcing an object in can break teeth or injure the mouth.

options.text: Ease him to the floor and cushion his head
options.rationale: A seated patient can fall and strike his head during a seizure. Easing him to the floor and padding his head prevents a fall and head injury.

options.text: Fainting from a low blood glucose
options.rationale: Fainting causes brief limpness, not stiffening and rhythmic jerking of all limbs. No glucose value or history suggests this cause.

options.text: Fall from dizziness on standing
options.rationale: Dizziness on standing causes a fall but not stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking. He was also seated, not standing.

options.text: Generalized tonic clonic seizure
options.rationale: A cry, loss of consciousness, stiffening, then jerking and incontinence describe a generalized tonic clonic seizure. A recent head injury raises his risk for one.

options.text: Agitation from an unmet toileting need
options.rationale: Agitation is purposeful movement in a conscious patient. He has lost consciousness, and the incontinence is part of the seizure.

options.text: Intake and output totals for the shift
options.rationale: Intake and output matter for fluid balance, not for seizure safety. They do not change what the nurse does in the next minutes.

options.text: Breathing and oral secretions
options.rationale: Secretions can block his airway during and after the seizure. Watching his breathing confirms that side lying is keeping his airway clear.

options.text: His fall risk score from admission
options.rationale: Fall risk matters later for planning, but an old score tells nothing about this event. It does not guide care during the seizure.

options.text: Duration of the seizure
options.rationale: Tracking how long the seizure lasts tells the nurse and provider when it is prolonged. A tonic clonic seizure usually ends within 1 to 3 minutes.

questions.takeaway: During a seizure, the nurse times it, stays with the patient, protects the head and body from injury, positions the patient on the side and puts nothing in the mouth.
questions.strategy: Holding the limbs and protecting the tongue feel protective. Both cause injury; protection comes from the floor, padding and side lying.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cry, loss of consciousness, stiffening, then jerking.
Floor, cushion the head, side lying, nothing in the mouth.
Seizure duration and airway.

elimination.verdict: Ease him to the floor and turn him to his side; tonic clonic seizure; monitor duration and breathing.

questions.stem: After a patient falls beside her bed, two staff members arrive to help. The nurse's assessment finds her right leg shorter than the left and turned outward, with right hip pain of 8 on a 0 to 10 scale. What is the nurse's next action?

options.text: Lift her to bed with the two staff, then call the provider
options.rationale: Returning her to bed feels kind, but moving a suspected fracture can worsen it. The assessment found injury, so she stays still until the provider directs care.

options.text: Keep her still and notify the provider of the findings
options.rationale: A shortened, outwardly turned leg with severe hip pain suggests a fracture. After assessing for injury, the next step is notifying the provider without moving her.

options.text: Review which fall precautions were in place
options.rationale: Reviewing the plan belongs after the patient is safe and treated. It is a later step and does nothing for her injury now.

options.text: Finish a head to toe assessment before calling anyone
options.rationale: A complete assessment matters, but the key finding is already clear. Delaying notification of a likely fracture delays her treatment.

questions.takeaway: When assessment after a fall finds a likely injury, the nurse keeps the patient still and notifies the provider before any move.
questions.strategy: Getting her off the floor feels like the caring choice, and two staff are present. The findings say not to move her yet.

steps.detail: A short, outwardly turned leg with severe pain points to a hip fracture.
Lifting could worsen the fracture.
A full assessment and plan review can follow notification.

elimination.verdict: Keep her still and notify the provider of the findings.

questions.stem: At a post fall huddle for a patient who fell at night, staff note that his plan listed the call light within reach, but it was found clipped to the wall behind the bed. Which contribution best serves the huddle?

options.text: "Let us wait for the manager to read the occurrence report first."
options.rationale: The huddle happens as soon as possible after a fall, while details are fresh. Waiting loses the information that explains the event.

options.text: "That planned step was not in place. How do we check it every round?"
options.rationale: This identifies a contributing factor, notes that a planned intervention was not in place and proposes what needs to change. Those are the questions a post fall huddle answers.

options.text: "He was taught to call for help, so we should teach him again more firmly."
options.rationale: Teaching again assumes he chose not to call. The call light was out of his reach, so more teaching cannot fix the cause.

options.text: "We should find out who last left the room so we can counsel them."
options.rationale: Assigning blame shifts the focus from the process to a person. The huddle is nonpunitive so that staff speak freely about what happened.

questions.takeaway: A post fall huddle asks what happened, what contributed, whether interventions were in place and what needs to change, without blame.
questions.strategy: Reteaching the patient sounds like a fix. The stem shows the planned intervention was not in place, which puts the cause in the process.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The call light was out of reach.
Counseling a person and waiting for the manager both stall learning.
Checking the call light every round fixes the gap.

elimination.verdict: Point out that the planned step was not in place and ask how to check it every round.

questions.stem: The night after bowel surgery, a patient who was calm and oriented all day becomes restless, picking at her nasogastric tube and trying to climb out of bed. Ninety minutes ago she received her first dose of a medication for nausea. She voided 30 minutes ago, says her pain is mild, and her vital signs are unchanged from the evening. Her partner, at the bedside, has moved her hand away from the tube twice. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Ask her partner to stay and redirect her through the night
options.rationale: Family presence is a sound alternative, and it is keeping her hand off the tube for now. It leaves the cause untreated, and restlessness that began soon after a first dose of a new drug points to the drug.

options.text: Apply hand mitts to protect the nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Mitts are the least restrictive device, but a restraint comes only after causes and alternatives fail. Her partner is protecting the tube for now, and the likely cause has not been addressed.

options.text: Report the behavior change and its timing to the provider
options.rationale: Medication effects are a common reason for sudden restlessness, and this change followed her first dose of the nausea drug. The provider can stop or change it, which may end the behavior at its source.

options.text: Offer the bedpan and a dose of pain medication
options.rationale: Toileting and pain are the first causes to check before any restraint. She voided 30 minutes ago and calls her pain mild, so neither need explains this sudden change.

questions.takeaway: When behavior changes soon after a new medication, the nurse treats the medication effect as a cause to report before turning to restraints or longer term alternatives.
questions.strategy: Keeping her partner at the bedside looks like the right restraint alternative. The first dose of a new drug just before the change names a likely cause, and finding the cause comes before managing the behavior.

steps.detail: Restlessness began soon after a first dose of a nausea drug.
She voided recently, her pain is mild and her vital signs are unchanged.
Her partner controls the risk now but does not remove the cause.

elimination.verdict: Report the behavior change and its timing to the provider.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities related to restraint use, restraint alternatives, and ongoing patient monitoring

questions.stem: During a chart review on a surgical unit, the nurse reads the plan of care for a patient with new confusion 2 days after lung surgery. He rates his incision pain 7 on a 0 to 10 scale each evening. Which entry in his plan does the nurse recognize as a restraint?

options.text: Recline his chair fully whenever he tries to rise
options.rationale: Any intervention that keeps a patient from moving freely counts as a restraint, even without a device. A chair tilted back so he cannot get up holds him in place the way a belt would.

options.text: Keep the bed low with a floor mat beside it
options.rationale: A low bed and floor mat reduce injury if he gets up, but they do not stop him from getting up. They are fall precautions that leave his movement free.

options.text: Give his prescribed pain medication, which leaves him drowsy
options.rationale: Drowsiness can make a drug look like a chemical restraint. This one treats the incision pain he rates each evening, so it is therapy for his condition rather than a way to control his behavior.

options.text: Keep his daughter at the bedside overnight
options.rationale: Family presence leaves him free to move while someone familiar watches and reorients him. It is one of the alternatives used to avoid a restraint, not a restraint itself.

questions.takeaway: A restraint is defined by its effect on movement, not by whether it is a device, and a medication that treats the patient's condition is not a chemical restraint.
questions.strategy: The drowsy pain medication tempts students who know about chemical restraint. Ask what each entry is for and whether it stops him from moving; only the reclined chair stops him from moving.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Does the entry keep him from moving freely?
It treats pain he rates 7, so it is treatment, not behavior control.
A family member, a low bed and a floor mat leave him free to move.

elimination.verdict: Recline his chair fully whenever he tries to rise.
