questions.stem: Two minutes after his convulsions stop, a patient admitted with bacterial meningitis lies on his back in bed. He is drowsy, does not know where he is, and is breathing with a wet, gurgling sound. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Report the event and its length to the provider
options.rationale: The provider does need to know about the seizure and how long it lasted. Calling first leaves him on his back with pooled secretions while the nurse is on the phone.

options.text: Reorient him and check his mouth for bites
options.rationale: Reorienting him and checking for injury are correct steps once a seizure ends. His gurgling breathing shows an airway problem, and the airway comes before orientation or the injury check.

options.text: Lower the bed and leave one side rail down
options.rationale: A low bed with one rail down is the right setup after a seizure. It prevents a later fall but does nothing for the secretions pooling in his airway now.

options.text: Turn him onto his side
options.rationale: Gurgling means saliva and mucus are pooling in his airway while he is too drowsy to clear them. Side lying lets the secretions drain and the tongue fall forward, which protects his breathing.

questions.takeaway: After a seizure, side lying to clear pooled secretions comes before reorientation, the injury check or a call to the provider.
questions.strategy: Reorienting him and checking his mouth is standard care after a seizure, so it looks right. The wet, gurgling breathing makes this an airway problem first.

steps.detail: Wet, gurgling breathing in a drowsy patient lying on his back.
Secretions in the airway outrank orientation and the injury check.
The bed setup and the call follow once he is on his side.

elimination.verdict: Turn him onto his side.

questions.stem: Walking past a room, the nurse sees a patient sitting on the floor beside his bed. No other staff are nearby. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Stay with him and assess for injury before he is moved
options.rationale: The nurse stays with him and assesses him where he is. Moving him before assessment could worsen an injury such as a fracture.

options.text: Call for assistance from the room
options.rationale: Help is needed to assess and move him safely. Calling from the room brings help while the nurse stays with him.

options.text: Notify the provider of the fall and the findings
options.rationale: The provider is notified once there are assessment findings to report. The findings guide what the provider orders next.

options.text: Document the event and complete an occurrence report
options.rationale: Documentation and the occurrence report come last so they include the assessment, the notification and the plan change. The report also lets the agency find trends.

options.text: Reassess his fall prevention plan
options.rationale: The plan did not prevent this fall, so it is reviewed and changed. A plan that stays the same invites the same fall.

questions.takeaway: After a fall, the nurse calls for help, stays and assesses for injury, notifies the provider, follows policy, reassesses the plan, and documents and completes an occurrence report.
questions.strategy: Getting him off the floor or calling the provider at once feels urgent. Neither comes before the nurse has help in the room and has assessed him.

steps.detail: Call from the room.
The provider needs findings.
Reassess the plan, then document and file the report.

elimination.verdict: Call for help, stay and assess, notify the provider, reassess the plan, document.

questions.stem: In a debriefing with her preceptor, a newly hired nurse describes how she handled several events this week. Which statement shows that she needs more teaching?

options.text: "I wiped up a spill by the sink and still reported the leaking faucet."
options.rationale: Cleaning the spill removed the immediate hazard, and reporting the faucet deals with its source. Both actions match how hazards are handled before anyone slips.

options.text: "I reported my own late insulin dose, though no harm came of it."
options.rationale: Reporting her own error can sound like needless self blame. In a culture of safety, errors are reported without fear of punishment so the unit can learn why they happen.

options.text: "I told the family the bed alarm was broken and that I reported it."
options.rationale: Communicating hazards to patients and families is part of safe practice. Telling them the alarm is broken and reported keeps them alert until it is repaired.

options.text: "I caught the wrong dose before I gave it, so no report was needed."
options.rationale: A near miss is reported even when no one is harmed, because it exposes a weak point that could hurt the next patient. Fixing it quietly keeps the hazard hidden from the team.

questions.takeaway: Errors, near misses and hazards are reported even when no harm occurred, because reporting is how the system learns and prevents the next event.
questions.strategy: Reporting her own late dose can look like the statement to correct. The statement that sounds most responsible, catching the error herself, is the one that keeps a hazard hidden.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Look for the statement that is wrong, not the one that is right.
Errors, near misses and hazards are all reported, harm or not.
Only the caught dose went unreported.

elimination.verdict: "I caught the wrong dose before I gave it, so no report was needed."

questions.objective: Identify patient, environmental, and health care related factors that increase the risk for injury

questions.stem: Each night around 0200, a patient with atrial fibrillation wakes to void and becomes dizzy as soon as she stands. She takes a heart rate medication at 2100 and has no dizziness during the day. She calls for help every time, but last night her knees gave way while an assistant was holding her arm. Which change to her plan addresses the cause of her risk?

options.text: Review her evening dose timing with the pharmacist
options.rationale: Dizziness only in the hours after an evening dose points to a medication effect. Working with the pharmacist on timing can move the peak effect away from her night trips to the bathroom.

options.text: Place a bedside commode next to her bed at night
options.rationale: A commode shortens the trip and is a sound safety step. She would still stand while dizzy from the drug, so it shortens the distance without changing the cause.

options.text: Offer a bedpan so she does not have to stand at night
options.rationale: A bedpan avoids standing, but it restricts her mobility more than her risk requires. It also manages the symptom rather than the medication timing behind it.

options.text: Add a second staff member for her night trips
options.rationale: More help can make her trips safer, and she already calls and waits for staff. Extra hands support her through the dizziness but leave the drug effect in place.

questions.takeaway: When a fall risk follows a medication's timing, the targeted fix is adjusting the timing with the pharmacist, while equipment and extra help only cushion the effect.
questions.strategy: A commode is a strong safety step, so it looks like the answer. The question asks for the cause, and dizziness only in the hours after the evening dose points to the drug's timing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dizziness comes only at night, hours after the 2100 dose.
The question asks for the cause, not for more safety.
A commode, a second helper and a bedpan cushion the effect; timing changes it.

elimination.verdict: Review her evening dose timing with the pharmacist.

questions.stem: A patient with long standing diabetic nerve damage in both feet has strong legs on strength testing and walked steadily in the lit hallway this afternoon. At 0200 he gets up to use the bathroom in his dark room, says he cannot tell where his feet are on the floor, and sways. Which plan does the nurse put in place for his night toileting?

options.text: Add leg strengthening exercises so he is steadier on his feet at night
options.rationale: Strengthening helps a patient whose legs are weak, and it would not harm him. His legs already test strong, so more strength does nothing for the lost sense of where his feet are.

options.text: Let him walk alone at night, since his hallway gait was steady
options.rationale: He was steady this afternoon because the hallway was lit and he could see his feet. In the dark that visual help disappears, and that is exactly when he swayed.

options.text: Light the path and walk beside him, cueing him to watch his feet
options.rationale: His legs are strong, so the missing piece is position sense in his feet, not muscle power. Light lets his eyes stand in for that lost awareness, and a nurse at his side protects his balance while he moves.

options.text: Keep him in bed overnight with a urinal until the nerve damage resolves
options.rationale: Bed rest prevents a fall tonight but adds the harms of immobility and removes safe mobility. Diabetic nerve damage does not clear quickly, so this plan has no realistic end point.

questions.takeaway: Balance needs proprioception as well as strength; when position sense is lost, vision and hands on support take its place.
questions.strategy: Strengthening tempts because weakness is the usual cause of unsteadiness. The stem rules it out: his legs test strong, and he swayed only when he could not see his feet.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Strong legs plus not knowing where the feet are points to lost proprioception.

steps.action: Match the fix to the deficit
steps.detail: Vision can replace position sense, so light and cueing to watch the feet address it.
Walking alone ignores the night finding, and bed until resolved restricts him with no end point.

elimination.verdict: Light the path and walk beside him, cueing him to watch his feet.

questions.stem: After 90 minutes in a chair, a patient with left sided weakness from a stroke is leaning to the left with her trunk curved and her left shoulder hanging lower than the right. She reports feeling tired and has a dull back ache. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Ask her to hold herself upright using the right armrest
options.rationale: Using her strong arm helps for a few minutes, so the idea is not unreasonable. She is already fatigued, and holding herself up with muscle effort adds to the tiredness rather than supporting her.

options.text: Recenter her trunk upright and support her left side and arm
options.rationale: Her slump puts uneven strain on her spine and joints, which is causing the fatigue and ache. Restoring alignment and propping the weak side spreads the load and keeps her balanced in the chair.

options.text: Return her to bed for the rest of the day to rest her back
options.rationale: Bed rest relieves the ache for now, but it trades the problem for the effects of immobility. The ache comes from how she is sitting, and that can be corrected in the chair.

options.text: Give her prescribed analgesic and recheck the ache in 30 minutes
options.rationale: An analgesic may ease the ache, and pain does need treating. It leaves the cause in place, so the poor alignment keeps straining her back while the medication wears off.

questions.takeaway: Proper alignment reduces joint stress and fatigue and improves balance, so the first fix for a slumped patient is support, not rest or medication.
questions.strategy: The analgesic is attractive because she reports pain. Ask what is causing the ache: the curved trunk is, and only support corrects it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ninety minutes of leaning to the weak side is a loss of alignment.

steps.action: Rule out treating the symptom only
steps.detail: Medication and bed rest relieve the ache without restoring posture.
Holding herself up with the right arm adds to her fatigue.

elimination.verdict: Recenter her trunk upright and support her left side and arm.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with a flare of ulcerative colitis is lying in bed with the head of the bed raised. The nurse performs the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool screening. Assuming the patient passes each request, place the nurse's requests in the order they are given.

options.text: March in place at the bedside
options.rationale: Level 4 starts with marching in place, which checks standing balance while weight shifts between feet. It comes only after the stand task has been passed.

options.text: Step one foot forward and back, then the other
options.rationale: Advancing and returning each foot is the last part of Level 4. Passing it shows the balance and stepping ability needed to progress to walking.

options.text: Raise your buttocks off the bed and hold for a count of 5
options.rationale: Level 3 tests whether the legs can lift the body toward standing. Holding the hover for a count of 5 shows enough strength to stand safely.

options.text: Sit at the side of the bed and hold that position unassisted
options.rationale: Level 1 begins by moving from semi reclined to sitting at the bedside. Sitting without help tests trunk strength and seated balance before anything else is tried.

options.text: Straighten one knee, then point and flex that foot
options.rationale: Stretch and point is Level 2 and checks lower leg strength and stability from a seated position. Each leg is tested in turn before standing is attempted.

options.text: Reach across your body and shake the nurse's hand
options.rationale: Reaching across midline and shaking hands completes the sit and shake task. Passing it shows enough trunk control to move on to the leg tasks.

questions.takeaway: The BMAT moves from trunk to legs to standing to stepping: sit and shake, stretch and point, stand, then walk, stopping at the first task the patient fails.
questions.strategy: Students often place standing before the leg stretch because standing feels like the main event. Each level builds on the one before, so leg strength is tested seated first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Start from where the patient is
steps.detail: The patient is semi reclined, so the first request is sitting up at the bedside.
Trunk balance comes before leg strength, and leg strength before weight bearing.
Marching precedes the single step forward and back.

elimination.verdict: Sit, reach and shake, stretch and point, hover for 5, march, then step.

questions.objective: Assess mobility, gait, range of motion, functional ability, and activity tolerance using relevant patient cues.

questions.stem: Weak after 2 weeks of influenza, a 79 year old patient rises from a chair with her feet touching each other and reaches forward for her walker, which stands an arm's length away. Her body sways as her trunk moves forward. What does the nurse teach her?

options.text: Set her feet apart and bring the walker close before rising
options.rationale: Feet apart widen her base of support, and a close walker keeps her center of gravity over that base. Older adults often stand with their feet close together, which narrows the base and upsets balance.

options.text: Stay seated for transfers until her strength fully returns
options.rationale: Staying seated avoids a fall today, but strength returns through activity, not rest. Inactivity would deepen her weakness and delay the recovery she needs.

options.text: Keep the walker in place and lean farther forward to reach it
options.rationale: Reaching farther shifts her center of gravity well in front of her feet. With her feet together that is the exact movement that made her sway.

options.text: Rise more quickly so less time is spent in the unsteady part
options.rationale: A quick rise shortens the wobble, which explains its appeal. Speed moves her center of gravity even faster past a narrow base, so it increases the chance that she falls.

questions.takeaway: A wide base of support with the center of gravity kept over it gives balance; older adults tend to narrow their base, so teach feet apart.
questions.strategy: Speed and staying seated both sound protective. The stem gives the cause: feet together and a long reach, so the fix changes the base and the reach.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Feet touching and an arm's length reach mean a narrow base and a forward shift of weight.

steps.action: Choose the option that fixes both
steps.detail: Feet apart widens the base; a close walker keeps the weight over it.
Waiting until strength fully returns keeps her weak.

elimination.verdict: Set her feet apart and bring the walker close before rising.

questions.stem: The nurse is about to write activity goals for a patient admitted with a heart failure flare who has an order for activity as tolerated. Which question does the nurse ask first?

options.text: "How far do you think you could walk right now?"
options.rationale: His current ability is useful and will be assessed. On its own it does not show whether today's distance is a loss, so it cannot set a realistic target.

options.text: "Would you like to try a walk in the hallway today?"
options.rationale: Offering a walk respects his choices and promotes activity. It is an intervention, and asking it before any assessment skips the step that tells the nurse whether a walk is safe.

options.text: "What could you do on a usual day before this illness?"
options.rationale: His prior function is the baseline that every activity goal is measured against. Without it the nurse cannot tell how much he has lost or what level he is working back toward.

options.text: "On a scale of 0 to 10, how is your breathing now?"
options.rationale: Dyspnea is part of activity tolerance and is worth tracking. It measures his response at rest, not what he could do before he became ill, so it does not anchor the goals.

questions.takeaway: Start the mobility assessment with the patient's baseline: what he could do before this illness is what his goals are measured against.
questions.strategy: Every option is a reasonable question, and the breathing scale looks like the safety priority. The stem asks what the goals rest on, which is the baseline.

steps.detail: The nurse is writing goals, which need a starting point.
Offering a walk acts before assessing.
Current distance and breathing describe today; only the usual day describes the baseline.

elimination.verdict: Ask what he could do on a usual day before this illness.

questions.stem: On day 2 of treatment for sepsis, the nurse helps a patient from a semi reclined position to sitting at the side of the bed. After 40 seconds the patient leans backward, needs the nurse's hands to stay upright, and cannot reach across midline. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Record Level 2, maximum assist, because sitting was reached
options.rationale: Level 2 describes a patient who keeps sitting balance but lacks leg strength. This patient reached sitting only with the nurse's hands, so the sitting balance itself is missing.

options.text: Go on to the stretch and point task with a second nurse holding the trunk
options.rationale: Stretch and point is the right next task once sit and shake is passed. Holding the trunk hides the very deficit being tested, and this patient has already failed the first level.

options.text: Ask the patient to rise toward standing to judge leg strength
options.rationale: Standing is the Level 3 task and tests leg strength. A patient who cannot hold a seated position has no safe way to attempt it.

options.text: Stop the screen and plan care at Level 1, total assist
options.rationale: The patient could not sit unassisted or reach across midline, so sit and shake is failed. The screen stops at the first failed task, and every move is planned at Level 1.

questions.takeaway: The BMAT stops at the first failed task; a patient who cannot sit unassisted, reach across midline and shake hands is Level 1, total assist.
questions.strategy: Being helped to sit can look like progress toward Level 2. The test is sitting unassisted, and this patient needed the nurse's hands.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sitting balance failed at 40 seconds with hands on, and midline reach failed.

steps.action: Remove options that move up the tool
steps.detail: Stretch and point and standing come only after sit and shake is passed.
Level 2 needs independent sitting balance, which this patient lacks.

elimination.verdict: Stop the screen and plan care at Level 1, total assist.

questions.note: Class teaching says the patient should sit unassisted for more than 2 minutes in sit and shake. The textbook describes unsupported seated balance for up to 1 minute and adds that tachycardia, sweating or light headedness during sitting also fails the task. Use more than 2 minutes on the course exam; for board style questions, rely on the textbook description.

questions.stem: The nurse is screening a patient on day 4 of a hospital stay for a bowel obstruction. The patient passes sit and shake and stretch and point. When asked to rise from the bed, the patient lifts the buttocks, holds for a count of 2, and sits back down. Which plan fits this result?

options.text: Score Level 2, maximum assist, because the standing attempt failed
options.rationale: The patient passed stretch and point, so the legs have strength and stability. A failed stand places the patient at Level 3, not back at Level 2.

options.text: Score Level 3, moderate assist, and do not start the walk task
options.rationale: The stand task requires holding the hover for a count of 5, and this patient held for 2. That stops the screen at Level 3, so walking is not attempted yet.

options.text: Score Level 4 and begin marching in place with a walker
options.rationale: The patient did clear the bed, which can look like a pass. Clearing the bed briefly is not the standard; the hold has to last for a count of 5.

options.text: Repeat the stand every 15 minutes until a count of 5 is held
options.rationale: Wanting to see progress is reasonable, and the BMAT is repeated with changes in status. Repeated attempts every 15 minutes tire the patient and raise the risk of a fall.

questions.takeaway: Failing the stand task, which requires holding the buttocks off the bed for a count of 5, places the patient at Level 3, moderate assist.
questions.strategy: Clearing the bed looks like success. The criterion is the count of 5, and the level is named by the task that was failed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A hold for 2 falls short of the count of 5.
Passing stretch and point rules out Level 2; failing stand rules out Level 4.
Frequent retesting adds fatigue and fall risk, not data.

elimination.verdict: Score Level 3, moderate assist, and do not start the walk task.

questions.stem: At 0800 a patient with liver failure passed sit and shake and stretch and point. At 1400 the nurse returns to attempt the stand task. Since noon the patient has been disoriented to place, has pulled at the oxygen tubing twice, and follows only some commands. Leg strength is unchanged. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Do the stand task now with a gait belt, since leg strength is unchanged
options.rationale: Leg strength is one part of the stand task, and it has not changed. The patient also has to understand and follow directions to stand safely, and that ability has been lost since noon.

options.text: Do the stand task with two staff, giving one short command at a time
options.rationale: Short commands and extra staff help a patient who is slow to process instructions. This patient follows only some commands, so extra hands cannot make standing predictable.

options.text: Postpone the stand task and report the new confusion to the provider
options.rationale: Cognition, orientation and delirium are checked before the stand task is attempted, so standing waits for now. Confusion that began at noon is an acute change in mental status, and the provider needs to know.

options.text: Return the patient to Level 1 handling and keep the patient on bed rest
options.rationale: Caution is right, but the patient still has the trunk and leg strength shown this morning. Dropping to Level 1 and bed rest overcorrects and adds the harms of immobility.

questions.takeaway: Before the stand task, check cognition, orientation and delirium; a patient who cannot follow directions does not progress, whatever the leg strength.
questions.strategy: The unchanged leg strength pulls toward testing. The stem adds a new cognitive change, and the BMAT treats the ability to follow directions as part of standing safely.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Disorientation and partial command following began at noon.

steps.action: Apply the rule for the stand task
steps.detail: Cognition and delirium are considered before standing is attempted.
The morning strength findings still hold, so Level 1 handling and bed rest go too far.

elimination.verdict: Postpone the stand task and report the new confusion to the provider.

questions.scenario: During a first hallway walk with the nurse, a patient recovering from a bleeding stomach ulcer walks 60 meters. Before the walk, the heart rate was 80 per minute, the respiratory rate 16 per minute, and the oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it shows the patient is tolerating the activity or not tolerating the activity.

rows.text: Respiratory rate 30 per minute, pausing for breath in the middle of sentences
rows.rationale: A rate nearly double the baseline with breaks in speech is marked dyspnea. The workload is more than this patient can handle right now.

rows.text: Oxygen saturation 88% on room air at the turnaround point
rows.rationale: A fall from 97% to 88% means oxygen supply is not keeping up with demand. That drop is a reason to stop and rest the patient.

rows.text: Reports feeling dizzy and reaches for the wall rail
rows.rationale: Dizziness signals that blood flow to the brain is not keeping up with the change in activity. Reaching for support shows a real risk of falling.

rows.text: Heart rate 100 per minute at the end of the walk and 84 per minute after 3 minutes of sitting
rows.rationale: A moderate rise with exercise is expected, and the return close to baseline within minutes is the recovery the nurse looks for. Quick recovery shows the heart handled the workload.

rows.text: Reports tired legs, and says the tiredness is gone after sitting for 2 minutes
rows.rationale: Some muscle fatigue is expected after a first walk following illness. Fatigue that clears within minutes of rest shows good ability to recover.

rows.text: Heart rate 118 per minute 10 minutes after returning to the chair
rows.rationale: A heart rate that stays high long after the activity has ended shows poor recovery. The ability to recover afterward is part of tolerance, not only the response during the walk.

questions.takeaway: Activity tolerance is judged by heart rate, breathing, oxygenation, dyspnea, fatigue, pain, dizziness, and how quickly the patient recovers afterward.
questions.strategy: A higher heart rate at the end of the walk looks like intolerance. The deciding cue is recovery: a rate that returns toward baseline is tolerance, and one still high after 10 minutes is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Compare each value with the baseline
steps.detail: The resting values give the reference point for every row.
A modest rise or brief fatigue is expected; doubling, desaturation and dizziness are not.
Values that settle within minutes show tolerance; values that stay high do not.

elimination.verdict: Tolerating: the heart rate that recovers and the leg fatigue that clears; all other findings show intolerance.

questions.stem: In the intensive care unit for 3 weeks with severe pancreatitis, a patient has had the left arm resting bent on a pillow to protect an IV in the left wrist. During range of motion, the left elbow stops 30 degrees short of where the right elbow fully straightens. Last week both elbows straightened fully. The patient reports stiffness but no pain. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Push the left elbow firmly through the resistance until it matches the right
options.rationale: Regaining the lost extension is the goal, so the intent is sound. Forcing a joint past resistance can injure the tissue; range of motion goes only to the point of resistance.

options.text: Add range of motion sessions and position the left elbow straighter between them
options.rationale: Comparing sides shows a new loss of motion on the side kept flexed, which points to an early contracture. More range of motion and positioning in extension can still reverse it.

options.text: Record the finding as expected after a long stay and change nothing
options.rationale: Loss of motion is common after a long stay, but common does not mean acceptable. A new difference between sides is a finding that calls for a change in care.

options.text: Keep the left arm resting bent on the pillow, since that causes no pain
options.rationale: A pain free position seems kind, and comfort matters. Holding the elbow bent for weeks is what shortened the tissue, so keeping it there will deepen the limitation.

questions.takeaway: Compare joints side to side and note stiffness, limitation and asymmetry; a new one sided loss after prolonged flexion is an early contracture to treat now.
questions.strategy: Recording it as expected feels accurate because the stay was long. The comparison with last week and with the right elbow shows a new, one sided change, which needs action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The left elbow lacks 30 degrees that the right still has.
Weeks of flexion on a pillow shorten muscles and tendons.

steps.action: Choose the option that reverses it
steps.detail: More range of motion and extended positioning treat an early contracture without forcing.

elimination.verdict: Add range of motion sessions and position the left elbow straighter between them.

questions.stem: After surgery to repair a torn ligament in a patient's right knee, the surgeon has restricted bending of that knee while it heals. The knee is swollen and painful. The patient wants to keep that leg as strong as possible while it heals. Which exercise does the nurse teach?

options.text: Tightening the right thigh with the knee straight, then relaxing
options.rationale: An isometric contraction works the muscle without moving the joint. That keeps the thigh strong while respecting the restriction and protecting the painful, healing knee.

options.text: Bending and straightening the right knee ten times each hour
options.rationale: Moving the knee through its range would build strength and flexibility. It breaks the order restricting knee bending and stresses a repair that is still healing.

options.text: Passive range of motion of the right knee by the nurse twice a day
options.rationale: Passive range of motion keeps joints flexible when a patient cannot move them. It still bends the restricted knee, and it does not strengthen the thigh muscle.

options.text: Resting the right leg on a pillow until the swelling and pain resolve
options.rationale: Rest eases swelling and pain, which is part of early care. Complete rest lets the thigh muscle weaken, which is the opposite of the patient's goal.

questions.takeaway: Isometric exercise contracts a muscle without joint movement, building static strength safely around a painful or healing joint.
questions.strategy: Passive range of motion sounds gentle. The restriction is on bending the knee, so any exercise that moves the joint is out, however it is performed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The knee may not bend.
Active and passive range of motion both move the knee.
Rest does not maintain strength; a muscle contraction without movement does.

elimination.verdict: Tighten the right thigh with the knee straight, then relax.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse her goal is to climb the 12 stairs to her bedroom at home. She is regaining strength after 3 weeks of limited activity from shingles pain, is now at Level 4 on the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool, and has no activity restrictions. Which exercise best supports her goal?

options.text: Tightening each thigh with the knee held straight, then relaxing
options.rationale: Isometric thigh tightening builds static strength and is useful when a joint must stay still. She has no restriction, and stairs need strength through movement, not only holding.

options.text: Passive range of motion of both knees by the nurse
options.rationale: Passive range of motion keeps joints flexible in a patient who cannot move. Her own muscles do none of the work, so it does nothing for her strength.

options.text: Holding a half squat against the wall without moving
options.rationale: A wall squat builds leg strength and looks close to stair climbing. It is isometric, holding the joint still, so it does not train the moving strength she needs.

options.text: Lifting and lowering each lower leg while seated
options.rationale: Isotonic exercise contracts the muscle while the joint moves, which builds the dynamic strength used in climbing. It trains the same movement pattern that stairs demand.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic exercise moves the joint while the muscle contracts, improving functional, dynamic strength; isometric exercise is the choice when a joint must stay still.
questions.strategy: The wall squat looks most like a functional leg exercise. Ask whether the joint moves: it does not, so it is isometric and less suited to a moving task.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Thigh tightening and the wall squat are isometric; the nurse moving the knees is passive.
Climbing stairs is dynamic movement, which isotonic exercise trains.
None apply, so there is no reason to keep the joint still.

elimination.verdict: Lifting and lowering each lower leg while seated.

questions.stem: Starting a home activity plan, a patient with coronary artery disease tells the nurse he will build strength by pushing as hard as he can against a doorframe and holding the push as long as he can. He has chest discomfort with heavy exertion that eases with rest. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Moderate walking with a warm up and cool down suits your heart better."
options.rationale: Hard, held isometric efforts increase the work of the heart and can be unsafe with heart disease. Moderate aerobic activity with gradual warm up and cool down strengthens him without sudden strain.

options.text: "Hold each push for less than 1 minute so it stays safe for your heart."
options.rationale: Shorter holds do reduce strain, so the advice sounds protective. A maximal held contraction still raises the work on his heart, so limiting time does not make the plan suitable.

options.text: "Do the doorframe pushes daily, and add walking once they feel easy."
options.rationale: Adding walking is a good idea. Keeping the maximal held pushes as the base of his plan leaves the heavy cardiac strain in place.

options.text: "Avoid all exercise until the chest discomfort has stopped completely."
options.rationale: Concern about his chest discomfort is appropriate. Avoiding all exercise denies him the benefit of regular moderate activity, which improves blood flow to the heart and reduces angina.

questions.takeaway: Activity plans are modified for coronary artery disease: favor moderate aerobic activity with warm up and cool down over maximal isometric straining.
questions.strategy: Shortening the hold sounds like a sensible compromise. The problem is the type of exercise, not its length, so only changing the exercise solves it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Maximal held isometric effort raises cardiac workload.
Avoiding all exercise removes the benefit he needs.
Shorter holds or adding walking keep the heavy straining.

elimination.verdict: Recommend moderate walking with a warm up and cool down.

questions.stem: A patient with a pelvic fracture has been on bed rest for 3 weeks. Her thigh muscles look thinner than on admission, and her knees are stiff when range of motion begins. Which other finding does the nurse recognize as an effect of her immobility?

options.text: Her pain rises from 3 to 5 of 10 when staff turn her in bed
options.rationale: Pain on turning is real and needs treatment. It comes from moving a fractured pelvis, so it is an effect of the injury rather than of the weeks in bed.

options.text: She has a fading bruise over the hip she landed on when she fell
options.rationale: Bruising is a finding to note on the skin assessment. It came from the impact of the fall that broke her pelvis, so it is not caused by her immobility.

options.text: She eats about a third of each meal and says she is never hungry
options.rationale: Decreased appetite is a metabolic effect of immobility, since her body's energy demand falls while she lies in bed. Poor intake also speeds the muscle loss already seen in her thighs.

options.text: She has a red, itchy rash where tape held her IV dressing in place
options.rationale: A skin problem in a patient on bed rest can look like an immobility effect. This rash sits exactly under the tape, so the adhesive caused it, not lying still.

questions.takeaway: Immobility causes metabolic effects such as decreased appetite and loss of lean muscle mass, along with musculoskeletal effects such as atrophy, weakness and joint stiffness.
questions.strategy: Every option is a real finding in a patient on bed rest. Ask what caused each one: the tape, the fracture, the fall or the weeks of lying still.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Trace each finding to its cause
steps.detail: The rash follows the tape, the pain follows the fracture and the bruise follows the fall.

steps.action: Match what is left to immobility
steps.detail: Low appetite fits the reduced metabolic demand of weeks in bed.

elimination.verdict: She eats about a third of each meal and says she is never hungry.

questions.nursesNote: 0900 Admitted from home with a urinary tract infection. Alert and oriented to person, place and time. Uses a cane at home and reports walking to the mailbox daily until 1 week ago. Walks with short shuffling steps and reaches for furniture to steady himself. Right knee bends to 90 degrees; left knee bends to 135 degrees. Skin warm and dry. Heart rate 78 per minute at rest, 92 per minute after walking 6 meters, and 80 per minute after 2 minutes of rest. Says he now needs his daughter's help to get out of the bathtub. Speech clear. Lungs clear in all fields.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow up in this patient's mobility assessment.

segments.text: Alert and oriented to person, place and time
segments.rationale: Full orientation is a normal finding for him and needs no follow up. It means he can understand and follow directions safely during mobility testing and walking.

segments.text: Uses a cane at home
segments.rationale: A cane he already uses at home is part of his baseline, not a new problem. The nurse makes sure it is available so he walks with his usual support.

segments.text: Walks with short shuffling steps and reaches for furniture to steady himself
segments.rationale: Short shuffling steps and grabbing furniture show an unsteady gait. These gait findings raise his fall risk and need follow up in the mobility plan.

segments.text: Right knee bends to 90 degrees; left knee bends to 135 degrees
segments.rationale: Comparing sides shows the right knee moves far less than the left. Asymmetric range of motion needs follow up to find the cause and protect his walking.

segments.text: Skin warm and dry
segments.rationale: Warm, dry skin is a normal finding that needs no follow up. It tells the nurse nothing that would change his mobility plan.

segments.text: Heart rate 78 per minute at rest, 92 per minute after walking 6 meters, and 80 per minute after 2 minutes of rest
segments.rationale: A modest rise with a quick return to near baseline is a normal response to activity. It shows he tolerated the short walk.

segments.text: Says he now needs his daughter's help to get out of the bathtub
segments.rationale: Needing help with bathing is a new loss of functional ability compared with his recent independence. A decline in performing daily activities shapes his care and discharge planning.

segments.text: Speech clear
segments.rationale: Clear speech is a normal neurological finding that needs no follow up. It does not point to any new problem that would limit his movement.

segments.text: Lungs clear in all fields
segments.rationale: Clear lungs in all fields are a normal finding that needs no follow up. Nothing about his breathing limits his activity at this point.

questions.takeaway: A mobility assessment pulls together gait, side to side range of motion, activity tolerance, and functional ability compared with the patient's baseline.
questions.strategy: The heart rate rise looks like intolerance, and the cane looks like a deficit. Ask what is new or abnormal against his baseline: the gait, the knee asymmetry, and the loss of bathing ability.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The cane is his usual aid; needing help in the tub is new.
A 45 degree difference between knees is asymmetry.
A rise that recovers within 2 minutes is normal.

elimination.verdict: The shuffling gait, the knee asymmetry, and the new need for bathing help require follow up.

questions.stem: A patient in a coma after a head injury has no voluntary movement of the ankles. Both feet rest pointed downward under blankets tucked tightly at the foot of the bed. The nurse can still bring each foot to a right angle by hand. Which plan does the nurse start?

options.text: Perform ankle range of motion once a day and leave the blankets as placed
options.rationale: Range of motion is part of the right plan, so this is close. The tight blankets keep pushing the feet into plantar flexion for the rest of the day, which undoes the exercise.

options.text: Support both feet in neutral alignment and perform ankle range of motion
options.rationale: The feet can still reach a right angle, so this is early foot drop that can be reversed. Neutral support between sessions and regular range of motion keep the ankle from shortening.

options.text: Tuck the blankets more firmly so the feet do not move during care
options.rationale: Keeping the feet still sounds protective. Tight blankets are what press the feet downward, so tucking them harder speeds the contracture.

options.text: Leave the feet as they rest and compare both ankles at the next shift
options.rationale: Comparing both sides is good assessment practice. Waiting allows the plantar flexion to become fixed while it is still correctable.

questions.takeaway: Foot drop is a plantar flexion contracture of prolonged immobility; prevent it with neutral alignment, range of motion and supportive devices as appropriate.
questions.strategy: Range of motion once a day sounds like enough. The cause is the constant downward pressure, so the plan must also hold the feet neutral between sessions.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pointed feet that still reach a right angle are early, correctable foot drop.
Tight blankets press the feet into plantar flexion.

steps.action: Choose the plan that removes the cause and moves the joint
steps.detail: Neutral support plus range of motion.

elimination.verdict: Support both feet in neutral alignment and perform ankle range of motion.

questions.stem: After 5 weeks mostly in bed during treatment for endocarditis, a patient is now cleared to stand and walk with a walker. He has no fluid restriction. A urine test shows a high level of calcium, and his provider notes that his bone density has decreased. Which plan targets the cause of both findings?

options.text: Give a calcium supplement with each meal to replace the lost bone
options.rationale: Replacing lost calcium seems logical when bone density falls. Without weight bearing the bones cannot use it, so extra calcium adds to what his kidneys must clear.

options.text: Turn him every 2 hours and continue range of motion exercises in bed
options.rationale: Turning and range of motion protect his skin and joints, so they belong in his care. They put no weight through his bones, and weight bearing is what slows bone loss.

options.text: Limit dairy foods and keep him in bed until the urine calcium falls
options.rationale: Cutting dietary calcium sounds like a direct fix for high urine calcium. The calcium is leaving his own unloaded bones, and more bed rest keeps that loss going.

options.text: Walk him with his walker several times a day and encourage fluids
options.rationale: Without weight bearing, bone releases calcium into the blood and urine, which weakens bone and raises the risk of kidney stones. Walking reloads the bones, and fluids dilute the urine so stones form less easily.

questions.takeaway: Immobility alters calcium metabolism: unloaded bones demineralize and release calcium into the urine, raising stone risk, so weight bearing activity and fluids address both.
questions.strategy: Limiting dairy and adding a supplement both focus on calcium intake, which tempts. The stem points to disuse as the shared cause, so the plan has to put weight back on his bones.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Falling bone density and high urine calcium both come from calcium leaving unloaded bone.
Less dairy or a supplement changes intake, not the bone loss from disuse.
Turning and range of motion in bed do not load the bones; walking does.

elimination.verdict: Walk him with his walker several times a day and encourage fluids.

questions.stem: A patient being treated for a bone infection in her spine has been on bed rest for 10 days. With the head of her bed at 60 degrees, she slips toward the foot of the bed every hour. Assistive personnel pull her back up by the arms, dragging her across the sheet. Her sacral skin is intact. What does the nurse change?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees so she stays fully upright
options.rationale: Sitting her straight up may seem to stop the slipping. A higher head of bed adds to the pull toward the foot of the bed, which increases shear on her sacrum.

options.text: Boost her on a friction reducing sheet with two staff, without dragging
options.rationale: Dragging scrapes the skin, and the slipping down the bed stretches the deep tissue, which is friction and shear. A friction reducing sheet lifts the drag off her skin and protects the staff.

options.text: Keep the method and check the sacrum for redness at each turn
options.rationale: Checking the sacrum is sound assessment for a patient at risk. It leaves the dragging in place, so the skin keeps taking friction and shear that cause the injury.

options.text: Massage her sacrum with lotion after each move to restore circulation
options.rationale: Massage sounds like it improves blood flow. Rubbing over a bony area at risk can damage fragile tissue, and it does nothing to stop the dragging.

questions.takeaway: Pressure, friction and shear cause pressure injuries in immobile patients; move patients up in bed with friction reducing devices instead of dragging.
questions.strategy: Checking for redness is good assessment, which makes keeping the method tempting. Ask what is causing harm now: the dragging, which the nurse can stop.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dragging is friction; sliding down at a high head of bed is shear.

steps.action: Remove options that keep the cause
steps.detail: Inspecting alone and massaging leave the dragging in place.

steps.action: Remove the option that worsens it
steps.detail: A higher head of bed increases shear.

elimination.verdict: Boost her on a friction reducing sheet with two staff, without dragging.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who spent 10 days in bed with a lower leg wound infection and is now cleared for activity as tolerated with no fluid restriction. He drinks about 700 mL a day, has not had a stool in 4 days, and passes small amounts of dark, cloudy urine. Which plan addresses both elimination problems?

options.text: Increase his fluids, use an upright commode, and add activity as tolerated
options.rationale: Low intake and inactivity cause both urinary stasis and slowed bowel movement. More fluid, an upright position and activity restore motility and bladder emptying together.

options.text: Limit his evening fluids and offer the bedpan every 4 hours
options.rationale: Limiting evening fluids can reduce night time urgency in some patients. He is already dry, and less fluid concentrates his urine further and hardens his stool.

options.text: Request a urinary catheter so the stagnant urine drains continuously
options.rationale: Draining the bladder sounds like a fix for stasis. A catheter adds infection risk to urine that already looks infected and does nothing for the constipation.

options.text: Request a laxative and keep offering the bedpan while he lies flat
options.rationale: A laxative may help the constipation, so it is partly right. The bedpan while lying flat works against bowel and bladder emptying and leaves the low intake and urine stasis unchanged.

questions.takeaway: Immobility causes urinary stasis, infection and stone risk, and slowed bowel motility with constipation; fluids, upright positioning and activity treat both.
questions.strategy: The laxative tempts because the stool problem is obvious. The stem asks for a plan that covers both problems, and they share the same causes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low fluid intake and inactivity drive both problems.
A laxative or a catheter addresses only one system.
Limiting fluids worsens both.

elimination.verdict: Increase his fluids, use an upright commode, and add activity as tolerated.

questions.concept: Urinary and bowel effects of immobility

questions.stem: In the hospital on bed rest for 2 weeks for a pregnancy complication, a patient has stopped talking with staff, sleeps through the day, and refuses her bath, saying, "What's the point? I can't even wash myself." Which action by the nurse is best?

options.text: Ask the provider to start a medication for depression today
options.rationale: Depression is a possible effect of immobility, and a lasting change may need provider follow up. Asking for medication before exploring her feelings skips the nursing assessment.

options.text: Reassure her that she will be up and about after the birth
options.rationale: Hope matters, and the reassurance is well meant. Brushing past her feelings tells her they are not worth discussing and does nothing for her loss of independence today.

options.text: Acknowledge her loss of independence and offer choices in her care
options.rationale: Her words show grief over lost independence and an altered self concept. Naming that feeling opens communication, and offering choices gives back some control.

options.text: Let her sleep and skip her bath today so that she can rest
options.rationale: Respecting her refusal sounds patient centered. Withdrawal and daytime sleeping are signs of the psychosocial effects of immobility, and leaving her alone deepens the isolation.

questions.takeaway: Immobility can cause isolation, loss of independence, anxiety, depression and altered self concept; acknowledge the feeling and restore control through choices.
questions.strategy: Medication can look like the thorough answer for possible depression. Assess and respond to the feeling first; the nurse explores before referring.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: She grieves her lost independence.

steps.action: Remove the option that dismisses the feeling
steps.detail: Reassurance about later skips what she feels now.
Skipping care isolates her; medication comes after assessment.

elimination.verdict: Acknowledge her loss of independence and offer choices in her care.

questions.scenario: The nurse is planning range of motion exercises for several patients on a medical unit.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate the type of range of motion exercise the nurse plans for the joints described.

rows.text: A patient who begins each wrist movement but tires before reaching the end of the arc, for the wrists
rows.rationale: Some voluntary movement is present, so passive exercise would waste the patient's effort. Help is needed only to complete the motion, which is active assistive range of motion.

rows.text: A patient weak after a long illness who raises the arm halfway to shoulder height and cannot go farther, for that shoulder
rows.rationale: The patient starts the motion with their own muscles but cannot finish the arc. The nurse supports the rest so the joint moves through full range while the muscles still work.

rows.text: A patient sedated on a ventilator who does not move any limb on command, for the elbows and wrists
rows.rationale: The patient cannot contract any muscles on request, so the nurse moves each joint. Passive range of motion keeps the joints flexible but does not build strength.

rows.text: A patient with paralysis of both legs from a spinal cord injury, for the hips and knees
rows.rationale: Paralyzed muscles cannot contract, so the joints must be moved for the patient. Passive range of motion prevents stiffness and contractures in those joints.

rows.text: A patient recovering from a hernia repair who moves both shoulders through full range without help, for the shoulders
rows.rationale: Full movement without help means the patient can do the exercise alone. The nurse teaches and observes, and the patient's own muscles do the work.

questions.takeaway: Active ROM is done by the patient, passive ROM is done for the patient, and active assistive ROM is started by the patient and completed with help.
questions.strategy: A weak patient looks like a passive candidate. If the patient can start the motion, use that effort and assist only for the rest of the arc.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask whether any voluntary movement exists
steps.detail: No movement or paralysis means passive.

steps.action: Ask whether the movement is complete
steps.detail: Full range without help means active.
Starting but not finishing the arc means active assistive.

elimination.verdict: Passive for the sedated and paralyzed patients, active for the hernia repair patient, active assistive for the two partial movers.

questions.stem: Two days after a hysterectomy, a patient gets out of bed for the first time. Her blood pressure lying down was 128/76 mm Hg. After 1 minute of sitting at the side of the bed, she reports dizziness, and her blood pressure is 102/60 mm Hg. What does the nurse do now?

options.text: Coach slow deep breaths with the incentive spirometer until the dizziness passes
options.rationale: Deep breathing prevents respiratory complications after surgery. It does not treat low blood pressure, and keeping her upright while dizzy risks a fall.

options.text: Apply sequential compression devices and continue the transfer to the chair
options.rationale: Compression devices improve venous return and help prevent clots. Applying them does not correct a pressure drop that is happening now, and continuing the transfer risks a fall.

options.text: Stand her up promptly with two staff so her calf muscles pump blood upward
options.rationale: Calf muscle action does help venous return, which makes this sound logical. Standing a dizzy patient whose pressure has already dropped raises the risk of fainting and falling.

options.text: Return her to lying, then raise the head of the bed in stages later
options.rationale: A systolic drop of 26 mm Hg with dizziness is orthostatic hypotension, so she goes back to bed. Gradual position changes then let her circulation adjust before the next attempt.

questions.takeaway: Immobility causes orthostatic hypotension; a systolic drop of 20 mm Hg or more with dizziness means return the patient to bed, then progress position changes gradually.
questions.strategy: Two staff standing her up feels safe and active. Ask what the dizziness and the pressure drop mean now: her circulation has not adjusted, so she lies back down first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Systolic fell from 128 to 102 mm Hg, a 26 mm Hg drop, with dizziness.
That is orthostatic hypotension from immobility.
Lying down restores blood flow to the brain; staged elevation comes next.

elimination.verdict: Return her to lying, then raise the head of the bed in stages later.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with 24 more hours of bed rest after surgery to drain a hip abscess. His sequential compression devices have been lying on a chair since his morning bath. What does the nurse do first to reduce his risk of thrombus formation?

options.text: Coach incentive spirometer use ten times each hour
options.rationale: Incentive spirometry prevents atelectasis by expanding the lungs. It is a respiratory intervention and does nothing to move blood through his leg veins while he lies still.

options.text: Place a pillow under both knees so his legs rest flexed
options.rationale: A pillow under the knees feels comfortable but presses on the vessels behind the knees. That pressure slows blood return and adds to venous stasis instead of preventing it.

options.text: Reapply the sequential compression devices to both legs
options.rationale: The devices squeeze the calves and push blood out of the leg veins, which counters venous stasis. They do nothing while they sit on a chair, so putting them back on comes first.

options.text: Plan progressive walking for when the bed rest order ends
options.rationale: Progressive activity is a key way to prevent thrombus, so it belongs in his plan. He must stay in bed for another day, so it cannot protect his veins right now.

questions.takeaway: Venous stasis from immobility is countered with sequential compression devices, leg exercises, adequate hydration and progressive activity, starting with the measure that works now.
questions.strategy: Progressive activity is a correct prevention measure, which makes it tempting. He is on bed rest for another day, so the measure that works right now comes first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Reject what does not help the veins
steps.detail: The knee pillow adds pressure and the spirometer treats the lungs.
Walking waits for the bed rest order to end; the devices work as soon as they are on.

elimination.verdict: Reapply the sequential compression devices to both legs.

questions.stem: A patient with three broken ribs is raised to Fowler's position to ease breathing. Three pillows behind the head push the chin toward the chest, the legs lie straight, and the patient has slid down toward the foot of the bed. What does the nurse correct?

options.text: Use one small head pillow and support the hips and knees flexed
options.rationale: Supported Fowler's keeps the cervical, thoracic and lumbar curves aligned and lets the hips and knees flex. Slight knee flexion also stops the slipping down the bed.

options.text: Add a fourth pillow behind the shoulders and raise the head of the bed
options.rationale: More support behind the shoulders may seem to fix the slump. More pillows push the head farther forward and a higher bed increases the slipping.

options.text: Keep the pillows in place and add a firm footboard for the straight legs
options.rationale: A footboard can stop the slipping toward the foot of the bed. It leaves the neck flexed against the chest and the hips and knees unsupported.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed flat so the patient stops sliding down
options.rationale: Lying flat would stop the slipping and straighten the spine. It removes the upright position that helps this patient breathe, which was the reason for Fowler's.

questions.takeaway: Supported Fowler's position flexes the hips and knees and keeps the normal curves of the cervical, thoracic and lumbar spine aligned.
questions.strategy: The footboard tempts because it stops the slipping. The stem lists two problems, a flexed neck and straight legs, and only one option corrects both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Neck flexed by three pillows; legs straight; patient sliding.

steps.action: Remove options that lose the purpose
steps.detail: Lying flat gives up the upright position.

steps.action: Pick the option that fixes every fault
steps.detail: One small pillow and supported hip and knee flexion.

elimination.verdict: Use one small head pillow and support the hips and knees flexed.

questions.stem: The nurse checks on a patient with Guillain Barré syndrome who cannot move the arms or legs. Assistive personnel have placed him supine and rested both arms on pillows raised out to the sides above shoulder level, at about 120 degrees. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and flex his hips and knees with support
options.rationale: Those changes describe supported Fowler's position, which is a different position. They leave the arms in the same unsafe placement.

options.text: Turn his head toward the left so it is not resting at midline
options.rationale: Turning the head is part of prone positioning. In supine the head rests at midline, which the assistive personnel have already done.

options.text: Leave the arms in place and check his hands for swelling in 2 hours
options.rationale: Checking the hands is reasonable follow up. Leaving the arms over shoulder level keeps the joint in a harmful position for 2 more hours.

options.text: Lower both arms to his sides or out at less than 90 degrees
options.rationale: In the supine position the arms rest at the sides or abducted less than 90 degrees. Holding them above shoulder level strains the shoulder joints and nerves of a patient who cannot move them.

questions.takeaway: In supine position the patient lies on the back with the arms at the sides or abducted less than 90 degrees.
questions.strategy: Checking for swelling sounds careful. Ask whether the position itself is correct: it is not, so the nurse fixes it now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Supine arms rest at the sides or below 90 degrees.
A turned head is prone; raised head and flexed knees are Fowler's.
Waiting 2 hours leaves the harm in place.

elimination.verdict: Lower both arms to his sides or out at less than 90 degrees.

questions.scenario: On day 3 after open abdominal surgery, a patient has stayed flat in bed and declines to turn or sit up because of incision pain. Respiratory rate 24 per minute and shallow. Breath sounds diminished in both lung bases. Cough is weak. Oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Temperature 37.6 °C. Calves soft and nontender. Urine clear yellow.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Apply sequential compression devices to both legs
options.rationale: Compression devices prevent venous stasis and are a sound immobility measure. His calves are soft and nontender, and the problem in front of the nurse is in the lungs.

options.text: Coach coughing, deep breathing and incentive spirometry
options.rationale: Deep breaths reopen collapsed air sacs, and coughing clears retained secretions. Together they treat the atelectasis and lower his pneumonia risk.

options.text: Let him stay flat until his incision pain has resolved
options.rationale: Rest feels kind when he is in pain, and pain does need treatment. Staying flat is what caused the collapse of his lung bases, so it worsens the problem.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and sit him upright
options.rationale: Sitting upright lets the diaphragm drop and the lungs expand into the bases. It directly counters the decreased lung expansion caused by lying flat.

options.text: Venous thrombus
options.rationale: A thrombus is a risk of his immobility, but his calves are soft and nontender. Nothing in his findings points to a clot.

options.text: Atelectasis
options.rationale: Shallow breathing, diminished bases, a weak cough and falling saturation after days lying flat fit collapse of the lung bases. Retained secretions put him on the path to pneumonia.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension
options.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension appears as dizziness and a blood pressure drop when rising. He has not been upright, and his findings are respiratory.

options.text: Urinary stasis
options.rationale: Urinary stasis is another effect of immobility. His urine is clear yellow, and his abnormal findings are all in the lungs.

options.text: Breath sounds in the lung bases
options.rationale: Diminished bases are the main sign of the problem. Breath sounds returning to the bases show the lungs are reexpanding.

options.text: Bowel sounds
options.rationale: Bowel sounds matter after abdominal surgery, and the nurse will check them. They do not measure the respiratory problem being treated here.

options.text: Oxygen saturation
options.rationale: His saturation of 91% shows gas exchange is already affected. Trending it shows whether the interventions are working.

options.text: Urine color and clarity
options.rationale: Urine checks help detect urinary stasis or dehydration. They do not track whether his lung bases are reopening.

questions.takeaway: Immobility decreases lung expansion, weakens the cough and lets secretions collect, leading to atelectasis and pneumonia; upright positioning and coughing and deep breathing reverse it.
questions.strategy: The compression devices are a correct immobility measure, which makes them tempting. Match each action to the problem in front of you: his findings are respiratory.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shallow breathing, diminished bases, weak cough and low saturation point to the lungs.
Soft calves and clear urine argue against a clot or urinary stasis.

steps.action: Pick actions and measures for the lungs
steps.detail: Upright position and coughing and deep breathing; track breath sounds and saturation.

elimination.verdict: Atelectasis: sit him upright, coach coughing, deep breathing and incentive spirometry, and monitor breath sounds and oxygen saturation.

questions.stem: In the intensive care unit, a critically ill patient with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome from COVID 19 is on a ventilator. In supported Fowler's position her oxygen saturation is 86% on high oxygen settings. Which position does the nurse prepare the team to place her in?

options.text: Left lateral recumbent, alternating with the right side every 2 hours
options.rationale: Regular side to side turning protects the skin and helps clear secretions. It is routine care, not the first line position for severe distress syndrome.

options.text: Prone, on her stomach with her head turned to one side
options.rationale: Prone positioning is first line for critically ill patients with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome. Lying on the stomach improves how air and blood meet in the lungs, raising oxygenation.

options.text: Supine, flat on her back with her arms at her sides
options.rationale: Supine is a basic resting position. Lying flat on her back compresses the back of the lungs, which tends to worsen oxygenation in this patient.

options.text: High Fowler's with her arms supported forward on an overbed table
options.rationale: Leaning forward upright helps an awake patient breathe more easily. A critically ill, ventilated patient cannot hold that position, and it is not the treatment for severe distress syndrome.

questions.takeaway: Prone positioning is first line therapy for critically ill patients with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome, such as from COVID 19.
questions.strategy: High Fowler's tempts because sitting up helps most patients breathe. The cues are critical illness, a ventilator and severe distress syndrome, which call for prone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Severe acute respiratory distress syndrome, ventilated, saturation 86%.
Prone, with the head turned to one side.
Supine and side lying are routine; high Fowler's suits an awake patient.

elimination.verdict: Prone, on her stomach with her head turned to one side.

questions.stem: A patient with lung cancer receives oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula. The nurse turns him onto his right side. He lies in good alignment and denies pain, but his oxygen saturation falls from 95% to 89%, and the cannula tubing now runs under his right shoulder. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Free the tubing from under his shoulder and confirm oxygen is flowing
options.rationale: After any repositioning the nurse checks tubes and lines and the ability to breathe comfortably. Tubing trapped under the shoulder can block flow, and freeing it treats the likely cause at once.

options.text: Increase the oxygen flow rate on the wall meter and recheck in 5 minutes
options.rationale: More oxygen seems logical when saturation falls. A kinked line delivers little at any flow, and changing the rate without an order is outside the nurse's role here.

options.text: Turn him back to his previous position and recheck the saturation
options.rationale: Returning to the earlier position might restore the saturation. It skips finding the cause, and the trapped tubing would still be kinked once he is moved again.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees and coach slow, deep breaths
options.rationale: Upright positioning and deep breathing support oxygenation in general. They cannot help if oxygen is not reaching him through pinched tubing.

questions.takeaway: After repositioning, reassess alignment, comfort, pressure areas, skin, tubes and lines, and breathing; check the equipment before changing treatment.
questions.strategy: Increasing the oxygen feels like the safest response to a falling saturation. Check the equipment first, because the stem shows tubing pinned under his shoulder.

steps.action: Link the change to the turn
steps.detail: The saturation fell right after repositioning.
The cannula tubing is trapped under his shoulder.

steps.action: Fix the cause before adding treatment
steps.detail: Freeing the tubing comes before changing flow or position.

elimination.verdict: Free the tubing from under his shoulder and confirm oxygen is flowing.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the chart of a patient on bed rest after spinal fusion surgery who had diminished breath sounds in both bases, a weak cough, and an oxygen saturation of 91% on room air. After 24 hours of sitting upright, deep breathing, coughing, and incentive spirometry, which finding best shows the plan is working?

options.text: Respiratory rate 12 per minute and shallow, dozing between checks
options.rationale: A rate of 12 per minute falls within the normal range, which makes this look reassuring. Shallow breathing while dozing is the pattern that lets the lung bases collapse.

options.text: Saturation 96% on oxygen at 2 L/min, with breath sounds in both bases still diminished
options.rationale: The saturation number looks better. It comes from added oxygen, and the bases are still diminished, so the lungs have not reexpanded.

options.text: Breath sounds in both bases, a strong cough, and 96% on room air
options.rationale: Each original problem has improved: air is reaching the bases, the cough clears secretions, and oxygenation is normal without help. That shows the lungs are expanding.

options.text: Reports no incisional pain while lying still and declines to cough
options.rationale: Pain control supports deep breathing, so this has some value. Declining to cough means secretions stay in the lungs, and the plan is not being carried out.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate respiratory interventions by the original cues: breath sounds in the bases, cough strength, and oxygenation without added support.
questions.strategy: The 96% on oxygen looks like success. Compare with the baseline, which was on room air with diminished bases; the added oxygen hides the unchanged lungs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Diminished bases, weak cough, saturation 91% on room air.

steps.action: Check each option against all three
steps.detail: Only one shows every cue improved.
Supplemental oxygen raises the number without fixing the lungs.

elimination.verdict: Breath sounds in both bases, a strong cough, and 96% on room air.

questions.stem: During mobility screening, a patient recovering from pneumonia sits unassisted at the side of the bed for 3 minutes and shakes the nurse's hand across midline. She cannot straighten either knee or point her toes. Assistive personnel ask how to move her to the chair. Which direction does the nurse give?

options.text: Stand her up with a gait belt and pivot her to the chair with two staff
options.rationale: A stand and pivot needs legs that can bear weight, and two staff makes it feel safe. She failed stretch and point, so her legs cannot be trusted to hold her during the pivot.

options.text: Have her hover her buttocks for a count of 5 before choosing
options.rationale: The hover is the Level 3 stand task. It is attempted only after stretch and point is passed, so trying it now risks a fall.

options.text: Walk her to the chair with a walker while staff give standby help
options.rationale: Walking with standby help fits a Level 4 patient. She stopped at Level 2, far short of the stand and step tasks that walking requires.

options.text: Move her with a mechanical lift and let her help from sitting
options.rationale: She failed stretch and point, which makes her Level 2, maximum assist, and that level calls for lift equipment for transfers. Her seated balance lets her take part, which supports her strength.

questions.takeaway: The BMAT level chooses the handling equipment; a Level 2 patient transfers by lift while taking part as much as her seated balance allows.
questions.strategy: Two staff with a gait belt feels safe, but staff numbers do not replace leg strength. Match the transfer to the last task she passed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Passed sit and shake, failed stretch and point: Level 2, maximum assist.
Pivoting and walking both need legs she cannot yet trust.

steps.action: Remove the out of order test
steps.detail: The hover is tried only after stretch and point is passed.

elimination.verdict: Move her with a mechanical lift and let her help from sitting.
