questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease has a high fall risk score. He is at Level 4 on the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool and walks steadily with his walker and standby assist. Assistive personnel report they kept him in bed with the bed alarm on all shift "so he would not fall." Which direction does the nurse give?

options.text: Continue keeping him in bed with the alarm, since his fall risk is high
options.rationale: His high fall risk is real and deserves a plan. Keeping him in bed is excessive restriction, and immobility worsens the weakness that makes falls more likely.

options.text: Walk him with his walker and standby assist at set times through the day
options.rationale: Fall prevention aims for safe mobility, not immobility. His level shows he can walk with standby help, and a schedule keeps him moving with support so he does not get up alone.

options.text: Move him with a mechanical lift for every trip out of bed
options.rationale: A lift feels like the safest handling choice. He passed the step task, and using a lift for a Level 4 patient removes the walking that maintains his strength.

options.text: Have him use a bedpan so that he does not need to get out of bed
options.rationale: A bedpan removes the trip to the bathroom and seems to remove the risk. It is another form of keeping him in bed and takes away function he still has.

questions.takeaway: Fall prevention does not mean keeping a patient in bed; match handling to the mobility level and aim for safe mobility.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option sounds cautious. Ask which one keeps him moving safely at the level he has shown he can manage.

steps.detail: Level 4: walks with walker and standby assist.
Bed with alarm and bedpan both keep him immobile.
A lift is meant for patients who cannot bear weight.

elimination.verdict: Walk him with his walker and standby assist at set times through the day.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.objective: Apply principles of safe patient handling to reduce injury risk for both patients and health care workers.

questions.stem: After cardiac surgery, a heavily sedated patient has been lying on his back for several hours without repositioning. Which areas does the nurse inspect for early pressure injury? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inner knees
options.rationale: The inner knees are a pressure site when the knees rest against each other in side lying. On his back the knees do not press together.

options.text: Back of the head
options.rationale: Lying supine places the weight of the head on the back of the skull. Little tissue covers the bone there, so pressure injury develops quickly.

options.text: Outer hips
options.rationale: The outer hips bear weight in side lying, not in the supine position. They are less at risk while he lies on his back.

options.text: Sacrum and buttocks
options.rationale: The sacrum carries the most body weight when lying on the back. It is one of the most common sites for pressure injury.

options.text: Shoulder blades
options.rationale: The shoulder blades bear the upper body's weight against the mattress when the patient is on his back. They are a common supine pressure site.

options.text: Heels
options.rationale: The heels carry the weight of the legs when lying flat, with almost no padding over the bone. Heel pressure injuries develop quickly in sedated patients.

options.text: Elbows
options.rationale: With arms at his sides, the elbows rest on the bed with little padding over the bone. They are at risk in the supine position.

questions.takeaway: Pressure injury sites depend on position; in supine the back of the head, shoulder blades, elbows, sacrum and heels bear the weight.
questions.strategy: Inner knees and outer hips are real pressure sites, which makes them tempting. Picture the patient on his back and ask which bony areas touch the mattress.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Supine means weight on the back surface of the body.

steps.action: Pick bony points touching the bed
steps.detail: Back of head, shoulder blades, elbows, sacrum, heels.
Inner knees and outer hips bear weight when lying on the side.

elimination.verdict: Back of the head, shoulder blades, elbows, sacrum and buttocks, and heels.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.objective: Describe the major respiratory, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, integumentary, elimination, and psychosocial effects of immobility.

questions.stem: After a long intensive care stay for kidney failure, a patient who weighs 110 kg is weak and cannot help with moving. Two assistive personnel plan to move him from the bed to a stretcher by lifting the draw sheet by hand. What does the nurse direct?

options.text: Lift on a count of three so that all staff move at the same moment
options.rationale: Moving together on a count helps coordination. It does not change the weight being lifted, so the risk of a back injury stays the same.

options.text: Have them bend their knees and keep their backs straight while lifting
options.rationale: Good body mechanics lower strain and are worth using. Body mechanics alone cannot make lifting a heavy, dependent person safe, so injuries still occur.

options.text: Add a third staff member so that the weight is shared by more people
options.rationale: More hands do spread the load, so this sounds safer. It is still a manual lift of a dependent patient, which is the task most likely to injure staff.

options.text: Use a friction reducing transfer device or a lift with enough staff
options.rationale: A dependent patient this heavy is far beyond what staff can lift safely by hand. Transfer devices and lifts take the load off the staff and protect the patient's skin.

questions.takeaway: Safe patient handling replaces manual lifting of dependent patients with transfer devices and mechanical lifts; good body mechanics alone are not enough.
questions.strategy: Body mechanics sounds like the textbook answer. For a dependent, heavy patient, equipment is the safety measure; technique is only a supplement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A manual lift of a dependent 110 kg patient.

steps.action: Remove options that keep the manual lift
steps.detail: More people, better posture and counting all still lift by hand.
A transfer device or lift removes the load.

elimination.verdict: Use a friction reducing transfer device or a lift with enough staff.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Potter).
questions.objective: Apply principles of safe patient handling to reduce injury risk for both patients and health care workers.

questions.stem: The nurse and an assistive personnel member are about to turn a patient toward themselves using a friction reducing sheet. The bed is raised to the nurse's waist height, and both stand close to the patient. The assistant's feet are together, and she leans forward from the waist to grip the sheet. Which correction does the nurse give her?

options.text: Pull the sheet fast so the turn takes less effort
options.rationale: A fast, jerking pull does not reduce the load on her back. It raises the strain on her spine and the chance of injury to both her and the patient.

options.text: Lower the bed so you are not working up so high
options.rationale: A lower bed sounds easier, but it forces more bending at the waist. The bed is already at a comfortable working height, which is where it belongs for the turn.

options.text: Set your feet wide apart and bend at the knees
options.rationale: A wide base of support keeps her center of gravity stable over her feet. Bending at the knees moves the work to the strong leg muscles instead of the lower back.

options.text: Step in closer to the patient before you pull
options.rationale: Standing close to the patient is a sound body mechanics principle. She is already close, so the step does nothing to fix her narrow stance and bent waist.

questions.takeaway: Body mechanics for the nurse: bed at working height, stand close, use a wide base of support, bend at the knees, tighten the abdomen and move the feet instead of twisting.
questions.strategy: Standing closer is a true principle, so it tempts. Match the correction to what is wrong in the stem: her feet are together and she bends at the waist.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The bed height and her distance from the patient are correct.
Feet together and bending at the waist call for a wide stance and bent knees.

elimination.verdict: Set your feet wide apart and bend at the knees.

questions.objective: Apply principles of safe patient handling to reduce injury risk for both patients and health care workers.

questions.stem: Three days into treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis, a patient sits at the side of the bed for the first time. At 1 minute she says she is lightheaded, so the nurse keeps her seated with her feet on the floor. At 3 minutes she says the lightheadedness is gone, and her blood pressure matches her lying reading. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Return her to lying and raise the head of the bed in stages
options.rationale: Returning to bed is right while dizziness and a pressure drop persist. Both have resolved after 3 minutes of sitting, so lying down again repeats a step she has already passed.

options.text: Help her stand with a gait belt and pause before walking
options.rationale: Her body has adjusted to sitting: the symptom is gone and her pressure is back to its lying value. The next gradual step is standing with support, pausing to check her before she walks.

options.text: Keep her seated until the next set of vital signs
options.rationale: Waiting seems cautious but serves no purpose once her symptom and pressure have recovered. Prolonged sitting delays mobility, which is the goal that prevents further deconditioning.

options.text: Stand her quickly so her leg muscles push blood upward
options.rationale: Leg muscle action does help venous return, but a quick rise is the opposite of a gradual position change. Standing fast after recent lightheadedness can bring the pressure drop back.

questions.takeaway: Gradual position change means advancing one step at a time once the patient's symptoms and blood pressure have recovered, not returning to bed after every brief symptom.
questions.strategy: Returning her to bed is right when dizziness persists, so it looks safe. Her symptom and her pressure have both recovered, so the next gradual step is standing.

steps.detail: Lightheadedness gone and pressure back to the lying value at 3 minutes.
Lying down fits persistent symptoms, which she no longer has.
A quick rise skips the gradual step.

elimination.verdict: Help her stand with a gait belt and pause before walking.

questions.stem: In skeletal traction for a broken thigh bone, a patient will stay on bed rest until surgery in 2 days. His sodium level is low, and the provider has restricted his fluids. A compression device is in place on his other leg. Which addition to his plan helps prevent a clot from forming?

options.text: Hourly ankle pumps and foot circles while awake
options.rationale: Ankle and foot exercises contract the calf muscles, which squeeze blood out of the leg veins and reduce venous stasis. They need no extra fluid and no change in his bed rest.

options.text: Dangling at the side of the bed twice a day
options.rationale: Progressive activity prevents clots once activity is allowed. Traction and a bed rest order until surgery mean he cannot sit at the side of the bed yet.

options.text: A pillow under both knees to ease leg strain
options.rationale: A pillow under the knees may feel comfortable, but it bends the knees and slows blood flow in the leg veins. That position raises the risk of venous stasis.

options.text: Extra fluids offered between meals and at bedtime
options.rationale: Hydration does help prevent clots by keeping blood less concentrated. His provider has restricted fluids for a low sodium level, so extra fluids would work against his treatment.

questions.takeaway: Clot prevention is fitted to the patient: hydration only as appropriate and activity only as allowed, with leg exercises available when both are limited.
questions.strategy: Fluids are a standard clot prevention step, so they look right. The fluid restriction rules them out and the bed rest rules out dangling, which leaves leg exercises.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluids are restricted and he must stay in bed.
Extra fluids break the restriction; dangling breaks the bed rest.
Ankle exercises move venous blood within both limits.

elimination.verdict: Hourly ankle pumps and foot circles while awake.

questions.stem: Halfway down a long hallway and far from any chair, a patient recovering from a kidney transplant tells the nurse her legs feel weak, and her knees begin to buckle. The nurse is at her side and slightly behind her, holding the gait belt. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Hold her upright and call out for a wheelchair
options.rationale: Calling for help is reasonable, and a wheelchair would end the walk safely. Her knees are already buckling, so holding her full weight until it arrives risks a fall for both of them.

options.text: Pull up on the gait belt to keep her standing
options.rationale: The belt gives a secure grip for guiding her, not for holding her full weight. Pulling up against buckling knees can injure her and strain the nurse's back.

options.text: Ease her to the floor along the nurse's leg
options.rationale: When a patient starts to fall, the safest response is a controlled descent to the floor. Sliding her down along the nurse's leg protects her head and spares the nurse's back.

options.text: Guide her quickly to the nearest chair
options.rationale: Sitting her in a chair is the safest choice when one is close by. She is far from any chair, so rushing her there on buckling knees invites an uncontrolled fall.

questions.takeaway: When a walking patient begins to fall with no seat nearby, the nurse uses the gait belt to guide a controlled descent to the floor rather than trying to hold her up.
questions.strategy: A chair or a wheelchair sounds safer than the floor. She is far from any chair and her knees are already giving way, so a controlled descent prevents an uncontrolled fall.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Far from any chair, with knees already buckling.
Pulling up or holding her full weight risks injury to both.
A guided descent along the nurse's leg protects her head.

elimination.verdict: Ease her to the floor along the nurse's leg.

questions.stem: Before a hallway walk with the nurse, a patient with left sided weakness from multiple sclerosis is at Level 4 on the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool. She has a feeding tube site on the left side of her upper abdomen. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lift her upright by the gait belt if her knees begin to buckle
options.rationale: Catching a falling patient is a natural instinct. A gait belt is for steadying, not lifting, and lifting a falling patient injures the nurse; the nurse eases her to the floor instead.

options.text: Have her sit at the side of the bed for 2 to 3 minutes before standing
options.rationale: Sitting first gives her circulation time to adjust to the upright position. It lets the nurse check for dizziness before she bears weight.

options.text: Fasten the gait belt snugly with room for two fingers underneath
options.rationale: A snug belt gives the nurse a secure hold if she loses balance. Room for two fingers keeps it from being so tight that it causes discomfort.

options.text: Walk on her right side so her stronger side can lead
options.rationale: Standing on the strong side is the rule for patients with orthopedic problems. With a neurological deficit she falls toward the weak side, so the nurse stands on the left.

options.text: Walk on her left side, holding the belt from behind
options.rationale: For a patient with a neurological deficit the nurse stands on the weak side. That is the side she is most likely to fall toward.

options.text: Place the belt so that it does not cross the feeding tube site
options.rationale: A belt over a tube or incision can dislodge the tube or injure the site. The nurse adjusts its position to avoid that area.

questions.takeaway: Use the gait belt to steady, never to lift; place it snugly away from tubes and incisions, dangle first, and stand on the weak side for a neurological deficit.
questions.strategy: Lifting by the belt feels protective, and standing on the strong side is a rule students remember. The belt only steadies, and the weak side rule applies to neurological deficits.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sitting at the bedside for 2 to 3 minutes comes before standing.
Snug, two fingers of room, away from the tube.

steps.action: Pick the side by the type of deficit
steps.detail: Neurological deficit: stand on the weak left side.

elimination.verdict: Dangle first, fasten the belt snugly away from the tube, and walk on her left side.

questions.stem: Once the nurse and an assistant turn a patient with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis onto her left side, the nurse reassesses her. Before the turn she spoke in full sentences. She says she is comfortable. Which finding does the nurse address first?

options.text: Her left ear is folded against the pillow
options.rationale: A folded ear is a pressure area that is easy to miss after a side lying turn. Smoothing it matters for comfort and skin, but it does not threaten her breathing.

options.text: She now speaks in short phrases between breaths
options.rationale: Breathing comfortably is part of every reassessment after a turn, and her shorter phrases show it has become harder. Her weak breathing muscles make this change the priority over lines and skin.

options.text: Her catheter tubing lies under her thigh, still draining urine
options.rationale: Tubes and lines are checked after every turn, and this tubing needs to be moved soon. Urine is still draining, so it ranks below a change in her breathing.

options.text: Her upper knee rests directly on her lower knee
options.rationale: Bony prominences resting on each other create a pressure area, so a pillow between the knees is needed. It is a skin risk that can wait minutes, unlike a breathing change.

questions.takeaway: After repositioning, the nurse checks alignment, pressure areas, tubes and breathing, and a change in breathing ranks first even when the patient says she is comfortable.
questions.strategy: The catheter tubing under her thigh is a clear, fixable problem and looks urgent. Her shorter phrases are a quieter cue, but with weak breathing muscles a breathing change outranks lines and skin.

steps.detail: She went from full sentences to short phrases.
Breathing outranks a draining catheter and pressure areas.
Free the tubing and pad the knees and ear next.

elimination.verdict: She now speaks in short phrases between breaths.

questions.stem: The morning after a patient recovering from a ruptured appendix fell without injury, the nurse reassesses her at Level 4 on the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool. She walks steadily with standby assist. She fell at 0300 while hurrying alone to the bathroom. Her husband asks that she stay in bed until discharge. Which plan revision does the nurse make?

options.text: Mechanical lift for every transfer for the rest of her stay
options.rationale: A lift is the right choice for a patient who fails the early screening levels. At Level 4 she can walk with standby help, so a lift takes away ability she still has.

options.text: Bed rest with a bed alarm until she goes home
options.rationale: Bed rest feels protective after a fall, and her husband asks for it. Immobility worsens weakness and leaves the real cause, rushing alone to the bathroom, untouched.

options.text: Bedside commode at night and walks only with physical therapy
options.rationale: A commode at night is reasonable, but limiting walks to therapy sessions restricts a patient who walks steadily with standby help. Less walking speeds weakness and raises her fall risk.

options.text: Night toileting rounds and hallway walks with staff nearby
options.rationale: Her fall came from rushing alone to the bathroom at night, so scheduled toileting targets that cause. Continued walks with standby assist keep the mobility that protects her strength.

questions.takeaway: After a fall, the plan is revised to target what caused it while keeping the patient as mobile as her reassessed level allows.
questions.strategy: The commode with therapy walks sounds like a careful middle ground. She walks steadily with standby assist, so any limit on walking restricts her more than her level calls for.

steps.detail: She fell rushing alone to the bathroom at 0300.
Level 4 with standby assist supports regular walks.
Bed rest, walks limited to therapy and a lift all restrict her more than needed.

elimination.verdict: Night toileting rounds and hallway walks with staff nearby.

questions.stem: On a medical unit, four patients have each had influenza with poor oral intake for 3 days, and their recorded intake and output are similar. None has kidney or heart disease. Which patient does the nurse monitor most closely for a fluid volume deficit?

options.text: An 83 year old woman of average build
options.rationale: Older adults have less total body water, about 50 to 55%, and women carry more fat and less muscle than men. She starts with the smallest reserve, so the same loss depletes her fastest.

options.text: A 47 year old man of average build
options.rationale: Adult men average about 60% body water, more than women and older adults. His loss is real, but it uses a smaller share of his reserve than an older woman's loss would.

options.text: A 31 year old man who lifts weights
options.rationale: Muscle holds more water than fat, so a young muscular man has the largest water reserve of the four. The same loss takes a smaller share of his total body water.

options.text: A 26 year old woman of average build
options.rationale: Being female does lower her total body water compared with a man her age. She lacks the drop in body water that comes with aging, so her reserve is still larger.

questions.takeaway: Older adults and women start with less total body water, so an equal loss puts them at higher risk for a deficit.
questions.strategy: Every patient has the same loss, so the choice turns on who has the smallest reserve. Age and sex both lower total body water, and only one option has both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: All four lost similar amounts, so compare starting reserves.
Older age and female sex each lower total body water.
Only the older woman carries both factors.

elimination.verdict: Monitor the 83 year old woman most closely.

questions.stem: Ten hours after admission for large burns, a patient has generalized swelling. His weight is unchanged from admission, heart rate is 126 per minute, blood pressure is 88/52 mm Hg and urine output is 15 mL per hour. A student nurse asks whether he has too much fluid. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Total body water has been lost through the burns
options.rationale: Burns do cause losses, and that is part of his risk. His weight has not dropped, so the main problem now is fluid sitting in the tissues rather than fluid gone from the body.

options.text: Water has moved out of the tissues into cells
options.rationale: Water entering cells is the picture of a hypotonic state such as hyponatremia, which shows first as cerebral changes. His cues point to low vascular volume with tissue swelling, not cell swelling.

options.text: Fluid has moved from the plasma into the tissues
options.rationale: Burns cause vascular dehydration, a plasma to interstitial shift with no true water loss. The swelling is fluid in the wrong compartment, while the fast pulse, low pressure and scant urine show his vessels are short.

options.text: The swelling means total body water is in excess
options.rationale: His unchanged weight argues against added water, and excess volume gives a bounding pulse and high blood pressure. He has a fast heart rate and low pressure instead.

questions.takeaway: Edema with a fast pulse and low blood pressure means plasma has shifted into the tissues: the vessels are short even though the body is swollen.
questions.strategy: The visible swelling pulls toward overload. The vital signs and the unchanged weight tip it: the vessels are short of fluid even though the tissues are full.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Heart rate 126, pressure 88/52 mm Hg and 15 mL per hour of urine mean low vascular volume.
No change since admission rules out both added water and true loss.
The swelling is plasma that moved into the interstitial space.

elimination.verdict: Fluid moved from the plasma into the tissues.

questions.objective: 1. Describe fluid compartments and how water/electrolytes move between them.
questions.concept: Vascular dehydration: plasma to interstitial shift

questions.scenario: On a medical unit, the nurse is caring for a patient with a serum sodium of 121 mEq/L who has a headache and is confused. The nurse considers how each IV solution that might be prescribed would move water between her cells and the fluid around them.
questions.stem: For each solution, indicate its effect on water in the patient's cells.

rows.text: D5W once the dextrose is metabolized
rows.rationale: Once the dextrose is used, what remains is free water, which acts as hypotonic. It moves into cells; that helps in hypernatremia and harms a patient whose sodium is low.

rows.text: D5 in 0.45% sodium chloride once the dextrose is metabolized
rows.rationale: This bag is hypertonic while it hangs, but the dextrose is metabolized after it enters the vein. What remains acts as hypotonic fluid and moves water into cells.

rows.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: At 0.45% the solution is hypotonic, below 270 mOsm/L, so water moves into the cells. That shift would add to the brain swelling causing her confusion and headache.

rows.text: 0.9% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Normal saline is isotonic, close to the 270 to 300 mOsm/L of body fluids. It expands the extracellular fluid without moving much water into or out of cells.

rows.text: 3% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: At 3% the solution is hypertonic, above 300 mOsm/L, so water leaves cells toward the higher solute concentration. For her swollen brain cells, that is the intended effect in severe hyponatremia.

questions.takeaway: Hypertonic fluid pulls water out of cells, hypotonic fluid pushes it in, and isotonic fluid stays mostly outside the cells.
questions.strategy: Judge the dextrose bags by what remains after the dextrose is metabolized, not by the label on the bag.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Body fluids are 270 to 300 mOsm/L.
3% is above that range, 0.9% sits in it and 0.45% is below it.

steps.action: Judge the dextrose bags after metabolism
steps.detail: Both leave free water behind, which acts as hypotonic.

elimination.verdict: Pulls: 3% sodium chloride. Little shift: 0.9% sodium chloride. Pushes: 0.45% sodium chloride, D5W and D5 in 0.45% sodium chloride.

questions.objective: 2. Explain the role of osmosis, diffusion, filtration, and hormonal regulation in fluid balance.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with right sided heart failure who has 3+ pitting edema in both lower legs. He asks why fluid collects in his legs when he already takes a water pill. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Salt inside your leg cells is drawing water into those cells
options.rationale: Osmosis does move water toward higher solute concentration, but edema is fluid in the tissue spaces, not swollen cells. Sodium pumps keep sodium about 10 times higher outside cells than inside them.

options.text: Pressure backing up in your veins pushes fluid out into your legs
options.rationale: Right sided heart failure raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, and filtration moves fluid from high to low pressure. Fluid is pushed out of the capillaries into the tissue, which forms the edema he sees.

options.text: Your water pill is making your kidneys hold water in your legs
options.rationale: A diuretic increases water and sodium loss through the kidneys rather than holding water back. Blaming the medication could also lead him to stop taking it, which would worsen the edema.

options.text: Too little protein in your blood is letting fluid leak out
options.rationale: Low blood protein lowers oncotic pressure and can cause edema in other conditions. Nothing in his history points to it; his failing right heart explains the raised pressure in the vessels.

questions.takeaway: Right sided heart failure raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, and filtration pushes fluid out of the vessels into the tissues.
questions.strategy: Two options name real edema mechanisms that do not fit this patient. Match the mechanism to the cause he has: a failing right heart backs up pressure in the veins.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Right sided heart failure raises pressure in the capillaries.
Fluid moving from high to low hydrostatic pressure is filtration.
Low protein is not in his history, cell swelling is not edema, and diuretics remove water.

elimination.verdict: Pressure backing up in the veins pushes fluid into the legs.

questions.objective: 2. Explain the role of osmosis, diffusion, filtration, and hormonal regulation in fluid balance.

questions.stem: In the clinic, a patient newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus has a blood glucose of 310 mg/dL and reports feeling tired and hungry. She asks, "If there is so much sugar in my blood, why do my cells need insulin?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Insulin helps glucose cross the cell membrane into your cells
options.rationale: Glucose enters cells by facilitated diffusion, which needs help crossing the membrane, and insulin provides that help. Without it, glucose stays in her blood while her cells go short, matching her fatigue and hunger.

options.text: Insulin pulls extra water into your cells to dilute the sugar
options.rationale: Moving water toward a higher solute concentration is osmosis, and insulin does not drive it. Insulin acts on the glucose itself by helping it get through the membrane.

options.text: Insulin helps your kidneys filter the extra sugar out of your blood
options.rationale: Filtration depends on hydrostatic pressure, and insulin is not what sends glucose into the urine. Insulin lowers blood glucose by letting it enter cells, not by excreting it.

options.text: Glucose moves into cells on its own; insulin just stores the extra
options.rationale: Plain diffusion does move solutes from high to low concentration, and her gradient is steep. Glucose cannot cross the membrane unassisted, so a steep gradient alone does not feed her cells.

questions.takeaway: Glucose enters cells by facilitated diffusion, and insulin is the helper that gets it across the membrane.
questions.strategy: The steep gradient makes plain diffusion tempting. What tips it is that glucose needs help crossing the membrane, and insulin is that help.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glucose is a solute, so osmosis and filtration describe the wrong process.
Glucose needs help, so this is facilitated diffusion.
Insulin provides that help.

elimination.verdict: Insulin helps glucose cross into the cells.

questions.objective: 2. Explain the role of osmosis, diffusion, filtration, and hormonal regulation in fluid balance.

questions.stem: The provider prescribes 0.45% sodium chloride IV at 100 mL per hour for a patient who drank several liters of plain water over a few hours as part of a cleansing diet. Her serum sodium is 119 mEq/L, she is confused and she had a brief seizure an hour ago. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Start the infusion at half the rate until the provider calls back
options.rationale: A slower rate feels like a safe compromise, but it still delivers a solution that moves water into cells. The problem is the type of fluid, not the speed.

options.text: Start the infusion and reassess her orientation in 1 hour
options.rationale: Reassessing orientation is a right step after a safe treatment has started. Starting a hypotonic fluid first lets more water into swollen brain cells before the error is caught.

options.text: Hold all IV fluid and give her oral water as she tolerates it
options.rationale: Plain water is even more hypotonic than 0.45% saline and would lower her sodium further. Excess water is what caused her low sodium in the first place.

options.text: Clarify the prescription with the provider before starting it
options.rationale: A 0.45% solution is hypotonic, and hypotonic fluid pushes water into cells, adding to the brain swelling behind her confusion and seizure. Severe hyponatremia like hers is treated with 3% hypertonic saline instead.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluid pushes water into cells, so it worsens the brain swelling of severe hyponatremia; question it before it runs.
questions.strategy: Reassessing and slowing the rate both feel careful. Each still delivers a fluid that moves water into her swollen brain cells, so only clarifying first protects her.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic.
Hypotonic fluid pushes water into cells, and her brain cells are already swelling.

steps.action: Drop the options that start it
steps.detail: Running it now or more slowly still gives the wrong fluid.

elimination.verdict: Clarify the prescription before starting it.

questions.objective: 2. Explain the role of osmosis, diffusion, filtration, and hormonal regulation in fluid balance.
questions.concept: Osmosis: hypotonic fluid moves water into cells

questions.stem: The nurse reviews new IV prescriptions for four patients before hanging the bags. Which prescription does the nurse clarify with the provider?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride: sodium 131 mEq/L after 2 days of vomiting
options.rationale: Vomiting is an actual sodium loss with a fluid deficit, and isotonic saline replaces both without shifting water into cells. This prescription fits the cause, so the nurse can hang it.

options.text: D5 in 0.45% sodium chloride: sodium 126 mEq/L, new confusion
options.rationale: The bag is hypertonic while it hangs, but once the dextrose is metabolized the fluid acts as hypotonic and pushes water into cells. Brain cells already swelling from this patient's low sodium would swell further.

options.text: D5W: sodium 150 mEq/L after 3 days of high fever
options.rationale: Fever causes water loss and cell shrinkage, and D5W becomes hypotonic once its dextrose is used, returning free water to the cells. It fits, provided the sodium is lowered gradually.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride: sodium 152 mEq/L with dry mucous membranes
options.rationale: Half normal saline is hypotonic and pushes water back into shrunken cells, which is the goal in hypernatremia from water loss. The nurse still watches the rate, because rapid correction risks cerebral edema.

questions.takeaway: D5 in 0.45% sodium chloride is hypertonic only in the bag; once the dextrose is metabolized it acts as hypotonic, so it worsens low sodium and cell swelling.
questions.strategy: The hypertonic label on the bag makes it look like a safe choice for low sodium. What tips it is how the fluid behaves after the dextrose is used: it adds free water.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Judge each fluid by its effect in the body
steps.detail: For dextrose fluids, count what remains after the dextrose is used.

steps.action: Match each effect to the sodium problem
steps.detail: Low sodium swells cells; high sodium shrinks them.
Free water given to a patient whose brain cells are already swelling.

elimination.verdict: Clarify the D5 in 0.45% sodium chloride for the sodium of 126 mEq/L.

questions.objective: 2. Explain the role of osmosis, diffusion, filtration, and hormonal regulation in fluid balance.
questions.note: The class material is internally inconsistent on hypernatremia fluids. The key points summary says to treat with isotonic fluids and restrict sodium; the intervention content says the goal is to replace free water and lower sodium gradually, and lists 0.9% NaCl alongside hypotonic D5W, 0.45% NS and D5 in 0.45% NS. The textbook and current practice use hypotonic free water for water loss hypernatremia and give isotonic saline first only when the patient is hypotensive or in shock. This item is keyed on how D5 in 0.45% NS behaves after metabolism, which both agree on. On the course exam, if a stem asks only for the treatment of hypernatremia, isotonic fluids with sodium restriction is the summary answer; on the NCLEX, choose hypotonic free water with gradual correction for a stable patient.

questions.stem: A patient with SIADH has a serum sodium of 126 mEq/L and is on a 1,000 mL per day fluid restriction. Assistive personnel report that his urine is scant and dark and ask whether to bring him extra water. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: Bring a sports drink instead, since it contains some sodium
options.rationale: Sodium sounds helpful when the level is low, but the drink is still mostly water. His problem is retained water, and any fluid counts against his restriction.

options.text: Keep the restriction but give him extra ice chips for thirst
options.rationale: Keeping the restriction is right, but ice chips melt into water that counts toward the daily limit. Unmeasured extra fluid undermines the treatment for his low sodium.

options.text: Keep the restriction; the hormone is making his kidneys hold water
options.rationale: Excess ADH makes the kidneys reabsorb water, so urine is scant and concentrated even while his body holds too much water. Extra water would dilute his sodium further.

options.text: Bring the water, since dark urine means he is getting dehydrated
options.rationale: Scant dark urine does point to a deficit in dehydration. In SIADH the same urine comes from ADH holding water back, so it is not a sign he needs more.

questions.takeaway: In SIADH, scant concentrated urine comes from excess ADH holding water, so the fluid restriction stays in place.
questions.strategy: Dark, scant urine pulls toward dehydration. In SIADH the kidneys are holding water under ADH, so the same urine means the opposite.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: ADH makes the kidneys reabsorb water.
Water held back leaves scant, concentrated urine despite the excess.
Sports drinks and ice chips both add water to a restricted intake.

elimination.verdict: Keep the restriction; ADH is holding water.

questions.objective: 2. Explain the role of osmosis, diffusion, filtration, and hormonal regulation in fluid balance.
questions.concept: ADH: water reabsorption and concentrated urine

questions.scenario: The nurse is caring for five patients whose bodies are responding to a change in fluid or sodium balance.
questions.stem: For each patient situation, indicate the hormone the body releases in response.

rows.text: A patient's serum osmolarity rises after 14 hours without fluids
rows.rationale: The posterior pituitary releases ADH when osmolarity is high. ADH makes the kidneys reabsorb water, which dilutes the blood back toward normal.

rows.text: A patient's serum sodium rises to 149 mEq/L after heavy sweating
rows.rationale: A high sodium means high osmolarity, the trigger for ADH. ADH holds water in the body to dilute the sodium, while thirst drives the patient to drink.

rows.text: A patient's blood volume and pressure rise after 3 L of IV fluid given quickly
rows.rationale: The heart releases natriuretic peptide when volume and pressure are high. It makes the kidneys excrete sodium and water, the body's own attempt to unload the extra fluid.

rows.text: A patient's serum sodium is 131 mEq/L after weeks of a very low salt diet
rows.rationale: Low sodium triggers aldosterone from the adrenal cortex. Aldosterone makes the kidneys reabsorb sodium and water and excrete potassium in exchange.

rows.text: A patient's blood pressure drops and her kidneys secrete renin
rows.rationale: Renin leads to angiotensin II, and angiotensin II increases aldosterone. The result is more sodium and water reabsorbed and a rise in blood volume and pressure.

questions.takeaway: ADH answers high osmolarity, aldosterone answers low sodium and the renin cascade, and natriuretic peptide answers high volume or pressure.
questions.strategy: Match each trigger to its hormone. Renin is a cue for aldosterone, because angiotensin II is what raises aldosterone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the trigger in each row
steps.detail: High osmolarity, low sodium, renin release or high volume.
ADH for osmolarity, aldosterone for low sodium and renin, natriuretic peptide for volume and pressure.
Hormones that save water answer losses; the heart's hormone answers excess.

elimination.verdict: ADH: rising osmolarity and high sodium. Aldosterone: low salt diet and renin release. Natriuretic peptide: rapid IV fluid.

questions.objective: 2. Explain the role of osmosis, diffusion, filtration, and hormonal regulation in fluid balance.
questions.concept: Hormonal regulation: ADH, aldosterone, natriuretic peptide and RAAS

questions.stem: After a motor vehicle crash, a patient has lost about 1,500 mL of blood. Her blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg, heart rate is 124 per minute and urine output is 12 mL per hour. A new nurse suggests asking for a diuretic to get her kidneys working. Which response by the experienced nurse is appropriate?

options.text: Her kidneys are saving fluid to raise her pressure; she needs volume
options.rationale: Low blood pressure and volume trigger renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone, which constrict vessels and cut urine output. The low output is compensation, so replacing volume, not forcing urine, is the fix.

options.text: The low output is from ADH released for low osmolarity
options.rationale: ADH does reduce urine output, but its trigger is high osmolarity, not low. The response this stem points to starts with low blood pressure and blood volume.

options.text: Natriuretic peptide is holding sodium, so a diuretic makes sense
options.rationale: Natriuretic peptide is released for high volume and pressure, and it excretes sodium and water. It works against what her body needs after blood loss.

options.text: A diuretic will help, since low output means her kidneys are failing
options.rationale: Very low output can signal kidney damage, and it must be reported. Here it follows blood loss and low pressure, and a diuretic would drain the volume her body is trying to keep.

questions.takeaway: After blood loss, the RAAS cuts urine output and constricts vessels to raise volume and pressure; treat the volume, not the urine.
questions.strategy: Low urine output pulls toward the kidneys as the problem. The blood loss and low pressure tip it: her kidneys are compensating on purpose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Link the urine to the cause
steps.detail: Output fell after blood loss with low pressure.
Low pressure starts renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone, which reduce urine output.
ADH answers high osmolarity and natriuretic peptide answers high volume, so neither fits.

elimination.verdict: Her kidneys are compensating; she needs volume.

questions.objective: 2. Explain the role of osmosis, diffusion, filtration, and hormonal regulation in fluid balance.
questions.concept: Hormonal regulation: ADH, aldosterone, natriuretic peptide and RAAS

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with a new ileostomy who has had high output for 2 days and is being treated for dehydration. Which finding does the nurse report to the provider first?

options.text: Heart rate of 98 per minute at rest
options.rationale: A heart rate near 100 can be early compensation for low volume. At this level it is a mild change compared with output under 500 mL per day.

options.text: Fatigue after walking the length of the hallway twice
options.rationale: Fatigue fits many postoperative states and is not specific to a fluid deficit. It does not show organ harm the way scant urine does.

options.text: Thirst and a dry mouth since this morning
options.rationale: Dry mucosa and thirst fit an early deficit and call for fluids. They are less urgent than a urine output showing that the kidneys are short of volume.

options.text: Urine output of 410 mL in 24 hours
options.rationale: Urine under 500 mL per day is the renal finding the nurse treats as concerning in dehydration. It means her kidneys are no longer getting enough volume, so it goes to the provider first.

questions.takeaway: In dehydration, urine output under 500 mL per day is a concerning finding that outranks early signs such as thirst.
questions.strategy: Every option fits dehydration, so the question is which shows the most harm. Urine under 500 mL per day tells you the kidneys are short of volume.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Each option can appear with a deficit.
Thirst and a heart rate of 98 are early compensation.
Output under 500 mL per day means poor kidney perfusion.

elimination.verdict: Report the 410 mL urine output first.

questions.objective: 3. Differentiate dehydration and fluid overload based on causes, assessment findings, and interventions.

questions.stem: Four days after a stroke, a patient has difficulty swallowing. She has dry mucous membranes, a heart rate of 108 per minute and concentrated urine. She is drowsy and coughs when given sips of water. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Obtain a prescription for IV crystalloid replacement
options.rationale: Oral replacement is for patients alert enough to swallow who can tolerate fluids by mouth. She is drowsy and coughs on sips, so fluid has to go by vein to correct her deficit safely.

options.text: Encourage her to drink 240 mL with each meal
options.rationale: Encouraging oral intake is the first line for a mild deficit. She cannot protect her airway with thin liquids right now, so larger volumes add risk without fixing the deficit.

options.text: Offer small sips of water every 15 minutes
options.rationale: Small, frequent sips are a sound approach for mild dehydration in an alert patient. Her coughing on sips shows she cannot swallow safely, so more sips risk aspiration.

options.text: Hold all fluids until her alertness improves
options.rationale: Holding fluids protects her airway but leaves the deficit untreated. Her fast pulse and concentrated urine show she needs replacement now by another route.

questions.takeaway: Oral replacement fits a mild deficit in a patient alert enough to swallow; a patient who cannot swallow safely gets IV crystalloids.
questions.strategy: Oral fluids feel like the gentler first step. Her coughing on sips tips it: the route has to change, not the goal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Oral replacement needs an alert patient who can swallow.
Coughing on sips is an aspiration risk.
Holding fluids leaves her dry, so switch to IV.

elimination.verdict: Obtain IV crystalloid replacement.

questions.objective: 3. Differentiate dehydration and fluid overload based on causes, assessment findings, and interventions.

questions.stem: A patient with large draining wounds from a crush injury has a blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg, heart rate of 112 per minute, urine output of 15 mL per hour and edema in both arms. Albumin is infused. Which finding 2 hours later shows the albumin had the intended effect?

options.text: Arm edema is the same as before the infusion
options.rationale: Edema can take longer to resolve, so no change is not a failure by itself. It also does not show that volume inside the vessels has improved, which is the goal.

options.text: Heart rate rises from 112 to 124 per minute
options.rationale: A faster heart rate means the body is compensating harder for low volume. That points to a worsening deficit, the opposite of the intended effect.

options.text: Urine output rises to 40 mL per hour
options.rationale: Albumin raises oncotic pressure, which holds water in the vessels and expands plasma volume. Better kidney perfusion shows up as more urine, the sign that vascular volume has improved.

options.text: Hematocrit is higher than before the infusion
options.rationale: A rising hematocrit means the blood is more concentrated, as happens with plasma loss. A colloid that expands plasma volume should dilute it instead.

questions.takeaway: Colloids raise oncotic pressure to hold water in the vessels; rising urine output and blood pressure show plasma volume is expanding.
questions.strategy: Edema is the visible problem, so its persistence feels like failure. The goal of a colloid is volume inside the vessels, and urine output measures that.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Albumin holds water in the vessels and expands plasma volume.
More kidney perfusion means more urine.
A faster pulse and a higher hematocrit mean less plasma.

elimination.verdict: Urine output rising to 40 mL per hour.

questions.objective: 3. Differentiate dehydration and fluid overload based on causes, assessment findings, and interventions.

questions.stem: The day after hip replacement surgery, a patient has received 4 L of IV fluid over 24 hours. The nurse notes these findings on the morning assessment. Which finding does the nurse act on first?

options.text: Pitting edema of 3+ in both lower legs
options.rationale: Deep pitting edema confirms excess fluid in the tissues and needs tracking. Fluid in the legs is uncomfortable but does not threaten breathing the way fluid in the lungs does.

options.text: Needed three pillows to breathe comfortably overnight
options.rationale: Needing to sit up to breathe means fluid is collecting in his lungs, an early sign of pulmonary edema. Breathing is threatened before anything else here, so this finding is acted on first.

options.text: Weight up 2.5 kg since the day before surgery
options.rationale: Rapid weight gain is the best measure of how much fluid he has retained, and it confirms overload. It measures the problem, while his breathing at night shows the danger.

options.text: Blood pressure 164/92 mm Hg, up from 132/78 mm Hg
options.rationale: A rise in blood pressure fits a larger blood volume and should be reported. The number looks the most alarming, but it does not show fluid reaching his lungs the way his breathing does.

questions.takeaway: In fluid overload, any sign that breathing is affected, even a quiet one like needing more pillows, comes before louder numbers such as weight or blood pressure.
questions.strategy: The blood pressure and weight are the loudest numbers, and weight is the best indicator of overload. The pillows are a breathing finding, and the ABCs put the lungs first.

steps.detail: Every finding fits fluid overload after 4 L of IV fluid.
Needing three pillows means he cannot breathe lying flat.
Weight and pressure track the overload; the lungs show the threat.

elimination.verdict: Act on his need for three pillows to breathe.

questions.objective: 3. Differentiate dehydration and fluid overload based on causes, assessment findings, and interventions.

questions.stem: A patient with an enterocutaneous fistula has drained large volumes for 3 days and has been NPO for a week. Which findings support a fluid volume deficit? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hematocrit above the reference range
options.rationale: Losing plasma water leaves the same red cells in less fluid. That hemoconcentration raises hemoglobin, hematocrit and osmolarity on the lab report.

options.text: Distended neck veins with the head of the bed at 45 degrees
options.rationale: Distended neck veins mean excess volume in the vessels. They belong to fluid overload, the opposite of what fistula losses produce.

options.text: Crackles in both lung bases
options.rationale: Crackles signal fluid backing into the lungs, a finding of fluid overload. A patient losing fluid through a fistula should have clear lungs unless another problem is present.

options.text: Heart rate 116 per minute with a weak pulse
options.rationale: A fast, weak pulse is the heart compensating for low vascular volume. It is one of the earliest cardiovascular findings of a deficit from ongoing fistula losses.

options.text: Blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg lying and 98/60 mm Hg standing
options.rationale: A drop in pressure on standing is orthostatic hypotension. There is not enough volume in the vessels to hold pressure up when gravity pulls blood toward the legs.

options.text: Urine output of 380 mL in 24 hours, dark amber
options.rationale: Concentrated urine under 500 mL per day is a concerning renal finding in dehydration. The kidneys are saving water because the vessels are short.

options.text: Weight up 1.2 kg since admission
options.rationale: Rapid weight gain is the best indicator of fluid overload. A deficit from days of fistula losses shows up as weight loss instead.

questions.takeaway: A fluid deficit shows as a fast weak pulse, an orthostatic drop, hemoconcentration and scant concentrated urine; neck veins, crackles and weight gain point to overload.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding by direction: too little volume or too much. Every overload finding is a distractor here.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fistula drainage removes extracellular fluid, so expect a deficit.
Fast weak pulse, orthostatic drop, high hematocrit, scant concentrated urine.
Neck vein distention, crackles and weight gain mean overload.

elimination.verdict: Heart rate, orthostatic pressures, hematocrit and urine output.

questions.objective: 3. Differentiate dehydration and fluid overload based on causes, assessment findings, and interventions.

questions.stem: The provider raised a patient's long term corticosteroid dose a month ago, and she has since gained weight and has swelling in both ankles. Which additional finding on her morning assessment supports fluid overload?

options.text: Skin over the sternum that stays tented after a pinch
options.rationale: Tenting over the sternum is a reliable sign of poor turgor from a fluid deficit. A patient holding extra water has full, often puffy tissue, not skin that stays pinched up.

options.text: Thready pulse that weakens each time she stands
options.rationale: A thready pulse that weakens on standing reflects low circulating volume and orthostatic changes. Fluid overload produces a bounding pulse, so this finding points the opposite way.

options.text: Hematocrit higher than the result drawn on admission
options.rationale: A rising hematocrit means the blood has become concentrated, which happens when plasma water is lost. Extra fluid dilutes the blood and lowers the hematocrit instead of raising it.

options.text: Neck veins distended with the head raised 45 degrees
options.rationale: Corticosteroids make the kidneys hold sodium and water, and the extra volume backs up into the veins. Neck veins that stay full with the head raised 45 degrees are a sign of overload.

questions.takeaway: Fluid overload shows as a bounding pulse, high blood pressure, distended neck veins, crackles and rapid weight gain; tenting, a thready pulse and a rising hematocrit point to a deficit.
questions.strategy: Every option is a real fluid finding, so recognizing the finding alone does not help. Read each one as more volume or less volume; only the full neck veins point toward more.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Steroids retain sodium and water, so look for excess volume.
Tenting, a thready pulse and hemoconcentration all show too little volume.
Distended neck veins show extra volume in the veins.

elimination.verdict: Neck veins distended with the head raised 45 degrees.

questions.objective: 3. Differentiate dehydration and fluid overload based on causes, assessment findings, and interventions.

questions.stem: A patient with late phase kidney failure weighed 76.4 kg at 0600 yesterday on the bed scale in a hospital gown. Today assistive personnel report 78.6 kg at 1030 on the standing scale, after breakfast, with him in street clothes and shoes. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Restrict his fluids further until the provider responds
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is part of overload care. Changing it based on a weight that may be off by clothing, shoes and breakfast treats a number that has not been confirmed.

options.text: Record 78.6 kg and compare with tomorrow's weight
options.rationale: Recording an unreliable weight sets a false baseline for every comparison after it. Daily weights only mean something when time, scale and clothing match.

options.text: Report a 2.2 kg gain to the provider now
options.rationale: A gain that fast would be a real concern in kidney failure, so the urge to report is right. The two weights used different scales, times and clothing, so the gain may not be fluid.

options.text: Reweigh him on the bed scale in a gown
options.rationale: Daily weights are compared at the same time, on the same scale and in the same clothing. Today's weight broke all three, so the nurse gets a matching weight before deciding whether he gained fluid.

questions.takeaway: Daily weights are only comparable at the same time, on the same scale and in the same clothing; confirm a surprising gain under matching conditions.
questions.strategy: Rapid weight gain is the best indicator of overload, which makes reporting feel urgent. Count the differences between the two weights before trusting the number.

steps.detail: Different time, scale, clothing and meal status.
Shoes, clothes and breakfast add weight that is not fluid.
Reweigh under matching conditions, then report a true gain.

elimination.verdict: Reweigh him on the bed scale in a gown.

questions.objective: 3. Differentiate dehydration and fluid overload based on causes, assessment findings, and interventions.
questions.concept: Daily weights: same time, scale, clothing

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing a patient for discharge after treatment for fluid overload. His plan includes a loop diuretic, fluid and sodium restriction and daily weights. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I'll drink extra water so the water pill doesn't dry me out."
options.rationale: Worry about drying out is understandable when taking a diuretic. Overload care restricts fluids, so extra water undoes the treatment.

options.text: "I'll weigh myself each morning after I urinate, in the same clothes."
options.rationale: Daily weights at the same time, on the same scale and in the same clothing are the best way to catch fluid gain early. Morning after voiding keeps the conditions alike from day to day.

options.text: "I'll weigh myself on Sundays so I can see the weekly trend."
options.rationale: Tracking a trend is useful, but weekly weights miss gains that build over 2 or 3 days. Rapid weight gain is the earliest sign, so weights are daily.

options.text: "I'll use more salt since the pill makes me lose so much."
options.rationale: A diuretic does increase sodium loss, which makes this sound logical. Water follows sodium, so extra salt makes his body hold water and works against the sodium restriction.

questions.takeaway: After fluid overload, the patient weighs daily under the same conditions and limits fluid and sodium.
questions.strategy: Each wrong statement rests on a believable reason. What tips it is which statement matches daily weights plus fluid and sodium restriction.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Daily weights, fluid restriction and sodium restriction.
Weekly weights miss a fast gain.
Extra water and extra salt both add retained fluid.

elimination.verdict: Weighing each morning after voiding in the same clothes.

questions.objective: 3. Differentiate dehydration and fluid overload based on causes, assessment findings, and interventions.

questions.stem: An 88 year old patient on a medical unit developed fluid overload from IV fluids given during treatment for sepsis and has received a loop diuretic for 3 days. She has lost 3.5 kg, her lungs are clear, her blood pressure is 92/56 mm Hg lying and 78/48 mm Hg sitting, and she is newly confused. The next diuretic dose is due. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Give the dose, since her overload was the reason it was prescribed
options.rationale: The original reason was real, but her findings have changed. Another dose in a patient who is now dry would lower her pressure further and deepen the confusion.

options.text: Give the dose and place her on fall precautions
options.rationale: Fall precautions are right for her orthostatic drop and confusion. Giving the dose still deepens the deficit that is causing both problems.

options.text: Hold the dose and report the findings to the provider
options.rationale: Clear lungs, a large weight loss, a sitting pressure drop and new confusion show she has moved from overload into a deficit. Older adults have less kidney concentrating ability and higher risk from diuretics, so the dose waits for the provider.

options.text: Give the dose and increase her fluid intake to balance it
options.rationale: Matching losses with intake sounds balanced, but it runs two opposing treatments at once. The safer step is to stop the cause of the deficit and get new orders.

questions.takeaway: Clear lungs, weight loss, an orthostatic drop and new confusion in an older adult on a diuretic mean the treatment for overload is now causing a deficit.
questions.strategy: Fall precautions are a correct action, which makes that option tempting. It treats the result while the dose keeps causing it.

steps.detail: Clear lungs and 3.5 kg lost: the overload is gone.
An orthostatic drop and new confusion mean a deficit in an older adult.

steps.action: Drop every option that gives the dose
steps.detail: Three options still deliver the diuretic.

elimination.verdict: Hold the dose and report.

questions.objective: 3. Differentiate dehydration and fluid overload based on causes, assessment findings, and interventions.

questions.stem: On a medical unit, a patient admitted with dehydration from diarrhea reported dizziness when he stood up this morning. He is receiving IV fluids and asks to walk to the bathroom. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Check his blood pressure and pulse while he lies flat
options.rationale: A lying baseline comes first so the nurse can tell whether pressure drops as he rises. He reported dizziness on standing, so orthostatic hypotension is the concern.

options.text: Walk with him to the bathroom, staying at his side
options.rationale: Walking comes last because it carries the greatest fall risk. Staying at his side follows the fall precautions a dehydrated patient needs.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and let him rest sitting up
options.rationale: Slow position changes are a dehydration safety measure. Sitting up in bed first lets his circulation adjust before his legs hang down.

options.text: Help him stand at the bedside with support
options.rationale: Standing comes only after his sitting and dangling pressures hold. Supporting him at the bedside keeps him near the bed if dizziness returns.

options.text: Have him dangle his legs and recheck his blood pressure
options.rationale: Dangling adds the next gravity challenge while he is still safe on the bed. A recheck here shows whether it is safe to stand before he puts weight on his legs.

questions.takeaway: A dehydrated patient changes position in stages with pressure checks, because orthostatic hypotension makes falls likely.
questions.strategy: The pull is to help him straight to the bathroom because he asked. Each stage adds gravity a little at a time, and the baseline has to come before any of it.

steps.detail: A lying pressure gives later readings meaning.
Sit, then dangle, then stand.
Walking carries the most fall risk.

elimination.verdict: Lying vital signs, sit up, dangle and recheck, stand, walk with him.

questions.objective: 3. Differentiate dehydration and fluid overload based on causes, assessment findings, and interventions.
questions.concept: Dehydration safety: slow position changes and falls

questions.stem: At the start of the shift, the nurse receives report on four patients on a medical unit. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: A man with a sodium of 128 mEq/L who is newly disoriented
options.rationale: Low sodium lets water into cells, and the brain has little room to swell inside the rigid skull. New confusion is a cerebral change that can progress to seizures, so he is seen first.

options.text: A man receiving IV fluid for dehydration who has a dry mouth
options.rationale: Dry mouth is expected in dehydration, and his treatment is already running. It is an expected finding that does not point to new harm.

options.text: A woman with a sodium of 147 mEq/L who is asking for water
options.rationale: Her sodium is slightly high, and thirst is the body's normal response to it. She is alert enough to ask, and a drink helps correct it, so she is less urgent.

options.text: A woman on bed rest with her usual 1+ ankle edema
options.rationale: Edema needs ongoing assessment, but this finding matches her usual baseline. An expected, stable finding can wait while a new neurologic change is assessed.

questions.takeaway: New confusion in hyponatremia is a cerebral change that comes first, because the brain swells within a rigid skull.
questions.strategy: Two patients have abnormal sodium values. What tips it is new versus expected: only one has a mental status change that is new.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Baseline edema and dry mouth in dehydration are expected.
Thirst at 147 mEq/L is a normal response; disorientation at 128 mEq/L is new.
Swelling inside the skull can progress to seizures.

elimination.verdict: See the man with a sodium of 128 mEq/L who is newly disoriented.

questions.objective: 4, 5, 6 (sodium). Compare hyponatremia and hypernatremia; recognize key assessment findings and safety concerns; identify priority nursing interventions and treatments.

questions.stem: After 3 days of vomiting, a patient who takes a diuretic has a serum sodium of 127 mEq/L. Her pulse is 114 per minute and thready, her blood pressure drops when she sits up and her mucous membranes are dry. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Extra plain water by mouth
options.rationale: Extra water does help a deficit, but plain water has no sodium and would dilute her level further. She is also vomiting, so oral intake will not stay down.

options.text: Fluid restriction of 1,000 mL per day
options.rationale: Fluid restriction treats hyponatremia from excess water, such as SIADH. She is short of fluid, so restriction would deepen the deficit and her low pressure.

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride infusion
options.rationale: Vomiting and a diuretic are actual sodium losses, and her thready pulse and orthostatic drop show a fluid deficit. Hyponatremia with a fluid deficit is treated with IV saline.

options.text: A vasopressin antagonist
options.rationale: Vasopressin antagonists treat hyponatremia with fluid excess by helping the kidneys shed water. She has a deficit, so removing more water would worsen her volume.

questions.takeaway: Determine the cause first: hyponatremia with a fluid deficit gets IV saline, while hyponatremia with excess water gets restriction or a vasopressin antagonist.
questions.strategy: Fluid restriction is the treatment students remember for low sodium. The thready pulse tips it: she is short of fluid, so the fix replaces sodium and volume.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vomiting and a diuretic are actual losses.
A thready pulse and orthostatic drop mean a deficit.
A deficit gets saline; restriction and vasopressin antagonists are for excess.

elimination.verdict: IV 0.9% sodium chloride.

questions.objective: 4, 5, 6 (sodium). Compare hyponatremia and hypernatremia; recognize key assessment findings and safety concerns; identify priority nursing interventions and treatments.

questions.stem: On an inpatient psychiatric unit, a patient has been drinking large amounts of water throughout the day. He reports a headache, is slow to answer questions and has had muscle weakness since this morning. His weight is up 1.8 kg from 2 days ago, his pulse is bounding and his serum sodium is 123 mEq/L. Which plan of care does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Fluid restriction with neurologic checks each shift
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is the right treatment for his water excess. With confusion and a sodium of 123 mEq/L, checking him once a shift leaves him unprotected if a seizure starts.

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride with seizure precautions
options.rationale: Seizure precautions are right for him, and saline treats hyponatremia when the patient is low on volume. His bounding pulse and weight gain show excess water, so saline would add to the overload.

options.text: Oral fluids with salty snacks between meals
options.rationale: Extra oral sodium and fluid fit hyponatremia from real sodium loss in a patient who is short on volume. He has too much water, and more fluid would dilute his sodium further.

options.text: Fluid restriction with seizure precautions
options.rationale: Weight gain and a bounding pulse show his low sodium comes from water he drank, so restriction treats the cause. His headache and slowed answers signal brain swelling, so seizure precautions protect him.

questions.takeaway: When hyponatremia comes with weight gain and a bounding pulse, the problem is excess water: restrict fluids and protect the brain with seizure precautions.
questions.strategy: Saline with seizure precautions is half right, which makes it tempting. Volume status decides the type of hyponatremia, and his bounding pulse and weight gain rule out adding fluid.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight up 1.8 kg and a bounding pulse: dilutional, from excess water.
Take water away; do not add sodium or fluid.
Headache and slowed thinking at 123 mEq/L call for seizure precautions.

elimination.verdict: Fluid restriction with seizure precautions.

questions.objective: 4, 5, 6 (sodium). Compare hyponatremia and hypernatremia; recognize key assessment findings and safety concerns; identify priority nursing interventions and treatments.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure has dilutional hyponatremia with a serum sodium of 125 mEq/L and new confusion. She is started on a vasopressin antagonist. Which finding 24 hours later shows the treatment is working?

options.text: She answers questions about place and time correctly
options.rationale: The drug helps her kidneys shed extra water, so sodium rises and brain cells lose the water they took on. Clearing confusion shows the cerebral effect of low sodium is easing.

options.text: Her serum sodium is now 123 mEq/L
options.rationale: A fall from 125 to 123 mEq/L means the dilution is getting worse. Treatment that works moves the level up toward the 135 mEq/L minimum.

options.text: Her weight is 1 kg higher than on admission
options.rationale: Weight gain means more retained water, which would dilute her sodium further. The drug should bring her weight down as water leaves.

options.text: Her urine output is lower than it was yesterday
options.rationale: Less urine would mean she is holding more water, the reverse of what the drug is meant to do. Success shows as more urine and a rising sodium.

questions.takeaway: A vasopressin antagonist treats hyponatremia from water excess; success shows as more urine, falling weight, rising sodium and clearing confusion.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option is a change in the wrong direction. Ask what removing extra water would do to urine, weight, sodium and the brain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Help the kidneys excrete extra water.
More urine, less weight, higher sodium, clearer thinking.
Only the orientation finding moves the right way.

elimination.verdict: She answers questions about place and time correctly.

questions.objective: 4, 5, 6 (sodium). Compare hyponatremia and hypernatremia; recognize key assessment findings and safety concerns; identify priority nursing interventions and treatments.
questions.concept: Vasopressin antagonist for hyponatremia with fluid excess

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the histories of four patients on a medical unit. Which patient does the nurse monitor most closely for hypernatremia?

options.text: A patient with SIADH after a head injury
options.rationale: SIADH does change sodium, which makes it tempting. The extra ADH makes the kidneys hold water, which dilutes the blood and lowers sodium below 135 mEq/L rather than raising it.

options.text: A patient with hyperaldosteronism and high blood pressure
options.rationale: Aldosterone makes the kidneys hold on to sodium, and too much of it keeps adding sodium to the blood. Sodium gain is one route to a level above 145 mEq/L, so this patient needs the closest watch.

options.text: A patient receiving only D5W IV for 3 days
options.rationale: D5W adds water with no sodium once its dextrose is used. Three days of only free water dilutes the blood and pushes the sodium down, not up.

options.text: A patient with heart failure who is retaining fluid
options.rationale: Heart failure does hold sodium, so it can look like a sodium gain. It holds even more water, which dilutes the sodium and causes dilutional hyponatremia instead.

questions.takeaway: Hypernatremia comes from sodium gain or water loss, such as hyperaldosteronism, excess sodium intake, fever and dehydration; SIADH, heart failure and free water dilute sodium instead.
questions.strategy: Every patient has a change in sodium balance, so the question is direction. Ask whether each condition adds sodium or adds water; heart failure tempts because it retains both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hypernatremia comes from sodium gain or water loss.
SIADH, heart failure and free water all add water and lower sodium.
Excess aldosterone retains sodium.

elimination.verdict: A patient with hyperaldosteronism and high blood pressure.

questions.objective: 4, 5, 6 (sodium). Compare hyponatremia and hypernatremia; recognize key assessment findings and safety concerns; identify priority nursing interventions and treatments.

questions.scenario: The nurse is assessing a patient who has vomited and had diarrhea for 2 days and cannot keep oral fluids down. Her mucous membranes are dry, heart rate is 112 per minute with a weak pulse, blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg lying and 84/52 mm Hg sitting, and her urine is dark. Serum sodium is 139 mEq/L, and hematocrit is above the reference range.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Give the prescribed antiemetic
options.rationale: Treating the cause is part of dehydration care, and vomiting is driving her loss. Stopping it reduces ongoing loss and may let her take fluids by mouth later.

options.text: Restrict her fluids to 1 L per day
options.rationale: Fluid restriction treats fluid overload and dilutional hyponatremia. She has lost fluid, so limiting intake works against the replacement she needs.

options.text: Request a loop diuretic for her dark, scant urine
options.rationale: A loop diuretic removes water and sodium, which treats fluid overload. In a patient who is already dry, it would deepen the deficit and drop her pressure further.

options.text: Infuse the prescribed IV 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: She cannot keep oral fluids down and has orthostatic changes, so replacement goes by vein. An isotonic crystalloid replaces the extracellular fluid she has lost.

options.text: Vascular dehydration from a plasma shift
options.rationale: A plasma to interstitial shift leaves swelling with low vascular volume and no true loss. She has true losses from vomiting and diarrhea and no edema.

options.text: Fluid overload
options.rationale: Overload brings a bounding pulse, high blood pressure and weight gain. She has a weak, fast pulse and a pressure drop on sitting, the opposite pattern.

options.text: Hypernatremia from water loss
options.rationale: Hypernatremia needs a sodium above 145 mEq/L, often with agitation or twitching. Her sodium is in range, so the loss is not water alone.

options.text: Isotonic dehydration
options.rationale: Her sodium is normal at 139 mEq/L, so she has lost water and sodium together from the extracellular fluid. This is the most common type, and it fits vomiting and diarrhea.

options.text: Hourly urine output
options.rationale: Dark, scant urine shows her kidneys are saving water. Rising output with lighter color shows that replacement is reaching her kidneys.

options.text: Deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Reflex changes go with electrolyte problems such as hyponatremia. Her sodium is normal, so reflexes do not track her main problem.

options.text: Capillary blood glucose
options.rationale: Nothing in her history points to a glucose problem. Checking it does not show whether her fluid deficit is correcting.

options.text: Orthostatic blood pressure and pulse
options.rationale: The pressure drop on sitting is one of her clearest deficit findings. When it closes, her vessels hold enough volume for upright positions and her fall risk drops.

questions.takeaway: Vomiting and diarrhea with a normal sodium is isotonic dehydration: replace with isotonic IV fluid, treat the cause and track orthostatic pressures and urine output.
questions.strategy: The normal sodium is the deciding cue: it rules out hypernatremia and makes this an isotonic loss. Restriction and diuretics belong to the opposite problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: At 139 mEq/L the loss is water and sodium together.
Isotonic IV fluid replaces the loss, and an antiemetic slows it.
Orthostatic pressures and urine output show whether volume is returning.

elimination.verdict: Isotonic dehydration: IV 0.9% sodium chloride and an antiemetic; monitor orthostatic vital signs and urine output.

questions.objective: 3. Differentiate dehydration and fluid overload based on causes, assessment findings, and interventions.

questions.stem: In the emergency department, a patient who was found at home after 3 days without water had a serum sodium of 158 mEq/L, agitation and twitching. Hypotonic IV fluid has run for 5 hours, and his sodium is now 142 mEq/L. He has a new headache, is harder to rouse and has vomited once. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the hypotonic infusion and notify the provider
