options.rationale: A drop of 16 mEq/L in 5 hours is rapid, and headache, drowsiness and vomiting point to water rushing into brain cells. Stopping the fluid that drives the shift comes before anything else.

options.text: Increase the rate to replace the fluid lost in vomiting
options.rationale: He did lose some fluid, which makes replacement sound logical. A faster hypotonic rate pushes even more water into brain cells that are already swelling.

options.text: Give an antiemetic and recheck his sodium in 4 hours
options.rationale: Treating vomiting eases a symptom, and a later recheck is reasonable. Both leave the hypotonic fluid running while his brain shows signs of swelling.

options.text: Continue the infusion, since his sodium is now in range
options.rationale: A normal sodium looks like success, but the speed of correction matters as much as the number. Lowering sodium gradually protects the brain from cerebral edema.

questions.takeaway: Hypernatremia is corrected gradually; a fast drop with new headache or drowsiness signals cerebral edema, so stop the hypotonic fluid and report.
questions.strategy: A sodium back in range invites the conclusion that treatment worked. The new neurologic signs tip it: the correction was too fast.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 158 to 142 mEq/L in 5 hours is fast.
Headache, drowsiness and vomiting point to brain swelling.
The hypotonic fluid is driving the shift.

elimination.verdict: Stop the hypotonic infusion and notify the provider.

questions.objective: 4, 5, 6 (sodium). Compare hyponatremia and hypernatremia; recognize key assessment findings and safety concerns; identify priority nursing interventions and treatments.
questions.concept: Hypernatremia treatment: restore volume, lower sodium gradually

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient receiving continuous tube feedings who has had large watery stools for 3 days, and his free water flushes were missed over the weekend. His serum sodium is 156 mEq/L. He is lethargic, his blood pressure is 80/46 mm Hg, his pulse is 128 per minute and weak, and his urine output is 10 mL per hour. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate first?

options.text: IV 3% sodium chloride infusion
options.rationale: A 3% solution is hypertonic and treats severe hyponatremia. Given here, it adds sodium to a level already above the 145 mEq/L maximum and pulls more water out of his cells.

options.text: IV D5W at a rapid rate
options.rationale: Free water is the eventual goal in hypernatremia, so D5W is a reasonable later choice. Run fast, it lowers sodium too quickly and risks cerebral edema, and little of it stays in his vessels to raise pressure.

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride infusion
options.rationale: His low pressure, weak fast pulse and scant urine show his vessels are critically short, so circulating volume comes first. Isotonic saline stays in the extracellular fluid and restores pressure without dropping his sodium suddenly.

options.text: IV furosemide
options.rationale: A diuretic has a place in hypernatremia when the cause is kidney related. His problem is water lost in stool, so removing more fluid would deepen his shock.

questions.takeaway: Hypernatremia with low blood pressure and scant urine gets isotonic saline first to restore volume; free water and gradual sodium correction follow once he is stable.
questions.strategy: D5W tempts because free water is the goal in hypernatremia. The blood pressure of 80/46 mm Hg tips it: restore circulation first with a fluid that stays in the vessels.

steps.detail: Low pressure, weak fast pulse and 10 mL per hour of urine mean poor perfusion.
3% saline raises sodium; furosemide removes volume he does not have.
Rapid D5W drops sodium too fast and leaves the vessels; isotonic saline stays in them.

elimination.verdict: IV 0.9% sodium chloride infusion.

questions.objective: 4, 5, 6 (sodium). Compare hyponatremia and hypernatremia; recognize key assessment findings and safety concerns; identify priority nursing interventions and treatments.
questions.concept: Hypernatremia treatment: restore volume, lower sodium gradually
questions.note: The class material is internally inconsistent on hypernatremia fluids: the key points summary says to treat with isotonic fluids and restrict sodium, while the intervention content says the goal is free water and lists hypotonic solutions beside 0.9% NaCl. The textbook and current practice give isotonic saline first only when hypernatremia comes with hypotension or shock, then hypotonic free water to lower sodium gradually. This stem makes the patient unstable, so both sources support isotonic saline here; on the NCLEX, a stable patient with water loss hypernatremia gets hypotonic free water instead.

questions.stem: A patient's daughter is taking her 81 year old father home after treatment for hypernatremia caused by poor fluid intake. Which instruction does the nurse give the daughter?

options.text: Check the skin on the back of his hand daily for tenting
options.rationale: Checking turgor shows thought about hydration. Skin on an older adult's hand tents from age alone, so turgor is checked over the sternum.

options.text: Offer him water on a schedule, even if he is not thirsty
options.rationale: Older adults have a decreased thirst reflex, so waiting for him to ask leaves him dry. Increasing water intake on a schedule helps keep hypernatremia from coming back.

options.text: Offer him water whenever he says he feels thirsty
options.rationale: Responding to thirst works for younger adults. His thirst reflex is blunted with age, so thirst comes late or not at all.

options.text: Add salt to his meals to help him hold on to fluid
options.rationale: Water does follow sodium, which makes this sound helpful. Extra salt raises his sodium further, and the plan restricts dietary sodium if needed.

questions.takeaway: Older adults have a blunted thirst reflex, so water is offered on a schedule rather than when they ask.
questions.strategy: Offering water when he is thirsty sounds patient centered. Age blunts thirst, so the cue that plan relies on is missing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Thirst is decreased in older adults.
Thirst and hand turgor both mislead at his age.
Extra salt raises an already high level.

elimination.verdict: Offer water on a schedule.

questions.objective: Special population: older adults (fluid balance changes with aging).
questions.concept: Decreased thirst reflex in older adults

questions.stem: An 86 year old patient is brought to the clinic by her son, who says she became confused yesterday. She takes a diuretic, an antihypertensive and a daily laxative, and she says she is not thirsty. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Accept that she is not thirsty and screen her memory
options.rationale: A memory screen describes the confusion without looking for its cause. Thirst is decreased in older adults, so her denial does not rule out a deficit.

options.text: Tell her son to stop all three medicines for now
options.rationale: Her medications do raise her risk, and they may need review. Stopping them without assessment or a provider's decision skips finding out what is wrong now.

options.text: Arrange a follow up visit if the confusion lasts a week
options.rationale: Waiting a week treats new confusion as minor. In an older adult it may signal an imbalance that is worsening today.

options.text: Check her lying and standing blood pressure and pulse
options.rationale: In an older adult, confusion may be the first sign of a fluid or electrolyte imbalance, and all three of her medications raise that risk. These checks look for a deficit before anything else is decided.

questions.takeaway: New confusion in an older adult may be the first sign of a fluid or electrolyte imbalance; assess for it, and do not rely on thirst.
questions.strategy: She denies thirst, which pulls toward ruling out dehydration. Thirst is blunted at her age, and the medication list is the risk cue.

steps.detail: A diuretic, an antihypertensive and a laxative all raise imbalance risk.
Older adults have a decreased thirst reflex.
Vital signs look for a deficit now.

elimination.verdict: Check lying and standing blood pressure and pulse.

questions.objective: Special population: older adults (fluid balance changes with aging).
questions.concept: Confusion as the first sign in older adults

questions.stem: In the emergency department, a 77 year old patient has had poor oral intake for 2 days. Skin pinched on the back of his hand stays tented. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Document the tenting as confirmed dehydration
options.rationale: Tenting can point to a deficit, but on an older adult's hand it may only reflect age. Recording it as confirmed would base his care on an unreliable site.

options.text: Check skin turgor over his sternum
options.rationale: Older adults lose skin elasticity, so hand skin can tent from age alone. Turgor is assessed at the sternum in older adults, which gives a finding the nurse can trust.

options.text: Repeat the pinch on his other hand to compare
options.rationale: Comparing sides sounds thorough, but both hands have the same age related loss of elasticity. A second hand gives the same unreliable result.

options.text: Ask whether he feels thirsty to confirm the finding
options.rationale: Thirst is decreased in older adults, so it cannot confirm or rule out a deficit. Asking swaps one unreliable cue for another.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, assess skin turgor over the sternum; tenting on the hand may reflect age rather than dehydration.
questions.strategy: His age changes where a routine technique is done. Two options keep using an unreliable site, and one uses an unreliable cue.

steps.detail: Both hand options use skin that loses elasticity with age.
Thirst is blunted in older adults.
The sternum gives a trustworthy turgor finding.

elimination.verdict: Check turgor over the sternum.

questions.objective: Special population: older adults (fluid balance changes with aging).
questions.concept: Skin turgor at the sternum in older adults

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that support hypernatremia or its likely cause.
questions.nursesNote: 0700 Admitted 84 year old woman from her long term care facility after 4 days of poor oral intake. Staff report she rarely asks for water. Alert and calm at baseline per staff. Now agitated, pulling at her gown and confused to place. Fine muscle twitching noted in both hands. Temperature 37.2°C. Mucous membranes dry and sticky. Lung sounds clear in all fields. Serum sodium 154 mEq/L. Ankles without edema.

segments.text: Staff report she rarely asks for water.
segments.rationale: Older adults have a decreased thirst reflex, so she does not ask for water even as she dries out. Low intake with weak thirst leads directly to water loss and a rising sodium.

segments.text: Alert and calm at baseline per staff.
segments.rationale: Her usual calm alertness is the baseline, not a sign of illness. It matters because it shows that the agitation and confusion that follow are new.

segments.text: Now agitated, pulling at her gown and confused to place.
segments.rationale: Hypernatremia causes increased excitability, which appears as agitation and confusion. Water leaving brain cells drives these changes, and they can progress to lethargy and coma.

segments.text: Fine muscle twitching noted in both hands.
segments.rationale: Twitching reflects the increased excitability that high sodium causes in nerves and muscles. Left untreated, it can progress to weakness.

segments.text: Temperature 37.2°C.
segments.rationale: A temperature of 37.2°C is within the normal range, so fever is not adding to her water loss. Her loss comes from poor intake instead.

segments.text: Mucous membranes dry and sticky.
segments.rationale: Dry, sticky mucosa shows a water deficit, the usual source of a high sodium. It ties her low intake to the lab value.

segments.text: Lung sounds clear in all fields.
segments.rationale: Clear lungs argue against fluid overload and are an expected normal finding. They do not support a high sodium.

segments.text: Serum sodium 154 mEq/L
segments.rationale: A sodium of 154 mEq/L is above the 145 mEq/L maximum. It confirms hypernatremia and explains why water is leaving her cells.

segments.text: Ankles without edema.
segments.rationale: No edema fits a deficit rather than an excess. The absence of swelling is a normal finding that does not point to hypernatremia.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, weak thirst and poor intake lead to hypernatremia, which shows as agitation, confusion, twitching and dry mucosa.
questions.strategy: The normal temperature and clear lungs are true findings but do not support the problem. Keep the cues that show water loss and increased excitability.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Poor intake and a weak thirst reflex.
Agitation, confusion and twitching.
Dry mucosa and a sodium of 154 mEq/L.

elimination.verdict: Rarely asks for water, agitation and confusion, twitching, dry mucosa and the sodium of 154 mEq/L.

questions.objective: 4, 5, 6 (sodium). Compare hyponatremia and hypernatremia; recognize key assessment findings and safety concerns; identify priority nursing interventions and treatments.
questions.concept: Hypernatremia findings in an older adult

questions.stem: On an observation unit, a landscaper is receiving IV fluids after a day of profuse sweating while working in the heat. At admission her blood pressure dropped and she felt faint when she stood. She has now received 1 L of fluid and asks to use the bathroom. Which action by assistive personnel requires the nurse to step in?

options.text: Raises the head of the bed slowly before she stands
options.rationale: Raising the head of the bed slowly lets her circulation adjust before she bears weight. This is the slow position change that prevents a fall from orthostatic hypotension, so it is correct.

options.text: Measures her blood pressure lying, sitting and then standing
options.rationale: Measuring lying, sitting and standing pressures can look like nursing assessment, but taking vital signs is within the role of assistive personnel. The nurse interprets the readings, so this needs no correction.

options.text: Keeps the bed in its lowest position with the call light in reach
options.rationale: A low bed and a call light within reach are standard fall precautions for a patient who has had orthostatic dizziness. Both are appropriate, so the nurse does not need to intervene.

options.text: Lets her walk there alone since her pressure in bed was normal
options.rationale: A normal pressure in bed does not show how her pressure responds to standing, and she nearly fainted on standing at admission. Walking alone skips the slow position change and support she still needs.

questions.takeaway: In dehydration, a normal blood pressure in bed does not clear a patient to stand and walk alone; slow position changes and support continue until standing is safe.
questions.strategy: Measuring orthostatic pressures looks like the action outside the role of assistive personnel, but taking vital signs is within it. The unsafe action is the one that treats a normal pressure in bed as proof she can walk alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the unsafe action.
Taking vital signs, even lying and standing, is within the role of assistive personnel.
A normal pressure in bed says nothing about her response to standing.

elimination.verdict: Step in when she is allowed to walk alone.

questions.concept: Dehydration safety: slow position changes and falls
questions.objective: 3. Differentiate dehydration and fluid overload based on causes, assessment findings, and interventions.

questions.stem: In the intensive care unit, the nurse is precepting a new graduate caring for a patient who has generalized edema and a low blood pressure the day after a long spinal surgery. Albumin has been prescribed. Which statement by the new graduate requires correction?

options.text: The albumin will rehydrate her cells faster than saline would
options.rationale: Albumin stays in the bloodstream and raises oncotic pressure, so its effect is on plasma volume, not cell water. Crystalloids are the fluids that replace water inside cells and in the extracellular space.

options.text: Her swelling is fluid that has shifted out of her bloodstream
options.rationale: Edema with a low blood pressure after a long surgery shows plasma that has moved into the tissues rather than water lost from the body. The statement is accurate and needs no correction.

options.text: The albumin should pull fluid from her tissues back into her vessels
options.rationale: It can sound wrong to expect fluid to leave swollen tissue, but higher oncotic pressure in the vessels draws water back from the interstitial space. That is the intended effect, so the statement is accurate.

options.text: Her urine output will tell us whether the albumin is working
options.rationale: A rising urine output shows the kidneys are receiving more blood volume, which is the goal of a colloid. Using it to judge the albumin is accurate, so this statement needs no correction.

questions.takeaway: Colloids such as albumin raise oncotic pressure and expand plasma volume; crystalloids are the fluids that replace water in the cells and the extracellular space.
questions.strategy: The statement about pulling fluid out of swollen tissue sounds backward, so students flag it. It describes oncotic pressure correctly; the error is crediting albumin with rehydrating cells.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the statement that is wrong.
Albumin raises oncotic pressure and holds water in the vessels.
Only the claim about cell water assigns albumin a crystalloid job.

elimination.verdict: Correct the claim that albumin rehydrates cells.

questions.objective: 3. Differentiate dehydration and fluid overload based on causes, assessment findings, and interventions.

questions.stem: During a home health visit, the nurse sees an older patient who has had a fever for 2 days and has drunk very little. His serum sodium yesterday was 153 mEq/L, and his wife says that last night he was restless and his hands twitched. Which finding today shows the imbalance has reached a later stage?

options.text: Says his mouth feels dry and sticky
options.rationale: A dry, sticky mouth fits the water loss behind his high sodium. It can be present at any point in the deficit and does not show the brain changes moving forward.

options.text: Knows his wife and where he is
options.rationale: Knowing his wife and his location shows his thinking is still intact. That points away from the later stage, which brings lethargy and then coma rather than clear orientation.

options.text: Lies quietly and is hard to keep awake
options.rationale: High sodium first irritates the brain, causing agitation and twitching, then progresses to lethargy and coma. A quiet patient who is hard to keep awake has moved past the restless stage, not recovered from it.

options.text: Snaps at his wife and will not stay in bed
options.rationale: Irritability and restlessness are true effects of high sodium, and more of them can look like worsening. They belong to the early, excitable stage his wife already described, so they do not show progression.

questions.takeaway: High sodium moves from agitation and twitching to lethargy, weakness and coma, so a patient who becomes quiet and drowsy is worsening, not settling.
questions.strategy: The quiet, drowsy patient looks calmer than the restless one, which tempts students to read it as improvement. High sodium progresses from excitation to depression, so the drowsy finding is the later stage.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Agitation and twitching come first; lethargy and weakness follow.
Restlessness and twitching are the early stage already present.
Only drowsiness shows a move to the later stage.

elimination.verdict: Lies quietly and is hard to keep awake.

questions.concept: Hypernatremia findings in an older adult
questions.objective: 4, 5, 6 (sodium). Compare hyponatremia and hypernatremia; recognize key assessment findings and safety concerns; identify priority nursing interventions and treatments.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews arterial blood gas results for four patients on a medical unit. Which result does the nurse report as outside the normal range?

options.text: pH 7.45, PaCO2 37 mm Hg, HCO3 25 mEq/L
options.rationale: A pH of 7.45 is the upper limit of normal, not alkalosis. Alkalosis begins only when the pH rises above 7.45, and the other two values are normal.

options.text: pH 7.36, PaCO2 45 mm Hg, HCO3 25 mEq/L
options.rationale: Every value here sits inside the normal limits, even though the PaCO2 is at the top of 35 to 45 mm Hg. A value at the boundary of the range still counts as normal.

options.text: pH 7.43, PaCO2 35 mm Hg, HCO3 22 mEq/L
options.rationale: The PaCO2 is at the bottom of its range and the HCO3 is at the bottom of 22 to 26 mEq/L. Both are still normal, and the pH is well inside 7.35 to 7.45.

options.text: pH 7.34, PaCO2 47 mm Hg, HCO3 25 mEq/L
options.rationale: Normal pH stops at 7.35, so 7.34 is acidosis, and the PaCO2 of 47 mm Hg is above the 45 mm Hg limit. This result needs to be reported and interpreted further.

questions.takeaway: Normal ABG values are pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaCO2 35 to 45 mm Hg and HCO3 22 to 26 mEq/L, and a value on the boundary is still normal.
questions.strategy: Boundary values tempt students to flag the normal results. Only one panel crosses a limit: a pH below 7.35 with a PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only 7.34 falls outside; 7.45 is the upper limit, not beyond it.
PaCO2 35 and 45 mm Hg and HCO3 22 mEq/L are the edges of normal, still inside.
PaCO2 47 mm Hg is above 45 mm Hg, matching the low pH.

elimination.verdict: pH 7.34 with PaCO2 47 mm Hg is the only result outside the normal range.

questions.objective: Explain how acids, bases, and buffers influence blood pH.

questions.scenario: At the start of the shift, the nurse reviews six ABG results.
questions.stem: For each result, indicate the level of compensation.

rows.text: pH 7.37, PaCO2 58 mm Hg, HCO3 32 mEq/L
rows.rationale: Both PaCO2 and HCO3 are abnormal, yet the pH has returned inside 7.35 to 7.45. A normal pH with two abnormal values means compensation is complete.

rows.text: pH 7.43, PaCO2 27 mm Hg, HCO3 17 mEq/L
rows.rationale: The PaCO2 and the HCO3 are both well outside their ranges. The pH is back inside 7.35 to 7.45, which defines full compensation even though both values remain abnormal.

rows.text: pH 7.31, PaCO2 54 mm Hg, HCO3 26 mEq/L
rows.rationale: The pH and the PaCO2 are both abnormal, so this is respiratory acidosis. The HCO3 is still inside 22 to 26 mEq/L, so the kidneys have not started compensating.

rows.text: pH 7.52, PaCO2 39 mm Hg, HCO3 31 mEq/L
rows.rationale: The high HCO3 explains the high pH, so this is metabolic alkalosis. The PaCO2 is still normal, so the lungs have not begun to compensate.

rows.text: pH 7.48, PaCO2 28 mm Hg, HCO3 20 mEq/L
rows.rationale: The low PaCO2 explains the high pH, so this is respiratory alkalosis. The HCO3 has dropped below 22 mEq/L in compensation, but the pH is still above 7.45.

rows.text: pH 7.33, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, HCO3 15 mEq/L
rows.rationale: The low HCO3 explains the low pH, so this is metabolic acidosis. The PaCO2 is also abnormal because the lungs are compensating, but the pH is still below 7.35.

questions.takeaway: Uncompensated: the other system is normal. Partial: both systems abnormal and the pH still abnormal. Full: both abnormal but the pH back to normal.
questions.strategy: A normal pH tempts students to call the gas normal. When the pH is normal, look at PaCO2 and HCO3 before deciding; two abnormal values with a normal pH is full compensation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Normal pH with abnormal values points to full compensation.

steps.action: If the pH is abnormal, check the other system
steps.detail: Normal other value: uncompensated. Abnormal other value: partial.

steps.action: Confirm the other value moves to offset
steps.detail: Compensation moves the pH back toward normal.

elimination.verdict: Two uncompensated, two partial, two full.

questions.objective: Describe respiratory and renal regulation of acid base balance.

questions.stem: At the finish of a long distance race, a patient collapses and is resting in the medical tent. Heavy exercise has flooded the blood with acid. A student nurse asks what limits the change in pH during the first seconds. Which response by the nurse is correct?

options.text: The kidneys excrete hydrogen ions as ammonium
options.rationale: Ammonium formation is a real renal method of trapping hydrogen ions for excretion. The kidneys take hours to days and about 24 to 48 hours to fully respond.

options.text: Chemical buffers bind the extra hydrogen ions
options.rationale: Chemical buffers act within seconds, and bicarbonate is the main buffer of the extracellular fluid. They bind free hydrogen ions before the lungs or kidneys have time to respond.

options.text: Hemoglobin releases hydrogen ions into the plasma
options.rationale: Hemoglobin is a protein buffer, but it works in the opposite direction. It binds excess hydrogen ions inside red blood cells, pulling them out of the blood.

options.text: Faster, deeper breathing blows off carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Breathing does lower carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions, and it starts quickly. It still takes minutes, so it follows the chemical buffers that act in seconds.

questions.takeaway: Chemical buffers act in seconds, the lungs in minutes and the kidneys over hours to days, though the kidneys are the most powerful.
questions.strategy: Faster breathing is the response students picture first, but it is minutes away. The words first seconds point to the chemical buffers.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: First seconds rules out any organ response.
Buffers in seconds, lungs in minutes, kidneys in hours to days.

steps.action: Check the direction of each claim
steps.detail: Hemoglobin binds hydrogen ions; it does not release them into plasma.

elimination.verdict: Chemical buffers such as bicarbonate act first.

questions.objective: Explain how acids, bases, and buffers influence blood pH.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient in septic shock who has a respiratory rate of 34 per minute with deep, regular breaths. ABG results: pH 7.27, PaCO2 29 mm Hg, HCO3 13 mEq/L. A new nurse suggests the patient has a respiratory problem causing the acid base change. Which reply is correct?

options.text: The low HCO3 is the cause; the lungs are compensating
options.rationale: The HCO3 is low and moves with the low pH, so the problem is metabolic. The deep, rapid breathing is the lungs blowing off carbon dioxide to raise the pH.

options.text: The fast breathing is the cause, so the patient has respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: A low PaCO2 does point toward alkalosis when breathing is the primary problem. This pH is 7.27, so the patient is acidotic, and the low CO2 cannot be the cause.

options.text: The kidneys will correct this within minutes by excreting acid
options.rationale: The kidneys can excrete acid and are the most powerful regulator. They are slow, needing 24 to 48 hours, so they are not the response the nurse sees now.

options.text: The lungs are retaining carbon dioxide to buffer the extra acid
options.rationale: Retaining carbon dioxide would add acid and push the pH lower. The PaCO2 of 29 mm Hg shows the lungs are getting rid of carbon dioxide, not keeping it.

questions.takeaway: When the problem is metabolic, the lungs compensate within minutes; in metabolic acidosis the patient breathes faster and deeper to blow off CO2.
questions.strategy: The rapid breathing tempts students to call this a respiratory problem. Match the pH to the value that moves with it: a low HCO3 with a low pH is metabolic.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 7.27 is acidosis, which rules out any alkalosis answer.

steps.action: Find which value explains the pH
steps.detail: HCO3 13 mEq/L is low with the low pH; metabolic equal.
The lungs are blowing off CO2 to compensate.

elimination.verdict: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.

questions.objective: Describe respiratory and renal regulation of acid base balance.
questions.concept: Respiratory compensation for a metabolic problem

questions.stem: Six hours after admission with three fractured ribs, a patient is taking shallow breaths because of pain. ABG results: pH 7.30, PaCO2 55 mm Hg, HCO3 26 mEq/L. The patient's partner asks why the body has not fixed the problem yet. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: The lungs are already correcting it by breathing faster now
options.rationale: The lungs are the cause here, because painful, shallow breathing is retaining carbon dioxide. A system that is causing the problem cannot also be compensating for it.

options.text: The body cannot correct an acid problem caused by breathing
options.rationale: Respiratory acidosis can be compensated, and the kidneys are the system that does it. Saying the body cannot correct it is an absolute that the physiology does not support.

options.text: The kidneys need a day or two to respond
options.rationale: The kidneys compensate for a respiratory problem by holding on to bicarbonate. They take 24 to 48 hours to fully respond, so 6 hours in, the HCO3 is still normal.

options.text: The kidneys only correct problems that start in the kidneys
options.rationale: The kidneys do correct metabolic problems, but that is not their only role. They also compensate for respiratory problems by adjusting bicarbonate and hydrogen ions.

questions.takeaway: The kidneys compensate for respiratory problems and are the most powerful regulator, but they take 24 to 48 hours to fully respond.
questions.strategy: The normal HCO3 tempts students to say the kidneys are not involved in respiratory problems. The time since the injury is what explains it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: pH low, PaCO2 high: respiratory, from shallow breathing.
For a respiratory problem it is the kidneys.
6 hours is short of the 24 to 48 hours the kidneys need.

elimination.verdict: The kidneys will compensate, but they need a day or two.

questions.objective: Describe respiratory and renal regulation of acid base balance.

questions.stem: A patient with a neuromuscular disease has shallow breathing, and her PaCO2 has been rising for several days. The nurse is reviewing her daily laboratory trend. Which finding shows that the kidneys are compensating for the problem?

options.text: Serum HCO3 rising from 25 to 31 mEq/L over 3 days
options.rationale: Holding on to bicarbonate is how the kidneys offset retained carbon dioxide. A steady rise over days fits the 24 to 48 hours the kidneys need to respond.

options.text: pH falling from 7.34 to 7.29 over 3 days
options.rationale: A falling pH means the acidosis is getting worse. Compensation moves the pH back toward normal, so this trend shows the opposite of what the nurse is looking for.

options.text: Serum HCO3 falling from 24 to 19 mEq/L over 3 days
options.rationale: Losing bicarbonate removes base and makes the acidosis worse. The kidneys compensate for retained carbon dioxide by reabsorbing bicarbonate, not by excreting it.

options.text: Respiratory rate rising from 14 to 26 per minute
options.rationale: Faster breathing is how the lungs compensate for a metabolic problem. Her problem is respiratory, and the stem asks about the kidneys, not the lungs.

questions.takeaway: The kidneys correct acidosis by reabsorbing bicarbonate and trapping hydrogen ions in the urine; rising HCO3 over days is renal compensation for respiratory acidosis.
questions.strategy: A rising respiratory rate looks like the body fighting back, but it is the wrong system. Kidney compensation shows up as HCO3 moving in the direction that offsets the problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The base side: HCO3.
Rising HCO3 offsets acid; falling HCO3 adds to it.
Respiratory rate is the lungs; a falling pH is worsening, not compensation.

elimination.verdict: A rising HCO3 over days shows renal compensation.

questions.objective: Describe respiratory and renal regulation of acid base balance.

questions.stem: On admission for a planned knee repair, a patient with 20 years of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is alert, talking in full sentences and says her breathing is at her usual. ABG results: pH 7.36, PaCO2 60 mm Hg, HCO3 33 mEq/L. How does the nurse interpret this result?

options.text: Fully compensated metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: A high HCO3 with a normal pH can look like this. Her long history of lung disease and a pH on the acid side of normal point to a respiratory cause.

options.text: Normal acid base balance
options.rationale: The pH is normal, and that is why this answer tempts. A normal pH can still hide a disorder, and here both PaCO2 and HCO3 are far outside their ranges.

options.text: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: Years of retained carbon dioxide explain the high PaCO2, and the kidneys have raised HCO3 to offset it. Because the pH has returned to normal, the compensation is full.

options.text: Partially compensated respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: Partial compensation would fit if the pH were still below 7.35. This pH is 7.36, inside the normal range, so the compensation is complete, not partial.

questions.takeaway: A normal pH can reflect a fully compensated disorder; connect the ABG to the patient's history to name the primary problem.
questions.strategy: The normal pH and her comfortable breathing pull toward a normal gas. The history of chronic lung disease tells the nurse which abnormal value came first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Do not stop at the pH
steps.detail: A normal pH can still reflect a fully compensated disorder.
PaCO2 and HCO3 are both abnormal.

steps.action: Use the history to name the primary problem
steps.detail: Twenty years of lung disease means CO2 retention came first.

elimination.verdict: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis.

questions.objective: Describe respiratory and renal regulation of acid base balance.

questions.stem: One hour after a patient became short of breath, the nurse receives an ABG result. Place the nurse's steps for interpreting the result in order.

options.text: Check whether the other system is normal or moving to correct the pH
options.rationale: Compensation is judged only after the primary problem is known. The other system tells the nurse whether the result is uncompensated, partial or full.

options.text: Classify the pH as acidosis, alkalosis or normal
options.rationale: The pH comes first because it shows the direction of the problem. It does not show the cause, so the nurse keeps going.

options.text: Connect the result to the patient's assessment and current treatment
options.rationale: An ABG is interpreted alongside the patient, not in isolation. The final step links the numbers to what the nurse sees and to the care already given.

options.text: Decide whether the PaCO2 or the HCO3 explains the pH
options.rationale: The value that moves to match the pH is the cause: respiratory opposite, metabolic equal. This step names the primary problem.

options.text: Compare the PaCO2 and HCO3 with their normal ranges
options.rationale: The nurse needs to know which values are abnormal before deciding which one caused the pH change. PaCO2 is the respiratory part and HCO3 the metabolic part.

questions.takeaway: Interpret an ABG in order: pH, then PaCO2 and HCO3, then which one explains the pH, then compensation, then the patient.
questions.strategy: Students often jump to compensation before naming the cause. Compensation can only be judged once the nurse knows which system started the problem.

steps.detail: The pH tells acidosis or alkalosis.
Compare PaCO2 and HCO3, then match one to the pH.
Judge the other system, then link to the assessment.

elimination.verdict: pH, values, cause, compensation, patient.

questions.objective: Differentiate respiratory and metabolic acid base disturbances.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with acute pancreatitis has had no oral intake for 2 days. ABG results: pH 7.30, PaCO2 31 mm Hg, HCO3 15 mEq/L. How does the nurse interpret this result?

options.text: Uncompensated metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: The diagnosis of metabolic acidosis is right. Uncompensated would need a normal PaCO2, and this PaCO2 of 31 mm Hg shows the lungs are already working on it.

options.text: Partially compensated metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: The low HCO3 moves with the low pH, which makes the problem metabolic. The low PaCO2 shows the lungs are compensating, but the pH has not yet returned to normal.

options.text: Partially compensated respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: A low PaCO2 does mean respiratory alkalosis when it causes the pH change. This pH is 7.30, which is acidosis, so the low PaCO2 cannot be the cause.

options.text: Fully compensated metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: Full compensation requires the pH to come back inside 7.35 to 7.45. At 7.30 the pH is still acidotic, so the compensation is only partial.

questions.takeaway: Partial compensation means the pH is still abnormal while both PaCO2 and HCO3 are abnormal.
questions.strategy: Students who spot the low HCO3 often stop there and choose uncompensated. Check the other system before naming the level of compensation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 7.30 is acidosis; cut the alkalosis option.
HCO3 low with pH low: metabolic equal.
PaCO2 low means compensation; pH still abnormal means partial.

elimination.verdict: Partially compensated metabolic acidosis.

questions.objective: Describe respiratory and renal regulation of acid base balance.

questions.stem: A patient with cancer of the larynx has a tumor narrowing his upper airway. Over the past hour his breathing has become noisy and labored at 26 per minute, and he is using his neck muscles to breathe. ABG results: pH 7.29, PaCO2 57 mm Hg, HCO3 26 mEq/L. How does the nurse interpret this result?

options.text: Partially compensated respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: Respiratory acidosis is the right problem. Partial compensation needs an abnormal HCO3, and 26 mEq/L is still inside the 22 to 26 mEq/L range.

options.text: Uncompensated metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: The pH does show acidosis. A metabolic cause needs a low HCO3, and this HCO3 is normal while the PaCO2 is high from air that cannot pass the tumor.

options.text: Uncompensated respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: A rate of 26 per minute does suggest he could be blowing off carbon dioxide. Little air moves past the narrowed airway, so his PaCO2 is high and his pH is below 7.35.

options.text: Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: The pH is low and the PaCO2 is high, moving in opposite directions, so the lungs are the cause. The HCO3 is still normal, so the kidneys have not begun to compensate.

questions.takeaway: Respiratory opposite: pH down with PaCO2 up is respiratory acidosis; a normal HCO3 means no compensation yet.
questions.strategy: His fast breathing tempts students toward alkalosis. A narrowed airway moves little air with each breath, so the PaCO2 climbs even at 26 breaths per minute; read the gas, not the rate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 7.29 is acidosis, so the fast rate is not causing an alkalosis.
pH down and PaCO2 up move opposite: respiratory.
26 mEq/L is normal, so uncompensated.

elimination.verdict: Uncompensated respiratory acidosis.

questions.objective: Differentiate respiratory and metabolic acid base disturbances.

questions.stem: On the third day of nasogastric suction after bowel surgery, a patient has these ABG results: pH 7.53, PaCO2 43 mm Hg, HCO3 35 mEq/L. How does the nurse interpret this result?

options.text: Uncompensated respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: The pH does show alkalosis. Respiratory alkalosis needs a low PaCO2 from fast breathing, and this PaCO2 is normal while the HCO3 is high.

options.text: Partially compensated metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: Metabolic alkalosis is the right problem, and a PaCO2 of 43 mm Hg is higher than average. It is still inside 35 to 45 mm Hg, so compensation has not started.

options.text: Uncompensated metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: The high HCO3 moves with the high pH, so the problem is metabolic, from acid lost through the suction. The PaCO2 of 43 mm Hg is still normal, so the lungs have not compensated.

options.text: Fully compensated metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: Full compensation would bring the pH back inside 7.35 to 7.45. A pH of 7.53 is still alkalotic, so the compensation is not full.

questions.takeaway: Metabolic equal: pH up with HCO3 up is metabolic alkalosis; judge compensation against the normal PaCO2 of 35 to 45 mm Hg.
questions.strategy: A PaCO2 in the low 40s looks like the lungs are starting to retain CO2. Normal PaCO2 runs 35 to 45 mm Hg, so 43 mm Hg is still normal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 7.53 is alkalosis.
pH up and HCO3 up move equal: metabolic.
43 mm Hg is inside 35 to 45 mm Hg, so uncompensated.

elimination.verdict: Uncompensated metabolic alkalosis.

questions.objective: Differentiate respiratory and metabolic acid base disturbances.
questions.note: One table in the class material lists PaCO2 as 35 to 40 mm Hg in metabolic acidosis, while the ABG normal values table and the interpretation steps use 35 to 45 mm Hg. Key 35 to 45 mm Hg on the course exam and on the NCLEX; under the 35 to 40 range this PaCO2 would look abnormal and change the compensation call.

questions.stem: In the emergency department, a patient who was found on the floor at home is breathing 18 times per minute. Arterial blood gas results: pH 7.41, PaCO2 39 mm Hg, HCO3 24 mEq/L, PaO2 64 mm Hg, SaO2 90%. How does the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: Normal results that need no follow up
options.rationale: The acid base values are normal, which makes this tempting. The PaO2 of 64 mm Hg and SaO2 of 90% are low, so the patient is not oxygenating well.

options.text: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: A normal pH can hide a compensated disorder. That requires abnormal PaCO2 and HCO3 values, and both are normal here.

options.text: Uncompensated respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: Respiratory alkalosis needs a pH above 7.45 and a low PaCO2. A low oxygen level alone does not change the acid base category.

options.text: Normal acid base balance with impaired oxygenation
options.rationale: The pH, PaCO2 and HCO3 are all normal, so there is no acid base problem. A PaO2 of 64 mm Hg is below the normal 80 to 100 mm Hg and an SaO2 of 90% is below 95%, an oxygenation problem evaluated separately.

questions.takeaway: For acid base, read pH, PaCO2 and HCO3; PaO2 and SaO2 answer a separate question: is the patient oxygenating?
questions.strategy: Students who see a normal pH, PaCO2 and HCO3 stop and call the gas normal. The last two values answer a different question.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: pH, PaCO2 and HCO3 are all normal.
PaO2 64 mm Hg and SaO2 90% are both low.
No acid base disorder, but impaired oxygenation.

elimination.verdict: Normal acid base, impaired oxygenation.

questions.objective: Differentiate respiratory and metabolic acid base disturbances.

questions.stem: During an acute asthma attack, a patient had these ABG results on arrival: pH 7.27, PaCO2 62 mm Hg, HCO3 27 mEq/L. She received a bronchodilator and oxygen therapy. Which repeat result 2 hours later shows her acidosis has resolved?

options.text: pH 7.49, PaCO2 32 mm Hg, HCO3 24 mEq/L
options.rationale: The acidosis is gone, but the pH is now above 7.45 with a low PaCO2. She has moved into respiratory alkalosis, which is a new imbalance, not a resolution.

options.text: pH 7.38, PaCO2 43 mm Hg, HCO3 25 mEq/L
options.rationale: The pH of 7.38 and PaCO2 of 43 mm Hg are back inside 7.35 to 7.45 and 35 to 45 mm Hg, so she is clearing carbon dioxide again. This result shows the treatment worked.

options.text: pH 7.24, PaCO2 66 mm Hg, HCO3 27 mEq/L
options.rationale: The PaCO2 has climbed and the pH has dropped further. She is retaining more carbon dioxide, which means the treatment is failing and she may need ventilation support.

options.text: pH 7.33, PaCO2 51 mm Hg, HCO3 26 mEq/L
options.rationale: This is better than her arrival result, and that makes it tempting. The pH is still below 7.35 and the PaCO2 is still high, so the acidosis has not resolved.

questions.takeaway: Repeat ABGs show whether treatment worked; resolution means pH and PaCO2 back in range, not just better or overcorrected.
questions.strategy: An improved result tempts students who read better as resolved. Compare each value with normal, a pH of 7.35 to 7.45 and a PaCO2 of 35 to 45 mm Hg, not with the arrival result.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Resolved means back to normal, not just improved.

steps.action: Cut the worse and the overshoot
steps.detail: A falling pH is failure; a pH above 7.45 is a new alkalosis.
Only one has pH and PaCO2 inside their ranges.

elimination.verdict: pH 7.38, PaCO2 43 mm Hg, HCO3 25 mEq/L.

questions.objective: Differentiate respiratory and metabolic acid base disturbances.

questions.stem: On a surgical unit, the nurse is reviewing the assigned patients. Which patients are at risk for metabolic alkalosis? Select all that apply.

options.text: A patient with a 4 minute seizure an hour ago
options.rationale: A seizure makes the muscles produce a burst of acid. That overproduction of hydrogen ions causes metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis.

options.text: A patient taking a high dose loop diuretic
options.rationale: High dose loop diuretics make the kidneys lose hydrogen ions along with fluid. Losing acid leaves a relative excess of base, which raises the HCO3 and the pH.

options.text: A patient with severe diarrhea for 2 days
options.rationale: Diarrhea does cause an acid base problem, and it is a GI loss like suction. It removes bicarbonate from the intestine, causing metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis.

options.text: A patient who received several units of blood
options.rationale: Stored blood carries a preservative that the body turns into bicarbonate. Several units add a load of base that the body must clear, raising the pH.

options.text: A patient who is hyperventilating from anxiety
options.rationale: Hyperventilation does cause alkalosis, which makes this tempting. It blows off carbon dioxide, so the alkalosis is respiratory, not metabolic.

options.text: A patient receiving total parenteral nutrition
options.rationale: The nutrient solution can carry more base than the body uses each day. When that base builds up, the HCO3 rises and the pH moves above 7.45.

options.text: A patient with a nasogastric tube to continuous suction
options.rationale: Gastric fluid is rich in acid, and suction removes it steadily. Losing acid leaves the blood with a relative excess of base, which is metabolic alkalosis.

questions.takeaway: Metabolic alkalosis comes from base excess (antacids, transfusion, IV bicarbonate, TPN) or acid deficit (vomiting, NG suction, high dose diuretics).
questions.strategy: Diarrhea tempts because it is a GI loss like suction. Upper GI loss removes acid; lower GI loss removes base.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Sort each patient as base gained or acid lost
steps.detail: TPN and blood add base; suction and the diuretic remove acid.

steps.action: Separate upper and lower GI losses
steps.detail: Gastric suction loses acid; diarrhea loses bicarbonate.
Hyperventilation is respiratory alkalosis; seizures overproduce acid.

elimination.verdict: Suction, TPN, the loop diuretic and blood transfusion.

questions.objective: Identify common causes and assessment findings of acidosis and alkalosis.

questions.stem: Three hours after the ventilator rate was increased for a sedated patient on mechanical ventilation, ABG results are pH 7.52, PaCO2 28 mm Hg, HCO3 22 mEq/L. Which change does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A reduction in the ventilator rate
options.rationale: The low PaCO2 with a high pH is respiratory alkalosis, and the ventilator is removing too much carbon dioxide. Lowering the rate treats the cause of the imbalance.

options.text: An infusion of IV sodium bicarbonate
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is a treatment for severe metabolic acidosis. Adding base to a patient whose pH is already 7.52 would make the alkalosis worse.

options.text: An IV infusion of potassium chloride
options.rationale: Alkalosis can shift potassium into cells, so potassium may need replacing later. No potassium value is given, and the ventilator setting is what is causing the alkalosis.

options.text: Supplemental oxygen at a higher flow
options.rationale: Oxygen is useful for respiratory problems and hypoxia, but nothing here shows low oxygen. More oxygen does not raise a PaCO2 that the ventilator is lowering.

questions.takeaway: Pairing pH up with PaCO2 down is respiratory alkalosis; when a treatment such as mechanical ventilation is the cause, stop or adjust it.
questions.strategy: Potassium replacement is linked to alkalosis and tempts students who remember the shift. Treating the cause comes before chasing a value that is not given.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: pH up and PaCO2 down: respiratory alkalosis.

steps.action: Find the cause in the stem
steps.detail: The ventilator rate went up 3 hours ago.

steps.action: Choose the action that treats the cause
steps.detail: Lower the rate so less CO2 is blown off.

elimination.verdict: Reduce the ventilator rate.

questions.objective: Differentiate respiratory and metabolic acid base disturbances.
questions.concept: ROME: respiratory alkalosis from mechanical ventilation

questions.stem: After 3 days of severe diarrhea, a patient has these ABG results: pH 7.29, PaCO2 37 mm Hg, HCO3 17 mEq/L. Which finding does the nurse expect on the neuromuscular assessment?

options.text: Hand spasm when the blood pressure cuff inflates
options.rationale: A positive Trousseau sign shows that nerves and muscles are overexcitable. It belongs with alkalosis, while this pH below 7.35 points to depressed nerve and muscle function instead.

options.text: Calf cramps with brisk reflexes in both knees
options.rationale: Cramping and brisk reflexes are real acid base findings, but they come from overexcited nerves and muscles. That is the alkalosis pattern, and this pH of 7.29 is acidotic.

options.text: Agitation with dizziness and tingling lips
options.rationale: Agitation, dizziness and tingling are central nervous system signs of alkalosis. Acidosis moves the brain the other way, toward lethargy, confusion and eventually coma.

options.text: Flaccid leg weakness with diminished reflexes
options.rationale: A pH of 7.29 with a low HCO3 is metabolic acidosis from base lost in the stool. Acidosis depresses nerves and muscles, so flaccid weakness with diminished reflexes is the expected finding.

questions.takeaway: Acidosis depresses the brain, nerves and muscles, causing lethargy, flaccid weakness and low reflexes; alkalosis overexcites them, causing cramps, tingling, tetany and brisk reflexes.
questions.strategy: Three options describe overexcitement, which tempts students who remember only that acid base problems cause muscle symptoms. Name the imbalance from the pH first; below 7.35, everything slows down.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: pH 7.29 is below 7.35 with a low HCO3: metabolic acidosis.
Acidosis depresses; alkalosis excites.
Cramps, the Trousseau sign and tingling all show overexcitement.

elimination.verdict: Flaccid leg weakness with diminished reflexes.

questions.objective: Identify common causes and assessment findings of acidosis and alkalosis.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient who has chewed antacid tablets many times a day for 2 weeks for heartburn. ABG results: pH 7.51, PaCO2 39 mm Hg, HCO3 30 mEq/L. Which finding requires follow up as an effect of the patient's acid base imbalance?

options.text: Burning behind the breastbone after each meal
options.rationale: The burning is a real problem that needs attention, but it is the heartburn that led to the antacid use. It is a cause of the alkalosis, not an effect of it.

options.text: Heart rate of 52 per minute and regular
options.rationale: Alkalosis tends to raise the heart rate, not slow it. A heart rate of 52 per minute fits the depressed cardiac function of acidosis better than this alkalotic result.

options.text: Tingling around the mouth and in both hands
options.rationale: A pH of 7.51 with a high HCO3 is metabolic alkalosis from the antacids. Alkalosis makes nerves fire too easily, and tingling around the mouth and hands is one of its hallmark signs.

options.text: Lethargy with diminished reflexes in both knees
options.rationale: Lethargy and diminished reflexes in both knees show a depressed brain and depressed muscles. That is the acidosis picture, while alkalosis brings brisk reflexes, dizziness and agitation instead.

questions.takeaway: Alkalosis overexcites nerves and muscles: tingling, dizziness, Trousseau and Chvostek signs, brisk reflexes and a faster heart rate; the problem that led to it is not one of its effects.
questions.strategy: The heartburn is the most familiar complaint and is a true finding. Ask whether each finding is caused by the high pH or is the reason the patient took the base.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: pH 7.51 with HCO3 30 mEq/L: metabolic alkalosis from the antacids.
The heartburn led to the antacids; it is not caused by the alkalosis.
A slow heart rate and diminished reflexes fit acidosis.

elimination.verdict: Tingling around the mouth and in both hands.

questions.objective: Identify common causes and assessment findings of acidosis and alkalosis.

questions.stem: An 87 year old patient who takes a daily aspirin and a diuretic is admitted to a medical unit with metabolic acidosis, and he answers questions slowly. His daughter says he is "a little forgetful at home." Which action best helps the nurse judge his mental status?

options.text: Ask him to state the date and record his answer
options.rationale: Orientation questions are a useful part of a mental status check. One answer without his baseline cannot show whether today is different from his usual.

options.text: Ask the daughter how today compares with his usual alertness
options.rationale: Mental status in an older adult is judged against his own baseline. The daughter knows his usual, so she can tell the nurse whether slow answers are new.

options.text: Ask the daughter whether he still drives a car
options.rationale: Driving gives a rough idea of how he functions at home. It does not compare his alertness today with his usual, which is the question the nurse needs answered.

options.text: Record that slow answers are expected at his age
options.rationale: Slower processing can be part of aging. Assuming it is normal skips the comparison with baseline and could miss acidosis affecting the brain.

questions.takeaway: Older adults are at greater risk from acid base imbalance; assess mental status against the person's own baseline, and ask about every prescribed and OTC drug.
questions.strategy: Accepting slowness as normal aging is the emotionally easy distractor. A change from his usual is what signals acidosis affecting the brain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Is his slowness new or his usual?
His daughter.
A single orientation answer or driving status does not compare with baseline.

elimination.verdict: Compare today's alertness with his usual through his daughter.

questions.objective: Identify common causes and assessment findings of acidosis and alkalosis.
questions.concept: Older adults: mental status vs baseline

questions.scenario: The nurse is caring for six patients and anticipates the acid base change each one's condition may cause.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate the imbalance the nurse anticipates.

rows.text: A visitor who flew to a mountain town at high altitude yesterday
rows.rationale: Thin air at high altitude makes the person breathe faster and deeper. That blows off carbon dioxide, lowering the PaCO2 and raising the pH.

rows.text: A patient breathing 30 per minute in the first hour of an acute lung injury
rows.rationale: Early in an acute lung problem the patient breathes fast and blows off carbon dioxide. The PaCO2 drops and the pH rises, before fatigue can slow the breathing.

rows.text: A patient with severe obesity whose chest cannot expand fully when lying flat
rows.rationale: Inadequate chest expansion means less carbon dioxide is exhaled with each breath. The retained carbon dioxide raises the PaCO2 and lowers the pH.

rows.text: A patient who has eaten almost nothing for 3 weeks
rows.rationale: Starvation makes the body break down fat for fuel, which overproduces acid. The extra hydrogen ions use up bicarbonate and lower the pH.

rows.text: A patient with severe dehydration after several days of poor fluid intake
rows.rationale: Dehydration lowers the body's production of bicarbonate, leaving a base deficit. With less base to balance the acid, the HCO3 and the pH both fall.

rows.text: A patient who choked on food and has a partial airway obstruction
rows.rationale: Air cannot move freely past the obstruction, so carbon dioxide is retained. Retained carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid and the pH falls.

questions.takeaway: Starvation and dehydration add acid or lose base; obstruction and poor chest expansion retain CO2; high altitude and early lung problems blow it off.
questions.strategy: A lung problem does not always mean acidosis. Early in an acute pulmonary problem the patient breathes fast, which lowers PaCO2.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Starvation and dehydration change the acid or base load through metabolism.

steps.action: For lung causes, ask whether CO2 is kept or lost
steps.detail: Obstruction and poor expansion keep CO2; fast breathing loses it.
Two rows per column.

elimination.verdict: Two metabolic acidosis, two respiratory acidosis, two respiratory alkalosis.

questions.objective: Identify common causes and assessment findings of acidosis and alkalosis.
questions.concept: Causes of acidosis and respiratory alkalosis

questions.stem: In the emergency department, a patient who drank windshield washer fluid containing methanol has a pH of 7.21, PaCO2 of 33 mm Hg and HCO3 of 13 mEq/L. Serum potassium is 6.3 mEq/L. He is confused and his respirations are deep and rapid. Which assessment does the nurse perform first?

options.text: Place him on a cardiac monitor and check rhythm
options.rationale: Acidosis pushes potassium out of cells, and a level of 6.3 mEq/L can trigger cardiac arrest. The cardiovascular system is assessed first for that reason.

options.text: Inspect his skin for color and temperature
options.rationale: Warm, flushed skin fits metabolic acidosis and helps confirm the type. It does not change the urgent risk from high potassium to the heart.

options.text: Test his deep tendon reflexes in all four limbs
options.rationale: Hyporeflexia is an expected neuromuscular effect of acidosis and hyperkalemia. It does not carry the immediate risk of death that a cardiac rhythm change does.

options.text: Check his orientation to person, place and time
options.rationale: His confusion is a real central nervous system effect of acidosis and needs tracking. A rhythm problem from high potassium can kill him faster, so the heart comes first.

questions.takeaway: In acidosis, hydrogen ions move into cells and potassium moves out, causing hyperkalemia; assess the cardiovascular system first.
questions.strategy: Confusion is the most noticeable finding and tempts students to start with the brain. The potassium makes the heart the life threat.

steps.detail: Acidosis plus a potassium of 6.3 mEq/L.
Hyperkalemia can trigger cardiac arrest.

steps.action: Pick the system that matches the danger
steps.detail: The heart, assessed with a monitor and rhythm check.

elimination.verdict: Cardiac monitor and rhythm first.

questions.objective: Explain the relationship between acid base balance and potassium shifts.
questions.concept: Acidosis and hyperkalemia: assess the heart first

questions.stem: While preparing a due digoxin dose, the nurse learns that a patient who also takes a high dose thiazide diuretic has nausea. ABG results: pH 7.51, PaCO2 40 mm Hg, HCO3 31 mEq/L. Serum potassium is 3.0 mEq/L. His pulse is 58 per minute and irregular. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the digoxin and report the findings to the provider
options.rationale: Alkalosis moves potassium into cells, and low potassium raises the risk of digoxin toxicity. His nausea and slow, irregular pulse suggest toxicity may already be present.

options.text: Give the digoxin and recheck his pulse in 1 hour
options.rationale: Rechecking the pulse seems cautious and reasonable. His low potassium, nausea and irregular pulse already point to toxicity, and another dose would add to it.

options.text: Offer an antacid for the nausea before the digoxin
options.rationale: Antiemetics fit nausea from vomiting, and an antacid seems like a gentle choice. Antacids are bases and would add to his metabolic alkalosis.

options.text: Give the thiazide diuretic early to correct the alkalosis
options.rationale: High dose thiazide diuretics are already a cause of his metabolic alkalosis. Giving more would lose more acid and potassium and make both problems worse.

questions.takeaway: In alkalosis, potassium shifts into cells, causing hypokalemia and a higher risk of digoxin toxicity.
questions.strategy: The antacid looks gentle and the recheck looks cautious. Both miss that low potassium raises the risk of digoxin toxicity and his findings already fit it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Interpret the gas and the potassium
steps.detail: Metabolic alkalosis with potassium of 3.0 mEq/L.
Low potassium raises digoxin toxicity risk.
Nausea and a slow, irregular pulse fit toxicity, so the dose is held.

elimination.verdict: Hold the digoxin and report.

questions.objective: Explain the relationship between acid base balance and potassium shifts.
questions.concept: Potassium shifts with acid base changes

questions.stem: A patient's wife tells the nurse, "He hasn't eaten anything with potassium in days. How can it be high?" He has chronic liver failure with metabolic acidosis, and his serum potassium is 5.8 mEq/L. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "His body makes extra potassium to replace the lost base."
options.rationale: Potassium and bicarbonate both carry a charge, so a trade between them sounds logical. The body cannot make potassium; the level rises because acid entering cells pushes potassium out.

options.text: "The level is probably a lab error, since he has not eaten potassium."
options.rationale: Low intake does make a high level seem unlikely. Acidosis explains the high level, so dismissing it as an error could miss a cardiac danger.

options.text: "His liver is releasing stored potassium because it is failing."
options.rationale: Liver failure is one cause of his metabolic acidosis, which makes this sound related. The rise in potassium comes from the acid shifting potassium out of cells, not from the liver.

options.text: "The acid moves into his cells and pushes potassium out."
options.rationale: Excess hydrogen ions move into cells for buffering, and potassium moves out to keep the electrical charge balanced. The potassium in his blood rises even without more intake.

questions.takeaway: In acidosis, H+ moves into cells and K+ moves out to keep cells electrically neutral, producing a relative hyperkalemia.
questions.strategy: Organ based explanations sound plausible. The shift is about electrical neutrality across the cell membrane: hydrogen in, potassium out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Recall the direction of the shift in acidosis
steps.detail: H+ into cells, K+ out.

steps.action: Cut the organ and production stories
steps.detail: The liver does not release it, and the body cannot make potassium.
A lab error claim ignores a known, dangerous cause.

elimination.verdict: Acid moves into cells and pushes potassium out.

questions.objective: Explain the relationship between acid base balance and potassium shifts.
questions.concept: Potassium shifts with acid base changes

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four patients who have acidosis. For which patient does the nurse anticipate a prescription for IV sodium bicarbonate?

options.text: pH 7.14, PaCO2 85 mm Hg, HCO3 28 mEq/L
options.rationale: This pH is the lowest of the four, so it draws the eye. The high PaCO2 makes it respiratory acidosis, which is treated with ventilation, not bicarbonate.

options.text: pH 7.16, PaCO2 24 mm Hg, HCO3 8 mEq/L
options.rationale: The low HCO3 matching the low pH shows metabolic acidosis, and the pH is below 7.2. That is the point where IV bicarbonate is used for metabolic acidosis.

options.text: pH 7.26, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, HCO3 13 mEq/L
options.rationale: This is metabolic acidosis and may need treatment of its cause. The pH is still above 7.2, so bicarbonate is not yet indicated.

options.text: pH 7.31, PaCO2 34 mm Hg, HCO3 16 mEq/L
options.rationale: This is a milder metabolic acidosis with the lungs starting to compensate. A pH of 7.31 is well above 7.2, so the cause is treated instead.

questions.takeaway: Identify the type of acidosis before treating; IV bicarbonate is for metabolic acidosis with pH below 7.2, while respiratory acidosis needs better ventilation.
questions.strategy: The lowest pH is the emotional pull. Bicarbonate fixes a base deficit; it does not remove the carbon dioxide behind respiratory acidosis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Name the type of each acidosis
steps.detail: High PaCO2 is respiratory; low HCO3 is metabolic.
Bicarbonate does not treat retained CO2.
Among the metabolic cases, only one pH is below 7.2.

elimination.verdict: pH 7.16, PaCO2 24 mm Hg, HCO3 8 mEq/L.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions for patients with acid base imbalances.
questions.concept: Metabolic acidosis treatment: treat the cause, bicarbonate only below pH 7.2

questions.stem: A patient admitted with pneumonia has thick secretions and can speak only 3 or 4 words between breaths. ABG results: pH 7.32, PaCO2 53 mm Hg, HCO3 27 mEq/L. Which intervention does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Lay her flat so her breathing muscles can rest
options.rationale: Rest sounds kind for a tired patient, but lying flat limits how far the chest can expand. Less expansion means less carbon dioxide leaves, so her acidosis would worsen.

options.text: Have her breathe slowly into a paper bag
options.rationale: Paper bag breathing makes a person rebreathe carbon dioxide and is used for anxiety driven respiratory alkalosis. She already has too much carbon dioxide, so rebreathing it would worsen her acidosis.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and coach coughing
options.rationale: Her PaCO2 of 53 mm Hg shows carbon dioxide retained from poor ventilation. Sitting upright lets her chest expand, and effective coughing clears the secretions that are blocking gas exchange.

options.text: Request IV sodium bicarbonate for the low pH
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is used for metabolic acidosis with a pH below 7.2. Her acidosis comes from retained carbon dioxide at a pH of 7.32, so the fix is better ventilation.

questions.takeaway: Respiratory acidosis is treated by improving ventilation: upright positioning, coughing and deep breathing, bronchodilators, mucolytics and oxygen; bicarbonate and rebreathing do not fit.
questions.strategy: Bicarbonate tempts because it raises a low pH. Name the source first: a high PaCO2 means the lungs are the problem, so choose the action that helps her move air.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: pH 7.32 with PaCO2 53 mm Hg: respiratory acidosis.
Better chest expansion and clear airways.
Bicarbonate is for metabolic acidosis; the paper bag is for alkalosis; lying flat limits expansion.

elimination.verdict: Raise the head of the bed and coach coughing.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions for patients with acid base imbalances.

questions.nursesNote: 0700: Patient with chronic kidney failure, missed dialysis for 4 days. Heart rate 46 per minute and regular. Reports itching on both arms. Blood pressure 86/50. Monitor shows tall T waves and a widened QRS. Temperature 36.9 C. Lethargic, opens eyes to voice, oriented to name only. Dialysis fistula in the left arm with a palpable thrill. Hand grips weak, reflexes diminished in both arms. Respirations 30 per minute, deep and regular. ABG: pH 7.25, PaCO2 31 mm Hg, HCO3 13 mEq/L.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow up as effects of the patient's acidosis.

segments.text: Heart rate 46 per minute and regular
segments.rationale: Acidosis slows the heart, and the slowing can progress to heart block. A rate of 46 per minute is bradycardia that needs follow up now.

segments.text: Reports itching on both arms
segments.rationale: Itching is common with kidney failure and is uncomfortable. It is not an effect of the acid itself and does not threaten the heart or brain.

segments.text: Blood pressure 86/50
segments.rationale: Acidosis weakens the heart and widens the blood vessels, so blood pressure falls. A pressure of 86/50 means the circulation is already affected.

segments.text: Monitor shows tall T waves and a widened QRS
segments.rationale: Tall T waves and a wide QRS are acidosis findings that also signal hyperkalemia. They warn that cardiac arrest is possible, so they are the most urgent finding.

segments.text: Temperature 36.9 C
segments.rationale: A temperature of 36.9 C is normal. Fever can add acid, but this patient does not have one, so it is not an effect of the acidosis.

segments.text: Lethargic, opens eyes to voice, oriented to name only
segments.rationale: Acidosis depresses the central nervous system, from lethargy and confusion to stupor and coma. Being oriented to name only is a real decline.

segments.text: Dialysis fistula in the left arm with a palpable thrill
segments.rationale: A palpable thrill shows the dialysis access has blood flowing through it. That is the expected finding for a working fistula, not an effect of acidosis.

segments.text: Hand grips weak, reflexes diminished in both arms
segments.rationale: Hyporeflexia and muscle weakness are neuromuscular effects of acidosis. They can progress to flaccid paralysis, so the nurse follows them closely.

questions.takeaway: Acidosis depresses the heart, brain and muscles: bradycardia, hypotension, tall T waves and wide QRS, lethargy, weakness and hyporeflexia.
questions.strategy: Itching and the fistula belong to kidney failure, not to the acidosis. The cardiac changes are where the risk to life lies, so start there.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bradycardia, hypotension, tall T waves and wide QRS.
Lethargy, weak grips and diminished reflexes.

steps.action: Remove what is normal or belongs to kidney failure
steps.detail: Normal temperature, itching and a working fistula.

elimination.verdict: The cardiac, neurologic and neuromuscular depression findings.

questions.objective: Identify common causes and assessment findings of acidosis and alkalosis.

questions.stem: During a continuous opioid infusion for kidney stone pain, a patient is difficult to rouse. Respiratory rate is 6 per minute and shallow. ABG results: pH 7.26, PaCO2 64 mm Hg, HCO3 28 mEq/L. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Notify the provider of the ABG results now
options.rationale: The provider does need to know, and soon. The nurse can stop the infusion and stimulate breathing right now, and waiting lets carbon dioxide keep rising.

options.text: Prepare an IV infusion of sodium bicarbonate
options.rationale: Bicarbonate raises pH in severe metabolic acidosis. This acidosis is respiratory from slow breathing, so bicarbonate does not treat the cause.

options.text: Draw a repeat ABG in 30 minutes to compare
options.rationale: A repeat gas is how the nurse will evaluate treatment later. Repeating it now delays the action this patient needs while he keeps hypoventilating.

options.text: Stop the opioid infusion and rouse the patient
options.rationale: The opioid is depressing his breathing and causing respiratory acidosis. Stopping it and rousing him to breathe treats the cause and supports his airway and breathing.

questions.takeaway: Acidosis is a sign, not a disease; when an opioid is depressing breathing, stop the cause and support ventilation first.
questions.strategy: Calling the provider feels safe and responsible. The nurse has an action within reach that treats the cause right now.

steps.detail: pH low, PaCO2 high: respiratory acidosis.
An opioid infusion with a respiratory rate of 6 per minute.

steps.action: Choose the action that fixes breathing now
steps.detail: Stop the infusion and stimulate him.

elimination.verdict: Stop the opioid and stimulate breathing.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions for patients with acid base imbalances.
questions.concept: Respiratory acidosis from respiratory depression: treat the cause

questions.stem: In the procedure area before a biopsy, a patient is breathing 36 times per minute and says, "I feel like I can't get enough air and my fingers are tingling." She is crying and says she is terrified of the procedure. Heart and lung assessment shows no other problem, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. ABG results: pH 7.54, PaCO2 26 mm Hg, HCO3 22 mEq/L. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Explain each step of the biopsy in detail
options.rationale: Teaching can ease fear of a procedure, and she will need it later. While she is breathing 36 times per minute and tingling, she cannot take in detail, so her breathing comes first.

options.text: Leave her to rest alone in a quiet room
options.rationale: A quiet room can help some anxious patients, but leaving her alone removes the support she needs. A frightened patient left by herself tends to keep breathing fast.

options.text: Stay with her and coach slow, even breaths
options.rationale: Her rate of 36 with a PaCO2 of 26 mm Hg shows fear blowing off carbon dioxide. Staying with her calms the fear, and coached slow breathing lets carbon dioxide build back up.

options.text: Encourage her to breathe deeply and cough
options.rationale: Deep breathing and coughing are good care for retained secretions and carbon dioxide. She has the opposite problem, and deeper breaths would blow off even more carbon dioxide.

questions.takeaway: For anxiety driven respiratory alkalosis, the nurse stays with the patient, gives calm reassurance and coaches slower breathing so carbon dioxide can build back up.
questions.strategy: Deep breathing sounds like standard respiratory care, which makes it tempting. She is losing too much carbon dioxide already, so the right action slows her breathing rather than deepening it.

steps.detail: pH 7.54 and PaCO2 26 mm Hg with a normal HCO3 and SpO2 99%: respiratory alkalosis from anxiety.
Slow her breathing so carbon dioxide is kept.
Explaining the biopsy waits until her breathing slows.

elimination.verdict: Stay with her and coach slow, even breaths.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions for patients with acid base imbalances.
questions.note: The class material lists breathing into a paper bag for anxiety driven hyperventilation, together with calm reassurance. Current practice cautions that paper bag rebreathing can cause hypoxia and is used only after cardiac and pulmonary causes are ruled out, so this item keys reassurance and coached slow breathing, which both accept. On the course exam, select the paper bag if it is offered for an anxious, hyperventilating patient with normal oxygenation; on the NCLEX, prefer reassurance and slowed breathing when they are offered.

questions.stem: Six hours after a cardiac arrest, a patient has a stable pulse and blood pressure and is still receiving the IV sodium bicarbonate infusion started during the arrest. ABG results: pH 7.57, PaCO2 40 mm Hg, HCO3 35 mEq/L. She reports muscle cramps. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Pause the infusion and contact the provider about the result
options.rationale: IV sodium bicarbonate adds base, and this gas shows metabolic alkalosis with cramps from overexcited muscles. Stopping or adjusting the treatment that causes the alkalosis comes first.

options.text: Continue the infusion and recheck the ABG in 1 hour
options.rationale: A repeat gas is a good way to evaluate treatment. Running more base for another hour means the nurse knowingly adds to an alkalosis that is already present.

options.text: Have her breathe into a paper bag to retain carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Rebreathing raises PaCO2 in respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation. Her problem is too much base, and her PaCO2 is normal.

options.text: Continue the infusion because it was ordered for the arrest
options.rationale: The order did exist and served a purpose during the arrest. Her pH is now 7.57, and more base would make the alkalosis worse.

questions.takeaway: In alkalosis, stop or adjust the causative treatment and prevent further loss of H+, K+, Ca2+ and Cl.
questions.strategy: A running order feels binding. The nurse questions any treatment that would worsen a result the nurse can already see.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: pH up and HCO3 up: metabolic alkalosis.
IV sodium bicarbonate given during the arrest.

steps.action: Choose the action that stops the cause
steps.detail: Pause the infusion and contact the provider.

elimination.verdict: Pause the bicarbonate infusion and contact the provider.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions for patients with acid base imbalances.
questions.concept: Stop or adjust the causative treatment

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy for cancer has vomited for 4 days. She feels weak and dizzy when she stands, and her blood pressure is 94/58 mm Hg. ABG results: pH 7.49, PaCO2 38 mm Hg, HCO3 28 mEq/L. An antiemetic and IV fluids with electrolyte replacement are prescribed. Which action does the nurse add to her plan of care?

options.text: Offer antacid tablets to settle her stomach
