options.rationale: Antacids may seem like comfort care for a stomach upset by vomiting. They add base, and with an HCO3 of 28 mEq/L that would make her alkalosis worse.

options.text: Start fall precautions before she gets up
options.rationale: Metabolic alkalosis brings muscle weakness, and her blood pressure of 94/58 mm Hg with dizziness on standing adds to the fall risk. Fall precautions protect her while the fluids and antiemetic correct the cause.

options.text: Coach her to breathe into a paper bag
options.rationale: Paper bag breathing is used for respiratory alkalosis caused by anxious hyperventilation. Her PaCO2 is normal and her HCO3 is high, so her problem is metabolic, not respiratory.

options.text: Walk her in the hall to rebuild strength
options.rationale: Walking builds strength once she is stable, and early activity is usually good care. Today she is dizzy on standing with a low blood pressure, so walking her now invites a fall.

questions.takeaway: Metabolic alkalosis care stops the cause, replaces fluid and electrolytes and adds fall precautions, because hypotension and muscle weakness make falls likely.
questions.strategy: Walking sounds like good care for a weak patient, and antacids sound like comfort. Her dizziness on standing and low blood pressure make safety the gap left in the plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: pH 7.49 with HCO3 28 mEq/L after 4 days of vomiting: metabolic alkalosis.
The antiemetic and fluids already treat the cause.
Dizziness on standing and a pressure of 94/58 mm Hg call for fall precautions.

elimination.verdict: Start fall precautions before she gets up.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions for patients with acid base imbalances.
questions.concept: Metabolic alkalosis interventions and fall precautions

questions.stem: During handoff report, the nurse hears about four patients with acid base imbalances. Which patient does the nurse assess first?

options.text: Metabolic acidosis, potassium 6.4 mEq/L, legs feel heavy
options.rationale: Acidosis pushes potassium out of cells, and heavy legs signal muscle weakness from a high potassium. The same effect on heart muscle can cause heart block or cardiac arrest, so this patient is assessed first.

options.text: Metabolic acidosis, deep breaths at 32 per minute, alert
options.rationale: Fast, deep breathing draws attention under the ABCs. In metabolic acidosis it is Kussmaul breathing, the lungs blowing off acid, and an alert patient moving air well is compensating, not failing.

options.text: Anxiety related hyperventilation, tingling fingers, lightheaded
options.rationale: Tingling and lightheadedness are expected with respiratory alkalosis from anxiety, and calm coaching will help soon. These findings are uncomfortable but do not threaten life the way a high potassium does.

options.text: Metabolic alkalosis after vomiting, pulse 104 per minute, calf cramps
options.rationale: A faster pulse and cramps are expected findings of alkalosis and need follow up. They are not the threat to the heart that a potassium of 6.4 mEq/L poses in acidosis.

questions.takeaway: In acidosis, a high potassium threatens the heart even when the patient looks well; Kussmaul breathing in an alert patient is compensation, not the emergency.
questions.strategy: Deep, rapid breathing pulls toward the ABCs. What tips it is that the breathing is working as compensation, while the potassium with weakness is the quiet sign of a heart at risk.

steps.detail: Kussmaul breathing, tingling and cramps fit their imbalances.
A potassium of 6.4 mEq/L with weakness in acidosis.
The heart is at risk of block or arrest.

elimination.verdict: Assess the patient with acidosis and a potassium of 6.4 mEq/L first.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions for patients with acid base imbalances.
questions.concept: Acidosis and hyperkalemia: assess the heart first

questions.scenario: In the emergency department, a patient with type 1 diabetes who has been skipping meals and missed two insulin doses has a blood glucose of 520 mg/dL, and her mucous membranes are dry. Respirations are 30 per minute and deep. Her skin is warm, dry and flushed. ABG results: pH 7.24, PaCO2 27 mm Hg, HCO3 11 mEq/L. Serum potassium is 5.9 mEq/L.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Coach the patient to slow the breathing rate
options.rationale: Slowing breathing helps when hyperventilation is the cause of the problem. Here the deep, fast breathing is compensating, and slowing it would lower the pH further.

options.text: Give IV sodium bicarbonate as a bolus
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is used for metabolic acidosis, which makes it tempting. It is reserved for a pH below 7.2, and this pH is 7.24.

options.text: Give IV insulin as prescribed
options.rationale: Insulin treats the cause, because ketoacidosis develops when there is too little insulin. Stopping the production of ketone acids corrects the acidosis at its source.

options.text: Give IV fluids for hydration as prescribed
options.rationale: Hydration helps correct metabolic acidosis, and her dry mucous membranes show she is dehydrated. Replacing fluid restores circulation so the body can clear the acid.

options.text: Metabolic acidosis from diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: The low HCO3 matches the low pH, and missed insulin with a glucose of 520 mg/dL points to ketoacidosis. Deep breathing and warm, flushed skin fit metabolic acidosis.

options.text: Respiratory acidosis from ineffective breathing
options.rationale: Respiratory acidosis needs a high PaCO2 from retained carbon dioxide. This PaCO2 is low, and the breathing is deep and effective.

options.text: Respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation
options.rationale: The fast breathing and low PaCO2 make this tempting. A pH of 7.24 is acidosis, so the low PaCO2 is compensation, not the cause.

options.text: Metabolic alkalosis from acid loss
options.rationale: Metabolic alkalosis needs a high HCO3 and a pH above 7.45. This pH is below 7.35 and the HCO3 is low, which is acidosis.

options.text: Rate and depth of respirations
options.rationale: Deep, rapid breathing is the lungs compensating for the acid. As the acidosis corrects, the breathing should slow, so it tracks the response to treatment.

options.text: Chvostek sign
options.rationale: A positive Chvostek sign is a finding of alkalosis from overexcited nerves. This patient is acidotic, so the sign does not track the problem.

options.text: Serum potassium level
options.rationale: Acidosis shifts potassium out of cells, and this level is already 5.9 mEq/L. High potassium can trigger dangerous heart rhythms, so it is watched closely.

options.text: Hourly abdominal girth
options.rationale: Abdominal girth tracks distension, which this patient does not have. It gives no information about the acidosis or the potassium.

questions.takeaway: Metabolic acidosis from DKA is treated with hydration and insulin; bicarbonate is reserved for pH below 7.2, and potassium and breathing are monitored.
questions.strategy: Bicarbonate tempts as a direct fix for low pH. The threshold is a pH below 7.2, and treating the cause comes first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: pH and HCO3 both low: metabolic acidosis; low PaCO2 is compensation.
Insulin and fluids for ketoacidosis; pH 7.24 is above the bicarbonate threshold.

steps.action: Monitor the danger and the response
steps.detail: Potassium for the heart, breathing for the trend.

elimination.verdict: Fluids and insulin; DKA; potassium and respirations.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions for patients with acid base imbalances.
questions.concept: Metabolic acidosis treatment: treat the cause, bicarbonate only below pH 7.2

questions.stem: On an orthopedic unit, a patient on bed rest with a fractured pelvis has been tearful and anxious all week. She suddenly says she cannot catch her breath and her lips are tingling, and she is breathing 32 times per minute. ABG results: pH 7.50, PaCO2 29 mm Hg, HCO3 22 mEq/L, PaO2 61 mm Hg. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Stay at her side and coach slow breathing
options.rationale: Calm coaching is right for hyperventilation driven by anxiety, and her tears make anxiety look likely. Her low PaO2 rules that out, because slower breathing does not correct a lack of oxygen.

options.text: Have her breathe into a paper bag
options.rationale: A paper bag is used only for anxiety driven hyperventilation once other causes are excluded. Rebreathing exhaled air would lower her oxygen further when her PaO2 is already low.

options.text: Give supplemental oxygen and call the provider
options.rationale: Her PaO2 of 61 mm Hg shows the fast breathing is driven by low oxygen, which points to an acute lung problem rather than anxiety. Oxygen treats the threat now, and the provider must evaluate the cause.

options.text: Give her as needed pain medication
options.rationale: Pain can speed breathing, and she has a fracture, but treating pain does not correct her low oxygen. Medication that slows breathing could also deepen her hypoxemia before the cause is found.

questions.takeaway: Respiratory alkalosis is treated according to its cause: coaching and reassurance fit anxiety, but a low PaO2 means the fast breathing answers a lack of oxygen and calls for oxygen and the provider.
questions.strategy: Her week of tears makes coached breathing look right, and it would be for anxiety. The PaO2, read separately from the acid base values, shows hypoxemia, so oxygen comes first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: pH up and PaCO2 down: respiratory alkalosis from fast breathing.
A PaO2 of 61 mm Hg shows hypoxemia, not anxiety alone.
Oxygen first; coaching and a paper bag do nothing for low oxygen.

elimination.verdict: Give oxygen and call the provider.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions for patients with acid base imbalances.

questions.stem: Two days after several units of blood for a bleeding stomach ulcer, a patient has these ABG results: pH 7.55, PaCO2 38 mm Hg, HCO3 32 mEq/L. Which pair of findings does the nurse expect on assessment?

options.text: Confusion with warm, flushed, dry skin
options.rationale: Confusion can occur with either imbalance, so it does not separate them. Warm, flushed, dry skin belongs to metabolic acidosis, and her pH and HCO3 are both high.

options.text: Leg weakness with brisk knee reflexes
options.rationale: Alkalosis overexcites nerves, so reflexes become brisk, yet it also weakens skeletal muscle. Weakness with brisk reflexes fits the base excess that her transfusions caused, shown by her high pH and HCO3.

options.text: Leg weakness with diminished knee reflexes
options.rationale: Leg weakness does occur in alkalosis, so half of this pair fits her. Diminished reflexes belong to acidosis, which depresses nerves, while her high pH brings brisk reflexes instead.

options.text: Hand cramping with a heart rate of 50 per minute
options.rationale: Hand cramping is a true effect of alkalosis on excitable muscle. A heart rate of 50 per minute fits acidosis instead, because alkalosis raises the heart rate rather than slowing it.

questions.takeaway: Alkalosis overexcites nerves but can still weaken skeletal muscle, so weakness with brisk reflexes fits it, while weakness with diminished reflexes points to acidosis.
questions.strategy: Weakness sounds like a depressed system, so students reject it or pair it with diminished reflexes. Alkalosis brings skeletal muscle weakness with hyperreflexia, so test both halves of every pair against the high pH.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: pH and HCO3 are both high: metabolic alkalosis from transfused blood.
A pair fits only if both findings fit alkalosis; one acidosis finding rules it out.
Alkalosis brings weakness with brisk, not diminished, reflexes.

elimination.verdict: Leg weakness with brisk knee reflexes.

questions.objective: Identify common causes and assessment findings of acidosis and alkalosis.

questions.stem: In the postanesthesia unit, a patient is recovering from general anesthesia. Before surgery he talked easily with the nurse without hearing aids. He now opens his eyes briefly to a firm touch on the shoulder but does not turn when his name is spoken. Which action is best?

options.text: Speak loudly into one ear to get him to respond
options.rationale: More volume does not help when the problem is the brain's awareness of sound rather than the ear receiving it. Shouting also startles a patient who is waking up.

options.text: Request a hearing evaluation before he goes home
options.rationale: A hearing evaluation would be reasonable if a problem persisted once he was fully awake. Requesting it now skips seeing whether the change clears as the anesthesia wears off.

options.text: Record a new hearing loss in his health history
options.rationale: He heard normally a few hours ago, and anesthesia gives a clear reason for the change. Recording a hearing loss now labels a deficit before he is alert enough to be tested.

options.text: Recheck his response to voice as he wakes further
options.rationale: Hearing a voice depends on the brain perceiving the sound, and perception depends on the level of consciousness that anesthesia is still lowering. Rechecking as he wakes shows whether his normal response returns.

questions.takeaway: Perception depends on the cortex and the level of consciousness, so a patient who is not fully awake may receive a stimulus without perceiving it.
questions.strategy: The tempting choices treat the cue as an ear problem. His normal hearing before surgery and the anesthesia still lowering his consciousness point to perception, which needs time to recover.

steps.detail: He heard normally before surgery, so the change is new and has an obvious cause.
Sound still reaches the ear; awareness of it needs an alert cortex.
Watch his response return as consciousness returns before calling it a deficit.

elimination.verdict: Recheck his response to voice as he wakes further.

questions.objective: Describe normal sensory function and types of sensory alterations.
questions.concept: Perception depends on level of consciousness

questions.stem: A patient in skeletal traction for a femur fracture has been on bed rest for 2 weeks in a private room. Her family lives out of state. She is now bored, irritable and unsure whether it is morning or evening. Her pain is well controlled. Which addition to the plan of care best addresses the cause of these changes?

options.text: Ask the provider about a drug for her low mood
options.rationale: Mood changes may need treatment if they persist once the cause is addressed. Starting with a drug skips the nursing action that targets the missing stimulation.

options.text: Cluster her care and add a daily quiet time
options.rationale: Clustering care and quiet time are the measures for sensory overload. Her room already gives too little input, so fewer visits from staff would deepen the deprivation.

options.text: Tell her the date and time at each shift change
options.rationale: Reorienting her helps and belongs in the plan. Two or three reminders a day leave the empty, restricted environment that is causing her confusion unchanged.

options.text: Add family photos, her own music and a wall clock
options.rationale: Meaningful stimuli such as photos, music and clocks are what prevent and treat the deprivation that weeks of bed rest in a closed room cause. The clock also helps her keep track of time.

questions.takeaway: Deprivation from bed rest and restricted rooms is treated by adding meaningful stimuli such as photos, music, clocks and contact with people.
questions.strategy: Clustering care and quiet time sound restful, but they treat overload. The empty room and absent family point to too little input, so add meaningful stimulation.

steps.detail: Two weeks of traction in a private room with no family: deprivation.
Quiet time and clustered care reduce stimulation, which she already lacks.

steps.action: Choose the cause over the symptom
steps.detail: Reminders and drugs treat the effects; meaningful stimuli treat the cause.

elimination.verdict: Add family photos, her own music and a wall clock.

questions.objective: Describe normal sensory function and types of sensory alterations.

questions.stem: For each patient, indicate whether the findings suggest sensory deprivation or sensory overload.
questions.scenario: A float nurse reviews six patients on different units. Each patient has a change in thinking, mood or perception that began during the current stay.

rows.text: In the emergency department for 9 hours beside the triage desk; thoughts are racing and he cannot finish a sentence
rows.rationale: The emergency department is a common setting for overload, with constant noise, people and activity. Racing thoughts and scattered attention show a brain that cannot filter what it receives.

rows.text: Neurological checks every 30 minutes through the night; keeps pulling at the dressing and needs constant reorientation
rows.rationale: Frequent monitoring through the night is a common source of overload. Handling dressings and needing constant reorientation are the behavior changes seen when the brain cannot respond to stimuli meaningfully.

rows.text: On strict bed rest at home and alone most of the day; misjudges how much time has passed
rows.rationale: Bed rest in an empty house removes most meaningful input for hours at a time. Misjudging time is a perceptual effect of deprivation, along with changes in spatial judgment.

rows.text: Neutropenic and alone in a protective room with no visitors for a week; now tearful with sudden mood swings
rows.rationale: A protective room with no visitors gives too little meaningful stimulation for days. Tearfulness and sudden mood swings are affective effects of deprivation, described as depression and emotional lability.

rows.text: Severe chronic pain that flares each evening on a busy medical unit; restless and anxious
rows.rationale: Chronic pain is itself a constant stimulus, and a busy unit adds more on top of it. Restlessness and anxiety appear when the brain cannot screen out that much input.

rows.text: Ten days in a single room on a quiet ward with nothing to look at; colors seem dull and her coordination has slipped
rows.rationale: A quiet room with nothing to look at is a restricted environment with little stimulation. Changes in color perception and coordination are perceptual effects of deprivation rather than of excess input.

questions.takeaway: Confusion and anxiety appear with both problems, so the setting decides: isolation, bed rest and restricted rooms point to deprivation, while emergency care, intensive care, chronic pain and frequent monitoring point to overload.
questions.strategy: Anxiety and confusion show up in both columns, so a single symptom misleads. Count the stimuli in each setting first, then check that the effects fit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Too little meaningful stimulation means deprivation; too much to filter means overload.
Isolation, bed rest and empty rooms against emergency care, chronic pain and frequent checks.
Mood swings, time and color changes fit deprivation; racing thoughts and tube pulling fit overload.

elimination.verdict: Deprivation: the protective room, bed rest at home and the quiet ward. Overload: the emergency department, the nightly neurological checks and the chronic pain.

questions.objective: Describe normal sensory function and types of sensory alterations.
questions.concept: Deprivation versus overload: settings and effects

questions.stem: In the intensive care unit, a patient is restless and calls staff by the wrong names when they approach. Alarm volumes were lowered and her care is already combined into fewer visits. Her family says she wears glasses and two hearing aids at home; both are in a bag in her bedside drawer. Which action is best now?

options.text: Arrange for a staff member to sit at her bedside
options.rationale: Constant observation keeps a restless patient safe, but it is more supervision than she needs yet. It also leaves her uncorrected vision and hearing deficits in place.

options.text: Put her glasses and hearing aids on her
options.rationale: The overload measures are in place, yet she still misreads people because she cannot see or hear them clearly. Patients often have more than one alteration, and her devices treat the deficit underneath.

options.text: Darken the room and extend her quiet time
options.rationale: More quiet time is a reasonable overload measure and is partly in place already. Darkness makes it even harder for a woman with poor vision to recognize who is approaching.

options.text: Reorient her to place and staff every hour
options.rationale: Frequent reorientation is a sound acute care measure. Telling her who people are does little when she cannot see their faces or hear their voices, so it works better once her devices are on.

questions.takeaway: Patients often have more than one sensory alteration; check for a deficit and restore working devices before adding more stimulus control.
questions.strategy: Every distractor treats overload, which is already managed. The bag of devices in the drawer is the unaddressed cue.

steps.detail: Alarms are lowered and care is combined, yet she still misidentifies staff.
Her glasses and hearing aids are in a drawer, so she has an uncorrected deficit.
Devices let her recognize people; the other choices add measures she may not need.

elimination.verdict: Put her glasses and hearing aids on her.

questions.objective: Describe normal sensory function and types of sensory alterations.

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating care for a resident of a long term care facility who became withdrawn and forgetful after his roommate moved out and family visits dropped off. His plan added weekly pet therapy visits, a radio tuned to his favorite station and a large calendar. Which finding 2 weeks later best shows the plan is working?

options.text: His daughter says the unit feels livelier now
options.rationale: Her impression is welcome, but it describes the setting rather than the patient. Evaluation needs a change in his own behavior or orientation.

options.text: He sleeps most of the day and rarely calls
options.rationale: Fewer calls can look like contentment to busy staff. Sleeping all day and asking for nothing show ongoing withdrawal, so the deprivation has not resolved.

options.text: He greets the dog by name and knows the day
options.rationale: Engaging with a meaningful stimulus and knowing the day show his mood and orientation are recovering. Those affective and cognitive effects of deprivation are what the plan targeted.

options.text: He plays the radio but asks what month it is
options.rationale: Using the radio shows the stimulus is in place and he is engaging with it. Still asking the month shows his disorientation persists, so the goal is only partly met.

questions.takeaway: Deprivation is resolving when the patient engages with meaningful stimuli and his orientation and mood improve, not when he becomes quiet.
questions.strategy: A quiet patient who asks for nothing can look improved. Choose the finding that shows both engagement and restored orientation in the patient himself.

steps.detail: Withdrawal and forgetfulness were the problems.
Sleeping and not calling are withdrawal, not recovery.
Engagement and orientation together show full improvement.

elimination.verdict: He greets the dog by name and knows the day.

questions.objective: Describe normal sensory function and types of sensory alterations.

questions.stem: Two days after starting an opioid for knee pain, a warehouse forklift driver who is back at work after knee surgery tells the occupational health nurse that she feels slowed and has twice misjudged the distance to a shelf. Her vision screening last month was normal. Which action is best?

options.text: Keep her off the forklift and contact the prescriber today
options.rationale: Opioids can impair perception, and her change began when the drug did, after a normal vision screening. Removing her from the forklift prevents injury while the prescriber reviews the cause.

options.text: Refer her for a repeat vision screening this week
options.rationale: A vision check fits a new problem with judging distance. Her screening was normal last month and the timing points to the new drug, so another screening misses the cause.

options.text: Tell her to raise the change at her next routine visit
options.rationale: Reporting to the prescriber is right, but waiting leaves her operating heavy machinery with impaired perception. The safety risk is present today, so the report cannot wait.

options.text: Teach her to slow down when turning near the shelves
options.rationale: Driving more slowly is sensible advice for any operator. It does not remove the hazard, because perception dulled by a drug is not corrected by trying harder.

questions.takeaway: Opioids and psychotropic drugs can impair perception; when a new drug matches a new change, remove the hazard and contact the prescriber now.
questions.strategy: Reporting at the next visit has the right idea but the wrong timing. The heavy machinery makes the risk immediate.

steps.detail: Slowed thinking and misjudged distance began with the opioid 2 days ago.
Her vision screening was normal last month.
Stop the hazardous task and contact the prescriber today.

elimination.verdict: Keep her off the forklift and contact the prescriber today.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect sensory perception and function.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with a leg infection has long standing hearing loss and followed conversation well with his hearing aids on admission. On day 4, in a quiet private room with both aids freshly checked and working, he cannot follow what staff say. Which item in his record most needs follow up?

options.text: No family visits since he was admitted
options.rationale: Lack of visitors can cause loneliness and deprivation over time. It does not explain a measurable drop in hearing in a quiet room with working aids.

options.text: His long standing hearing loss in both ears
options.rationale: His baseline loss is real, but hearing aids corrected it well on admission. A worsening that begins in the hospital is new and cannot be blamed on a loss that was already managed.

options.text: An aminoglycoside antibiotic started on admission
options.rationale: Aminoglycosides are ototoxic, and his hearing worsened in the days after the drug began while his aids work normally. A new decline in that time frame needs a prompt report to the provider.

options.text: A diuretic he has taken daily for 10 years
options.rationale: Diuretics can also damage hearing, so this is the near miss. He heard well on admission after a decade on it, so it does not explain a change that began this week.

questions.takeaway: A new hearing decline after an ototoxic drug is started needs prompt follow up; match the onset of the change to what changed in the record.
questions.strategy: Two choices are ototoxic drugs. The one that began just before the change is the cause; the one he took for years while hearing well is not.

steps.action: Rule out the environment and devices
steps.detail: The room is quiet and both aids were checked and work.
Both can harm hearing; only the antibiotic is new.
Hearing dropped in the days after admission, when the aminoglycoside began.

elimination.verdict: An aminoglycoside antibiotic started on admission.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect sensory perception and function.

questions.stem: During a work physical at a community clinic, a patient who moved to the country 2 years ago and speaks limited English holds the intake form at arm's length and squints, and through her daughter she says print in her own language has also become blurry. She has not had an eye examination in 10 years because of cost and bus travel. Which action is best?

options.text: Use an interpreter and refer her to a low cost eye clinic
options.rationale: Cost and travel are access barriers that help explain higher rates of vision impairment in some groups. A trained interpreter ensures she understands, and an affordable referral removes the barrier the nurse can address.

options.text: Have her daughter read the form and fill it in
options.rationale: Family help gets the form finished today. It relies on her daughter to interpret health information and leaves the missed screening and blurry vision unaddressed.

options.text: Suggest she buy reading glasses at a local pharmacy
options.rationale: Pharmacy reading glasses cost little and may help her read. They skip the examination she has missed for 10 years, so another cause of her blurry vision could go undetected.

options.text: Advise her to book an eye exam once she has health insurance
options.rationale: Insurance may come later, and the barrier she describes is real. Waiting leaves an unexamined vision problem in place when the nurse could connect her with affordable care now.

questions.takeaway: Disparities in vision and hearing impairment are tied to barriers in access to care; the nurse detects the problem and refers to care the patient can reach.
questions.strategy: The pharmacy glasses and the daughter's help solve today's form. Choose the option that removes the access barrier behind 10 years without an examination.

steps.detail: She squints and sees blurry print in her own language, so this is vision, not only language.
Cost and bus travel have kept her from care for 10 years.
An interpreter for clear communication and an affordable eye clinic.

elimination.verdict: Use an interpreter and refer her to a low cost eye clinic.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect sensory perception and function.
questions.concept: Cultural factors and access to care

questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.
questions.scenario: On the second day after abdominal surgery, a patient is recovering on a busy surgical unit. Staff enter about every 15 minutes for separate tasks, his roommate's television runs until 0200, and the hallway lights stay bright all night. He is restless, says his thoughts are racing, cannot follow the plan for walking and keeps picking at his abdominal dressing. His pain is 2 on a 0 to 10 scale, his oxygen saturation is 97% on room air, and he stated the correct date this morning.

options.text: Schedule rest periods with a quiet time and dimmed lights at night
options.rationale: Scheduled rest and quiet time give his brain a break from input it cannot filter. Dimming the lights at night also supports sleep, which overload disrupts.

options.text: Apply mitts so he cannot reach the dressing
options.rationale: Protecting the incision is a fair concern, but mitts are more restrictive than his situation calls for. Reducing the stimulation that drives the picking comes first.

options.text: Add a radio at the bedside for distraction
options.rationale: Music is a meaningful stimulus that helps deprivation. For a patient already overwhelmed, it adds one more input his brain cannot screen out.

options.text: Combine assessments, medications and dressing care into fewer visits
options.rationale: Staff entering every 15 minutes is a major source of his stimulation. Combining activities cuts the interruptions without withholding any care he needs.

options.text: Sensory deprivation
options.rationale: Deprivation also causes confusion and poor problem solving. His room has far too much input rather than too little, so the setting rules it out.

options.text: A new hearing deficit
options.rationale: A missed deficit can cause mismatched responses and confusion. Nothing suggests he cannot hear; he hears plenty and cannot filter it.

options.text: Sensory overload
options.rationale: Frequent entries, late television and constant light give excessive stimulation on a busy unit. Racing thoughts, restlessness and handling the dressing are classic overload effects.

options.text: Uncontrolled postoperative pain
options.rationale: Pain can cause restlessness after surgery and deserves checking. His pain is 2 on a 0 to 10 scale, which does not explain this degree of agitation.

options.text: Restlessness and handling of the dressing
options.rationale: These behaviors are direct effects of his overload. If they settle after stimulation is reduced, the plan is working.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks fluid balance after surgery and may be ordered for other reasons. It shows nothing about whether his sensory overload is improving.

options.text: Ability to follow conversation and instructions
options.rationale: Scattered attention kept him from following the walking plan. Being able to follow instructions again shows his brain is processing input meaningfully.

options.text: Number of visitors each day
options.rationale: Visitor numbers matter for a patient at risk of isolation and deprivation. More visitors would add stimulation for him, so counting them does not measure his recovery.

questions.takeaway: Overload is managed by cutting stimulation: combine care, schedule rest and quiet time, and watch whether restlessness settles and attention returns.
questions.strategy: Restraining him or adding distraction are the near misses; one ignores the cause and the other adds input. His controlled pain and normal oxygen saturation rule out the physical causes.

steps.detail: Oxygen saturation 97% and pain 2 on a 0 to 10 scale do not explain his behavior.
Entries every 15 minutes, a television until 0200 and bright lights all night: overload.
Combine care and schedule rest; reject mitts and a radio.
Restlessness, dressing handling and ability to follow conversation.

elimination.verdict: Overload; combine care into fewer visits and schedule rest with quiet time; monitor restlessness with dressing handling and his ability to follow instructions.

questions.objective: Describe normal sensory function and types of sensory alterations.

questions.stem: At a workplace screening, a 46 year old machinist says he turns the television up more than he did last year. He works 10 hours daily beside grinding machines and wears safety glasses but no ear protection. Which action is best?

options.text: Advise him to add side shields to his safety glasses
options.rationale: Side shields improve eye protection against flying particles. His symptom is hearing loss, and his ears are the part left unprotected.

options.text: Teach ear protection at work and refer him for a hearing test
options.rationale: Prolonged noise exposure is a preventable cause of hearing loss, and he has a daily exposure with no protection. Teaching and referral are the nurse's role in prevention and early detection.

options.text: Explain that hearing declines in the 40s and recheck him next year
options.rationale: Hearing changes can begin in the 40s, so his age is a real factor. Blaming age ignores an unprotected noise exposure that is still harming his hearing every workday.

options.text: Suggest he keep the television volume low at home
options.rationale: Lower volume at home is reasonable for anyone. The damaging noise is ten hours a day at work, so this advice misses the main source.

questions.takeaway: Do not settle for age as the explanation when an unprotected noise exposure is present; teach protection and refer for testing.
questions.strategy: Age in the 40s is a true factor, which makes blaming it attractive. The daily unprotected noise is the cause the nurse can change.

steps.detail: Ten hours daily beside grinders with no ear protection.
Age is real, but it does not account for an active hazard.
Teach protection and refer for testing.

elimination.verdict: Teach ear protection at work and refer him for a hearing test.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect sensory perception and function.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a 68 year old patient who says that over the last few years he has had to watch his feet on the stairs, and he feels unsteady on them at night. He takes no new medications, his vision examination last month was normal, and his provider found no new cause at a checkup last week. Which teaching is best?

options.text: Move his bedroom downstairs and stop using the stairs
options.rationale: Avoiding the stairs removes one hazard but limits his mobility more than his problem requires. A gradual, expected change can be managed with simple adaptations instead.

options.text: Report the unsteadiness to the provider today
options.rationale: Sudden changes need prompt reporting rather than being blamed on age. His change came on gradually over years and his provider found no new cause last week, so it fits expected aging after 60.

options.text: Ask his eye doctor for stronger glasses
options.rationale: Seeing the steps better would help, but his vision examination was normal last month. Stronger glasses would not replace the position sense he has lost.

options.text: Light the stairway at night and use the handrail
options.rationale: Position sense declines after 60, so older adults depend more on sight to place their feet. Good lighting and a secure handrail make up for that loss and lower his fall risk.

questions.takeaway: Proprioceptive changes after 60 make older adults rely on vision for balance; lighting and handrails reduce fall risk.
questions.strategy: Reporting today is right for sudden change, which makes it tempting. A change that developed gradually over years with no new drug fits expected aging.

steps.detail: Gradual over several years, no new drugs, and a provider checkup last week found nothing new.
Position sense declines after 60, and vision compensates.
Light the stairs and use the handrail; avoid all or nothing restrictions.

elimination.verdict: Light the stairway at night and use the handrail.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect sensory perception and function.

questions.stem: On day 5 of contact isolation, a patient who has had no visitors has become withdrawn and tearful. His daughter tells the nurse that putting on a gown and gloves is a bother and that he just sleeps anyway. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: You can phone the unit each day, and we will pass on your messages.
options.rationale: Messages keep some contact and are better than nothing. They do not replace the face to face social interaction whose absence is causing his withdrawal.

options.text: It is safer for you to stay away until his isolation ends.
options.rationale: Contact isolation allows visitors who wear the right protective equipment. Telling her to stay away removes his main social contact and deepens the isolation behind his low mood.

options.text: Visits help him while he is isolated. I can show you how to gown.
options.rationale: Absence of visitors leads to isolation, loneliness and depression, which match his withdrawal and tears. Teaching her to gown removes her barrier and makes visiting safe for both of them.

options.text: I will ask the provider if a medication could help his mood.
options.rationale: A drug may be considered if low mood persists after the cause is addressed. The cause here is a lack of social contact, which the nurse can fix directly.

questions.takeaway: Lack of visitors causes isolation, loneliness and depression; make visiting possible by teaching family how to use protective equipment.
questions.strategy: Staying away sounds like infection control, but contact isolation permits protected visits. The best response treats his loneliness and her barrier together.

steps.detail: Five days without visitors and new tearful withdrawal.
Contact isolation allows visitors in a gown and gloves.
Teach the daughter to gown so she can visit.

elimination.verdict: Visits help him while he is isolated. I can show you how to gown.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect sensory perception and function.

questions.stem: During an admission interview, a woman gives answers that do not match the questions and nods at everything the nurse says. Her daughter reports that her mother was managing her own bills at home yesterday. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Ask the daughter whether her mother uses hearing aids or glasses
options.rationale: Mismatched answers and nodding are cues of a hearing problem, and her daughter's report shows her thinking was sharp yesterday. Establishing her baseline and her devices comes before judging her cognition.

options.text: Review her medication list for drugs that cloud thinking
options.rationale: Drugs can cloud thinking and deserve review at some point. The cues point first to a missed hearing deficit, which one question to the daughter can confirm.

options.text: Complete a mental status examination using standard questions now
options.rationale: A mental status examination may be needed later. If she cannot hear the questions, the results will wrongly suggest confusion, so the hearing question comes first.

options.text: Orient her to the room, the bathroom and the call light
options.rationale: Orientation is part of every admission and keeps her safe. Teaching she cannot hear will not stick, so the communication barrier has to be identified first.

questions.takeaway: Establish the patient's baseline and any existing deficit before interpreting her behavior; a hearing deficit can look like confusion.
questions.strategy: The mental status examination looks like the logical assessment, but its results depend on her hearing the questions. Find out about her devices first.

steps.detail: Mismatched answers and nodding at everything suggest she is not hearing.
Managing her own bills yesterday argues against confusion.
Confirm hearing aids or glasses before testing cognition or teaching.

elimination.verdict: Ask the daughter whether her mother uses hearing aids or glasses.

questions.objective: Assess patients for sensory deficits and related safety risks.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with gradually worsening vision in both eyes who lives alone and fills his own weekly pill organizer for several heart medications. Which assessment gives the nurse the most information about his safety at home?

options.text: Ask him to state the date, the place and his address
options.rationale: Orientation questions assess his mental status. His problem is vision, and a fully oriented man can still misread a label he cannot see.

options.text: Ask whether he keeps his glasses where he can find them
options.rationale: Accessible glasses are part of assessing assistive devices. Keeping glasses nearby does not prove he can read small print with them, which only watching him can show.

options.text: Ask how often family or friends stop by his home
options.rationale: Social support matters for someone who lives alone and is part of the assessment. It does not show whether he can read his labels and dose his drugs correctly.

options.text: Watch him read his bottle labels and fill the organizer
options.rationale: Functional ability means whether he can safely perform tasks such as reading labels. Watching him do the task shows directly whether his vision allows accurate dosing.

questions.takeaway: Assess functional ability by observing the patient perform the actual task, such as reading labels, rather than by asking about it.
questions.strategy: Every choice is a real part of the sensory assessment. The tiebreaker is which one shows whether he can dose his drugs safely.

steps.detail: Misreading labels could lead to wrong doses of heart drugs.
Watching the task gives better evidence than asking about it.
Functional ability tests the task itself.

elimination.verdict: Watch him read his bottle labels and fill the organizer.

questions.objective: Assess patients for sensory deficits and related safety risks.

questions.stem: At an annual clinic visit, the nurse reviews a patient's health history. Which findings increase this patient's risk for a sensory alteration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Has had hypertension for 12 years
options.rationale: Hypertension is a health status factor that increases the risk of sensory problems. Long standing high blood pressure can damage the small vessels that serve the eyes and other sense organs.

options.text: Wears safety goggles when using a power drill at home
options.rationale: Flying objects from tools are an occupational hazard to the eyes. Wearing goggles is the protective behavior that lowers the risk instead of raising it.

options.text: Takes a psychotropic medication every night
options.rationale: Psychotropic drugs are among the medications that can impair perception. Taking one nightly is a medication factor the nurse should note during the history.

options.text: Keeps a dog and listens to the radio each morning
options.rationale: Pets and music are meaningful stimuli that help prevent deprivation. They protect sensory function rather than threaten it.

options.text: Sprays crop pesticides each week without wearing goggles
options.rationale: Chemical exposure is an occupational hazard that can injure the eyes and impair sight. Spraying without goggles leaves her eyes open to splashes and drift every week.

options.text: Walks with a neighborhood group three times a week
options.rationale: Regular social contact with a group is protective against isolation. It adds meaningful stimulation and does not raise sensory risk.

options.text: Has lived alone with no visitors since moving 6 months ago
options.rationale: Lack of social interaction leads to isolation, loneliness and depression over time. Six months without visitors removes a major source of meaningful stimulation.

questions.takeaway: Unprotected chemical exposure, chronic illness such as hypertension, perception altering drugs and social isolation raise risk; pets, music, social contact and protective gear lower it.
questions.strategy: Several distractors mention a hazard but describe the protective behavior. Read each for whether it adds risk or reduces it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Environmental, health status, medication and social factors each appear.
Goggles, pets, music and group walks protect; they do not add risk.
Unprotected chemical spraying, hypertension, a psychotropic drug and isolation.

elimination.verdict: Pesticide spraying without goggles, hypertension, the nightly psychotropic drug and 6 months without visitors.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect sensory perception and function.
questions.concept: Factors that raise risk of sensory alteration

questions.stem: A patient with low vision is on strict bed rest and uses reading glasses and a handheld magnifier to choose his meals and read his teaching sheets. During morning rounds, which finding should the nurse follow up?

options.text: He takes his glasses off to sleep and puts them on to read
options.rationale: Taking glasses off for sleep is a normal habit and does not limit his reading. The problem would be where they go afterward, which this finding does not show to be unsafe.

options.text: His glasses are in a case on the windowsill across the room
options.rationale: Devices help only when they are accessible, and a man on strict bed rest cannot reach a windowsill across the room. Placing the glasses within reach lets him read without getting up unsafely.

options.text: He reads his menu choices aloud correctly with his glasses on
options.rationale: Reading his choices correctly shows his glasses are functional for the task. Watching him use the device is good evidence, and here it confirms there is nothing to correct.

options.text: His magnifier is on the overbed table next to his menu
options.rationale: The magnifier sits exactly where he needs it for choosing meals. A device that is within reach for the task it serves shows this part of his care is working.

questions.takeaway: Assess assistive devices for both function and access; a working device placed out of reach does not help the patient and invites an unsafe attempt to get it.
questions.strategy: Three findings show the devices working, which makes the room look fine. Strict bed rest is the cue that turns a case on a far windowsill into a safety risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Does each device work, and can he reach it from bed?
He reads his menu with his glasses, so they work.
Glasses across the room are out of reach for a man on strict bed rest.

elimination.verdict: His glasses are in a case on the windowsill across the room.

questions.objective: Assess patients for sensory deficits and related safety risks.

questions.stem: On admission to an unfamiliar hospital room, a patient who has had very little vision in either eye for several years tells the nurse that he usually walks to the bathroom twice each night, that he misses his wife, and that he feels nervous about being in a strange place. Which nursing diagnosis is the priority?

options.text: Impaired socialization
options.rationale: Missing his wife is real and deserves attention during his stay. Loneliness is a belonging need, which ranks below a risk of injury that could happen tonight.

options.text: Anxiety
options.rationale: His nervousness is an actual problem and should be addressed with orientation and reassurance. A fall at night could cause serious injury, so safety outranks it even though anxiety is already present.

options.text: Impaired verbal communication
options.rationale: Vision loss does not affect his speech or hearing, and he states his needs clearly. Nothing in his report suggests a barrier to communication.

options.text: Risk for falls
options.rationale: Walking at night through a room he cannot see and does not know is a direct threat to his physical safety. Safety needs come before the psychosocial needs he also describes.

questions.takeaway: Risk for injury or falls is the priority diagnosis for a patient with sensory loss in an unfamiliar setting, ahead of socialization and anxiety.
questions.strategy: Anxiety is an actual problem and fall risk is only a risk, which tempts students to pick anxiety. A threat to physical safety tonight outranks a psychosocial problem.

steps.detail: Night walks in an unknown room, loneliness and nervousness.
Physical safety comes before belonging and emotional needs.
He speaks and hears normally, so communication is not impaired.

elimination.verdict: Risk for falls.

questions.objective: Assess patients for sensory deficits and related safety risks.
questions.concept: Priority nursing diagnosis with sensory loss

questions.stem: The nurse is interviewing a 78 year old patient who says reading print has become harder over the past several years. She adds that since she woke this morning she cannot see clearly out of her right eye. Her yearly eye examination is scheduled for next month. Which action is best?

options.text: Report the change in her right eye to the provider today
options.rationale: Her gradual trouble with print fits aging, but vision loss in one eye since this morning is sudden and new. Sudden changes are not assumed to be age related and need prompt reporting.

options.text: Teach her to use a magnifier and large print labels
options.rationale: Magnifiers and large print help with her slow decline in reading. They do nothing for a sudden loss in one eye, which needs evaluation first.

options.text: Tell her to mention the right eye at next month's examination
options.rationale: Her yearly examination is the right place to follow the gradual change. Waiting a month to report a sudden loss treats a new problem as if it were expected aging.

options.text: Arrange a home safety assessment for this week
options.rationale: A home safety assessment suits her gradual loss of vision and may be needed soon. Arranging it does not address the new change that began this morning.

questions.takeaway: Gradual change can fit aging, but a new or sudden change is never assumed to be age related; report it promptly.
questions.strategy: The magnifier and home safety choices answer the gradual problem she mentions first. The sudden change since this morning is what decides the priority.

steps.detail: Years of slow print difficulty and a sudden change since this morning.
New or sudden changes are not blamed on age.
Report today rather than wait a month.

elimination.verdict: Report the change in her right eye to the provider today.

questions.objective: Assess patients for sensory deficits and related safety risks.
questions.concept: New or sudden changes are not aging

questions.stem: A patient with aphasia after a left sided stroke does not answer when asked his name or the date, and assistive personnel report that he is confused. When the nurse asks, he follows a two step command and points to the correct pictures on a picture board. Which action is best?

options.text: Reorient him to person, place and date at every visit
options.rationale: Reorientation helps a patient who is disoriented. He is not, so repeating it treats a problem he does not have and can feel demeaning to him.

options.text: Add a bed alarm and move him near the nurses' station
options.rationale: A bed alarm suits a confused patient who may get up unsafely. His cognition is intact, so the label driving this restriction is wrong.

options.text: Record that he understands speech, and use the board
options.rationale: Following commands and pointing correctly show his thinking and understanding are intact; his deficit is in producing speech. Recording this corrects the confusion label and keeps the method that works.

options.text: Repeat the orientation questions and wait longer for an answer
options.rationale: Allowing extra time is a good strategy with aphasia in general. Asking for spoken answers he cannot produce tests his speech rather than his orientation and adds frustration.

questions.takeaway: Assess mental status through the patient's behavior during interaction and his communication method; a speech deficit is not confusion.
questions.strategy: The report of confusion invites reorientation. His response to commands and the picture board is the evidence that overrules it.

steps.detail: No spoken answers led to a report of confusion.
He follows a two step command and points correctly.
Record intact understanding and keep using the board.

elimination.verdict: Record that he understands speech, and use the board.

questions.objective: Assess patients for sensory deficits and related safety risks.

questions.stem: A home health nurse visits a woman with low vision in both eyes. Highlight the findings that need follow up for her safety.
questions.nursesNote: 1400 Home visit. Lives alone in a two story house; her daughter visits every Sunday. States she feels her way down the stairs, which have plain gray carpet and no handrail on the left side. Wearing her current glasses, she reads her large print calendar without difficulty. Two loose throw rugs lie in the front hall. Kitchen is lit by a bright fluorescent tube, and she says the glare at the counter makes it hard to see. Keeps her pill bottles in the same basket on the table. Grab bars are installed beside the toilet. States she has not left the house in 3 weeks and has stopped calling friends.

segments.text: her daughter visits every Sunday
segments.rationale: A weekly visit from family is a source of support and a chance to notice problems. It is a strength in her social situation, not a hazard.

segments.text: plain gray carpet and no handrail on the left side
segments.rationale: Stairs without contrast at the edges and with a missing handrail are a major fall risk for someone with low vision. Painting the edges and adding a secure rail are needed.

segments.text: she reads her large print calendar without difficulty
segments.rationale: Reading the calendar with her current glasses shows her devices work for large print. This finding supports her independence rather than signaling a risk.

segments.text: Two loose throw rugs lie in the front hall
segments.rationale: Throw rugs are a classic trip hazard, especially for a person who cannot see the edges. They should be removed from her walking paths.

segments.text: the glare at the counter makes it hard to see
segments.rationale: Fluorescent lighting creates glare that lowers what she can see while she prepares food. Warm incandescent light adjusted to reduce glare is safer.

segments.text: Keeps her pill bottles in the same basket on the table
segments.rationale: Keeping objects in a consistent place helps a person with low vision find them reliably. This is a safe habit to encourage.

segments.text: Grab bars are installed beside the toilet
segments.rationale: Grab bars address bathroom safety, one of the hazards the nurse assesses. Their presence shows that this risk is already managed.

segments.text: has not left the house in 3 weeks and has stopped calling friends
segments.rationale: Withdrawing from friends and staying home for weeks shows impaired socialization, which sensory loss often causes. It needs follow up as much as the physical hazards do.

questions.takeaway: Assess the home for trip risks, lighting, stairs and bathroom safety, and ask about social contact, since withdrawal signals impaired socialization.
questions.strategy: Several findings mention a safety feature that is already in place. Highlight only what still poses a risk to her now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stairs without contrast or a full handrail, loose rugs, glare from fluorescent light.
Three weeks at home and no calls to friends point to impaired socialization.
Weekly visits, readable calendar, consistent pill basket and grab bars.

elimination.verdict: Highlight the stairs, the throw rugs, the glare and her withdrawal from friends.

questions.objective: Assess patients for sensory deficits and related safety risks.
questions.concept: Environmental hazards and social support at home

questions.stem: The daughter of an older patient with low vision in both eyes lists four changes she plans for his new apartment, which has fluorescent ceiling tubes, throw rugs in the hall and a carpeted staircase. Which change should the nurse support?

options.text: Tape the hall throw rugs firmly to the floor
options.rationale: Taping keeps the rugs from sliding, so it looks like a reasonable compromise. Their edges can still catch his feet, and the safe step is to remove throw rugs from his walking paths.

options.text: Swap the tube lights for shaded warm incandescent lamps
options.rationale: Fluorescent tubes create glare that cuts what a person with low vision can see. Warm incandescent light with shades to soften the brightness is the recommended way to light his home.

options.text: Put the brightest bulbs available in every room
options.rationale: Older eyes do need more light, so brighter bulbs seem like the obvious fix. Maximum brightness adds glare, though, and lighting should be adjusted to reduce glare rather than pushed to its highest level.

options.text: Cover the stairs with one dark runner to match
options.rationale: A matching runner makes the stairs look tidy and adds some grip underfoot. It erases the contrast he needs to see each step; stair edges should stand out, such as with bright yellow paint.

questions.takeaway: For low vision, light the home with warm, glare reduced lamps rather than the brightest bulbs, remove throw rugs instead of taping them, and give stair edges sharp contrast.
questions.strategy: Brighter bulbs and taped rugs are partial fixes that feel helpful but leave glare or a trip edge in place. Choose the change that removes the hazard instead of softening it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warm, shaded light beats maximum brightness, which adds glare.
Throw rugs are removed, not taped down.
Stair edges should stand out, not blend into a dark runner.

elimination.verdict: Support swapping the tube lights for shaded warm incandescent lamps.

questions.objective: Apply nursing interventions to promote safety and effective communication.
questions.concept: Home safety adaptations for low vision

questions.stem: After home safety teaching for the son of a patient with low vision who lives alone, the nurse evaluates his understanding. Which statement by the son shows the teaching needs follow up?

options.text: I took up the rugs in the hallway and the bedroom.
options.rationale: Removing throw rugs clears her paths of a common trip hazard. This statement shows he understood the teaching.

options.text: I put a bright yellow strip along the edge of each step.
options.rationale: Sharp contrast on stair edges helps her see where each step ends. This is a correct adaptation that needs no correction.

options.text: Each time I visit, I move her kitchen things to better spots.
options.rationale: Moving her things, even into better places, removes the consistent locations she relies on to find them. She needs a predictable space, so the son needs more teaching.

options.text: I swapped the tube lights for warm bulbs with shades.
options.rationale: Warm, shaded lighting reduces the glare that fluorescent tubes cause. This change matches the teaching on lighting for low vision.

questions.takeaway: Keeping objects in consistent locations is a safety measure; well meant rearranging undoes it.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement sounds helpful and caring. Ask whether each change keeps her space predictable.

steps.detail: Look for the statement that shows a misunderstanding.
Rugs removed, contrast added and glare reduced are all correct.
Moving her things each visit undoes predictable placement.

elimination.verdict: Each time I visit, I move her kitchen things to better spots.

questions.objective: Apply nursing interventions to promote safety and effective communication.
questions.concept: Home safety adaptations for low vision

questions.stem: Assistive personnel caring for a newly admitted patient with severe vision loss in both eyes and normal hearing tell the nurse, 'I talk to him loudly and slowly so he understands me.' Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: Speak normally, describe objects, and let him touch them
options.rationale: His hearing is normal, so a loud, slow voice is unnecessary and can feel condescending. Detailed description and touch replace the information his eyes cannot give him.

options.text: Do his grooming and meal setup so he does not get hurt
options.rationale: Protecting him from injury is a fair goal for assistive personnel. Taking over his care removes independence he can keep with orientation and description.

options.text: Keep the slow pace and add large print labels to his things
options.rationale: Large print can help a patient with some usable vision. Severe loss in both eyes may make print useless, and the slow pace is still unneeded for a man who hears normally.

options.text: Use a normal voice, and set the call light wherever is handy
options.rationale: Speaking normally is correct for a patient with vision loss. Placing the call light in a different spot each time defeats consistent placement, so he cannot find it when he needs help.

questions.takeaway: With vision loss, speak normally, describe objects in detail and allow touch; save slow, face to face speech for hearing loss.
questions.strategy: One distractor starts with the right voice and then breaks consistent placement. Read the whole option before choosing.

steps.detail: Vision is lost; hearing is normal.
Loud, slow speech is the hearing loss strategy and is not needed here.
A normal voice plus an inconsistent call light still fails.

elimination.verdict: Speak normally, describe objects, and let him touch them.

questions.objective: Apply nursing interventions to promote safety and effective communication.
questions.concept: Communicating with a patient who has vision loss

questions.stem: While teaching about a new medication, the nurse notes that a patient with hearing loss in both ears cannot follow. The nurse is standing at the foot of the bed, looking down at the chart while talking. Which change is best?

options.text: Leave a written sheet for him to read on his own later
options.rationale: Written information is part of good teaching for hearing loss. Leaving it without explaining in person gives him no chance to ask questions or show understanding.

options.text: Move closer and speak much louder into one of his ears
options.rationale: Moving closer seems helpful, but shouting distorts words and can sound angry. Standing at his ear also hides the nurse's face, which he needs to see.

options.text: Teach his wife and ask her to explain it to him at home
options.rationale: Including family can reinforce teaching after discharge. Bypassing him when he can learn with the right approach denies him his own teaching.

options.text: Face him, speak slowly, and add written information
options.rationale: Facing him lets him see the nurse's lips and expressions, and slow, clear speech is easier to follow than volume. Written information backs up what he may miss.

questions.takeaway: For hearing loss, face the patient, speak slowly and clearly without shouting, and add written information.
questions.strategy: Louder speech is the instinct, but it distorts words. The fix is position and pace, not volume.

steps.detail: Standing at the foot of the bed looking down hides the nurse's face.
Shouting distorts speech.
Face him, slow down, and back it up in writing.

elimination.verdict: Face him, speak slowly, and add written information.

questions.objective: Apply nursing interventions to promote safety and effective communication.
questions.concept: Communicating with a patient who has hearing loss

questions.stem: At 2200, a patient who hears poorly even with both hearing aids in is moved to a new room and needs to learn the call light now. Her reading glasses were left at home. Which approach is best?

options.text: Hand her a printed sheet and point to each step
options.rationale: Written information is a standard support for hearing loss. Without her reading glasses she may not read the sheet, so it cannot carry the teaching tonight.

options.text: Face her, speak slowly and have her show the steps back
options.rationale: Face to face, slow speech is the main strategy for hearing loss and does not depend on her reading. Having her show the steps confirms she can call for help tonight.

options.text: Wait until family bring her glasses in the morning
options.rationale: Her glasses would help with written material. Waiting leaves her in a new room overnight unable to call for help, which is a safety risk now.

options.text: Speak loudly near her ear and repeat all the steps twice
options.rationale: Repetition helps, but shouting distorts words and hides the nurse's face. Lip reading and facial cues are lost when the nurse stands at her ear.

questions.takeaway: Choose the communication strategy that fits all of the patient's deficits at once, and confirm understanding by return demonstration.
questions.strategy: Written information is the usual backup for hearing loss, which makes the printed sheet attractive. Her missing glasses take it away tonight.

steps.detail: Poor hearing with aids, and no reading glasses.

steps.action: Cut what depends on the missing sense
steps.detail: Printed sheets need her glasses.
Teach face to face now and check with return demonstration.

elimination.verdict: Face her, speak slowly and have her show the steps back.

questions.objective: Apply nursing interventions to promote safety and effective communication.
questions.concept: Communicating with a patient who has hearing loss

questions.stem: On a medical unit, the nurse admits a patient who has almost no vision in either eye. Place the nurse's actions in the order they should be performed.

options.text: Walk her from the bed to the bathroom, describing each object and letting her touch it
options.rationale: Complete orientation to the environment is the core acute care measure for vision loss. Describing objects in detail and allowing touch help her build a mental map.

options.text: Say her name and introduce yourself as you enter the room
options.rationale: A patient who cannot see needs to know who has entered before anything else happens. Announcing yourself prevents startling her and builds trust for the rest of the admission.

options.text: Have her find the call light and the bathroom on her own
options.rationale: Her own demonstration shows whether the orientation worked before you leave her alone. It is the evaluation step that confirms she can stay safe.

options.text: Place the call light within reach and guide her hand to it
options.rationale: An accessible call light is a key safety measure once she knows the room. Guiding her hand lets her locate it by touch rather than by sight.

options.text: Ask what she can see and how she prefers to be guided
options.rationale: Assessment comes before intervention, and her remaining vision and preferences shape how you orient her. Engaging the patient in what works best makes the orientation fit her.

questions.takeaway: Announce yourself, learn how the patient prefers to be helped, orient her by description and touch, secure the call light, then confirm she can find things on her own.
questions.strategy: Students often place the call light first because it is a safety measure. She cannot use a call light she has not located, so orientation comes before it and her own demonstration comes last.

steps.detail: A patient who cannot see needs to know who is in the room.
Ask what she sees and how she likes to be guided.
Walk the room, then place and show the call light.
She finds the call light and bathroom herself.

elimination.verdict: Introduce yourself, ask her preferences, orient her to the room, place the call light, then have her find things on her own.

questions.objective: Apply nursing interventions to promote safety and effective communication.
questions.concept: Orientation to the environment on admission

questions.stem: After a head injury from a fall, a patient has aphasia. He understands speech but struggles to produce words. While trying to tell the nurse where he hurts, he stops partway through and grows frustrated. His wife is at the bedside. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Finish his sentence with the word he seems to want
options.rationale: Supplying the word looks kind and may ease his frustration for a moment. It risks putting the wrong words in his mouth, while listening patiently and allowing time lets him say what he means.

options.text: Speak louder and more slowly so he can follow
options.rationale: Slow, clear speech helps a patient who has hearing loss. He already understands speech, so his problem is producing words, and a louder voice adds nothing and may feel condescending.

options.text: Return to ask about the pain once he is calmer
options.rationale: Giving him a break can lower frustration, and calm does help communication. Leaving now leaves his pain unexplained and unrelieved, and he needs a way to answer now rather than later.

options.text: Ask yes or no questions about where the pain is
options.rationale: Yes or no questions let him answer with a nod or one word he can produce. They narrow down where he hurts without demanding speech he cannot form right now.

questions.takeaway: With aphasia, listen patiently, allow time, and use yes or no questions or communication boards so the patient can answer without producing full speech.
questions.strategy: Finishing his sentence and coming back later feel like kindness to a frustrated patient. Both take away his chance to say where he hurts now; pick the option that works around the speech deficit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He understands speech but cannot produce words.
A louder voice fixes a hearing problem he does not have.

steps.action: Keep his voice in the answer
steps.detail: Yes or no questions let him report the pain himself; finishing his words or leaving does not.

elimination.verdict: Ask yes or no questions about where the pain is.

questions.objective: Apply nursing interventions to promote safety and effective communication.
questions.concept: Communicating with a patient who has aphasia

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient who recently started a job with 7 hours of screen work daily and reports tired, burning eyes by midafternoon. Her eye examination last month was normal. Which teaching is correct?

options.text: Book another eye examination for later this month
options.rationale: A new examination would suit a change in vision. Her eyes were normal last month and the symptoms fit screen use, so prevention teaching comes first.

options.text: Every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds
options.rationale: Looking at a distant object every 20 minutes relaxes the focusing muscles that screen work keeps tense. Brief, frequent breaks prevent the strain that builds over a long day.

options.text: Every 20 minutes, close both eyes tightly for 20 seconds
options.rationale: The timing matches the rule, and closing the eyes feels restful. The rule calls for focusing on something far away, which is what relaxes the eye muscles.

options.text: Every 2 hours, step away from the screen for a 20 minute rest
options.rationale: Longer breaks help, and the number 20 makes this sound familiar. Two hours is too long between breaks, so strain builds well before each rest.

questions.takeaway: Prevent digital eyestrain with a break every 20 minutes to look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
questions.strategy: Two distractors borrow the number 20 in the wrong place. Check all three parts: how often, how far and how long.

steps.detail: Every 20 minutes, 20 feet away, 20 seconds.
Two hours and closed eyes each break one part.
A normal examination last month and screen related symptoms call for teaching.

elimination.verdict: Every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.

questions.objective: Apply nursing interventions to promote safety and effective communication.
questions.concept: Health promotion: screening, protection and prevention

questions.stem: At a community woodworking class, the nurse reviews eye and ear safety with participants. Which participant statement needs follow up?

options.text: I get my hearing checked again, though last year's test was normal.
options.rationale: A normal result can make another test seem wasteful, yet screening continues at regular, age appropriate intervals. Planning the next check shows the participant understood that point.

options.text: I take out my contact lenses and clean them before a nap.
options.rationale: Taking lenses out before sleep and cleaning them as instructed is proper contact lens care. It lowers the risk of an eye infection, so this statement shows sound understanding.

options.text: I skip earplugs for quick saw cuts, since each lasts a minute.
options.rationale: Brief cuts feel harmless, but a power saw is loud enough that short, repeated exposures add up to permanent hearing damage. Protection is worn every time the hazard is present, not only for long jobs.

options.text: I wear safety glasses even when I am only sweeping sawdust.
options.rationale: Sweeping seems too minor to need protection, but it stirs fine particles into the air near the eyes. Wearing eye protection whenever particles fly is correct and needs no follow up.

questions.takeaway: Eye and hearing protection is worn every time a hazard is present, however brief, and screening continues at regular intervals even after a normal result.
questions.strategy: The statements that sound overly careful are the correct ones, which makes them tempting to flag. What tips it is that noise damage builds with every exposure, so a short job is no exception.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Look for the one statement that leaves the eyes or ears unprotected.
Glasses while sweeping, lens care before sleep and a repeat hearing check are all correct.

steps.action: Find the exception the participant made
steps.detail: Skipping earplugs because a cut is short ignores that each exposure adds damage.

elimination.verdict: I skip earplugs for quick saw cuts, since each lasts a minute.

questions.objective: Apply nursing interventions to promote safety and effective communication.
questions.concept: Health promotion: screening, protection and prevention

questions.stem: At a senior center blood pressure clinic, a woman who has worn hearing aids for years for slowly worsening hearing says that about an hour ago, while she was talking on the phone, the sound in her left ear went silent. A staff member checked both aids since then and found them clean and working, and the right aid still helps her hear well. Her audiology visit is set for next month. She says, "It is just my age catching up with me." Which action is the priority?

options.text: Arrange for her provider to see her today
options.rationale: A loss that appeared within the last hour is new and needs prompt evaluation rather than being blamed on age. Both aids were just checked and work, so the device does not explain it.

options.text: Add the new loss to her audiology visit next month
options.rationale: The audiology visit will give her a full hearing test, which she does need. Waiting a month on a loss that began an hour ago treats a sudden change as aging and delays its evaluation.

options.text: Suggest an amplified phone for calls on her left side
options.rationale: Amplified phones are useful devices for long standing hearing loss. Fitting a device to a loss that began an hour ago treats it as permanent before anyone has looked for its cause.

options.text: Sit on her right side and speak face to face
options.rationale: Facing her from her better hearing side is the right way to talk with her now. It helps this conversation but does nothing about a new loss that needs a provider's evaluation today.

questions.takeaway: A sudden change in hearing or vision is never assumed to be age related, even in a patient with a known gradual loss.
questions.strategy: Her long, slow loss and her own words invite the age explanation, and talking from her good side is good care. The sudden onset and working aids make prompt evaluation the priority.

steps.action: Separate the old loss from the new one
steps.detail: Years of gradual loss, then one ear went silent within the hour.
Both aids checked clean and working, and the right one still helps.
A sudden change needs evaluation today, not next month.

elimination.verdict: Arrange for her provider to see her today.

questions.concept: New or sudden changes are not aging
questions.objective: Assess patients for sensory deficits and related safety risks.

questions.stem: On her third night after shoulder surgery, a patient with profound hearing loss cannot tell the nurse where she is or what day it is. The admission note says she answered every written question correctly and wrote out her own medication list.
