options.rationale: A midline tip ends below the axilla in a peripheral vein, so it is not a central line. Vesicants can leak into tissue and cause severe damage, so they need central access.

options.text: An IV analgesic every 4 hours as needed
options.rationale: Analgesics are an appropriate use for midline catheters. A nonvesicant pain medication given every few hours is appropriate through this device.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride for hydration
options.rationale: Hydration therapy is an appropriate use for midline catheters. Isotonic saline is well within the 600 mOsm/L limit for this device.

options.text: An IV antibiotic every 8 hours
options.rationale: Antibiotics are an appropriate use for midline catheters. A nonvesicant drug given on a schedule fits the device.

questions.takeaway: A midline is a peripheral device for nonvesicant drugs under 600 mOsm/L; vesicants, TPN and continuous vasopressors need central access.
questions.strategy: Midlines are long and sit in the upper arm, so they feel central. Their tip is still peripheral, which sets the limits.

steps.detail: A midline ends below the axilla, outside the central circulation.
No vesicants, TPN or continuous vasopressors.
The vesicant is the only one on that list.

elimination.verdict: A vesicant chemotherapy drug.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: A patient with limited arm veins needs a nonvesicant IV antibiotic for 10 days. The antibiotic's osmolarity is well under 600 mOsm/L. Which device does the nurse expect to be placed?

options.text: Implanted port
options.rationale: A port is a surgically placed device for intermittent long term therapy such as months of chemotherapy. A 10 day antibiotic course does not justify surgery.

options.text: Short peripheral IV
options.rationale: A short peripheral IV suits short term therapy, and this course lasts 10 days. With limited veins, repeated restarts would use up the few sites left.

options.text: Midline catheter
options.rationale: A midline carries nonvesicant drugs under 600 mOsm/L and dwells well beyond a short IV. Therapy longer than 6 days in a patient with poor veins fits it well.

options.text: Nontunneled central venous catheter
options.rationale: A nontunneled central line is for short term acute care and carries the highest infection risk among central lines. A nonvesicant drug does not need central access.

questions.takeaway: Therapy longer than 6 days with a nonvesicant drug under 600 mOsm/L points to a midline catheter.
questions.strategy: A central line can carry anything, which makes it feel safest. The least invasive device that fits the drug and duration is the right one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 10 days is too long for a short peripheral IV.
Nonvesicant and under 600 mOsm/L does not need central access.
A midline fits therapy longer than 6 days.

elimination.verdict: Midline catheter.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices
questions.note: The class material says a midline can dwell up to 4 weeks. The textbook gives indications of more than 6 days and up to 14 days, so a 10 day course fits both. On the course exam, use up to 4 weeks. On NCLEX, use more than 6 days and up to 14 days, and expect a PICC for longer therapy.

questions.stem: At an oncology clinic, a patient with breast cancer who will receive chemotherapy every 3 weeks for the next 6 months and swims laps most mornings asks which long term device fits this plan. Which device does the nurse expect the team to recommend?

options.text: Implanted port
options.rationale: A port sits completely under the skin, so there is no external catheter to protect while swimming. It has the lowest infection risk and suits intermittent long term therapy such as chemotherapy.

options.text: Midline catheter
options.rationale: A midline works for short term therapy with solutions that are not vesicants. Chemotherapy over 6 months needs central access, and its external line would also have to stay dry.

options.text: Tunneled central catheter
options.rationale: A tunneled catheter does suit long term therapy, and its cuff lowers infection risk. Its external portion needs daily care and must stay dry, which conflicts with swimming laps every morning.

options.text: PICC
options.rationale: A PICC gives central access for weeks to months, so it could deliver the chemotherapy. Its external catheter must stay covered and dry, and swimming is not allowed with one in place.

questions.takeaway: Implanted ports suit intermittent long term therapy: they have the lowest infection risk and no external catheter to protect.
questions.strategy: Every central option can deliver the drug; the daily swimming and the gaps between treatments decide it, because only a port leaves nothing outside the skin.

steps.detail: Six months of chemotherapy needs a central device, so the midline is out.
The PICC and the tunneled catheter both have an external portion that must stay dry.

elimination.verdict: An implanted port fits intermittent therapy and daily swimming.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: A patient with aplastic anemia is prescribed a unit of packed red blood cells. Type and crossmatch are complete, and baseline vital signs were recorded at 1300. At 1310, the blood bank calls to say the unit is ready, and a coworker offers to pick it up right away. In what order does the nurse carry out these steps?

options.text: Check the chart for a signed transfusion consent form
options.rationale: Consent must be on file before blood leaves the blood bank, even when the unit is ready and help is offered. Once issued, the unit cannot wait while paperwork is sorted out.

options.text: Recheck vital signs 15 minutes after the unit starts
options.rationale: The first reassessment comes 15 minutes after the start and is compared with the 1300 baseline. Reactions often begin early, so this check catches them while little blood has been given.

options.text: Match the unit label to the patient's band with a second licensed nurse
options.rationale: Two licensed nurses compare the label with the patient's band, type, unit number and expiration. The check needs both the unit and the patient present, so it happens at the bedside.

options.text: Start the unit through tubing primed with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: The infusion starts only after the bedside check confirms the right unit for the right patient. Saline is the only solution that may run with blood.

options.text: Pick up the unit from the blood bank
options.rationale: The unit is retrieved only once consent is confirmed. Issue starts the 4 hour limit for infusing it, so the remaining steps follow without delay.

options.text: Recheck vital signs when the unit is complete
options.rationale: Vital signs are checked again when the unit finishes, after checks every 30 to 60 minutes during it. This final set shows how the patient tolerated the whole transfusion.

questions.takeaway: Even when the unit is ready and help is offered, consent is confirmed first; then retrieve, verify at the bedside with two licensed nurses, start with saline and reassess at 15 minutes and at completion.
questions.strategy: The ready unit and the offer of help push toward picking it up first. Consent has to be on file before the blood is issued, and the 4 hour clock starts at issue.

steps.detail: Consent is confirmed before anyone goes to the blood bank.
Two nurses verify with the unit and the patient together.
Saline primed tubing, then vital signs at 15 minutes and at completion.

elimination.verdict: Consent, retrieve, verify, start, recheck at 15 minutes, recheck at completion.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: The nurse reviews four patients with new prescriptions for total parenteral nutrition (TPN). For which patient does the nurse hold the TPN and contact the provider?

options.text: Tunneled chest catheter used for 3 weeks of home infusions
options.rationale: A tunneled catheter is a central line built for long term therapy such as TPN. It has been in use for weeks, so its tip position was confirmed long ago.

options.text: PICC placed today, brisk blood return, x ray still pending
options.rationale: A PICC counts as central only once an x ray confirms its tip in the lower superior vena cava. A blood return shows the catheter is in a vein, not where its tip lies.

options.text: Subclavian catheter placed yesterday, tip confirmed on x ray
options.rationale: A nontunneled subclavian catheter is central, and its tip has been confirmed. It carries the highest infection risk, which calls for careful site care but does not stop TPN.

options.text: Implanted chest port accessed today with a noncoring needle
options.rationale: An implanted port is a central device, and a noncoring needle is the correct way to access it. TPN can run through it once the needle is in place.

questions.takeaway: TPN needs central access, and a central device is not ready for use until an x ray confirms its tip position; a blood return does not prove where the tip lies.
questions.strategy: A PICC is a central line, which makes it look ready for TPN. What tips it is the pending x ray: until the tip is confirmed, the line cannot be treated as central.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The PICC, port, tunneled and subclavian catheters all are.
Only the PICC has no confirmed tip position.
A blood return shows a vein, not tip location.

elimination.verdict: Hold the TPN for the patient whose PICC x ray is pending.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: A patient with end stage kidney disease has a tunneled hemodialysis catheter in the right chest. The patient's peripheral IV infiltrated, and an IV antibiotic is due now. The nurse cannot find a new vein after two attempts. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the antibiotic until the next dialysis session
options.rationale: Holding delays a dose that is due now for an infection. Other access can be obtained without waiting.

options.text: Ask the dialysis nurse to give the antibiotic through the catheter
options.rationale: Dialysis trained staff manage the catheter, but only for dialysis. Who accesses it does not change the rule against routine infusions.

options.text: Give the antibiotic through the dialysis catheter
options.rationale: A hemodialysis catheter is never used for routine IV infusion. Using it risks infection and damage to the patient's dialysis access.

options.text: Ask the vascular access specialist to place a new IV
options.rationale: The vascular access specialist is trained for difficult access and can use tools such as ultrasound. The dialysis catheter is reserved for dialysis and is not an option.

questions.takeaway: A hemodialysis catheter is for dialysis only; difficult IV access goes to the vascular access specialist.
questions.strategy: Having a dialysis nurse access the catheter sounds like a safe compromise. The rule is about the device's use, not the person handling it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dialysis catheters are never used for routine IV access.
Holding a due antibiotic leaves the infection untreated.
The vascular access specialist handles difficult access.

elimination.verdict: Ask the vascular access specialist to place a new IV.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: A year after a left mastectomy with lymph node removal, a right handed woman has her right forearm IV removed this morning for phlebitis at a site 6 cm above the wrist. She needs 2 more days of IV antibiotics. Which site does the nurse choose for the new IV?

options.text: Left forearm, in the nondominant arm
options.rationale: The nondominant arm is usually preferred for comfort and mobility. After a mastectomy with lymph node removal, that arm is avoided because lymph drainage is impaired and infection risk rises.

options.text: Right hand, a vein below the inflamed site
options.rationale: Starting distal is the usual rule for a first site, which makes the hand appealing. Sites distal to phlebitis are avoided because the infused fluid would flow into the inflamed vein.

options.text: Right forearm, a vein above the inflamed site
options.rationale: The mastectomy rules out the left arm, so the right arm is the only choice. Moving proximal to the phlebitis keeps the new catheter out of the damaged stretch of vein.

options.text: A vein on the top of the right foot
options.rationale: The foot avoids both the mastectomy arm and the inflamed vein. Lower extremity sites are avoided in adults because they raise the risk of clots and infection.

questions.takeaway: When the other arm is ruled out, a new IV after phlebitis goes proximal to the old site in the same arm, never distal to it.
questions.strategy: The distal first rule and the nondominant arm rule each point to a wrong site. The mastectomy removes the left arm, and the phlebitis rules out everything below it on the right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The left arm is avoided regardless of dominance.

steps.action: Rule out sites below the phlebitis
steps.detail: The right hand is distal to the inflamed vein.
Adult lower extremities are avoided.

elimination.verdict: Right forearm, in a vein above the inflamed site.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: The nurse has removed a right handed patient's left forearm IV for phlebitis. He needs 3 more days of IV antibiotics. Both arms have soft, visible veins. Which site does the nurse choose for the new IV?

options.text: A straight vein in the right forearm
options.rationale: The right forearm has no contraindication, and a straight, soft forearm vein is a preferred site. Avoiding the injured vein outweighs using the nondominant arm.

options.text: A dorsal vein of the left hand
options.rationale: Starting distal and moving up is the usual habit, but this vein drains into the inflamed one. Sites distal to prior phlebitis are avoided.

options.text: The left antecubital fossa
options.rationale: The antecubital fossa is avoided for short peripheral IVs because elbow bending dislodges the catheter. It is also on the same arm as the inflamed vein.

options.text: The left forearm, 2 cm below the old site
options.rationale: A site just below the old one sits distal to the phlebitis, so fluid would flow into the inflamed vein. That placement is avoided.

questions.takeaway: Avoid sites distal to prior phlebitis or infiltration; otherwise start at the most distal appropriate site and move up.
questions.strategy: Most distal first is a rule students know well, which makes the hand vein tempting. A prior phlebitis site changes the rule for that arm.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The left forearm vein has phlebitis.

steps.action: Rule out sites draining into it
steps.detail: Left hand and below the old site are distal to it.
The antecubital fossa is avoided for short IVs.

elimination.verdict: A straight vein in the right forearm.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: Before a peripheral IV attempt in a patient with edematous arms, the nurse is orienting a new graduate to a near infrared vein illumination device. Which statement by the new graduate requires correction?

options.text: The edema is one reason to use the device.
options.rationale: Edema hides veins under swollen tissue, and it is one of the indications for vein illumination. This statement is correct and needs no change.

options.text: It uses no radiation, so repeated use is safe.
options.rationale: Near infrared light carries no radiation, so the device can be used again as needed. This statement is accurate.

options.text: This can cut down on needle sticks for the patient.
options.rationale: Seeing a vein map helps the nurse choose a vein on the first try. Fewer needle sticks is a real benefit of the device.

options.text: With the map, I can skip palpating the vein.
options.rationale: A vein finder shows where veins lie but not whether they are soft, straight and resilient. It does not replace clinical assessment, so palpation is still required.

questions.takeaway: Vein illumination reduces needle sticks but does not replace palpating and assessing the vein.
questions.strategy: Three statements are true benefits of the device. The one that needs correction treats the tool as a substitute for the nurse's hands.

steps.detail: Find the incorrect statement.
No radiation, fewer sticks and edema as an indication are all true.
Skipping palpation drops a required assessment.

elimination.verdict: With the map, I can skip palpating the vein.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.scenario: In the emergency department, the nurse is choosing peripheral catheter sizes for several new patients.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate the catheter gauge the nurse selects.

rows.text: A patient with stable anemia scheduled for 2 units of packed red blood cells
rows.rationale: An 18 gauge catheter is preferred for blood products. It gives adequate flow without damaging red cells or causing excessive resistance.

rows.text: A patient with a ruptured abdominal aneurysm headed to emergency surgery
rows.rationale: Major surgery with massive blood loss needs rapid volume replacement. A large bore catheter gives the fastest possible flow.

rows.text: A patient with multiple injuries from a car crash who is bleeding heavily
rows.rationale: Large bore catheters allow the high flow rates needed for rapid fluid resuscitation. Trauma with heavy bleeding calls for the largest gauge.

rows.text: An older adult with small, fragile veins who needs an IV antibiotic
rows.rationale: Fragile veins tear and infiltrate easily with a large catheter. The smallest effective gauge protects the vein and still delivers the antibiotic.

rows.text: A 4 year old who needs maintenance IV fluids
rows.rationale: Children have small veins, so a small bore catheter limits vein trauma. Maintenance fluids run well through a 22 to 24 gauge catheter.

rows.text: A patient going for a CT scan with IV contrast
rows.rationale: Contrast media is given quickly and is thick, so it needs a moderate bore. An 18 gauge catheter is preferred for contrast.

questions.takeaway: Larger gauge numbers mean smaller catheters: 14 to 16 for trauma, 18 for blood and contrast, 22 to 24 for children and fragile veins.
questions.strategy: The numbering runs backward, so a bigger number means a smaller catheter. Match the flow the patient needs to the lumen that can deliver it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Smaller gauge numbers mean wider lumens.
Heavy bleeding needs the widest; blood and contrast need moderate.
Children and fragile veins get 22 to 24 gauge.

elimination.verdict: Trauma and aneurysm 14 to 16; blood and contrast 18; child and older adult 22 to 24.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: After placing a peripheral IV on the second attempt, the nurse writes: "0915: 20 gauge catheter in right forearm basilic vein. Vein soft and straight. Transparent dressing applied. Patient tolerated with brief discomfort. Distal forearm chosen to preserve upper veins for 5 days of antibiotics." Which entry does the note still need?

options.text: The time of the next tubing change
options.rationale: Tubing is labeled with its date so the next change can be timed. That label is separate from the insertion note.

options.text: The patient's blood type
options.rationale: Blood type matters for transfusion orders and verification. It has no place in a note about placing a peripheral IV.

options.text: The number of insertion attempts
options.rationale: The number of attempts is a required part of insertion documentation. It shows how much the vein was traumatized and guides site choice later.

options.text: The patient's most recent oral intake
options.rationale: Oral intake belongs in the intake and output record. It is not part of documenting an IV insertion.

questions.takeaway: Insertion notes include site, gauge, number of attempts, vein condition, dressing, patient tolerance and the rationale for the site.
questions.strategy: The note looks complete because it is long. Check it against the list: site, gauge, attempts, vein condition, dressing, tolerance, rationale.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Site, gauge, attempts, vein condition, dressing, tolerance, rationale.
Everything is there except attempts.
Intake, tubing labels and blood type belong elsewhere.

elimination.verdict: The number of insertion attempts.

questions.objective: Document Infusion Care

questions.stem: Before discharge, the nurse removes a patient's left forearm peripheral IV at 1410. The catheter tip is intact, the site has no redness or swelling, bleeding stops after 1 minute of pressure, and the patient says the removal did not hurt. Which note documents the removal completely?
questions.takeaway: A removal note includes the time, catheter tip integrity, site appearance and patient tolerance.
questions.strategy: Each note is accurate and sounds thorough, so look for what is missing rather than what is there. Check every note against the four required elements: time, tip, site and tolerance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Time, tip integrity, site appearance and patient tolerance.
One lacks the tip, one lacks the time, one lacks the site.
A room number or pressure time does not replace a missing element.

elimination.verdict: The note with the time, intact tip, site appearance and pain report.

questions.objective: Document Infusion Care

options.text: Catheter removed, tip intact. Site without redness or swelling. Patient reports no pain at discharge.
options.rationale: This note covers the tip, the site and tolerance, so it looks complete. It has no removal time, which is required because it marks when the device came out.

options.text: 1410: Catheter removed, tip intact. Site without redness or swelling. Patient reports no pain.
options.rationale: This note records the removal time, tip integrity, site appearance and patient tolerance. Those four elements together make up complete documentation of an IV removal.

options.text: 1410: Catheter removed, tip intact, pressure held 1 minute. Patient reports no pain.
options.rationale: Holding pressure until bleeding stops is correct care and worth noting. The note leaves out the site appearance, which is required as a baseline for any later problem.

options.text: 1410: Catheter removed in room 412. Site without redness or swelling. Patient reports no pain.
options.rationale: The room number adds nothing, and the note leaves out the tip inspection. Recording an intact tip shows that no piece of the catheter was left in the vein.

questions.stem: The nurse is checking vascular access dressings on four patients. Each dressing is clean, dry and intact. Which dressing does the nurse change today?

options.text: A gauze dressing on a tunneled catheter, dated 3 days ago
options.rationale: Gauze dressings are changed every 2 days, so a 3 day old gauze dressing is overdue. It needs changing even though it looks clean.

options.text: A transparent dressing on a PICC, dated 2 days ago
options.rationale: Transparent dressings are changed every 7 days, or sooner if wet or soiled. At 2 days and intact, this one is not yet due.

options.text: A transparent dressing on a midline, dated 4 days ago
options.rationale: A 4 day old transparent dressing has 3 days left before its 7 day change. It can stay while intact.

options.text: A transparent dressing on a nontunneled catheter, dated 6 days ago
options.rationale: A clean, intact transparent dressing is changed every 7 days. At 6 days old, this one is due tomorrow, not today.

questions.takeaway: Transparent dressings are changed every 7 days and gauze dressings every 2 days, or sooner if wet or soiled.
questions.strategy: The oldest transparent dressing draws attention first. Gauze has a much shorter interval, so the 3 day gauze is the one that is overdue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One gauze, three transparent.
Gauze every 2 days; transparent every 7 days.
Gauze at 3 days.

elimination.verdict: A gauze dressing on a tunneled catheter, dated 3 days ago.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.objective: Document Infusion Care

questions.stem: Ten days after bowel surgery, a patient with Crohn disease who receives TPN at home through a tunneled chest catheter is readmitted with fever, shaking chills, low blood pressure and new confusion. Which additional finding makes the catheter a less likely source of these signs?

options.text: Chills that began soon after a TPN bag was hung
options.rationale: Symptoms that start soon after a new bag is hung point toward the infusion system. That timing raises suspicion of the catheter or the infused solution rather than lowering it.

options.text: A red abdominal incision draining pus
options.rationale: A red, draining incision is another identifiable source that could explain the fever, chills and low blood pressure. Catheter related bloodstream infection is the diagnosis when no other source is found, so this finding points elsewhere.

options.text: A catheter in place for the past 8 months
options.rationale: Long dwell time makes the catheter more likely, not less likely, to be the source. Every extra day a central catheter stays in place adds to the risk of bloodstream infection.

options.text: No redness or drainage at the exit site
options.rationale: A clean exit site does argue against a local skin infection where the catheter enters. Bloodstream infection from a catheter often shows no exit site signs at all, so a clean site does not lower suspicion of the catheter.

questions.takeaway: Catheter related bloodstream infection is fever, chills, hypotension and altered mental status with no other identifiable source, and it often has no exit site signs.
questions.strategy: The clean exit site feels like evidence against the catheter, but bloodstream infection from a line rarely announces itself at the skin. Only a second source of infection changes the explanation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: These systemic signs with no other source define a catheter related bloodstream infection.
Dwell time and bag timing point toward the line; a clean site is neutral.
A draining incision can explain the same signs.

elimination.verdict: The red incision draining pus points away from the catheter.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: The charge nurse on a surgical unit reviews a registered nurse's (RN's) plan for a licensed practical nurse (LPN) and assistive personnel (AP). Facility policy and the state nurse practice act let LPNs flush established central and peripheral lines and hang fluids that are not high alert. Which assignment does the charge nurse ask the RN to change?

options.text: The AP reports a wet IV dressing to the RN
options.rationale: Reporting site appearance is within the AP role, and the RN then assesses the site. The AP is observing and reporting, not judging what the wet dressing means.

options.text: The LPN flushes an established PICC with saline
options.rationale: A PICC is a central line, which makes this flush feel like an RN task. Policy here lets the LPN flush established central lines, so this routine task is delegated correctly.

options.text: The LPN hangs lactated Ringer's on an established IV
options.rationale: Lactated Ringer's is not a high alert fluid, and hanging it on an established line is delegable to the LPN. The RN keeps responsibility for checking that the patient tolerates it.

options.text: The LPN does the PICC discharge teaching
options.rationale: Patient and family education on infusion therapy is an RN task, because the RN plans the teaching and judges whether it worked. An LPN may reinforce that teaching but does not take it over.

questions.takeaway: Initial patient and family education on infusion therapy stays with the RN, even when an LPN may handle the line itself.
questions.strategy: The central line flush draws attention because PICCs feel like RN territory, but the stem's policy allows it. Teaching is the task that requires RN planning and evaluation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flushing established lines, central included, and hanging non high alert fluids are delegable.
Reporting site appearance is an AP role.
Patient education on infusion therapy stays with the RN.

elimination.verdict: Change the LPN PICC discharge teaching assignment.

questions.objective: Apply Clinical Judgment

questions.stem: During discharge teaching, a patient going home with a PICC in the left upper arm makes several statements. Which statements show that the patient understands the teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will have my blood pressure taken on my right arm."
options.rationale: Blood pressure cuffs and needle sticks are kept off the PICC arm. Using the right arm protects the catheter from pressure and damage.

options.text: "If the flush is hard to push, I will push harder to clear it."
options.rationale: Resistance during a flush means the line may be blocked or damaged. Forcing it can rupture the catheter, so the patient stops and calls.

options.text: "I will call right away for a temperature above 38°C or chills."
options.rationale: Fever above 38°C or chills can signal a bloodstream infection from the catheter. Calling right away gets early treatment.

options.text: "I can carry my 20 lb grandchild with my left arm."
options.rationale: Lifting more than 10 lb with the PICC arm is limited. Lifting can move the catheter or damage the vein.

options.text: "A short swim is fine as long as the dressing stays sealed."
options.rationale: The PICC arm is never submerged, even with a sealed dressing. Pool water can seep under the dressing and contaminate the site.

options.text: "I will carry my PICC card with the catheter details."
options.rationale: The identification card tells other caregivers what device is in place. Carrying it is part of the safety teaching.

options.text: "I will wear a waterproof cover over the site when I shower."
options.rationale: The PICC dressing must stay clean, dry and intact at all times. A waterproof cover keeps shower water off the site and protects it.

questions.takeaway: PICC teaching: keep the dressing dry, no submerging, no blood pressure or sticks on that arm, limit lifting, never force a flush and report fever or chills.
questions.strategy: A sealed dressing makes swimming sound safe. The rule is no submerging the arm at all, whatever the dressing looks like.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No cuff, no lifting over 10 lb, no submerging.
Stop if a flush meets resistance.
Fever, chills and site changes need prompt care.

elimination.verdict: Right arm blood pressure, shower cover, call for fever or chills, carry the PICC card.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: After scrubbing a patient's forearm with chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) for 30 seconds and letting it air dry, the nurse can no longer see the vein she located by touch before the prep. She needs to feel the vein again to find it. What does the nurse do before inserting the catheter?

options.text: Palpate, then blot the site with sterile gauze
options.rationale: Blotting with sterile gauze does not remove the organisms the fingertip left on the skin. CHG also needs to air dry to work, so blotting weakens the prep further.

options.text: Wipe a fingertip with alcohol, then palpate
options.rationale: An alcohol wipe on a fingertip does not make the finger sterile. The finger still carries skin flora onto the prepared site, so the CHG no longer protects the patient.

options.text: Palpate, then repeat the CHG scrub and drying
options.rationale: Touching the prepared skin recontaminates it, so the antisepsis has to be repeated after palpating. A fresh 30 second scrub that air dries restores the protection before the catheter goes in.

options.text: Palpate wearing a fresh pair of clean gloves
options.rationale: Clean gloves are better than bare fingers, which makes this choice look safe. They are not sterile, so touching the prepared site with them still recontaminates it and the prep is lost.

questions.takeaway: Any touch of the site after CHG antisepsis cancels the prep, so the scrub and air drying are repeated before insertion.
questions.strategy: Clean gloves sound like an acceptable shortcut, but they are not sterile. The stem says she must touch the site again, so the only safe plan is to redo the prep afterward.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The stem says she must feel the vein again.
Clean gloves and an alcohol wiped finger are still unsterile.
Repeat the 30 second scrub and let it air dry.

elimination.verdict: Palpate, then repeat the CHG scrub and drying.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: A patient injured in a motorcycle crash still has the femoral central venous catheter placed in the emergency department 4 days ago. It is used once a day for a nonvesicant IV antibiotic that will continue for 3 more days. His forearm veins are soft and easy to see, the site is clean, and he has no fever. Which question does the nurse raise with the provider today?

options.text: Can a peripheral IV replace this central line?
options.rationale: Dwell time is a main risk factor for bloodstream infection, and the femoral site carries the highest risk. A nonvesicant antibiotic for 3 days can run through a peripheral IV in his good forearm veins.

options.text: Should the femoral dressing be changed daily?
options.rationale: Daily changes of an intact dressing add handling without lowering infection risk. Transparent dressings are changed every 7 days unless soiled, and the larger risk here is the line itself.

options.text: Should the catheter stay until the antibiotic ends?
options.rationale: The catheter is still in use, so keeping it until the course ends seems reasonable. Each extra day raises infection risk, and a nonvesicant drug with good forearm veins means the line is no longer necessary.

options.text: Should the catheter tip be cultured now?
options.rationale: Routine tip or hub cultures do not prevent infection in a patient without signs of one. Cultures guide treatment when infection is suspected, and he has a clean site and no fever.

questions.takeaway: Daily line necessity review asks whether the catheter is still needed, and a line that is still used can be unnecessary when a peripheral route would do.
questions.strategy: A catheter that is still in use feels necessary, which makes keeping it look safe. The nonvesicant drug, short remaining course and good forearm veins mean the central line no longer earns its risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Is this catheter still necessary?

steps.action: Match the therapy to a device
steps.detail: A nonvesicant drug for 3 days fits a peripheral IV.
Femoral access carries the highest infection risk.

elimination.verdict: Ask whether a peripheral IV can replace the central line.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: On the postpartum unit, a nurse new to the unit is preparing to transfuse packed red blood cells for a woman who bled heavily after a cesarean birth. Her only IV is a 20 gauge forearm catheter infusing 5% dextrose in 0.9% sodium chloride. Which statement by the new nurse needs correction?

options.text: "Her 20 gauge forearm catheter can be used for the blood."
options.rationale: An 18 gauge catheter is preferred for blood, so a 20 gauge can look too small. Blood products may run through 18 to 20 gauge access, so her 20 gauge catheter is acceptable.

options.text: "Two licensed nurses must check the unit at her bedside."
options.rationale: Two licensed nurses verify the label, unit number and ABO/Rh type against her band before the unit starts. This statement is accurate, so it needs no correction.

options.text: "Her vital signs get rechecked 15 minutes after it starts."
options.rationale: Vital signs are reassessed 15 minutes after the start, when early reactions tend to show. This statement is accurate, so the new nurse needs no correction here.

options.text: "Her dextrose and saline fluid can prime the blood tubing."
options.rationale: Dextrose in the bag or tubing damages red cells, even when the fluid also contains saline. Blood products run only with 0.9% sodium chloride, so the tubing needs its own plain saline bag.

questions.takeaway: Blood runs only with 0.9% sodium chloride; a fluid that adds dextrose to saline is still not compatible.
questions.strategy: The word saline in her fluid makes it look compatible, and the 20 gauge catheter looks too small. Dextrose is the problem, while 18 to 20 gauge access is acceptable for blood.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It contains dextrose as well as saline.
Blood may run through 18 to 20 gauge access.
Two nurse verification and the 15 minute recheck are correct.

elimination.verdict: Correct the plan to prime the tubing with dextrose and saline.

questions.objective: IV Solution Types
questions.concept: Blood products with 0.9% sodium chloride only

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with a retinal disease who says that faces straight ahead look blank and that red and green now look alike. He still walks safely down a dim hallway and notices people moving at the edges of his vision. Which interpretation fits these findings?

options.text: The lens is clouding and scattering light across the whole retina
options.rationale: A clouded lens does blur vision and fade colors, so this is a reasonable guess. It blurs the whole field, though, and would not spare his side vision so cleanly.

options.text: The cones of the retina are failing while the rods still work
options.rationale: Cones handle color and central vision, and those are the losses he describes. His safe walking in dim light and his side vision show that the rods are still working.

options.text: The rods of the retina are failing while the cones still work
options.rationale: Rods handle peripheral and low light vision, so rod failure would make the dim hallway and side vision hard. Those are the abilities he still has.

options.text: The drainage of aqueous humor is blocked and the pressure is rising
options.rationale: Raised pressure damages the nerve fibers from the periphery inward, so side vision goes first. He has the opposite pattern, with central loss and intact side vision.

questions.takeaway: Rods serve peripheral and low light vision; cones serve color and central vision.
questions.strategy: Two options name retinal cells, so the choice turns on which cell does which job. Match central and color loss to the cell that provides them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Central vision and color are lost; dim light and side vision remain.
Cones give central and color vision, rods give peripheral and low light vision.
Pressure damage takes side vision first, the reverse of his pattern.

elimination.verdict: Cone failure with rods still working.

questions.objective: 5. Describe basic anatomy and function of the eye

questions.stem: A patient with raised intraocular pressure (IOP) tells the nurse, "I have cut back to two glasses of water a day so my eye pressure will come down." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Eye pressure rises because the lens hardens with age, so the pressure will settle once the lens is replaced"
options.rationale: The lens does harden with age, but that causes presbyopia and cataracts. It is not the mechanism of raised IOP, and lens replacement treats cataracts.

options.text: "Eye pressure follows your total body fluid, so cutting back on water is a reasonable way to lower it"
options.rationale: This reinforces a harmful plan. IOP depends on the fluid the eye makes and drains, so limiting water gives no benefit and can dehydrate her.

options.text: "Eye pressure depends on the fluid your eye makes and drains, so drinking less will not lower it"
options.rationale: IOP comes from the balance between aqueous humor production and drainage inside the eye. Restricting drinking water does not change that balance and only risks dehydration.

options.text: "Eye pressure comes from blood flow in the retina, so lowering your blood pressure is the main way to fix it"
options.rationale: Blood pressure control does protect the eye, which makes this tempting. IOP itself is set by aqueous humor production and drainage, not by retinal blood flow.

questions.takeaway: IOP is the balance of aqueous humor production and drainage; it is not lowered by drinking less.
questions.strategy: The patient's plan sounds logical because pressure and fluid seem linked. Ask which fluid sets IOP.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Aqueous humor, made and drained inside the eye.
Retinal blood flow, lens hardening and body fluid do not set IOP.

elimination.verdict: Explain that IOP depends on aqueous production and drainage.

questions.objective: 5. Describe basic anatomy and function of the eye

questions.stem: Long after a chemical splash injured her eye, a patient has a scarred, cloudy cornea. Ophthalmoscopy shows a healthy retina and optic disc. She asks, "If the back of my eye is healthy, why is everything blurry?" Which explanation should the nurse give?

options.text: "Your cones have stopped working, so the center of your vision has lost its sharp focus"
options.rationale: Cones do give sharp central vision, but they sit in the retina, which is healthy. The problem is in front of the retina, where light first enters.

options.text: "Light must pass clearly through the cornea before it can focus on the retina"
options.rationale: The cornea, aqueous humor, lens and vitreous humor all bend light toward the retina. A cloudy cornea scatters the light before it arrives, so a healthy retina still gets a blurred image.

options.text: "The cornea makes the fluid that feeds the eye, so a scar starves the retina of nutrients"
options.rationale: Aqueous humor is not made by the cornea, and her retina is healthy on examination. The cornea matters here because it is the first surface that bends light.

options.text: "The scar raises the pressure inside your eye, and that pressure is what makes your vision blurry"
options.rationale: Trauma can lead to secondary glaucoma, so this is not impossible. Her findings are a cloudy cornea and a healthy optic disc, which point to blocked light, not pressure damage.

questions.takeaway: The cornea, aqueous humor, lens and vitreous humor bend light toward the retina; clouding anywhere along that path blurs vision.
questions.strategy: A healthy retina makes students hunt for a hidden retinal problem. Follow the light from front to back instead.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The cornea is cloudy; the retina and disc are healthy.
Light must pass clear refractive media to focus on the retina.

elimination.verdict: A cloudy cornea blocks clear light from reaching a healthy retina.

questions.objective: 5. Describe basic anatomy and function of the eye
questions.concept: refractive media bend light toward the retina

questions.stem: An 83 year old woman is admitted for a hip fracture. During the admission interview, she describes several changes in her vision. Which findings should the nurse recognize as expected age related changes? Select all that apply.

options.text: Her eyes feel dry and gritty by the end of the day
options.rationale: Tear production falls with age, so dry eyes are an expected finding. Artificial tears and comfort measures fit, not an emergency workup.

options.text: She saw sudden flashes of light in one eye this morning
options.rationale: Posterior vitreous detachment becomes more common with age, so this may seem harmless. Sudden flashes point to a retinal tear or detachment, which is an emergency.

options.text: She needs much more light than before to read in the evening
options.rationale: The aging pupil is less able to dilate, so less light reaches the retina. Older adults adapt poorly to the dark and need brighter light to see.

options.text: She has been bumping into door frames on both sides
options.rationale: Loss of side vision is not part of normal aging. It suggests glaucoma, which damages vision from the periphery inward and needs evaluation.

options.text: She has to hold the newspaper farther away to read it
options.rationale: The aging lens hardens and loses elasticity, so it cannot focus up close. That is presbyopia, an expected change that reading glasses correct.

options.text: She has trouble telling her navy and green sweaters apart
options.rationale: Color discrimination declines with age, especially for blues, greens and violets. Telling dark blues from greens is a classic expected change.

questions.takeaway: Expected aging changes: a stiffer lens, a smaller pupil needing more light, weaker blue and green discrimination and drier eyes; lost side vision and sudden flashes are not expected.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option could be explained away by age. Anything sudden or any loss of side vision falls outside normal aging.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lens, pupil, color and tears change with age.
Side vision loss and sudden flashes need evaluation.

elimination.verdict: Needs more light, dry eyes, color confusion and farther reading distance are expected.

questions.objective: 6. Recognize normal age related changes in vision

questions.stem: At a community screening, a patient with no eye symptoms has tonometry readings of 18 mmHg in each eye. She is worried because her friend's reading was 14 mmHg. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Your readings are normal, so you will not need your eye pressure checked again"
options.rationale: The first half is correct, which makes this tempting. Screening grows more frequent with age, so a normal reading today does not end future checks.

options.text: "Your pressure is higher than your friend's, so you need a glaucoma referral this week"
options.rationale: Comparing her with a friend feels meaningful, but normal is judged against the range, not another person. Her 18 mmHg readings do not call for a referral.

options.text: "Both of your readings fall within the normal range, so keep your routine eye exams"
options.rationale: A reading of 18 mmHg is normal under every accepted range, and she has no symptoms. Routine screening continues, because normal pressure today does not replace future checks.

options.text: "Your pressure is close to the open angle glaucoma range, so you should start eyedrops"
options.rationale: The open angle range begins at 22 mmHg, so 18 mmHg is not there. Drops are prescribed for raised pressure or nerve damage, not for a normal reading.

questions.takeaway: Normal IOP on tonometry is about 10 to 21 mmHg; a normal reading keeps routine screening, not referral.
questions.strategy: The friend's lower number pulls toward alarm. Judge the value against the normal range and keep screening going.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 18 mmHg is inside 10 to 20 and 8 to 21 mmHg.
"Will not need checked again" ignores screening that increases with age.

elimination.verdict: Normal; continue routine screening.

questions.objective: 5. Describe basic anatomy and function of the eye
questions.note: Your instructor's material gives normal eye pressure two ways: 10 to 20 mmHg with the eye assessment techniques and 8 to 21 mmHg with glaucoma. Standard references give about 10 to 21 mmHg, and both versions agree that 22 mmHg or higher is raised, where the open angle glaucoma range begins. The reading in this item sits clearly inside or outside every version, so the key is the same either way. On the course exam, use the range a question states; if a reading of exactly 21 mmHg appears with no range given, it is normal by the glaucoma figure but raised by the assessment figure, so check the stem's wording. For NCLEX, treat a reading above 21 mmHg as raised.

questions.stem: After 2 days of vomiting, an alert 80 year old patient is admitted. His eyes look dry and his sclerae look yellowish. The assistive personnel says, "His eyes show he is dehydrated and jaundiced." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Dry eyes are expected with age, so he is probably not dehydrated after the vomiting"
options.rationale: Dry eyes are an aging change, but that does not rule out dehydration. Two days of vomiting is a real risk, so the nurse still assesses hydration another way.

options.text: "His eyes show both problems, so I will start encouraging fluids and record his output"
options.rationale: Fluids may well be needed after vomiting, but this accepts unreliable cues as proof. The nurse assesses with reliable findings before acting on a conclusion.

options.text: "Yellow sclerae mean jaundice, so I will notify the provider about liver problems right away"
options.rationale: Yellow sclerae do signal jaundice in younger adults, and that makes this tempting. At his age the sclera is not used to judge jaundice, so this rushes a conclusion.

options.text: "At his age his eyes are not reliable signs, so I will check other findings"
options.rationale: In older adults, dry eyes and yellowed sclerae are common aging changes and are not reliable signs. Vomiting still puts him at risk, so the nurse uses other hydration findings and laboratory results.

questions.takeaway: Do not use the sclera or eye appearance to judge hydration or jaundice in older adults; use other findings.
questions.strategy: The vomiting makes dehydration feel certain, so the eye cues seem to confirm it. The issue is whether these cues are valid at his age.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dry eyes and yellowed sclerae are common aging changes.
Vomiting still calls for a hydration assessment.
Other hydration signs and labs.

elimination.verdict: Assess hydration and jaundice with other findings.

questions.objective: 6. Recognize normal age related changes in vision
questions.concept: sclera not used for hydration or jaundice in older adults

questions.stem: In a long term care facility, an alert, oriented 89 year old resident has knocked over her water glass twice at night in her dimly lit room. She also mixes up her blue pill organizer and her green one. Which change to her plan of care best fits these findings?

options.text: Add brighter light and use contrasting organizer colors
options.rationale: Her aging pupil admits less light, so dim rooms cause errors. Blues and greens are hard for older adults to tell apart, so contrasting colors make the organizers distinct.

options.text: Ask the provider about a cognitive screen because she confuses objects
options.rationale: Confusing objects can signal cognitive change, and that makes this tempting. She is alert and oriented, and the errors match lighting and color changes of aging.

options.text: Refer her for an urgent eye exam to check for a retinal detachment
options.rationale: A retinal detachment causes sudden flashes, floaters or a curtain over vision. Her problems are gradual and fit expected changes in the pupil and color perception.

options.text: Move her water out of reach at night and offer drinks during rounds
options.rationale: This would stop the spills but limits her independence and her fluids. It also leaves the real problem, poor vision in dim light, untouched.

questions.takeaway: Older adults need more light and see blues and greens poorly; adapt lighting and color contrast.
questions.strategy: Mixing up objects pushes toward a cognitive cause. Her orientation points back to the eye.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Alert and oriented makes a cognitive cause less likely.
Dim light errors: pupil change. Blue and green confusion: color change.

elimination.verdict: Better lighting and color contrast.

questions.objective: 6. Recognize normal age related changes in vision

questions.stem: During a home health visit, a 76 year old patient tells the nurse that vision in his left eye went dim and blurry yesterday afternoon. He says, "I am getting old; my eyes were bound to go." His right eye is unchanged. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Suggest he have his reading glasses rechecked
options.rationale: A new prescription helps presbyopia, which develops over years in both eyes. Sudden blur in one eye calls for an examination, not new glasses.

options.text: Agree that slow vision decline is part of aging
options.rationale: Some vision changes do come with age, so his comment sounds reasonable. His change was sudden and one sided, so agreeing with him delays care.

options.text: Arrange an eye examination for him today
options.rationale: A change in one eye that appeared within a day is not a normal aging pattern. New or sudden vision changes are evaluated promptly rather than blamed on age.

options.text: Teach him to use brighter lighting when he reads
options.rationale: Brighter light does help the aging eye, so this is a reasonable general measure. It treats a gradual change and leaves a sudden one unexamined.

questions.takeaway: New or sudden vision changes are never assumed to be age related.
questions.strategy: The patient offers the explanation himself, and it is easy to accept. Sudden and one sided are the words that rule out aging.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Yesterday afternoon, one eye only.
Aging changes are gradual and usually in both eyes.

elimination.verdict: Same day evaluation.

questions.objective: 6. Recognize normal age related changes in vision
questions.concept: sudden change is not age related

questions.stem: During vision screening with her glasses on, a patient reads 20/200 with the right eye and 20/40 with the left eye on the Snellen chart. Her son asks whether she now counts as legally blind. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Yes. Her right eye qualifies, and her left eye is also below the normal 20/20"
options.rationale: Both facts are true, but neither meets the definition. One eye at 20/200 is not enough, and 20/40 is far better than 20/200.

options.text: "Yes. A reading of 20/200 with glasses on in either eye meets the definition"
options.rationale: 20/200 with correction is the right number, and that is why this is tempting. The definition uses the best eye, so one poor eye does not meet it.

options.text: "No. Legal blindness is judged without glasses, so she needs to be tested again"
options.rationale: Testing again sounds careful, but the definition uses corrected vision. She was tested with her glasses on, so the result already applies.

options.text: "No. It is judged by the better eye with glasses, which reads 20/40"
options.rationale: Legal blindness is 20/200 or worse in the best eye with correction. Her better eye reads 20/40, so she does not meet the definition.

questions.takeaway: Legally blind is 20/200 or worse in the best eye with correction.
questions.strategy: The number 20/200 in the stem pulls toward yes. Check which eye the definition uses.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 20/200 or worse, best eye, corrected.
She was tested with glasses, and her best eye reads 20/40.

elimination.verdict: No, because her better eye reads 20/40.

questions.objective: 7. Differentiate common eye and vision disorders, including cataracts, glaucoma, retinal detachment, and refractive errors

questions.stem: The nurse is taking the history of a patient who comes to the eye clinic with blurred vision. Which findings from his history should the nurse explore further? Select all that apply.

options.text: He welds at work without wearing eye protection
options.rationale: Occupation is part of the eye history because of flying object and chemical hazards. Welding without protection exposes his eyes to injury and calls for teaching.

options.text: He has taken oral corticosteroids every day for 3 years for asthma
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are a known cause of cataracts and of secondary glaucoma. Long term daily use is drug history directly tied to his blurred vision.

options.text: He had an appendectomy without complications 20 years ago
options.rationale: Surgical history is part of a complete history, but an old abdominal surgery has no link to the eye. It does not explain his blurred vision.

options.text: He drinks one cup of coffee every morning before work
options.rationale: Social habits are part of the eye history, and that makes this tempting. A single daily cup of coffee has no known link to cataracts or glaucoma.

options.text: He has had type 2 diabetes for 12 years
options.rationale: Diabetes raises the risk of cataracts and of secondary glaucoma from new blood vessel growth. A long history of diabetes is key systemic health data.

options.text: His father lost his sight to glaucoma
options.rationale: Family history is a glaucoma risk factor. A parent with vision loss from glaucoma raises his own risk and calls for pressure testing.

questions.takeaway: The eye history covers drugs, systemic disease, family history and occupation; corticosteroids and diabetes cause cataracts and secondary glaucoma.
questions.strategy: Every option is real history data. Select the items with a known path to eye damage.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Corticosteroids and diabetes cause cataracts and secondary glaucoma.
A parent with glaucoma and unprotected welding raise risk.
An old surgery and one coffee carry no eye risk.

elimination.verdict: Corticosteroids, diabetes, family history of glaucoma and unprotected welding.

questions.stem: At a workplace health fair, a 45 year old African American man whose mother has glaucoma reports no eye symptoms. Tonometry reads 26 mmHg in each eye. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Reassure him that glaucoma is unlikely because he has no symptoms
options.rationale: Lack of symptoms feels reassuring, which makes this tempting. Open angle glaucoma is the silent thief of sight and is often symptom free until vision is lost.

options.text: Refer him for a full glaucoma evaluation with an eye care provider
options.rationale: A reading of 26 mmHg is in the open angle glaucoma range, and he has two risk factors: African American over 40 and a family history. Open angle glaucoma is often silent until late, so he needs evaluation now.

options.text: Advise a repeat pressure check at age 60 when his risk begins
options.rationale: Age 60 is a risk threshold for the general population and for Hispanic or Latino adults. For African American adults risk starts at 40, and his pressure is already raised.

options.text: Teach him to watch for halos and return if he notices any
options.rationale: Halos can occur with open angle glaucoma, so this sounds like useful teaching. Waiting for symptoms means waiting for nerve damage that cannot be reversed.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma risk: age 60 and older, African American 40 and older, Hispanic or Latino 60 and older, family history; open angle glaucoma is often silent.
questions.strategy: The absence of symptoms pulls toward reassurance. Raised pressure plus risk factors call for referral regardless of symptoms.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 26 mmHg sits in the open angle range of 22 to 32 mmHg.
African American over 40 and a family history.
Symptoms appear late, after permanent loss.

elimination.verdict: Refer for a full glaucoma evaluation.

questions.note: Your instructor's material gives normal eye pressure two ways: 10 to 20 mmHg with the eye assessment techniques and 8 to 21 mmHg with glaucoma. Standard references give about 10 to 21 mmHg, and both versions agree that 22 mmHg or higher is raised, where the open angle glaucoma range begins. The reading in this item sits clearly inside or outside every version, so the key is the same either way. On the course exam, use the range a question states; if a reading of exactly 21 mmHg appears with no range given, it is normal by the glaucoma figure but raised by the assessment figure, so check the stem's wording. For NCLEX, treat a reading above 21 mmHg as raised.

questions.stem: The nurse is interviewing a patient who reports bumping into door frames on both sides of her body for several months and seeing halos around lights. She has a mild ache in both eyes. Reading straight ahead is unchanged, and she asks for stronger glasses. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "New glasses will not restore side vision, so you need an eye pressure check"
options.rationale: Gradual loss of side vision with halos and a mild ache fits open angle glaucoma. That vision loss is not reversible with glasses, so the next step is pressure testing and referral.

options.text: "Stronger glasses should help, since this sounds like the normal focusing change of aging"
options.rationale: The aging lens does cause near focus trouble, which makes glasses seem logical. Her reading is unchanged, and lost side vision is not a normal aging change.

options.text: "Your symptoms are an emergency, so go to the emergency department right now"
options.rationale: Sudden pain, vision loss and redness signal an angle closure emergency. Her changes developed over months with only a mild ache, which fits the gradual form.

options.text: "These symptoms come from a cloudy lens, so you will likely need cataract surgery"
options.rationale: Cataracts also cause glare and halos, so this is a near miss. Cataracts blur the whole field, while she has lost side vision with central vision intact.

questions.takeaway: Open angle glaucoma: gradual peripheral vision loss, halos and a mild ache; the loss is not reversible with glasses.
questions.strategy: Halos appear in both cataracts and glaucoma. The loss of side vision with central vision intact tips it to glaucoma.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Side vision gone, central vision intact.
Months, not hours, so not angle closure.
Glasses do not restore glaucoma vision loss.

elimination.verdict: Pressure check and referral; glasses will not help.

questions.stem: A patient with extreme nearsightedness calls the clinic triage line. Two hours ago he suddenly saw flashes of light and new floaters in his right eye. Now a dark shadow covers part of his vision in that eye. He has no pain. What should the nurse tell him?

options.text: "Floaters are common with age, so mention them at your next routine visit"
options.rationale: Floaters do become more common with aging, so this sounds reasonable for an isolated floater. New floaters with flashes and a shadow are not routine.

options.text: "Since there is no pain, rest your eyes tonight and call back if it spreads"
options.rationale: Lack of pain feels reassuring, which is the trap here. Retinal detachment is typically painless, and waiting lets the detachment progress.

options.text: "Put on dark glasses and avoid bright light until the flashes settle down"
options.rationale: Dark glasses are used after cataract surgery, so this sounds like eye care. It treats light sensitivity and does nothing for a detaching retina.

options.text: "These symptoms need emergency eye care now, so go to be examined right away"
options.rationale: Flashes, floaters and a curtain over vision are the classic signs of retinal detachment, and extreme myopia is a risk factor. It is an emergency even without pain.

questions.takeaway: Sudden flashes, floaters and a curtain over vision, without pain, signal retinal detachment, an emergency.
questions.strategy: No pain is the cue that pulls toward waiting. Sudden visual change is the deciding feature.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flashes, floaters, curtain, sudden.
Extreme myopia.
Retinal detachment is painless.

elimination.verdict: Emergency examination now.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a college student who sleeps in his contact lenses and has right eye pain, tearing and a hazy right cornea. Fluorescein staining shows a green area on the cornea. He asks to come back next week after his exams. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "A corneal infection can damage the eye quickly, so you need treatment to start today"
options.rationale: Pain, a hazy cornea and green fluorescein staining in a contact lens wearer point to corneal ulceration or infection. The cornea has no separate blood supply, so infection is an emergency.

options.text: "Take your lenses out for a week, and come back after exams if the pain continues"
options.rationale: Lenses do stay out, so part of this is correct. Delay is the problem, because the cornea cannot fight infection well without a blood supply.

options.text: "This is a scratch that heals by itself, so use artificial tears until next week"
options.rationale: A simple abrasion can heal, and that makes this tempting. A hazy cornea with tearing in someone who sleeps in lenses raises infection risk, which needs antibiotics now.

options.text: "Your eye pressure is probably high, so you will need a glaucoma check next week"
options.rationale: Angle closure also causes pain and a hazy cornea. The green stain and contact lens history point to the corneal surface, not to raised pressure.

questions.takeaway: A painful hazy cornea with green fluorescein staining in a lens wearer is an emergency because the cornea has no separate blood supply.
questions.strategy: His schedule makes a delay sound acceptable. The cornea's lack of a blood supply sets the timing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Green fluorescein means a corneal defect.
Sleeping in lenses raises infection risk.
No blood supply means infection is an emergency.

elimination.verdict: Treatment today.

questions.stem: During an eye examination, a delivery driver says he can read his phone clearly but cannot read highway signs until he is almost under them. His eye care provider prescribes corrective lenses. He asks why his eyes work this way. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Your lens has lost its elasticity with age, so it can no longer focus up close"
options.rationale: This correctly describes presbyopia, the loss of lens elasticity with age. It affects near vision, and he reads his phone without trouble.

options.text: "Your cornea is curved unevenly, so images are distorted at every distance"
options.rationale: This correctly describes astigmatism. His problem depends on distance, with near vision clear, so uneven distortion at all distances does not fit.

options.text: "Your eye focuses images in front of the retina; a concave lens corrects it"
options.rationale: Clear near vision with blurry distance vision is myopia, or nearsightedness. The image falls in front of the retina, and a concave lens corrects it.

options.text: "Your eye focuses images behind the retina, and a convex lens moves the focus forward"
options.rationale: This correctly describes hyperopia, or farsightedness. Hyperopia blurs near objects more than distant ones, which is the reverse of his complaint.

questions.takeaway: Myopia: image focuses in front of the retina, corrected with a concave lens; hyperopia: behind the retina, corrected with a convex lens.
questions.strategy: Each option is a true statement about some refractive error. Match the one to the distance he cannot see.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Near clear, far blurry: nearsighted.
Focus in front of the retina, concave correction.

elimination.verdict: Myopia with concave lens correction.

questions.nursesNote: 0900 Admission eye assessment. Patient has worn glasses for distance for 20 years. Left upper eyelid droops over the top of the iris; patient's wife says this began 2 weeks ago. Both eyes are symmetric in position. Sclerae white, corneas clear. Right pupil 3 mm, left pupil 6 mm. Both pupils constrict when light is shone into either eye. Red reflex present on the right, absent on the left. Snellen 20/20 right eye with glasses.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that need follow up.

segments.text: Patient has worn glasses for distance for 20 years.
segments.rationale: Long term use of corrective lenses is common history for an adult. It explains the glasses during acuity testing and needs no follow up on its own.

segments.text: Left upper eyelid droops over the top of the iris
segments.rationale: A drooping eyelid is ptosis, which is checked for during inspection. Ptosis that started 2 weeks ago is a new change and is reported.

segments.text: Both eyes are symmetric in position.
segments.rationale: Symmetric eye position means there is no exophthalmos or enophthalmos on inspection. This is a normal finding and needs no follow up.

segments.text: Sclerae white, corneas clear.
segments.rationale: White sclerae and clear corneas are the normal color and clarity checked on inspection. Nothing here needs follow up.

segments.text: Right pupil 3 mm, left pupil 6 mm.
segments.rationale: PERRLA requires pupils that are equal in size. A difference of 3 mm between the two pupils is abnormal and is reported.

segments.text: Both pupils constrict when light is shone into either eye.
segments.rationale: Constriction of the other pupil is the normal consensual response, and both eyes have it. This finding is expected.

segments.text: absent on the left
segments.rationale: An absent red reflex can signal a mature cataract. It needs follow up with ophthalmoscopy and slit lamp examination by the eye care provider.

segments.text: Snellen 20/20 right eye with glasses.
segments.rationale: A reading of 20/20 is normal visual acuity on the Snellen chart. The right eye is well corrected with glasses and needs no follow up.

questions.takeaway: Inspection checks ptosis and symmetry; PERRLA checks equal pupils with direct and consensual responses; an absent red reflex suggests a mature cataract.
questions.strategy: The consensual response looks odd to students but is normal. Check each finding against what normal looks like.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New ptosis is abnormal; symmetry and clear corneas are normal.
Unequal size fails PERRLA; consensual constriction is normal.
Absent left red reflex is abnormal; 20/20 is normal.

elimination.verdict: New ptosis, unequal pupils and the absent left red reflex.

questions.stem: The nurse is interviewing a 47 year old patient who has always had good vision and says she now holds menus at arm's length to read them. Her distance vision is clear, and she has no pain or flashes. Which conclusion should guide the nurse's teaching?

options.text: This is farsightedness she has had since birth, and it is now worsening
options.rationale: Farsightedness also blurs near vision, which makes this a near miss. She has always had good vision, and her change began in midlife.

options.text: This is an expected loss of lens elasticity that reading glasses correct
options.rationale: Presbyopia is the loss of lens elasticity that begins in the 40s, so near focus fails first. Her age, new onset and clear distance vision fit it.

options.text: This is open angle glaucoma, and she needs a pressure check today
options.rationale: Age is a glaucoma risk factor, so screening has value. Glaucoma takes side vision first, while her problem is focusing up close.

options.text: This is an early cataract, and she will need surgery once it worsens
options.rationale: Cataracts do develop with age and blur vision. They blur vision at all distances, fade colors and make night driving hard, none of which she reports.

questions.takeaway: Presbyopia: age related loss of lens elasticity starting in the 40s, causing trouble with near focus.
questions.strategy: Hyperopia and presbyopia both blur near vision. Lifelong versus new in midlife separates them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New in her late 40s after a lifetime of good vision.
Near focus only; distance is clear.

elimination.verdict: Presbyopia; reading glasses.

questions.objective: 7. Differentiate common eye and vision disorders, including cataracts, glaucoma, retinal detachment, and refractive errors

questions.stem: At a pediatric clinic visit, the nurse learns that a 9 year old boy holds his books at arm's length and rubs his eyes after homework, but he reads the board clearly from the back of the classroom. He has no eye disease, pain or injury, and his new glasses use convex lenses. His mother asks what the problem is. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: His lenses are losing elasticity as they age
options.rationale: Loss of lens elasticity also blurs near vision and pushes reading material farther away. That is presbyopia, which begins in the 40s, so it does not explain this change in a 9 year old.

options.text: His corneas are curved unevenly, distorting all images
options.rationale: Astigmatism comes from uneven corneal curvature and can make the eyes tired, so it may seem to fit. It distorts images at every distance, and his clear view of the board rules it out.

options.text: His eyes focus distant images in front of the retina
options.rationale: Myopia, or nearsightedness, focuses images in front of the retina and blurs distant objects. He reads the board from the back row, and myopia is corrected with a concave lens, not a convex one.

options.text: His eyes focus near images behind the retina
options.rationale: Hyperopia, or farsightedness, focuses images behind the retina, so close work blurs and tires the eyes. A convex lens moves the focus forward, which matches his new glasses.

questions.takeaway: Hyperopia blurs near vision and is corrected with a convex lens; myopia blurs distance and takes a concave lens; astigmatism distorts at every distance; presbyopia begins in the 40s.
questions.strategy: Presbyopia is the near miss because it also blurs near vision. His age rules it out, and the convex lens plus a clear distant view point to farsightedness.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Near work blurs; the board is clear.
A convex lens moves focus forward, which corrects images that fall behind the retina.
Presbyopia starts in the 40s, not in childhood.

elimination.verdict: His eyes focus near images behind the retina.

questions.concept: myopia, hyperopia and astigmatism with lens correction

questions.stem: A 52 year old landscaper with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has not had an eye exam in 6 years. His vision is 20/20 and he has no eye symptoms. He asks how often he really needs his eyes checked. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: Every year once you turn 60, when risk begins
options.rationale: Age 60 is a real glaucoma risk threshold for some groups, so this answer sounds familiar. Annual exams start after 40 when risk factors are present, and he already has two of them.

options.text: Every year, since your age and health raise your risk
options.rationale: Screening frequency increases with age, and exams are annual after 40, especially with risk factors. Diabetes and hypertension are major risk factors that can damage the eye before vision changes.

options.text: Every 5 years, as long as your vision stays at 20/20
options.rationale: Normal acuity is reassuring, and a long interval can suit a younger adult with no risks. Diabetes and hypertension can harm the eye while vision is still 20/20, so 5 years is far too long.

options.text: Only when you notice a change in your vision
options.rationale: Waiting for symptoms seems sensible when his vision is clear. Many eye diseases, such as open angle glaucoma, cause no symptoms until damage is done, and screening is meant to catch them first.

questions.takeaway: Eye exams become annual after 40, especially with risk factors such as diabetes and hypertension, because damage can begin before vision changes.
questions.strategy: His 20/20 vision tempts a longer interval. Age over 40 plus diabetes and hypertension call for yearly exams no matter how well he sees.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He is over 40 and has diabetes and hypertension.
Exams are annual after 40, especially with risk factors.
Normal vision does not mean a healthy eye.

elimination.verdict: Every year, since his age and health raise his risk.

questions.stem: A patient with cataracts in both eyes can no longer read his medication labels or cook safely because of blurred vision. He asks whether eyedrops could clear his lenses. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Surgery is the only treatment, and it is done once your better eye reaches 20/200"
options.rationale: Surgery is right here too, but 20/200 in the better eye is the line for legal blindness. Waiting for that would leave him unsafe for far too long.

options.text: "Surgery is the only treatment, and it is done once the pupil has turned bluish white"
options.rationale: Surgery is the right treatment, which makes this tempting. A bluish white pupil describes a mature cataract, while the timing of surgery is set by daily function.

options.text: "Surgery is the only treatment, and it is done once daily activities are affected"
options.rationale: No drops or medicines clear a cataract, so surgery is the only treatment. It is timed by function, and unsafe cooking and unreadable labels meet that point.

options.text: "Eyedrops used every day lower the pressure in the eye and slow the lens clouding"
options.rationale: Daily pressure lowering drops are the treatment for glaucoma. They do nothing to clear or slow a cloudy lens.

questions.takeaway: Cataracts are treated only by surgery, performed when ADLs are affected.
questions.strategy: Three options name surgery. Compare the trigger each one attaches to it.

steps.detail: Pressure lowering drops treat glaucoma.
Pupil color, an acuity number, or daily function; the stem describes lost function.

elimination.verdict: Surgery, timed by daily activities.
