questions.concept: cataract surgery as the only treatment, timed by ADLs

questions.stem: The nurse gives discharge teaching to a patient going home 2 hours after phacoemulsification of her right eye with a lens implant. Which statement shows that the discharge teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will have my grandson lift the laundry and I will not bend to tie shoes"
options.rationale: Bending, lifting more than 10 lb and straining raise IOP and are avoided after cataract surgery. Her plan avoids both.

options.text: "If my eye suddenly hurts tonight, I will take pain medicine and call next week"
options.rationale: Mild discomfort can be managed at home, which makes this tempting. Sudden pain is one of the findings she must report right away.

options.text: "I can go back to lifting weights at the gym as long as I keep my head up"
options.rationale: Keeping her head up avoids bending, so part of this is correct. Lifting heavy weights still strains and raises IOP, which is avoided after surgery.

options.text: "My vision should be at its sharpest by tomorrow morning when I take the patch off"
options.rationale: Vision does start to improve soon after surgery, so this sounds hopeful. Best vision takes 4 to 6 weeks, and expecting it tomorrow may make her think normal healing has failed.

questions.takeaway: After cataract surgery: dark glasses, no bending, lifting over 10 lb or straining, report sudden pain or vision loss; best vision in 4 to 6 weeks.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option is half right. Check every statement against the IOP rule and the report rule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No bending, lifting over 10 lb or straining.
Best vision at 4 to 6 weeks, not the next day.
Sudden pain is reported now.

elimination.verdict: Avoiding lifting and bending shows understanding.

questions.nursesNote: 1015 Clinic visit. Patient reports vision in both eyes has slowly blurred over the past 2 years. States, "I think I just need stronger glasses." Denies eye pain. Reports bright lights at night make driving difficult. Side vision intact on confrontation. Says colors look faded and yellowish. Tonometry 15 mmHg both eyes. Denies flashes or floaters. Pupil of the right eye appears bluish white.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that point to cataracts.

segments.text: slowly blurred over the past 2 years
segments.rationale: Gradual blurring over months to years is the typical cataract course. It separates cataracts from the sudden onset of retinal detachment or angle closure glaucoma.

segments.text: "I think I just need stronger glasses."
segments.rationale: Patients with early cataracts often blame their glasses or contacts. This comment fits the slow, painless blur the lens causes.

segments.text: Denies eye pain.
segments.rationale: Cataracts are painless, so this agrees with the diagnosis. Open angle glaucoma and retinal detachment can also be painless, so it does not point to cataracts on its own.

segments.text: bright lights at night make driving difficult
segments.rationale: Difficulty with night driving is a classic cataract complaint. The cloudy lens scatters the light from headlights and streetlights, causing glare.

segments.text: Side vision intact on confrontation.
segments.rationale: Intact side vision helps rule out glaucoma. It is a normal finding rather than a sign of cataracts.

segments.text: colors look faded and yellowish
segments.rationale: A clouded, yellowed lens reduces color perception, so colors look dull. Faded colors are a common cataract finding.

segments.text: Tonometry 15 mmHg both eyes.
segments.rationale: This pressure is normal, which argues against glaucoma. Cataracts do not raise eye pressure, so the reading does not point to them.

segments.text: Pupil of the right eye appears bluish white.
segments.rationale: A bluish white pupil is a sign of a mature cataract. The ophthalmoscope would also show an absent red reflex in that eye.

questions.takeaway: Cataracts: painless, gradual blur, faded colors, night driving trouble, blaming glasses, and a bluish white pupil when mature.
questions.strategy: Painless and normal pressure fit cataracts but do not separate them from other problems. Highlight the findings that point to the lens.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gradual blur, faded colors, night driving, bluish white pupil.
No pain and normal pressure do not point to cataracts alone.

elimination.verdict: Gradual blur, blaming glasses, night driving trouble, faded colors and the bluish white pupil.

questions.stem: Two days after cataract removal from his left eye, a man phones the clinic. Yesterday the eye felt mildly scratchy. One hour ago he developed sudden sharp pain in that eye, and his vision in it is now dimmer. What should the nurse advise?

options.text: Expect the best vision only 4 to 6 weeks after the surgery
options.rationale: This is true and would answer a patient whose vision is slowly clearing. It does not explain vision that worsened within an hour.

options.text: Rest with dark glasses on and call again if the pain lasts 24 hours
options.rationale: Dark glasses and rest suit the mild scratchiness he had yesterday. The new findings are sudden pain and dimmer vision, which cannot wait a day.

options.text: Stop bending and lifting, then recheck the eye in the morning
options.rationale: Avoiding bending and lifting is correct aftercare, but it prevents complications. It does not address a complication that has already started.

options.text: Have the eye examined by the surgeon today for the new pain
options.rationale: Sudden pain and vision loss are the findings patients are taught to report after cataract surgery. Both are present, so the eye is examined now.

questions.takeaway: After cataract surgery, sudden pain or sudden vision loss is reported and examined right away.
questions.strategy: Yesterday's scratchiness and today's pain are different findings. Answer the newest cue and the word sudden.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mild scratchiness yesterday, sudden pain and dimmer vision now.
Sudden pain and vision loss are both on it.

elimination.verdict: Examination by the surgeon today.

questions.stem: Four patients arrive at an urgent eye care clinic at the same time. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: A patient whose left eye feels scratchy after rubbing it, with clear vision
options.rationale: A scratchy eye after rubbing deserves an exam for a small surface injury. Clear vision with no sudden pain or redness makes it the least urgent problem in the group.

options.text: A patient whose right eye turned painful, red and foggy 40 minutes ago
options.rationale: Pain, redness and clouded vision that began suddenly fit angle closure glaucoma, in which pressure climbs fast and can damage the optic nerve within hours. It is a medical emergency, so this patient is seen first.

options.text: A patient with glaucoma who ran out of drops 2 days ago and now sees halos with a mild ache
options.rationale: Missed drops with new halos and an ache are a real concern, and this patient needs drops and a pressure check today. Those are signs of the gradual, open angle form, which is not the immediate threat.

options.text: A patient whose cataract was removed 3 weeks ago and whose vision is not yet fully sharp
options.rationale: Vision that is still a little soft 3 weeks after cataract removal is expected, since the best vision comes 4 to 6 weeks after surgery. Nothing here signals a complication.

questions.takeaway: Sudden pain, redness and clouded vision point to angle closure glaucoma, an emergency that outranks the gradual signs of open angle glaucoma even when drops were missed.
questions.strategy: The word glaucoma and the missed drops pull toward the patient with halos, but halos and a mild ache are signs of the slow form. The patient with no diagnosis named, whose symptoms began suddenly, is the emergency.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The patient with glaucoma named is not the one whose eye changed suddenly.
One eye became painful, red and foggy within the last hour.
Halos with a mild ache are gradual glaucoma; the scratchy eye has clear vision; soft vision at 3 weeks is expected.

elimination.verdict: The adult whose right eye turned painful, red and foggy 40 minutes ago.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the chart of a patient with open angle glaucoma whose pressures were 17 mmHg on prostaglandin eyedrops 6 months ago. Today both eyes read 27 mmHg. Pharmacy records show one bottle refilled in 6 months. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ask the patient how and how often the drops are being used at home
options.rationale: A pressure rise with too few refills suggests missed doses, and strict adherence is critical in glaucoma. Assessing use first tells the team whether the drug failed or was not taken.

options.text: Teach the patient that the vision already lost will return once pressure falls
options.rationale: Lowering pressure does matter, but the teaching is wrong. Glaucoma treatment prevents further damage and does not restore lost vision.

options.text: Prepare the patient for laser trabeculoplasty because the drops have failed
options.rationale: Surgery is the next step when drops fail, so this is logical. The refill record suggests the drops were not used, so failure has not been shown yet.

options.text: Ask the provider to add a second type of eyedrop to lower the pressure
options.rationale: Adding a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor or a beta blocker is a real option when one drug is not enough. Doing it before checking adherence may add a drug the patient also will not use.

questions.takeaway: In glaucoma, strict adherence to eyedrops is critical; assess use before concluding treatment failed.
questions.strategy: Rising pressure invites escalation. The refill record points to assessment first.

steps.detail: One bottle in 6 months.
Ask how the drops are used before surgery or new drugs.

elimination.verdict: Assess adherence first.

The reading in this item sits clearly inside or outside every version, so the key is the same either way. On the course exam, use the range a question states; if a reading of exactly 21 mmHg appears with no range given, it is normal by the glaucoma figure but raised by the assessment figure, so check the stem's wording. questions.stem: Before starting beta blocker eyedrops for open angle glaucoma, a patient has a resting heart rate of 58 beats per minute. Which instruction best limits the amount of drug that reaches the rest of the body?

options.text: "Blink several times right after the drop so it spreads across your eye"
options.rationale: Blinking does spread the drop, so this sounds helpful. It also pumps the drug into the tear duct, which raises systemic absorption.

options.text: "Put in two drops each time so that enough of the drug stays in the eye"
options.rationale: Extra drops feel like they would work better. More drug means more drains to the body, which raises the risk of slowing his heart further.

options.text: "After each drop, press gently on the inner corner of your eye near your nose"
options.rationale: Punctal occlusion blocks the tear duct, so less drug drains into the nose and bloodstream. With a heart rate of 58, limiting the systemic beta blocker effect matters.

options.text: "Take your pulse once a week and skip the drops if it is below 60"
options.rationale: Watching the heart rate is reasonable with beta blockers. Skipping doses breaks the strict adherence glaucoma needs, and it does not reduce absorption.

questions.takeaway: Punctal occlusion, pressing the inner corner of the eye after drops, reduces systemic absorption of glaucoma eyedrops.
questions.strategy: The heart rate makes monitoring options attractive. The stem asks how to limit absorption, which points to technique.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Limit the drug reaching the body.
Pressure on the inner corner blocks drainage.

elimination.verdict: Punctal occlusion.

questions.objective: 10. Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common vision disorders

questions.stem: A patient with open angle glaucoma started eyedrops 3 months ago and has used every dose. His eye pressure is now controlled, but the side vision he lost before diagnosis has not returned. He says, "The drops are not working, so I want to stop them." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: Stronger glasses will bring back the side vision the drops cannot
options.rationale: Glasses correct focusing problems such as nearsightedness and farsightedness. Glaucoma vision loss comes from nerve damage, so it is not reversible with glasses or any other treatment.

options.text: The drops protect the vision you still have, so keep using them
options.rationale: Glaucoma treatment aims to prevent further damage, not to restore vision already lost. His controlled pressure shows the drops are working, and treatment continues for the rest of his life.

options.text: You may stop once your pressure stays controlled for a full year
options.rationale: A year of controlled pressure sounds like a reasonable point to reassess. Glaucoma treatment is lifelong, and stopping the drops lets the pressure rise and damage the nerve again.

options.text: Ask about laser surgery, since the drops have not restored your vision
options.rationale: Laser trabeculoplasty is a real option when drops fail to lower the pressure. His pressure is controlled, so the drops have not failed, and no surgery restores lost side vision.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma treatment is lifelong and prevents further damage without restoring lost vision; surgery is for drops that fail to control the pressure.
questions.strategy: Laser surgery is the near miss because it is the next step when drops fail. Controlled pressure means the drops are doing their job, which is protecting the vision he has left.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The goal is to stop further damage, not to restore vision.
Controlled pressure means the drops have not failed.
Treatment is lifelong.

elimination.verdict: Keep using the drops to protect the vision he still has.

questions.objective: 10. Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common vision disorders
questions.concept: glaucoma treatment goal and lifelong adherence

questions.scenario: At an eye clinic, the nurse reviews tonometry results and symptoms for several patients.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate which finding the pressure and symptoms best fit.

rows.text: 19 mmHg in each eye; no symptoms
rows.rationale: A reading of 19 mmHg falls inside every accepted normal range. With no symptoms, this patient continues with routine screening.

rows.text: 48 mmHg in the right eye; sudden severe pain and redness for 1 hour
rows.rationale: Angle closure pressures run 30 mmHg or higher. Sudden pain and redness show the drainage angle has closed, which is an emergency.

rows.text: 36 mmHg in the left eye; sudden blurred vision and a hazy cornea
rows.rationale: A pressure above 30 mmHg with sudden vision loss fits angle closure. The hazy cornea is corneal edema from the abrupt pressure rise.

rows.text: 13 mmHg in each eye; gradual blur and faded colors
rows.rationale: 13 mmHg is normal, so glaucoma is not the explanation. Gradual blur with faded colors points to cataracts, which do not raise pressure.

rows.text: 26 mmHg in each eye; slow loss of side vision over a year
rows.rationale: 26 mmHg sits in the open angle range of 22 to 32 mmHg. Gradual peripheral loss matches the slow course of open angle glaucoma.

rows.text: 24 mmHg in each eye; no symptoms, found at a yearly checkup
rows.rationale: 24 mmHg is in the open angle range even though the patient feels fine. Open angle glaucoma is often silent until late, so the lack of a complaint does not make the pressure normal.

questions.takeaway: Normal pressure is about 10 to 21 mmHg; open angle glaucoma runs about 22 to 32 mmHg and is gradual; angle closure runs 30 mmHg or higher and is sudden and painful.
questions.strategy: Two patients have no symptoms, and pressure alone can mislead near the cutoffs. Place the number first, then use the onset and symptoms to separate the gradual form from the sudden one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Normal, 22 to 32 mmHg, or 30 mmHg and higher.
Sudden and painful means angle closure; gradual means open angle.

elimination.verdict: Normal: 19 and 13 mmHg. Open angle: 26 and 24 mmHg. Angle closure: 48 and 36 mmHg.

questions.objective: 7. Differentiate common eye and vision disorders, including cataracts, glaucoma, retinal detachment, and refractive errors
questions.concept: open angle versus angle closure glaucoma
questions.note: Your instructor's material gives normal eye pressure two ways: 10 to 20 mmHg with the eye assessment techniques and 8 to 21 mmHg with glaucoma. Standard references give about 10 to 21 mmHg, and both versions agree that 22 mmHg or higher is raised, where the open angle glaucoma range begins. The reading in this item sits clearly inside or outside every version, so the key is the same either way. On the course exam, use the range a question states; if a reading of exactly 21 mmHg appears with no range given, it is normal by the glaucoma figure but raised by the assessment figure, so check the stem's wording. For NCLEX, treat a reading above 21 mmHg as raised.

questions.stem: On the surgical unit, a patient is awaiting scleral buckling surgery for a left retinal detachment. She wants to walk the hall and read on her phone to pass the time. Which action by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: Explain that her activity is restricted and the eye patch stays on
options.rationale: Before repair, head movement and activity are restricted and an eye patch reduces eye movement. Both limit further pulling on the detached retina.

options.text: Remove the patch so she can see well enough to walk safely
options.rationale: Seeing clearly does help safety, so this sounds kind. The patch reduces eye movement, and removing it allows more strain on the retina.

options.text: Allow both activities, since restrictions begin after the surgery
options.rationale: Many restrictions do follow surgery, which makes this tempting. For retinal detachment, restriction of head movement starts before surgery.

options.text: Encourage hall walks to prevent clots, but ask her to avoid reading
options.rationale: Early walking prevents clots after many surgeries, so this sounds like good care. Before retinal repair, activity is restricted to protect the retina.

questions.takeaway: Before retinal detachment surgery: restrict head movement and activity and use an eye patch to reduce eye movement.
questions.strategy: Clot prevention makes walking feel like standard surgical care. The retina's needs come first here.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Restrict head movement and activity; patch the eye.
Walking, reading and removing the patch all increase movement.

elimination.verdict: Restrict activity and keep the patch.

questions.objective: 10. Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common vision disorders

questions.stem: After scleral buckling surgery for a right retinal detachment, a patient is preparing to go home. Which statement shows that he needs more teaching?

options.text: I will put off reading and other close work for the first week.
options.rationale: Reading and close work keep the eyes moving constantly, so they are avoided for the first week. This statement is accurate and needs no further teaching.

options.text: My wife will carry the groceries, and I will not bend over.
options.rationale: Lifting and bending raise intraocular pressure, which he must avoid while the eye heals. Letting his wife carry the groceries shows he understood the activity limits.

options.text: I will keep my head in the position the surgeon showed me.
options.rationale: Positioning per the surgeon's instructions helps the gas or oil hold the retina in place. This statement is correct and shows he understood that part of the teaching.

options.text: If eye pain comes with nausea, I will rest and wait.
options.rationale: Pain with nausea after retinal surgery is a warning sign that must be reported right away. Waiting it out at home could delay care for a problem that threatens his vision.

questions.takeaway: After retinal detachment repair, follow the surgeon's positioning, avoid IOP raising activities and close work for the first week, and report sudden pain, pain with nausea or sudden vision change at once.
questions.strategy: Three statements describe careful behavior at home. The one that waits out pain with nausea delays a report that must be made immediately.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Look for the statement that is unsafe.
Positioning, no lifting or bending and no close work are all correct.
Pain with nausea is reported right away, not watched.

elimination.verdict: The plan to rest and wait with eye pain and nausea needs more teaching.

questions.objective: 10. Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common vision disorders

questions.stem: The provider prescribes broad spectrum antibiotic eyedrops every hour for the first 24 hours for a graduate student with a right corneal ulcer. She plans to sleep through the night and catch up on the doses in the morning. What should the nurse teach?

options.text: "Put in several drops at bedtime so the medicine lasts until morning"
options.rationale: This tries to make up for the missed doses, which sounds practical. Extra drops at once run out of the eye and do not keep drug levels up for hours.

options.text: "Sleep through the night, since rest helps the cornea heal faster"
options.rationale: Rest does support healing, so this sounds caring. Skipping hours of antibiotic during the first day lets the infection grow.

options.text: Set an alarm so each dose goes in on time through the night
options.rationale: Antibiotics are often given hourly for the first 24 hours because the cornea has no separate blood supply. Missing a night of doses lets the infection progress.

options.text: "Wear your contact lens at night to hold the medicine against the cornea"
options.rationale: Keeping drug in contact with the cornea sounds logical. Contact lenses stay out until the cornea is fully healed.

questions.takeaway: Corneal infections are often treated with broad spectrum antibiotic drops hourly for the first 24 hours, including overnight.
questions.strategy: Sleep and rest sound healthy. The schedule exists because the cornea cannot fight infection without a blood supply.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every hour for 24 hours.
No separate blood supply in the cornea.
Bunched doses, skipped doses and lenses do not meet the schedule.

elimination.verdict: Hourly drops overnight.

questions.objective: 10. Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common vision disorders

questions.stem: On day 4 of antibiotic eyedrops for infection of both corneas, a patient says the pain is gone. Which statement shows that the patient understood the teaching?

options.text: I will save the leftover drops in case this comes back.
options.rationale: Saving medicine may seem thrifty, but the full antibiotic course must be completed. Stopping early to keep leftovers lets the infection return in a cornea with no separate blood supply.

options.text: I wipe the bottle tip between eyes so one bottle is enough.
options.rationale: Keeping the tip clean is a good habit with any eyedrop. Wiping does not reliably remove organisms, and the teaching for infection in both eyes is a separate bottle for each.

options.text: I use one bottle for my right eye and another for my left.
options.rationale: Separate bottles keep organisms from one eye from reaching the other on the dropper tip. With both corneas infected, a bottle for each eye is what the teaching called for.

options.text: I wear my contacts for a few hours now that the pain is gone.
options.rationale: Feeling better on day 4 is a good sign that the antibiotic is working. Contact lenses stay out until the cornea is fully healed, not just until the pain stops.

questions.takeaway: Corneal infection teaching: a separate bottle for each infected eye, the full antibiotic course, and no contact lenses until the cornea has fully healed.
questions.strategy: Wiping the tip sounds like careful technique and is the closest distractor. The teaching for infection in both eyes is separate bottles, not a cleaner shared one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two infected eyes need two bottles.
Finish every dose; do not save leftovers.
They stay out until healing is complete.

elimination.verdict: A separate bottle for each eye.

questions.objective: 10. Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common vision disorders

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient who is considering LASIK surgery to correct nearsightedness. After teaching, which statement shows that the patient understood the procedure and its risks?

options.text: "The laser reshapes my retina, so I must avoid reading for the first week"
options.rationale: Avoiding reading and close work for the first week is teaching after retinal detachment repair. LASIK changes the cornea, not the retina.

options.text: "The laser reshapes my cornea, and I may have dry eyes or halos afterward"
options.rationale: LASIK uses a laser to reshape the cornea. Dry eyes, halos and, rarely, light sensitivity are the complications to expect and report.

options.text: "The laser replaces my lens with an implant, so I will not get cataracts later"
options.rationale: Lens replacement with an implant is cataract surgery, not LASIK. LASIK works on the cornea and leaves the lens alone.

options.text: "The laser opens a drain in my eye, so I will need pressure drops for life"
options.rationale: Laser treatment that improves drainage belongs to glaucoma care. LASIK reshapes the cornea and has nothing to do with eye pressure.

questions.takeaway: LASIK reshapes the cornea; complications include dry eyes, halos and, rarely, light sensitivity.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option borrows a laser or a restriction from a different eye surgery. Ask which structure LASIK changes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: LASIK reshapes the cornea.
Dry eyes and halos.

elimination.verdict: Cornea reshaped; dry eyes or halos possible.

questions.objective: 10. Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common vision disorders

questions.scenario: In the emergency department, a patient reports severe right eye pain that began suddenly 1 hour ago. The right eye is red, the cornea looks hazy, and vision in that eye is blurred. Tonometry reads 46 mmHg in the right eye and 16 mmHg in the left eye. He does not wear contact lenses and reports no injury.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Patch the eye and schedule a clinic visit tomorrow
options.rationale: An eye patch is used before retinal detachment surgery to limit eye movement. Delaying care for a day risks permanent vision loss here.

options.text: Notify the provider immediately of the findings
options.rationale: Sudden pain, redness, corneal edema and a pressure of 46 mmHg signal an emergency. Rapid treatment is needed to prevent permanent optic nerve damage.

options.text: Irrigate the right eye with sterile saline
options.rationale: Saline irrigation treats a foreign body on the eye surface. He reports no injury, and irrigation does nothing for a blocked drainage angle.

options.text: Prepare the patient for laser peripheral iridotomy
options.rationale: Laser peripheral iridotomy is the first line emergency treatment for angle closure. It opens a path for aqueous humor to drain.

options.text: Angle closure glaucoma
options.rationale: Sudden pain, vision loss, a red eye and corneal edema with a pressure of 30 mmHg or higher are the angle closure pattern. The iris has blocked drainage.

options.text: Corneal ulceration
options.rationale: A corneal ulcer also causes pain and a hazy cornea. There is no contact lens use or injury, and the very high pressure points to blocked drainage.

options.text: Retinal detachment
options.rationale: Retinal detachment is also sudden and an emergency. It is painless, with flashes, floaters and a curtain, and it does not raise the pressure.

options.text: Open angle glaucoma
options.rationale: Open angle glaucoma also raises pressure, which makes it a near miss. It is gradual and nearly symptom free, with pressures of about 22 to 32 mmHg.

options.text: Fluorescein staining of the cornea
options.rationale: Fluorescein staining finds corneal abrasions and ulcers on the eye surface. It does not measure the pressure problem causing this emergency.

options.text: Intraocular pressure in the right eye
options.rationale: IOP shows whether treatment is opening the drainage angle. A falling pressure means aqueous humor is draining again.

options.text: Color discrimination in both eyes
options.rationale: Color changes are expected with aging and occur with cataracts. They do not track an acute pressure crisis.

options.text: Pain level and vision in the right eye
options.rationale: Pain and vision track the pressure on the optic nerve. Easing pain and stable vision show the treatment is working.

questions.takeaway: Angle closure glaucoma is an emergency: sudden pain, vision loss, redness, corneal edema and IOP of 30 mmHg or higher; laser peripheral iridotomy is first line.
questions.strategy: Corneal ulcer and angle closure share pain and a hazy cornea. The 46 mmHg reading and absence of lens use or injury tip it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sudden pain plus 46 mmHg means angle closure.
Notify now and prepare for iridotomy.
Pressure, pain and vision.

elimination.verdict: Angle closure glaucoma: notify, prepare for iridotomy, monitor IOP and pain with vision.

questions.objective: 10. Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common vision disorders
questions.note: Your instructor's material gives normal eye pressure two ways: 10 to 20 mmHg with the eye assessment techniques and 8 to 21 mmHg with glaucoma. Standard references give about 10 to 21 mmHg, and both versions agree that 22 mmHg or higher is raised, where the open angle glaucoma range begins. The reading in this item sits clearly inside or outside every version, so the key is the same either way. On the course exam, use the range a question states; if a reading of exactly 21 mmHg appears with no range given, it is normal by the glaucoma figure but raised by the assessment figure, so check the stem's wording. For NCLEX, treat a reading above 21 mmHg as raised.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes after grit blew into his right eye, a machinist has an eye that is tearing, irritated and sensitive to light. A loose speck lies on the surface of the eye, and nothing protrudes from it. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Fluorescein examination and irrigation of the eye with saline
options.rationale: Tearing, irritation and light sensitivity with a loose surface speck fit a foreign body. Fluorescein shows any scratch and saline irrigation washes the particle out.

options.text: A CT scan of the orbits followed by surgical removal
options.rationale: Imaging and surgery are needed when an object has penetrated the eye. Nothing here has entered the eye, so this plan is excessive.

options.text: Leave the speck in place and wait for the eye care provider
options.rationale: Leaving an object in place is the rule for a protruding, penetrating object. A loose speck on the surface is irrigated out.

options.text: An eye patch and restriction of head movement until surgery
options.rationale: A patch and limited head movement are preoperative care for retinal detachment. They do nothing to remove a surface particle.

questions.takeaway: A surface foreign body causes irritation, tearing and light sensitivity and is treated with a fluorescein exam and saline irrigation.
questions.strategy: The machinist detail may suggest a penetrating injury. The stem says the speck is loose and nothing protrudes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Loose surface speck, nothing protruding.
Fluorescein plus saline irrigation.

elimination.verdict: Fluorescein exam and saline irrigation.

questions.objective: 10. Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common vision disorders

questions.stem: In the emergency department, a carpenter injured in a nail gun accident has a metal fragment protruding from his left eye. He asks the nurse to pull it out because it hurts. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Tape a firm pressure patch over the eye to steady it
options.rationale: Steadying the object sounds protective, and the eye does need shielding. Firm pressure on a penetrating injury can drive the fragment deeper and push the eye's contents out.

options.text: Gently pull the fragment out and cover the eye with gauze
options.rationale: Removing the source of pain feels caring. Pulling the object out can tear the eye and push its contents out.

options.text: Irrigate the eye with saline to wash the fragment loose
options.rationale: Saline irrigation treats a loose surface foreign body. Irrigating around a penetrating object can push contaminants deeper and move the object.

options.text: Leave the fragment in place and notify the eye care provider
options.rationale: A protruding object is never removed by the nurse, because pulling it out can cause more damage. Only the eye care provider assesses and removes it.

questions.takeaway: Never remove a protruding object from the eye; only the eye care provider assesses and removes it.
questions.strategy: His pain makes removal feel kind. The nurse's role with a protruding object is to leave it alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Protruding metal: penetrating.
Never remove; the eye care provider does.

elimination.verdict: Leave it in place and notify the provider.

questions.objective: 10. Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common vision disorders

questions.stem: After a grinding wheel shattered, a factory worker may have a metal fragment inside his right eye. Orders before surgery are: MRI of the orbits, CT of the orbits, IV antibiotics and a tetanus booster. Which order should the nurse question?

options.text: The MRI of the orbits
options.rationale: MRI is contraindicated when a metal fragment is suspected, because the magnet can move the metal. Moving metal can cause further injury to the eye.

options.text: The CT of the orbits
options.rationale: CT is one of the imaging tests preferred when metal may be in the eye. It does not use a magnet, so it is safe.

options.text: The tetanus booster
options.rationale: A tetanus booster is given before surgery for a penetrating eye injury. A dirty metal fragment is a tetanus prone wound.

options.text: The IV antibiotics
options.rationale: IV antibiotics are given before surgery for a penetrating eye injury. They lower the risk of infection inside the eye.

questions.takeaway: Suspected metal in the eye: no MRI; use x ray or CT, and give IV antibiotics and a tetanus booster before surgery.
questions.strategy: Three orders are correct and one is unsafe. The word metal should stop you at the magnet.

steps.detail: Three orders are correct; question the one that is not.
CT is preferred; MRI is contraindicated with metal.

elimination.verdict: Question the MRI.

questions.objective: 10. Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common vision disorders

questions.stem: Last week, an eye care provider told a patient that the new floaters in her right eye came from a vitreous change that is common with aging. She calls the clinic because the floaters seem thicker today, and when she looks at a doorway with that eye, its lower half is missing. Her eye does not hurt. What should the nurse tell her?

options.text: Floaters from that change often thicken before they fade
options.rationale: A vitreous change with aging does cause floaters, so the earlier reassurance had a basis. The missing lower half of the doorway is a new field loss that this reassurance does not cover.

options.text: Schedule a visit for an updated glasses prescription
options.rationale: New glasses correct refractive errors, which blur the whole image. They cannot restore part of the visual field that has gone dark because the retina is separating.

options.text: Call back if the eye becomes painful or red
options.rationale: Pain and redness do signal other eye emergencies such as angle closure glaucoma. Retinal detachment is painless, so waiting for pain lets the detachment spread and her vision loss grow.

options.text: Come in for an emergency eye examination now
options.rationale: A missing part of the visual field after new floaters fits a curtain over vision, and retinal detachment is an emergency. The lost area matches where the retina has pulled away, so she needs care now.

questions.takeaway: Floaters explained as an aging vitreous change become an emergency once any part of the visual field goes missing, even without pain.
questions.strategy: The earlier explanation and the lack of pain both invite reassurance. The doorway that is half gone is a field loss, the curtain sign in the patient's own words.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Half a doorway missing is a shadow over part of her vision.

steps.action: Connect it to the vitreous change
steps.detail: Vitreous detachment with aging often leads to retinal detachment.
Detachment is painless, so pain is not the trigger to act.

elimination.verdict: Come in for an emergency eye examination now.

questions.objective: 7. Differentiate common eye and vision disorders, including cataracts, glaucoma, retinal detachment, and refractive errors

questions.stem: At a follow up visit in a pulmonary clinic, a patient who has taken an oral corticosteroid daily for years for asthma says that over the past year the television picture has looked dull and hazy, as if through a dirty window, and the new glasses she bought in the spring did not help. She denies eye pain. When the nurse shines a penlight, the pupil of her left eye looks bluish white. Which condition do her findings suggest?

options.text: Presbyopia
options.rationale: Presbyopia is a common lens change from the 40s and does lead to new glasses. It blurs close work, while her haze affects a distant screen, did not improve with glasses and shows in the pupil.

options.text: Cataract
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are a toxic cause of cataract, and slow painless haze with dull colors is its typical pattern. A bluish white pupil marks a mature cataract, a cloudy lens seen right through the pupil.

options.text: Secondary glaucoma
options.rationale: Long term steroid use can cause secondary glaucoma, and its loss is also gradual, painless and not fixed by glasses. Glaucoma does not turn the pupil bluish white, and it takes side vision before causing overall haze.

options.text: Retinal detachment
options.rationale: Retinal detachment is also painless and can follow eye changes with aging. It starts suddenly with flashes, floaters or a curtain, and her haze has built slowly over a year.

questions.takeaway: Gradual painless haze, dull colors and a bluish white pupil point to cataract; corticosteroids raise the risk of both cataract and secondary glaucoma.
questions.strategy: Her steroid use and glasses that did not help both fit glaucoma. The bluish white pupil is a lens finding that glaucoma does not produce.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A year of slow haze rules out a sudden detachment.
A distant screen and colors, not only close work, so not presbyopia.
A bluish white pupil is a lens change that glaucoma does not cause.

elimination.verdict: Cataract.

questions.objective: 7. Differentiate common eye and vision disorders, including cataracts, glaucoma, retinal detachment, and refractive errors

questions.scenario: The emergency department nurse triages several adults who arrive with eye complaints.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate whether the problem needs emergency care now or can wait for a routine eye appointment.

rows.text: Cloudy cornea and worsening pain 2 days after a tree branch scratched the eye
rows.rationale: A hazy cornea with rising pain after a scratch points to corneal infection. The cornea has no separate blood supply, so infection is treated as an emergency before it damages vision.

rows.text: Blurred near vision that began in the patient's mid 40s
rows.rationale: This fits presbyopia, an age related loss of lens elasticity. Reading glasses correct it, and there is no threat to the eye.

rows.text: Faded colors and glare that have worsened over 2 years
rows.rationale: Slowly worsening colors and glare fit cataracts. Surgery is planned when daily activities are affected, not in the emergency department.

rows.text: Sudden floaters with a shadow over part of the vision
rows.rationale: Floaters with a shadow or curtain point to retinal detachment. It is painless but an emergency because vision is lost as the retina separates.

rows.text: Corneal cut from broken glass with a clear fluid leak
rows.rationale: A corneal laceration is an emergency because eye contents can prolapse through the wound. It may need microscopic suturing and antibiotics.

questions.takeaway: Corneal lacerations, retinal detachment and corneal infection are emergencies; presbyopia and cataracts are routine.
questions.strategy: No pain in retinal detachment pulls it toward routine. Sudden change and threat to the eye decide urgency.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the sudden or open injuries
steps.detail: Laceration, sudden floaters with a shadow, a cloudy painful cornea after a scratch.
Presbyopia and cataracts.

elimination.verdict: Emergency: laceration, floaters with a shadow, infected scratch. Routine: presbyopia, cataracts.

questions.objective: 10. Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common vision disorders
questions.concept: urgency of eye trauma and disorders

questions.stem: Five days into antibiotic eyedrops for an infection of her left cornea, a patient who wears contact lenses returns to the clinic and says the eye feels normal. The nurse reviews her home care. Which statement by the patient needs follow up?

options.text: I will wear my glasses until the provider says it has healed
options.rationale: Waiting for the provider can sound overly cautious once the eye feels normal. Glasses until healing is confirmed is exactly the plan, so this statement shows understanding.

options.text: I will finish every dose even though the eye feels fine
options.rationale: Stopping when symptoms fade is a common error, so this may look like a statement to question. Completing the full antibiotic course is the correct plan and needs no follow up.

options.text: I will switch to new daily lenses now that it feels better
options.rationale: New lenses sound hygienic, but no contact lenses of any kind go in until the cornea is fully healed. Feeling normal is not the same as healed, and a lens over the cornea risks reinfection.

options.text: I will use this bottle only in my left eye
options.rationale: Keeping a bottle for the infected eye prevents carrying the organism to the healthy eye. This statement is correct teaching, so it does not need follow up.

questions.takeaway: After a corneal infection, no contact lenses, even new ones, until the cornea is fully healed; relief of symptoms does not mean healing.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is dressed as good hygiene, and the correct ones sound overly cautious. Sort each by the rule: no lenses until healed, full course, separate bottle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the statement that needs follow up.

steps.action: Test each statement against the rule
steps.detail: Full course, one bottle per infected eye, glasses until healed are all correct.
New lenses are still lenses on an unhealed cornea.

elimination.verdict: I will switch to new daily lenses now that it feels better.

questions.objective: 10. Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common vision disorders

questions.stem: A patient applying for disability benefits reads 20/400 with each eye on the Snellen chart without glasses. With his glasses on, his better eye reads 20/70. He says, "Without my glasses I can barely see the big E, so I must be legally blind." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: The weaker eye is what counts, so you meet the definition
options.rationale: Vision is often recorded for each eye separately. The definition uses the better eye, because a person with one good eye can still function with that eye.

options.text: The definition uses corrected vision, so you do not meet it
options.rationale: Legal blindness is 20/200 or worse in the better eye with correction. His better eye reaches 20/70 with glasses, so he does not meet it, though his vision is still impaired.

options.text: Each eye reads worse than 20/200 uncorrected, so you meet it
options.rationale: His uncorrected readings are worse than 20/200, which makes this sound right. The definition uses vision with glasses on, and his corrected better eye reads 20/70.

options.text: Only total loss of sight in both eyes meets the definition
options.rationale: Many people believe legal blindness means seeing nothing at all. The cutoff is 20/200 or worse in the better eye with correction, so some people who are legally blind still see.

questions.takeaway: Legal blindness is judged in the better eye with correction; uncorrected readings, however poor, do not decide it.
questions.strategy: Both uncorrected readings are far past 20/200, which makes the patient's claim feel right. The words best eye and corrected are both in the definition, and his glasses change the answer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 20/200 or worse, better eye, with correction.
His corrected better eye: 20/70.
20/70 is better than 20/200, so he does not meet it.

elimination.verdict: The definition uses corrected vision, so you do not meet it.

questions.objective: 7. Differentiate common eye and vision disorders, including cataracts, glaucoma, retinal detachment, and refractive errors

questions.stem: On a medical unit, a new graduate nurse caring for an 90 year old patient admitted with liver disease shares her assessment plan with her preceptor. Which statement by the new graduate needs correction?

options.text: I will check his bilirubin result and ask about urine color
options.rationale: This plan looks beyond the eyes, which is the right approach in an older adult. Laboratory values and history give a more reliable picture of jaundice than the sclerae.

options.text: I will offer lubricating drops per order for his dry eyes
options.rationale: Dry eyes can look like a sign of dehydration, so this may seem to need follow up. Reduced tear production is a normal aging change, and lubricating drops treat it.

options.text: His sclerae look white, so I will chart no jaundice
options.rationale: Eye appearance is unreliable for jaundice or hydration in older adults, so white sclerae do not rule jaundice out. In a patient with liver disease, that charting could hide a real problem.

options.text: I will turn on more light before he reads his menu
options.rationale: This adjusts for the aging pupil, which dilates less and needs more light. The statement shows a correct understanding of normal eye changes and needs no correction.

questions.takeaway: In older adults the sclerae cannot rule jaundice or dehydration in or out; use other data such as laboratory results.
questions.strategy: Most students know a yellow sclera is unreliable in older adults but accept a white one as reassuring. The rule works in both directions, so the white sclerae prove nothing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is wrong.

steps.action: Apply the aging rule both ways
steps.detail: Eye appearance cannot confirm or exclude jaundice in older adults.
Lab review, drops for dry eyes and more light are all correct.

elimination.verdict: His sclerae look white, so I will chart no jaundice.

questions.concept: sclera not used for hydration or jaundice in older adults
questions.objective: 6. Recognize normal age related changes in vision

questions.stem: Since a cold began a week ago, a patient has had muffled hearing in the right ear. The provider found fluid behind an intact right eardrum. The patient asks, "Is my hearing nerve damaged?" Which explanation does the nurse give?

options.text: "The fluid keeps the small ear bones from passing the sound inward."
options.rationale: Sound travels from the eardrum across the ossicles to the cochlea, and middle ear fluid dampens that vibration. The nerve is not involved, so this kind of loss is often correctable.

options.text: "The eardrum has torn, so it can no longer vibrate with sound."
options.rationale: A perforation would block conduction, but the provider found the eardrum intact. The fluid behind it is what is damping the vibration of the eardrum and ossicles.

options.text: "The fluid has injured the cochlea, so the loss will be permanent."
options.rationale: The cochlea sits in the inner ear, and nothing in the findings points to inner ear damage. Middle ear fluid blocks transmission, which is usually correctable rather than permanent.

options.text: "Swelling from the cold is pressing on the nerve to the brain."
options.rationale: Cranial nerve VIII carries sound to the brain only after the cochlea receives it. The stated problem is fluid in the middle ear, which stops vibration before it ever reaches the nerve.

questions.takeaway: Sound moves from air to eardrum, ossicles, cochlea, cranial nerve VIII and the auditory cortex; a block before the cochlea causes a conductive, often correctable, loss.
questions.strategy: The patient fears nerve damage, and two distractors agree with that fear. Trace the pathway: fluid sits in the middle ear, before the cochlea and the nerve.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It is behind the eardrum, in the middle ear where the ossicles sit.
The eardrum is intact, so the torn eardrum option contradicts the findings.
Vibration is stopped before the cochlea and nerve, so neither is damaged.

elimination.verdict: Middle ear fluid blocks the ossicles from passing sound inward.

questions.objective: Describe basic anatomy and function of the ear
questions.concept: sound pathway through the middle ear

questions.stem: A patient admitted with inflammation of the inner ear of the left side reports that the room spins when she turns her head. Hearing in the left ear is reduced. She wants to walk to the shower by herself. Which action is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Dim the lights and limit visitors to reduce stimulation
options.rationale: A quiet room can ease discomfort, but dim light makes a walk to the shower more dangerous. It does not address the balance loss from the inner ear.

options.text: Speak on her right side when giving instructions
options.rationale: Using the better hearing ear is a sound communication strategy for her reduced left sided hearing. It does nothing for the vertigo that could cause a fall on the way to the shower.

options.text: Provide a written board for instructions during the shift
options.rationale: Written communication helps a patient with hearing loss. Her loss is in one ear only, and the more urgent problem is balance, which threatens her safety right now.

options.text: Walk with her to the shower and back
options.rationale: The semicircular canals and vestibule in the inner ear control balance, so inner ear inflammation causes vertigo. Spinning with movement makes falling her most immediate risk.

questions.takeaway: The inner ear holds both the cochlea for hearing and the semicircular canals and vestibule for balance, so inner ear disorders raise fall risk.
questions.strategy: The hearing loss tempts a communication answer. The spinning with head movement tells you the balance organs are involved, and a fall injures faster than a missed word.

steps.detail: Reduced hearing on the left and spinning with movement.
Vertigo during a walk to the shower can cause a fall and injury now.
Dim light adds to the fall risk.

elimination.verdict: Assist her with ambulation because the inner ear governs balance.

questions.objective: Describe basic anatomy and function of the ear

questions.stem: In an ear clinic, the nurse reviews the findings of four patients before the provider sees them. Which patient's problem is located in the middle ear?

options.text: Pain when the tragus is pressed and a swollen canal
options.rationale: Tragus pain with a swollen canal points to external otitis. The canal and pinna are parts of the external ear, so this problem sits outside the middle ear.

options.text: Hearing loss after an antibiotic damaged the organ of Corti
options.rationale: The organ of Corti lies in the cochlea and turns vibration into nerve signals. Damage there is an inner ear problem that causes sensorineural loss rather than a middle ear one.

options.text: A stapes held still by new bone growth around it
options.rationale: The stapes is one of the three ossicles that carry vibration across the middle ear. When bone growth fixes it in place, sound stops in the middle ear before it reaches the cochlea.

options.text: Hard, dry cerumen packed tightly in the ear canal
options.rationale: Cerumen is made by glands that line the ear canal. A packed canal is an external ear problem that blocks sound before it ever reaches the eardrum.

questions.takeaway: External ear: pinna, canal, cerumen glands and eardrum; middle ear: ossicles and eustachian tube; inner ear: cochlea with the organ of Corti plus the semicircular canals and vestibule.
questions.strategy: The stapes sits right next to the cochlea, which pulls some students toward the inner ear. The ossicles, including the stapes, belong to the middle ear.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Tragus, canal and cerumen are external; the organ of Corti is inner.
The stapes is an ossicle, and the ossicles are middle ear structures.

elimination.verdict: The stapes held still by new bone growth.

questions.objective: Describe basic anatomy and function of the ear
questions.concept: structures of the external, middle and inner ear

questions.scenario: A 74 year old man is admitted for elective knee surgery, and the nurse completes an admission ear assessment.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected age related change or needs follow up.

rows.text: Coarse hair grows thickly at the opening of each ear canal
rows.rationale: Canal hair coarsens with age, more often in men. It is expected and needs no action unless it traps cerumen and blocks the canal.

rows.text: His pinnae look longer than in a photo from 20 years ago
rows.rationale: The pinna elongates with age, especially in men. It is a normal structural change and does not affect hearing.

rows.text: Swelling and tenderness over the bone behind his right ear
rows.rationale: The mastoid area is checked for pain and swelling during the ear exam. These findings suggest infection spreading from the ear and are never part of normal aging.

rows.text: Both eardrums look dull and slightly retracted on the provider's exam
rows.rationale: The tympanic membrane loses elasticity with age and may look dull or retracted. Without pain, drainage or fever, this matches normal aging.

rows.text: Ringing in both ears since a new medication was started 5 days ago
rows.rationale: Tinnitus that begins after a new drug suggests an ototoxic effect. It is a new change with a clear trigger, so it is reported rather than blamed on age.

rows.text: Hard cerumen blocks the left canal, and he cannot hear a whisper on that side
rows.rationale: Drier cerumen is an aging change, but an impaction that blocks hearing is a correctable problem. The nurse reports it so it can be softened and removed.

questions.takeaway: Pinna elongation, coarse canal hair and a dull eardrum are expected with aging; mastoid swelling, new tinnitus after a drug and an impaction that blocks hearing need follow up.
questions.strategy: The cerumen row catches students; dry cerumen is expected, but an impaction that blocks hearing is a problem to fix.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Longer pinna, coarse hair and dull eardrum are expected.

steps.action: Look for a trigger or new symptom
steps.detail: New ringing after a drug and mastoid swelling are not aging.
Dry cerumen is expected; a blocked canal with lost hearing is not.

elimination.verdict: Three expected changes, three findings that need follow up.

questions.objective: Recognize normal age related changes in hearing

questions.stem: During a hearing assessment, an 75 year old patient says he understands his son on the phone but cannot follow his granddaughter's speech, and he mixes up words such as "fish" and "sip." His ear canals are clear. Which action by the nurse fits this finding?

options.text: Request irrigation of both ear canals
options.rationale: Irrigation treats cerumen impaction, which is a common cause of reduced hearing in older adults. His canals are clear, so there is nothing to remove.

options.text: Raise the voice so every word is louder
options.rationale: Volume seems helpful, but raising the voice usually raises its pitch and distorts it. Shouting is specifically avoided because it pushes speech toward the frequencies he has already lost.

options.text: Ask his granddaughter to speak directly into his ear
options.rationale: Being close makes speech louder, but she keeps the same high pitch. Speaking into the ear also removes his view of her face and lips, which he needs.

options.text: Face him and speak in a lower pitched voice
options.rationale: High frequency sounds are lost first with aging, so a higher voice and soft consonants fade out. A lower pitch moves speech into the range he still hears, and facing him adds visual cues.

questions.takeaway: Aging takes high frequency sounds first, so lower your pitch rather than your volume.
questions.strategy: Clear canals rule out the correctable cause. Then the choice is between louder and lower, and only lower reaches the frequencies he still hears.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No cerumen, so irrigation is off the table.
He hears a male voice but loses a child's voice and soft consonants: high pitch loss.
Shouting raises pitch; a lower voice stays in his range.

elimination.verdict: Face him and lower the pitch of your voice.

questions.objective: Recognize normal age related changes in hearing

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an 85 year old patient admitted for a hip fracture who followed television at a normal volume last week. For 2 days she has not heard speech from the left side. Her daughter says, "It is just her age." What does the nurse do?

options.text: Inspect the left ear canal and ask how the change began
options.rationale: A new, one sided change over 2 days is not the pattern of gradual aging loss. Older adults' cerumen dries and impacts easily, so the nurse checks for a correctable cause.

options.text: Record it as an expected aging change and continue routine care
options.rationale: Age related loss develops slowly and affects both ears. A sudden change on one side should never be assumed to be aging, and accepting it could miss a correctable cause.

options.text: Speak only into her right ear for the rest of her stay
options.rationale: Using the better ear is a good communication strategy. On its own it accepts the new loss without assessing it, and the cause may be easy to correct.

options.text: Ask the provider for a hearing aid referral before discharge
options.rationale: A hearing aid may help a permanent loss later. Ordering one before the canal is checked skips assessment, and a blocked canal may need only cerumen removal.

questions.takeaway: New or sudden hearing changes are not assumed to be age related; assess every older adult individually.
questions.strategy: The daughter's explanation is the emotional pull. A 2 day, one sided change is the cue that it is something other than aging.

steps.detail: Normal last week, gone on one side for 2 days: sudden, not gradual.
The hearing aid and better ear options act before anyone looks in the canal.
Dry cerumen impacts easily in older adults.

elimination.verdict: Inspect the canal and take a history before accepting or treating the change.

questions.objective: Recognize normal age related changes in hearing
questions.concept: sudden change is not assumed to be aging

questions.stem: A patient with gradual hearing loss in both ears ran a jackhammer for 25 years without ear protection. His canals are clear and his eardrums are intact. He asks, "Can you clean my ears out so I can hear again?" Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Surgery to replace a small ear bone will restore it."
options.rationale: Stapedectomy replaces the stapes for otosclerosis, a conductive cause. His ossicles are not the problem; the damage is in the inner ear, where that surgery does not help.

options.text: "This damage usually lasts, so protect the hearing you have."
options.rationale: Prolonged loud noise damages the inner ear, causing sensorineural loss that is often permanent. Clear canals mean there is nothing to clean, and protection prevents further loss.

options.text: "Cleaning the canals usually brings this kind of hearing back."
options.rationale: Cleaning helps when cerumen blocks the canal and causes a conductive loss. His canals are already clear, so cleaning would not change a noise related inner ear loss.

options.text: "Hearing returns over a few months once the noise stops."
options.rationale: Avoiding noise prevents more damage, but it does not repair hair cells already lost. Promising recovery gives him false hope about a loss that is usually permanent.

questions.takeaway: Noise exposure causes sensorineural loss, which is often permanent, while conductive loss is often correctable.
questions.strategy: The surgery and cleaning options are real treatments for conductive loss. Clear canals and intact eardrums point away from conduction toward inner ear damage.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear canals and intact eardrums rule out the usual conductive blocks.
Years of loud noise damage the inner ear: sensorineural.
Neither time off noise nor middle ear surgery restores hair cells.

elimination.verdict: Tell him the loss is likely permanent and teach protection of remaining hearing.

questions.objective: Differentiate conductive, sensorineural, and mixed hearing loss

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient who reports reduced hearing in the right ear for a month and says her left ear hears normally. During the Weber test, with the vibrating tuning fork on the top of the head, she hears the tone louder in the left ear. Which conclusion do these findings support?

options.text: Conductive loss in the right ear
options.rationale: In conductive loss the tone lateralizes toward the affected ear because room noise is blocked out on that side. Her tone moved away from the poor ear, which rules this out.

options.text: Conductive loss in the left ear
options.rationale: A left conductive loss would make the tone louder on the left. She says her left ear hears normally and her complaint is the right ear, so this does not fit.

options.text: Sensorineural loss in the right ear
options.rationale: In sensorineural loss the damaged inner ear or nerve cannot sense bone conducted sound well. The tone therefore sounds louder in the healthy left ear, away from her complaint.

options.text: Normal hearing in both ears
options.rationale: A normal Weber result is a tone heard equally in both ears. She hears it louder on one side, so the result is abnormal.

questions.takeaway: Weber checks whether sound is heard equally in both ears: it lateralizes toward the poor ear in conductive loss and toward the good ear in sensorineural loss.
questions.strategy: Students expect the tone to be louder in the good ear for every loss. That is true only for sensorineural loss; conductive loss pulls the tone toward the poor ear.

steps.detail: Normal is equal in both ears; hers lateralized.
Louder on the left, the ear she does not complain about.
Toward the good ear means sensorineural loss in the poor ear.

elimination.verdict: The tone moved away from the poor right ear: sensorineural loss on the right.

questions.objective: Differentiate conductive, sensorineural, and mixed hearing loss

questions.stem: During the Rinne test on the left ear, a patient who reports muffled hearing in that ear hears the tuning fork longer when it rests on the mastoid bone than when it is held beside the ear canal. Which conclusion do these findings support?

options.text: A normal result for the left ear
options.rationale: A normal Rinne result is air conduction heard longer than bone conduction. His result is the reverse, so it is abnormal.

options.text: Sensorineural loss in the left ear
options.rationale: In sensorineural loss air conduction still outlasts bone, though both are shortened. Bone outlasting air points to a block in transmission, not inner ear damage.

options.text: Mixed loss in both ears
options.rationale: The test was done on the left ear only and shows a transmission problem there. Nothing in the finding shows inner ear damage or tells anything about the right ear.

options.text: Conductive loss in the left ear
options.rationale: Normally air conduction lasts longer than bone conduction. When bone outlasts air, something is blocking sound from passing through the canal and middle ear.

questions.takeaway: Rinne compares air to bone conduction: air outlasts bone normally, and bone outlasting air signals conductive loss in that ear.
questions.strategy: The trap is thinking that any abnormal tuning fork result means nerve damage. Bone longer than air is the specific pattern of a conduction block.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Air conduction lasts longer than bone conduction.
Bone lasted longer: reversed.
A reversed result means sound is blocked on its way in: conductive.

elimination.verdict: Bone outlasting air in the left ear means conductive loss in that ear.

questions.objective: Differentiate conductive, sensorineural, and mixed hearing loss

questions.scenario: In an audiology clinic, the nurse reviews the histories of six patients who each have hearing loss.
questions.stem: For each history, identify the type of hearing loss it most likely causes.

rows.text: Otosclerosis in one ear plus years of loud factory noise
rows.rationale: Otosclerosis blocks transmission through the middle ear, while noise damages the inner ear. Having both a conductive and a sensorineural cause produces a mixed loss.

rows.text: Thick middle ear fluid after repeated ear infections
rows.rationale: Fluid in the middle ear damps the vibration of the ossicles before sound reaches the cochlea. The inner ear itself is intact, so the loss is conductive.

rows.text: Twenty years of firearm noise without ear protection
rows.rationale: Prolonged loud noise damages the hair cells of the inner ear. That damage is sensorineural and usually permanent, which makes noise a major preventable cause.

rows.text: A tumor growing on cranial nerve VIII
rows.rationale: Cranial nerve VIII carries sound information from the cochlea to the brain. A tumor on it damages the nerve pathway, so the loss is sensorineural.

rows.text: Gradual loss in both ears in an older adult from cochlear nerve degeneration
rows.rationale: This is presbycusis, the age related loss from degeneration of the cochlear nerve. It is sensorineural and permanent, though aids and devices can help.

rows.text: A perforated eardrum after a blow to the ear
rows.rationale: A hole in the eardrum keeps it from vibrating normally, which blocks sound transmission. This kind of loss is often correctable once the eardrum heals or is repaired.

questions.takeaway: Conductive loss is an obstruction of sound transmission (cerumen, fluid, perforation, otosclerosis); sensorineural is inner ear or nerve damage (aging, noise, ototoxic drugs, tumors); mixed is both.
questions.strategy: Otosclerosis catches students because it is a conductive cause even though it is permanent without surgery. Ask where the problem sits, in front of or inside the cochlea.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Eardrum, ossicles or middle ear fluid: conductive.

steps.action: Look for inner ear or nerve damage
steps.detail: Noise, nerve tumor and nerve degeneration: sensorineural.

steps.action: Spot two causes in one row
steps.detail: A middle ear cause plus noise damage makes a mixed loss.

elimination.verdict: Location decides the type: transmission problems are conductive, inner ear or nerve damage is sensorineural.

questions.objective: Differentiate conductive, sensorineural, and mixed hearing loss
questions.concept: classifying conductive, sensorineural and mixed loss

questions.stem: The nurse is taking the home history of a patient with a new sensorineural hearing loss in both ears. Which finding does the nurse explore further as a likely contributor?

options.text: Takes a bulk fiber supplement every evening
options.rationale: Supplements belong on every medication history. Bulk fiber is not among the ototoxic drug groups, which are NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, diuretics, quinine based drugs and chemotherapy agents.

options.text: Takes a quinine based drug nightly for leg cramps
options.rationale: Quinine based drugs are ototoxic and can damage the inner ear. Nightly use is a medication risk the nurse explores as a cause of this new sensorineural loss.

options.text: Mows the lawn each week while wearing earmuffs
options.rationale: Lawn mowers are loud, and prolonged noise is a major preventable cause of sensorineural loss. Wearing earmuffs each time protects the patient's hearing, so this habit lowers the risk.

options.text: Had hard cerumen removed from both ears last month
options.rationale: Cerumen impaction is a common cause of hearing loss, so it seems worth exploring. It causes a conductive loss that clears once the canal is open, so it does not explain new inner ear damage.

questions.takeaway: Ototoxic drug groups include NSAIDs, aminoglycoside antibiotics, diuretics, quinine based drugs and chemotherapy agents; unprotected loud noise is a major preventable cause of sensorineural loss.
questions.strategy: The old cerumen impaction is the near miss because it did affect hearing. It causes conductive loss, while the quinine based drug can damage the inner ear and cause sensorineural loss.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sensorineural loss means inner ear or nerve damage.
Quinine based drugs are ototoxic; fiber is not.
Earmuffs protect, and cerumen causes a conductive loss.

elimination.verdict: The nightly quinine based drug.

questions.objective: Differentiate conductive, sensorineural, and mixed hearing loss
questions.concept: ototoxic drugs and noise in the history

questions.stem: An audiologist reports that a patient has a 35 dB hearing loss in both ears. The nurse must give the patient discharge teaching on a busy surgical unit. Which plan fits this result?

options.text: Teach face to face in a quiet room with the door closed
options.rationale: A 20 to 40 dB loss causes mild difficulty hearing in noise. Removing background noise and facing the patient lets normal speech, around 60 dB, come through clearly.

options.text: Raise the voice to a shout so it carries over the noise
options.rationale: Shouting distorts speech and raises its pitch, so it is avoided with any hearing loss. The fix for trouble hearing in noise is to remove the noise.

options.text: Give the teaching in writing and skip the spoken review
options.rationale: Written material is a good supplement for hearing loss. Skipping the spoken review removes the chance to ask questions and confirm understanding.

options.text: Stand right beside the patient's ear for every sentence
options.rationale: Standing right next to the speaker is needed for a severe loss of 71 to 90 dB. A mild loss does not require it, and leaning at the ear blocks the patient's view of the face.

questions.takeaway: A 20 to 40 dB loss means mild difficulty in noise, so control the environment; a 71 to 90 dB loss means the patient must be right next to the speaker.
questions.strategy: Standing at the ear is right for a severe loss and wrong for this one. Read the number: 35 dB is a mild loss whose problem is background noise.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 35 dB falls in the 20 to 40 dB range: mild difficulty in noise.

steps.action: Match the plan to the problem
steps.detail: The problem is noise, so remove it.
Shouting distorts; writing only skips confirming understanding.

elimination.verdict: Teach face to face in a quiet room.

questions.objective: Differentiate conductive, sensorineural, and mixed hearing loss

questions.stem: During an admission interview, a woman leans forward, tilts her head toward the nurse, and answers "Tuesday" when asked about allergies. Assistive personnel tell the nurse she seems confused. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Document new confusion and start fall precautions
options.rationale: Documenting confusion records a conclusion the evidence does not yet support. Her cues fit hearing loss, so labeling her confused could mislead the whole team.

options.text: Face her in good light and repeat the question
options.rationale: Leaning forward, tilting the head and mismatched answers are behavioral cues of hearing loss. Repeating the question face to face tests that explanation before anyone labels her confused.

options.text: Complete a mental status screening before going on
options.rationale: A mental status screen is reasonable if confusion persists. Her behaviors point first to hearing loss, and a screen she cannot hear would give a false result.

options.text: Ask a family member to answer the remaining questions
options.rationale: Family can add information, but this bypasses a patient who may be fully able to answer. It also leaves the possible hearing loss unassessed.

questions.takeaway: Tilting the head, leaning forward, saying "What?" and mismatched answers are cues of hearing loss, not confusion.
questions.strategy: The confusion label from assistive personnel is the trap. Her behaviors describe someone straining to hear, and the next step tests that.

steps.detail: Leaning in and tilting the head are signs of straining to hear.
Repeat the question in a way she can hear and see.
Documenting confusion and asking family both accept it without evidence.

elimination.verdict: Face her and repeat the question before concluding anything.

questions.objective: Recognize common ear and hearing conditions and their clinical manifestations

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who has had 2 days of deep, throbbing pain in the left ear that feels like pressure, with muffled hearing, a low pitched ringing and mild dizziness. Her temperature is 38.6 C. Moving the pinna and tragus does not change the pain, and the canal is not swollen. The provider sees a red, bulging eardrum and prescribes an antibiotic and an analgesic. Which additional measure does the nurse include in her care?

options.text: Irrigate the left canal with warm water to ease pressure
options.rationale: Warm water might seem soothing for pressure pain. Irrigation is never done when otitis media or a perforation is suspected, because it can spread the infection.

options.text: Follow a low sodium diet to reduce fluid in the ear
options.rationale: A low sodium diet reduces endolymph in Ménière disease. Her fever and bulging eardrum point to infection in the middle ear, not excess fluid in the inner ear.

options.text: Avoid water and earbuds in that ear for 7 to 10 days
options.rationale: Avoiding water and earbuds is the right teaching for external otitis. Her pain does not change with pinna or tragus movement and the canal is normal, so the infection is behind the eardrum.

options.text: Apply mild heat over the left ear for comfort
options.rationale: Pressure pain, fever and a red, bulging eardrum point to acute otitis media. Mild heat is part of its nonsurgical care, along with analgesics, bed rest and the full antibiotic course.

questions.takeaway: Acute otitis media causes pressure pain, conductive loss, low pitched tinnitus, fever and dizziness; care includes the full antibiotic course, analgesics, mild heat and bed rest, and never irrigation.
questions.strategy: Water and earbud restriction is the near miss, since it is correct for an infection of the ear canal. No tragus pain and a bulging eardrum place this infection in the middle ear.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pressure pain, fever and a bulging eardrum point to acute otitis media.
No tragus pain rules out external otitis; fever and a bulging eardrum rule out Ménière disease.
Mild heat helps; irrigation is never done.

elimination.verdict: Apply mild heat over the left ear.

questions.objective: Recognize common ear and hearing conditions and their clinical manifestations
questions.concept: acute otitis media recognition and care

questions.stem: A patient with acute otitis media of the right ear rated his ear pain 8 of 10 an hour ago. He has had no analgesic since then. The pain is now 2 of 10, and there is fresh yellow drainage on his pillow. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Assess the drainage and report a possible perforated eardrum
options.rationale: As pressure builds, the eardrum bulges and can perforate, and pain eases when it does. Sudden relief without an analgesic plus new drainage points to rupture, which the provider must know.

options.text: Record the lower pain score as a sign the infection is clearing
options.rationale: Less pain often means improvement. Here it came suddenly, without medication, and with new drainage, which signals a ruptured eardrum rather than healing.

options.text: Give the scheduled analgesic to keep the pain controlled
