options.rationale: Pain control is part of otitis media care. His pain is now 2 of 10, and giving a drug before assessing the drainage skips the finding that matters most.

options.text: Irrigate the right ear canal to clear the drainage
options.rationale: Clearing the canal seems helpful for comfort. Irrigation is never done when perforation or otitis media is suspected, because it spreads the infection inward.

questions.takeaway: In otitis media, sudden pain relief with drainage means the eardrum has likely perforated; assess and report, and never irrigate.
questions.strategy: The lower pain score looks like good news. Relief that comes with no analgesic and new drainage is the classic sign of perforation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No analgesic was given.
Fresh drainage on the pillow.
Irrigation is contraindicated with suspected perforation.

elimination.verdict: Assess the drainage and report a possible perforation.

questions.objective: Recognize common ear and hearing conditions and their clinical manifestations

questions.scenario: On day 4 of an IV aminoglycoside antibiotic for a bone infection, a patient who also takes a daily diuretic reports new ringing in both ears this morning and says voices sound muffled. When she stands, she feels unsteady and reaches for the wall. Both ear canals are clear, she has no ear pain, and her temperature is 36.8 C. The next antibiotic dose is due in 30 minutes.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Hold the next dose and report the findings to the prescriber
options.rationale: New tinnitus and hearing loss during an aminoglycoside course are signs of inner ear damage. Holding the dose and reporting lets the prescriber act before more damage occurs.

options.text: Start fall precautions and assist her with every transfer
options.rationale: The inner ear controls balance as well as hearing, and she is already unsteady. Assisting her prevents a fall while the drug effect is evaluated.

options.text: Give the dose on time and recheck her hearing in 1 hour
options.rationale: Giving the dose on time keeps the infection treatment on schedule. It also adds more of the drug that is likely harming her inner ear, so the nurse holds it.

options.text: Instill a ceruminolytic into both ear canals
options.rationale: A ceruminolytic softens impacted cerumen. Her canals are clear, so there is nothing to soften, and it would delay addressing the drug effect.

options.text: Cerumen impaction
options.rationale: Impaction can cause fullness, hearing loss and dizziness. Her canals are clear, and impaction would not explain ringing that began during drug therapy.

options.text: Ménière disease
options.rationale: Ménière disease brings vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss in episodes, usually on one side. Her symptoms began in both ears during an ototoxic drug course, which fits the drug instead.

options.text: Acute otitis media
options.rationale: Otitis media can cause hearing loss, tinnitus and dizziness. She has no ear pain and a normal temperature, which makes a middle ear infection unlikely.

options.text: Ototoxic drug effect
options.rationale: New ringing, muffled hearing and unsteadiness during an aminoglycoside course, with a diuretic added, fit inner ear damage from ototoxic drugs. Clear canals and no pain point away from other causes.

options.text: Her report of ringing and hearing in both ears
options.rationale: Tracking tinnitus and hearing shows whether the inner ear damage is worsening or stabilizing once the dose is held. These are the earliest signs of ototoxicity.

options.text: Any drainage from her ear canals
options.rationale: Drainage from the canal points to a perforated eardrum or a canal infection. Her canals are clear and painless, so drainage does not track the inner ear damage that is her problem.

options.text: Her balance and steadiness when she stands
options.rationale: Vestibular damage shows as unsteadiness and is a direct fall risk. Watching her balance guides how much help she needs to move safely.

options.text: Her pain when the tragus is pressed
options.rationale: Tragus pain is a sign of external otitis. She has no ear pain, so this finding does not track her actual problem.

questions.takeaway: New tinnitus or hearing loss during an aminoglycoside or other ototoxic drug means hold the dose, report, protect against falls, and monitor hearing and balance.
questions.strategy: The scheduled dose and the infection are a strong pull to keep giving the drug. New inner ear symptoms during therapy are the cue to hold and report.

steps.action: Link the symptoms to the drugs
steps.detail: Ringing, muffled hearing and unsteadiness began during an aminoglycoside course.
Clear canals, no pain and no fever rule out impaction and infection.
Hold and report for the drug, assistance for the balance loss.

elimination.verdict: Ototoxic drug effect: hold and report, prevent falls, monitor hearing and balance.

questions.objective: Differentiate conductive, sensorineural, and mixed hearing loss
questions.concept: ototoxic drugs and noise in the history

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with right ear pain who wears earbuds during daily gym workouts and cleans his ears with cotton swabs. The pain sharply worsens when the nurse touches the tragus. The canal is swollen and he says the ear feels plugged. Which instruction belongs in his teaching?

options.text: Flush the canal with warm tap water each evening
options.rationale: Rinsing seems to clean the ear. Water in the canal feeds the inflammation, and cleaning is done by the provider, not the patient at home.

options.text: Dry the canal with a cotton swab after every shower or swim
options.rationale: Keeping the canal dry is a good goal. Cotton swabs injure canal skin and are a common cause of external otitis, so this would worsen it.

options.text: Avoid water and earbuds in that ear for 7 to 10 days
options.rationale: Pain with tragus movement, a swollen canal and a plugged sensation fit external otitis. Earbuds and moisture irritate the inflamed canal skin, so both are avoided while it heals.

options.text: Avoid air travel and nose blowing until the ear has fully healed
options.rationale: These precautions protect the middle ear after stapedectomy. His inflammation is in the external canal, where pressure changes play no part.

questions.takeaway: External otitis causes pain with pinna or tragus movement, canal swelling and a plugged feeling; teach avoidance of water and earbuds for 7 to 10 days and no cotton swabs.
questions.strategy: The cotton swab option sounds like good drying advice. Swabs are one of the causes, so it would injure the canal again.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Name the condition from the cues
steps.detail: Tragus pain and canal swelling point to the external ear.
Cotton swabs and water both irritate the canal.

steps.action: Cut the wrong part of the ear
steps.detail: Air travel and nose blowing matter for the middle ear.

elimination.verdict: Teach him to keep water and earbuds out of the ear for 7 to 10 days.

questions.objective: Recognize common ear and hearing conditions and their clinical manifestations

questions.stem: A veteran with blast exposure has had constant ringing in both ears for months. Testing has ruled out other causes, and he says the ringing keeps him awake every night. Which suggestion by the nurse fits his plan of care?

options.text: Ask for a hearing test that will confirm the ringing
options.rationale: Hearing tests are done for tinnitus, but they rule out other causes rather than confirm the ringing. His other causes are already ruled out.

options.text: Keep the bedroom completely silent so the ringing is easier to track
options.rationale: Silence makes tinnitus seem louder because nothing competes with it. Tracking the ringing does not help him sleep.

options.text: Play a sound machine or soft background noise at bedtime
options.rationale: Masking with background noise or a sound machine makes the ringing less noticeable in a quiet room. It is a listed tinnitus strategy that targets his sleep problem.

options.text: Take aspirin at bedtime to ease the ear discomfort
options.rationale: Aspirin is one of the drugs that can cause or worsen tinnitus. It would add to his problem rather than relieve it.

questions.takeaway: Tinnitus has no confirming test; management includes masking, tinnitus retraining therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy, and ototoxic drugs such as aspirin can worsen it.
questions.strategy: Aspirin sounds like a harmless comfort measure. It is one of the drugs that causes tinnitus.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Background sound masks ringing; silence exposes it.
No test confirms tinnitus; testing only rules out causes.
Aspirin can cause tinnitus.

elimination.verdict: Suggest a sound machine at bedtime.

questions.objective: Recognize common ear and hearing conditions and their clinical manifestations

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the history of a patient who has had three episodes this month of spinning that lasted for hours with nausea and vomiting. Each came with roaring in the right ear and reduced hearing on that side. She has no ear pain or fever, and her ear canals are clear. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: An oral antibiotic taken for the full course
options.rationale: A full antibiotic course treats otitis media. She has no pain or fever, and the episodic pattern of vertigo points to an inner ear fluid problem rather than infection.

options.text: A ceruminolytic followed by ear irrigation
options.rationale: Cerumen impaction can cause hearing loss and dizziness. Her canals are clear, and impaction does not cause repeated episodes of vertigo lasting hours.

options.text: Topical antibiotic and steroid ear drops
options.rationale: These drops treat external otitis. She has no ear pain or canal swelling, and the problem is in the inner ear, which drops cannot reach.

options.text: A low sodium diet with a diuretic
options.rationale: Episodic vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss is the classic triad of Ménière disease, caused by excess endolymph. Low sodium intake and a diuretic reduce that fluid volume.

questions.takeaway: Ménière disease presents as episodic vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss from excess endolymph, treated with low sodium intake and diuretics.
questions.strategy: Each distractor treats a real ear condition that shares one symptom. Only the full triad in episodes, without pain or fever, fits excess inner ear fluid.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Episodic vertigo, tinnitus and one sided hearing loss is the triad.
No pain, no fever, clear canals.
Lower endolymph volume with sodium restriction and a diuretic.

elimination.verdict: Anticipate a low sodium diet and a diuretic.

questions.objective: Recognize common ear and hearing conditions and their clinical manifestations
questions.concept: Ménière disease recognition and acute care

questions.stem: A roofer with Ménière disease says that twice this week he suddenly fell to the ground with no dizziness or warning beforehand, and he did not lose consciousness. Which teaching point is the priority?

options.text: Stay off roofs and ladders while these episodes continue
options.rationale: Sudden falls with no warning are Tumarkin crisis drop attacks. Because there is no warning to act on, avoiding heights is the only protection from a serious fall at work.

options.text: Begin vestibular rehabilitation exercises for balance
options.rationale: Vestibular rehabilitation improves balance over time and is part of management. It does not protect him from a sudden drop while he is working at a height.

options.text: Use background sound at night to mask the ringing
options.rationale: Masking helps tinnitus, which is part of Ménière disease. Ringing does not threaten his life, while a fall from a roof does.

options.text: Lie down as soon as the first dizziness begins
options.rationale: Lying down at the first sign of vertigo is sound advice for a typical attack. These drops come with no dizziness first, so there is no moment to act on.

questions.takeaway: Tumarkin crisis causes sudden drop attacks without warning, so avoiding heights, ladders and driving is the priority safety teaching.
questions.strategy: Lying down at the first dizziness is the textbook answer for a usual attack. The stem says there is no warning, which removes that option.

steps.detail: No dizziness or warning before he falls.
A fall from a roof can be fatal.

steps.action: Cut the long term or comfort measures
steps.detail: Masking and exercises do not stop a sudden drop.

elimination.verdict: Teach him to avoid roofs and ladders.

questions.objective: Recognize common ear and hearing conditions and their clinical manifestations

questions.stem: On day 4 of a 10 day oral antibiotic for acute otitis media, a patient's ear pain is 0 of 10 and her temperature is 36.9 C. She says she will stop the antibiotic now that she feels well. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Save the remaining doses in case the pain returns later."
options.rationale: Saving doses seems thrifty, but it leaves the infection partly treated now. A later partial course would be too short to clear a returning infection.

options.text: "Finish every dose; an infection that returns can damage your hearing."
options.rationale: Feeling better does not mean the infection is gone. Untreated or partly treated otitis media can lead to perforation, ossicle damage and permanent conductive hearing loss.

options.text: "Stop the antibiotic and use mild heat until the ear feels normal."
options.rationale: Mild heat is part of otitis media comfort care. It does not treat infection, and stopping the antibiotic early risks the complications that threaten hearing.

options.text: "Take it until day 7, since most acute ear infections clear by then."
options.rationale: Acute otitis media can take up to 3 weeks to resolve. Choosing an earlier stop day still ends the prescribed course early and invites a return of infection.

questions.takeaway: Patients with otitis media complete the full antibiotic course, because untreated infection can perforate the eardrum and cause permanent conductive loss.
questions.strategy: The day 7 option sounds like a compromise grounded in fact. Any stop before the prescribed course ends is still stopping early.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No pain and no fever on day 4 do not mean the infection is gone.
Stopping now, saving doses and stopping on day 7 all end the course early.
Untreated infection can cause permanent hearing loss.

elimination.verdict: Teach her to finish every dose.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders
questions.concept: complete the antibiotic course for otitis media

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a patient with recurrent otitis media who is scheduled for a myringotomy with placement of a tube in the eardrum. Which statement by the patient shows that the nurse's teaching was understood?

options.text: "The surgeon will replace the small bone that stopped moving."
options.rationale: Replacing the stapes with a prosthesis is a stapedectomy, done for otosclerosis. His problem is recurrent infection with fluid, not a fixed ossicle.

options.text: "The tube lets fluid drain so pressure stops building up."
options.rationale: A myringotomy opens the eardrum to drain fluid and relieve pain. The tube keeps that opening patent, so it is chosen when infections keep coming back.

options.text: "After the tube goes in, I will never get an ear infection again."
options.rationale: The tube lowers pressure and the chance of repeat infections. A promise that infection can never return is an absolute that the procedure cannot guarantee.

options.text: "The surgery rebuilds my eardrum so it can vibrate again."
options.rationale: Rebuilding the eardrum is a tympanoplasty, done for a conductive loss from a damaged eardrum. A myringotomy makes a small opening instead of repairing one.

questions.takeaway: Myringotomy drains middle ear fluid and relieves pain; a tube is placed when otitis media keeps recurring.
questions.strategy: Three ear surgeries share similar language. Match the procedure to its purpose: drain (myringotomy), rebuild the drum (tympanoplasty), replace the stapes (stapedectomy).

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rebuilding the drum and replacing a bone are other surgeries.
"Never get an ear infection again" overpromises.
Draining fluid matches a myringotomy with a tube.

elimination.verdict: He understands that the tube drains fluid and prevents pressure buildup.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders
questions.concept: myringotomy and tube for recurrent otitis media

questions.nursesNote: 0900 Admitted for elective hernia repair. Worked 30 years on an airport ground crew with ear protection worn only some of the time. Walks 3 km each morning. Has a thyroid disorder treated with daily hormone replacement. Allergic to penicillin. Takes an NSAID every day for knee pain. Wears reading glasses for small print. Flew home from overseas 2 days ago; right ear has felt plugged since the plane landed. Lives with his wife, who drives him to appointments.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings in the history that the nurse explores further as risks for hearing loss.

segments.text: Admitted for elective hernia repair.
segments.rationale: A hernia repair is the reason for admission and has no link to the ear. It does not change his hearing risk.

segments.text: Worked 30 years on an airport ground crew with ear protection worn only some of the time.
segments.rationale: Prolonged loud noise exposure is a major preventable cause of hearing loss. Thirty years near jet engines with patchy protection is a strong risk to explore.

segments.text: Walks 3 km each morning.
segments.rationale: Daily walking is a healthy habit that supports his recovery. It has no effect on the ear or hearing.

segments.text: Has a thyroid disorder treated with daily hormone replacement.
segments.rationale: Thyroid disorders are among the systemic conditions screened in a hearing history. The nurse asks whether any hearing change has come with it.

segments.text: Allergic to penicillin.
segments.rationale: The allergy matters for safe drug choices during his stay. It is not a cause of hearing loss.

segments.text: Takes an NSAID every day for knee pain.
segments.rationale: NSAIDs are ototoxic drugs, and daily use adds steady exposure. The nurse asks about ringing or hearing change since he started it.

segments.text: Wears reading glasses for small print.
segments.rationale: Reading glasses correct an age related change in near vision. They tell the nurse nothing about his ears or his risk for hearing loss.

segments.text: Flew home from overseas 2 days ago; right ear has felt plugged since the plane landed.
segments.rationale: Air travel is part of the hearing history because pressure changes stress the eustachian tube and middle ear. A plugged ear since landing needs follow up.

segments.text: Lives with his wife, who drives him to appointments.
segments.rationale: His wife is useful social support at discharge. Her presence does not raise or lower his risk for hearing loss.

questions.takeaway: A hearing history covers noise exposure, ototoxic drugs, air travel, ear trauma, surgery and infections, and systemic conditions such as diabetes, autoimmune disease, HIV and thyroid disorders.
questions.strategy: The allergy and glasses look clinically important but belong to other systems. Keep only findings that touch noise, ototoxic drugs, pressure change or a screened systemic condition.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Thirty years of airport work with patchy protection.

steps.action: Look for drugs and systemic disease
steps.detail: Daily NSAID and a thyroid disorder.
Recent flight with a plugged ear since landing.

elimination.verdict: Highlight the noise exposure, thyroid disorder, daily NSAID and recent flight with a plugged ear.

questions.objective: Recognize common ear and hearing conditions and their clinical manifestations

questions.stem: On day 5 of antibiotic and steroid drops for external otitis of the left ear, a patient with type 1 diabetes phones the clinic. Her ear pain was 3 of 10 two days ago and is now 9 of 10. The skin behind the ear is red and swollen, and her temperature is 38.9 C. What does the nurse advise?

options.text: Come in to be examined today
options.rationale: Worsening pain, fever and spreading redness in a patient with diabetes suggest necrotizing otitis. This rare complication can be fatal, so she needs a same day evaluation.

options.text: Keep using the drops, since healing takes 7 to 10 days
options.rationale: External otitis does take days to settle, and water avoidance lasts 7 to 10 days. Her pain tripled with a new fever and spreading swelling, which is worsening, not slow healing.

options.text: Apply heat to the ear and call back in 48 hours
options.rationale: Heat is a comfort measure for external otitis. Waiting 2 days with a high fever and spreading infection in a patient with diabetes delays care for a dangerous complication.

options.text: Rinse the ear with warm water before the next dose
options.rationale: Rinsing seems to help the drops reach the canal. Water worsens external otitis, and rinsing does nothing for an infection spreading beyond the canal.

questions.takeaway: In a patient with diabetes or a weak immune system, worsening external otitis with fever and spreading swelling may be necrotizing otitis and needs same day care.
questions.strategy: Keep using the drops sounds patient and correct for a slow condition. Rising pain, fever and spread in a patient with diabetes is a change in course, not slow progress.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pain rose from 3 to 9 with a new fever.
Diabetes raises the risk of necrotizing otitis.
Waiting, heat and rinsing all postpone evaluation.

elimination.verdict: She needs to be examined today.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders

questions.stem: The provider prescribes irrigation today for a patient with impacted cerumen in the right ear who received a ceruminolytic yesterday. Which finding leads the nurse to hold the irrigation and contact the provider?

options.text: A feeling of fullness that began 3 days ago
options.rationale: Fullness is a typical sign of cerumen impaction. It confirms the reason for the procedure and does not make irrigation unsafe.

options.text: Mild dizziness when the patient first stands
options.rationale: Dizziness can come with cerumen impaction, and it calls for help when standing. It does not suggest a damaged eardrum, so irrigation can proceed with safe positioning.

options.text: Itching deep inside the canal since yesterday
options.rationale: Impacted wax often makes the canal itch. It fits the problem being treated and is not a reason to hold the irrigation.

options.text: Ear pain with a temperature of 38.4 C
options.rationale: Pain with fever suggests otitis media, and the eardrum behind the cerumen may be inflamed or perforated. Irrigating could push water and infection into the middle ear.

questions.takeaway: Never irrigate the ear when eardrum perforation or otitis media is suspected, because the water spreads infection.
questions.strategy: Dizziness is the tempting safety answer, but it is a known sign of impaction itself. Pain with fever is the cue that the eardrum may not be intact.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fullness, itching and dizziness are all signs of cerumen impaction.
Pain with fever points to infection behind the eardrum.
Suspected otitis media or perforation means no irrigation.

elimination.verdict: Hold the irrigation for ear pain with fever.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders
questions.concept: never irrigate with suspected perforation or otitis media

questions.stem: In the clinic, a gardener says a dried seed went into her right ear while she was planting. The provider is on the way. A coworker suggests flushing the ear with warm water to wash the seed out. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Flush the canal gently with warm water to move it out
options.rationale: Irrigation removes cerumen well. A seed expands with water, which would make it harder to remove and more painful.

options.text: Instill oil into the canal to stop the seed from moving
options.rationale: Oil is used to suffocate a live insect before removal. A seed is not alive and will not crawl, so oil only adds material to the canal.

options.text: Keep the canal dry until the provider removes it
options.rationale: Vegetable matter such as a seed absorbs water and swells. Irrigating could wedge it tighter in the canal, so the provider removes it dry.

options.text: Try to lift the seed out with a cotton swab
options.rationale: A cotton swab seems gentle, but it pushes objects deeper and injures canal skin. Removal belongs to the provider with proper instruments.

questions.takeaway: Never irrigate when the foreign body is vegetable matter, because it swells with water.
questions.strategy: Irrigation is the right answer for cerumen and the oil step is right for an insect. The object type decides: a seed swells with water.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A dried seed is vegetable matter.
Vegetable matter expands with water, so no irrigation.
Oil is for live insects only.

elimination.verdict: Keep the canal dry and let the provider remove the seed.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders
questions.concept: vegetable foreign body is not irrigated

questions.stem: After an insect crawled into his left ear while he slept outdoors, a patient arrives at urgent care. He hears buzzing and feels it moving, and he is frightened. The provider prescribes removal. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Irrigate the canal to flush the insect out
options.rationale: Irrigation clears cerumen. A live insect is never irrigated, because water can drive it deeper and make it struggle against the eardrum.

options.text: Instill the prescribed oil to suffocate the insect
options.rationale: A live insect is suffocated with oil before removal so it stops moving and cannot sting or scratch the eardrum. Removal is then safer and less distressing.

options.text: Reach in with a cotton swab to draw the insect out
options.rationale: A cotton swab pushes objects deeper and can injure the canal. A moving insect could also be driven against the eardrum.

options.text: Instill a ceruminolytic and wait 2 days before removal
options.rationale: A ceruminolytic softens cerumen and has no effect on an insect. Waiting 2 days leaves a live insect moving in his ear.

questions.takeaway: Suffocate a live insect with oil before removal; never irrigate a live insect.
questions.strategy: Irrigation is the familiar ear procedure and feels like it would wash the insect away. The live insect rule rules it out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It is moving and buzzing.
Live insects are suffocated with oil, never irrigated.
Cotton swabs push it deeper; ceruminolytics are for cerumen.

elimination.verdict: Instill the oil first.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders

questions.stem: A patient having an acute Ménière attack has severe spinning and is vomiting. Her blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg and her pulse is 108 beats per minute; her usual blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. An antiemetic is prescribed as needed. She is trying to get out of bed to reach the bathroom. What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Keep her in bed safely and give the antiemetic
options.rationale: During an attack, vertigo makes any attempt to walk a fall risk, and vomiting needs control. Rises in blood pressure, pulse and respirations can occur as part of the acute attack itself.

options.text: Request an antihypertensive for the raised blood pressure
options.rationale: Her pressure is well above her usual level. Rising blood pressure, pulse and respirations can occur during an acute attack, and treating the number ignores the fall that is about to happen.

options.text: Walk her to the bathroom with a gait belt
options.rationale: A gait belt makes walking safer for many patients. During severe vertigo with vomiting, even assisted walking is likely to end in a fall.

options.text: Begin balance exercises to help her adapt to the spinning
options.rationale: Vestibular rehabilitation is part of long term management. It is not done during an acute attack, when movement worsens vertigo and vomiting.

questions.takeaway: During an acute Ménière attack, keep the patient safe in bed and control nausea; vital sign rises can be part of the attack.
questions.strategy: The blood pressure is a number that pulls attention. The immediate harm is a fall from trying to walk during severe vertigo.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She is trying to get up during severe vertigo.
Rises in blood pressure and pulse can be part of the attack.
Movement worsens vertigo and invites a fall.

elimination.verdict: Keep her in bed and give the antiemetic.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders
questions.concept: Ménière disease recognition and acute care

questions.stem: For a patient with a cerumen impaction in the left ear, the provider prescribes a ceruminolytic followed by irrigation. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Instill the prescribed ceruminolytic drops into the left canal
options.rationale: The ceruminolytic softens hard cerumen so it can be removed. It comes after screening and before any attempt at removal.

options.text: Allow the drops the prescribed time to soften the cerumen
options.rationale: Hard, dry cerumen needs time to loosen. Irrigating too soon is less effective and more uncomfortable for the patient.

options.text: Reassess hearing in the left ear
options.rationale: Cerumen impaction causes a conductive loss that is often correctable. Rechecking hearing shows whether removal worked or another cause needs referral.

options.text: Ask about ear pain, drainage and any past eardrum perforation
options.rationale: Irrigation is unsafe if perforation or otitis media is suspected. Screening first decides whether the procedure can go ahead at all.

options.text: Irrigate the left canal as prescribed
options.rationale: Once the cerumen is softened, irrigation or manual removal clears the canal. This is the step that relieves the blockage.

questions.takeaway: Cerumen removal: screen for perforation or infection, soften with a ceruminolytic, wait, irrigate or remove, then reassess hearing.
questions.strategy: Students often start with the drops. Screening for perforation or infection comes first because it decides whether irrigation is allowed.

steps.detail: The history rules out perforation and infection.
Drops and waiting time come before irrigation.
Hearing is rechecked last.

elimination.verdict: Screen, instill, wait, irrigate, reassess.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient newly diagnosed with Ménière disease who takes a diuretic. Which statement by the patient shows that the teaching was understood?

options.text: I will rest from balance exercises until the attacks stop.
options.rationale: Resting during an acute attack makes sense. Vestibular rehabilitation exercises are meant to improve balance between attacks, so stopping them until attacks end removes a helpful therapy.

options.text: I will skip my water pill on days I feel fine.
options.rationale: Feeling well between attacks is common, and the drug may seem unneeded then. The diuretic lowers endolymph volume over time, so skipping doses lets the fluid build up again.

options.text: I will drive slowly if an attack starts on the road.
options.rationale: Slowing down sounds cautious, but vertigo can make the patient lose control of the car. Driving is avoided during attacks, so the safe plan is to pull over and stop.

options.text: I will check food labels and choose low sodium foods.
options.rationale: A low sodium diet helps limit the excess endolymph that distends the inner ear. Checking labels for sodium shows the patient understood this lifestyle measure.

questions.takeaway: Ménière teaching: low sodium diet, take the diuretic, avoid caffeine, stress and fatigue, no driving or ladders during attacks, and balance exercises between attacks.
questions.strategy: Each wrong statement sounds cautious or sensible on a good day. Ménière care works through steady habits, so pick the statement that keeps a measure going rather than pausing it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low sodium is correct.
The diuretic is taken daily, not skipped.
No driving during attacks; balance exercises continue between them.

elimination.verdict: Checking food labels and choosing low sodium foods.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders

questions.stem: The day before a right labyrinthectomy for Ménière disease that has not responded to drugs or other treatment, a patient says, "The spinning will stop, and I will finally hear my family on that side again." What does the nurse do?

options.text: Explain that hearing improves 4 to 6 weeks after surgery
options.rationale: That timeline belongs to stapedectomy for otosclerosis. After labyrinthectomy, hearing in that ear is lost, so this statement is false.

options.text: Agree that the spinning should stop after the operation
options.rationale: The surgery does stop vertigo, so part of his statement is true. Agreeing without addressing the hearing outcome leaves his misunderstanding in place.

options.text: Tell the surgeon that he expects his hearing to return
options.rationale: A labyrinthectomy stops vertigo but causes total hearing loss on the operative side. His statement shows he lacks information for informed consent, which the surgeon must address before surgery.

options.text: Review the fall precautions he will need after surgery
options.rationale: Fall teaching is part of care for any ear surgery affecting balance. It does not address the false belief that could invalidate his consent.

questions.takeaway: Labyrinthectomy is a last resort that stops vertigo but causes total hearing loss on the operative side.
questions.strategy: Agreeing with the true half of his statement is the trap. The false half, about hearing returning, is what makes consent unsafe.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Spinning stops: true. Hearing returns: false.
Consent based on a false belief is not informed.
4 to 6 weeks belongs to stapedectomy.

elimination.verdict: Notify the surgeon of his misunderstanding before surgery.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders

questions.stem: A patient with severe sensorineural hearing loss in both ears from inner ear damage has used powerful hearing aids for years and still cannot understand speech. She asks what else might help. Which option does the nurse expect the provider to discuss?

options.text: A stapedectomy
options.rationale: A stapedectomy replaces the stapes for otosclerosis, which is a conductive problem. Her damage is in the inner ear, past where this surgery works.

options.text: A tympanoplasty
options.rationale: A tympanoplasty rebuilds the eardrum or ossicles for conductive loss. Her eardrum and ossicles are not the problem.

options.text: A cochlear implant
options.rationale: A cochlear implant bypasses the damaged cochlea and stimulates the nerve directly. It is used for sensorineural loss when hearing aids no longer give useful speech.

options.text: A personal sound amplification product
options.rationale: Amplification products make sound louder, like a simple hearing aid. Powerful aids have already failed her, so more amplification will not help.

questions.takeaway: Cochlear implants are for sensorineural loss and bypass the damaged cochlea; tympanoplasty and stapedectomy treat conductive loss.
questions.strategy: Both surgeries sound like stronger fixes. They repair conduction, and her problem is the inner ear itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sensorineural, from inner ear damage.
Stapedectomy and tympanoplasty fix the middle ear.
Powerful aids already failed.

elimination.verdict: Anticipate discussion of a cochlear implant.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders
questions.concept: hearing aids and cochlear implants by type of loss
questions.note: Class content states that hearing aids help conductive loss more than sensorineural loss. Current practice agrees that aids give the clearest result when the inner ear is intact, but most people who wear aids have sensorineural loss, including presbycusis, and aids are first line for it; cochlear implants are for severe loss that aids cannot help. For the course exam, use the class statement; for NCLEX, know that aids are first line for most sensorineural loss.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with otosclerosis in both ears who has decided to delay a stapedectomy. Testing shows that her cochlea and auditory nerve work normally. She asks whether a hearing aid is worth trying in the meantime. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "You will need a cochlear implant, since an aid will not help."
options.rationale: A cochlear implant bypasses a damaged cochlea and is used for sensorineural loss. Her cochlea and nerve work normally, so there is nothing that needs to be bypassed.

options.text: "Aids only help nerve damage, so surgery is your only choice."
options.rationale: Aids are widely used for nerve related loss, but they are not limited to it. With a conductive loss, louder sound reaches a working inner ear, so an aid can help her now.

options.text: "An aid cannot push sound past a stapes that does not move."
options.rationale: The fixed stapes does damp vibration, and that is the cause of her hearing loss. Amplified sound still carries enough vibration through the ossicles and skull bone to reach her working cochlea.

options.text: "An aid often works well when sound is blocked, as yours is."
options.rationale: An aid makes sound louder so more vibration gets past the stiff stapes, and her healthy cochlea and nerve turn it into clear speech. Aids help conductive loss more than sensorineural loss for this reason.

questions.takeaway: Hearing aids help conductive loss more than sensorineural loss, because an intact inner ear turns amplified sound into clear hearing.
questions.strategy: The surgery and implant options sound like stronger fixes. A working cochlea and nerve mean that louder sound alone can restore useful hearing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Otosclerosis fixes the stapes: a conductive loss.
A normal cochlea and nerve can use amplified sound.
"Only" and "cannot" overstate what aids do.

elimination.verdict: An aid is worth trying, because her inner ear is intact.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders
questions.concept: hearing aids and cochlear implants by type of loss
questions.note: Class content states that hearing aids help conductive loss more than sensorineural loss. Current practice agrees that aids give the clearest result when the inner ear is intact, but most people who wear aids have sensorineural loss, including presbycusis, and aids are first line for it; cochlear implants are for severe loss that aids cannot help. For the course exam, use the class statement; for NCLEX, know that aids are first line for most sensorineural loss.

questions.stem: A patient with severe hearing loss who lives alone removes her hearing aids at night and says she worries she would not hear the smoke alarm or a knock at the door. Which device does the nurse suggest?

options.text: A flashing alert system for the alarm and doorbell
options.rationale: Flashing alert systems turn sounds into light signals she can see without her hearing aids. This protects her at night, when her aids are out.

options.text: Wearing her hearing aids every night while she sleeps
options.rationale: Keeping aids in would let her hear an alarm. Aids are removed at night for comfort and care of the device and ear, so this is not a practical plan.

options.text: A personal sound amplification product for use in the daytime
options.rationale: Amplification products help her hear during the day. They would be out or off at night, when the alarm risk she describes occurs.

options.text: An amplified telephone for calls to her family
options.rationale: Amplified phones make calls easier and are a useful assistive device. They do not alert her to a fire or a visitor.

questions.takeaway: Assistive devices such as flashing alert systems, amplified phones and personal sound amplification products support safety and independence with hearing loss.
questions.strategy: Several devices help hearing loss in general. Match the device to the stated risk: alarms at night when the aids are out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Missing an alarm or knock at night.
Her aids are out while she sleeps.
A visual alert does not depend on hearing.

elimination.verdict: Suggest a flashing alert system.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders
questions.concept: assistive devices for safety at home

questions.stem: The nurse is giving preoperative instructions to a patient with hearing loss who hears better with her right ear. Which actions does the nurse use? Select all that apply.

options.text: Speak slowly and clearly in a lower pitch
options.rationale: Slow, clear speech is easier to follow, and a lower pitch suits the high frequency loss common with hearing impairment. Volume alone does not help.

options.text: Arrange interpreter services if she uses sign language
options.rationale: Interpreter services are part of effective communication, which is a legal and ethical duty for safe care. Her preferred language may be signed.

options.text: Sit on her right side, facing her
options.rationale: Moving to the better hearing ear and facing her lets her hear more and see the nurse's face. Both are listed communication strategies for hearing loss.

options.text: Talk while gathering supplies across the room
options.rationale: Talking while working saves time. Distance and turning away remove the visual cues she depends on and reduce the sound reaching her.

options.text: Give the instructions in writing as well
options.rationale: Written communication backs up what she may miss by ear. She can review it later and check details before surgery.

options.text: Shout the most important points
options.rationale: Shouting seems to make key points stand out. It distorts speech and raises its pitch, making it harder for her to understand.

options.text: Stand with the bright window behind the nurse
options.rationale: Standing near a window seems to give good light. Bright light behind the speaker shadows the face, so she cannot read lips or expressions.

questions.takeaway: With hearing loss: face the patient in good light, avoid standing in front of windows, speak slowly and clearly in a lower pitch, use the better ear, write, and use interpreters; never shout.
questions.strategy: The window option sounds like good lighting. Light behind the speaker puts the face in shadow.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Facing her with light on the nurse's face, not behind it.
Better ear, slower speech, lower pitch, no shouting.
Writing and interpreter services.

elimination.verdict: Select the right side seating, lower pitch, written instructions and interpreter options.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders
questions.concept: communicating with a hearing impaired patient

questions.stem: Two hours after a left stapedectomy for otosclerosis, a woman says she feels steady and wants to walk to the bathroom by herself. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Have her sit at the bedside for 10 minutes, then walk alone
options.rationale: Dangling first is a reasonable step before standing. Walking alone afterward still leaves her without help if vertigo starts on the way.

options.text: Walk beside her and assist her to the bathroom
options.rationale: Vertigo risk is high after a stapedectomy because surgery is close to the inner ear. Feeling steady in bed does not predict balance when she stands, so the nurse assists.

options.text: Let her walk alone with the call light in reach
options.rationale: Respecting her wish for independence matters. A call light helps only after a problem begins, and sudden vertigo could drop her before she reaches it.

options.text: Keep her in bed and offer a bedpan until morning
options.rationale: A bedpan removes the walking risk. It is more restrictive than needed, since assisted ambulation keeps her safe and mobile.

questions.takeaway: After stapedectomy, assist with ambulation because vertigo risk is high.
questions.strategy: Her report of feeling steady pulls toward independence. The procedure, not her feeling, decides that she needs help.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stapedectomy carries a high vertigo risk.
A call light or dangling does not cover sudden vertigo.
A bedpan is more than she needs.

elimination.verdict: Walk beside her and assist.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders

questions.stem: The day after a stapedectomy for otosclerosis, a patient is preparing to go home. Which statement shows that he understood the discharge teaching?

options.text: "I won't blow my nose or strain on the toilet for now."
options.rationale: Straining and nose blowing raise pressure in the middle ear and can dislodge the prosthesis. Avoiding them is a listed postoperative priority.

options.text: "Getting dizzy when I stand means I should call 911."
options.rationale: Vertigo after stapedectomy is common and calls for help with walking, not emergency services. Calling 911 for expected dizziness misreads the teaching.

options.text: "If my hearing is not back by tomorrow, the surgery failed."
options.rationale: Wanting quick results is understandable. Hearing usually improves about 4 to 6 weeks after surgery, so muffled hearing tomorrow is expected.

options.text: "I can fly to my daughter's wedding at the end of this week."
options.rationale: A family trip is important to him. Air travel changes middle ear pressure and is avoided after stapedectomy, so this plan needs to wait.

questions.takeaway: After stapedectomy: no straining, nose blowing or air travel, prevent infection, and expect hearing to improve over about 4 to 6 weeks.
questions.strategy: The dizziness statement sounds cautious, which can feel like the safe pick. Dizziness is expected after this surgery and calls for help walking, not emergency services.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No nose blowing, straining or flying.
Hearing improves over 4 to 6 weeks, not overnight.
Vertigo is expected; it calls for help walking.

elimination.verdict: He understands to avoid nose blowing and straining.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders

questions.stem: The nurse teaches hearing protection to a patient who just started work at a sawmill. Which statement shows that the teaching was understood?

options.text: "Ringing after a shift goes away overnight, so it means no harm."
options.rationale: Ringing often fades by morning, which feels reassuring. Ringing after noise is a warning of inner ear stress, and repeated exposure leads to lasting damage.

options.text: "I'll wear earplugs or earmuffs for every shift, even short ones."
options.rationale: Prolonged loud noise is a major preventable cause of permanent hearing loss. Protection is needed every time he is exposed, not only on long days.

options.text: "I'll get a hearing test only if I notice trouble hearing."
options.rationale: Waiting for symptoms seems efficient. Regular hearing screening catches loss early, before he notices it and after damage has begun.

options.text: "Only noise that hurts my ears can damage my hearing."
options.rationale: Pain does signal very loud sound. Damage happens with prolonged loud noise well below the level that hurts, so waiting for pain leaves him unprotected.

questions.takeaway: Prolonged loud noise is a major preventable cause of hearing loss; protect the ears every exposure and screen regularly.
questions.strategy: The ringing statement is tempting because the ringing does fade. A sign that passes is still a warning of damage.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every shift, even short ones.
Pain and ringing are not safe thresholds.
Regular exams, not only when symptoms appear.

elimination.verdict: He understands to protect his ears for every exposure.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders

questions.stem: In the preoperative holding area, the nurse reviews the chart of a patient scheduled for a left labyrinthectomy for Ménière disease that drugs and diet have not controlled. Which finding does the nurse bring to the surgeon before the procedure?

options.text: Expects that the spinning will stop after surgery
options.rationale: Patient expectations are worth checking before surgery, and a wrong one is reported. This one is accurate, because labyrinthectomy does stop vertigo, so there is nothing to correct.

options.text: Low sodium diet and a daily diuretic for a year
options.rationale: Diet and drug history matter before any procedure. A year of failed sodium restriction and diuretic therapy shows that surgery is the last resort it should be, which supports the plan.

options.text: Profound hearing loss in the right ear since birth
options.rationale: A labyrinthectomy destroys all hearing on the operative side. With almost no hearing in the right ear, removing the left labyrinth would leave the patient unable to hear, so the surgeon must know before surgery.

options.text: Tinnitus and fullness in the left ear this morning
options.rationale: New ear symptoms can deserve a report in many patients. Ringing and fullness on the diseased side are part of Ménière disease and are the reason for the operation.

questions.takeaway: Labyrinthectomy stops vertigo but removes all hearing on that side, so poor hearing in the other ear changes the whole plan.
questions.strategy: Checking the patient's expectation feels like the safe report; this expectation is correct. The other ear decides whether the patient will hear at all afterward.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Recall the cost of the operation
steps.detail: Labyrinthectomy causes total hearing loss on the operative side.
The right ear already hears almost nothing.
Tinnitus, failed diet and drugs, and the hope that vertigo stops all fit the plan.

elimination.verdict: Report the right ear hearing loss before surgery.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders

questions.stem: The day after gallbladder surgery, assistive personnel report that a patient gives answers that do not match their questions and keeps saying "What?" They ask whether he is becoming confused. Which finding best tells the nurse that hearing, not confusion, explains his answers?

options.text: States his own name when the nurse asks
options.rationale: Knowing his name shows some orientation. Orientation to person is the last to be lost, so a patient with new confusion can still give his name correctly.

options.text: Turns one ear toward people when they speak
options.rationale: Turning an ear toward a speaker is a behavioral cue of hearing loss. A confused patient can also have hearing loss, so this cue does not show that his thinking is clear.

options.text: Stops talking when his visitors arrive
options.rationale: Social withdrawal is a functional sign of hearing loss. It is not specific, because pain, fatigue, low mood and confusion after surgery can all cause it too.

options.text: Responds correctly to a printed note
options.rationale: Correct, prompt responses to a printed note show that his thinking is clear when the words reach him. The mismatched spoken answers then come from not hearing the question.

questions.takeaway: When answers do not match the question, test the message another way; correct responses to a printed note point to hearing loss, not confusion.
questions.strategy: Turning an ear toward speakers is a true hearing cue, so it is tempting. Only the printed note separates clear thinking from confusion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The item asks which finding rules out confusion, not which finding suggests hearing loss.
Ear turning and withdrawal can occur with confusion and hearing loss together.
A printed note skips hearing and tests thinking directly.

elimination.verdict: Correct responses to a printed note show that hearing, not confusion, explains his answers.

questions.objective: Recognize common ear and hearing conditions and their clinical manifestations

questions.nursesNote: Postoperative day 1, right stapedectomy. 0800 Packing in place in the right ear. Reports hearing in the right ear is muffled. Right corner of mouth droops when she smiles; left side lifts normally. Pain 2 of 10. Temperature 38.4 C. Taking clear fluids without nausea. Got up alone to the bathroom at 0630 and says the room spun. Husband at bedside. Ear dressing has a small amount of foul smelling yellow drainage.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that the nurse follows up.

segments.text: Packing in place in the right ear.
segments.rationale: Packing is placed during surgery and stays for a time afterward. Its presence is expected on day 1.

segments.text: Reports hearing in the right ear is muffled.
segments.rationale: Packing and swelling muffle hearing at first, and hearing improves about 4 to 6 weeks after surgery. Muffled hearing on day 1 is expected.

segments.text: Right corner of mouth droops when she smiles; left side lifts normally.
segments.rationale: The facial nerve, cranial nerve VII, runs close to the stapes. One sided droop on the operative side suggests facial nerve damage and is reported.

segments.text: Pain 2 of 10.
segments.rationale: Mild pain is expected the day after ear surgery. A score of 2 of 10 shows her pain is controlled.

segments.text: Temperature 38.4 C.
segments.rationale: Preventing infection is a postoperative priority. A fever on day 1 can signal infection near the inner ear and needs follow up.

segments.text: Taking clear fluids without nausea.
segments.rationale: Tolerating fluids without nausea is a good recovery sign. Nausea would come with vertigo, and she has none now.

segments.text: Got up alone to the bathroom at 0630 and says the room spun.
segments.rationale: Vertigo risk is high after stapedectomy, and she walked without help. The nurse reinforces assisted ambulation and checks that she was not hurt.

segments.text: Husband at bedside.
segments.rationale: Her husband's presence is useful support for her recovery and discharge. It is not a clinical finding that needs follow up.

segments.text: Ear dressing has a small amount of foul smelling yellow drainage.
segments.rationale: Foul smelling yellow drainage on the dressing suggests a wound infection. Together with the fever, it needs to be reported to the surgeon promptly.

questions.takeaway: After stapedectomy, watch for facial nerve damage, infection and vertigo; muffled hearing and mild pain early on are expected.
questions.strategy: Muffled hearing looks like a surgical failure. Hearing is expected to improve only over 4 to 6 weeks, so on day 1 it is normal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A one sided droop points to cranial nerve VII.
Fever and foul drainage.
Walking alone with vertigo.
Packing, muffled hearing, mild pain.

elimination.verdict: Highlight the facial droop, fever, unassisted walk with vertigo and foul drainage.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders

questions.stem: In a long term care facility, a woman with hardened cerumen in the left ear has received a ceruminolytic for 3 days, and irrigation is prescribed for today. Before starting, the nurse asks about the ear. Which report leads the nurse to hold the irrigation?

options.text: That ear has felt full and plugged for about a week or more.
options.rationale: Fullness can come from fluid behind the eardrum, so it sounds like a middle ear warning. It is also the classic sign of cerumen impaction, the very problem the irrigation was prescribed to treat.

options.text: My other ear needed this same cleaning done last year.
options.rationale: A history of impaction in the other ear is worth charting. Past irrigation of a different ear says nothing about the eardrum on this side, so it is no reason to stop.

options.text: A bad ache last week stopped at once and left my pillow wet.
options.rationale: Severe pain that suddenly stops, followed by drainage, is the sign of a perforated eardrum. Irrigation is never done when perforation is suspected, because it can push water and infection into the middle ear.

options.text: Sounds on that side have seemed faint ever since this began.
options.rationale: Hearing loss on one side can point to a middle ear problem. Cerumen blocking the canal also muffles sound, so this report fits the known impaction rather than a reason to hold.

questions.takeaway: Before irrigating, ask about the eardrum: severe pain that suddenly stopped and was followed by drainage means suspected perforation, so hold and report.
questions.strategy: Fullness and faint hearing sound like middle ear trouble, which makes them tempting. Both are signs of the cerumen itself; only the sudden end of a bad ache with drainage points to perforation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fullness and muffled hearing fit the known impaction.
A bad ache that stopped at once with a wet pillow means the eardrum likely ruptured.
Suspected perforation means no irrigation.

elimination.verdict: Hold the irrigation for the ache that stopped at once with drainage.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders
questions.concept: never irrigate with suspected perforation or otitis media

questions.stem: During a telehealth visit, a patient who was just prescribed an antibiotic for acute otitis media repeats the home instructions. Which statement by the patient needs follow up?

options.text: "If the pain stops suddenly and the ear drains, I can stop the pills."
options.rationale: Sudden pain relief with drainage means the eardrum has perforated, not that the infection is gone. The patient must report it and still finish the full antibiotic course to prevent lasting hearing loss.

options.text: "I can take a pain reliever with the antibiotic to help me feel better."
options.rationale: Taking two drugs together may seem like something to question. Analgesics are part of the treatment plan for otitis media, so this statement is correct.

options.text: "A warm pack held over the sore ear may help ease the pain at home."
options.rationale: Heat over an infected area can sound unsafe. Mild heat is part of the nonsurgical treatment of otitis media and eases the pressure pain, so this statement is correct.

options.text: "I plan to stay in bed and rest for the next day or two while I heal."
options.rationale: Bed rest can sound outdated for an ear problem. Rest is part of the nonsurgical plan for acute otitis media, so this statement shows that the teaching was understood.

questions.takeaway: Sudden pain relief with drainage in otitis media signals perforation, not cure; the patient reports it and finishes the whole antibiotic course.
questions.strategy: Heat, rest and analgesics can each sound wrong for an infection, yet all are part of the plan. Pain that suddenly stops sounds like healing but means the eardrum broke.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The item asks for the statement that is wrong.
Mild heat, rest and analgesics all belong to otitis media care.
Pain relief with drainage is perforation, and the course is still finished.

elimination.verdict: The statement about stopping the pills after sudden relief needs follow up.

questions.objective: Explain priority nursing care, treatment, patient education, and prevention strategies for common hearing disorders
questions.concept: complete the antibiotic course for otitis media

questions.stem: On a medical unit, the nurse prepares discharge teaching for a patient recovering from pneumonia. His audiogram shows an 80 dB hearing loss in both ears, he does not use sign language, and his hearing aids were lost during the admission. Which plan does the nurse use?

options.text: Raise the voice and speak in a higher pitch
options.rationale: Raising the voice seems to help a patient who cannot hear. Higher pitches are lost first and shouting distorts words, so the nurse lowers the pitch instead of raising it.

options.text: Sit right next to him, facing him, and speak slowly
options.rationale: A loss of 71 to 90 dB means the listener must be right next to the speaker to hear speech. Facing him adds lip reading and facial cues, and a slow pace makes each word clearer.

options.text: Hand him the written sheet and skip the spoken part
options.rationale: Written material is a useful support for hearing loss. Skipping the spoken teaching removes the chance to answer questions and check understanding before he goes home.

options.text: Face him from the foot of the bed in a quiet private room
options.rationale: Facing the patient in a quiet room is the right plan for a mild loss of 20 to 40 dB. At 80 dB he cannot follow speech from the foot of the bed.

questions.takeaway: Match the plan to the audiogram: a mild loss needs a quiet room, while a 71 to 90 dB loss needs the speaker right beside the patient.
questions.strategy: A quiet room facing the patient is the textbook answer and feels complete. The 80 dB result means distance itself blocks speech, so the nurse must be right next to him.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 80 dB falls in the range where the speaker must be right beside the patient.
It fits a mild loss, not this one.

steps.action: Cut the pitch and skip errors
steps.detail: A higher pitch and written only teaching both fail him.

elimination.verdict: Sit right next to him, face him and speak slowly.

questions.objective: Differentiate conductive, sensorineural, and mixed hearing loss

questions.stem: After a patient twists the left knee while skiing, the knee feels loose and shifts sideways when the patient stands on it, but it does not lock or catch. The x ray shows no fracture, and the patient can tighten the thigh muscle and lift the straight leg off the bed. Which structure does the nurse suspect is injured?

options.text: The muscle
options.rationale: Skeletal muscle produces movement and supports the joint, but this patient tightens the thigh muscle and lifts the leg on command. Strength is present, so the looseness comes from another structure.

options.text: A tendon
options.rationale: A tendon connects muscle to bone, so a torn thigh tendon would stop the patient from lifting the straight leg. This patient lifts the leg, which shows the muscle still pulls on bone.

options.text: The cartilage
options.rationale: Cartilage reduces friction inside the joint, and a torn piece often makes the knee lock, catch or grind. This knee does neither; it shifts sideways, which points to a loss of stability instead.

options.text: A ligament
options.rationale: Ligaments connect bone to bone and keep a joint stable, so a tear lets the joint shift out of line. Intact bones on x ray and a working thigh muscle point to the ligament.

questions.takeaway: A joint that shifts out of line with intact bones and working muscles points to a torn ligament, the bone to bone connector.
questions.strategy: Students pick tendon because it sounds like a sports injury; the patient lifting the straight leg proves the muscle to bone connection still works.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The x ray shows no fracture.
The patient tightens the thigh and lifts the leg.
Instability between two bones is a ligament problem.

elimination.verdict: A torn ligament.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.objective: Perform a focused musculoskeletal assessment including history, posture, gait, joint movement, muscle strength, and neurovascular status.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses a patient whose right lower leg cast came off today after six weeks for a fracture. The right calf is visibly thinner than the left, the skin is intact, the foot is pink and warm, and the patient pushes the right foot against the nurse's hand with less force than the left. How does the nurse interpret the thinner calf?

options.text: A new deformity to report
options.rationale: A new deformity is a change in the shape or alignment of bone or joint after injury. A smaller muscle on a limb that was immobilized is the expected result of disuse.

options.text: Muscle loss from aging
options.rationale: Muscle atrophy with aging is gradual and affects both sides about equally. Here only the casted leg changed, and the change matches the six weeks of inactivity.

options.text: Rapid swelling to report
options.rationale: Rapid swelling makes a limb larger and tighter, and it is a red flag after injury. This calf is smaller than the other side, which is the opposite finding.

options.text: Muscle atrophy from inactivity
options.rationale: Skeletal muscle strength and size change with activity and inactivity, and six weeks without use shrinks the calf. Normal color and warmth show the circulation is intact.

questions.takeaway: A muscle shrinks and weakens when it is not used; one sided loss that matches a period of immobilization is disuse atrophy.
questions.strategy: The word thinner tempts students toward a red flag; red flags are sudden, larger or cooler, while a smaller muscle after a cast fits inactivity.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The calf is smaller, not larger, so swelling is out.
Six weeks in a cast means six weeks without muscle work.
Pink, warm skin rules out a vascular cause.

elimination.verdict: Atrophy from inactivity.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.objective: Perform a focused musculoskeletal assessment including history, posture, gait, joint movement, muscle strength, and neurovascular status.
questions.concept: Skeletal muscle strength changes with inactivity

questions.stem: During a health history for stiffness and grinding in the right knee that has worsened over the past year, a patient says, "It probably doesn't matter, but I tore something in that knee playing football 30 years ago." Which action by the nurse is best?

options.text: Move on to testing strength of the knee
options.rationale: Strength testing is part of the physical assessment and will come later. The history comes first because it tells the nurse which areas need the closest attention.

options.text: Refer the patient to physical therapy now
options.rationale: A therapist may help later with gait and function, but no assessment has been completed yet. Referring before the history and examination skips the data that shows what help is needed.

options.text: Note the old tear as a likely factor
options.rationale: An injury from many years ago can lead to joint damage and arthritis long after the event. The history directs the physical assessment, so the old tear is recorded and weighed now.

options.text: Leave out events older than five years
options.rationale: Recent events matter, but leaving out old injuries loses the likely cause of a slowly worsening joint. Past trauma and sports injuries are asked about no matter when they happened.

questions.takeaway: Ask about every past injury and sports activity, however long ago; old trauma often explains a joint problem today.
questions.strategy: The patient tells you the injury does not matter; the trap is agreeing because it was long ago.

steps.detail: The nurse is still taking the history.
An old knee tear fits a knee that is slowly getting worse.
Strength testing and referral come after the history.

elimination.verdict: Note the old tear as a factor.

questions.stem: After a minor fall at home, a patient is found to have a compression fracture of a vertebra. During the history the nurse looks for factors that raise the risk of further bone loss. Which findings does the nurse flag for follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Takes a daily calcium and vitamin D supplement
options.rationale: Adequate calcium and vitamin D support bone, so this habit lowers risk rather than raising it. The nurse records it as a protective factor.

options.text: Walks briskly for 30 minutes most days
options.rationale: Walking is weight bearing exercise, which helps keep bone strong. This habit protects bone, so it is a strength to reinforce rather than a risk to follow up.

options.text: Avoids milk and cheese because of lactose intolerance
options.rationale: Dairy foods are a main source of calcium, and avoiding them can leave intake too low to keep bone dense. The nurse follows up on other calcium and vitamin D sources.

options.text: Works at a library returning books to shelves
options.rationale: This job keeps the patient standing, walking and lifting light loads through the day. Nothing about it points to bone loss, so it needs no follow up.

options.text: Smokes about one pack of cigarettes a day
options.rationale: Tobacco use harms bone health, and avoiding tobacco is one of the ways to promote musculoskeletal health. Smoking is a changeable risk the nurse can address with teaching.

options.text: Drinks four or five glasses of wine each night
options.rationale: Excessive alcohol works against bone health, and limiting it is part of promoting musculoskeletal health. This amount is well beyond light drinking, so it needs follow up.

options.text: Mother had osteoporosis with a hip fracture
options.rationale: Osteoporosis tends to run in families, so a family history raises the patient's own risk. The nurse records it and flags it for bone density follow up.

questions.takeaway: Low calcium intake, tobacco, heavy alcohol use and a family history of osteoporosis all raise the risk of bone loss.
questions.strategy: Every option describes a habit; sort each one by whether it builds bone or wears it down.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Avoiding dairy cuts calcium intake.
Tobacco and heavy alcohol use both harm bone.
Osteoporosis in a parent raises risk.
Walking and supplements help bone.

elimination.verdict: Dairy avoidance, smoking, heavy alcohol use and family history.

questions.stem: The nurse observes an 83 year old patient with osteoporosis who stands with a rounded upper back and her head forward. She walks with her feet wide apart, sways when she turns, and holds the furniture as she moves around her room. Which action does the nurse take based on these findings?

options.text: Encourage her to walk faster to build strength
options.rationale: Activity does build strength, but movement slows with aging and hurrying an unsteady patient invites a fall. The nurse does not rush her.

options.text: Assess her need for a cane or walker
options.rationale: Kyphosis shifts the center of gravity forward, and a wide, unsteady gait raises the risk of falls. An ambulatory device gives her support so she can stay mobile with better balance.

options.text: Report the rounded back as a new deformity
options.rationale: A new deformity after injury is a red flag, but kyphosis from osteoporosis develops over years. Nothing in her findings suggests a sudden change, so the focus is her gait safety.

options.text: Keep her in bed until her balance improves
options.rationale: Bedrest would protect her from a fall today, but it speeds muscle and bone loss and makes balance worse. The goal is to maintain function with support, not remove activity.

questions.takeaway: Kyphosis and a widened gait shift balance and raise fall risk; support mobility with the right device rather than restricting it.
questions.strategy: Bedrest feels safe but is the least helpful choice; the findings call for support while she keeps moving.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A forward rounded back moves the center of gravity.
Wide stance, swaying and holding furniture mean she needs support.
Bedrest and hurrying both make outcomes worse.

elimination.verdict: Assess for a cane or walker.

questions.stem: A 73 year old patient comes to the clinic for a yearly checkup with no new complaints. During the general inspection, which finding does the nurse follow up?

options.text: Right knee red, warm and swollen
options.rationale: Redness, warmth and swelling on one side point to inflammation or injury in that joint. Inspection always compares sides, and this knee does not match the other.

options.text: Slow, steady gait with an even stride
options.rationale: Movement slows with aging, but this gait is steady and even on both sides. A slow pace without limping, swaying or asymmetry needs no follow up.

options.text: Calf muscles slightly thinner on both legs
options.rationale: Muscle atrophy is an expected change of aging, and here it is equal on both legs. Symmetric, gradual thinning in an older adult is recorded as baseline.

options.text: Shoulders level when he stands upright
options.rationale: Level shoulders show good alignment and symmetry of the upper body. This is a normal posture finding that the nurse documents.

questions.takeaway: Inspection looks for asymmetry, swelling, redness and deformity; one sided change stands out against symmetric aging findings.
questions.strategy: Several options describe older adult changes that look abnormal; the finding that differs from the other side is the one that needs follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only the knee differs between right and left.
Equal thinning and a slow even gait fit aging.
Red, warm and swollen.

elimination.verdict: The red, warm, swollen right knee.

questions.stem: In a long term care facility, an 92 year old patient has a stooped upper back, thin arms and legs, and a slow walk, all unchanged for years and equal on both sides. At this month's general inspection, her left ankle is puffy and pinker than the right, and she now puts less weight on that foot. She says it does not hurt and is just old age. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Chart the ankle as a change of aging
options.rationale: Her stooped back, thin limbs and slow walk count as aging changes because they are long standing and symmetric. The ankle changed recently and only on the left, so her own label does not fit it.

options.text: Teach weight bearing exercise for her bone loss
options.rationale: Weight bearing exercise does help protect aging bones and suits her stooped posture. It does nothing to explain a swollen, pink ankle that she now avoids loading, so it is not the action now.

options.text: Report the left ankle findings
options.rationale: Aging changes come slowly and affect both sides, but this ankle is swollen, pink and favored on one side only. Swelling and redness on inspection need follow up even when she denies pain.

options.text: Recheck the ankle at next month's inspection
options.rationale: The absence of pain makes waiting seem reasonable, and the ankle will be rechecked. A month of delay leaves one sided swelling and redness unexplained, and painless findings still need reporting.

questions.takeaway: On general inspection, swelling, redness or a change in gait on one side is followed up even when the patient denies pain and calls it aging.
questions.strategy: Her own explanation and the lack of pain pull toward charting or waiting. What tips it is that the ankle finding is recent and one sided, unlike her symmetric aging changes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The stooped back, thin limbs and slow walk are years old; the ankle is new.
Only the left ankle is puffy, pink and spared from weight.
No pain and a patient's label of aging do not make a one sided change normal.

steps.action: Pick the action that gets it evaluated
steps.detail: Exercise teaching and waiting leave the ankle unexplained.

elimination.verdict: Report the left ankle findings.
