questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse that pain in the right hand makes buttoning a shirt hard. When asked, the patient makes a full fist and touches each fingertip to the thumb with the left hand. With the right hand the patient cannot close the fist fully and stops, saying the knuckles hurt. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Inspect and palpate the right knuckles
options.rationale: The right hand has limited, painful movement that the left hand does not, so the nurse looks more closely at those joints. Swelling, redness, warmth or deformity there would explain the limit.

options.text: Record the right hand range of motion as normal
options.rationale: The patient cannot finish the fist with the right hand, so the movement is limited. Calling it normal would hide the very finding the patient came in with.

options.text: Push the right fingers into a full fist
options.rationale: Gently checking passive movement can follow when active movement is limited, but forcing painful joints risks injury. The nurse first inspects and palpates the joints that hurt.

options.text: Repeat the fist test on the left hand
options.rationale: Comparing sides is correct, and the left hand has already been tested and is normal. Repeating it adds no new data about the painful right hand.

questions.takeaway: When movement is limited or painful on one side, compare with the other side, then inspect and palpate the affected joints.
questions.strategy: Forcing the fingers closed seems thorough, but it hurts painful joints; look and feel before pushing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The left hand is normal; the right is limited and painful.
The right knuckles need inspection and palpation.
Pushing hurts and retesting the left adds nothing.

elimination.verdict: Inspect and palpate the right knuckles.

questions.stem: After a stroke, a patient can move the left leg side to side across the mattress but cannot lift the leg off the bed. The nurse uses the 0 to 5 muscle strength scale. Which grade does the nurse record for the left leg?

options.text: 4 out of 5
options.rationale: A grade of 4 means movement against some resistance from the examiner. This patient cannot even overcome gravity, so resistance has not been reached.

options.text: 3 out of 5
options.rationale: A grade of 3 means the patient can lift the limb against gravity. This patient cannot raise the leg off the mattress, so the grade is lower.

options.text: 1 out of 5
options.rationale: A grade of 1 is a trace contraction that the nurse can feel or see, with no movement of the limb. This patient moves the whole leg across the bed.

options.text: 2 out of 5
options.rationale: A grade of 2 means the muscle moves the limb only when gravity is taken away, as when it moves across the bed. The patient cannot lift the leg, so the grade is not higher.

questions.takeaway: Sliding on the bed is movement without gravity, grade 2; lifting off the bed is against gravity, grade 3.
questions.strategy: Students mix up 2 and 3; ask whether the leg left the bed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Yes, so it is above 1.

steps.action: Ask if it lifted against gravity
steps.detail: No, so it is below 3.
Movement with gravity eliminated.

elimination.verdict: 2 out of 5.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected change of aging or needs follow up.
questions.scenario: A 72 year old patient is admitted to a skilled nursing unit for strengthening after pneumonia. The nurse completes a musculoskeletal assessment and compares the findings with what is expected for her age.

rows.text: Left ankle swollen since yesterday; right ankle normal
rows.rationale: Swelling that is new and on one side only does not match the gradual, symmetric pattern of aging. It needs follow up for injury, inflammation or a circulation problem.

rows.text: Cannot lift her right arm today; she could yesterday
rows.rationale: Sudden loss of movement is a red flag that aging does not explain. A change from yesterday to today needs to be reported right away.

rows.text: Thigh muscles slightly smaller on both legs
rows.rationale: Muscle tissue atrophies with aging, and here the change is equal on both legs. Symmetric loss is expected, and exercise can help her keep strength.

rows.text: Walks more slowly than she did a few years ago, with even steps
rows.rationale: Movement slows with aging, and her steps are still even on both sides. A slower pace without limping or swaying is recorded as baseline.

rows.text: Shoulders raise a little less far than in younger adults, equal on both sides
rows.rationale: Range of motion decreases with age as joint cartilage becomes less elastic. The loss is mild and equal, which fits aging rather than injury.

rows.text: New tingling in the toes of her left foot
rows.rationale: New numbness or tingling is a red flag for nerve or blood flow problems. Aging does not cause sudden new sensation changes in one foot.

questions.takeaway: Aging is slow and symmetric; anything new, sudden or one sided needs follow up.
questions.strategy: Several expected findings sound like problems in a patient recovering from illness; judge each by how fast it changed and whether both sides match.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Changes over years fit aging; changes since yesterday do not.
Equal on both sides fits aging; one sided needs a look.
Sudden loss of movement and new tingling are always reported.

elimination.verdict: Expected, expected, follow up, expected, follow up, follow up.

questions.stem: The nurse is monitoring a patient after surgery on the lower back. At 0800 the patient held both legs up against the nurse's firm pressure, equal on both sides. At 1200 the patient can lift the right leg off the bed but it falls as soon as the nurse presses lightly. The left leg is unchanged. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Help the patient do leg exercises to build strength
options.rationale: Exercise builds strength when weakness comes from inactivity. A sudden drop within hours after spine surgery suggests a nerve problem, which exercise will not fix.

options.text: Report the change in right leg strength now
options.rationale: Strength dropped from full to movement against gravity only within four hours, which is a sudden loss of movement. A sudden change is a red flag that is reported right away.

options.text: Document the right leg strength as 3 out of 5
options.rationale: Grading the leg as 3 out of 5 is accurate, but documenting alone stops one step short. The finding is a sudden decline from the 0800 baseline and needs to be reported.

options.text: Reassess the right leg strength at 1600
options.rationale: Regular reassessment is part of care, but waiting four more hours delays action on a sudden loss of strength. The change is already present and needs a response now.

questions.takeaway: A strength grade matters most compared with the last one; a sudden drop is reported, not just recorded.
questions.strategy: Grading the leg correctly feels like the task; the real decision is what a fall from 5 to 3 in four hours means.

steps.detail: Full strength at 0800, against gravity only at 1200.
Four hours makes it sudden.
Sudden loss of movement is reported now.

elimination.verdict: Report the change now.

questions.stem: On a rehabilitation unit, the nurse reviews arm strength findings for four patients. Which finding does the nurse record as 3 out of 5 on the muscle strength scale?

options.text: The arm lifts off the bed but drops with the lightest pressure
options.rationale: Lifting the arm off the bed shows movement against gravity. Dropping with the lightest pressure means it cannot move against any resistance, so the grade stops at 3.

options.text: The muscle tightens under the fingers, but the arm stays still
options.rationale: A contraction the nurse can feel shows the muscle is not fully paralyzed. With no movement of the limb at all, the finding is a trace contraction, grade 1.

options.text: The arm holds against light pressure but gives way to firm pressure
options.rationale: This arm does lift against gravity, which grade 3 also requires. Holding against some resistance takes it one step higher, so the nurse records grade 4.

options.text: The arm moves across the bed but cannot be lifted off it
options.rationale: Moving across the bed is real movement, so this arm is stronger than a trace contraction. Sliding along the mattress removes gravity, and movement without gravity is grade 2.

questions.takeaway: Muscle strength is graded by what the muscle overcomes: movement without gravity is 2, against gravity is 3, and against some resistance is 4.
questions.strategy: Grades 2 and 4 sit right beside 3, so each is a near miss. Ask whether the arm beats gravity, then whether it beats any resistance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lifting off the bed beats gravity; sliding across the bed does not.
The arm that holds light pressure is a 4; the arm that drops is a 3.

elimination.verdict: The arm lifts off the bed but drops with the lightest pressure.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing upper arm strength for a patient who reports that the left arm has felt weak for a week. Which technique gives the nurse the most useful data?

options.text: Watch the patient raise the left arm overhead
options.rationale: Raising the arm shows movement against gravity, but without resistance the nurse cannot tell grade 3 from grade 5. Testing one arm also gives nothing to compare.

options.text: Ask the patient to rate the arm weakness from 0 to 10
options.rationale: The patient's report matters and starts the assessment, but it is not a measure of strength. The nurse needs to see what the muscle can move against.

options.text: Measure around both upper arms with a tape
options.rationale: Muscle size may show wasting, but size does not tell how strong the muscle is. Strength is judged by movement against gravity and resistance.

options.text: Press down on both arms as the patient raises them
options.rationale: Strength is tested by asking the patient to move against the nurse's resistance. Testing both arms at the same time lets the nurse compare the weak side with the normal side.

questions.takeaway: Test strength by having the patient move against your resistance, and test both sides together for comparison.
questions.strategy: Watching the arm rise looks like a strength test, but without resistance and without the other arm, it cannot grade or compare.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Movement against resistance.
Testing both arms at once.
A rating and a tape measure do not show strength.

elimination.verdict: Press down on both arms.

questions.stem: This morning a patient's left forearm was placed in a cast, and the nurse is now completing a neurovascular check. The nurse has recorded the color, temperature and capillary refill of the left fingers, the left radial pulse, finger movement and pain. Which assessment does the nurse still need to complete?

options.text: Ask the patient to rate the anxiety level
options.rationale: Anxiety can rise after an injury and is worth assessing for comfort. It is not part of the neurovascular check, which looks at circulation, sensation and movement.

options.text: Ask whether the fingers feel numb or tingly
options.rationale: Sensation is one of the parts of a neurovascular check, along with color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, movement and pain. It is the only part the nurse has not checked.

options.text: Measure the patient's blood pressure
options.rationale: Blood pressure is a useful vital sign, but it tells nothing about blood flow or nerves below the cast. The neurovascular check looks at the injured limb itself.

options.text: Check the skin over the patient's elbow
options.rationale: Skin near the cast edge can be inspected later, but the elbow is above the fracture. The neurovascular check focuses on the fingers below the injury.

questions.takeaway: A neurovascular check covers color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, sensation, movement and pain, compared with the other side.
questions.strategy: Movement and sensation are easy to blend together; moving the fingers does not show that the patient can feel them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Color, temperature, capillary refill, pulse, movement, pain.
Sensation.
Blood pressure, elbow skin and anxiety are not the check.

elimination.verdict: Ask about numbness or tingling.

questions.stem: A patient has a crush injury of the right foot from a dropped crate. The right foot is pink and warm, the toes move on request, sensation is intact and capillary refill is brisk. The right pedal pulse feels faint. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Raise the right leg on two pillows
options.rationale: Raising an injured limb may help swelling, but it does not answer whether the pulse is normal for this patient. The pulse still needs to be judged before choosing an intervention.

options.text: Report a diminished pulse to the provider
options.rationale: A diminished pulse can be a red flag, but this foot is pink and warm with brisk refill and normal sensation. The nurse compares with the left foot before deciding the pulse is diminished.

options.text: Feel the left foot's pedal pulse
options.rationale: Every neurovascular finding is compared with the other side, and some people have faint pedal pulses on both feet. All other findings on the right are normal, so the comparison comes first.

options.text: Record the right pedal pulse as normal
options.rationale: The pulse may turn out to be normal for this patient, but the nurse cannot know that yet. Without the comparison, recording it as normal is a guess.

questions.takeaway: Judge a neurovascular finding against the other side before calling it abnormal.
questions.strategy: Reporting looks safe, but every other finding is reassuring; the comparison is the missing piece of data.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Color, warmth, refill, movement and sensation are normal.
The faint pulse has not been compared.
Check the left foot first.

elimination.verdict: Feel the left pedal pulse.

questions.stem: The day after surgery to repair a fractured right ankle, a patient wears a padded splint that leaves the top of the foot uncovered. The nurse cannot feel a pulse on the top of the right foot. The right toes are pink and warm, capillary refill is brisk, the patient wiggles the toes, and sensation is normal. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Remove the splint to check the ankle
options.rationale: Taking off a prescribed splint after surgery is not the nurse's decision and could harm the repair. The pulse can be checked without removing it.

options.text: Check the pedal pulse with a Doppler
options.rationale: A Doppler uses high frequency sound waves to detect blood flow that fingers cannot feel. With every other finding normal, the nurse uses it to find the pulse before calling it absent.

options.text: Record the right pedal pulse as absent
options.rationale: The pulse could not be felt, but warm pink toes with brisk refill show blood is reaching the foot. Charting it absent without a Doppler check would be inaccurate.

options.text: Report an absent pulse to the surgeon
options.rationale: An absent pulse is a red flag, but this foot is warm, pink and moving normally. The nurse confirms the pulse with a Doppler first so the report is accurate.

questions.takeaway: When a pulse cannot be felt, use a Doppler to find it before calling it absent.
questions.strategy: Absent pulse is on the red flag list, so reporting is tempting; the other normal findings say to confirm with a Doppler first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pink, warm, brisk refill, normal movement and sensation.
A Doppler hears flow the fingers miss.
Removing the splint is unsafe, and reporting comes after confirming.

elimination.verdict: Use a Doppler.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that the nurse reports as red flags.
questions.nursesNote: 0900: Patient admitted with a fracture of the left upper arm, arm in a sling. Talking with family at the bedside. Reports left arm pain 9 out of 10, up from 4 out of 10 at 0700. Right hand pink and warm with brisk capillary refill. Left hand pale and cool to touch. Left radial pulse present, equal to the right. Says the left fingers "feel like pins and needles" since 0830. Ate most of breakfast. Can no longer bend the left fingers, which moved at 0700.

segments.text: Talking with family at the bedside
segments.rationale: Talking with family shows the patient is alert and has support nearby. It says nothing about blood flow or nerves in the injured arm.

segments.text: Reports left arm pain 9 out of 10, up from 4 out of 10 at 0700
segments.rationale: Severe pain, especially pain that is climbing quickly after an injury, is a red flag. It can mean pressure is building on the tissue of the arm.

segments.text: Right hand pink and warm with brisk capillary refill
segments.rationale: The right arm is uninjured, and these findings serve as the normal for comparison. They help show how much the left hand has changed.

segments.text: Left hand pale and cool to touch
segments.rationale: A cool, pale hand on the injured side, while the other hand is pink and warm, points to poor blood flow. It is one of the red flags to report.

segments.text: Left radial pulse present, equal to the right
segments.rationale: An equal pulse is reassuring on its own, so it is not a red flag. A present pulse does not rule out a problem, so the other changes still need to be reported.

segments.text: Says the left fingers "feel like pins and needles" since 0830
segments.rationale: New tingling shows that the nerves in the arm are being affected. New numbness or tingling is a red flag that needs reporting.

segments.text: Ate most of breakfast
segments.rationale: Good intake is useful to know for nutrition and healing. It has nothing to do with the circulation or nerves of the injured arm.

segments.text: Can no longer bend the left fingers, which moved at 0700
segments.rationale: A loss of movement that was present two hours ago is a sudden change. Sudden loss of movement is a red flag and adds urgency to the report.

questions.takeaway: Severe or rising pain, a cool pale limb, new tingling and sudden loss of movement are red flags even when the pulse is still present.
questions.strategy: The equal pulse tempts students to relax; a present pulse does not cancel the other changes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pain is higher and movement is lost.
The left hand is pale and cool; the right is pink and warm.
Pins and needles since 0830.
Family, breakfast and the uninjured hand.

elimination.verdict: Rising pain, pale cool hand, new tingling, lost movement.

questions.concept: Neurovascular red flags: who to see first

questions.stem: On an orthopedic unit, the nurse receives report on four patients. Which patient does the nurse assess first?

options.text: Has hip arthritis with pain of 4 out of 10
options.rationale: Moderate pain from long standing arthritis needs attention, but it is chronic and stable. It can wait until the patient with a new red flag has been seen.

options.text: Has a bruise on the shin that is the same size
options.rationale: A bruise that has not grown shows no ongoing bleeding or rapid swelling. It is expected after an injury and does not need to be seen first.

options.text: Has right leg strength of 4 out of 5, unchanged
options.rationale: Grade 4 strength is reduced, but it has not changed since the last check. A stable finding is a lower priority than a new one.

options.text: Has an elbow fracture and new numbness of the fingers
options.rationale: New numbness after a fracture is a red flag that blood flow or nerves may be compromised. It is a new and unstable change, so this patient is seen first.

questions.takeaway: A new red flag outranks stable or chronic findings, even when the stable patient has pain.
questions.strategy: Pain is an emotionally strong option, but stable arthritis pain does not outrank new numbness after a fracture.

steps.detail: Only the numbness is new.
Arthritis pain is chronic.
New numbness or tingling is on it.

elimination.verdict: The patient with new finger numbness.

questions.concept: Neurovascular red flags: who to see first

questions.stem: After arthroscopy of the left shoulder, a patient returns to the surgical recovery area. A dressing covers the small incisions and the arm is in a sling. Which assessment does the nurse perform first?

options.text: Pulses and sensation in the left hand
options.rationale: After arthroscopy the priority is the neurovascular status of the affected limb. The nurse checks pulses, color, warmth, capillary refill, sensation, movement and pain in the left arm.

options.text: The patient's knowledge of home exercises
options.rationale: Teaching will be needed before discharge, but it comes after the patient's safety is confirmed. The arm must be checked first.

options.text: Strength of both legs against resistance
options.rationale: Leg strength is not affected by a shoulder procedure. Testing it delays the check of the limb that was operated on.

options.text: Range of motion of the left shoulder
options.rationale: Exercises may be taught for later, but range of motion may not be allowed right after the procedure. Moving the shoulder is not the first assessment after surgery.

questions.takeaway: After a joint procedure, check the neurovascular status of that limb first.
questions.strategy: Shoulder movement feels like the natural focus after shoulder surgery, but circulation and nerve function come before range of motion.

steps.detail: The left arm.
Neurovascular status comes first.
Range of motion and teaching come later.

elimination.verdict: Neurovascular check of the left hand.

questions.stem: A patient hurt in a car crash has a pelvic x ray showing a fracture with the bone broken into several pieces, and the surgeon wants a more detailed picture of the bone to plan the repair. Which test does the nurse expect to be ordered next?

options.text: DEXA scan
options.rationale: A DEXA scan measures bone mineral density to check for osteoporosis. It does not show the shape or position of the broken pieces.

options.text: Ultrasound
options.rationale: Ultrasound can assess tendons, muscles and fluid collections. It does not give a detailed view of the inside of a broken bone.

options.text: CT scan
options.rationale: CT gives more detailed images of bone than an x ray and is useful for complex fractures. The images can be viewed from many angles to plan surgery.

options.text: Bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan finds hidden fractures, infection or tumors when an x ray looks normal. This fracture is already seen, and the surgeon needs detail, not detection.

questions.takeaway: When the fracture is known and complex, CT gives the detailed bone picture the surgeon needs.
questions.strategy: A bone scan sounds like the bone test, but it is for finding hidden problems, not for detailing a fracture already seen.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The x ray shows the fracture.
More bone detail for surgery.
CT gives detailed bone images.

elimination.verdict: CT scan.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the chart of a patient treated for breast cancer two years ago who now has aching in several ribs and the lower back. X rays of the painful areas look normal. The provider wants to look at the whole skeleton for areas of increased bone activity. Which test does the nurse prepare the patient for?

options.text: Ultrasound
options.rationale: Ultrasound assesses tendons, muscles and fluid collections near the surface. It cannot survey the entire skeleton for bone changes.

options.text: DEXA scan
options.rationale: A DEXA scan measures bone mineral density, mainly to assess osteoporosis. It is not used to search the skeleton for spots of increased activity.

options.text: Arthroscopy
options.rationale: Arthroscopy places a scope inside a single joint to view it directly. It cannot look at the ribs and spine, and it is invasive.

options.text: Bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan views the whole skeleton and can detect tumors, infection, hidden fractures and areas of increased bone activity. It can find changes before they show on an x ray.

questions.takeaway: A bone scan surveys the whole skeleton for tumors, infection, hidden fractures and increased bone activity when x rays look normal.
questions.strategy: DEXA is the test students link with bone, but it measures density; the request to look at the whole skeleton for activity points to the bone scan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The problem is not visible on plain film.
Several areas and the whole skeleton.
A bone scan shows areas of increased bone activity.

elimination.verdict: Bone scan.

questions.stem: The provider suspects a fluid collection in a soft, rounded swelling behind a patient's right knee that has grown over a month, and wants a quick test that needs no needle or special preparation. Which test does the nurse expect?

options.text: DEXA scan
options.rationale: A DEXA scan measures bone mineral density. It gives no information about a soft swelling behind the knee.

options.text: X ray
options.rationale: An x ray shows bone clearly, but soft tissue and fluid are not well separated on it. It would not show what is inside the swelling.

options.text: Ultrasound
options.rationale: Ultrasound uses sound waves to view soft tissue, muscles, tendons and fluid collections. It needs no injection and no special preparation or care afterward.

options.text: Bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan needs an injection of radioactive material and looks at bone activity. The swelling is in soft tissue, and the provider wants no needle.

questions.takeaway: Ultrasound shows tendons, muscles and fluid collections without a needle or preparation.
questions.strategy: An x ray is the usual first study, but it is for bone; a soft swelling suspected to hold fluid calls for ultrasound.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Soft tissue and fluid, not bone.
No needle and no preparation.
Ultrasound.

elimination.verdict: Ultrasound.

questions.stem: After a fall, a patient is found on the floor, having lain there for many hours. The thigh and buttock muscles are tender and weak, and the patient has no fracture. Which laboratory result supports injury to the skeletal muscle?

options.text: Elevated creatine kinase MM
options.rationale: Damaged muscle releases enzymes into the blood, and creatine kinase MM is the form found in skeletal muscle. A high level supports injury from hours of pressure on the muscles.

options.text: Decreased serum lactate dehydrogenase
options.rationale: Lactate dehydrogenase also leaks from damaged muscle, so injury raises the level. A decrease points the wrong way.

options.text: Decreased aldolase
options.rationale: Aldolase is one of the muscle enzymes, but injury raises it rather than lowering it. A low level would not support muscle damage.

options.text: Normal serum aspartate aminotransferase
options.rationale: Aspartate aminotransferase rises with skeletal muscle trauma. A normal value would not support the injury the nurse suspects.

questions.takeaway: Creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate aminotransferase and aldolase all rise when skeletal muscle is damaged.
questions.strategy: Every option names a correct muscle enzyme, so the decision rests on direction: injury makes muscle enzymes rise.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: All four are muscle enzymes.
Damage releases enzymes, so levels go up.
Elevated creatine kinase MM.

elimination.verdict: Elevated creatine kinase MM.

questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.
questions.scenario: Six hours after surgery to repair a fracture of the right thigh bone, a patient in a long leg splint reports severe pain that has not eased since the last check, and says the toes feel numb. The right toes are pale and cool and the patient cannot wiggle them. The left foot is pink and warm, with toes that move normally.

options.text: Do range of motion exercises on the right toes
options.rationale: Exercise helps prevent stiffness from immobility, but the patient has lost movement from a new problem. Moving the toes does not address the cause.

options.text: Give prescribed pain medicine, recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: Pain does need treatment, and medicine may be given as prescribed. Waiting an hour to recheck leaves pale, cool, numb toes unreported while blood flow to the leg may be failing.

options.text: Recheck the right toes and compare with the left
options.rationale: Repeated checks against the other foot show whether the leg is getting better or worse. Comparing sides is part of every neurovascular assessment.

options.text: Report the findings to the provider now
options.rationale: Pale, cool toes with numbness, severe pain and lost movement are red flags. They are reported promptly because blood flow and nerves in the leg may be at risk.

options.text: Muscle weakness from inactivity
options.rationale: Inactivity makes muscles weaker over days to weeks, not within six hours. It also does not make the toes pale, cool and numb.

options.text: Poor blood flow to the right leg
options.rationale: Pale, cool toes with numbness, severe pain and lost movement on one side point to reduced circulation and nerve function. The left foot is normal, so the problem is in the injured leg.

options.text: A torn ligament in the knee
options.rationale: A torn ligament makes a joint unstable, but it does not explain pale, cool, numb toes. These findings point to the blood and nerve supply.

options.text: Expected pain after a fracture
options.rationale: Some pain after a fracture is expected, but severe pain that does not ease, with numbness and pale toes, is not. Those added findings rule out a routine course.

options.text: Color and temperature of the right toes
options.rationale: Color and temperature show whether blood is reaching the toes. A change toward pink and warm, or toward pale and cold, tells the nurse which way the leg is going.

options.text: Strength of the left leg
options.rationale: The left leg is normal and serves as the comparison for the injured side. Tracking its strength does not show how the right leg is responding.

options.text: Sensation and movement of the right toes
options.rationale: Feeling and movement show whether the nerves of the leg are working. Their return or further loss guides how urgent the situation is.

options.text: Blood pressure in the left arm
options.rationale: Blood pressure shows overall circulation, but it does not show flow in the injured leg. A normal reading would not rule out a problem below the splint.

questions.takeaway: Red flags in an injured limb are reported at once, and the limb is rechecked against the other side for color, warmth, sensation and movement.
questions.strategy: Pain medicine and range of motion both sound like good care for a painful leg that will not move. Severe pain with numb, pale toes and lost movement is a warning sign, so the report cannot wait.

steps.detail: Pale, cool, numb, painful and not moving on one side.
Poor blood flow to the injured leg.
Report now and keep comparing with the other foot.
Color, warmth, feeling and movement of the right toes.

elimination.verdict: Report, recheck and compare; poor blood flow; watch color, warmth, sensation and movement.

questions.stem: In the clinic two days after a needle biopsy of the left hip bone, a patient has a site check. Which finding at the biopsy site does the nurse report to the provider?

options.text: Mild soreness rated 2 out of 10
options.rationale: Some tenderness after a needle biopsy is expected and can be eased with a mild pain reliever. Low, steady soreness alone is not a reason to call the provider.

options.text: Redness and warmth spreading around the site
options.rationale: After a bone biopsy the nurse watches for bleeding and for redness, warmth or tenderness that could mean infection. Spreading redness and warmth need to be reported.

options.text: A faint bruise under the clear dressing
options.rationale: A small bruise near a needle puncture is common after the procedure. It is not spreading redness and shows no active bleeding.

options.text: A small dry dressing that is intact
options.rationale: A dry, intact dressing shows no bleeding from the puncture site. It is the finding the nurse hopes to see.

questions.takeaway: After a biopsy, watch the site for bleeding and for redness, warmth or tenderness that signals infection.
questions.strategy: A bruise and soreness look worrying, but both are expected after a needle biopsy; spreading redness and warmth point to infection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bleeding and infection.
Only spreading redness and warmth fits either risk.
Mild soreness, a dry dressing and a faint bruise.

elimination.verdict: Spreading redness and warmth.

questions.stem: A postmenopausal patient learns from a DEXA scan that her bone density is low. She walks 30 minutes most days, takes calcium and vitamin D, and smokes half a pack of cigarettes a day. Which teaching point does the nurse add?

options.text: Swim laps in place of your walks to protect your bones
options.rationale: Swimming is good exercise, but the water carries the body's weight. Walking is weight bearing exercise that builds bone, so trading it away would weaken her plan.

options.text: Cut back on dairy foods so your joints stay healthy
options.rationale: Dairy foods supply calcium and vitamin D, which bones need. Cutting back would lower her intake and add to her bone loss rather than protect her joints.

options.text: Rest more and limit walking so you avoid a fracture
options.rationale: Fear of a fracture makes rest sound safe for fragile bones. Less activity speeds bone and muscle loss, and regular activity is how she maintains function over time.

options.text: Stop smoking, and ask about a program to help you quit
options.rationale: Tobacco speeds bone loss, and avoiding it is part of promoting musculoskeletal health. She already walks and takes calcium and vitamin D, so smoking is the gap left in her plan.

questions.takeaway: Promoting musculoskeletal health means regular and weight bearing activity, calcium and vitamin D, adequate nutrition, avoiding tobacco and limiting alcohol.
questions.strategy: Swimming and rest both sound gentle on fragile bones. Look at what she already does and pick the habit still missing from her plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Walking and calcium with vitamin D are in place.
Smoking is the remaining risk, and the other options would remove protective habits.

elimination.verdict: Stop smoking, and ask about a program to help you quit.

questions.stem: At a follow up visit, the nurse checks what a patient with osteopenia learned about keeping his bones and muscles healthy. Which statement shows that he needs more teaching?

options.text: "I switched to one drink on weekends instead of nightly."
options.rationale: Limiting excessive alcohol protects bone health. Cutting from nightly drinking to one drink on weekends shows he applied the teaching.

options.text: "I have milk or yogurt with breakfast and lunch."
options.rationale: Dairy foods provide calcium that bone needs to stay dense. Having them at two meals a day shows he understood the teaching about nutrition.

options.text: "I quit my daily walks and only do seated arm exercises."
options.rationale: Seated arm exercise keeps some muscle active, but it does not put weight through the hips, spine and legs. Stopping walking removes the weight bearing exercise that slows bone loss.

options.text: "I go outside in the sun and take my vitamin D."
options.rationale: Vitamin D helps the body absorb the calcium that bone needs. Sun exposure and his supplement show he is meeting the goal for appropriate vitamin D intake.

questions.takeaway: Weight bearing activity is the exercise that protects bone; replacing it with seated exercise is a gap to correct.
questions.strategy: Seated arm exercise sounds active and safe; the key word is weight bearing, which seated exercise is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is wrong.
Dairy, less alcohol and vitamin D all match.
No more weight bearing walks.

elimination.verdict: Quitting walks for seated exercise.

questions.stem: At urgent care, a patient who felt a sudden snap at the back of the left heel while sprinting for a bus cannot rise onto the toes of that foot. When she tries, the nurse feels the calf muscle tighten under her hand, but the heel does not lift. The nurse can move the foot through its full range, and the ankle does not slip, lock or catch. Which structure does the nurse suspect is injured?

options.text: The cartilage
options.rationale: Cartilage reduces friction inside the joint, and damage often causes locking or catching. Her ankle moves through its full range smoothly, which does not fit a cartilage injury.

options.text: A tendon
options.rationale: The calf muscle contracts, yet its pull never reaches the heel bone, and tendons connect muscle to bone. The ankle is stable and moves smoothly, so the break in the chain is the tendon.

options.text: The muscle
options.rationale: Weakness on rising to the toes does point toward the muscle at first. The nurse felt the calf tighten on command, so the muscle is working and its force is being lost further along.

options.text: A ligament
options.rationale: Ligaments connect bone to bone and keep a joint stable, so they are a common ankle injury. This ankle does not slip during full movement, which argues against a torn ligament.

questions.takeaway: When a muscle contracts but the bone does not move, and the joint is stable and smooth, the link between them, the tendon, is injured.
questions.strategy: Weakness makes the muscle the obvious answer. The nurse felt the muscle contract, so the problem lies between the muscle and the bone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It tightens on command, so it works.
Full ankle movement with no slipping or catching clears the ligament and cartilage.
Force from a working muscle that does not move the bone points to the tendon.

elimination.verdict: A tendon is the likely injury.

questions.stem: Three weeks into an intensive care stay for sepsis, a patient has been on bed rest the whole time and had no injury to either leg. Both legs have been equally still. Today the nurse finds the left thigh visibly thinner than the right, and the left leg pushes against her hand with less force. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Report the left thigh wasting
options.rationale: Bed rest affects both legs alike, so disuse should cause wasting on both sides. Wasting and weakness on one side after equal inactivity is unexpected and needs the provider's evaluation.

options.text: Measure both thighs again next week
options.rationale: Measuring both thighs gives a useful baseline for later comparison. Waiting a week delays evaluation of a one sided change that inactivity alone does not explain.

options.text: Begin strengthening exercises for both legs
options.rationale: Strengthening is the right response to disuse atrophy, which this long bed rest will cause. Inactivity cannot explain a difference between two legs that were equally still, so exercise comes after evaluation.

options.text: Document atrophy expected from bed rest
options.rationale: Muscle does shrink with inactivity, and three weeks of bed rest makes atrophy likely. Disuse atrophy is symmetric, though, and charting this one sided finding as expected misses a new problem.

questions.takeaway: Disuse atrophy follows the inactivity: equal inactivity should give equal wasting, so a one sided difference is reported.
questions.strategy: Strengthening fits the long bed rest and sounds proactive. The detail that both legs were equally still rules out disuse as the cause of a one sided difference.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Equal bed rest should cause equal atrophy.
Only the left thigh is thinner and weaker.
An unexplained one sided change is reported before any exercise plan.

elimination.verdict: Report the left thigh wasting.

questions.stem: For each clinical question, indicate the imaging test the nurse expects to be ordered.
questions.scenario: In an outpatient imaging center, the nurse reviews the reason for each patient's test before preparing them.

rows.text: A patient with back pain and leg weakness needs a view of the spinal structures and discs
rows.rationale: MRI shows spinal structures, discs and bone marrow in detail. An x ray would show the bones of the spine but not the soft structures around them.

rows.text: A patient treated for low bone density has a follow up to see whether density improved
rows.rationale: A DEXA scan is repeated to measure bone mineral density over time. It shows whether treatment is slowing or reversing bone loss.

rows.text: A postmenopausal patient with a thin build is being screened for osteoporosis
rows.rationale: A DEXA scan measures bone mineral density and is the common test for osteoporosis. It shows how dense the bone is before any fracture happens.

rows.text: A patient's finger is swollen and bent out of line after being caught in a door, and a fracture is suspected
rows.rationale: An x ray shows fractures, dislocations and alignment, and it is the first study when a broken bone is suspected. It is fast and shows bone clearly.

rows.text: A patient with hip stiffness for years is checked for joint wear
rows.rationale: An x ray shows degenerative changes in a joint, such as a narrowed joint space. It is the usual first look at a joint that has worn over time.

rows.text: A patient cannot raise the arm after a fall, and a torn shoulder tendon is suspected
rows.rationale: MRI is best for soft tissues such as tendons, ligaments, muscles and cartilage. A tendon tear does not show well on an x ray, which mainly shows bone.

questions.takeaway: X ray for bone injury, alignment and joint wear; MRI for soft tissue and the spine; DEXA for bone density.
questions.strategy: MRI sounds more advanced, so students over choose it; the clinical question decides the test, and suspected fractures start with an x ray.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what tissue is in question
steps.detail: Bone, soft tissue or bone density.
X ray.
MRI.
DEXA scan.

elimination.verdict: X ray, MRI, DEXA scan, x ray, MRI, DEXA scan.

questions.stem: On a medical unit, the nurse watches assistive personnel walk a patient admitted for dehydration. The patient has a rounded upper back, holds her head forward and walks with her feet set wide apart. Which action by the assistive personnel does the nurse correct?

options.text: Coaching her to place her feet closer together
options.rationale: A rounded upper back moves her center of gravity forward, and the wide stance widens her base of support to keep her balanced. Narrowing her steps removes that compensation and raises fall risk.

options.text: Letting her hold the hallway rail as she walks
options.rationale: Holding the rail can look like a habit that keeps her dependent. A shifted center of gravity raises fall risk, and the rail gives support, so this action is safe.

options.text: Having her use her walker in the hallway
options.rationale: A walker can seem unnecessary for a short walk on the unit. Kyphosis and a wide gait raise fall risk, and a device supports her mobility, so this action is correct.

options.text: Walking beside her at the pace she sets
options.rationale: A slow pace can look like the walk is not building strength. Rushing a patient whose balance is already shifted invites a fall, so letting her set the pace is correct.

questions.takeaway: A wide based gait with a rounded upper back is a compensation for a shifted center of gravity; support it rather than correct it.
questions.strategy: Coaching better posture sounds helpful and looks like good teaching. The wide stance is keeping her upright, so narrowing it is the unsafe action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The item asks for the action that is wrong.
A rounded upper back shifts the center of gravity forward.
The wide stance widens her base; narrowing it makes falling more likely.

elimination.verdict: Correct the coaching to bring her feet closer together.

questions.stem: In the same day surgery unit, an hour after arthroscopy of the right knee, a patient rates his knee pain 8 of 10, up from 3 of 10 in the recovery area, and asks for the prescribed analgesic. An ice pack and elevation are in place. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Teach the home exercises before discharge
options.rationale: Exercise teaching is part of preparing for discharge after arthroscopy. A patient with sudden severe pain cannot focus on teaching, and the limb needs assessment first.

options.text: Refill the ice pack and raise the leg higher
options.rationale: Ice and elevation are comfort measures after knee surgery. They treat the pain without explaining its sharp rise, and they delay finding a circulation or nerve problem.

options.text: Check pulses and sensation in the right foot
options.rationale: A sharp rise in pain after arthroscopy can signal a circulation or nerve problem in the limb. Checking the foot first shows whether the pain is a red flag that needs reporting.

options.text: Give the prescribed analgesic for the knee pain
options.rationale: Pain relief is needed and the analgesic is prescribed. Severe pain that rises sharply is a red flag, so the limb is checked before the drug masks a change.

questions.takeaway: After arthroscopy, a sudden rise in pain calls for a neurovascular check of the limb before the pain is treated.
questions.strategy: Giving the prescribed analgesic answers the patient's request and is a good action, but one step early. The sharp rise from 3 to 8 makes the pain a finding to assess first.

steps.detail: Pain rose sharply within an hour.
Severe pain is a red flag for circulation or nerve problems in the limb.
Check the foot, then give the analgesic.

elimination.verdict: Check the right foot first.

questions.stem: In a spine clinic, a patient reports a month of neck pain that shoots down the right arm, with tingling in the fingers. Neck x rays show only mild wear of the bones. The provider wants a detailed image to see whether the cushion between two neck bones is bulging onto a nerve. Which test does the nurse expect to be ordered?

options.text: Bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan looks for occult fractures, infection, tumors and increased bone activity. It shows bone metabolism, not a disc pressing on a nerve.

options.text: CT scan
options.rationale: CT gives more detailed images than an x ray, and the request for detail makes it tempting. Its strength is bone, as in complex fractures, while this question is about a disc and a nerve.

options.text: Ultrasound
options.rationale: Ultrasound does image some soft tissue, such as tendons, muscles and fluid collections, with no special preparation. It is not the test for spinal structures, so it cannot show a disc pressing on a nerve.

options.text: MRI
options.rationale: The cushion between neck bones is a disc, and discs and nerves are spinal soft tissue that MRI images best. It can show a disc pressing on a nerve that an x ray cannot.

questions.takeaway: MRI is the test for soft tissue and spinal structures such as discs and nerves; CT is for detailed bone images, and ultrasound for tendons, muscles and fluid.
questions.strategy: The request for a detailed image and the bone wear on x ray pull toward CT. The target is a disc and a nerve, which are spinal soft tissue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A disc and a nerve are soft tissue.
MRI images soft tissue best; CT images bone best.
Bone scan shows bone activity, and ultrasound is not used for spinal structures.

elimination.verdict: MRI is the expected test.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient admitted yesterday with a newly found cerebellar tumor. He is alert, oriented and follows commands. His grip is strong and equal in both hands. He asks to walk to the bathroom by himself for the first time. Which plan fits the part of the brain involved?

options.text: Let him go alone, since his grip strength is equal
options.rationale: Equal grip is a good motor finding, but grip tests hand strength rather than coordination. A cerebellar problem can leave strength normal while balance and steadiness on his feet are impaired.

options.text: Walk beside him and watch his gait and balance
options.rationale: The cerebellum controls balance and coordination, so strong grip and clear thinking do not show that he can walk safely. Walking beside him while watching his gait tests the function that is at risk.

options.text: Recheck his pupils before he gets out of bed
options.rationale: Pupil checks belong in his neurologic monitoring, but they say nothing about whether he can walk steadily. The risk this tumor creates is a fall from poor balance and coordination.

options.text: Ask him the date, the place and why he is here
options.rationale: Orientation tests awareness, which he has already shown is intact. Asking again adds nothing about the balance and coordination problem that a cerebellar tumor causes.

questions.takeaway: The cerebellum controls balance and coordination, so a patient with a cerebellar problem can have normal strength and thinking and still fall when walking.
questions.strategy: Equal grip strength is the reassuring distractor. What tips it is matching the plan to what the cerebellum does: balance and coordination.

steps.detail: The cerebellum handles balance and coordination.

steps.action: Match the check to the job
steps.detail: Grip, pupils and orientation test other functions.

steps.action: Choose the check that protects him
steps.detail: Watching his gait while beside him tests balance and prevents a fall.

elimination.verdict: Walk beside him and watch his gait and balance.

questions.stem: A patient with a brain abscess has become drowsy. Today's CT report states that new swelling around the abscess is pressing on the brainstem. Which assessment is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Light touch sensation on both forearms
options.rationale: A side to side sensory check belongs in a full exam and finds new sensory loss. It does not reach the breathing and circulation risk that brainstem pressure creates.

options.text: Orientation to person, place, time and situation
options.rationale: Orientation shows awareness, and drowsiness may change it. A confused patient who is breathing well is less urgent than one whose breathing may slow or stop from brainstem pressure.

options.text: Grip strength in both hands, compared side to side
options.rationale: Comparing grip is part of the motor check and may change later. It does not test the vital functions the brainstem controls, which are the ones that fail first with pressure there.

options.text: Breathing pattern, heart rate and blood pressure
options.rationale: The brainstem controls vital functions such as breathing and heart rate, so pressure on it threatens those first. Checking breathing and circulation also follows the ABCs for a patient who is getting drowsy.

questions.takeaway: The brainstem controls vital functions, so pressure on it makes breathing and circulation the first things the nurse checks.
questions.strategy: Every option is a real neurologic check. The CT names the brainstem, and the brainstem runs breathing and heart rate, which also wins under the ABCs.

steps.detail: The brainstem controls vital functions.
Breathing and circulation come before grip, orientation or touch.

elimination.verdict: Breathing pattern, heart rate and blood pressure.

questions.objective: Describe the basic nervous system organization and function

questions.stem: A patient with a herniated disc compressing a spinal nerve in his lower back cannot feel light touch, pain or temperature on the top of his right foot. He moves the right foot and ankle with full strength, equal to the left. Which plan fits these findings?

options.text: Report a new brain problem, since sensation is interpreted in the brain
options.rationale: Sensation is interpreted in the brain, but the compressed spinal nerve belongs to the peripheral nervous system. The loss matches that nerve's area on one foot, which the known disc compression explains.

options.text: Teach him to warm the foot with a heating pad when it feels numb
options.rationale: Warmth may feel comforting, but he cannot sense temperature on that skin and could be burned without knowing. Heat on a foot without sensation is a safety hazard rather than a treatment.

options.text: Check bath water temperature for him and inspect the foot each shift
options.rationale: Signals carrying sensation toward the central nervous system are blocked, so he cannot feel heat or injury on that skin. Testing the water for him and inspecting the foot protect the area he cannot feel.

options.text: Use a gait belt because the nerve to his foot muscles is damaged
options.rationale: A gait belt fits leg weakness, but his strength is full and equal on both sides. The pathway carrying signals out to his muscles is working; only the sensory pathway is affected.

questions.takeaway: Spinal nerves are part of the PNS; when one loses its afferent signals, sensation goes while strength stays, so the nurse protects the skin the patient cannot feel.
questions.strategy: The gait belt is the trap for students who see a nerve injury and think weakness. His strength is full; the only loss is feeling, so the plan protects the skin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Feeling lost, strength full and equal.
A spinal nerve is peripheral, not brain.
Heat is the hazard, so the nurse checks the water and the skin.

elimination.verdict: Check bath water temperature for him and inspect the foot each shift.

questions.objective: Differentiate CNS, PNS, and autonomic nervous system
questions.concept: PNS spinal nerve: afferent loss with intact strength

questions.scenario: During morning assessments, the nurse checks several patients who have nerve injuries in the arms or legs. Each finding below is new since the injury.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it shows a problem in an afferent pathway or an efferent pathway.

rows.text: Cannot tell whether bath water on the right forearm is warm or cold
rows.rationale: Telling warm from cold depends on signals carried from the skin toward the central nervous system. Losing that ability leaves the forearm open to a burn the patient will not feel.

rows.text: Feels the nurse's touch on the right hand normally but cannot lift the right wrist
rows.rationale: Touch reaches the central nervous system, so the incoming pathway is intact. The wrist cannot lift because signals traveling away from the central nervous system to the muscle are blocked.

rows.text: Grip in the left hand is weak, although touch on the palm feels normal
rows.rationale: Normal touch on the palm shows the sensory pathway is working. A weak grip means the signals sent outward from the central nervous system to the hand muscles are impaired.

rows.text: Left foot drags while walking, although she feels the floor under it
rows.rationale: She feels the floor, so sensory signals are arriving. The foot drags because commands leaving the central nervous system are not reaching the muscles that lift it.

rows.text: Does not notice a blister forming on the left heel
rows.rationale: A blister normally hurts enough that a patient mentions it. Not noticing one means pain signals from the heel are not traveling toward the central nervous system.

rows.text: Cannot feel a pinprick on the left shin but kicks the left leg with full strength
rows.rationale: The leg muscles respond normally, so signals going out to them are working. The missing feeling means signals traveling from the shin toward the central nervous system are not getting through.

questions.takeaway: Afferent pathways carry signals toward the CNS, so their loss shows up as lost feeling; efferent pathways carry signals away to muscles and organs, so their loss shows up as lost movement.
questions.strategy: Most rows pair something that works with something that does not. Decide which half failed: lost feeling points afferent, lost movement points efferent.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the failed function in each row
steps.detail: Feeling lost or movement lost.
Toward the CNS is afferent; away to muscles is efferent.

elimination.verdict: Afferent for the shin, blister and bath water rows; efferent for the wrist, foot drag and grip rows.

questions.objective: Describe the basic nervous system organization and function

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient awaiting a knee replacement who was frightened this morning; her heart rate was 108 per minute and her pupils were wide. After the anesthesia team answers her questions, she eats lunch and naps. Which finding shows that her parasympathetic response is now dominant?

options.text: Heart rate 64 per minute with active bowel sounds
options.rationale: A slower heart rate and active digestion are both rest and digest effects. Seeing them together after a meal and a nap shows the parasympathetic system has taken over from the morning stress response.

options.text: Blood glucose higher than her morning value
options.rationale: Raising blood glucose is how the fight or flight response mobilizes energy for the muscles. A rising value points toward sympathetic activity, not toward the energy conserving parasympathetic response.

options.text: Pupils wide and equal while she rests quietly
options.rationale: Resting quietly fits rest and digest, but the pupils tell a different story. Dilated pupils are a fight or flight effect, so they show the sympathetic system is still active.

options.text: Heart rate 104 per minute with a relaxed expression
options.rationale: A relaxed face suggests her fear has eased, which is tempting. Her heart rate is still nearly as fast as this morning, so the sympathetic response has not yet settled.

questions.takeaway: Parasympathetic means rest and digest: a slower heart rate, active digestion and conserved energy; a fast heart rate, wide pupils and rising glucose still mean fight or flight.
questions.strategy: A calm face or quiet rest can look like rest and digest. Check every body effect in the option, because one sympathetic effect rules the whole option out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Slow heart and digestion are parasympathetic; fast heart, wide pupils and rising glucose are sympathetic.
A relaxed face does not cancel a heart rate of 104 per minute.

elimination.verdict: Heart rate 64 per minute with active bowel sounds.

questions.objective: Differentiate CNS, PNS, and autonomic nervous system

questions.stem: In the emergency department, a patient with a kidney stone rates his pain 9 of 10 and says he is scared. His heart rate is 116 per minute, up from 78 an hour ago. His pupils are 5 mm, equal and brisk, up from 3 mm. He is alert, oriented and follows commands. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Record the findings as normal and continue routine checks
options.rationale: The findings likely reflect stress, but a heart rate of 116 per minute with pain of 9 of 10 still calls for action. Recording and moving on leaves the cause untreated and the explanation unconfirmed.

options.text: Treat his pain and fear, then recheck heart rate and pupils
options.rationale: Equal, brisk pupils and a faster heart rate during severe pain and fear fit the fight or flight response. Relieving the stressor and then rechecking confirms that cause rather than assuming it.

options.text: Begin Glasgow Coma Scale checks every 15 minutes
options.rationale: Frequent coma scale scoring fits a patient whose consciousness is changing. He is alert, oriented and follows commands, so these checks add work without treating the cause of his findings.

options.text: Call a rapid response for the change in his pupil size
options.rationale: A change in pupils from baseline does deserve attention. Here both widened equally, react briskly and stay within 2 to 6 mm while he is fully alert, which points to stress rather than brain injury.

questions.takeaway: Pain and fear trigger the sympathetic response: a faster heart and equally dilated, brisk pupils in an alert patient. Treat the stressor and recheck before calling it a neurologic emergency.
questions.strategy: Dilated pupils pull toward the neuro emergency. What tips it is that both pupils changed together, still react briskly, and he is fully alert during severe pain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Check the pupils against danger signs
steps.detail: Equal, brisk and in range; nothing one sided or sluggish.
Alert, oriented and following commands.
Pain of 9 of 10 and fear explain fight or flight.

elimination.verdict: Treat his pain and fear, then recheck heart rate and pupils.

questions.objective: Differentiate CNS, PNS, and autonomic nervous system

questions.stem: The nurse admits a patient with a seizure disorder to the unit. No neurologic findings have been recorded for her during this hospital stay. She is awake and talking with her husband. Which assessment does the nurse perform?

options.text: No neurologic exam until a seizure or a change occurs
options.rationale: Waiting for a seizure removes the comparison that makes a change visible. Setting a baseline at admission is what lets the nurse detect a change later in the stay.

options.text: A pupil check, followed by a full exam if her pupils are unequal
options.rationale: Pupils are part of the exam, but checking one area first assumes a problem must appear before the rest is done. She has no baseline at all, so the full exam comes first.

options.text: A focused check of the functions linked to her seizures
options.rationale: A focused assessment targets a suspected problem or a change from baseline. She has no recorded baseline yet, so there is nothing for a focused check to be compared against.

options.text: A complete neurologic exam to set her baseline
options.rationale: A comprehensive assessment is the broad baseline exam used for new admissions and neurologic concerns. Without a baseline, any later change in her findings cannot be recognized as a change.

questions.takeaway: New admissions and neurologic concerns get a comprehensive baseline exam; focused exams come later, to follow a known condition or a change from that baseline.
questions.strategy: The focused check sounds efficient for a known seizure disorder. What tips it is that no baseline exists yet, and a focused check needs one to compare against.

steps.detail: None has been recorded.

steps.action: Match the exam to the moment
steps.detail: New admission means comprehensive.

elimination.verdict: A complete neurologic exam to set her baseline.

questions.objective: Perform a focused neurologic assessment

questions.stem: Two days after neck surgery, a patient whose complete neurologic exam was recorded at admission says this morning that her left hand feels numb and weaker than it did yesterday. Which assessment does the nurse perform now?

options.text: Compare sensation and grip in both hands with baseline
options.rationale: A focused assessment targets the suspected problem once a change from baseline is reported. Comparing her hands side to side and against the admission exam shows how much has changed.

options.text: Reassure her that numbness is common while the incision heals
options.rationale: Some symptoms are expected after surgery, but a new change in feeling and strength is a neurologic cue. Reassuring her before assessing skips the step that shows whether it is serious.

options.text: Check her left hand only and record what she reports
options.rationale: Checking the hand she reports is a start, but without the right hand there is nothing to compare it with. Strength and sensation are always compared right with left.

options.text: Repeat the full admission neurologic exam before reporting anything
options.rationale: A full exam was right at admission to set the baseline. Now a specific change is reported, so a targeted check gets the needed findings faster without delaying the report.

questions.takeaway: Once a baseline exists, a reported change gets a focused assessment of that area, compared right with left and against the baseline.
questions.strategy: The full exam looks thorough. What tips it is that a baseline already exists and the change is specific, so a targeted comparison answers the question fastest.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A complete baseline is on record.
Left hand numbness and weakness.
Both hands, and against admission.

elimination.verdict: Compare sensation and grip in both hands with baseline.

questions.objective: Perform a focused neurologic assessment

questions.stem: A patient admitted with a concussion after a car crash asks the nurse the same questions about his injury every few minutes. The nurse wants to assess his memory of recent events. Which request does the nurse use?

options.text: Count backward from 100 by 7s
options.rationale: Counting backward by 7s is a common mental status task. It tests attention and calculation, so he could do it well and still have no memory of recent events.

options.text: Tell me how you came to the hospital
options.rationale: Describing how he arrived requires him to recall recent events, which tests memory directly. The nurse can compare his account with what is already known about the crash.

options.text: Copy this word onto the paper
options.rationale: Copying a word checks that he can see, follow an instruction and write. It does not require him to remember anything, so it cannot show a memory problem.

options.text: Explain what the saying 'better late than never' means
options.rationale: Explaining a saying tests abstract thinking. A patient can explain a familiar saying well and still be unable to recall anything that happened today.

questions.takeaway: To test recent memory, ask the patient to recall recent events, such as how he came to the hospital; calculation and abstract thinking tasks test other functions.
questions.strategy: Counting backward by 7s feels like the classic brain test. What tips it is asking which task needs him to remember something that happened recently.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Calculation, abstract thinking, copying, recall.

steps.action: Keep the one that needs recall
steps.detail: Only describing his arrival requires memory.

elimination.verdict: Tell me how you came to the hospital.

questions.objective: Perform a focused neurologic assessment

questions.stem: After a procedure done with sedation, a patient returns to the unit. The nurse assesses his level of consciousness. Which actions belong in this assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask him to squeeze the nurse's hand and then let go
options.rationale: Command following is the third part of level of consciousness. A simple two part command shows whether he can take in an instruction and act on it.

options.text: Measure his blood pressure and heart rate
options.rationale: Vital signs matter after sedation, but they are not part of judging level of consciousness. An alert patient and a drowsy one can have the same blood pressure.

options.text: Ask him what is happening to him today
options.rationale: Awareness asks whether he understands what is happening around him. Asking about today's events shows whether he grasps his situation after sedation, not just whether his eyes are open.

options.text: Check his pupils for size and reaction to light
options.rationale: Pupil checks are part of a neurologic assessment, but they test cranial nerve function. Level of consciousness is judged by alertness, awareness and command following.

options.text: Note whether he wakes when his name is spoken
options.rationale: Alertness is the first part of level of consciousness: is he awake and responsive to stimulation. Waking to his name shows how much stimulation he needs to respond.

options.text: Compare light touch on both of his forearms
options.rationale: Comparing touch side to side belongs in the sensory assessment. It shows whether feeling is equal, not how awake or aware he is.

questions.takeaway: Level of consciousness has three parts: alertness, awareness and command following. Pupils, sensation and vital signs are assessed too, but they are not LOC.
questions.strategy: Everything listed belongs somewhere in post sedation care. Ask which item tells how awake he is, how aware he is, or whether he can follow a command.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Alertness, awareness, command following.
Name, today's events and hand squeeze fit; pupils, touch and vitals do not.

elimination.verdict: Waking to his name, asking about today, and the hand squeeze command.

questions.objective: Assess level of consciousness, language, speech, movement, and sensation
questions.concept: LOC components: alertness, awareness, command following

questions.stem: On a medical unit, the nurse checks four patients who were all alert and oriented at the start of the shift. Which patient's finding shows a decline in level of consciousness?

options.text: Is wide awake and chatting but says the year is 2019
options.rationale: Saying the wrong year is a change in orientation that also needs follow up. She is fully awake, though, and level of consciousness asks how awake a patient is.

options.text: Is awake and asks for his glasses so he can read the menu
options.rationale: Asking for glasses is an ordinary request from an awake patient who knows what he wants to do. It shows alertness and awareness rather than any decline.

options.text: Wakes only to a loud voice and shaking, then drifts off
options.rationale: Level of consciousness describes how awake a patient is, and needing a loud voice and touch to rouse him is a clear drop in alertness. Difficulty staying aroused is a change that needs assessment now.

options.text: Is awake and calm but has forgotten the nurse's name from this morning
options.rationale: Forgetting the name of someone met hours earlier is common in awake, oriented people. It says nothing about how awake she is and is not a change in consciousness.

questions.takeaway: Level of consciousness asks how awake the patient is; orientation asks whether the patient knows person, place, time and situation. A patient can be awake but disoriented.
questions.strategy: The wrong year is a real change and pulls students in. What tips it is the question's term: level of consciousness means how awake, and she is wide awake.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Define the term in the stem
steps.detail: Level of consciousness means how awake.
Disoriented but awake is orientation, not consciousness.
Only one patient is hard to keep awake.

elimination.verdict: Wakes only to a loud voice and shaking, then drifts off.

questions.objective: Assess level of consciousness, language, speech, movement, and sensation

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient who had a stroke 2 days ago and has new slurred, garbled speech. He points to the correct object when the nurse names it, follows a two step command and writes his daughter's name correctly. Which communication approach fits these findings?

options.text: Speak louder and more slowly so that he can hear the words
options.rationale: Raising the voice helps a hearing problem. He follows spoken commands, so hearing and understanding are fine; his difficulty is forming the words.

options.text: Ask only yes or no questions and discourage writing
options.rationale: Yes or no questions can save effort for some patients. Discouraging writing removes the tool he uses best, because his written language is intact.

options.text: Give him extra time and offer a pen and paper
options.rationale: He understands and uses words, so language is intact; his problem is producing speech, which is a motor function. Extra time and writing let him use the language skills he still has.

options.text: Use pictures and gestures, since he cannot understand words
options.rationale: Pictures and gestures help a patient who cannot understand words. He points to named objects and follows a two step command, so his understanding is intact.

questions.takeaway: Speech is the physical production of words, a motor function; language is understanding and using words, a cognitive function. A patient with only a speech problem can still understand and write.
questions.strategy: Pictures and gestures are the usual stroke communication tip. What tips it is that he understands everything and writes well, so only the motor act of speaking is affected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He points to objects and follows commands.
He writes a name correctly.
Only speech production, a motor problem.

elimination.verdict: Give him extra time and offer a pen and paper.

questions.objective: Assess level of consciousness, language, speech, movement, and sensation

questions.stem: A patient admitted with encephalitis speaks clearly and at a normal rate, but many of her words are the wrong ones. When the nurse says 'raise your right arm,' she smiles and nods without moving. Her arm strength is equal on both sides. How does the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: A new problem with language
options.rationale: Language is the cognitive ability to understand and use words. Clear speech full of wrong words, plus a command she does not follow despite normal strength, points to language rather than a motor problem.

options.text: A new problem with speech
options.rationale: A speech problem is a motor problem in forming words, so words sound slurred or garbled. Her words come out clearly and at a normal rate, so speech production is working.

options.text: Weakness of the right arm
options.rationale: Weakness could explain an arm that does not rise. Her strength is equal on both sides, so the unfollowed command comes from not understanding it.

options.text: Drowsiness from her infection
options.rationale: Drowsiness would lower her alertness and slow her answers. She is awake, smiling and talking at a normal rate, so how awake she is does not explain the findings.

questions.takeaway: Clear, normal rate words that are the wrong words, with trouble understanding commands, mean a language problem; slurred or garbled words with intact understanding mean a speech problem.
questions.strategy: Students hear a talking problem and pick speech. What tips it is that her words come out clearly; the trouble is choosing and understanding them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear words at a normal rate, so speech works.
She cannot follow a simple command.
Strength is equal.

elimination.verdict: A new problem with language.

questions.objective: Assess level of consciousness, language, speech, movement, and sensation

questions.stem: At an outpatient oncology visit, a patient receiving chemotherapy for colon cancer says his feet have felt 'different' for about a month. The nurse plans a sensory assessment of his legs and feet. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Test light touch on both legs and leave pain and temperature for later
options.rationale: Light touch is one part of the exam. Pain and temperature are also tested, and losing them is what puts his feet at risk of an injury he does not feel.

options.text: Test matching spots on both legs and ask if they feel the same
options.rationale: Sensory findings are always compared right with left, using the same spot on each side. Asking whether they feel the same shows any difference between sides, which is the finding to report.

options.text: Test only the foot that he says feels different
options.rationale: Starting with the foot he mentions is reasonable, but testing it alone gives no comparison. A loss shows up as a difference between sides, so both sides are tested.

options.text: Ask whether his feet feel numb and record his answer
options.rationale: His own description is useful history, but it is not an assessment of sensation. The nurse tests touch, pain and temperature directly and compares the sides rather than relying on his report.

questions.takeaway: Assess touch, pain and temperature, and always compare right with left by asking whether it feels the same on both sides.
questions.strategy: Testing the foot he complains about seems focused and efficient. What tips it is that a sensory finding only means something when compared with the other side.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only one option tests both sides.
Touch, pain and temperature are all tested.

steps.action: Reject report in place of testing
steps.detail: Asking is history, not assessment.

elimination.verdict: Test matching spots on both legs and ask if they feel the same.

questions.objective: Assess level of consciousness, language, speech, movement, and sensation

questions.stem: While the nurse assesses an 84 year old patient admitted for a urinary tract infection, the patient says light touch feels duller on her left forearm than on her right. Six months ago, sensation was recorded as equal on both sides. Her daughter says numbness comes with age. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Teach her to protect the left arm from heat and pressure
options.rationale: Protecting skin with less feeling is a useful later step. Teaching first treats the finding as settled before the nurse has assessed it or reported the change.

options.text: Recheck both forearms at the next scheduled assessment
options.rationale: Rechecking is part of good monitoring, but waiting leaves a new neurologic change unreported. The difference between sides is a cue that needs assessment and a report now.

options.text: Agree with the daughter and record it as expected aging
options.rationale: Aging does decrease sensitivity to touch, which makes the daughter's view tempting. Aging changes do not explain a new difference between her two arms, so it is not assumed to be age.

options.text: Assess both arms further and report the new difference
options.rationale: A difference between sides that was not there six months ago is a new sensory change, which is documented and reported. A new change is never assumed to be aging before it has been assessed.

questions.takeaway: Do not assume a new neurologic change is due to aging: a new difference between sides is assessed and reported.
