questions.strategy: Decreased touch sensation is a real aging change, so the daughter sounds right. What tips it is that the loss is on one side only and is new since the last record.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Equal six months ago, unequal now.
Aging does not create a one sided difference.
Find out more and report.

elimination.verdict: Assess both arms further and report the new difference.

questions.objective: Assess level of consciousness, language, speech, movement, and sensation

questions.stem: An 81 year old patient on the orthopedic unit is 2 days after surgery to repair a hip fracture. The nurse compares today's motor findings with the admission record. Which findings does the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.

options.text: Slow, steady walking with a walker, as therapy taught
options.rationale: Slow walking with a walker is expected 2 days after hip surgery. Steady use of the device as taught shows safe mobility rather than a new neurologic problem.

options.text: Left hand grip weaker than the right, first noted today
options.rationale: Hand strength is always compared right with left, and new asymmetry is a sign of neurologic dysfunction. Being first noted today means it differs from her baseline and needs to be reported.

options.text: A slight head tremor, recorded at admission and unchanged
options.rationale: A tremor is worth noting, but this one was recorded at admission and has not changed. An unchanged finding is part of her baseline rather than a new cue.

options.text: Right hand shaking at rest that began this morning
options.rationale: A tremor is one of the findings the motor exam looks for. This one is new since this morning, so it is a change from her baseline that the provider needs to know about.

options.text: Left arm cannot be raised as high as the right, first noted today
options.rationale: Movement is compared right with left, and the two arms now move unequally. A new difference between sides is a neurologic change that is reported, not explained away by surgery or age.

options.text: Slower movements than a younger adult, as at admission
options.rationale: Slower movement is an expected change with aging. It matches her admission record, so it is part of her baseline rather than a new finding to report.

questions.takeaway: Motor findings are compared right with left and against baseline; new asymmetry or a new tremor is reported, while slower movement with aging and unchanged findings are not new cues.
questions.strategy: Several findings are abnormal for a young adult. What tips each one is whether it is new since admission or different between the two sides.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The head tremor and slowness were already there.
Grip and arm lift now differ left from right.
Slow walking with a walker is expected.

elimination.verdict: The weaker left grip, the new right hand tremor and the left arm that cannot rise as high.

questions.objective: Assess level of consciousness, language, speech, movement, and sensation
questions.concept: Motor assessment: compare right vs left

questions.stem: A patient with an ear infection that has spread to the bone behind his right ear says that water dribbles out of the right side of his mouth when he drinks. Which assessment does the nurse perform next?

options.text: Ask him to stick out his tongue and move it side to side
options.rationale: Tongue movement tests CN XII, the hypoglossal nerve. His problem is liquid leaking from one corner of the mouth, which points to weak facial muscles rather than the tongue.

options.text: Ask him to follow the nurse's finger with his eyes
options.rationale: Following a finger tests the nerves for eye movement, CN III, IV and VI. Those nerves do not control the lips and cheeks that keep water in his mouth.

options.text: Ask him to shrug his shoulders against the nurse's hands
options.rationale: A shoulder shrug tests CN XI, the accessory nerve. That nerve moves the shoulders and head, not the muscles that close the lips around a cup.

options.text: Ask him to smile, raise his eyebrows and show his teeth
options.rationale: Dribbling from one side of the mouth suggests weakness of the facial nerve, CN VII, which controls facial expression. Smiling, raising the eyebrows and showing the teeth let the nurse compare the two sides.

questions.takeaway: CN VII controls facial expression; the nurse checks it by having the patient smile, raise the eyebrows and show the teeth while watching for drooping or asymmetry.
questions.strategy: The tongue option is tempting because drinking involves the mouth. What tips it is that the leak comes from a weak corner of the lips, which the facial nerve controls.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Name the nerve behind each test
steps.detail: Shrug is XI, tongue is XII, eye tracking is III, IV and VI.
One sided lip weakness is facial expression, CN VII.

elimination.verdict: Ask him to smile, raise his eyebrows and show his teeth.

questions.objective: Identify basic cranial nerve assessment findings

questions.stem: Following thyroid surgery, a patient who is NPO says it feels hard to swallow his saliva. Assistive personnel offer to give him a few sips of water to see whether he coughs. Which response by the nurse is correct?

options.text: Give him ice chips instead, since they melt in such small amounts
options.rationale: Ice chips seem harmless because each one melts into only a little water, but they still put fluid in his throat. The order is NPO, and his swallowing complaint raises the risk of aspiration.

options.text: Do not give water; keep him NPO while I assess this
options.rationale: Swallowing, controlled by CN IX and X, is not tested in a patient who is NPO. His reported difficulty also signals aspiration risk, so the nurse assesses further and reports it.

options.text: Give the sips while I stay with him and watch for coughing
options.rationale: Watching for coughing is how swallowing is observed when testing is clinically appropriate. It is not appropriate here, because he is NPO and already reports difficulty.

options.text: Give the sips with the head of the bed raised
options.rationale: Raising the head of the bed does lower aspiration risk when a patient eats or drinks. Swallowing is not tested in a patient who is NPO, so no sips are given in any position.

questions.takeaway: Swallowing (CN IX and X) is observed only when clinically appropriate and never tested in a patient who is NPO; a reported swallowing problem is an aspiration risk to report.
questions.strategy: Watching him closely while he sips sounds safe. What tips it is the NPO order: no intake means no swallow test, however carefully it is done.

steps.detail: NPO means nothing by mouth, ice chips included.

steps.action: Cut every option that gives fluid
steps.detail: Three options still put fluid in his throat.
Assess and report the swallowing difficulty.

elimination.verdict: Do not give water; keep him NPO while I assess this.

questions.objective: Identify basic cranial nerve assessment findings
questions.concept: Swallowing CN IX and X: not tested if NPO

questions.stem: The nurse is monitoring a patient with a subdural hematoma whose pupils were 3 mm, equal and brisk at 1400. At 1600 his right pupil is 3 mm and brisk, and his left pupil is 5 mm and sluggish. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Complete a neurologic check and notify the provider now
options.rationale: One pupil getting larger and slower while the other stays the same is a change from his baseline, and changes from baseline matter most. He needs a full neurologic check and a report now.

options.text: Dim the room lights and recheck in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Room lighting changes pupil size, but it changes both pupils together. One pupil enlarging and slowing while the other stays brisk is not a lighting effect, and waiting delays action.

options.text: Recheck both pupils at the next scheduled check
options.rationale: Rechecking on schedule fits findings that are stable. This is a new change from baseline in a patient with bleeding around the brain, so waiting delays needed action.

options.text: Record that both pupils are within the 2 to 6 mm range
options.rationale: Both sizes do fall within 2 to 6 mm, which makes recording them tempting. The pupils are now unequal and one reacts slowly, and that change from baseline matters more than the range.

questions.takeaway: Pupils should be equal, round and reactive; a new difference in size or reaction from the patient's baseline needs a neurologic check and a report, even within 2 to 6 mm.
questions.strategy: The normal range misleads, because both numbers are in it. What tips it is that the pupils were equal and brisk two hours ago and now are not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Equal and brisk at 1400; unequal and sluggish at 1600.
Change from baseline outranks the normal range.
A new change needs action now.

elimination.verdict: Complete a neurologic check and notify the provider now.

questions.objective: Identify basic cranial nerve assessment findings

questions.stem: A newly graduated nurse wants to call a rapid response for an 86 year old patient admitted for dehydration. She is alert and oriented. Her pupils are 3 mm, equal and slow to react to light in both eyes, recorded the same way at admission 2 days ago. Which guidance is best?

options.text: Recheck her pupils every 15 minutes for the next hour
options.rationale: Frequent checks fit a pupil that has just changed. Hers are equal and unchanged for 2 days while she stays alert, so extra checks add nothing.

options.text: Call the rapid response, since sluggish pupils signal brain injury
options.rationale: Sluggish pupils can be a serious sign when they are new or one sided. Hers are equal, unchanged in 2 days and explained by aging, so they are her baseline.

options.text: This matches her baseline; continue routine pupil checks
options.rationale: Pupils react more slowly to light with aging, and hers are equal, unchanged since admission and paired with normal alertness. A finding that matches the baseline is monitored, not escalated.

options.text: Notify the provider, because a slow reaction is never normal
options.rationale: A slow reaction would concern the nurse in a younger adult or if it were new. Slower pupil reaction is an expected change with aging, so it is not abnormal for her.

questions.takeaway: Pupils react more slowly with aging; an equal, unchanged finding that matches baseline is monitored, while a new or one sided change is escalated.
questions.strategy: Sluggish pupils are a classic danger sign, so calling for help feels safe. What tips it is that both pupils are equal, nothing has changed since admission, and she is alert.

steps.detail: Same as admission 2 days ago.
Pupils react more slowly in older adults.
A slow reaction is not always abnormal.

elimination.verdict: This matches her baseline; continue routine pupil checks.

questions.objective: Identify basic cranial nerve assessment findings

questions.stem: In the emergency department, a patient brought in after an assault opens her eyes when her name is called. She says random words that do not answer the nurse's questions. When pressure is applied to her nail bed, she reaches across with her other hand to push the nurse's hand away. Which Glasgow Coma Scale total does the nurse record?

options.rationale: This total scores her motor response as withdrawal, which is 4. Reaching across to push the stimulus away is localizing, which scores 5, so the total is one point higher.
Opening to voice scores 3, words that do not answer questions score 3, and pushing the stimulus away is localizing, which scores 5. The total is 11 on a scale of 3 to 15.
This total scores her verbal response as confused, which is 4. She gives only random words that do not answer the questions, which scores 3.
This is the total for opening to voice, confused speech and obeying commands. She uses random words rather than confused sentences, and she localizes rather than obeys.

questions.takeaway: GCS adds eye opening (1 to 4), verbal response (1 to 5) and motor response (1 to 6) for a total of 3 to 15; reaching to push a stimulus away is localizing, scored 5.
questions.strategy: Withdrawal and localizing are the common mix up. Pulling away from pain is withdrawal; reaching toward the stimulus to remove it is localizing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Opens to her name: 3.
Random words: 3.
Reaches to push the hand away: localizes, 5.

questions.objective: Explain the purpose of the Glasgow Coma Scale

questions.scenario: On a neurology unit, the nurse performs cranial nerve checks on several patients. Each finding below is new.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate which cranial nerve the nurse documents as affected.

rows.text: Voice is hoarse and he coughs each time he swallows
rows.rationale: Voice and swallowing are functions of CN IX and X. Coughing with each swallow suggests food or fluid entering the airway, which is an aspiration risk.

rows.text: Right corner of his mouth droops when he smiles
rows.rationale: Smiling tests the muscles of facial expression supplied by CN VII. A droop on one side of the mouth is a facial nerve finding, so the two sides are compared and reported.

rows.text: Left forehead does not wrinkle when she raises her eyebrows
rows.rationale: Raising the eyebrows tests facial expression, which the facial nerve controls. A forehead that moves on one side only is the asymmetry the nurse documents for CN VII.

rows.text: Right upper eyelid droops and he cannot fully raise it
rows.rationale: Eyelid elevation is one of the oculomotor nerve's jobs. A new droop of one upper eyelid that he cannot lift points to CN III.

rows.text: Left pupil stays large when a light is shone into it
rows.rationale: Pupil constriction is controlled by the oculomotor nerve. A pupil that does not get smaller in light shows that CN III on that side is not working normally.

rows.text: No gag when the back of her throat is touched
rows.rationale: The gag reflex depends on the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves. Losing it also raises the risk of aspiration, so the nurse documents and reports it promptly.

questions.takeaway: CN III raises the eyelid, constricts the pupil and moves the eye; CN VII controls facial expression; CN IX and X handle the gag reflex, swallowing and voice.
questions.strategy: Eyelid and forehead findings both involve the area around the eye, which mixes students up. Raising the lid is CN III; wrinkling the forehead is facial expression, CN VII.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lid elevation and pupil constriction belong to CN III.
Forehead and smile asymmetry belong to CN VII.
Gag, voice and swallowing belong to CN IX and X.

elimination.verdict: CN III for the eyelid and pupil, CN VII for the forehead and mouth, CN IX and X for the gag and the hoarse voice.

questions.objective: Identify basic cranial nerve assessment findings

questions.stem: A patient with a skull fracture had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14 at 1400 and 14 at 1500. At 1600 his score is 12. His next check is due at 1700. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Complete a full neurologic check now and notify the provider
options.rationale: A declining score signals deterioration, and a drop from 14 to 12 in one hour is a decline. It needs immediate assessment and a report rather than another scheduled check.

options.text: Reorient him to place and time every hour
options.rationale: Reorienting can help a confused patient feel secure. It does not find or treat the cause of a falling score, which needs assessment and a report now.

options.text: Recheck the score at 1700 as scheduled
options.rationale: Scheduled checks fit a stable score. His score has fallen since the last check, and waiting an hour lets a deteriorating patient go unassessed and unreported.

options.text: Record the score, since a 2 point drop is small
options.rationale: Two points can sound minor on a 3 to 15 scale. The trend matters more than the size of one score, and a falling score is exactly the change that requires immediate action.

questions.takeaway: Trend over time is the point of the GCS: a declining score signals deterioration and requires immediate action, even if the drop is small.
questions.strategy: A score of 12 still looks fairly good, which invites waiting. What tips it is the direction: 14, 14, then 12 means he is getting worse.

steps.detail: Stable twice, then down 2 points.
A declining score requires immediate action.
Neither assesses the decline.

elimination.verdict: Complete a full neurologic check now and notify the provider.

questions.objective: Explain the purpose of the Glasgow Coma Scale

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on two patients. One, with an anoxic brain injury after a cardiac arrest, has scored 9 on the Glasgow Coma Scale at every check for 2 days. The other, admitted after a bicycle crash, scored 15 an hour ago and now scores 13. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: The patient with the anoxic injury, because 9 is the lower score
options.rationale: A lower score is worse, which makes this choice tempting. A score of 9 that has not changed for 2 days is that patient's known state, while the other score is falling now.

options.text: The patient from the bicycle crash, after the other patient's routine check
options.rationale: This is the right patient at the wrong time. A falling score signals deterioration and needs assessment now, not after a routine task for a stable patient.

options.text: The patient from the bicycle crash, because his score is falling
options.rationale: A drop from 15 to 13 in one hour is a declining trend, which signals deterioration and requires immediate action. A score that is changing outranks a lower score that is stable.

options.text: The patient with the anoxic injury, because 9 means deep coma
options.rationale: Deep coma is a score of 3, the bottom of the scale. A score of 9 is serious, but it has stayed the same for 2 days and signals no new deterioration.

questions.takeaway: Prioritize the patient whose GCS is changing: a declining trend outranks a lower score that has been stable.
questions.strategy: Both scores are abnormal, and 9 looks worse than 13. What tips it is which score moved and in which direction.

steps.detail: 9 for 2 days against 15 to 13 in one hour.
The falling score is the new cue.
First means now, not after another task.

elimination.verdict: The patient from the bicycle crash, because his score is falling.

questions.objective: Explain the purpose of the Glasgow Coma Scale

questions.stem: In the intensive care unit, a patient with a large brain hemorrhage does not open his eyes or speak. With a painful stimulus, his arms bend inward toward his chest and his wrists and fingers curl inward, while his legs extend. Which documentation and action by the nurse are correct?

options.text: Withdrawal from pain, motor score 4; recheck at the next check
options.rationale: Withdrawal, scored 4, would be the answer if he pulled the limb away from the pain. His arms bend into a fixed inward posture instead, which is abnormal flexion and scores 3.

options.text: Decorticate posturing, motor score 3; recheck at the next check
options.rationale: The posture and score are named correctly in this entry. Waiting for the next routine check is unsafe, because both forms of abnormal posturing require immediate assessment and intervention.

options.text: Decerebrate posturing, motor score 2; notify the provider now
options.rationale: Notifying the provider now is correct for any abnormal posture. Decerebrate posturing is extension with the arms straightening away from the body, and his arms flex inward instead.

options.text: Decorticate posturing, motor score 3; notify the provider now
options.rationale: Arms flexing toward the core with curled wrists and fingers is decorticate posturing, scored 3 on the motor scale. Any abnormal posturing needs immediate assessment and intervention, so the provider is notified now.

questions.takeaway: Decorticate posturing is flexion toward the core, means damage above the brainstem, scores 3 on the GCS motor scale, and needs immediate assessment and intervention.
questions.strategy: Any arm movement to pain can look like withdrawal, and a correct label can hide a wrong action. The fixed inward posture names it; the abnormal posture makes it urgent.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Arms toward the core is decorticate, not decerebrate.
Abnormal flexion is 3, not withdrawal at 4.
Abnormal posturing means notify now, not at the next check.

elimination.verdict: Decorticate posturing, motor score 3; notify the provider now.

questions.objective: Recognize abnormal motor responses

questions.stem: A patient with brain swelling after a near drowning showed decorticate posturing, a Glasgow Coma Scale motor score of 3, at 0600. At 0800, assistive personnel report that when his nail bed is pressed, he now straightens both arms away from his body and his feet point down. They say he is moving more and seems to be improving. Which response by the nurse is correct?

options.text: He is getting worse; I will assess him and call the provider
options.rationale: A change from flexion to extension means damage now involves the brainstem, which is more severe. His motor score falls from 3 to 2, so the nurse assesses and reports now.

options.text: Please bend his arms back and pad the side rails
options.rationale: Repositioning treats the posture as a comfort problem. The posture is a sign of brainstem involvement, so the nurse assesses and reports instead of correcting the limbs.

options.text: He may be waking up; let's see if he will squeeze a hand
options.rationale: Checking command following is part of a neurologic check, but the finding is not waking. Abnormal extension replacing flexion is deterioration that needs immediate assessment and a report.

options.text: That is good news; let's record it and keep checking hourly
options.rationale: Straightening sounds like more movement and so like progress. Extension posturing scores 2, lower than flexion at 3, and points to brainstem involvement, which is a decline.

questions.takeaway: Decerebrate posturing is extension away from the body, means brainstem involvement and is more severe than decorticate; a change from flexion to extension is deterioration.
questions.strategy: Assistive personnel offer the hopeful reading, and more movement sounds like progress. What tips it is the motor scale: extension scores lower than flexion.

steps.detail: Arms extend away, feet point down: decerebrate.
Brainstem involvement is worse than above it.
Assess now and notify the provider.

elimination.verdict: He is getting worse; I will assess him and call the provider.

questions.objective: Recognize abnormal motor responses

questions.stem: A 79 year old patient admitted to the medical unit with pneumonia was alert and oriented at 0800. At 1000, assistive personnel report that she does not know where she is and is pulling at her oxygen tubing. Which assessment does the nurse perform first?

options.text: Medication record review
options.rationale: Medications can cause sudden confusion. Reviewing records takes time and does not address a breathing problem that may be happening at this moment.

options.text: Electrolyte results
options.rationale: Electrolyte problems can cause confusion and are worth checking. Lab results are slower to obtain and less urgent than oxygenation in a patient pulling at her oxygen.

options.text: Temperature
options.rationale: Infection can cause sudden confusion, and she has pneumonia. Fever does not threaten her right now the way low oxygen does, so oxygenation is checked first.

options.text: Oxygen saturation
options.rationale: A sudden change in mental status needs immediate assessment, and poor oxygenation is a fast, dangerous cause. With pneumonia and displaced tubing, checking oxygen saturation also follows the ABCs.

questions.takeaway: A sudden change in mental status is a new cue needing immediate action; check oxygenation first, then glucose, infection, medications and electrolytes.
questions.strategy: Every option is a real cause of sudden confusion. What tips it is the ABCs and the cue that she is pulling at her oxygen tubing.

steps.detail: Oriented at 0800, confused at 1000.
Oxygenation comes before infection, drugs or labs.
She may have pulled her oxygen off.

elimination.verdict: Oxygen saturation.

questions.objective: Identify neurologic changes requiring intervention
questions.concept: Sudden mental status change: oxygenation first

questions.scenario: One day after abdominal surgery, a patient was alert and oriented at 2000. At 2300 she is hard to arouse and mumbles when spoken to. She received an opioid pain medication at 2130. Her respiratory rate is 8 per minute, oxygen saturation is 86% on room air, capillary blood glucose is 112 mg/dL and temperature is 37.0 °C.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Check her electrolyte results before calling anyone
options.rationale: Electrolyte imbalance is one cause of confusion. Her breathing and oxygen findings already explain the change, and waiting for labs delays urgent action.

options.text: Let her sleep and recheck at the next routine check
options.rationale: Rest after surgery is normal, which makes this tempting. A respiratory rate of 8 per minute with low oxygen is not normal sleep, and waiting risks further decline.

options.text: Notify the provider of the acute change now
options.rationale: A sudden change from alert to hard to arouse is a new cue requiring immediate action. The provider needs the findings now to treat the cause.

options.text: Stay with her and support her airway and breathing
options.rationale: Her breathing is slow and her oxygen saturation is low, so airway and breathing come first under the ABCs. Staying with her lets the nurse act if her breathing worsens.

options.text: Infection
options.rationale: Infection can cause sudden confusion after surgery. Her temperature is 37.0 °C and the change came soon after a medication dose, which points elsewhere.

options.text: Acute change in mental status from poor oxygenation
options.rationale: She went from alert to hard to arouse within hours, with slow breathing and low oxygen after an opioid dose. Poor oxygenation linked to the medication explains the change.

options.text: Low blood glucose
options.rationale: Low glucose is a common cause of sudden confusion. Her capillary glucose is 112 mg/dL, which rules it out as the cause here.

options.text: Normal tiredness after surgery
options.rationale: Tiredness after surgery is expected, but a tired patient still rouses easily and breathes normally. Slow breathing and low oxygen make this an acute change.

options.text: Level of consciousness compared with her baseline
options.rationale: She was alert and oriented at 2000, which is her baseline. Comparing her alertness against it shows whether treatment is working.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks fluid balance over days. It says nothing about the breathing and alertness problem that needs watching tonight.

options.text: Bowel sounds
options.rationale: Bowel sounds are checked after abdominal surgery, but they do not change with this problem. They will not show whether her breathing or alertness is recovering.

options.text: Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation
options.rationale: These two values show the oxygenation problem driving her change. Watching them shows whether her breathing is improving or getting worse.

questions.takeaway: A sudden drop in consciousness is an act now cue: check oxygenation, glucose, infection, medications and electrolytes, support the ABCs and notify the provider.
questions.strategy: Her glucose and temperature are listed so they can be ruled out. What tips it is the timing after the opioid dose plus a respiratory rate of 8 per minute and saturation of 86%.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Rule out causes with the data
steps.detail: Glucose 112 mg/dL and temperature 37.0 °C are normal.
Slow breathing and low oxygen after an opioid.

steps.action: Pick actions and monitors that match
steps.detail: Airway, report, breathing values and alertness.

elimination.verdict: Support airway and breathing and notify the provider; poor oxygenation; monitor breathing values and level of consciousness.

questions.objective: Identify neurologic changes requiring intervention
questions.concept: Sudden mental status change: oxygenation first

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with diabetes mellitus admitted for cellulitis of the leg who becomes confused and sweaty at 1000. Her oxygen saturation is 97% on room air, unchanged from 0800, and her respiratory rate is 16 per minute. She received insulin at 0730 and ate almost none of her breakfast. Which assessment does the nurse perform next?

options.text: Body temperature
options.rationale: Cellulitis is an infection, and infection can cause confusion. Insulin given with almost no food points more directly to low blood glucose, which a bedside check confirms in a minute.

options.text: Capillary blood glucose
options.rationale: Her oxygenation is normal, so the nurse moves to the next fast bedside check, blood glucose. Insulin given with almost no food makes low glucose the most likely cause of her sudden confusion and sweating.

options.text: Medication list review
options.rationale: Medications can cause confusion, and insulin is the medication involved here. Reconciling her medication list takes time and does not measure the glucose level the insulin may have lowered.

options.text: Serum electrolytes
options.rationale: Electrolyte imbalance can cause confusion and may be checked later. Nothing in the stem points to them, and a lab draw is slower than a bedside glucose check.

questions.takeaway: When oxygenation is normal, work down the causes of sudden confusion; insulin given without food points to blood glucose.
questions.strategy: Infection is a real cause and she has one. What tips it is the antecedent: insulin at 0730 with almost no breakfast.

steps.detail: Saturation 97%, unchanged.
Insulin given, breakfast not eaten.
A capillary glucose answers it now.

elimination.verdict: Capillary blood glucose.

questions.objective: Identify neurologic changes requiring intervention
questions.concept: Sudden mental status change: blood glucose

questions.stem: An 93 year old patient is on day 2 of a hospital stay for heart failure. The nurse reviews her neurologic findings. Which finding does the nurse assess further now?

options.text: Forgets the nurse's name but recalls it when reminded
options.rationale: Mild memory changes are expected with aging, so this looks like a lapse that matters. She recalls the name with a reminder, which fits normal aging rather than a sudden change.

options.text: Answers questions slowly, but every answer is correct
options.rationale: Slower processing speed and reaction time are expected with aging. Her answers are correct, so her thinking is intact even though she takes longer to reply.

options.text: Cannot name the month, which she named at breakfast
options.rationale: Losing orientation within a few hours is a sudden change, not aging. Sudden or acute changes always need immediate assessment of causes such as oxygenation, glucose and infection.

options.text: Ankle reflexes diminished on both sides, as at her last visit
options.rationale: Deep tendon reflexes diminish with aging. These are equal on both sides and unchanged from her last visit, which makes them part of her baseline rather than a new cue.

questions.takeaway: Slower processing, mild memory changes and diminished reflexes on both sides are expected with aging; a sudden change, such as losing orientation within hours, always needs immediate assessment.
questions.strategy: Each finding would be abnormal in a young adult, which pulls toward the memory lapse. What tips it is timing: only one finding changed since this morning.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Slow answers, low reflexes on both sides and mild memory lapses fit aging.
The month was known at breakfast and is not known now.

elimination.verdict: Cannot name the month, which she named at breakfast.

questions.objective: Identify neurologic changes requiring intervention
questions.concept: Expected aging changes vs new changes

questions.stem: A patient with a frontal lobe injury from a fall is impulsive and shows poor judgment. He speaks clearly and understands what is said to him. An hour after he correctly showed the nurse how to use the call light, he is found standing unsteadily beside the bed without having called. After the nurse helps him back to bed, which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Use a picture board for communication
options.rationale: A picture board helps a patient who cannot understand or use words. He speaks clearly and understands what is said, so his problem is impulsive behavior, which a picture board does not address.

options.text: Enable the bed alarm
options.rationale: Frontal lobe injury impairs judgment and impulse control, so his safety cannot depend on him choosing to call. A bed alarm alerts staff when he gets up without relying on his judgment.

options.text: Reteach the call light and have him show it again
options.rationale: Teaching is a reasonable, least restrictive measure. He already showed correct use and still did not call, because using it depends on the judgment the injury has impaired.

options.text: Place all items directly in front of him
options.rationale: Placing items in front helps a patient who does not notice things to one side. His risk comes from getting up impulsively, which item placement does not prevent.

questions.takeaway: With frontal lobe injury, judgment and impulse control are impaired, so choose safety measures such as a bed alarm that do not depend on the patient deciding to ask for help.
questions.strategy: Reteaching the call light is the tempting safe answer. What tips it is that he already knew how and still got up, so teaching cannot fix the problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He knew the call light and did not use it.
Impulsivity and poor judgment, not language or vision.

steps.action: Choose what works without his judgment
steps.detail: An alarm brings staff to him.

elimination.verdict: Enable the bed alarm.

questions.objective: Apply neurologic findings to clinical situations
questions.concept: Frontal lobe injury: safety without relying on judgment

questions.stem: The provider prescribes a lumbar puncture for a patient with fever, a severe headache and a stiff neck. Which statement shows that she understood the nurse's teaching about what the test looks at?

options.text: It takes quick pictures of my skull to look for bleeding or a fracture
options.rationale: Quick images of the brain and skull for bleeding or fractures describe a CT scan. A lumbar puncture does not produce images; it analyzes fluid.

options.text: It measures how fast blood is flowing through the arteries in my brain
options.rationale: Measuring blood flow in brain arteries describes a transcranial Doppler. A lumbar puncture samples cerebrospinal fluid and does not measure blood flow.

options.text: They will test the fluid around my spinal cord for infection
options.rationale: A lumbar puncture removes cerebrospinal fluid so it can be analyzed for infection, bleeding or inflammation. With fever and a stiff neck, infection is what the fluid is checked for.

options.text: It records the electrical activity in my brain to look for seizures
options.rationale: Recording brain electrical activity describes an EEG, which looks for seizures and abnormal brain activity. A lumbar puncture analyzes fluid and does not measure electrical activity.

questions.takeaway: A lumbar puncture analyzes CSF for infection, bleeding or inflammation; EEG records electrical activity, CT gives quick images for bleeding, and transcranial Doppler measures cerebral blood flow.
questions.strategy: Each distractor describes a real neurologic test. Match the test name to what it looks at: lumbar puncture means spinal fluid.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Name the test each statement describes
steps.detail: EEG, transcranial Doppler, CT and lumbar puncture.
Lumbar puncture analyzes cerebrospinal fluid.

elimination.verdict: They will test the fluid around my spinal cord for infection.

questions.objective: Apply neurologic findings to clinical situations

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient scheduled for electromyography (EMG) whose hand weakness and muscle twitching have worsened over several months. Which statement shows that he understood the nurse's teaching about the test?

options.text: It records my brain waves to find abnormal activity
options.rationale: Recording brain waves describes an EEG, which looks for seizures and brain dysfunction. An EMG looks at the nerves and muscles in his body, not the brain's activity.

options.text: It shows whether blood vessels in my brain are narrowing
options.rationale: Looking for narrowed brain arteries describes a transcranial Doppler, which detects vasospasm and changes in blood flow. An EMG does not look at blood vessels.

options.text: It makes detailed pictures of my spinal cord and nerves
options.rationale: Detailed soft tissue pictures of the spinal cord and nerves describe an MRI. An EMG tests how nerves and muscles function rather than producing images.

options.text: It checks how well my nerves and muscles are working
options.rationale: Electromyography looks for nerve and muscle disorders. Weakness and twitching that have worsened over months are the kind of problem it is used to evaluate.

questions.takeaway: EMG evaluates nerve and muscle disorders; MRI gives detailed soft tissue images, EEG records brain electrical activity, and transcranial Doppler measures cerebral blood flow.
questions.strategy: Detailed pictures of nerves sounds close because nerves are involved. What tips it is that EMG tests how nerves and muscles work, not what they look like.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Name the test each statement describes
steps.detail: MRI, transcranial Doppler, EEG and EMG.

steps.action: Keep the nerve and muscle function statement
steps.detail: That is EMG.

elimination.verdict: It checks how well my nerves and muscles are working.

questions.objective: Apply neurologic findings to clinical situations

questions.stem: On a cardiac unit, a patient admitted with atrial fibrillation was alert and oriented 30 minutes ago. The nurse now notices new confusion, slurred speech and weakness of his right arm. Place the nurse's actions in the order they are performed.

options.text: Compare the findings with his prior baseline
options.rationale: Comparing the new findings with the earlier record shows exactly what has changed and since when. That timing and detail are what the provider will need.

options.text: Recognize the findings as a change from his baseline
options.rationale: Every later step depends on seeing that something is new. Confusion, slurred speech and one sided weakness in a patient oriented 30 minutes ago are a change from baseline.

options.text: Assess him immediately at the bedside
options.rationale: A new neurologic change means acting now, so the nurse stays and assesses him. The assessment gives the details needed for every step after it.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the rapid response
options.rationale: Notification comes once the nurse has the findings to report. Calling with specific changes and vital signs lets the team respond quickly and appropriately.

options.text: Assess airway, breathing, circulation and vital signs
options.rationale: The nurse checks the ABCs and vital signs to find any immediate threat to life. These values also go into the report to the provider.

questions.takeaway: A new neurologic change means act now: recognize the change, assess immediately, compare with baseline, check ABCs and vital signs, then notify the provider or activate a response.
questions.strategy: The pull is to call for help the instant something looks wrong. The report goes after the bedside findings, so the caller has something specific to say.

steps.detail: Nothing happens until the change is seen.
Bedside findings, baseline comparison, ABCs and vital signs.
Notify with the findings in hand.

elimination.verdict: Recognize, assess, compare with baseline, check ABCs and vital signs, notify.

questions.objective: Identify neurologic changes requiring intervention
questions.concept: Act now sequence for a new neurologic change
questions.note: Instructor's order: recognize the change, assess immediately, compare with baseline, check ABCs and vital signs, then notify; use that order on the unit exam. On NCLEX, failing airway or breathing comes before everything else, and suspected stroke findings are reported without delay.

questions.stem: Five days after a ruptured brain aneurysm, a patient's provider wants to check, at the bedside and repeatedly over the next several days, how well blood is moving through the large arteries of her brain. Which test does the nurse prepare her for?

options.text: Transcranial Doppler study
options.rationale: A transcranial Doppler measures cerebral blood flow in the major brain arteries. It can be repeated at the bedside, which suits a provider who wants to follow her arteries day by day.

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: An MRI gives the most detailed soft tissue images of the brain and spinal cord. It is a picture of tissue, not a measure of blood flow, and it cannot be done at the bedside.

options.text: Electroencephalogram
options.rationale: An EEG records the electrical activity of the brain, not the movement of blood. It gives no information about how well blood is flowing through her large brain arteries.

options.text: Computed tomography scan
options.rationale: A CT scan quickly shows structural problems such as bleeding, so it fits a ruptured aneurysm at first. It shows structure rather than how fast blood is flowing through her arteries.

questions.takeaway: CT shows structural abnormalities, MRI gives detailed soft tissue images, EEG records electrical activity, and transcranial Doppler measures cerebral blood flow.
questions.strategy: A ruptured aneurysm pulls toward CT, because CT is the test for bleeding. The provider's question here is about blood flow, which only one test measures.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blood flow through the brain arteries, repeated at the bedside.

steps.action: Match each test to what it looks at
steps.detail: CT structure, MRI soft tissue, EEG electrical activity, Doppler flow.

elimination.verdict: Transcranial Doppler study.

questions.objective: Apply neurologic findings to clinical situations
questions.concept: Diagnostic tests: CT vs MRI vs transcranial Doppler

questions.stem: On a rehabilitation unit, a patient with a spinal cord injury from 6 weeks ago says he has stopped answering his friends' calls and sees no point in going to therapy. His motor and sensory findings are unchanged from yesterday. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Ask the provider to order more frequent neurologic checks
options.rationale: Frequent checks fit a changing physical exam. His motor and sensory findings are unchanged, and the new cues are emotional, so more physical checks miss the problem.

options.text: Encourage him to call one friend today to lift his mood
options.rationale: Social contact can help mood, and the idea is kind. Giving advice before assessing his mood skips the depression screening his statements call for.

options.text: Screen him for depression and ask about his coping and support
options.rationale: Withdrawing from friends and losing interest in therapy are cues for depression, which is screened for in chronic neurologic conditions. Asking about coping and support addresses the whole patient.

options.text: Tell him that therapy is the best way to get stronger
options.rationale: Therapy does help recovery, which makes this sound supportive. Telling him so skips his feelings and does not assess the hopelessness he just described.

questions.takeaway: A complete neurologic assessment includes psychosocial status: emotional response, coping, support systems and depression screening, especially with chronic neurologic conditions.
questions.strategy: Encouraging therapy or a phone call sounds helpful. What tips it is that he has just described withdrawal and hopelessness, which calls for assessment before advice.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Withdrawal from friends, no point in therapy.
Motor and sensory findings are unchanged.
Screen for depression and explore coping.

elimination.verdict: Screen him for depression and ask about his coping and support.

questions.objective: Apply neurologic findings to clinical situations
questions.concept: Psychosocial assessment: depression, coping and support

questions.stem: Since admission, a patient with swelling of the cerebellum after a viral illness has walked with a wide, unsteady gait and has had a tremor when reaching for objects. This morning the nurse notes several findings. Which finding does the nurse act on first?

options.text: Her breathing has become slow and irregular
options.rationale: Swelling in the cerebellum can press on the brainstem, which controls breathing, heart rate and blood pressure. Slow, irregular breathing signals that pressure and threatens oxygenation, so the nurse acts on it first.

options.text: She knocks over her cup when reaching for it
options.rationale: Knocking over a cup fits the reaching tremor and poor coordination she has had since admission. It threatens her safety, but it does not threaten breathing the way a new breathing pattern does.

options.text: She says she is afraid to walk to the bathroom
options.rationale: Fear of walking is a real concern after repeated unsteadiness, and it deserves a response. It is a psychosocial need, and a physical threat to breathing outranks it under the ABCs.

options.text: She now sways when sitting on the edge of the bed
options.rationale: Swaying while sitting is a new loss of balance and does need follow up and fall precautions. Slow, irregular breathing threatens a vital function, so the breathing finding comes before the balance finding.

questions.takeaway: Cerebellar problems cause imbalance and poor coordination, but swelling there can press on the brainstem, so a change in breathing outranks any new balance finding.
questions.strategy: The new sway while sitting looks like the cerebellar change to report. What tips it is that slow, irregular breathing is a brainstem vital function and comes first under the ABCs.

steps.detail: Unsteady gait and reaching tremor are her known cerebellar findings.
Swelling in the cerebellum sits next to the brainstem, which runs breathing.
A breathing change outranks balance, coordination and fear.

elimination.verdict: Her breathing has become slow and irregular.

questions.objective: Describe the basic nervous system organization and function

questions.stem: At breakfast, a patient admitted for a flare of multiple sclerosis coughs and clears her throat after each sip of coffee, and her voice now sounds wet. She has a regular diet prescribed and no NPO order. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Offer thicker foods, since liquids cause the coughing
options.rationale: A texture change may later be part of her plan, but it assumes the cause before anyone evaluates it. Coughing and a wet voice call for stopping intake and reporting first.

options.text: Watch her swallow another sip with the head of the bed raised
options.rationale: Watching a swallow is allowed when a patient is not NPO and it is clinically appropriate. She already coughs with every sip and sounds wet, so another sip adds risk without new information.

options.text: Ask her to shrug her shoulders against resistance
options.rationale: A shoulder shrug tests cranial nerve XI, the accessory nerve. Her problem involves swallowing and voice, which belong to cranial nerves IX and X, so this check misses the finding that matters.

options.text: Stop oral intake and report signs of aspiration risk
options.rationale: Coughing with each sip and a wet voice are signs of aspiration risk that the nurse notes and reports. Stopping intake protects her airway until her swallowing can be evaluated safely.

questions.takeaway: The NPO rule is not the only limit on swallowing checks: swallowing is observed only when clinically appropriate, and signs of aspiration risk mean stop intake and report.
questions.strategy: Because she has no NPO order, watching another swallow seems allowed. What tips it is that she already shows signs of aspiration risk, so testing again is not clinically appropriate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Coughing with every sip and a wet voice point to cranial nerves IX and X.
She is already failing the swallow, so another sip only adds risk.
Stop intake and report before anything else.

elimination.verdict: Stop oral intake and report signs of aspiration risk.

questions.objective: Identify basic cranial nerve assessment findings
questions.concept: Swallowing CN IX and X: not tested if NPO

questions.stem: Each hour, the nurse checks a patient with liver cirrhosis. At 1300 she was awake and watching television. At 1400 she again names herself, the hospital, the date and the reason she is there, but she falls asleep between questions and opens her eyes only when the nurse speaks loudly and touches her arm. Which entry does the nurse chart?

options.text: Awake but disoriented
options.rationale: Awake but disoriented describes a patient who stays awake and answers wrongly. She falls asleep between questions and her answers are correct, so both parts of this entry are wrong.

options.text: Difficult to arouse; oriented when awakened
options.rationale: Level of consciousness is how awake she is, while orientation is what she understands. Needing a loud voice and touch to open her eyes is a decline in arousal, even though her orientation is intact.

options.text: Alert and oriented to person, place, time and situation
options.rationale: She does answer all four orientation questions correctly, which makes this entry tempting. She cannot stay awake and needs a loud voice and touch to open her eyes, so she is not alert.

options.text: Unresponsive to voice and touch
options.rationale: Unresponsive means no response at all to voice or touch. She opens her eyes to a loud voice with touch and then answers correctly, so she still responds.

questions.takeaway: Orientation and level of consciousness are separate: a patient can answer every orientation question and still show a falling level of consciousness.
questions.strategy: A perfect orientation check pulls toward alert and oriented. What tips it is that she now needs a loud voice and touch to open her eyes, a change since 1300.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: How awake is she, and does she know person, place, time and situation?
Eyes open only to a loud voice and touch, then she drifts off.
All four answers are correct.

elimination.verdict: Difficult to arouse; oriented when awakened.

questions.objective: Assess level of consciousness, language, speech, movement, and sensation

questions.nursesNote: 0900: 71 year old man admitted 2 days ago for a COPD exacerbation. Awake, answering questions slowly but correctly. Oriented to person, place, time and situation. Pupils 3 mm, equal, react slowly to light, unchanged from admission. Speech newly slurred since breakfast. Hand grips strong and equal. Says the left side of his face feels numb when touched, which he did not report yesterday. Gait slow and steady with his cane, as at admission. Coughed twice while drinking water at breakfast. Naps in the afternoon and wakes often at night.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow up by the nurse.

segments.text: answering questions slowly but correctly
segments.rationale: Slower processing is an expected change with aging. His answers are correct, so his thinking is intact and this needs no follow up.

segments.text: Oriented to person, place, time and situation
segments.rationale: Full orientation is a normal finding. It shows his awareness is intact even though other findings in the note have changed.

segments.text: react slowly to light, unchanged from admission
segments.rationale: Pupils react more slowly with aging, and his are equal and unchanged since admission. That makes this his baseline rather than a new cue.

segments.text: Speech newly slurred since breakfast
segments.rationale: Slurred speech is a motor problem with producing words, and this began this morning. A new speech change may signal neurologic dysfunction and needs assessment now.

segments.text: Hand grips strong and equal
segments.rationale: Strong, equal grips show no motor difference between sides. This is a normal finding that helps the nurse describe the other changes accurately.

segments.text: left side of his face feels numb when touched, which he did not report yesterday
segments.rationale: New numbness on one side of the face is a new sensory change with a difference between sides. New sensory changes are documented and reported, not assumed to be aging.

segments.text: Gait slow and steady with his cane, as at admission
segments.rationale: Slower movement and gait changes are expected with aging. His gait matches admission and he is steady, so this is his baseline.

segments.text: Coughed twice while drinking water at breakfast
segments.rationale: Coughing while drinking is a sign of trouble swallowing and an aspiration risk. Swallowing involves CN IX and X, and with his new slurred speech it needs follow up.

segments.text: Naps in the afternoon and wakes often at night
segments.rationale: Altered sleep and wake cycles with more nighttime waking are expected with aging. This pattern does not point to a new neurologic problem.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, sort each finding by whether it is new or one sided; slow answers, slow pupils, slow gait and altered sleep can be aging, but new slurred speech, one sided numbness and coughing with drinks need follow up.
questions.strategy: Many findings in the note sound abnormal for a young adult. The cue that tips each one is the word showing whether it is new or matches admission.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pupils, gait and slow answers are unchanged or aging.
Slurred speech since breakfast, face numbness not reported yesterday.
Coughing with water means aspiration risk.

elimination.verdict: New slurred speech, new left facial numbness and coughing while drinking.

questions.objective: Identify neurologic changes requiring intervention
questions.concept: Expected aging changes vs new changes

questions.stem: Yesterday, a patient with brain injury from carbon monoxide poisoning straightened both arms away from his body, with his feet pointed down, when his nail bed was pressed. Today the same stimulus makes his arms bend stiffly toward his chest with his wrists curled. His wife says, "He's moving more, so his brain is healing." Which reply by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Less severe than before, but still abnormal."
options.rationale: Decerebrate extension points to brainstem involvement and is more severe than decorticate flexion. Flexion toward the chest is still abnormal posturing that requires immediate assessment, so this reply is honest without overpromising.

options.text: "Yes, his brain is recovering from the injury."
options.rationale: Moving from extension to flexion is a shift toward a less severe posture, so her hope has some basis. Both postures are abnormal neurologic signs, so calling this recovery promises more than the finding shows.

options.text: "He is pulling away from the pain normally."
options.rationale: Pulling away from pain is withdrawal, a purposeful movement scored higher than abnormal flexion. Stiff arms bent to the chest with curled wrists describe decorticate posturing, not withdrawal.

options.text: "No, bending inward is worse than straightening."
options.rationale: Decorticate flexion, with the arms bent toward the core, indicates damage above the brainstem. Decerebrate extension is the more severe posture, so this reply reverses the two.

questions.takeaway: Decerebrate extension is more severe than decorticate flexion, so a change toward flexion is less severe, but both remain abnormal signs that need immediate assessment.
questions.strategy: Her hopeful statement is partly true, which makes agreeing with her appealing. What tips it is that the new posture is still abnormal, so the accurate reply concedes the change without calling it healing.

steps.detail: Arms straight away from the body, feet pointed down: decerebrate.
Arms stiffly bent to the chest, wrists curled: decorticate.
Less severe, yet both postures are abnormal.

elimination.verdict: "Less severe than before, but still abnormal."

questions.objective: Recognize abnormal motor responses

questions.stem: A warehouse worker struck on the head by a falling shelf is brought in drowsy and has vomited twice. The provider needs to know right away whether he is bleeding inside his skull. Which statement by a nursing student needs correction?

options.text: "A CT can also show whether his skull is fractured."
options.rationale: Besides bleeding, CT quickly detects fractures, masses and swelling. A falling shelf could fracture his skull, so this statement is accurate and needs no correction.

options.text: "A CT scan can show bleeding in his brain quickly."
options.rationale: CT quickly detects bleeding inside the skull, which is the question the provider needs answered now. This statement is accurate for a drowsy, vomiting patient after a head blow, so it needs no correction.

options.text: "An EEG records electrical activity, so it will not show bleeding."
options.rationale: An EEG measures brain electrical activity and detects seizures and abnormal activity. It does not image bleeding, so this statement is accurate and needs no correction.

options.text: "An MRI should come first, since its images are more detailed."
options.rationale: MRI does give more detailed soft tissue images and is best for tumors, nerves and demyelinating disease. The provider needs an answer about bleeding right away, and CT detects bleeding quickly, so this needs correction.

questions.takeaway: When bleeding must be ruled out fast, CT comes first because it detects bleeding quickly; MRI gives more detail but fits questions about tumors, nerves and demyelinating disease.
questions.strategy: More detail sounds like a better test, so the MRI statement looks correct. What tips it is that the provider needs a fast answer about bleeding, which is what CT provides.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the one statement that is wrong.
Is he bleeding, answered right away.
CT detects bleeding quickly; MRI adds soft tissue detail.

elimination.verdict: "An MRI should come first, since its images are more detailed."

questions.objective: Apply neurologic findings to clinical situations
questions.concept: Diagnostic tests: CT vs MRI vs transcranial Doppler

questions.stem: While caring for a patient admitted for pneumonia, the nurse notes at 1015 that she suddenly cannot see objects on her right side and staggers when she stands. Her face is symmetric, arm strength is equal and her speech is clear. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Keep observing, since face, arm and speech are normal
options.rationale: A normal face, arm and speech check misses strokes that appear only as balance or vision changes. Balance and Eyes sit in front of FAST to catch exactly these patients.

options.text: Return her to bed and recheck her in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Getting her back to bed does protect her from a fall. Waiting 30 minutes to see whether the deficits clear spends brain tissue that treatment might have saved.

options.text: Activate the stroke response and note the onset time
options.rationale: Sudden loss of balance and a new loss of vision on one side are the Balance and Eyes checks of BE FAST. Either one can be a stroke, so the response starts now with an exact onset time.

options.text: Check lying and standing blood pressures for orthostasis
options.rationale: A drop in pressure on standing can make a patient unsteady. It does not explain sudden vision loss on one side, and checking it first delays the stroke response.

questions.takeaway: BE FAST adds Balance and Eyes to the face, arm and speech checks; sudden imbalance or vision loss alone is enough to activate the stroke response.
questions.strategy: The normal face, arm and speech findings pull toward watching. Two sudden new deficits, even outside FAST, tip it to activation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sudden one sided vision loss and new unsteadiness, both at 1015.
Balance and Eyes are stroke signs in their own right.
Observing or rechecking later loses time.

elimination.verdict: Activate the stroke response and record the onset time.

questions.objective: Recognize signs and symptoms of neurologic emergencies

questions.stem: The nurse teaches BE FAST to the husband of a patient who had a transient ischemic attack last month. Which statement by the husband shows that he needs more teaching?

options.text: "I'll call 911 rather than drive him in myself."
options.rationale: Time in BE FAST means calling 911 right away. Emergency crews start assessment and alert the stroke team before arrival, which a private car cannot do, so this is correct.

options.text: "If his speech slurs, then clears, I won't call."
options.rationale: His last episode cleared, so waiting it out feels reasonable to him. A sign that clears may be another transient attack, a warning of stroke, and it still needs an immediate 911 call.

options.text: "If he suddenly loses his balance, I'll call 911."
options.rationale: Sudden loss of balance or coordination is the Balance check. It counts as a stroke sign even when his face and arms look normal, so this statement is correct.

options.text: "If part of his vision suddenly goes, I'll call 911."
options.rationale: A sudden change in vision is the Eyes check and can be the only sign of a stroke. Calling 911 is the right response, so this statement shows understanding.

questions.takeaway: BE FAST: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time; any sudden sign means calling 911 right away, even if it clears.
questions.strategy: The question asks for the wrong statement, and the earlier attack that passed makes waiting sound sensible. A sign that clears still means a call, because it can warn of a stroke.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is unsafe.
Balance, vision and calling 911 all lead to an immediate call.
Speech that clears is still a reason to call.

elimination.verdict: "If his speech slurs, then clears, I won't call."

questions.objective: Recognize signs and symptoms of neurologic emergencies
questions.concept: BE FAST teaching: time and calling 911

questions.nursesNote: 0900: Day 2 after a large left hemisphere ischemic stroke. Right arm weakness unchanged from admission. Halting, word finding speech unchanged from admission. Now opens eyes only when his name is called loudly; awake and talking at 0700. Blood pressure 148/86 mm Hg, same as 0700. Reports a new severe headache. Blood glucose 116 mg/dL. Cannot see the nurse standing on his right side, which he could at 0700. Oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that signal neurologic deterioration and need to be reported now.

segments.text: Right arm weakness unchanged from admission
segments.rationale: This weakness is his known deficit from the stroke. It is his baseline and has not changed, so it is not new deterioration.

segments.text: Halting, word finding speech unchanged from admission
segments.rationale: Word finding trouble fits his left hemisphere stroke. It is unchanged, so it does not signal worsening on its own.

segments.text: Now opens eyes only when his name is called loudly; awake and talking at 0700
segments.rationale: He was awake and talking two hours ago and now needs a loud voice to open his eyes. A declining level of consciousness is the earliest sign of deterioration and rising ICP.

segments.text: Blood pressure 148/86 mm Hg, same as 0700
segments.rationale: His pressure is unchanged from the earlier reading. A steady value does not rule out trouble, but it is not itself a new finding to report.

segments.text: Reports a new severe headache
segments.rationale: A new severe headache after a stroke can mean bleeding or swelling in the brain. It is listed with declining consciousness as a change that matters.

segments.text: Blood glucose 116 mg/dL
segments.rationale: This glucose is in a safe range and rules out low blood sugar as a cause of his change. It needs no report of its own.

segments.text: Cannot see the nurse standing on his right side, which he could at 0700
segments.rationale: A visual deficit that was not present two hours ago is a new neurologic finding. New deficits can signal a worsening or new stroke.

segments.text: Oxygen saturation 97% on room air
segments.rationale: His saturation is normal on room air, so hypoxia is not adding to brain injury. There is nothing to report here.

questions.takeaway: Compare every neurologic finding to baseline: declining LOC, a new severe headache and a new visual deficit signal deterioration, even with stable vital signs.
questions.strategy: Sort each line into new or unchanged. Unchanged stroke deficits are baseline, however serious they look.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Arm weakness and speech are unchanged from admission.
Pressure is unchanged, glucose and saturation are normal.
Harder to arouse, new headache, new visual loss.

elimination.verdict: Declining consciousness, new severe headache and new visual deficit.

questions.objective: Recognize early signs of increased ICP
questions.concept: LOC change is the earliest sign of increased ICP

questions.stem: A 78 year old patient is seen in clinic a week after a transient ischemic attack. She smokes a pack a day, rarely exercises, and her father had a stroke. She says, "Strokes run in my family and I've already had a warning, so nothing I do will matter." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "You're right; your family history outweighs the rest."
options.rationale: Family history does raise her risk and cannot be changed. Agreeing with her leaves out the modifiable risks she has, which are the ones teaching can lower.

options.text: "Quitting smoking and walking daily can lower your risk."
options.rationale: Smoking and physical inactivity are modifiable risks she can change starting today. Naming them answers her belief that nothing matters with specific steps that lower her stroke risk.

options.text: "Aspirin will cancel out the risk from your father."
options.rationale: Aspirin when appropriate is part of stroke prevention. Family history is nonmodifiable, and no medication erases it, so this promise is false and may stop her changing her habits.

options.text: "Treating the attack you had can reverse that risk."
options.rationale: Her recent attack does demand action, which makes this sound hopeful. A previous TIA is a nonmodifiable risk; it cannot be undone, only offset by changing the risks she controls.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable stroke risks are hypertension, diabetes, smoking, obesity, high cholesterol and inactivity; older age, family history, previous stroke and previous TIA are nonmodifiable.
questions.strategy: The recent attack feels like something to fix, but the event itself cannot be changed. Ask which response names a risk she can change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age, family history and the TIA are fixed; smoking and inactivity can change.
Nothing reverses a TIA or cancels family history.

steps.action: Pick the response that gives her a target
steps.detail: Smoking cessation and activity.

elimination.verdict: "Quitting smoking and walking daily can lower your risk."

questions.objective: Recognize signs and symptoms of neurologic emergencies
questions.concept: Modifiable and nonmodifiable stroke risk factors

questions.stem: Before discharge after an ischemic stroke, a patient reviews his medications with the nurse. He has a new antihypertensive, a cholesterol medication, daily aspirin as prescribed, and a nicotine patch. Which statement by him needs follow up?

options.text: "I'm using the patch so I don't go back to smoking."
options.rationale: Smoking cessation is the S of ABCS. Using nicotine replacement to stay off cigarettes supports prevention and does not need correction.

options.text: "I'll take the aspirin every day the way it was prescribed."
options.rationale: Aspirin when appropriate is the A of ABCS, and his provider has prescribed it. Taking it as directed is the correct plan and needs no follow up.

options.text: "I'll keep my lab visit to have my cholesterol rechecked."
options.rationale: Cholesterol management is the C of ABCS. Rechecking levels shows whether the medication works, so this statement is correct.

options.text: "My pressure is normal now, so I can stop those pills."
options.rationale: A normal reading on the medication shows the drug is working, not that it is no longer needed. Stopping it lets pressure climb again and removes the B of ABCS, so this needs correction.

questions.takeaway: ABCS of stroke prevention: Aspirin when appropriate, Blood pressure control, Cholesterol management, Smoking cessation; controlled pressure still needs its medication.
questions.strategy: Three statements are correct ABCS behaviors. The one that needs follow up sounds like good news but stops a prevention measure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Needs follow up means find the wrong belief.
Aspirin, cholesterol and smoking statements fit.
Stopping pressure pills once pressure is normal removes blood pressure control.

elimination.verdict: Stopping the antihypertensive once pressure is normal.

questions.objective: Recognize signs and symptoms of neurologic emergencies

questions.stem: A patient with an intracerebral hemorrhage was alert and oriented at 0000. At 0200 she is restless, picking at her gown and unsure where she is. Her headache, blood pressure and pulse are unchanged from 0000. What does this change mean?

options.text: Pressure inside her skull may be rising
options.rationale: A change in level of consciousness, such as new restlessness or confusion, is the earliest sign of increased ICP. A bleed adds volume in the skull, so she is at risk and this is reported now.

options.text: Her stable vital signs rule out a problem
options.rationale: Steady vital signs are reassuring in many patients. In rising ICP, vital signs change late, so stable numbers do not cancel a new change in consciousness.

options.text: Her pain is causing the restlessness
options.rationale: Pain can make a patient restless. Her headache has not changed since she was oriented, so pain does not explain the new confusion.

options.text: Night time confusion is expected in hospital
options.rationale: Patients can become disoriented at night in hospital. Assuming that here would miss a new change in a patient whose bleed puts her at high risk.

questions.takeaway: A decline in LOC, such as restlessness or new confusion, is the earliest sign of increased ICP and early deterioration.
questions.strategy: Three findings are unchanged and one is new. Build the answer on the new one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Orientation and behavior changed between 0000 and 0200.
Unchanged pain cannot explain a new change.
Consciousness changes first; vital signs follow later.

elimination.verdict: Possible rising ICP; report it now.

questions.objective: Recognize early signs of increased ICP
questions.concept: LOC change is the earliest sign of increased ICP

questions.stem: On a stroke unit, the nurse receives report on four patients. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: A man with aphasia who is upset because he cannot find the words he wants
options.rationale: His frustration deserves a calm, patient response. Aphasia is an expected deficit of his stroke, and he is stable.

options.text: A woman 3 days after a stroke who is asking when her swallow study will be done
options.rationale: Her question matters, and she stays NPO until she is screened. She is alert and asking questions, which shows stable consciousness.

options.text: A man 1 day after a stroke who is newly drowsy since the last check
options.rationale: A drop in level of consciousness is the earliest sign of deterioration and rising ICP. It is a new, unstable change, so he is seen first.

options.text: A woman with left sided neglect who keeps forgetting her left arm on the armrest
options.rationale: Neglect is a real safety concern and needs positioning and cues. It is her known deficit, not a new change, so she can wait briefly.

questions.takeaway: A new decline in LOC outranks stable stroke deficits; it is the earliest sign of deterioration.
questions.strategy: Each patient has a real need. Only one has a change from the last assessment.

steps.detail: Only the drowsy man is different from his last check.
Known deficits are stable; new drowsiness is not.
Consciousness changes come first.

elimination.verdict: The newly drowsy man.

questions.objective: Recognize early signs of increased ICP
questions.concept: Prioritizing a change in level of consciousness

questions.stem: The nurse is monitoring a patient with brain swelling after a large ischemic stroke who was drowsy but woke to his name at 1400. At 1600 he opens his eyes only to a painful stimulus. His blood pressure is 196/70 mm Hg, up from 150/84 mm Hg; his pulse is 48/min, down from 82/min; and his breathing is irregular with pauses. How does the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: Normal changes in vital signs during deep sleep
options.rationale: Pulse and breathing do slow somewhat in sleep. Sleep lowers blood pressure rather than raising it, and a sleeping patient wakes to his name, which he no longer does.

options.text: A late sign of severely raised intracranial pressure
options.rationale: Rising systolic pressure with a widening pulse pressure, a slow pulse and irregular breathing form the Cushing triad. It appears late, after consciousness has already fallen, and needs emergency action now.

options.text: Pain from a headache raising his blood pressure
options.rationale: Pain can raise blood pressure. Pain also speeds the pulse, and his pulse has slowed to 48/min while he barely responds, so pain does not explain the pattern.

options.text: An early sign of rising pressure to recheck in an hour
options.rationale: Rising pressure inside the skull is the right idea. The early sign was his falling level of consciousness at 1400; these vital sign changes come late, so waiting an hour is unsafe.

questions.takeaway: Decreased LOC is the earliest sign of increased ICP; the Cushing triad of hypertension with widened pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular respirations is a late sign.
questions.strategy: The slow pulse and pauses in breathing can look like sleep. A rising systolic pressure with a slowing pulse in a patient who no longer wakes to his name points to the late pattern.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Consciousness fell first; vital signs changed after.
High systolic pressure, wide pulse pressure, slow pulse, irregular breathing.
Pain speeds the pulse; sleep lowers pressure.

elimination.verdict: A late sign of severely raised intracranial pressure.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.objective: Recognize early signs of increased ICP
questions.concept: Early versus late signs of increased ICP

questions.scenario: On a neurology unit, the nurse monitors several patients at risk for increased intracranial pressure and compares each new finding with that patient's earlier assessment.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an early sign or a late sign of increased intracranial pressure.

rows.text: New restlessness and picking at the bed sheets
rows.rationale: Restlessness is a change in level of consciousness, which appears before vital signs change. Catching it gives the team time to act before pressure rises further.

rows.text: Irregular breathing with long pauses
rows.rationale: Irregular respirations complete the Cushing triad. Pressure is now affecting the brainstem centers that control breathing, which happens late.

rows.text: Disoriented to place after being oriented this morning
rows.rationale: New confusion is one of the first ways rising pressure shows itself. Orientation changes before the pulse or breathing do, so it is an early cue.

rows.text: Slower to answer questions than an hour ago
rows.rationale: A slower response is a subtle drop in level of consciousness. It is the earliest kind of change and is reported even when vital signs are normal.

rows.text: Pulse 46/min, down from 88/min
rows.rationale: A slowing pulse is part of the Cushing triad. It appears only once pressure inside the skull is severely raised, well after consciousness has changed.

rows.text: Blood pressure 210/68 mm Hg, up from 148/82 mm Hg
rows.rationale: Systolic pressure is climbing while diastolic falls, so the pulse pressure is widening. This is the hypertension of the Cushing triad, a late finding.

questions.takeaway: Early signs of increased ICP are changes in LOC such as restlessness, new confusion and slowed responses; late signs are the Cushing triad of hypertension with widened pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular respirations.
questions.strategy: Subtle behavior changes are easy to dismiss as minor. Consciousness changes first, so behavior rows are early and vital sign rows are late.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Restlessness, confusion and slow answers reflect consciousness.
Slow pulse, wide pulse pressure and irregular breathing are the triad.
Consciousness changes early; the triad comes late.

elimination.verdict: Early, early, late, late, late, early.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.objective: Recognize early signs of increased ICP
questions.concept: Early versus late signs of increased ICP
