questions.stem: In the emergency department, a patient reports 20 minutes of numbness in his right hand and trouble finding words this morning. Both resolved, and his neurologic examination is now normal. He asks to go home. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: "This warns that a stroke may follow, so you need evaluation today."
options.rationale: Symptoms that cleared with a normal examination point to a transient ischemic attack, which leaves no permanent damage. It is a warning sign of an impending stroke, so evaluation happens now.

options.text: "Learn the BE FAST signs, and call us if they ever return."
options.rationale: BE FAST teaching is useful and belongs in his discharge plan. Teaching alone without evaluating the cause of this warning misses the chance to prevent a stroke.

options.text: "This was a small stroke, and the damage it caused is permanent."
options.rationale: A stroke leaves persistent deficits from injured or dead brain tissue. His deficits resolved fully, so calling the damage permanent is inaccurate and needlessly frightening.

options.text: "Nothing lasting happened, so a clinic visit next week is enough."
options.rationale: It is true that a transient attack leaves no lasting damage. Its meaning is a warning of stroke to come, so waiting a week leaves him unprotected.

questions.takeaway: A TIA resolves within minutes to hours and causes no permanent damage, but it warns of an impending stroke and needs prompt evaluation.
questions.strategy: Two options say something true about a TIA. Only one acts on what the TIA means: a stroke may be coming.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Symptoms resolved and the examination is normal: a transient attack.
No persistent deficit means no permanent damage.
A warning sign needs evaluation now, not next week.

elimination.verdict: Explain that it is a warning and evaluation happens today.

questions.objective: Differentiate TIA, ischemic, and hemorrhagic stroke

questions.stem: Forty minutes after sudden left arm weakness and slurred speech began, a patient arrives in the emergency department. Her speech has cleared, but her left arm still drifts down when she holds it out. Her daughter says, "It's going away, so it's one of those mini strokes." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Agree with the daughter and begin stroke prevention teaching
options.rationale: Prevention teaching belongs later in her care. Labeling this a transient attack while a deficit persists is premature and could stop a time sensitive workup.

options.text: Recheck the arm in an hour to confirm the deficit resolves
options.rationale: Improving speech is encouraging, and a recheck will be part of her care. Waiting an hour before imaging uses up the treatment window while a deficit remains.

options.text: Ask the provider to cancel imaging since symptoms are improving
options.rationale: Improvement does happen, and it can tempt the team to scale back. Imaging is still needed because a remaining deficit means brain tissue is at risk now.

options.text: Continue the stroke response and prepare her for brain imaging
options.rationale: A transient attack is diagnosed only after every deficit resolves, and her arm drift persists. Persistent dysfunction is treated as a stroke in progress, so imaging and treatment decisions continue.

questions.takeaway: Until every deficit resolves, the patient is treated as having a stroke; improving symptoms do not make it a TIA.
questions.strategy: The family's label and the cleared speech both pull toward waiting. The arm drift that is still there decides it.

steps.detail: The left arm still drifts.
A transient attack requires full resolution.
Keep the stroke response moving to imaging.

elimination.verdict: Continue the stroke response and prepare for imaging.

questions.objective: Differentiate TIA, ischemic, and hemorrhagic stroke

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with sudden right sided weakness whose last known well was 60 minutes ago. The CT scanner is occupied for the next 15 minutes and the fibrinolytic has arrived from pharmacy. His wife says, "Time is brain, please start it now." Which action is correct?

options.text: Give the bolus now and send him to CT during the infusion
options.rationale: This saves minutes, and minutes do matter in stroke. If the scan then shows a bleed, the drug has already made the bleeding worse.

options.text: Repeat the NIHSS and start the drug if the score has risen
options.rationale: A rising NIHSS score does show worsening and is worth reporting. It cannot separate a clot from a bleed, so it cannot clear him for a fibrinolytic.

options.text: Hold the drug until a CT scan excludes bleeding
options.rationale: A fibrinolytic dissolves clots and would worsen a hemorrhagic stroke, and only imaging can tell the two apart. The drug waits for the scan, even with time pressure.

options.text: Draw clotting studies and start the drug once they are sent
options.rationale: Clotting studies such as PT and INR are part of the workup. Sending labs does not rule out a bleed in the brain; only imaging does.

questions.takeaway: Brain imaging to exclude hemorrhage comes before any fibrinolytic, because the drug treats only ischemic stroke.
questions.strategy: The wife quotes a true principle, which makes the fast options appealing. Speed never replaces the scan that rules out bleeding.

steps.detail: Clot or bleed is not yet known.
Only brain imaging separates them.
Labs and the NIHSS cannot exclude a bleed.

elimination.verdict: Hold the fibrinolytic until CT excludes hemorrhage.

questions.objective: Differentiate TIA, ischemic, and hemorrhagic stroke

questions.stem: In the emergency department, a patient's noncontrast CT shows an intracerebral hemorrhage 50 minutes after her symptoms began. A student nurse asks whether to prepare a fibrinolytic because the patient is inside the treatment window. Which reply by the nurse is correct?

options.text: "Yes, she is well within the 4.5 hour window from last known well."
options.rationale: The 4.5 hour window is real for eligible ischemic strokes. Timing does not make a bleed eligible, so this answer misapplies the rule.

options.text: "No, she is bleeding into the brain, and the drug would increase it."
options.rationale: A hemorrhagic stroke is a burst vessel, and a fibrinolytic breaks down clots that would help stop that bleeding. The time window applies only to eligible ischemic stroke.

options.text: "No, the drug waits until a second scan locates the clot."
options.rationale: This reply correctly declines the drug but gives the wrong reason. Her scan already shows bleeding, and there is no clot to find and dissolve.

options.text: "Yes, once her blood pressure is brought down first."
options.rationale: Blood pressure control is part of preparing an ischemic stroke patient for the drug. Lowering pressure does not change the fact that this vessel is bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Fibrinolytics are for eligible ischemic stroke only; a hemorrhagic stroke on CT rules them out regardless of time.
questions.strategy: The time window is tempting because it is a true fact. It belongs to ischemic stroke, and this scan shows a bleed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Intracerebral hemorrhage: a burst pipe.

steps.action: Match the drug to the type
steps.detail: Fibrinolytics treat clogged pipes only.
Of the two no answers, only one gives the right reason.

elimination.verdict: No, the drug would worsen the bleeding.

questions.objective: Differentiate TIA, ischemic, and hemorrhagic stroke
questions.concept: Fibrinolytics are not for hemorrhagic stroke

questions.stem: The provider reviews a patient's noncontrast CT, which shows no bleeding, and explains that a clot formed in place inside a narrowed artery in her brain. Her facial droop has not improved since yesterday. Her son asks what kind of stroke this is. Which reply by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "A blocked vessel: an ischemic stroke from an embolus."
options.rationale: This is an ischemic stroke, so the first half is right. An embolus is a clot that travels from elsewhere, and her clot formed in place, which makes it a thrombus.

options.text: "A warning attack: it will clear without lasting damage."
options.rationale: A transient attack resolves within minutes to hours with no permanent damage. Her droop has lasted since yesterday, so brain tissue is injured and this is a stroke.

options.text: "A burst vessel: a hemorrhagic stroke with bleeding."
options.rationale: A hemorrhagic stroke is a burst pipe with bleeding into or around the brain. Her CT shows no bleeding, so a ruptured vessel does not fit her findings.

options.text: "A blocked vessel: an ischemic stroke from a thrombus."
options.rationale: A thrombus forms in place and blocks the artery, a clogged pipe that causes ischemia. The droop has lasted since yesterday and the CT shows no bleeding, so this is an ischemic stroke.

questions.takeaway: TIA is temporary with no permanent damage; ischemic stroke is a blocked vessel, from a thrombus that forms in place or an embolus that travels; hemorrhagic stroke is a vessel that ruptures and bleeds.
questions.strategy: Two options share the right category, so the second half decides. Where the clot formed separates a thrombus from an embolus.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A droop since yesterday rules out a transient attack.
No bleeding on CT rules out hemorrhagic stroke.
A clot that formed in place is a thrombus.

elimination.verdict: "A blocked vessel: an ischemic stroke from a thrombus."

questions.objective: Differentiate TIA, ischemic, and hemorrhagic stroke
questions.concept: Classifying TIA, ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke

questions.stem: A patient admitted with a subarachnoid hemorrhage is at risk for increased intracranial pressure. Which actions does the nurse include in her plan of care to avoid raising her ICP? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place a rolled pillow behind her head to tuck her chin
options.rationale: A pillow behind the head can feel supportive. Tucking the chin flexes the neck, which squeezes the neck veins and traps blood in the skull.

options.text: Keep her head and neck in a midline position
options.rationale: Turning the head to one side can kink the neck veins and slow drainage from the brain. A midline head keeps that outflow open.

options.text: Give prescribed oxygen to keep her saturation up
options.rationale: Low oxygen makes brain vessels widen, which adds blood volume inside the skull. Avoiding hypoxia also protects injured brain tissue from secondary injury.

options.text: Group her bath, linen change and suctioning together
options.rationale: Grouping care does save her interruptions. Back to back activities stack their pressure rises on top of each other, so care is spaced out instead.

options.text: Raise the knee gatch so her hips are sharply flexed
options.rationale: Raising the knees may seem comfortable. Sharp hip flexion raises pressure in the abdomen and chest, which slows blood return from the brain and raises ICP.

options.text: Space her care with rest periods between tasks
options.rationale: Each activity, such as turning or suctioning, briefly raises intracranial pressure. Rest between tasks lets the pressure settle before the next rise.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed raised to 30 degrees
options.rationale: Raising the head of the bed helps blood drain from the brain through the neck veins. Better venous drainage lowers the volume inside the skull.

questions.takeaway: To avoid raising ICP: head of bed elevated with the head midline, no neck or hip flexion, care spaced rather than clustered, and no hypoxia.
questions.strategy: Clustering care is good practice for many patients, which makes it tempting here. With raised ICP, anything that stacks activities or kinks venous drainage is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Elevation and a midline head help; neck and hip flexion hinder.
Spacing care helps; grouping tasks adds rises together.
Avoiding hypoxia keeps brain vessels from widening.

elimination.verdict: Head of bed raised, head midline, care spaced out and oxygen as prescribed.

questions.coverage: Covered in Lecture PPT and Reading (Iggy).
questions.objective: Recognize early signs of increased ICP

questions.stem: Eighteen hours after a large ischemic stroke, a patient's oxygen saturation falls from 96% to 89% on room air while he dozes. His breath sounds are clear and he has no secretions. Oxygen is prescribed as needed. Which action protects his brain now?

options.text: Apply the prescribed oxygen and recheck the saturation
options.rationale: Injured brain tissue next to the stroke depends on the oxygen it still receives. Correcting hypoxia now prevents secondary injury, and the recheck shows whether it worked.

options.text: Lay the bed flat to send more blood to his head
options.rationale: Lying flat may seem to help blood reach the brain. It does not raise his oxygen level and increases his risk of aspiration after a large stroke.

options.text: Recheck the saturation at the next scheduled vital signs
options.rationale: Rechecking is a reasonable step after acting. Waiting hours leaves already injured brain tissue short of oxygen, which is the secondary injury to avoid.

options.text: Suction his airway to clear any secretions
options.rationale: Suctioning helps when secretions block the airway. His breath sounds are clear with no secretions, so suctioning adds no oxygen and can irritate the airway.

questions.takeaway: Prevent secondary brain injury after stroke by avoiding hypoxia and hypotension; act on a falling saturation now.
questions.strategy: Two options are good care in other situations. The finding here is low oxygen with a clear airway.

steps.detail: Saturation 89% with clear breath sounds.
Hypoxia worsens injury around the stroke.
Apply the prescribed oxygen and recheck.

elimination.verdict: Apply oxygen now and recheck.

questions.objective: Explain impacts on perfusion and cognition

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the latest findings of a patient on day 1 after an ischemic stroke. Which finding does the nurse report to the provider first?

options.text: Asks for her reading glasses so she can see the menu
options.rationale: This shows she is alert and engaged. It is a comfort request that can be met after the pressure is addressed.

options.text: Temperature 37.3 C, up from 37.0 C at 0800
options.rationale: Her temperature rose slightly since morning. It is still within the normal range and does not threaten brain perfusion right now.

options.text: Blood pressure 86/50 mm Hg, from 152/88 mm Hg at 0800
options.rationale: A sudden drop in pressure reduces blood flow to brain tissue that is already short of perfusion. Hypotension causes secondary injury, so this is reported first.

options.text: Left arm weakness that is unchanged since her admission
options.rationale: Arm weakness is a real deficit from her stroke. It is unchanged, so it is her baseline and not a new problem to report.

questions.takeaway: After a stroke, hypotension reduces brain perfusion and causes secondary injury; a sudden pressure drop is reported promptly.
questions.strategy: Low pressure can look less alarming than a stroke deficit. The brain needs perfusion, and the drop is the only new threat.

steps.detail: Pressure fell from 152/88 to 86/50 mm Hg.
Low pressure means less blood to injured brain.
Baseline weakness, normal temperature and a comfort request can wait.

elimination.verdict: The drop to 86/50 mm Hg.

questions.objective: Explain impacts on perfusion and cognition

questions.stem: A patient with a right hemisphere stroke has left leg weakness. He is alert and oriented, says, "My leg is fine," and has tried twice to stand alone despite call light teaching. Which plan addresses this behavior?

options.text: Apply a vest restraint whenever staff leave the room
options.rationale: A restraint would stop him from standing. It is not the least restrictive option and adds injury risk while supervision has not been tried.

options.text: Ask his family to convince him the leg is weak
options.rationale: Family support helps in recovery. Arguing about the leg does not change impaired judgment from the stroke, so the fall risk remains.

options.text: Supervise him closely at every transfer
options.rationale: Right hemisphere damage impairs judgment and causes impulsivity, so he overestimates what he can do. Teaching cannot fix that, but close supervision keeps him from falling.

options.text: Repeat the call light teaching and have him say it back
options.rationale: Teach back is a good way to check learning. He already knows about the call light; the problem is impaired judgment, not missing information.

questions.takeaway: Right hemisphere stroke impairs perception, judgment and impulse control; safety comes from supervision, not from more teaching.
questions.strategy: Teaching is the instinctive fix for a patient who ignores instructions. A right hemisphere patient knows the rule; the stroke removed his judgment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Right hemisphere: impulsive with poor judgment.
He has been taught; knowledge is not the gap.
Supervision before restraint.

elimination.verdict: Supervise him closely at every transfer.

questions.objective: Explain impacts on perfusion and cognition
questions.concept: Right hemisphere: impulsivity and poor judgment

questions.stem: During a meal, a patient with a right hemisphere stroke eats with her right hand, finishes only the food on the right half of her plate and does not notice her left arm hanging off the chair. She says she is full when asked about the rest of the meal. How does the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: Aphasia that keeps her from asking for help
options.rationale: Aphasia is a language problem that comes from left hemisphere damage. She speaks clearly about being full, so language is not her problem.

options.text: Left sided neglect from the right hemisphere stroke
options.rationale: Right hemisphere damage reduces awareness of the left side of space and body. Ignoring the left half of the plate and her own left arm fits neglect, which creates injury risk.

options.text: Poor appetite from the stress of hospitalization
options.rationale: Stress can reduce appetite, and she does say she is full. Poor appetite would not explain her ignoring her own left arm.

options.text: Weakness of the right arm from the stroke
options.rationale: One sided weakness does follow a stroke. A right hemisphere stroke affects the left side, and she uses her right hand to eat.

questions.takeaway: Right hemisphere stroke can cause left sided neglect: the patient ignores the left side of space and body, which is a safety risk.
questions.strategy: Her statement about being full makes appetite tempting. The arm hanging off the chair points to an awareness problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Right hemisphere affects the left side.
Left half of the plate and left arm both ignored.
Her speech is clear and her right hand works.

elimination.verdict: Left sided neglect.

questions.objective: Explain impacts on perfusion and cognition

questions.stem: "I waaant sooome waaater," a patient says in slow, slurred speech 2 days after a stroke. His speech has been like this since admission. He follows commands, names objects correctly and uses the right words in every sentence. His wife asks whether he has lost his ability to understand language. Which reply by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "No, slurred speech means the stroke is getting worse."
options.rationale: The nurse would report any new slurring at once. His speech has been the same since admission, so it is not a sign of worsening.

options.text: "Yes, he hears you but cannot make sense of what you say."
options.rationale: Trouble understanding spoken language is a receptive language problem. He follows commands and names objects correctly, which shows he understands.

options.text: "Yes, his brain is having trouble finding the right words."
options.rationale: Trouble finding words is aphasia, a language problem. He uses the correct words every time, so this is not what is happening.

options.text: "No, his words are right; the muscles that form them are weak."
options.rationale: He chooses correct words and follows commands, so his language is intact. Slurred speech from weak or uncoordinated muscles is dysarthria, a speech muscle problem.

questions.takeaway: Aphasia is a language problem with wrong or missing words; dysarthria is a speech muscle problem with correct words that are slurred.
questions.strategy: Slurred speech is easy to call aphasia. The words are right, which places the problem in the muscles, not in language.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every word is correct.
He follows commands and names objects.
Slurred but correct: dysarthria.

elimination.verdict: Language is intact; the speech muscles are affected.

questions.objective: Explain impacts on perfusion and cognition

questions.scenario: The nurse is caring for two patients on a stroke unit: one with a left hemisphere stroke and one with a right hemisphere stroke.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate which hemisphere is most likely affected.

rows.text: Ignores food on the left side of the tray
rows.rationale: The right hemisphere manages spatial awareness. Damage causes left sided neglect, so the patient misses the left half of the tray.

rows.text: Weakness and numbness of the right arm and leg
rows.rationale: Each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body. Right sided motor and sensory deficits come from the left hemisphere.

rows.text: Climbs out of bed without help, saying nothing is wrong
rows.rationale: Impulsivity with poor judgment follows right hemisphere damage. This patient overestimates ability and needs close supervision for safety.

rows.text: Cannot add up the cost of a meal
rows.rationale: Math and logic are left hemisphere functions in most people. Difficulty with calculations, such as adding a bill, is an expected left hemisphere deficit.

rows.text: Moves slowly and cautiously, checking each step
rows.rationale: Slow, cautious behavior is linked to left hemisphere damage. It contrasts with the impulsive behavior of right hemisphere damage.

rows.text: Cannot find words to name a cup
rows.rationale: Language and speech are controlled by the left hemisphere in most people. Losing words is aphasia, which follows left hemisphere damage.

questions.takeaway: Left hemisphere: aphasia, agraphia, calculation trouble, right sided deficits, slow and cautious. Right hemisphere: left neglect, impulsivity, poor judgment, left sided deficits.
questions.strategy: Behavior is the hard row: cautious belongs to the left hemisphere and impulsive to the right. Body side is always opposite the hemisphere.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Words and calculations are left hemisphere.
Right body deficits mean left hemisphere damage.
Impulsive and neglect are right; slow and cautious are left.

elimination.verdict: Left, right, left, right, left, left.

questions.objective: Explain impacts on perfusion and cognition

questions.stem: A patient with a left hemisphere stroke says, "I want... the... thing... drink," then cries. She raises her left hand when asked and points to the water jug. This pattern is unchanged since admission. Her son says, "She's confused now." Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "She understands you, but her brain can't find the words."
options.rationale: She follows a command and points to what she wants, so she knows what she means. Losing the words is aphasia from left hemisphere damage, and her tears show she knows it.

options.text: "Her speech muscles are weak, so her words come out slurred."
options.rationale: Weak speech muscles cause dysarthria, with correct words that come out slurred. Her words are clear when she finds them; her problem is missing words, not slurring.

options.text: "She cannot understand speech, so explaining things won't help."
options.rationale: Some aphasia does affect understanding. She raised her hand on request and pointed to the jug, so she understands what is said.

options.text: "This new confusion suggests pressure rising in her skull."
options.rationale: A new change in consciousness would be reported at once. This pattern has been the same since admission, so it is not new.

questions.takeaway: Aphasia is a language problem from left hemisphere damage; the patient may know exactly what she wants and still not find the words.
questions.strategy: The son's word confused invites an ICP answer. Unchanged since admission and following commands point to aphasia.

steps.detail: She follows a command and points correctly.
Missing words, not slurred words.
Unchanged since admission, so not new deterioration.

elimination.verdict: Aphasia: she understands but cannot find the words.

questions.objective: Explain impacts on perfusion and cognition
questions.concept: Aphasia: knows what she wants, cannot find the words

questions.stem: In the emergency department, a patient arrives at 0705 with a left facial droop and left arm weakness that she woke with at 0610. She went to bed at 2230 after watching television and talking normally with her husband. Which time does the nurse report as last known well?

options.rationale: Arrival time matters for tracking how fast the department delivers care. It says nothing about when the stroke began or when she was last normal.
Last known well is when she was last known to be normal. Nobody knows when during the night symptoms began, so the time she went to bed normal is used.

options.text: Unknown
options.rationale: It is true that no one saw the symptoms start. A last known well time can still be set from when she was last seen normal.
This is when the symptoms were discovered, not when she was last normal. Using it would make her look eligible for treatment that she may not qualify for.

questions.takeaway: Last known well is the last time the patient was known to be normal; for symptoms found on waking, that is when the patient was last seen normal before sleep.
questions.strategy: Discovery time feels like onset. Last known well works backward to the last moment she was normal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Talking normally at bedtime, 2230.
Waking at 0610 and arrival at 0705 come after onset.
A last normal time exists.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI
questions.concept: Last known well when symptoms are found on waking

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes who takes insulin is brought in with slurred speech, confusion and right arm weakness that began 80 minutes ago. He is breathing easily with an oxygen saturation of 97%. Which assessment does the nurse complete before he goes to CT?

options.text: Capillary blood glucose
options.rationale: Low blood glucose can cause slurred speech, confusion, weakness and altered consciousness, which mirror a stroke. A fingerstick takes a minute, and he takes insulin.

options.text: Repeat oxygen saturation every 5 minutes
options.rationale: Oxygenation is monitored after a stroke. His saturation is 97% and he breathes easily, so repeating it does not answer the stroke or mimic question.

options.text: Full medication reconciliation with his pharmacy
options.rationale: Current medications are part of the stroke history. A full reconciliation takes too long to finish before CT, and the team needs the key items now.

options.text: Swallow screen with sips of water
options.rationale: A swallow screen is required before any oral intake. He is not about to eat or drink, so it does not need to come before imaging.

questions.takeaway: Check blood glucose promptly in every suspected stroke; hypoglycemia can mimic stroke with slurred speech, confusion and weakness.
questions.strategy: The diabetes and insulin history are the cue. Each distractor is real stroke care at a different moment.

steps.detail: Insulin use raises the chance of low glucose.
Slurred speech, confusion and weakness fit both.
A fingerstick glucose before CT.

elimination.verdict: Capillary blood glucose.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI
questions.concept: Check blood glucose promptly: stroke mimic

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with sudden slurred speech and left arm weakness who had a blood glucose of 52 mg/dL and received treatment per protocol. Her glucose is now 104 mg/dL, but the slurred speech and left arm weakness are unchanged. Last known well was 95 minutes ago. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Cancel the stroke alert, because low glucose explains it
options.rationale: Low glucose can mimic a stroke, and that is why it was treated first. Her deficits did not resolve with a normal glucose, so it does not explain them.

options.text: Ask for the fibrinolytic to be started now
options.rationale: Speed does matter with 95 minutes already gone. A fibrinolytic is never given before brain imaging has excluded bleeding, and she has not been scanned.

options.text: Recheck the glucose every 15 minutes for an hour first
options.rationale: Rechecking glucose after treatment is sensible. Delaying imaging an hour while deficits persist uses up her treatment window.

options.text: Keep the stroke alert active and continue to brain imaging
options.rationale: Treating the low glucose came first, and reassessment shows the deficits persist with a normal glucose. A stroke is still possible, so the stroke pathway continues.

questions.takeaway: Treat hypoglycemia first, then reassess neuro status; deficits that persist after glucose is normal keep the stroke pathway active.
questions.strategy: Finding low glucose feels like solving the case. The reassessment, not the low number, decides whether it was a mimic.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Treat the low glucose, then reassess.
Glucose is normal; deficits persist.
Imaging before any treatment decision.

elimination.verdict: Keep the stroke alert active and go to imaging.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI
questions.concept: Check blood glucose promptly: stroke mimic

questions.stem: The team is considering a fibrinolytic for a patient whose noncontrast CT shows no hemorrhage 110 minutes after last known well. His daughter arrives and says he takes a blood thinner for an irregular heartbeat. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Start a second IV line for the infusion
options.rationale: IV access per protocol is part of the nurse's role. Preparing for the drug before the team knows about the anticoagulant moves toward a possibly unsafe treatment.

options.text: Begin frequent neuro and blood pressure checks
options.rationale: Frequent neuro and blood pressure checks are essential during treatment. They monitor for bleeding later but do not help the team decide eligibility now.

options.text: Tell the stroke team about the blood thinner now
options.rationale: An anticoagulant raises bleeding risk and may make the fibrinolytic unsafe. Eligibility depends on history and medications, so the team needs this before deciding.

options.text: Reassure the daughter that the clear CT makes it safe
options.rationale: A clear CT does exclude a bleed already present. It does not account for bleeding risk from his medication, so the reassurance is false.

questions.takeaway: Obtaining and communicating the medical history and current medications is a nursing role that directly affects fibrinolytic eligibility.
questions.strategy: The clear CT makes the drug feel cleared. New information about a contraindication goes to the decision makers before anyone moves forward.

steps.detail: He takes an anticoagulant.
A fibrinolytic plus a blood thinner raises bleeding risk.
The team decides eligibility with complete history.

elimination.verdict: Report the blood thinner to the stroke team now.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI

questions.nursesNote: 1000: Day 1 after an ischemic stroke with left sided weakness. NIHSS 6 at 0600 and 6 at 1000. Left arm drift less than at 0600. Left facial droop unchanged from 0600. Now cannot feel light touch on her left forearm, which she felt at 0600. Speech clear with correct words, as at 0600. Newly slow to answer and dozes off between questions. Blood pressure 152/84 mm Hg, within her prescribed range. Reaches past her cup with her left hand, which she did not do at 0600. Pupils equal and brisk, as at 0600.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that signal neurologic worsening and need to be reported now.

segments.text: NIHSS 6 at 0600 and 6 at 1000
segments.rationale: An unchanged total looks reassuring, but improvement on one item can offset new deficits on others. The NIHSS standardizes the assessment and does not replace looking at each finding.

segments.text: Left arm drift less than at 0600
segments.rationale: Less drift means her left arm strength has improved since the baseline. Improvement is documented and welcome, but it is not a sign of worsening.

segments.text: Left facial droop unchanged from 0600
segments.rationale: The droop was present at the 0600 baseline and has not changed. A deficit that matches the baseline is not new and does not signal worsening.

segments.text: Now cannot feel light touch on her left forearm, which she felt at 0600
segments.rationale: Sensation is one of the areas the NIHSS checks, and this loss is new since the baseline. Even a subtle new deficit can signal a worsening or new stroke, so it is reported now.

segments.text: Speech clear with correct words, as at 0600
segments.rationale: Her speech and language match the baseline. A finding that is the same as at 0600 is not a new change and does not need an urgent report.

segments.text: Newly slow to answer and dozes off between questions
segments.rationale: A decline in level of consciousness is one of the earliest signs that the brain is worsening. It is new since 0600, so it is reported now even though the total score held.

segments.text: Blood pressure 152/84 mm Hg, within her prescribed range
segments.rationale: Her blood pressure sits inside the range the provider set for her. It is monitored closely, but it does not show a change in her neurologic status.

segments.text: Reaches past her cup with her left hand, which she did not do at 0600
segments.rationale: Missing a target she can see is a new coordination problem, another area the NIHSS checks. Because it was absent at 0600, it counts as a new deficit to report.

segments.text: Pupils equal and brisk, as at 0600
segments.rationale: Equal, brisk pupils match her baseline and are reassuring for now. They do not cancel out the other new findings, which still need to be reported.

questions.takeaway: Compare each NIHSS area with the baseline; an unchanged total can hide new deficits when another area improves.
questions.strategy: The steady total of 6 pulls toward calling her stable. New sensory loss, drowsiness and missed reaching are each worse than at 0600, and the improved arm offsets them in the score.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Compare every finding with 0600.
An improved arm can hide new deficits in the score.

steps.action: Keep what is new and worse
steps.detail: Sensory loss, drowsiness and missed reaching.

elimination.verdict: The new sensory loss, the drowsiness and the missed reaching.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI
questions.concept: NIHSS baseline and change over time

questions.stem: On day 3 after a left hemisphere stroke, a patient has had right arm weakness since admission, and her NIHSS score at 0800 was unchanged from day 2. At 1000 she has a new right facial droop and cannot lift her right leg, which she lifted at 0800. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Position the right leg in alignment and request a therapy referral
options.rationale: Positioning and therapy support function after a stroke. Treating this as an old deficit misses that the leg weakness is new today.

options.text: Compare her NIHSS score at the next scheduled check
options.rationale: The NIHSS is used to track change over time. Waiting for the next scheduled check ignores a change the nurse has already found.

options.text: Document the change and watch whether it clears within the hour
options.rationale: Documentation is required for any change. Watching for an hour delays action on a possible new stroke, which is time sensitive.

options.text: Report the new deficits now, using 0800 as her baseline
options.rationale: The 0800 assessment is the baseline, and the facial droop and leg weakness are new since then. Even subtle changes can mean a worsening or new stroke, so they are reported now.

questions.takeaway: The NIHSS sets a baseline and tracks change; any new deficit compared with baseline is reported at once.
questions.strategy: Her existing right arm weakness makes new right sided findings look like more of the same. The 0800 baseline shows they are new.

steps.detail: At 0800 she could lift her right leg and had no facial droop.
Both are new at 1000.
New deficits are reported immediately.

elimination.verdict: Report the new deficits now.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI
questions.concept: NIHSS baseline and change over time

questions.stem: Three hours after admission for an ischemic stroke, a patient has no swallow screen documented. He says he is very thirsty, and his oral aspirin is due now. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Offer ice chips to ease his thirst
options.rationale: Ice chips seem harmless and his thirst is real. They melt into liquid he could aspirate, so they are held until he is screened.

options.text: Give the aspirin with a small sip of water
options.rationale: Aspirin is part of stroke care when appropriate. A sip of water with a tablet is still oral intake, which is unsafe before the screen.

options.text: Complete a swallow screen before giving anything by mouth
options.rationale: No food, fluids or medications are given until a swallow screen is completed. Aspiration can cause pneumonia and raises the risk of serious illness and death after a stroke.

options.text: Hold the aspirin but give water slowly with him upright
options.rationale: Holding the tablet is correct, and upright positioning lowers risk. Water is still oral intake, and being thirsty does not make it safe.

questions.takeaway: Every stroke patient stays NPO, including oral medications and water, until a swallow screen is completed.
questions.strategy: Thirst and a due medication create pressure to give something by mouth. Every oral option is the same unsafe step.

steps.detail: No swallow screen is documented.
Aspirin, ice chips and water are all oral intake.
Screen first.

elimination.verdict: Complete the swallow screen first.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI
questions.concept: NPO until swallow screen, including medications

questions.stem: At lunchtime on a stroke unit, a patient with right sided weakness after a stroke needs help eating. Assistive personnel offer to feed her. No swallow screen is documented today. Which action does the nurse take before delegating the feeding?

options.text: Ask the family to feed her instead
options.rationale: Family members can help with meals later. Changing who feeds her does not answer whether she can swallow safely.

options.text: Confirm that a swallow screen has been passed
options.rationale: The registered nurse must confirm swallowing safety before feeding is delegated. Once she has passed the screen, assistive personnel can help her eat.

options.text: Teach assistive personnel to stop if she coughs
options.rationale: Knowing when to stop is useful for anyone feeding her. Without a passed screen, coughing would mean aspiration has already happened.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 30 degrees
options.rationale: Raising the head of the bed is part of safe feeding and lowers aspiration risk. It does not show whether she can swallow, which only the screen answers.

questions.takeaway: Feeding can be delegated to assistive personnel only after the RN confirms the patient has passed a swallow screen.
questions.strategy: Each distractor makes feeding safer, which makes them appealing. None answers whether she can swallow.

steps.detail: No screen documented today.
Swallowing safety is confirmed by the RN first.
Coaching, family feeding and positioning do not replace the screen.

elimination.verdict: Confirm the swallow screen first.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI
questions.concept: Delegating feeding after the swallow screen

questions.stem: A patient admitted with a stroke has word finding difficulty, right sided weakness and urinary incontinence. Saliva is pooling in the right corner of his mouth, and his breathing sounds gurgly. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Assess his airway and gag reflex
options.rationale: Pooled saliva and gurgly breathing point to a threat to his airway. Airway is the first nursing priority after a stroke, so it comes before hygiene or comfort.

options.text: Provide perineal care and skin protection
options.rationale: Perineal care protects his skin and dignity and will be done soon. It does not address a threatened airway, which comes first.

options.text: Begin his speech and language exercises
options.rationale: Communication is part of function after a stroke. Working on speech now ignores the airway finding and is not a first action.

options.text: Change his wet gown and linens
options.rationale: Wet linens need changing for comfort and skin integrity. Like perineal care, this is important but can wait until his airway is secure.

questions.takeaway: After a stroke, protect the airway first: airway, brain checks, swallow, safety, function, and monitoring for deterioration.
questions.strategy: Incontinence is the visible problem and invites cleanup. The gurgling is the threat to life.

steps.detail: Pooled saliva and gurgly breathing.
Airway before skin and comfort.
Speech work comes later.

elimination.verdict: Assess his gag reflex and airway.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI
questions.concept: Airway is the first nursing priority after stroke

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with a suspected acute ischemic stroke who arrived 70 minutes after his last known well time. His wife has given his history, and he is waiting for brain imaging while the team decides whether he is a fibrinolytic candidate. Which action by the nurse is appropriate at this stage?

options.text: Give his scheduled oral aspirin with sips of water
options.rationale: Aspirin is part of stroke prevention when appropriate. Nothing goes by mouth before a swallow screen, and an antiplatelet before imaging could worsen a bleed nobody has ruled out.

options.text: Verify working IV access per protocol
options.rationale: Obtaining or verifying IV access is a nursing role while eligibility is decided. Imaging, labs and possible treatment all depend on it, so checking it now prevents delay.

options.text: Tell his wife that he qualifies for the clot dissolving drug
options.rationale: The nurse gathers much of the data behind eligibility. The decision rests on a full clinical and imaging evaluation by the provider team, and his imaging is not done yet.

options.text: Start the fibrinolytic so that it runs during the scan
options.rationale: Starting fast seems to save brain tissue, which makes this tempting. Imaging must exclude hemorrhage first, so a fibrinolytic never starts before the scan.

questions.takeaway: While eligibility is decided, the nurse obtains last known well and history, verifies IV access, monitors vital signs and performs frequent neurologic checks; the team decides treatment after imaging.
questions.strategy: The wrong options either take the team's decision or act before imaging. The right one prepares for treatment without starting it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Eligibility belongs to the team after imaging.

steps.action: Ask whether it acts before imaging
steps.detail: Aspirin and the fibrinolytic both do.
IV access is the nurse's job now.

elimination.verdict: Verify working IV access per protocol.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI
questions.concept: Nursing role in fibrinolytic candidate evaluation

questions.stem: In an outpatient clinic, the nurse finds a patient with sudden right facial droop and arm weakness. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Prepare the patient for brain imaging
options.rationale: Imaging excludes hemorrhage and is required before a fibrinolytic. It follows activation and history so the team can act on the result.

options.text: Activate the emergency stroke response
options.rationale: Once a stroke is recognized, the response is activated without delay. Every minute of delay costs brain tissue, so the call comes before the detailed history.

options.text: Establish and communicate the last known well time
options.rationale: The last known well time drives treatment eligibility. It is gathered once help is on the way and reported to the stroke team.

options.text: Recognize the stroke signs using BE FAST
options.rationale: Recognition comes first, because nothing else starts until someone sees the stroke. BE FAST gives a quick structured check of balance, eyes, face, arm and speech.

options.text: Support the team as it determines treatment
options.rationale: The treatment decision comes last because it needs the time, the history and the imaging. The nurse then monitors closely whatever is chosen.

questions.takeaway: Time is brain: recognize, activate, establish last known well, image, then determine treatment.
questions.strategy: Gathering the history before calling for help feels thorough. Activation comes right after recognition so the team is moving while the nurse gathers facts.

steps.detail: Nothing happens until the stroke is seen.
Activate, then gather last known well.
Imaging before the treatment decision.

elimination.verdict: Recognize, activate, last known well, imaging, treatment decision.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI
questions.concept: Time is brain: stroke alert sequence

questions.stem: A patient receiving alteplase for an ischemic stroke with left arm weakness is 20 minutes into the infusion. She has an indwelling urinary catheter. Which new finding does the nurse recognize as a possible sign of bleeding?

options.text: Mild ache at the IV site with no oozing
options.rationale: Bleeding from puncture sites is a warning sign, so an IV site complaint deserves a look. An ache with no blood shows no bleeding, so it is not the sign here.

options.text: Left hand grip stronger than before the infusion
options.rationale: A change during the infusion can feel alarming. A stronger grip shows improvement from restored blood flow, which is the hoped for effect of the drug, not bleeding.

options.text: Pink tinged urine in her catheter bag
options.rationale: Blood in the urine is one of the bleeding signs watched for after a thrombolytic. It shows the drug is impairing clotting, so bleeding elsewhere, including the brain, is possible.

options.text: Dry mouth with a request for a drink of water
options.rationale: A dry mouth is a comfort concern, and she stays NPO until a swallow screen is done. It does not suggest bleeding and does not change her monitoring.

questions.takeaway: After a thrombolytic, watch for bleeding: new or worsening deficits, severe headache, acute hypertension, nausea and vomiting, and bleeding from puncture sites, urine or the GI tract.
questions.strategy: The IV site option sounds like puncture site bleeding but shows no blood. Bleeding can appear far from the brain, so check the urine, puncture sites and stool too.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only the urine shows blood; the IV site does not ooze.
Stronger grip and dry mouth are not bleeding.

elimination.verdict: Pink tinged urine in her catheter bag.

questions.objective: Apply findings to NCLEX style clinical situations

questions.stem: The nurse reassesses a patient who finished a fibrinolytic infusion 2 hours ago. His left hand grip was weak before treatment, and his blood glucose was 110 mg/dL ten minutes ago. Which finding does the nurse act on first?

options.text: Opens his eyes only when his name is called repeatedly
options.rationale: A drop in level of consciousness after a thrombolytic can signal bleeding in the brain. It is the most dangerous change listed and calls for urgent evaluation.

options.text: Pink tinged urine in the urinal, first seen this hour
options.rationale: Hematuria is a listed bleeding sign and will be reported. It is less urgent than a sign that the brain itself may be bleeding.

options.text: Left hand grip weaker than the right, as before treatment
options.rationale: Weakness is worth tracking after a stroke. This one matches his pretreatment baseline, so it is not a new change.

options.text: Blood oozing at the IV site, first seen this hour
options.rationale: Puncture site bleeding is a real warning sign that needs pressure and a report. It is not the threat to his brain that a fall in consciousness is.

questions.takeaway: After a thrombolytic, a decline in LOC or new neurologic worsening outranks other bleeding signs because it may mean intracranial hemorrhage.
questions.strategy: Three findings are real bleeding signs or deficits. The one in the brain and new since treatment wins.

steps.detail: The weak grip was present before treatment.
Glucose was normal 10 minutes ago.
A brain bleed outranks oozing and hematuria.

elimination.verdict: His decline in consciousness.

questions.objective: Apply findings to NCLEX style clinical situations

questions.stem: Two days after a bowel resection, a patient walked to the bathroom with the nurse's help at 0200, talking clearly and moving both arms normally. At 0400 the nurse saw her asleep during rounds. At 0600 she is woken for vital signs and has a new left facial droop and slurred speech. Which time does the nurse report as last known well?

options.text: Unknown, since she was asleep
options.rationale: A sleeping patient's onset time is unknown, but her last normal time is not. The nurse confirmed normal speech and movement at 0200, so that time is reported.
At 0400 she was seen, and it is tempting to use the latest time anyone saw her. She was asleep, so nobody could tell whether her face and speech were normal then.
At 0600 the deficits were found, which is not when they began. Reporting the discovery time could make her look eligible for treatment that depends on time when she may not be.
Last known well is the last time she was known to be normal. At 0200 the nurse watched her walk and talk normally, which is the latest confirmed normal time.

questions.takeaway: Last known well is the last time someone confirmed the patient was normal; seeing a patient asleep does not confirm anything.
questions.strategy: The 0400 rounds feel like the most recent good time. What tips it is that she was asleep then, so only the 0200 walk confirms normal function.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Last known well means last known to be normal.
0400 was sleep, 0600 was discovery.
At 0200 she walked and talked normally.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI
questions.concept: Last known well when symptoms are found on waking

questions.stem: The nurse is talking with a patient admitted yesterday with a stroke. Speaking takes her great effort, she pauses between words, and she tires after a few sentences. Which additional finding shows a language problem rather than a speech muscle problem?

options.text: She calls her toothbrush a spoon
options.rationale: Calling an object by the wrong name is a problem forming the right word, which is aphasia. Weak speech muscles slur words but do not swap one word for another.

options.text: Saliva pools at the corner of her mouth
options.rationale: Pooled saliva shows weak mouth and face muscles, which fits dysarthria and also signals aspiration risk. It says nothing about whether she can find or understand words.

options.text: Her words come out thick and slurred
options.rationale: Thick, slurred words come from weak or uncoordinated speech muscles, which is dysarthria. This finding points away from a language problem, not toward one.

options.text: She cries when she cannot finish a sentence
options.rationale: Frustration fits a patient who knows what she wants but cannot say it. Speech already takes her great effort, so tears can follow muscle fatigue as easily as missing words.

questions.takeaway: Aphasia shows as wrong or missing words and trouble understanding; slurred, effortful speech with the right words is dysarthria, and frustration can occur with either.
questions.strategy: Crying over an unfinished sentence matches the picture of a patient who knows what she wants. What tips it is that her speech is already effortful, so only the wrong word points clearly to language.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Note what the stem already shows
steps.detail: Effortful, paused, tiring speech fits either problem.
Slurring and pooled saliva point to muscles.
Wrong names for objects mean language.

elimination.verdict: She calls her toothbrush a spoon.

questions.objective: Explain impacts on perfusion and cognition
questions.concept: Aphasia: knows what she wants, cannot find the words

questions.stem: At the start of the night shift, one room within sight of the nurses' station opens up. The nurse is caring for four patients who each had a stroke or warning symptoms this week. Which patient does the nurse move to that room?

options.text: Left hemisphere stroke, dense right leg weakness, asks before each move
options.rationale: Dense weakness raises fall risk, which makes this patient tempting. Left hemisphere damage brings slow, cautious behavior, and he asks for help before each move, so his own caution lowers the risk.

options.text: Right hemisphere stroke, mild left sided weakness, oriented
options.rationale: Right hemisphere damage affects perception and judgment and causes impulsivity, so his mild weakness is the danger: he may feel able to stand and try alone. Close observation fits that risk best.

options.text: Left hemisphere stroke, aphasia, walks steadily with a cane
options.rationale: Aphasia makes asking for help harder, but she walks steadily with a cane and left hemisphere damage favors cautious behavior. Her fall risk is lower than that of an impulsive patient.

options.text: Transient ischemic attack, symptoms fully resolved, walking unaided
options.rationale: A transient ischemic attack leaves no permanent tissue damage, and his symptoms have fully resolved. He walks without help and has no deficit that raises his fall risk tonight.

questions.takeaway: Right hemisphere strokes impair judgment and cause impulsivity, so mild weakness can carry the highest fall risk; left hemisphere strokes bring slow, cautious behavior.
questions.strategy: Dense weakness looks like the biggest fall risk. What tips it is behavior: the left hemisphere patient asks before each move, while right hemisphere damage brings impulsivity.

steps.detail: Fall risk depends on behavior as much as strength.
Right: impulsive, poor judgment. Left: slow, cautious.
The impulsive patient with mild weakness.

elimination.verdict: Right hemisphere stroke, mild left sided weakness, oriented.

questions.objective: Explain impacts on perfusion and cognition
questions.concept: Right hemisphere: impulsivity and poor judgment

questions.scenario: Thirty five minutes into an alteplase infusion for an ischemic stroke, a patient's speech, which had begun to clear, is garbled again, and she reports a sudden severe headache. She vomits once. Her blood pressure has risen from 162/90 to 204/114 mm Hg.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Slow the infusion and recheck her in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Slowing seems like a careful compromise. Any more of the drug can worsen a bleed, and waiting 15 minutes delays the scan.

options.text: Prepare her for an emergency head CT
options.rationale: Urgent evaluation for these signs includes a head CT. The scan shows whether bleeding has started in the brain.

options.text: Give an analgesic and recheck her pain in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Her headache is real and does need relief. Treating it as pain and waiting 30 minutes ignores a likely bleed.

options.text: Stop the alteplase infusion and notify the provider now
options.rationale: Severe headache with neurologic worsening after a thrombolytic means immediate attention. Stopping the drug prevents further clot breakdown while the provider is reached.

options.text: Intracranial hemorrhage from the fibrinolytic
options.rationale: New headache, vomiting, returning deficit and a pressure spike during the infusion fit bleeding in the brain. Bleeding is the major concern with fibrinolytics.

options.text: Hypoglycemia mimicking a new stroke
options.rationale: Low glucose can mimic stroke signs. It would not cause a severe headache and a sudden pressure spike during the infusion.

options.text: Expected effect of restored blood flow
options.rationale: Restored flow is the goal of the drug. Its expected effect is improvement, not returning deficits and a severe headache.

options.text: Migraine headache from stress
options.rationale: Stress can trigger a migraine with headache and vomiting. A migraine would not explain her returning speech deficit and pressure spike during a fibrinolytic.

options.text: Blood pressure
options.rationale: Acute hypertension is one of her warning signs and raises bleeding risk. Frequent blood pressure monitoring is a priority after a thrombolytic.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks fluid balance over days. It tells the nurse nothing about bleeding happening in the next hour.

options.text: Bowel sounds
options.rationale: Bowel sounds are part of a full assessment. They do not track the bleeding or pressure that threatens her now.

options.text: Level of consciousness and neurologic status
options.rationale: Frequent neuro checks show whether she is worsening. A further decline in consciousness would signal growing bleeding or pressure.

questions.takeaway: Severe headache plus neurologic worsening after a thrombolytic means possible intracranial hemorrhage: stop the drug, notify, prepare for head CT, and monitor neuro status and blood pressure closely.
questions.strategy: Each wrong action treats one symptom or waits. The combination of headache, returning deficit and pressure spike points to bleeding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Headache, vomiting, returning deficit and hypertension during alteplase.
Stop the drug, notify and prepare for a head CT.
Neuro status and blood pressure.

elimination.verdict: Intracranial hemorrhage: stop, notify, CT; monitor neuro status and blood pressure.

questions.objective: Apply findings to NCLEX style clinical situations

questions.stem: At a home health visit, a patient recovering from a subarachnoid hemorrhage describes what he is doing to prevent another stroke. Which statement needs follow up by the nurse?

options.text: "I can't change my family history, so I focus on my pressure."
options.rationale: This sounds like giving up, which makes it tempting to correct. Family history is nonmodifiable and blood pressure control is a modifiable prevention step, so his plan is accurate.

options.text: "I haven't smoked since the bleed and threw out my lighters."
options.rationale: Smoking cessation is a core prevention step whatever kind of stroke he had. Removing his lighters makes a relapse harder, so this statement shows sound understanding and needs no follow up.

options.text: "I check my blood pressure each morning and write it down."
options.rationale: Blood pressure control is a core prevention step, and daily readings help his provider adjust treatment. This statement shows the teaching worked and needs no follow up.

options.text: "I started a daily aspirin, like my neighbor takes."
options.rationale: Aspirin belongs in stroke prevention only when appropriate, because it slows clotting. After a bleed in the brain, starting it on his own could invite another bleed, so the nurse follows up.

questions.takeaway: In ABCS the A is aspirin when appropriate: after a hemorrhagic stroke, self started aspirin needs follow up, while blood pressure control and smoking cessation always apply.
questions.strategy: Aspirin is the A in ABCS, so this statement looks like good prevention. What tips it is the bleed: aspirin is not appropriate for him without his provider's direction.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that needs follow up.
A subarachnoid hemorrhage is a burst vessel.
Aspirin is only when appropriate, and slows clotting.

elimination.verdict: "I started a daily aspirin, like my neighbor takes."

questions.objective: Recognize signs and symptoms of neurologic emergencies

questions.stem: On a rehabilitation unit, the charge nurse lists four lunch assignments for assistive personnel. Each patient had a stroke. Which assignment does the nurse question?

options.text: Set up the tray for the patient who passed and feeds himself
options.rationale: Setting up a tray for a patient who passed his screen and feeds himself fits the role of assistive personnel. Nothing new has changed his swallowing, so this assignment stands.

options.text: Feed the patient with aphasia who passed her screen this morning
options.rationale: Aphasia can make it hard for her to say she is struggling, so this assignment looks risky. She passed her swallow screen this morning, so feeding her is safe to delegate.

options.text: Feed the patient with a new facial droop since his screen yesterday
options.rationale: Delegation is safe only after the RN confirms that swallowing is safe. A new facial droop is a change since his screen, so the RN reassesses swallowing before anyone feeds him.

options.text: Feed the patient with right arm weakness who passed her screen today
options.rationale: Arm weakness is why she needs feeding help, not a sign that her swallowing has changed. Her screen was passed today, so this assignment is safe to delegate.

questions.takeaway: A passed swallow screen clears delegation only while it still reflects the patient; a new neurologic change means the RN reassesses swallowing before feeding is delegated.
questions.strategy: The patient with aphasia seems least able to signal trouble. What tips it is that only one patient has a new change since his screen, which leaves that screen out of date.

steps.detail: Find the assignment that is not safe to delegate.
All four passed a screen.

steps.action: Look for change since the screen
steps.detail: A new facial droop means swallowing must be reassessed.

elimination.verdict: Feed the patient with a new facial droop since his screen yesterday.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing assessments for stroke and TBI
questions.concept: Delegating feeding after the swallow screen

questions.stem: A woman with months of heavy menstrual bleeding is dizzy when she stands and tires after walking a short distance. Her lungs are clear, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 97% on room air, and hemoglobin is 7.1 g/dL. Which action addresses the cause of her symptoms?
questions.takeaway: Low oxygen carrying capacity causes hypoxia despite a normal saturation; oxygen therapy treats hypoxemia, so the underlying cause must be addressed.
questions.strategy: Applying oxygen feels like the safe move for a dizzy patient. The normal saturation shows her blood is not short of oxygen per molecule; it is short of hemoglobin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 97% means the hemoglobin present is well loaded with oxygen.
7.1 g/dL means too little carrier: a carrying capacity problem, not hypoxemia.

steps.action: Match the action to the cause
steps.detail: Only treatment of the low hemoglobin restores delivery to the tissues.

elimination.verdict: Report the hemoglobin and dizziness for treatment.

questions.objective: Explain ventilation, diffusion and perfusion in gas exchange

options.text: Report the hemoglobin and her dizziness to the provider for treatment
options.rationale: A hemoglobin of 7.1 g/dL is far below the expected minimum of about 12 g/dL for women, so her blood carries much less oxygen even though it is well saturated. Treating the low hemoglobin and its cause restores oxygen to her tissues.

options.text: Continue routine monitoring, since saturation and breathing rate are normal
options.rationale: Her saturation and rate are normal, which makes this choice tempting. A saturation describes the hemoglobin present, not how much there is, and her dizziness shows her tissues are short of oxygen now.

options.text: Coach slow, deep breathing before each walk in the hallway
options.rationale: Deep breathing improves ventilation, and her ventilation is already adequate with clear lungs and a normal rate. Her problem is too little hemoglobin to carry oxygen, which breathing exercises cannot change.

options.text: Apply oxygen by nasal cannula and recheck the saturation in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Oxygen raises the saturation of the hemoglobin she has, and hers is already 97%. It cannot replace the missing hemoglobin, so delivery to her tissues stays low and the cause goes untreated.

questions.stem: A patient with a urinary tract infection has a temperature of 39.6 °C and is shivering. Over the past hour her respiratory rate rose from 18 to 26 breaths per minute and her oxygen saturation fell from 96% to 92% on room air. Her lungs are clear, and her blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg with a strong radial pulse. Which explanation for the change in her oxygenation should guide the nurse's care?
questions.takeaway: An increased metabolic rate, as with fever and shivering, raises oxygen demand and can lower saturation even when the lungs are clear.
questions.strategy: Clear lungs push students toward anxiety or a hidden lung cause. Match each explanation to the findings in the stem; only raised demand fits fever with shivering.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear lungs argue against fluid in the alveoli.
No low blood pressure or weak pulse is reported.

steps.action: Find the cause in the stem
steps.detail: Fever and shivering are the named antecedent; both raise oxygen use.

elimination.verdict: A raised metabolic rate explains the change.

questions.objective: Explain ventilation, diffusion and perfusion in gas exchange

options.text: Fluid in the alveoli is keeping oxygen from crossing into the blood
options.rationale: Fluid in the alveoli would cause a diffusion problem, but her lungs are clear. Nothing in her findings points to the membrane, so this explanation sends care in the wrong direction.

options.text: Low blood volume is keeping blood from reaching the alveoli
options.rationale: Hypovolemia does reduce oxygenation, and fever can dehydrate a patient over time. Her blood pressure of 124/78 mm Hg and strong pulse do not support a perfusion problem now.

options.text: Anxiety about the infection is making her breathe faster
options.rationale: Anxiety can raise the respiratory rate, but it does not explain a falling saturation. Labeling the change as anxiety would delay care for a measurable rise in oxygen demand.

options.text: A raised metabolic rate is using oxygen faster than it is replaced
options.rationale: Fever and shivering raise the metabolic rate, so the tissues use more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide. Treating the fever and shivering as prescribed lowers that demand while the nurse monitors her saturation.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it mainly affects ventilation, diffusion or perfusion.
questions.takeaway: Ventilation moves air, diffusion moves gas across the alveolar capillary membrane, and perfusion delivers blood; an open airway does not guarantee oxygenation.
questions.strategy: The pull is to call every breathing problem a ventilation problem. Ask where the failure sits: air movement, the membrane, or the blood flow.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trace air from the mouth to the alveoli, across the membrane, then into the blood.
Air not moving is ventilation; fluid on the membrane is diffusion; too little blood is perfusion.

elimination.verdict: Ventilation, diffusion, perfusion, ventilation.

questions.objective: Explain ventilation, diffusion and perfusion in gas exchange
questions.scenario: The nurse is reviewing four patients on a medical unit to decide which part of gas exchange is most affected for each.

rows.text: After major blood loss in surgery, a patient has a blood pressure of 80/48 mm Hg and cool, pale skin
rows.rationale: Low blood volume means less blood reaches the alveoli and the tissues. The airway can be open and the lungs clear while the tissues still go short of oxygen.

rows.text: A patient with weak respiratory muscles cannot take a deep breath or cough forcefully
rows.rationale: Weak breathing muscles limit how much air moves in and out of the lungs. The failure is in air movement, so it happens before gas ever reaches the alveoli.

rows.text: A patient with painful rib fractures takes shallow breaths at 10 per minute to avoid pain
rows.rationale: Shallow, slow breaths taken to avoid pain move too little air into and out of the lungs. That is a ventilation problem, even when the alveoli and the blood flow are normal.

rows.text: A patient with pneumonia has fluid filling the alveoli of one lobe
rows.rationale: Fluid in the alveoli adds a barrier that oxygen must cross to reach the capillaries. Air still moves in, but gas cannot pass well across the alveolar capillary membrane.

questions.stem: In a long term care facility, a 77 year old woman has been newly confused since this morning and pulled out her hearing aids. Her temperature is 37.4 °C, respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation is 90% on room air, down from 96% last week. She denies shortness of breath. What should the nurse conclude?
questions.takeaway: In an older adult, new confusion with a rising respiratory rate can be the first cue of hypoxemia or infection, before fever or dyspnea appear.
questions.strategy: The normal temperature and her denial of dyspnea pull toward reassurance. A reduced response to hypoxia in aging means the cues show up as confusion instead.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Confusion that began this morning is a change, not her baseline.
Rate up and saturation down over a week point to the lungs.
A normal temperature and no dyspnea do not rule out infection in an older adult.

elimination.verdict: Suspect a respiratory cause and assess now.

questions.objective: Aging and respiratory changes
questions.concept: expected aging changes versus new dyspnea

options.text: A saturation of 90% is acceptable at her age, so the nurse rechecks it tomorrow
options.rationale: Aging lowers respiratory reserve, but a drop from 96% to 90% in a week is a change, not a baseline. Waiting a day risks missing worsening hypoxemia in a patient who cannot report it.

options.text: The confusion signals worsening dementia, so the nurse updates her care plan
options.rationale: Dementia progresses slowly, and this confusion is new since this morning. Pairing it with a rising rate and a falling saturation makes a physical cause far more likely.

options.text: She may have a respiratory infection that needs a full respiratory assessment now
options.rationale: Older adults have a reduced response to hypoxia and a higher infection risk, so confusion and a fast rate can appear before fever or dyspnea. Her falling saturation supports a respiratory cause that needs assessment now.

options.text: Without a fever or dyspnea, infection is unlikely, so the nurse reorients her
options.rationale: Reorienting her is kind but treats the confusion as the problem rather than as a cue. Older adults often have little or no fever early in an infection, so the missing fever does not rule it out.

questions.stem: Before his newborn daughter is discharged home, a father who smokes is learning how to protect her lungs. Which statement shows he needs more teaching?
questions.takeaway: Respiratory health promotion includes avoiding thirdhand smoke, the residue left on skin, hair and clothing, as well as secondhand smoke and vaping aerosol.
questions.strategy: The garage plan sounds responsible, which is the trap. Ask whether the baby still meets the smoke by another route.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Look for the one statement that is wrong.
Smoke residue travels on the father even when he smokes elsewhere.

elimination.verdict: The garage plan still exposes her to thirdhand smoke.

questions.objective: Respiratory health promotion and smoking cessation support

options.text: "I will ask my provider for help with quitting for good."
options.rationale: Quitting is the surest way to protect the baby from every kind of smoke exposure. Asking for help shows he understood that support makes quitting more likely to succeed.

options.text: "I will smoke only in the garage, then come in and hold her."
options.rationale: Smoking away from the baby limits secondhand smoke, which is a good step. Smoke residue on his hair, skin and clothes is thirdhand smoke, and it still reaches her when he holds her.

options.text: "No one will be allowed to vape inside our house or our car."
options.rationale: Vaping aerosol is an airway irritant that the baby should not breathe. Keeping both the home and the car free of it shows he understood the teaching.

options.text: "I will keep her vaccinations on schedule."
options.rationale: Maintaining vaccinations prevents respiratory infections and is part of respiratory health promotion. This statement is correct, so it does not show a need for more teaching.

questions.stem: At a clinic visit, a patient who refinishes furniture in his basement workshop reports a cough that is worse on days he sands wood and sprays finishes. He has never smoked, and his lungs are clear today. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: Take a cough suppressant on the days he works in the shop
options.rationale: A suppressant may quiet the cough for a day. The dust and fumes still reach his airways, so the irritation continues while the symptom that reveals it is hidden.

options.text: Wear a protective mask and ventilate the shop while he works
options.rationale: Dust and spray fumes are respiratory irritants, and his cough follows the days he is exposed. Protective equipment and better ventilation reduce what reaches his airways, which treats the cause of the cough.

options.text: Drink extra water on the days he works in the shop
options.rationale: Hydration can thin secretions and is part of respiratory health promotion. It does nothing to lower the dust and fumes he breathes, which are what trigger his cough.

options.text: Do his sanding in the evening so the dust settles overnight
options.rationale: Dust does settle over time, which makes this sound sensible. He still breathes the dust while he sands, so changing the hour does not reduce his exposure.

questions.takeaway: Respiratory health promotion includes reducing occupational and environmental irritants and using protective equipment in hazardous environments.
questions.strategy: Fluids and cough medicine feel like caring for the cough. The cough tracks his exposure, so the instruction that cuts the exposure wins.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Link the cough to its trigger
steps.detail: It worsens on sanding and spraying days.
Only the mask and ventilation reduce what he breathes.

elimination.verdict: Wear a protective mask and ventilate the shop.

questions.objective: Respiratory health promotion and smoking cessation support

questions.stem: A patient with a chronic cough tells the nurse that he smokes a pack and a half a day. When asked, he says, "Nobody ever told me the cough was from cigarettes." Using the 5 A's, what does the nurse do next?
questions.takeaway: The 5 A's run in order: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange; a patient who has never been told to quit needs clear advice next.
questions.strategy: Every option is a real cessation step, so the question is only about sequence. His statement shows Ask is done and Advise never happened.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: His use is known, so Ask is complete.
He was never advised, so Advise comes before Assess, Assist and Arrange.

elimination.verdict: Advise him clearly to quit.

questions.objective: Respiratory health promotion and smoking cessation support

options.text: Schedule a follow up visit in 1 week to review his smoking
options.rationale: Arrange is the final A, setting up follow up once a quit plan exists. A visit to review progress means little when no advice or plan has been given.

options.text: Offer nicotine replacement and a referral to a counseling program
options.rationale: Assist provides counseling and medication, but only after readiness is assessed. Offering treatment to someone who has not been advised or assessed jumps two steps ahead.

options.text: Ask whether he is willing to set a quit date in the next 30 days
options.rationale: Assessing readiness to quit is the third A, and it matters. Asking it before he has been advised skips the step that gives him a reason to consider quitting.

options.text: Tell him clearly that quitting is the most important step for his lungs
options.rationale: The nurse has asked about and recorded his use, and he has never been told to quit. Advise comes next: clear, personal advice that links his cough to smoking and urges him to stop.

questions.stem: At a smoking cessation visit, a patient who works night shifts says she is ready to quit. She says, "Just give me the patch. Talking to someone will not help me." Which plan should the nurse propose?
questions.takeaway: Smoking cessation is most effective with an individualized plan that combines counseling with medication such as nicotine replacement, bupropion or varenicline.
questions.strategy: Honoring her request looks patient centered, which is the trap. The individualized plan keeps her preference for the patch and still adds counseling she can fit around night shifts.

steps.detail: Patch alone and counseling alone each leave out half of what works.
