Every medication at once ignores her and is not individualized.
Counseling plus medication, fitted to her schedule.

elimination.verdict: Pair the patch with counseling in a format she chooses.

questions.objective: Respiratory health promotion and smoking cessation support

options.text: The patch paired with a counseling format she chooses and can attend
options.rationale: Cessation works best with an individualized approach that combines counseling with medication. Letting her choose a counseling format that fits her work hours addresses her reluctance and keeps both parts of the plan.

options.text: The patch with bupropion and varenicline started at once for the strongest effect
options.rationale: Bupropion and varenicline are cessation treatments, but stacking every medication together is not individualized care. It also skips the counseling that makes medication more effective.

options.text: Counseling first, adding medication only if the first attempt fails
options.rationale: Counseling is half of the effective combination. Holding medication until she fails removes the support she asked for and lowers her chance of success on this attempt.

options.text: The nicotine patch alone, because the plan must follow her stated preference
options.rationale: Her preference matters, and an individualized plan respects it. Medication alone is less effective than medication with counseling, so the nurse explains why both help before accepting the patch alone.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected aging change or requires follow up.
questions.takeaway: A gradual decline in cough strength, endurance and chest expansion fits aging; new shortness of breath or new confusion does not.
questions.strategy: The trap is filing every finding under age. Look at timing: changes over years fit aging, while changes since yesterday or this morning do not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Years of slow change point to aging; a new change in a day points to illness.
Reduced expansion that is equal on both sides fits aging.

elimination.verdict: Weaker cough, lower stair endurance and equal reduced expansion are expected; new dyspnea and new confusion need follow up.

questions.objective: Aging and respiratory changes
questions.concept: expected aging changes versus new dyspnea
questions.scenario: During the admission interview for a hip repair, an 82 year old man and his daughter describe several changes in his breathing.

rows.text: His chest expands less on a deep breath, equally on both sides
rows.rationale: Reduced chest wall compliance with aging limits expansion, and here the change is equal on both sides. Unequal expansion would be the finding that needs follow up.

rows.text: His cough has become weaker over the past several years
rows.rationale: A less effective cough reflex is an expected respiratory change with aging. It develops gradually over years and raises infection risk, so it shapes teaching rather than needing urgent follow up.

rows.text: He became short of breath while sitting in a chair yesterday
rows.rationale: New or severe shortness of breath is not normal aging at any age. Dyspnea at rest that began yesterday needs a focused respiratory assessment now.

rows.text: His daughter says he has seemed confused since this morning
rows.rationale: Older adults have a reduced response to hypoxia, so confusion may be the first sign of low oxygen or infection. A new change in mental status is never written off as age.

rows.text: He tires sooner climbing a flight of stairs than he did ten years ago
rows.rationale: Reduced respiratory muscle strength and chest wall compliance lower endurance gradually. A slow decline over a decade fits aging, unlike a change that appears over a day.

questions.stem: The nurse is taking a history from a patient with a cough that started 3 weeks ago and is worse at night. The nurse has recorded his smoking history, workplace exposures, allergies, current medications and family history. Which question should the nurse ask next to complete the focused respiratory history?
questions.takeaway: A focused respiratory history covers symptom timing and pattern, smoking and vaping, exposures, recent infections and travel, allergies, medications, family history, and the effect on sleep and daily activities.
questions.strategy: Three options pull back toward smoking because the patient smokes. List what is already recorded and choose the category still missing.

steps.detail: Smoking, exposures, allergies, medications and family history are recorded.
Three return to smoking; one opens infections and travel.
Quit dates and nicotine products are counseling, not history.

elimination.verdict: Ask about recent infections and travel.

questions.objective: Conduct focused respiratory history and physical assessment
questions.concept: components of the focused respiratory history

options.text: "How many cigarettes do you smoke on a typical day?"
options.rationale: The amount smoked is part of the history, but the nurse has already recorded his smoking history. Repeating it adds nothing and leaves recent infections and travel unasked.

options.text: "Which nicotine replacement products have you tried?"
options.rationale: Past cessation attempts help plan treatment later. This question adds nothing to the focused history of his cough and leaves infection and travel unasked.

options.text: "Have you had a recent infection or traveled anywhere lately?"
options.rationale: Recent infections and travel belong in a focused respiratory history and point toward infectious causes of a new cough. They are the remaining gap after smoking, exposures, allergies, medications and family history.

options.text: "Are you ready to set a date to quit smoking?"
options.rationale: Readiness to quit belongs to cessation counseling, which follows the completed history. Asking it now leaves the cause of his new cough incompletely explored.

questions.stem: During an admission history, a patient tells the nurse she smoked 2 packs a day for 15 years, then cut down to 1 pack a day for the 10 years before she quit 2 years ago. Which smoking history should the nurse document?
questions.takeaway: Pack years equal packs per day times years smoked; when the daily amount changed, calculate each period and add them.
questions.strategy: Each distractor is a real arithmetic slip: adding years, using one period, or applying the higher amount throughout. The 2 years since quitting do not count.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 15 years at 2 packs and 10 years at 1 pack.
30 plus 10.
Years after quitting add nothing.

elimination.verdict: 40 pack years.

questions.objective: Conduct focused respiratory history and physical assessment

options.text: 40 pack years
options.rationale: Packs per day times years smoked is figured for each period: 2 times 15 is 30, and 1 times 10 is 10. Together they give 40 pack years.

options.text: 25 pack years
options.rationale: Adding the years gives 25 years of smoking, but pack years multiply packs per day by years smoked. Counting years alone ignores that she smoked 2 packs a day for 15 of them.

options.text: 30 pack years
options.rationale: Thirty pack years is correct for the first period alone, 2 packs times 15 years. It leaves out the 10 later years at 1 pack a day, which add 10 more.

options.text: 50 pack years
options.rationale: Fifty would result from counting 2 packs a day for all 25 years. Her daily amount fell to 1 pack for the last 10 years, so fifty overstates her exposure.

questions.stem: A patient with dyspnea is wearing a heavy sweatshirt. A nursing student listened through it over the left posterior chest from apex to base, planned to do the right side next, and reports faint sounds. Which correction should the nurse make?
questions.takeaway: Auscultate on bare skin, compare symmetrical areas side to side from apex to base, and listen through the full respiratory cycle.
questions.strategy: Two options fix the clothing and keep a second error. The key is the only one that corrects both the fabric and the one side at a time pattern.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Listening through fabric and finishing one side before the other.

steps.action: Check each option for both fixes
steps.detail: Bare skin alone is not enough; side to side comparison is also needed.
Inspiration only drops expiratory sounds.

elimination.verdict: Bare skin, matching sites, side to side.

questions.objective: Conduct focused respiratory history and physical assessment

options.text: Listen on bare skin at matching sites, during inspiration only
options.rationale: Bare skin and matching sites are correct. Listening only during inspiration misses expiratory sounds such as wheezes, so the nurse listens through the full respiratory cycle.

options.text: Listen on bare skin, comparing each left site with the matching right site
options.rationale: Clothing muffles and distorts breath sounds, so the stethoscope goes on bare skin. Moving side to side at matching sites from apex to base lets each area be compared with its mirror.

options.text: Press the stethoscope firmly through the sweatshirt, then do the right side
options.rationale: Firm pressure improves contact, but fabric still adds noise and dampens faint sounds. Finishing one whole side before the other also loses the side to side comparison.

options.text: Listen on bare skin over the whole left side, then over the whole right side
options.rationale: Moving to bare skin fixes the main error. Listening to one whole side and then the other makes it hard to compare matching areas, which is how subtle differences are found.

questions.stem: The nurse begins a thorax examination on a man admitted for a scheduled knee replacement who is breathing comfortably. The nurse has observed his chest shape, symmetry, and the pattern and effort of his breathing. What does the nurse do next?
questions.takeaway: The thorax examination follows inspect, palpate, percuss, auscultate, comparing symmetrical areas from apex to base on bare skin.
questions.strategy: Auscultation feels like the real respiratory assessment, so students jump to it. The sequence moves from what is seen to what is felt, then tapped, then heard.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Place the nurse in the sequence
steps.detail: Inspection is done, so palpation is next.
Percussion is third and auscultation is last.
Listening through a gown is never correct.

elimination.verdict: Place both hands on his back to feel chest expansion.

questions.objective: Conduct focused respiratory history and physical assessment

options.text: Listen over the front of his chest through the gown
options.rationale: Listening through clothing muffles breath sounds and adds noise from the fabric. It also skips palpation and percussion, which come before auscultation.

options.text: Listen on bare skin from apex to base
options.rationale: This is the correct auscultation technique, so it sounds right. Auscultation comes last in the sequence, after palpation and percussion, not straight after inspection.

options.text: Place both hands on his back to feel chest expansion
options.rationale: Palpation follows inspection and confirms by touch whether both sides expand equally. It builds on what the nurse just saw and comes before percussion and auscultation.

options.text: Tap over matching areas of the chest to compare sounds
options.rationale: Percussion belongs in the thorax examination, which makes this tempting. It comes third, after palpation, because the sequence moves from looking to feeling to tapping to listening.

questions.stem: After abdominal surgery, a patient has coarse, low pitched sounds over the trachea and large airways that become quieter after he coughs. His oxygen saturation is 95% on room air, and he speaks in full sentences. Which action should the nurse take?
questions.takeaway: Rhonchi come from secretions in the trachea and large airways; coughing and deep breathing, with splinting after surgery, help clear them.
questions.strategy: Fluid restriction tempts students who confuse rhonchi with crackles. The change after coughing places the sound in secretions that he can clear.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Coarse sounds over large airways that change with a cough are secretions.
Full sentences and 95% rule out an emergency.

steps.action: Choose the action that clears secretions
steps.detail: Splinted coughing and deep breathing.

elimination.verdict: Help him splint and cough.

questions.objective: Conduct focused respiratory history and physical assessment

options.text: Call the rapid response team for an upper airway obstruction
options.rationale: A blocked upper airway causes stridor and distress, which this patient does not have. He speaks in full sentences with a normal saturation, so emergency help is not needed.

options.text: Restrict his oral fluids to reduce the fluid in his lungs
options.rationale: Restricting fluids makes secretions thicker and harder to cough up. These sounds come from secretions in the airways, so hydration continues unless it is restricted for another reason.

options.text: Document the sounds as expected over the large airways
options.rationale: Bronchial sounds are expected over the trachea, but coarse sounds that change with coughing are adventitious. Documenting them as normal leaves the secretions untreated.

options.text: Help him splint the incision while he coughs and deep breathes
options.rationale: Sounds that clear with coughing come from secretions in the large airways, which are rhonchi. Splinting the incision makes coughing less painful, so he can clear the secretions himself.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate what it most likely represents.
questions.takeaway: Rhonchi are coarse sounds from secretions in the large airways that change with coughing; every other sound is judged by its location and cause.
questions.strategy: Low pitch and a wet quality tempt you to call the base sounds secretions. Location and the response to a cough separate rhonchi from vesicular sounds and crackles.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bronchial at the trachea, bronchovesicular at the sternum and vesicular at the bases are expected.
Only the coarse sound over the large airways changes when mucus moves.
Persistent fine popping is fluid; persistent musical sounds are narrowing.

elimination.verdict: Three expected sounds, one secretion sound and two other adventitious sounds.

questions.objective: Conduct focused respiratory history and physical assessment
questions.scenario: A woman admitted with acute bronchitis has a productive cough. The nurse auscultates her chest, asks her to cough, and listens again.

rows.text: High pitched, musical sounds on expiration that do not change after coughing
rows.rationale: Wheezes come from narrowed airways, not from mucus that a cough can move. Bronchitis can cause both sounds, but a musical sound that persists after coughing points to narrowing.

rows.text: Coarse, low pitched rattling over the large airways that softens after a strong cough
rows.rationale: Rhonchi come from secretions in the trachea and large airways. Coughing moves the mucus, so a coarse sound that softens afterward points to secretions rather than fluid deep in the lungs.

rows.text: Medium pitched sounds near the sternum
rows.rationale: Bronchovesicular sounds are normal near the sternum over the main bronchi. Their medium pitch fits a spot between the trachea and the smaller airways, so no follow up is needed.

rows.text: Soft, low pitched sounds over the lung bases
rows.rationale: Vesicular sounds are the normal soft, low pitched sounds at the bases. Low pitch alone does not mean secretions; rhonchi are coarse and heard over the large airways.

rows.text: Loud, high pitched sounds over the trachea, unchanged after a cough
rows.rationale: Bronchial sounds belong over the trachea, where air moves through a large airway. Their loudness is expected there, and a cough does not change a normal sound.

rows.text: Fine popping at both bases on inspiration, unchanged after coughing
rows.rationale: Crackles mean fluid in the airways, and like rhonchi they sound wet. Unlike rhonchi, they are heard at the bases and do not clear with a cough, so they point to a different problem.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes ago, a patient who arrived short of breath had loud wheezes in both lungs. Now the nurse hears almost no breath sounds on either side. He is drowsy and can say only one word at a time. How should the nurse interpret this change?
questions.takeaway: Silent breath sounds after wheezing, with drowsiness or inability to speak, mean air movement is failing and need emergency help.
questions.strategy: Quiet lungs sound like improvement. Check the rest of the patient: improvement does not come with drowsiness and one word speech.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Wheezes need moving air.
Silence plus drowsiness plus one word speech means little air is moving.
Stay and call for help.

elimination.verdict: Air movement is failing; stay and call for help.

questions.objective: Recognize findings requiring immediate nursing intervention

options.text: Air movement is failing, so the nurse stays and calls for help
options.rationale: Wheezes need moving air, so silent breath sounds with drowsiness mean air movement is failing. The nurse stays with the patient and calls for emergency help now.

options.text: The stethoscope is misplaced, so the nurse listens again at the bases
options.rationale: Rechecking technique is reasonable when one finding is odd. Here the silence matches the drowsiness and the one word speech, so repeating auscultation only delays help.

options.text: The patient is exhausted, so the nurse dims the lights for rest
options.rationale: He is exhausted, but from the work of breathing against failing air movement. Leaving him to rest misses respiratory failure that needs help now.

options.text: The airways have opened, so the nurse documents the improvement
options.rationale: Wheezes do fade when narrowed airways open, which makes this choice the trap. Improvement would come with easier breathing and clearer speech, not drowsiness and one word answers.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who was extubated 1 hour ago after surgery. The nurse hears a new harsh, high pitched sound over her neck on inspiration and sees the skin between her ribs pulling in with each breath. Oxygen saturation is 95% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula. What does the nurse do first?
questions.takeaway: Stridor with retractions signals upper airway obstruction; the nurse stays, keeps the patient upright and calls for help, even when the saturation is normal.
questions.strategy: The normal saturation invites more checking. Stridor and retractions are concerning signs on their own, and the airway comes before the number.

steps.detail: Harsh, high pitched, over the neck on inspiration is stridor.
A normal number does not cancel a narrowing airway.
Stay, position upright, call the rapid response team.

elimination.verdict: Stay with her and call the rapid response team.

questions.objective: Recognize findings requiring immediate nursing intervention

options.text: Auscultate all lung fields to compare with the earlier assessment
options.rationale: A full lung assessment gives useful detail. Stridor comes from the upper airway, so listening to every lung field delays the emergency call without changing it.

options.text: Move the oximeter to another finger to confirm the 95% reading
options.rationale: Checking the sensor is useful when a reading does not match the patient. Here the 95% reading is believable but misleading, because saturation can stay normal while the airway narrows.

options.text: Stay with her, keep her upright and call the rapid response team
options.rationale: A harsh, high pitched inspiratory sound over the neck is stridor, from upper airway obstruction, and retractions show hard work to breathe. The airway can close before the saturation falls, so she needs help now.

options.text: Increase the oxygen to 4 L/min and recheck the saturation in 15 minutes
options.rationale: More oxygen does not open a narrowing airway, and the prescription sets the flow. Waiting 15 minutes for a number risks complete obstruction.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report that a postoperative patient's oxygen saturation is 89% and that he keeps pulling at the sensor and "is not making sense." He was oriented 2 hours ago. What does the nurse do first?
questions.takeaway: New confusion is a concerning respiratory sign; with a low saturation, the nurse goes to the patient and assesses breathing and mental status before anything else.
questions.strategy: Fixing the sensor looks reasonable because he is moving. The confusion is a finding in its own right and points to hypoxemia, not a bad probe.

steps.detail: Low reading plus new confusion.
An unstable patient is assessed by the nurse.
Rate, effort, color and mental status at the bedside.

elimination.verdict: Go to him and assess.

questions.objective: Recognize findings requiring immediate nursing intervention

options.text: Review his record for medications that could explain the confusion
options.rationale: Medications can cause confusion, and the record will matter later. Reviewing it before seeing the patient delays assessment of a possible airway or breathing problem.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to apply oxygen and report back in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Oxygen may be needed, but the patient needs a nurse's assessment first. Delegating care of a newly unstable patient and waiting 15 minutes leaves the cause unknown.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to tape the sensor and repeat the reading
options.rationale: A moving finger can give a falsely low reading, so checking placement has a place. New confusion is itself a sign of low oxygen, so the nurse cannot assume the number is wrong.

options.text: Go to him and assess breathing rate, effort, color and mental status
options.rationale: New confusion with a low reading is a concerning sign until proven otherwise. The nurse assesses the patient directly, because an unstable patient is not delegated and assessment comes before action.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients on a medical unit. Which patient should the nurse see first?
questions.takeaway: An airway threat such as stridor outranks expected findings of a known diagnosis, oxygen side effects and chronic symptoms.
questions.strategy: The pneumonia patient has the most abnormal findings, which is the pull. Ask which findings are new and threaten the airway; crackles and fever are expected for that diagnosis.

steps.detail: A new high pitched inspiratory sound is an upper airway problem.
Crackles and fever fit pneumonia; a morning cough fits smoking.
Dry nasal passages are a comfort issue.

elimination.verdict: See the patient with new hoarseness and stridor first.

questions.objective: Recognize findings requiring immediate nursing intervention

options.text: A patient who smokes daily and has a cough with white sputum every morning
options.rationale: A morning cough with white sputum is common in people who smoke and is a chronic finding. It calls for cessation counseling, not the nurse's first visit.

options.text: A patient with a new hoarse voice who now has a high pitched sound on each inspiration
options.rationale: A high pitched sound on inspiration is stridor, and with new hoarseness it points to a narrowing upper airway. Airway comes first, so this patient is seen before those with stable, expected findings.

options.text: A patient with pneumonia who has crackles at the right base and a temperature of 38.3 °C
options.rationale: Crackles and fever fit the pneumonia this patient is being treated for. They need monitoring, but they are expected findings for the diagnosis rather than a sign of a threatened airway.

options.text: A patient receiving oxygen by nasal cannula who reports dry nasal passages and a sore nose
options.rationale: Dry mucous membranes are a known complication of oxygen therapy and need nasal care. They are uncomfortable, but they do not threaten the airway or breathing.

questions.stem: On a medical unit, a patient tells the nurse, "I feel like I can't get enough air." Her respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 96% on room air, and her lungs are clear. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.takeaway: Dyspnea is subjective: the nurse believes and explores the patient's report, along with appearance, speech, endurance, anxiety and mental status, rather than relying on numbers alone.
questions.strategy: Normal numbers tempt the nurse to reassure. The patient's report is data, so the best response gathers more of it.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Normal numbers and anxiety both brush her report aside.
Oxygen without assessment or prescription.
Explore onset and activity.

elimination.verdict: Ask her to describe when it started and what she was doing.

questions.objective: Recognize findings requiring immediate nursing intervention

options.text: "Your oxygen level and breathing rate are normal, so your lungs are fine."
options.rationale: The numbers are reassuring, but dyspnea is what the patient feels, and normal values do not disprove it. Dismissing her report can miss an early change and damages trust.

options.text: "Tell me more about when this feeling started and what you were doing."
options.rationale: Dyspnea is subjective, so the patient's report is the measure. Exploring onset and activity gathers the data to judge severity and find a cause while the nurse watches her other indicators.

options.text: "Try to relax; anxiety often makes people feel short of breath."
options.rationale: Anxiety can cause a sense of breathlessness, and it is one indicator the nurse assesses. Naming it before exploring her report assumes a cause and closes off assessment.

options.text: "I will put some oxygen on you to make breathing easier."
options.rationale: Oxygen treats hypoxemia, and her saturation is 96% on room air. Applying it without a prescription or a reason skips assessment of what she is feeling.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require immediate nursing intervention.
questions.takeaway: Concerning respiratory signs include retractions, cyanosis, confusion, inability to speak in sentences and a posture that shows effort; fever alone in a known infection is not one.
questions.strategy: The fever and throat pain are abnormal, which is the trap. Highlight findings that show breathing failing now, not findings that fit the known diagnosis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Effort, speech, color and mental status reflect oxygenation.
Fever and mild throat pain fit the diagnosis.
Breath sounds in all lobes are good news.

elimination.verdict: Posture, speech, cyanosis, retractions and new confusion.

questions.objective: Recognize findings requiring immediate nursing intervention
questions.concept: concerning signs: retractions, cyanosis, confusion, speech
questions.nursesNote: 0815: Day 2 of admission for fever and cough. Temperature 38.1 °C. Sitting upright, leaning forward with hands on knees. Skin warm and dry. Speaks 2 or 3 words between breaths. Reports throat pain 2 of 10 from coughing. Lips and nail beds bluish. Breath sounds heard in all lobes. Skin between ribs pulls in with each breath. Oriented to person only; was oriented to person, place and time yesterday.

segments.text: Temperature 38.1 °C
segments.rationale: A temperature of 38.1 °C fits the infection she was admitted with and needs routine treatment and monitoring. It does not signal failing oxygenation the way her posture, speech, color and mental status do.

segments.text: Sitting upright, leaning forward with hands on knees
segments.rationale: Posture is an indicator of respiratory adequacy, and leaning forward on the knees helps the chest expand. A patient who needs this position is working hard to breathe.

segments.text: Skin warm and dry
segments.rationale: Warm, dry skin is consistent with a fever and adequate skin perfusion. It does not point to a breathing problem that needs immediate action.

segments.text: Speaks 2 or 3 words between breaths
segments.rationale: Speech ability shows how much breath a patient has to spare. Only 2 or 3 words between breaths means breathing is taking most of her effort.

segments.text: Reports throat pain 2 of 10 from coughing
segments.rationale: Mild throat pain from coughing is expected with a cough and deserves comfort measures. It does not threaten her airway or oxygenation.

segments.text: Lips and nail beds bluish
segments.rationale: Cyanosis of the lips and nail beds is a concerning sign of poor oxygenation. It needs immediate action, not routine monitoring.

segments.text: Breath sounds heard in all lobes
segments.rationale: Breath sounds in all lobes show that air is reaching every part of the lungs. This finding is reassuring, unlike silent breath sounds.

segments.text: Skin between ribs pulls in with each breath
segments.rationale: Skin pulling in between the ribs is retraction, a concerning sign of increased work of breathing. It means she is using extra effort to move air.

segments.text: Oriented to person only; was oriented to person, place and time yesterday
segments.rationale: New confusion is a concerning sign that the brain is not getting enough oxygen. A decline from full orientation yesterday is a change that needs immediate action.

questions.stem: In the emergency department, a patient brought in after hours outside in the cold is talking in full sentences, with pink lips and a respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute. The oximeter clipped to a cold finger with dark nail polish reads 84%. What should the nurse do?
questions.takeaway: Cold extremities, poor circulation, movement, nail polish and improper placement distort pulse oximetry; always correlate the reading with the patient.
questions.strategy: An 84% reading triggers emergency instincts. The patient in front of the nurse contradicts the number, so fix the measurement before treating it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Full sentences, pink lips and a normal rate do not fit 84%.
Cold finger and dark polish.
Warm site without polish.

elimination.verdict: Correct the sensor site and recheck.

questions.objective: Assessment and diagnostics: pulse oximetry and invasive respiratory procedures

options.text: Warm the hand or use a site without polish, then recheck
options.rationale: Cold extremities, poor circulation and nail polish all cause falsely low readings. Moving the sensor to a warm site without polish and comparing the result with how the patient looks gives a reading to trust.

options.text: Apply a nonrebreather mask right away and call the rapid response team
options.rationale: A true saturation of 84% would need urgent oxygen. This reading does not match a patient who speaks in full sentences with pink lips, so emergency treatment based on it is premature.

options.text: Coach deep breathing until the reading rises above 90%
options.rationale: Deep breathing helps when ventilation is shallow, but this patient is breathing normally. Coaching toward a number that may be false treats the device rather than the patient.

options.text: Document 84% and recheck at the next scheduled vital signs
options.rationale: Documenting an unverified value records a number that may be false. Waiting also risks missing true hypoxemia if the reading turns out to be correct.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes after a bronchoscopy done under sedation, a patient is back on the unit. His oxygen saturation is 98% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula. He is hard to wake and breathes 8 times per minute with shallow breaths. What should the nurse do?
questions.takeaway: Pulse oximetry does not measure ventilation or carbon dioxide; a sedated patient breathing slowly and shallowly needs action even with a normal saturation.
questions.strategy: The 98% reading is the distractor everyone trusts. Monitoring sedation and airway status after a procedure means watching rate, depth and arousal, not only the oximeter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Saturation only, not ventilation or carbon dioxide.
8 shallow breaths and hard to wake is failing ventilation.
Stimulate, stay and call for help.

elimination.verdict: Stimulate him, stay and call for help.

questions.objective: Assessment and diagnostics: pulse oximetry and invasive respiratory procedures

options.text: Let him sleep, because a saturation of 98% shows adequate breathing
options.rationale: A saturation of 98% is the trap. Oxygen keeps the hemoglobin saturated even as carbon dioxide builds from too few breaths, so the number cannot show adequate ventilation.

options.text: Request capnography and review the readings at the next hourly check
options.rationale: Capnography does measure exhaled carbon dioxide and would show the problem. Waiting an hour to review it leaves a patient with failing ventilation unattended now.

options.text: Increase the oxygen flow and recheck the saturation in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Oxygen treats hypoxemia, but his saturation is already high and his problem is poor ventilation. More oxygen does nothing for the carbon dioxide building up, and waiting delays help.

options.text: Stimulate him, stay at the bedside and call for help
options.rationale: Pulse oximetry measures saturation, not ventilation or carbon dioxide, and supplemental oxygen can keep it high while he breathes too little. Slow, shallow breathing with difficult arousal after sedation needs stimulation and help now.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing a patient for a thoracentesis on the left side. The consent is signed, and his allergies and bleeding risk have been reviewed. His breath sounds were last documented on admission 2 days ago. What should the nurse do before the procedure starts?
questions.takeaway: Before bronchoscopy, thoracentesis or lung biopsy, the nurse verifies preparation and consent, reviews allergies and bleeding risk, and obtains current baseline respiratory findings.
questions.strategy: Consent and allergies look like the safety checks, but the stem says both are done. The gap is a baseline from today.

steps.detail: Consent, allergies and bleeding risk are complete.
Breath sounds are 2 days old.
A current baseline lets the nurse detect a complication later.

elimination.verdict: Assess his respiratory status now.

questions.objective: Assessment and diagnostics: pulse oximetry and invasive respiratory procedures

options.text: Have him sign the consent again with the nurse as the witness
options.rationale: Verifying consent is a nursing responsibility, and the consent is already signed. Repeating it adds nothing, while the outdated respiratory findings are a gap that matters.

options.text: Plan to compare breath sounds afterward with the admission findings
options.rationale: Comparing before and after findings is the right idea. Findings from 2 days ago may not match today, so a change after the procedure could be missed or wrongly blamed on it.

options.text: Assess his respiratory rate, effort and breath sounds now
options.rationale: A baseline taken just before the procedure is what later findings are compared with. If breath sounds drop afterward, the nurse can tell whether a complication such as pneumothorax has occurred.

options.text: Review his allergies again with a family member
options.rationale: Allergies have already been reviewed, and repeating that review with family adds little. The missing piece is a current set of respiratory findings to compare against.

questions.stem: Two hours after a lung biopsy on the right side, a patient suddenly becomes short of breath, with a respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute. Breath sounds heard on the right before the procedure are now absent there. She is awake and alert, and the dressing is dry. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
questions.takeaway: After bronchoscopy, thoracentesis or lung biopsy, sudden dyspnea with newly absent breath sounds on the procedure side points to pneumothorax.
questions.strategy: Bleeding comes to mind first after any biopsy. The one sided loss of breath sounds is the finding that only pneumothorax explains.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Absent on the procedure side means air or collapse there.
Dry dressing argues against bleeding; a fast rate argues against oversedation.
Anxiety does not change breath sounds.

elimination.verdict: Pneumothorax.

questions.objective: Assessment and diagnostics: pulse oximetry and invasive respiratory procedures

options.text: Pneumothorax
options.rationale: Air leaking into the pleural space collapses lung tissue, so breath sounds disappear on that side and dyspnea starts suddenly. A lung biopsy can puncture the pleura, which makes this the likely cause.

options.text: Oversedation
options.rationale: Oversedation slows and weakens breathing rather than speeding it. This patient breathes fast and is alert, and sedation would not remove breath sounds from one side.

options.text: Anxiety
options.rationale: Anxiety can raise the respiratory rate, but it cannot silence breath sounds on one side. Calling this anxiety would delay care for a collapsing lung.

options.text: Bleeding at the biopsy site
options.rationale: Bleeding is a real risk after biopsy and is watched for. A dry dressing and the loss of breath sounds on one side point to air in the pleural space instead.

questions.stem: On a medical unit, a patient uses a nasal cannula connected to a portable oxygen cylinder for walks in the hallway. The nurse finds dry, cracked lips and reddened skin above both ears. A family member has brought petroleum jelly for the lips. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
questions.takeaway: Oxygen safety means no flames or petroleum products near the equipment, secured cylinders, skin checks under tubing, and oral and nasal care for dryness.
questions.strategy: Applying the jelly to the lips only sounds like a compromise. The lips sit right in the oxygen flow, so the fire risk remains.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Any petroleum product near oxygen is out.
Removing the cannula interrupts prescribed oxygen.
Padding, oral and nasal care, secured cylinder.

elimination.verdict: Water based lubricant, padding, oral and nasal care, secured cylinder.

questions.objective: Hypoxemia, hypoxia and oxygen therapy: devices, safety and complications

options.text: Provide oral and nasal care on a regular schedule
options.rationale: Oxygen dries the mucous membranes of the mouth and nose. Regular oral and nasal care relieves the dryness and lowers the risk of infection.

options.text: Make sure the portable cylinder is secured in its holder
options.rationale: An unsecured cylinder can fall, break its valve and become a dangerous hazard. Securing cylinders is one of the basic oxygen safety priorities.

options.text: Let the family member apply the jelly to the lips only
options.rationale: Keeping the jelly away from the nose does not make it safe, because the lips sit in the oxygen flow. Any petroleum based product near oxygen adds a fire risk.

options.text: Offer a water based lubricant for the lips and nares instead of the jelly
options.rationale: Petroleum based products are avoided around oxygen equipment because they add a fire hazard. A water based product treats the dryness of the lips and nares safely.

options.text: Remove the cannula for 1 hour each shift to rest the skin
options.rationale: Removing oxygen for an hour interrupts prescribed therapy and can cause hypoxemia. Pressure is relieved by padding and repositioning the tubing instead.

options.text: Pad the tubing and inspect the skin above both ears each shift
options.rationale: Reddened skin above the ears is early pressure from the tubing. Padding and regular skin inspection prevent it from becoming a pressure injury.

questions.stem: A woman admitted with a pulmonary embolism is receiving oxygen by simple face mask, prescribed at 6 L/min. She returned from an imaging test an hour ago. She is now drowsier than before the test and reports a new headache. Her oxygen saturation is 95%, her respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and the flowmeter reads 2 L/min. What does the nurse do first?
questions.takeaway: A simple mask must run at its minimum prescribed flow; below it, exhaled carbon dioxide is rebreathed even when the saturation looks normal.
questions.strategy: The saturation of 95% invites leaving her alone. The flowmeter reading and new drowsiness point to carbon dioxide rebreathing, which the oximeter cannot show.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2 L/min is below the 6 L/min prescribed for her mask.
Drowsiness and a headache fit rebreathed carbon dioxide; her saturation is normal.
Restore the flow, reassess, then report if she does not improve.

elimination.verdict: Raise the flow to 6 L/min and reassess her.

questions.objective: Hypoxemia, hypoxia and oxygen therapy: devices, safety and complications

options.text: Switch to a nasal cannula at 2 L/min to match the flow
options.rationale: A nasal cannula at that flow would not trap exhaled air, so part of this idea is sound. Changing the device and dose departs from her prescription, and the fix is to restore the prescribed flow.

options.text: Notify the provider of the new drowsiness and headache
options.rationale: New drowsiness is worth reporting, and the nurse reports it if she does not improve. The likely cause is in front of the nurse, so correcting the flow comes before the call.

options.text: Let her rest, since a saturation of 95% is adequate
options.rationale: A saturation of 95% is reassuring about oxygen. Pulse oximetry does not measure carbon dioxide, so it cannot rule out the rebreathing that a low flow on a simple mask causes.

options.text: Raise the flow to 6 L/min and reassess her
options.rationale: A simple mask below its minimum flow lets exhaled carbon dioxide build up inside it, which can cause drowsiness and a headache. Restoring the prescribed flow fixes the cause at the bedside.

questions.stem: The nurse learns that assistive personnel turned a patient's simple face mask oxygen below the prescribed minimum after she said the air felt too strong. Her oxygen saturation is 95%. What should the nurse do?
questions.takeaway: A simple face mask must run at no less than its minimum prescribed flow to prevent carbon dioxide rebreathing.
questions.strategy: A 95% saturation makes the lower flow look harmless. The risk is carbon dioxide rebreathing, which pulse oximetry does not measure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A simple mask has a minimum flow.
Saturation does not show carbon dioxide.
Device changes and breaks are not ordered.

elimination.verdict: Restore the minimum flow and explain.

questions.objective: Hypoxemia, hypoxia and oxygen therapy: devices, safety and complications

options.text: Remove the mask for 10 minutes each hour so she can rest
options.rationale: Rest breaks interrupt prescribed oxygen and lower the concentration she receives. Comfort concerns are met with explanation and skin and mouth care, not by stopping therapy.

options.text: Return the flow to the prescribed minimum and explain why
options.rationale: A simple mask needs at least its minimum prescribed flow to flush exhaled carbon dioxide out of the mask. Explaining this to the patient and the assistive personnel prevents a repeat.

options.text: Switch her to a nasal cannula so the air feels gentler
options.rationale: A cannula may feel gentler, but changing the device needs a prescription. The nurse uses the ordered device and settings and corrects the flow instead.

options.text: Leave the flow lower, since her saturation is 95%
options.rationale: The saturation is acceptable now, which makes this choice tempting. Below the minimum flow, exhaled carbon dioxide stays in the mask and she rebreathes it, which the saturation cannot show.

questions.stem: Ten minutes after a patient is placed on a nonrebreather mask for hypoxemia, his saturation has fallen from 94% to 88%, and the reservoir bag collapses flat when he breathes in. What should the nurse do first?
questions.takeaway: A nonrebreather mask works only when its reservoir stays inflated and its one way valves function; a flat bag means little oxygen is being delivered.
questions.strategy: Changing devices feels like decisive action. The device is right; the equipment problem in front of the nurse is what needs fixing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A flat reservoir means no oxygen store.
Restore flow and check the valves.
The cause is visible now.

elimination.verdict: Restore the flow and check the valves.

questions.objective: Hypoxemia, hypoxia and oxygen therapy: devices, safety and complications

options.text: Change to a Venturi mask for a more controlled concentration
options.rationale: A Venturi mask gives a controlled concentration, but not the high concentration this patient needs. The nonrebreather is the right device; it is not working.

options.text: Keep the mask in place and recheck the saturation in 10 minutes
options.rationale: Rechecking is part of monitoring the response, but the cause is visible now. A flat reservoir will not fix itself, so waiting lets hypoxemia worsen.

options.text: Check the oxygen flow and valves so the bag stays partly inflated
options.rationale: A flat bag means the reservoir is not filling, so he is receiving little oxygen. Restoring the flow keeps the bag partly inflated, and checking the one way valves confirms the device works.

options.text: Loosen the straps so room air can enter around the mask
options.rationale: Loosening the mask lets room air dilute the oxygen and lowers the concentration further. The problem is the empty reservoir, not the fit of the mask.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who has been on a Venturi mask for 6 hours. The prescription allows the nurse to adjust the concentration to keep oxygen saturation between 92% and 96%. For the past hour her saturation has read 99%, and she is breathing comfortably. What should the nurse do?
questions.takeaway: Oxygen is given at the lowest effective concentration consistent with the prescribed goal, because excess oxygen risks toxicity and absorption atelectasis.
questions.strategy: A high saturation looks like success, which is the trap. The prescribed range has a maximum, and staying above it is a problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 99% is above the 96% maximum.
Lower within the prescription rather than stopping or switching.
Check the response after the change.

elimination.verdict: Lower the concentration and reassess.

questions.objective: Hypoxemia, hypoxia and oxygen therapy: devices, safety and complications

options.text: Lower the concentration within the prescription and reassess
options.rationale: Oxygen is given at the lowest effective concentration that meets the prescribed goal. At 99% she is above the 96% maximum, so lowering the setting reduces the risk of oxygen toxicity and absorption atelectasis.

options.text: Keep the current setting, since she is doing well
options.rationale: She is doing well, which makes leaving the setting feel safe. A saturation above the prescribed maximum means she is receiving more oxygen than she needs, which raises complication risk.

options.text: Remove the mask and watch her saturation on room air
options.rationale: Stopping oxygen jumps past the stepwise lowering the prescription allows. She may still need some oxygen, and her goal range is set with the mask in use.

options.text: Change her to a nasal cannula for comfort
options.rationale: A nasal cannula may be more comfortable, but changing devices needs a prescription. The prescription already gives the nurse a way to lower the dose.

questions.stem: During discharge teaching for home oxygen, a patient says she heats her house with a wood stove and lights candles most evenings. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?
questions.takeaway: Home oxygen teaching keeps open flames, smoking and ignition sources away from the patient and the equipment, whatever the flow rate.
questions.strategy: Taking the cannula off sounds like a safe compromise. Oxygen lingers in the tubing, hair and clothing, so any flame near her stays a hazard.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the flame in each statement
steps.detail: The stove, the candles and the lighter are all flame sources.

steps.action: Ask whether distance or flow fixes it
steps.detail: Low flow or a removed cannula still leaves oxygen around her.

elimination.verdict: Put the candles away and keep the oxygen clear of the stove.

questions.objective: Hypoxemia, hypoxia and oxygen therapy: devices, safety and complications

options.text: "I can sit close to the wood stove as long as my oxygen flow is low."
options.rationale: Even low flow oxygen enriches the air around her and her clothing, so a flame nearby can ignite quickly. The equipment stays away from the stove regardless of the flow.

options.text: "I can light my candles if I take the cannula off first."
options.rationale: Taking the cannula off seems to separate her from the oxygen. The tubing keeps releasing oxygen and her hair and clothes hold it, so a flame beside her is still a fire risk.

options.text: "I will keep a lighter in my pocket so the stove is easy to start."
options.rationale: A lighter is handy for starting the stove, which makes this sound practical. Carrying an ignition source on her body, inside the oxygen enriched air around her face, invites a fire.

options.text: "I will put my candles away and keep my oxygen clear of the stove."
options.rationale: Oxygen makes any flame burn hotter and spread faster, so open flames are kept away from it. Removing the candles and keeping the equipment away from the stove removes both flame sources.

questions.stem: On arrival to the unit, a patient with suspected pneumonia has an oxygen saturation of 91% on room air. Prescriptions include oxygen by nasal cannula, sputum culture and sensitivity, blood cultures, and the first dose of an intravenous antibiotic. Place the nurse's actions in order.
questions.takeaway: In suspected pneumonia, treat hypoxemia first, collect sputum and blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose, then give the antibiotic and evaluate the response.
questions.strategy: Giving the antibiotic early feels most urgent for infection. Cultures drawn after it may grow nothing, so they come first, right after oxygen.

steps.detail: Oxygen for a saturation of 91%.
Cultures before the antibiotic.
Reassess the response.

elimination.verdict: Oxygen, cultures, antibiotic, reassess.

questions.objective: Pneumonia

options.text: Give the first dose of the intravenous antibiotic
options.rationale: The antibiotic follows the cultures without delay, because it treats the infection driving the pneumonia. Starting it promptly also helps prevent sepsis.

options.text: Apply oxygen by nasal cannula as prescribed
options.rationale: Hypoxemia is treated promptly, so oxygen comes first for a saturation of 91%. Cultures and medication can follow within minutes without risk to breathing.

options.text: Reassess saturation, respiratory effort and lung sounds
options.rationale: Monitoring the response comes last, to evaluate whether gas exchange is improving. The findings guide whether the oxygen setting or plan needs to change.

options.text: Collect the sputum and blood cultures
options.rationale: Cultures are collected right before the first antibiotic dose so the organism can still grow in the lab. They are obtained promptly, because an antibiotic given first can cause a falsely negative result.

questions.stem: In an assisted living facility, a resident developed fever, chills, a severe headache and muscle aches suddenly 10 hours ago. Two other residents have confirmed influenza. Which action by the nurse best supports her recovery?
questions.takeaway: Antiviral agents for influenza may be effective if started within 24 to 48 hours of symptom onset, so early recognition matters.
questions.strategy: Rest and fluids are true care for influenza, which is the trap. The 10 hour onset is the cue that makes the antiviral window the priority.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Symptoms began 10 hours ago.
Antivirals work best within 24 to 48 hours.
A vaccine does not treat active illness.

elimination.verdict: Arrange evaluation today for antiviral treatment.

questions.objective: Influenza: seasonal and pandemic
questions.note: The 24 to 48 hour window is keyed as taught in class. CDC guidance says antiviral benefit is greatest when started within 48 hours of onset, and patients who are hospitalized or at high risk are treated even after 48 hours. Use the class wording on the course exam; on NCLEX, "within 48 hours" is the expected window.

options.text: Encourage rest and fluids and reassess her in 3 days
options.rationale: Rest and fluids support recovery from influenza. Waiting 3 days passes the window when antiviral medication works best, so this choice leaves out the time sensitive action.

options.text: Arrange a provider evaluation today so antiviral treatment can begin
options.rationale: Antiviral agents may be effective if started within 24 to 48 hours of symptoms. Her symptoms began 10 hours ago, so arranging evaluation today keeps that window open.

options.text: Give an influenza vaccine today to shorten the illness
options.rationale: Vaccination prevents influenza or reduces its severity, but it does not treat an infection already present. It belongs in prevention, not in care of active illness.

options.text: Wash hands well and keep her in the shared dining room for meals
options.rationale: Handwashing is critical to stop the spread of influenza, which makes this choice partly correct. Keeping a resident with likely influenza in a shared dining room exposes others.

questions.stem: A patient admitted after a positive rapid test for seasonal influenza is coughing frequently. Which transmission based precautions does the nurse use when entering the room?
questions.takeaway: Seasonal influenza calls for droplet precautions added to standard precautions; contact and airborne precautions are for pandemic influenza until its routes of spread are known.
questions.strategy: Contact and airborne is tempting because it was taught alongside influenza. That pairing belongs to pandemic influenza before the type is known.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: This strain is identified and seasonal.
Large droplets call for droplet precautions with a mask.

steps.action: Reject too little and too much
steps.detail: Standard alone is too little; airborne is more than droplets need.

elimination.verdict: Droplet precautions plus standard precautions.

questions.objective: Influenza: seasonal and pandemic

options.text: Contact and airborne precautions until the strain is identified
options.rationale: Contact and airborne precautions are used for pandemic influenza until its type and routes of spread are known. This patient's seasonal strain is already identified and spreads by droplets.

options.text: Airborne precautions with a fitted respirator and a negative pressure room
options.rationale: Airborne precautions are for organisms that stay suspended in the air over a distance. Seasonal influenza droplets fall within a short distance, so a mask meets the need.

options.text: Droplet precautions with a mask, in addition to standard precautions
options.rationale: Seasonal influenza spreads by large respiratory droplets, so droplet precautions with a mask are added to standard precautions. Handwashing remains critical before and after every contact.

options.text: Standard precautions alone, because gloves and hand hygiene prevent spread
options.rationale: Standard precautions apply to every patient, but they do not call for a mask at every entry. A patient coughing with influenza spreads droplets that need added protection.

questions.stem: During a regional outbreak of a newly identified influenza strain whose routes of spread are not yet known, a traveler arrives at the emergency department. He has had sudden fever, chills, severe muscle aches and weakness since yesterday. What should the nurse do first?
questions.takeaway: For suspected pandemic influenza, early recognition and quarantine come first, with contact and airborne precautions until the routes of transmission are known.
questions.strategy: Taking the history first feels thorough. Precautions start on suspicion, and the history follows once others are protected.

steps.detail: Routes of spread are not yet known.
Contact and airborne until the strain is understood.
History follows isolation.

elimination.verdict: Isolate him with contact and airborne precautions.

questions.objective: Influenza: seasonal and pandemic

options.text: Take a full travel history, then decide on precautions
options.rationale: Travel history matters for diagnosis and public health reporting. Delaying precautions to collect it exposes staff and other patients during the wait.

options.text: Give an influenza vaccine before he leaves
options.rationale: Vaccination prevents or lessens influenza, but it does not treat an active illness. A vaccine for a newly identified strain may not exist, and it does nothing to stop spread now.

options.text: Isolate him with contact and airborne precautions
options.rationale: Early recognition and quarantine limit the spread of pandemic influenza. Until the type and its routes of transmission are known, contact and airborne precautions are used.

options.text: Isolate him with droplet precautions, as for seasonal influenza
options.rationale: Droplet precautions fit seasonal influenza, whose spread is known. A new strain with unknown routes needs broader protection until transmission is understood.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with pneumonia is breathing comfortably on his prescribed oxygen. Prescriptions include a sputum culture, blood cultures and the first dose of an intravenous antibiotic, to be given now. He coughed up a sputum specimen that went to the laboratory 10 minutes ago. The laboratory says it can send someone to draw the blood cultures in 1 hour. What does the nurse do?
questions.takeaway: Collect every prescribed culture before the first antibiotic dose, and collect it promptly so the antibiotic still starts on time.
questions.strategy: The sputum already sent makes the cultures feel done, and holding the dose feels safe. Blood cultures and a prompt first dose are both needed, so the nurse draws them now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sputum is collected; blood cultures are not.
Cultures come before the first antibiotic dose.
Collection, not results, must come first, and the dose is due now.

elimination.verdict: Draw the blood cultures now, then give the antibiotic.

questions.objective: Pneumonia

options.text: Hold the antibiotic until the culture results return
options.rationale: Cultures must be collected, not resulted, before the first dose. Results take days, and waiting for them would leave the infection untreated and raise the risk of sepsis.

options.text: Give the antibiotic now, since a sputum culture was sent
options.rationale: The sputum specimen was collected correctly before the antibiotic. The blood cultures have not been drawn, and an antibiotic given first can make them falsely negative.

options.text: Hold the antibiotic until the laboratory draws the cultures
options.rationale: This keeps cultures before the antibiotic, which is the right order. It delays a dose prescribed for now by an hour, and prompt treatment helps prevent sepsis.

options.text: Draw the blood cultures now, then give the antibiotic
options.rationale: Blood cultures are collected before the first antibiotic dose so the organism can still grow in the laboratory. Drawing them now meets that rule without holding a dose prescribed to start now.

questions.stem: At urgent care triage, a patient reports nausea and diarrhea for 2 days and, since this morning, a cough and fatigue. Her sense of taste and smell is unchanged. A coworker tested positive for COVID 19 last week. How should the nurse proceed?
questions.takeaway: COVID 19 presentation varies: gastrointestinal symptoms may come first and loss of taste or smell is now less common, so exposure and new symptoms prompt precautions and testing.
questions.strategy: Normal taste and smell and a gut onset both pull away from COVID 19. Neither rules it out, and the known exposure tips the decision.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A positive coworker last week.
Gut onset and normal taste do not rule it out.
Precautions start on suspicion.

elimination.verdict: Apply COVID 19 precautions and arrange testing.

questions.objective: COVID 19

options.text: Apply the facility's COVID 19 precautions and arrange testing
options.rationale: Presentation varies, and gastrointestinal symptoms may come before cough. With a known exposure and new respiratory symptoms, the nurse starts facility precautions and arranges antigen or PCR testing.

options.text: Seat her in the waiting room, since her taste and smell are normal
options.rationale: Loss of taste or smell can occur but is now less common than early in the pandemic. Its absence does not rule out COVID 19, and seating her with others risks spread.

options.text: Use contact precautions for gastroenteritis, since the illness began in the gut
options.rationale: Gastrointestinal symptoms have many causes. In COVID 19 they may appear before respiratory findings, and her new cough and known exposure make COVID 19 the likely cause to address.

options.text: Complete a full respiratory history before deciding on precautions
options.rationale: A full history is needed and comes soon. Precautions start as soon as infection is suspected, so delaying them while interviewing exposes others.

questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.
questions.takeaway: In pneumonia, new confusion with fever, a fast heart rate, low blood pressure, low urine output and a high lactate signals sepsis and needs immediate escalation.
questions.strategy: Each finding alone has a mild explanation, which is the trap. Taken together with the lactate, they show infection affecting perfusion across the body.

steps.detail: Fever, fast heart rate, low pressure, confusion, low urine and high lactate.
Sepsis explains every cue; the other choices explain one or two.
Escalate, culture, and watch pressure, heart rate and mental status.

elimination.verdict: Sepsis: escalate, obtain blood cultures, monitor blood pressure, heart rate and mental status.

questions.objective: Pneumonia
questions.concept: preventing and recognizing sepsis in pneumonia
questions.scenario: Two days after admission for pneumonia, a patient is restless and confused. Temperature is 39.2 °C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 86/50 mm Hg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 90% on 4 L/min by nasal cannula. Urine output was 60 mL over the past 4 hours. Serum lactate is 4.1 mmol/L.

options.text: Notify the rapid response team or provider of the findings now
options.rationale: These findings show a patient getting worse quickly, and sepsis needs rapid treatment. Escalating now brings the team that can start that treatment.

options.text: Recheck the vital signs in 4 hours
options.rationale: Routine rechecks are too slow for a patient with low blood pressure and new confusion. Waiting 4 hours lets her perfusion keep falling without treatment.

options.text: Obtain the prescribed blood cultures
options.rationale: Blood cultures identify organisms that have entered the bloodstream and guide treatment. They are part of the workup when pneumonia may have progressed to sepsis.

options.text: Restrict oral fluids to protect the lungs
options.rationale: Restricting fluids worsens the low circulating volume behind her low blood pressure and low urine output. In sepsis the problem is too little effective volume, not too much.

options.text: Anxiety from hospitalization
options.rationale: Anxiety can cause restlessness and a fast heart rate. It does not lower the blood pressure, reduce urine output or raise the lactate level.

options.text: The expected course of pneumonia
options.rationale: Fever and crackles are expected in pneumonia. Low blood pressure, new confusion and a high lactate are not, and they show the infection spreading beyond the lungs.

options.text: Dehydration from fever
options.rationale: Fever does increase fluid loss, and low urine output fits dehydration. Dehydration alone would not explain a high lactate with new confusion and a saturation of 90% on 4 L/min oxygen.

options.text: Sepsis
options.rationale: Fever, a fast heart rate, low blood pressure, new confusion, low urine output and a lactate well above the expected 2 mmol/L together show infection impairing perfusion across the body. That cluster is sepsis, which pneumonia care aims to prevent and catch early.

options.text: Weight each morning
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks fluid balance over days. It changes too slowly to guide care of a patient whose perfusion is failing now.

options.text: Mental status
options.rationale: New confusion reflects poor oxygen and blood flow to the brain. Clearer thinking is one sign that treatment is restoring perfusion.

options.text: Pain at the intravenous site
options.rationale: Site checks are routine care for any infusion. They do not show whether sepsis is improving or worsening.

options.text: Blood pressure and heart rate
options.rationale: Blood pressure and heart rate show whether circulation and perfusion are improving with treatment. A falling pressure signals worsening sepsis.

questions.stem: A patient hospitalized with COVID 19 has a respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute and an oxygen saturation of 92% on prescribed oxygen. She becomes short of breath walking to the bathroom and is drinking little because she feels tired. Which nursing action is indicated?
questions.takeaway: COVID 19 nursing care includes positioning for ventilation, monitoring oxygenation trends, clustering care, supporting hydration, nutrition, rest and mobility, and escalating worsening findings promptly.
questions.strategy: Fluid limits and strict bed rest sound protective. Her cues point to a fluid volume deficit and activity intolerance, so both work against her, while clustering care lowers her oxygen demand.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dyspnea on walking means activity intolerance; drinking little means risk for fluid volume deficit.
Fluid limits, strict bed rest and delayed reporting each make a risk worse.
Clustering care saves her effort and oxygen.

elimination.verdict: Group her vital signs, medications and hygiene into one visit.

questions.objective: COVID 19

options.text: Save changes in her breathing rate to report at rounds
options.rationale: Worsening findings are escalated promptly, not held for the provider's next visit. A rising rate can signal clinical deterioration that needs action now.

options.text: Group her vital signs, medications and hygiene into one visit
options.rationale: Clustering care reduces how often she must exert herself and lowers her oxygen demand. Rest between visits helps her tolerate the activity she still needs.

options.text: Limit her oral fluids so her lungs stay dry
options.rationale: Limiting fluids sounds protective for the lungs, but she is already drinking little. She is at risk for a fluid volume deficit, so hydration is supported, not limited.

options.text: Keep her on strict bed rest until oxygen is stopped
options.rationale: Rest is supported, which makes this tempting. Strict bed rest weakens her and lets secretions pool, so mobility is encouraged within her tolerance and paired with rest.

questions.stem: In the emergency department, a patient with COVID 19 is sitting upright on his prescribed nasal cannula. Over 2 hours his oxygen saturation fell from 94% to 91% and his respiratory rate rose from 22 to 28 breaths per minute. He answers questions appropriately. What should the nurse do?
questions.takeaway: In COVID 19, a falling saturation with a rising respiratory rate is a trend toward deterioration that the nurse escalates promptly, even when each value looks acceptable.
questions.strategy: Every single value looks acceptable, which is the trap. The direction of both values over 2 hours is the finding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Saturation down, rate up over 2 hours.
Flow above the prescription is not the nurse's call.
Report now and stay.

elimination.verdict: Report the trend now and stay.

questions.objective: COVID 19

options.text: Walk him in the room to expand his lungs and move secretions
options.rationale: Mobility is supported in COVID 19 care, but walking raises oxygen demand. A patient whose breathing is worsening needs rest and escalation, not added exertion.

options.text: Raise the cannula flow above the prescription and recheck in 30 minutes
options.rationale: More oxygen may be needed, but the nurse uses the ordered settings. Changing the flow without a prescription and waiting 30 minutes delays the report the trend requires.

options.text: Report the 2 hour trend now and stay to monitor his breathing
options.rationale: Escalating worsening findings promptly is a core nursing action in COVID 19. The trend matters more than any single value, and staying lets the nurse catch further decline.

options.text: Continue hourly monitoring, since he is alert and above 90%
options.rationale: Alertness and a saturation above 90% are reassuring on their own. Together, a falling saturation and a rising rate over 2 hours show a trend toward deterioration that needs reporting now.

questions.stem: On a medical unit, a woman with an asthma flare had wheezes throughout both lungs before her prescribed nebulizer treatment. She has worn a nasal cannula all morning. Thirty minutes after the treatment, the nurse hears far fewer wheezes. Which finding best shows that the change reflects improvement?

options.text: She has become quiet and sleepy
options.rationale: Growing drowsiness after hard breathing points to exhaustion and failing air movement. With fewer wheezes, it makes a silent chest more likely, so the nurse calls for help.

options.text: She now talks in full sentences
options.rationale: Full sentences mean enough air is moving to support speech, so fewer wheezes reflect opening airways. When a chest goes quiet from failing air movement, speech shortens to single words.

options.text: Her oxygen saturation has risen to 95%
options.rationale: A rising saturation is welcome and can come with improvement. She has worn oxygen all morning, and saturation does not measure air movement, so it cannot tell opening airways from a silent chest.

options.text: She leans forward with hands on knees
options.rationale: Leaning forward with the hands on the knees is a posture of hard work to breathe. It signals ongoing distress, so the quieter chest may mean less air is moving.

questions.takeaway: Fewer wheezes mean improvement only when the patient also shows better air movement, such as longer speech and better alertness; otherwise suspect a silent chest.
questions.strategy: The saturation looks like proof, but she is on oxygen and saturation does not measure air movement. Speech is the direct sign of how much air she moves.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Quieter wheezes can mean opening airways or failing air movement.
She is on oxygen, and saturation does not show ventilation.
Full sentences require moving air.

elimination.verdict: Full sentences show the quieter chest is improvement.

questions.objective: Recognize findings requiring immediate nursing intervention

questions.stem: An hour before a bronchoscopy with biopsy, the nurse is completing preparation for a man being evaluated for 2 weeks of blood streaked sputum. His consent is signed, and he has no allergies. Which finding does the nurse report to the provider before the procedure?

options.text: He has had nothing by mouth since midnight
options.rationale: Nothing by mouth since midnight is expected preparation for a procedure done under sedation. It shows he is ready, so there is nothing to report.

options.text: He coughed up blood streaked sputum today
options.rationale: Blood in the sputum belongs in his baseline findings before the procedure. It is the reason for the bronchoscopy and not a new change, so it does not need a report before the start.

options.text: He is anxious and asks how long it lasts
options.rationale: Anxiety before a procedure is common, and the nurse answers his question and offers support. It does not change the safety of the procedure, so it needs no report to the provider.

options.text: He took his blood thinner with breakfast
options.rationale: A blood thinner taken this morning raises his bleeding risk during the biopsy. Bleeding risk is reviewed before an invasive procedure, so the provider needs to know before it starts.

questions.takeaway: Preparation for an invasive respiratory procedure includes reviewing bleeding risk, and a finding that raises it is reported before the procedure starts.
questions.strategy: Blood in the sputum sounds alarming, but the stem says it is the reason for the procedure. The blood thinner is the new risk to the biopsy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Consent, allergies, bleeding risk and baseline findings.
Blood streaked sputum is why he is having the procedure.
A blood thinner taken today raises it.

elimination.verdict: Report the blood thinner taken with breakfast.

questions.objective: Assessment and diagnostics: pulse oximetry and invasive respiratory procedures

questions.stem: Since lunch, a woman admitted with heart failure has been on a nasal cannula whose flow the nurse may adjust to keep her saturation within the prescribed goal. Her reading has been above the goal for the past hour, and the nurse plans to lower the flow. Which finding makes the nurse assess further before lowering it?

options.text: She now uses her neck muscles to breathe
options.rationale: Neck muscle use is increased work of breathing, a sign she is struggling despite a high reading. The nurse assesses her breathing and its cause before lowering oxygen she may need.

options.text: She speaks in full sentences while eating
options.rationale: Speaking in full sentences while eating shows breathing that is easy and well supported. It supports lowering the flow toward the lowest effective level.

options.text: Her nose is dry and her nares are sore
options.rationale: Dry, sore nares are a real oxygen complication, and they call for nasal care. They are a further reason to use the lowest effective flow rather than a reason to hold the change.

options.text: Her lips and nail beds are pink
options.rationale: Pink lips and nail beds show no sign of cyanosis. Along with a reading above the goal, this finding supports lowering the flow and reassessing her response.

questions.takeaway: Lower oxygen toward the lowest effective concentration only when the whole patient is stable, not on the saturation number alone.
questions.strategy: The sore nose is a true complication that seems to demand action, but it supports lowering the flow. Only the work of breathing finding says she may still need the oxygen.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A reading above goal supports lowering the flow.
Neck muscle use is increased work of breathing.
Sore nares, full sentences and pink lips support lowering.

elimination.verdict: Neck muscle use calls for more assessment first.

questions.objective: Hypoxemia, hypoxia and oxygen therapy: devices, safety and complications

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing discharge teaching for a patient who smokes and was treated for pneumonia. He has no fluid restriction. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
questions.takeaway: Pneumonia prevention teaching includes vaccination, avoiding crowds in influenza season, coughing and deep breathing with movement, about 3 liters of fluid unless restricted, rest, and stopping smoking.
questions.strategy: Bed rest sounds restful, which is the trap. Rest and sleep are encouraged, but movement keeps the lungs expanded and the secretions moving.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluids, deep breathing and movement keep airways clear.
Avoiding crowds and vaccination prevent new infection.
Prolonged bed rest and smoking again.

elimination.verdict: Fluids, coughing and deep breathing, avoiding crowds, vaccination.

questions.objective: Pneumonia

options.text: Stay in bed as much as possible for the first 2 weeks
options.rationale: Rest and sleep support recovery, which makes this partly true. Staying in bed lets secretions pool and the lungs expand less, which works against recovery.

options.text: Avoid crowded places during influenza season
options.rationale: Crowds raise his exposure to respiratory infections while his lungs are recovering. Avoiding them during influenza season lowers the chance of another pneumonia.

options.text: Plan to smoke again once his cough has cleared
options.rationale: Stopping smoking protects the airways and lowers the risk of another pneumonia. Smoke damages the lungs whether or not he has symptoms, so a cleared cough changes nothing.

options.text: Cough, turn, move and deep breathe several times a day
options.rationale: Coughing, moving and deep breathing expand the lungs and clear secretions. These actions keep his airways open as he recovers.

options.text: Ask his provider which vaccinations he needs
options.rationale: Vaccination is a key way to prevent pneumonia and the infections that lead to it. Checking his vaccination status before he leaves supports prevention.

options.text: Drink about 3 liters of water each day
options.rationale: About 3 liters of water a day keeps secretions thin and easier to cough up. The amount applies to him because he has no fluid restriction.

questions.stem: Going home after treatment for pneumonia, a man who receives hemodialysis three times a week and follows a daily fluid limit reviews his instructions with the nurse. Which instruction does the nurse change for this patient?

options.text: Cough, turn, move and deep breathe often
options.rationale: Coughing, turning, moving and deep breathing keep secretions moving and the lungs expanded. His dialysis and fluid limit do not affect this advice, so it stays.

options.text: Drink about 3 liters of water daily
