options.rationale: The 3 liter goal applies only when fluids are not restricted, and his dialysis fluid limit is a restriction. Drinking that much could overload him between treatments, so the nurse adjusts this instruction.

options.text: Get extra rest and sleep while recovering
options.rationale: Rest can seem to clash with the advice to keep moving, which makes it look like the instruction to change. Rest and sleep are part of pneumonia recovery and fit with regular movement.

options.text: Get an influenza shot every year
options.rationale: Kidney failure weakens his defenses against infection, which can make a vaccine seem risky for him. The influenza shot contains no live virus and lowers his risk of another respiratory infection, so this advice stays.

questions.takeaway: The 3 liter water goal after pneumonia applies only when fluids are not restricted.
questions.strategy: The vaccine looks risky for a patient with kidney failure, but the shot is recommended for him. His fluid limit is the stated detail that changes the 3 liter water goal.

steps.detail: All four are usual pneumonia instructions.
He follows a dialysis fluid limit.
3 liters daily applies only without a restriction.

elimination.verdict: Change the 3 liter water instruction.

questions.objective: Pneumonia

questions.stem: During chemotherapy for leukemia, a patient becomes breathless walking to the bathroom. Her lungs are clear, her saturation is 99% on room air, and her hemoglobin is 6.8 g/dL. A nursing student makes several statements about her care. Which statement shows a misunderstanding?

options.text: "Too few red cells are carrying her oxygen."
options.rationale: This statement is correct, because hemoglobin carries most of the oxygen in the blood. A low hemoglobin lowers oxygen carrying capacity even when the lungs work well.

options.text: "Her breathlessness on walking needs to be reported."
options.rationale: This statement is correct, because new breathlessness with activity reflects tissue hypoxia. The provider needs to know so the cause, her low hemoglobin, can be treated.

options.text: "At 99%, her tissues have enough oxygen."
options.rationale: A saturation of 99% means the few red cells she has are full, not that her tissues get enough oxygen. With a hemoglobin this low, total oxygen delivery falls, so her tissues can be hypoxic.

options.text: "Extra oxygen will do little for her breathlessness."
options.rationale: Withholding help from a breathless patient sounds wrong, which makes this look like the error. Her hemoglobin is already fully saturated, and oxygen treats hypoxemia, not hypoxia from too few red cells.

questions.takeaway: A normal saturation with a very low hemoglobin can still leave tissues hypoxic, because oxygen therapy treats hypoxemia, not decreased oxygen carrying capacity.
questions.strategy: The statement about oxygen doing little sounds uncaring, so students pick it as the error. The high saturation is the reassurance that misleads, because it says nothing about how much hemoglobin there is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hypoxemia is low arterial oxygen; hypoxia is low tissue oxygen.
Saturation is full, but hemoglobin is very low.
A full saturation does not mean enough oxygen reaches tissues.

elimination.verdict: The 99% statement shows the misunderstanding.

questions.objective: Explain ventilation, diffusion and perfusion in gas exchange

chapters.title: Assessment of the Skin, Hair, and Nails

questions.stem: In the emergency department, a patient who fell from a bicycle has large areas on both thighs where the outer layer of skin is scraped away, leaving moist pink tissue. Which problem does the nurse monitor for most closely while these areas heal?

options.text: Loss of cushioning over the thigh bones
options.rationale: Cushioning comes from the subcutaneous tissue, which lies below the dermis and is intact here. A scrape that removed only the outer layer leaves the padding over the bones unchanged.

options.text: Loss of pressure sensation in the thighs
options.rationale: Pressure receptors sit in the subcutaneous tissue, which this scrape did not reach. A wound limited to the outer layer leaves those receptors working, so sensation is not the main concern.

options.text: Less vitamin D made by the injured skin
options.rationale: The epidermis does make vitamin D, so this names a true function of the lost layer. A short loss over two thighs causes no problem the nurse can see now, while infection and fluid loss can.

options.text: Infection and fluid loss through the open areas
options.rationale: The epidermis is the barrier against microbes and the layer that prevents dehydration. Losing it over a large area opens a path in for bacteria and a path out for fluid.

questions.takeaway: Loss of the epidermis removes the barrier against microbes and fluid loss, so infection and dehydration are the risks to watch.
questions.strategy: Vitamin D is a true epidermal function, which makes it tempting. Pick the loss that can harm this patient now: an open barrier lets microbes in and fluid out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only the outer layer, the epidermis, is gone; the subcutaneous tissue is intact.
Cushioning and pressure receptors belong to the subcutaneous tissue.
Vitamin D loss is slow and unseen; infection and fluid loss can start within days.

elimination.verdict: Monitor for infection and fluid loss.

questions.objective: Use knowledge of anatomy and physiology to perform a focused assessment of the skin, hair, and nails.

questions.stem: Two days after sutures closed a deep glass cut on the right forearm, a patient says the skin just beside the incision feels numb when the nurse touches it lightly. What does this finding mean for the patient's care?

options.text: Injury to the area may go unfelt, so the nurse inspects it often
options.rationale: The dermis contains the nerves for pain, touch and temperature, and damage there leaves the area numb. The patient may not feel pressure or heat on it, so the nurse inspects it regularly.

options.text: The area can no longer make vitamin D, so the nurse plans sun exposure
options.rationale: Vitamin D is made in the epidermis, and its loss would not explain numbness. Sun on a healing cut adds injury, so planning sun exposure is wrong for this patient.

options.text: The area will close on its own, so the nurse stops wound checks
options.rationale: Numbness shows nerve damage in the dermis, the layer that also supports wound healing. A cut that reaches the dermis still needs checks, and numbness gives no reason to stop them.

options.text: The area has lost its fat padding, so the nurse adds a cushion
options.rationale: Cushioning comes from subcutaneous tissue, which lies below the dermis. Lost padding would not make the skin numb to a light touch, so a cushion does not address this finding.

questions.takeaway: The dermis holds the nerves for pain, touch and temperature and supports wound healing; a numb area cannot warn the patient of further injury.
questions.strategy: The distractors name real functions of other layers. Match the numbness to the layer that holds the nerves, then choose the action that protects a patient who cannot feel injury.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Numbness to light touch is lost sensation.
Nerves for pain, touch and temperature are in the dermis.
An area that cannot feel needs regular inspection.

elimination.verdict: Injury to the area may go unfelt, so the nurse inspects it often.

questions.objective: Use knowledge of anatomy and physiology to perform a focused assessment of the skin, hair, and nails.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced lung cancer has lost most of the fat beneath the skin over the past 6 months, and the hip bones and spine are now prominent. Which risks does this change create for the patient? Select all that apply.

options.text: Loss of vitamin D production in the skin
options.rationale: Vitamin D is made in the epidermis, not in the fat layer below the dermis. Losing subcutaneous fat does not stop the skin from making it.

options.text: Injury to the skin over the hips and spine
options.rationale: Subcutaneous tissue cushions and protects the body. Without it, bone presses on the skin with little padding, so the skin over the hips and spine is injured more easily.

options.text: Feeling cold in a room others find comfortable
options.rationale: Subcutaneous tissue stores fat that insulates the body for warmth. With little fat left, the patient loses heat faster and may feel cold when others in the room do not.

options.text: Inability to cool the body through sweat
options.rationale: Cooling through sweat is an epidermal function, and losing fat does not remove sweat glands. The patient can still sweat even though the fat layer is thin.

options.text: Distress about the change in appearance
options.rationale: Changes in fat stores can affect body image. A patient who sees prominent bones in the mirror may grieve the change, so the nurse asks how the patient feels about it.

options.text: Loss of strength and elasticity in the skin
options.rationale: Strength and elasticity come from the dermis, a separate layer above the fat. Fat loss makes the bones prominent but does not remove the dermal support that gives skin its stretch.

questions.takeaway: Subcutaneous tissue cushions, insulates and holds pressure receptors, so losing it raises the risk of feeling cold, skin injury over bones and body image distress.
questions.strategy: Every wrong choice names a real skin function, so match each one to its layer. Only the functions of the fat layer are lost here.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fat beneath the skin is subcutaneous tissue.
Cushion and protect, store fat and insulate, hold pressure receptors, affect body image.
Sweat and vitamin D belong to the epidermis; strength and elasticity belong to the dermis.

elimination.verdict: Cold, skin injury over bones and body image distress.

questions.objective: Use knowledge of anatomy and physiology to perform a focused assessment of the skin, hair, and nails.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient who has had an itchy rash on the trunk for 2 days. The skin history shows four facts. Which fact does the nurse follow up first?

options.text: Has used the same laundry soap for 2 years
options.rationale: Allergens are part of the history, so asking about soap is reasonable. A product used without trouble for 2 years is an unlikely trigger for a rash that began this week.

options.text: Started a new prescribed drug 4 days ago
options.rationale: Skin changes that begin after a new drug are a key history finding, and the timing fits this rash. The nurse asks about the drug first and reports the link to the provider.

options.text: Has a parent with psoriasis
options.rationale: Family history and genetic risk belong in the skin history, so the fact is worth recording. Psoriasis causes scaly plaques, not an itchy rash that began 2 days after a drug was started.

options.text: Worked in the garden without gloves 1 month ago
options.rationale: Outdoor contact is a possible allergen source and worth asking about. Contact with plants a month ago does not fit the timing of a rash that started 2 days ago.

questions.takeaway: When a rash appears, ask what drugs were started recently; skin changes after a new drug are a key history finding.
questions.strategy: Every fact belongs in a skin history. Timing tips the choice: only the drug change came shortly before the rash.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rash for 2 days; drug started 4 days ago.
Soap unchanged for 2 years; garden a month ago; parent's psoriasis is a different lesion.
The new drug is the likeliest cause.

elimination.verdict: Follow up the new drug first.

questions.objective: Use knowledge of anatomy and physiology to perform a focused assessment of the skin, hair, and nails.
questions.concept: Skin history: new drugs and allergens

questions.stem: While assessing a patient who is recovering from a viral illness, the nurse sees small pink spots scattered across the abdomen. In the room's light the nurse cannot tell whether the spots are flat or raised. Which action answers the question?

options.text: Measure several of the spots with a ruler
options.rationale: A ruler gives the width of each spot, which is useful to record. Width says nothing about height, so measuring cannot settle whether the rash is macular or papular.

options.text: Inspect the spots using the ABCDE method
options.rationale: The ABCDE method screens pigmented lesions for features of skin cancer. It does not tell whether a rash of small pink spots is flat or raised.

options.text: Pinch the skin over the abdomen and release it
options.rationale: Pinching and releasing the skin tests turgor, which is skin elasticity. It gives no information about whether these spots are flat or raised.

options.text: Palpate the spots with gloved fingertips
options.rationale: Palpation confirms the size and consistency of lesions and tells a flat macular rash from a raised papular rash. Fingertips can feel a slight rise that the eye misses in dim light.

questions.takeaway: Inspection finds a lesion; palpation confirms its size and consistency and tells a macular rash from a papular one.
questions.strategy: Each wrong choice is a real skin technique used for another question. Ask which technique answers flat versus raised.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flat or raised.
Turgor is elasticity; a ruler is width; ABCDE screens moles.
Palpation feels height and consistency.

elimination.verdict: Palpate the spots.

questions.objective: Use knowledge of anatomy and physiology to perform a focused assessment of the skin, hair, and nails.

questions.stem: At a clinic visit, a woman reports coarse dark hair growing on her chin and chest over the past 4 months and asks which hair removal method is safest. Which information does the nurse obtain first?

options.text: Recent drug changes and signs of hormone imbalance
options.rationale: Excess body hair comes from a hormonal imbalance or a side effect of drug therapy. Finding the cause comes before choosing how to remove the hair.

options.text: Hair removal products tried and any skin reaction
options.rationale: Product history matters once removal is planned, and a reaction would be worth recording. It does not explain why new hair began growing 4 months ago.

options.text: How often she shampoos and which products she uses
options.rationale: Shampoo habits relate to scalp cleanliness and dandruff. They do not cause coarse new hair to grow on the chin and chest.

options.text: Whether relatives have had thinning hair
options.rationale: Family history belongs in the skin history, but thinning hair is the opposite problem. It does not explain new excess hair growth in a woman.

questions.takeaway: New excess body hair in a woman is hirsutism; look for a hormonal imbalance or a drug side effect before addressing removal.
questions.strategy: She asks about hair removal, which pulls toward product history. Assess the cause of the new growth before answering the question she asked.

steps.detail: New coarse hair on chin and chest is hirsutism.
Hormonal imbalance or drug therapy.
Removal products come after the cause is known.

elimination.verdict: Ask about recent drugs and hormone changes.

questions.objective: Use knowledge of anatomy and physiology to perform a focused assessment of the skin, hair, and nails.

questions.stem: A patient with psoriasis has thick, scaly plaques on both forearms. It is a hot day, and he is wearing long sleeves. He says, "I don't want anyone to see my arms." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Psoriasis is not contagious, so other people have no reason to worry."
options.rationale: The fact is true and may help later in teaching. It answers a worry he did not voice and moves past what he said about his own feelings.

options.text: "Many people have psoriasis, and most people will not notice."
options.rationale: Reassurance that others will not notice denies what he has told the nurse he feels. It closes the topic rather than opening it.

options.text: "You seem worried about how your arms look. Tell me more."
options.rationale: Skin diseases can affect body image, and his words and long sleeves show that this one has. An open response invites him to share the feelings behind what he is doing.

options.text: "Long sleeves will make you overheat, so wear short sleeves today."
options.rationale: Heat is a fair concern on a hot day, but this reply tells him what to do with his body. It dismisses his distress instead of exploring it.

questions.takeaway: Skin, hair and nail changes can affect body image; explore the patient's feelings before teaching or reassuring.
questions.strategy: The contagion fact is true and sounds helpful. He spoke about his feelings, so the best reply opens that topic.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: He hides his arms and does not want them seen.
Both close the topic or redirect him.
It names his worry and invites more.

elimination.verdict: Explore his feelings about his appearance.

questions.stem: Ten days after a stroke, a patient who has needed help with all hygiene since admission has not had his hair washed in that time. The nurse finds patchy white and gray scales on the surface of his scalp; the scalp skin beneath is intact. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Report a possible scalp infection to the provider
options.rationale: An infection would bring changes in the scalp skin itself, and his scalp is intact. Surface scales after 10 days with no shampoo point to dandruff and a hygiene need.

options.text: Document hair loss and assess the hair's distribution
options.rationale: Distribution is part of the hair assessment, so checking it has merit. The finding is scales on the scalp surface, not missing hair, so hair loss is the wrong finding to record.

options.text: Leave the scalp alone until he can shampoo himself
options.rationale: Waiting delays hygiene for a patient who needs help with all care. The nurse encourages shampooing and helps when the patient cannot do it alone.

options.text: Document dandruff and arrange a shampoo
options.rationale: Patchy white or gray scales on the surface of an intact scalp are dandruff. Shampooing is hygiene he needs help with, so the nurse records the finding and arranges it.

questions.takeaway: Patchy white or gray scales on the scalp surface are dandruff; keep up shampooing for patients who cannot do it themselves.
questions.strategy: Scales can sound like disease. Intact scalp skin and 10 days without help with hair care point to dandruff and a hygiene need.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Surface scales, scalp intact.
Dandruff.
Hygiene help, not a report or waiting.

elimination.verdict: Document dandruff and shampoo his hair.

questions.scenario: During a focused skin assessment, a patient with long standing diabetes and recent weight loss describes several skin problems.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate which skin layer's function is most affected.

rows.text: Now feels the hard chair seat against the bones of the buttocks
rows.rationale: Subcutaneous tissue cushions and protects the body and holds pressure receptors. Weight loss thins that layer, so bone sits closer to the chair with less padding.

rows.text: Sweats less than before and overheats in warm weather
rows.rationale: Cooling through sweat is an epidermal function. When sweating drops, the body loses that cooling, so the patient overheats in warm weather.

rows.text: Dry, cracked skin on the heels has become infected
rows.rationale: The epidermis protects against microbes and prevents drying. Cracks in that outer layer give bacteria a way in, which explains the infection.

rows.text: A small cut on the shin has taken weeks to close
rows.rationale: The dermis supports wound healing and gives skin its strength. Slow closure of a cut points to a problem with that healing work in the dermis.

rows.text: Did not notice that the bath water was hot enough to redden both feet
rows.rationale: The dermis contains the nerves for pain, touch and temperature. Failing to sense hot water points to those dermal nerves and puts the patient at risk for burns.

questions.takeaway: Epidermis guards against microbes, drying and heat through sweat; dermis carries nerves and heals wounds; subcutaneous tissue cushions and insulates.
questions.strategy: Read each row for the function that failed, then place it. Temperature appears in two layers: sensing heat belongs to dermal nerves, while cooling by sweat belongs to the epidermis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sensation, healing, barrier, cushioning or cooling.
Not feeling hot water is nerves in the dermis; less sweat is the epidermis.
Feeling bone against a chair after weight loss is lost subcutaneous cushioning.

elimination.verdict: Dermis: rows 1 and 2. Epidermis: rows 3 and 5. Subcutaneous tissue: row 4.

questions.stem: At a community health fair, a woman with fair skin says she uses a tanning bed every spring to build a base tan and that it protects her skin all summer. She spends weekends on her boat without sunscreen. Which teaching does the nurse give?

options.text: Stop tanning bed use; wear sunscreen and limit sun time
options.rationale: A tanning bed is a source of ultraviolet light, the exposure the nurse teaches adults to reduce. Sunscreen and less time in the sun protect her on the boat.

options.text: Keep the base tan and add sunscreen on the sunniest days
options.rationale: Adding sunscreen is right, so this choice is partly correct. Keeping the base tan continues ultraviolet exposure, and sunscreen only on the sunniest days leaves her unprotected on others.

options.text: Keep the base tan, since a monthly skin check matters most
options.rationale: Monthly skin checks find changes early, but they do not prevent them. Accepting the base tan leaves a major source of ultraviolet exposure in place.

options.text: Shorten the tanning bed sessions and check all skin every month
options.rationale: Monthly skin checks are correct teaching, so this choice is half right. Shorter sessions still expose her to ultraviolet light, which she needs to stop, not reduce.

questions.takeaway: Teach adults to use sunscreen and reduce sun and ultraviolet exposure; a tanning bed is ultraviolet exposure, not protection.
questions.strategy: Two choices contain a correct teaching point attached to keeping the tan. Reject any choice that leaves the ultraviolet exposure in place.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The tanning bed and the boat are both ultraviolet.
Any choice that keeps the base tan or only shortens sessions keeps the exposure.
Stop the tanning bed, use sunscreen, limit sun.

elimination.verdict: Stop the tanning bed and protect her skin in the sun.

questions.objective: Teach evidence based health promotion activities to help prevent skin, hair, and nail health problems or trauma.

questions.stem: The nurse has taught skin self examination to a patient whose father had melanoma. Which statement by the patient shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "Once a year, on my birthday, I will check all of my skin for any change."
options.rationale: He has the extent right, since he plans to check all of his skin for change. The timing is wrong, because self examination is done monthly so that changes are found early.

options.text: "Every month I will check all of my skin, back included, for any change."
options.rationale: Adults are taught to examine all of their skin monthly and to watch for new or changing lesions. He names the right timing, the full extent of skin and the change that matters most.

options.text: "Every month I will check my face, neck and arms, where the sun hits."
options.rationale: Sun exposed areas matter, and monthly timing is correct. The teaching is to examine all skin, because lesions also develop on the back, scalp and other covered areas.

options.text: "Every month I will check my spots, but only the ones larger than 6 mm."
options.rationale: He has the timing right, and a diameter over 6 mm is one warning sign. A smaller spot that is changing or irregular still needs evaluation, so size alone cannot limit the check.

questions.takeaway: Teach monthly self examination of all skin, front and back, watching for any new or changing lesion with the ABCDE features.
questions.strategy: Each wrong statement gets two parts right and one part wrong. Check timing, extent and what to look for in every statement before choosing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Monthly; once a year is too seldom.
All skin; sun exposed areas alone miss the back and scalp.
Any change counts; a size over 6 mm is only one sign.

elimination.verdict: "Every month I will check all of my skin, back included, for any change."

questions.stem: On a medical unit, a 76 year old patient with thin, fragile skin has slid down in bed. Assistive personnel prepare to pull him up by grasping under both arms and dragging him toward the headboard. What does the nurse direct instead?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed first so the pull is shorter
options.rationale: Raising the head of the bed lets him sink farther toward the foot of the bed and adds to shearing. A shorter pull still drags his skin across the sheet.

options.text: Leave him where he is until his next 2 hour position change
options.rationale: Waiting leaves him slumped, with pressure and shear on his sacrum and heels. He needs repositioning now, done with a lift sheet.

options.text: Move him up with a lift sheet and a second staff member
options.rationale: Dragging the body across the sheet causes shearing, which tears fragile skin. A lift sheet with two staff raises him off the surface so his skin does not drag.

options.text: Turn him to the side, then pull him up under the arms
options.rationale: Turning first does not change how he is moved up, so his skin still drags across the sheet. Pulling under the arms also strains his shoulders.

questions.takeaway: Use lift sheets when moving patients so the skin is lifted, not dragged; dragging causes shearing injury to fragile skin.
questions.strategy: Each wrong choice changes the timing or the angle but still drags him. The fix is lifting rather than pulling.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dragging fragile skin causes shearing.
Does the skin still drag across the sheet?
Lift sheet with two staff.

elimination.verdict: Use a lift sheet with a second staff member.

questions.stem: While caring for a patient with obesity who is on bed rest, the nurse observes assistive personnel giving care during the shift. The patient has moist skin in the fold beneath her abdomen. Which action needs correction?

options.text: Positions her so air reaches the skin beneath the abdominal fold
options.rationale: Positioning to let air circulate to skinfolds keeps moist skin from breaking down. This is the right action for her abdominal fold, so it needs no correction.

options.text: Trims and cleans her fingernails while she is on bed rest
options.rationale: Fingernails are kept clean and trimmed so the patient does not scratch and injure her skin. Bed rest is no reason to skip nail care, so this action is correct.

options.text: Reports which skin areas looked different at each turn
options.rationale: Position changes are the time to note areas of compromised tissue integrity. Reporting them lets the nurse assess the changes promptly, so this action is correct.

options.text: Turns her every 4 hours overnight so that she can sleep
options.rationale: Patients on bed rest are repositioned at least every 2 hours, overnight included. Wanting her to sleep is kind, but 4 hours leaves her skin under pressure twice as long.

questions.takeaway: Reposition at least every 2 hours, day and night; let air reach skinfolds, keep nails clean and trimmed, and report skin changes.
questions.strategy: The wrong action comes with a kind reason, which makes it look acceptable. Judge the turning interval against the rule, not the reason given for it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the action that is wrong.
Every 4 hours is longer than at least every 2 hours.
Air to skinfolds, nail care and reporting changes are all correct.

elimination.verdict: Turns her every 4 hours overnight so that she can sleep.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with pneumonia has dark brown skin and respirations of 28 per minute. Assistive personnel report that his skin color looks unchanged, so he is not cyanotic. Where does the nurse look next?

options.text: His forearms for areas darker than nearby skin
options.rationale: Darker patches can mean inflammation or irritation in dark skin tones. That finding does not tell the nurse whether his oxygenation is poor.

options.text: His lips and tongue for a gray or white color
options.rationale: In dark skin tones, cyanosis is hard to see in the skin itself. The lips and tongue may look gray or white, and the nail beds and palms may show a bluish tinge.

options.text: His hard palate and inner sclera for yellowing
options.rationale: The hard palate and the sclera near the cornea are where the nurse checks for jaundice. They do not answer whether this breathless patient is cyanotic.

options.text: His cheeks, forehead and forearms for a blue tinge to the skin
options.rationale: Looking for blue skin works in light skin tones, and it is the reason the report missed the problem. Cyanosis in dark skin shows in the lips, tongue, palms and nail beds.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, look for cyanosis in the lips and tongue (gray or white) and the palms, soles, conjunctiva and nail beds (bluish tinge).
questions.strategy: The report sounds reassuring because skin color is unchanged. Unchanged skin is the expected finding in dark skin even when cyanosis is present.

steps.detail: Respirations of 28 per minute raise concern for oxygenation.
Skin color misses cyanosis in dark skin tones.
Lips and tongue, then nail beds and palms.

elimination.verdict: Inspect his lips and tongue.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect health equity for patients with skin, hair, or nail health problems.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that need follow up.
questions.nursesNote: 0800 Admitted with heart failure; he reports more shortness of breath since yesterday. Skin on the inner upper arms is medium brown and even. Lips and tongue appear gray. Thick calluses on both heels look yellow. Nail beds have a bluish tinge. Lengthwise brown bands on four fingernails; he states they have been present for 20 years. Sclera next to each cornea is white. Oral mucosa has an ash gray tone. Skin over the left shin is darker than the surrounding skin, warm and tender.

segments.text: Skin on the inner upper arms is medium brown and even
segments.rationale: The inner upper arm gets little sun, so it shows his baseline skin tone. An even medium brown there is the normal comparison point, not a problem.

segments.text: Lips and tongue appear gray
segments.rationale: In dark skin, cyanosis shows as gray or white lips and tongue. In a patient with heart failure this suggests poor oxygenation and needs follow up now.

segments.text: Thick calluses on both heels look yellow
segments.rationale: Callused soles can look yellow without jaundice. The sclera next to the cornea is white, so this finding is expected.

segments.text: Nail beds have a bluish tinge
segments.rationale: A bluish tinge in the nail beds is another sign of cyanosis in dark skin. Together with the gray lips, it points to poor oxygenation.

segments.text: Lengthwise brown bands on four fingernails
segments.rationale: Pigmented nail bands are common in people with dark skin, and he reports they have been present for 20 years. A long standing, unchanged finding is not a new problem.

segments.text: Sclera next to each cornea is white
segments.rationale: The sclera closest to the cornea is the most accurate site for jaundice in dark skin. White sclera there means no jaundice.

segments.text: Oral mucosa has an ash gray tone
segments.rationale: A gray or ash gray tone of the mucous membranes is how pallor shows in dark skin. It suggests poor perfusion or low hemoglobin and needs follow up.

segments.text: Skin over the left shin is darker than the surrounding skin, warm and tender
segments.rationale: In dark skin, inflammation often looks darker than the surrounding skin rather than red. Warmth and tenderness confirm a change that needs assessment.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, look for cyanosis in lips, tongue and nail beds, pallor in mucous membranes, jaundice in the sclera by the cornea, and inflammation as darker skin.
questions.strategy: Yellow calluses and brown nail bands look abnormal but are expected in dark skin. Gray lips and mucosa and a darker, warm shin are the problems.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The inner upper arm shows his normal tone.
Yellow calluses, long standing nail bands and white sclera.
Gray lips, bluish nail beds, ash gray mucosa, darker warm shin.

elimination.verdict: Gray lips and tongue, bluish nail beds, ash gray mucosa and the darker, warm, tender shin.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect health equity for patients with skin, hair, or nail health problems.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with a bleeding stomach ulcer whose hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL. She has dark brown skin, and the nurse checks her for pallor. Which assessment gives the most reliable information?

options.text: Mucous membranes for an ash gray tone in halogen light
options.rationale: Pallor in dark skin tones shows best in the mucous membranes, which look gray or ash gray. Ambient or halogen light gives the clearest view of that color.

options.text: Palms and soles for a yellow tone in daylight
options.rationale: Yellow is the color the nurse looks for with jaundice, and calluses can make palms look yellow anyway. Neither finding answers whether she is pale.

options.text: Forearm skin for color return after firm pressure
options.rationale: Pressing and watching for color return tests blanching, which is hard to see in dark skin. It does not show the gray tone of pallor.

options.text: Face compared with the upper chest for a lighter shade
options.rationale: Comparing two areas of skin sounds careful, but both may lose color equally. Pallor in dark skin is judged in the mucous membranes.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, check pallor in the mucous membranes under ambient or halogen light; brown skin may look yellow brown and very dark skin ash gray.
questions.strategy: Blanching and skin comparison are real techniques that work poorly in dark skin. Go where pigment does not hide the color.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pallor.
Mucous membranes, under good light.
Yellow palms are jaundice or calluses; blanching tests a different thing.

elimination.verdict: Inspect her mucous membranes for an ash gray tone.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect health equity for patients with skin, hair, or nail health problems.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with hepatitis works in construction, has dark brown skin and has thick calluses on both palms. Assistive personnel report that his palms look yellow. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Inspect the nail beds and conjunctiva for a bluish tinge
options.rationale: A bluish tinge in the nail beds and conjunctiva is how cyanosis shows in dark skin. It does not answer whether he is jaundiced.

options.text: Compare the yellow of the right palm with the left palm
options.rationale: Both palms are callused, so both may look yellow for the same reason. Comparing them adds nothing about jaundice.

options.text: Inspect the hard palate and the sclera next to the cornea
options.rationale: Callused palms can look yellow without jaundice, so the report is not proof. The hard palate and the sclera closest to the cornea give the most accurate check.

options.text: Report new jaundice to the provider and request a bilirubin level
options.rationale: Hepatitis makes jaundice plausible, so reporting feels safe. Yellow on callused palms is not reliable, and the nurse confirms the finding before reporting it.

questions.takeaway: Callused palms and soles can look yellow without jaundice; check the hard palate and the sclera closest to the cornea.
questions.strategy: Hepatitis primes the student to accept jaundice and report it. The site of the finding is unreliable, so confirm at a reliable site first.

steps.detail: Calluses can look yellow on their own.
Oral mucosa, hard palate and sclera next to the cornea.
A confirmed finding is what the provider needs.

elimination.verdict: Inspect the hard palate and the sclera next to the cornea.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect health equity for patients with skin, hair, or nail health problems.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the chart of a patient with leukemia whose platelet count is 18,000 per mm3. She has dark brown skin, and assistive personnel inspected her arms, legs and trunk in bright light and report no petechiae. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Repeat the inspection of her limbs under halogen light
options.rationale: Better light helps with pallor in the mucous membranes. Petechiae can stay hidden in dark skin under any light, so the limbs are still the wrong site.

options.text: Inspect her oral mucosa and conjunctiva
options.rationale: Petechiae are often not visible on darkly pigmented skin, so a normal skin check does not rule them out. The oral mucosa and conjunctiva show them more reliably.

options.text: Record no petechiae and recheck her skin each shift
options.rationale: Rechecking each shift sounds thorough, but she would keep being checked in the wrong place. Documenting "no petechiae" from skin alone may hide bleeding.

options.text: Palpate her arms and legs for tender, raised areas
options.rationale: Tender, raised areas suggest an ecchymosis with a hematoma, which is worth knowing with low platelets. Petechiae are tiny flat spots that palpation will not find.

questions.takeaway: Petechiae are often not visible on dark skin; inspect the oral mucosa and conjunctiva.
questions.strategy: Repeating the skin check under better light feels like a fix. The problem is the site, not the light.

steps.detail: A very low platelet count makes bleeding into the skin likely.
Skin inspection misses petechiae in dark skin.
Oral mucosa and conjunctiva.

elimination.verdict: Inspect her oral mucosa and conjunctiva.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect health equity for patients with skin, hair, or nail health problems.

questions.stem: Two days after falling onto his right hip, a patient with dark brown skin has an area over the hip that is darker than his usual skin tone and is tender and raised to the touch. How does the nurse interpret this finding?

options.text: Petechiae from bleeding under the skin
options.rationale: Petechiae are tiny spots that are often not visible on dark skin at all. A larger raised, tender area after a fall is not petechiae.

options.text: Skin irritation from lying on the right hip
options.rationale: Irritation can also look darker in dark skin, so this is a near miss. Irritation does not make a raised, tender lump, and the fall gives a clear cause for bleeding.

options.text: Cyanosis from poor blood flow to the hip
options.rationale: Cyanosis in dark skin shows as gray lips and tongue or bluish nail beds, not as one dark area. Nothing here suggests poor oxygenation.

options.text: An ecchymosis with a hematoma beneath it
options.rationale: In dark skin, an ecchymosis looks darker than the usual skin tone. Tenderness and a raised feel point to a hematoma beneath, which fits a fall 2 days ago.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, ecchymoses look darker than usual skin tone and may be tender or palpable when a hematoma lies beneath.
questions.strategy: Irritation and ecchymosis both look darker in dark skin. Palpation and the antecedent separate them: a raised, tender area after a fall is bleeding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A fall onto the hip 2 days ago.
Tender and raised suggests a hematoma.
Petechiae are tiny; cyanosis shows in lips and nail beds.

elimination.verdict: An ecchymosis with a hematoma.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect health equity for patients with skin, hair, or nail health problems.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report no redness under the straps of a knee brace that a patient with dark brown skin has worn for 3 days. The nurse sees a band of skin under one strap that is darker than the surrounding skin. What is the best action?

options.text: Palpate the band and compare it with the other leg
options.rationale: In dark skin, irritation and inflammation often appear darker than the surrounding skin instead of red. Palpating for warmth and firmness and comparing sides confirms a change from her normal.

options.text: Document no erythema and recheck at the next routine skin check
options.rationale: The report of no redness is accurate but misses how irritation shows in dark skin. Waiting for a routine check leaves pressure from the strap in place.

options.text: Record the darker band as her normal pigmentation
options.rationale: Normal pigmentation does not appear as a band under a strap after 3 days of wear. Its shape and location point to irritation from the brace.

options.text: Inspect her oral mucosa and conjunctiva for small dark spots
options.rationale: The mucosa and conjunctiva are where the nurse looks for petechiae in dark skin. That check does not address the band under the strap.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, erythema and inflammation may show as an area darker than the surrounding skin; palpate and compare sides.
questions.strategy: "No redness" is true and still misleading. Darker skin under a strap is the finding to follow up.

steps.detail: No redness does not mean no irritation in dark skin.
A band under a strap points to the brace.
Palpate and compare with the other leg.

elimination.verdict: Palpate the band and compare sides.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect health equity for patients with skin, hair, or nail health problems.
questions.concept: Inflammation and irritation in dark skin tone

questions.scenario: At a community clinic, the nurse reviews skin findings from five older adults seen today.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected aging change or needs follow up.

rows.text: A woman's forearm skin stays tented after a pinch; she has vomited four times since last night
rows.rationale: Tenting can come from aging alone, but here it comes with a cause of fluid loss. Vomiting since last night makes dehydration likely, so this finding needs follow up.

rows.text: A man's hand skin stays tented after a pinch; his mouth is moist and he drinks well
rows.rationale: Aging skin loses elasticity, so tenting on the hand is common in older adults. His moist mouth and good intake give no sign of fluid loss, so the tenting alone fits aging.

rows.text: A woman's shins have thin, translucent, paper like skin with loss of skin markings
rows.rationale: Thin, paper like skin with lost markings is atrophy, a common aging change. It raises her risk of skin tears and is protected, but it is not a new problem.

rows.text: A man has flat brown spots on the backs of both hands, unchanged for years
rows.rationale: Flat brown spots on sun exposed skin that have not changed are common with age. Stable color, shape and size do not call for follow up.

rows.text: A man's mouth is dry and sticky, and his urine has been dark amber since yesterday
rows.rationale: A dry mouth and dark urine point to fluid loss without relying on turgor. Because aging makes tenting less reliable, findings like these carry the weight in judging hydration.

questions.takeaway: Tenting is less reliable in aging skin; judge hydration by the history and other findings, such as intake, vomiting, mouth moisture and urine color.
questions.strategy: Two rows show the same tented skin, which tempts the same answer for both. The vomiting history, not the tenting, decides which one needs follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Aging skin is less elastic, so tenting by itself is weak evidence.
Vomiting, a dry mouth and dark urine point to fluid loss.
Atrophy and stable brown spots are expected.

elimination.verdict: Three expected aging changes; the dry mouth and the vomiting patient need follow up.

questions.objective: Explain how genetic implications and physiologic aging of the skin, hair, and nails affect tissue integrity.

questions.stem: During an admission assessment, the nurse wants a baseline skin tone to compare with later color changes. The patient has dark brown skin, and his face and forearms are deeply tanned after a month at the beach. Which area does the nurse inspect?

options.text: The forearms, which are easy to expose
options.rationale: Ease of access is practical, but the forearms are tanned from the beach. Their tone reflects facultative pigmentation, not his genetic skin tone.

options.text: The backs of both hands
options.rationale: Comparing sides is useful for spotting one sided changes. The backs of the hands get daily sun, so both show added pigment rather than his baseline.

options.text: The inner upper arm
options.rationale: Constitutive pigmentation is the genetic skin tone, and facultative pigmentation is added by ultraviolet exposure. The inner upper arm gets little sun, so it shows his true baseline.

options.text: The face, under a halogen light
options.rationale: Good lighting helps the nurse see color, so the light is a sound choice. The face is heavily sun exposed, so its tone includes the tan and is not his baseline.

questions.takeaway: Assess skin tone in areas least exposed to ultraviolet light, where constitutive (genetic) pigmentation shows without facultative (sun) pigment.
questions.strategy: Halogen light and side to side comparison are real techniques, which makes them tempting. The site still has to be one the sun does not reach.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Genetic tone versus tone added by sun.
Inner upper arm.
Face, hands and forearms are all tanned.

elimination.verdict: Inspect the inner upper arm.

questions.objective: Explain how genetic implications and physiologic aging of the skin, hair, and nails affect tissue integrity.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an 87 year old patient who eats and drinks well, and her intake has matched her output for 3 days. Her skin is thin and wrinkled. When assistive personnel pinch the skin on the back of her hand, it stays tented, and they report that she is dehydrated. How does the nurse respond?

options.text: Tenting points to edema; press over both ankles to check for pitting
options.rationale: Edema makes skin tight and swollen, which is the opposite of skin that stays tented. Checking the ankles does not explain the tenting on her hand.

options.text: Aging skin is less elastic; weigh tenting against her other findings
options.rationale: Turgor measures skin elasticity, and thin, wrinkled aging skin can stay tented without fluid loss. Her matched intake and output weigh against dehydration, so the nurse reads turgor with them.

options.text: Tenting confirms dehydration; offer fluids every hour and record intake
options.rationale: Offering fluids is right when dehydration is present, so the action is not harmful. Treating one tented pinch as proof ignores her balanced intake and output.

options.text: Tenting is expected at her age, so turgor no longer needs assessment
options.rationale: The nurse distinguishes normal variations from abnormal findings, and turgor stays part of that. Her age changes how the result is read, not whether it is checked.

questions.takeaway: Turgor is skin elasticity, which falls with aging; in an older adult, interpret tenting together with other fluid findings.
questions.strategy: The report sounds like a clear finding with a clear fix. Aging skin can tent on its own, and her intake and output say otherwise.

steps.detail: Skin elasticity.
Thin, wrinkled skin is less elastic.
Matched intake and output do not fit dehydration.

elimination.verdict: Interpret the tenting with her other findings.

questions.objective: Explain how genetic implications and physiologic aging of the skin, hair, and nails affect tissue integrity.

questions.stem: During a skin assessment, the nurse finds several raised lesions on a patient's chin, each smaller than 1 cm and filled with cloudy yellow fluid. Which term does the nurse use to document these lesions?

options.text: Papules
options.rationale: Papules are small, firm, raised lesions under 1 cm, so the size and height fit. A papule is solid, and these lesions are filled with fluid.

options.text: Bullae
options.rationale: Bullae are blisters with clear fluid that are larger than 1 cm. These lesions are under 1 cm and cloudy, so both features rule it out.

options.text: Pustules
options.rationale: Pustules are vesicles filled with cloudy or purulent fluid, often seen with acne. The cloudy yellow fluid is the feature that sets these lesions apart.

options.text: Vesicles
options.rationale: Vesicles are raised blisters smaller than 1 cm, so the size fits. Their fluid is clear, and these lesions hold cloudy yellow fluid.

questions.takeaway: Raised, under 1 cm and fluid filled: clear fluid is a vesicle, cloudy or purulent fluid is a pustule; over 1 cm with clear fluid is a bulla.
questions.strategy: Vesicle matches the size and the blister shape. The color of the fluid decides it.

steps.detail: Under 1 cm rules out bulla.
Fluid filled rules out papule.
Cloudy, not clear, makes it a pustule.

elimination.verdict: Pustules.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings for patients with a suspected or actual skin, hair, or nail problem.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with impetigo who has several kinds of lesions on his arms and legs. Which lesion does the nurse document as a pustule?

options.text: A honey colored, dried layer where a raised spot broke open
options.rationale: Impetigo pustules often break and leave this layer, so it may have begun as a pustule. Dried serum or pus is a crust, a secondary lesion, and is documented as such.

options.text: A 5 mm raised, firm red spot that holds no fluid
options.rationale: A raised lesion under 1 cm matches a pustule in size. It is solid and holds no fluid, which makes it a papule rather than a fluid filled lesion.

options.text: A 5 mm raised spot with clear, watery contents under a thin roof
options.rationale: This lesion has the same size and shape as a pustule. Its clear fluid makes it a vesicle; only cloudy or purulent fluid makes a pustule.

options.text: A 5 mm raised spot with milky yellow contents under a thin roof
options.rationale: A pustule is a vesicle filled with cloudy or purulent fluid, and milky yellow contents are pus. Its size under 1 cm and thin roof fit a fluid filled primary lesion.

questions.takeaway: A pustule is a vesicle with cloudy or purulent fluid; once it breaks and dries, what remains is a crust, a secondary lesion.
questions.strategy: The crust tempts because impetigo crusts come from pustules. The nurse documents what is present now, and only the intact lesion with milky contents is a pustule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Same size and roof; milky versus clear contents decides.
A broken, dried lesion is a crust.
No fluid means a papule.

elimination.verdict: The raised spot with milky yellow contents.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings for patients with a suspected or actual skin, hair, or nail problem.

questions.scenario: In the outpatient clinic, a woman reports months of fatigue and very heavy menstrual periods. Her fingernail plates are flattened and smoother than usual. The angle at each nail base is 160 degrees, and the base is firm. She has no history of diabetes, psoriasis or nail injury.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Ask about her usual diet and food intake
options.rationale: Nutrition is part of the skin history, and a diet low in iron adds to losses from heavy periods. Her answers guide teaching and the plan of care.

options.text: Apply oxygen by nasal cannula
options.rationale: Oxygen treats hypoxia, which causes clubbing rather than spoon nails. Her nail angle is a normal 160 degrees, so nothing here points to low oxygen.

options.text: Review her hemoglobin and iron results
options.rationale: Early spoon nails point to iron deficiency, with or without anemia, and heavy periods are a source of iron loss. Laboratory results confirm whether that is the cause.

options.text: Inspect her scalp and elbows for plaques
options.rationale: Psoriasis matters for late spoon nails and for pitting. She has early flattening, no psoriasis history and a clear source of iron loss.

options.text: Prolonged hypoxia
options.rationale: Prolonged hypoxia causes clubbing, which widens the nail angle and softens the base. Her angle is a normal 160 degrees with a firm base.

options.text: Psoriasis
options.rationale: Psoriasis is linked to late spoon nails and to pitting, not to early flattening. She has no psoriasis history, and heavy periods explain the finding better.

options.text: Iron deficiency
options.rationale: Flattened, smoother nail plates are early koilonychia, linked to iron deficiency with or without anemia. Heavy periods and fatigue fit, and the history rules out diabetes, psoriasis and injury.

options.text: Acute severe illness
options.rationale: Acute severe illness causes Beau's lines, which are horizontal grooves across all nails. Her nails are flattened, not grooved, and she reports no recent severe illness.

options.text: Oxygen saturation
options.rationale: Oxygen saturation tracks hypoxia, the cause of clubbing. Her nails and history do not point to a breathing problem, so it is not a priority parameter.

options.text: Blood glucose level
options.rationale: Poorly controlled diabetes over many years can cause spoon nails, so this is tempting. She has no diabetes history, and her heavy periods explain the finding.

options.text: Hemoglobin level
options.rationale: Iron deficiency can lead to anemia, so the hemoglobin level shows how far the problem has gone. Repeat results show whether treatment is working.

options.text: Fatigue with daily activity
options.rationale: Her main complaint is fatigue, which worsens as iron and hemoglobin fall. Tracking how she tolerates daily activity shows whether her condition is improving.

questions.takeaway: Flattened, smoother nail plates are early spoon nails (koilonychia), linked to iron deficiency; check hemoglobin and iron and ask about diet and blood loss.
questions.strategy: Spoon nails have several causes, and glucose and psoriasis are real ones. Her history removes them and leaves a clear source of iron loss.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flattened, smoother plates are early koilonychia.
Heavy periods and fatigue; no diabetes, psoriasis or injury.
Iron studies, diet, hemoglobin and fatigue.

elimination.verdict: Iron deficiency: review iron results, ask about diet, monitor hemoglobin and fatigue.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings for patients with a suspected or actual skin, hair, or nail problem.

questions.stem: At a clinic visit, a patient shows the nurse a thick, leathery patch on the back of the neck with deep, exaggerated skin lines. Which question does the nurse ask first?

options.text: "How long have you been rubbing or scratching this area?"
options.rationale: Thickened skin with exaggerated markings is lichenification, which comes from chronic rubbing or scratching. Asking about that habit finds the cause and the itch behind it.

options.text: "Have you recently started any new drugs?"
options.rationale: A new drug is an important question when a rash appears suddenly. A thick, leathery patch takes a long time to form, so a recent drug change is unlikely to explain it.

options.text: "Did the area start as a blister that broke open?"
options.rationale: Broken blisters leave crusts or erosions, which are moist or dried surface lesions. They do not produce thick, leathery skin with deep markings.

options.text: "Has this patch changed in size, shape or color?"
options.rationale: Asking about change is the E of ABCDE, used for pigmented lesions that may be skin cancer. A thick, leathery patch with deep lines points to long term rubbing instead.

questions.takeaway: Lichenification is thickened, leathery skin with exaggerated markings from chronic rubbing or scratching; ask about the habit and the itch.
questions.strategy: The ABCDE question sounds thorough for any skin patch. Thick, leathery skin with deep lines describes a long term response to rubbing, not a changing mole.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Thick, leathery, deep lines.
Lichenification.
Chronic rubbing or scratching.

elimination.verdict: Ask how long the patient has been rubbing or scratching.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings for patients with a suspected or actual skin, hair, or nail problem.

questions.stem: On admission for a hernia repair, a patient with long standing emphysema breathes comfortably, and his oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. Viewed from the side, each fingernail meets the proximal nail fold at a 180 degree angle, and the nail bases feel spongy. A nursing student says the nails need no follow up because his saturation is normal. How does the nurse respond?

options.text: This is early clubbing from long term low oxygen; it needs follow up
options.rationale: A 180 degree angle with a spongy base is early clubbing, which reflects hypoxia over time. His emphysema explains it, and it is documented and reported even when today's saturation is normal.

options.text: Spongy nail bases point to low iron; ask about his diet
options.rationale: Iron deficiency is linked to spoon nails, which have flattened or concave plates. Spongy bases with a straightened angle point to low oxygen, not low iron.

options.text: A 180 degree angle is normal, and the spongy bases come from aging
options.rationale: The normal angle is 160 degrees with a firm base. A straightened angle with a spongy base is early clubbing, and aging does not soften the nail base.

options.text: His saturation is normal now, so the nails need no follow up
options.rationale: A normal reading today is reassuring about his oxygen at this moment. Clubbing develops over a long period of low oxygen, so one normal reading does not rule it out.

questions.takeaway: Clubbing reflects long term hypoxia; early clubbing straightens the nail angle to 180 degrees with a spongy base, and a normal saturation today does not rule it out.
questions.strategy: The normal saturation makes the student's view sound safe. Clubbing records months of low oxygen, and a 180 degree angle is its early form, not a normal variant.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A 160 degree angle with a firm base.
180 degrees with spongy bases is early clubbing.
Clubbing reflects long term hypoxia; saturation shows only this moment.

elimination.verdict: Early clubbing from long term low oxygen; it needs follow up.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings for patients with a suspected or actual skin, hair, or nail problem.

questions.stem: Three months after treatment in intensive care for sepsis, a patient has recovered. Today the nurse sees a horizontal groove about 1 mm wide across every fingernail, partway up each nail. She has no fever and feels well. How does the nurse interpret the grooves?

options.text: As clubbing from low oxygen during her stay
options.rationale: Clubbing changes the angle at the nail base and makes the base spongy. A groove across the nail plate is a different finding with a different cause.

options.text: As a sign that her infection has returned
options.rationale: The grooves record a past pause in nail growth, not a current illness. She has no fever and feels well, so nothing today points to a new infection.

options.text: As pitting from a skin disease such as psoriasis
options.rationale: Pitting is many small dents scattered over the nail, often with psoriasis. These are single horizontal grooves across every nail, which fits a pause in growth.

options.text: As growth arrest during her severe illness
options.rationale: Beau's lines are 1 mm horizontal grooves across all nails caused by growth arrest during acute severe illness or prolonged fever. Her sepsis 3 months ago explains them, and she is well now.

questions.takeaway: Beau's lines are 1 mm horizontal grooves across all nails from growth arrest during acute severe illness, prolonged fever or severe malnutrition.
questions.strategy: A finding linked to sepsis can look like a sign of new infection. The grooves are a record of the past; today's fever and symptoms tell the present.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Horizontal grooves across all nails.
Growth arrest from acute severe illness.
No fever and she feels well.

elimination.verdict: Growth arrest from her severe illness.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings for patients with a suspected or actual skin, hair, or nail problem.

questions.stem: At a yearly skin check, a woman says none of her moles have changed. The nurse compares four of her moles with the measurements and photos recorded at last year's visit. Which mole does the nurse flag for evaluation?

options.text: Arm: 4 mm, even tan, smooth edge; flat, as it was last year
options.rationale: This mole is small, even in color and smooth, and it has stayed flat. Nothing about it meets an ABCDE warning sign, so it is rechecked at the next visit.

options.text: Back: 5 mm, even brown, smooth edge; flat last year, raised now
options.rationale: Becoming raised since last year is a change in elevation, the E in ABCDE. A lesion that is evolving needs evaluation even when she has not noticed it and its other features are reassuring.

options.text: Chest: 5 mm, raised, even dark brown; raised, as it was last year
options.rationale: A raised, darker mole can look worrying at first glance. It was raised and the same color last year, so it is stable and shows no ABCDE warning sign.

options.text: Neck: 3 mm, soft, raised, skin colored; unchanged since last year
options.rationale: Being raised is not a warning sign by itself. This soft, skin colored lesion is small, even and stable over a year, so it does not need evaluation now.

questions.takeaway: Evolving means any change in size, shape, color or elevation over time; compare with the earlier record, because the patient may not notice the change.
questions.strategy: Her report that nothing changed and the darker raised mole both pull attention elsewhere. Only the comparison with last year's record shows which mole has evolved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every mole is small, symmetric, smooth edged and one color.
Only the back mole changed: flat then, raised now.
She did not notice the change; the record did.

elimination.verdict: The back mole that is now raised.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings for patients with a suspected or actual skin, hair, or nail problem.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse that a mole on her left shoulder became raised and itchy over the past 2 months. It is 4 mm across, symmetric, one even brown color, with a smooth border. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Teach monthly skin checks and recheck it next year
options.rationale: Monthly self checks are good teaching, so part of this is correct. Waiting a year to recheck a mole that is changing now delays evaluation.

options.text: Palpate the mole and document it as a papule
options.rationale: Palpation confirms size and consistency, and recording the finding is reasonable. Documenting alone stops short, because a changing mole needs evaluation.

options.text: Arrange an evaluation of the mole now
options.rationale: Evolving or changing features are the E of ABCDE, and this mole has changed in height and sensation. One warning feature is enough to need evaluation, whatever the size.

options.text: Reassure her, because it is small, even and smooth
options.rationale: The mole meets four of the five criteria for a reassuring lesion, which makes this tempting. A mole that is changing still needs evaluation, so reassurance is not appropriate.

questions.takeaway: Any one ABCDE feature, including change alone in a small, even, smooth mole, is a reason for evaluation.
questions.strategy: Four reassuring features pull toward reassurance. The fifth, change, is enough by itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shape, border, color and size are all reassuring.
It has changed: raised and itchy.
Change alone needs evaluation now.

elimination.verdict: Arrange an evaluation now.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings for patients with a suspected or actual skin, hair, or nail problem.

questions.stem: The nurse inspects the fingernails of an 80 year old man during a head to toe assessment. Which findings need follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: A 160 degree angle between nail plate and proximal nail fold
options.rationale: A 160 degree angle with a slightly convex plate and a firm base is the normal nail shape. It is the standard the other findings are compared with.

options.text: Nail plates that curve inward like a spoon
options.rationale: A concave nail plate is late koilonychia, linked to psoriasis, chemical irritants or a developmental abnormality. It is not an aging change.

options.text: Spongy nail bases with a 180 degree angle
options.rationale: A straightened 180 degree angle with a spongy base is early clubbing. It is linked to hypoxia and lung cancer and needs follow up.

options.text: Lengthwise ridges and a yellow tint on all nails
options.rationale: Ridged, yellowed nails are an expected change with aging in an older adult. On their own, without other changes in shape, they need no follow up.

options.text: Many small pits across several fingernails
options.rationale: Multiple small pits are linked to psoriasis and alopecia areata. Aging does not cause them, so they need follow up.

questions.takeaway: Ridged, yellowed nails are expected with aging; clubbing, pitting and spoon shaped nails are not.
questions.strategy: Age makes every nail change look expected. Only ridging and yellowing come with aging, and a 160 degree angle is normal at any age.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 160 degrees, firm base.
Ridged, yellowed nails.
Early clubbing, pitting, late spoon nails.

elimination.verdict: Early clubbing, pitting and spoon shaped nails need follow up.

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings for patients with a suspected or actual skin, hair, or nail problem.

questions.stem: The provider orders a wound culture of a draining lesion on a patient's left lower leg. Assistive personnel offer to steady the leg with bare hands, saying they will touch only intact skin. What does the nurse direct?

options.text: Cover the lesion with a dressing, then steady the leg barehanded
options.rationale: Covering the lesion would also block the culture that is about to be taken. Standard Precautions still call for gloves before contact.

options.text: Wash hands and put on gloves before touching the leg
options.rationale: Hand hygiene and Standard Precautions apply to any care of a patient with impaired tissue integrity. Gloves protect the worker from drainage and protect the lesion from new organisms.

options.text: Steady the leg with bare hands, then wash hands afterward
options.rationale: Washing hands afterward is correct, so this choice is partly right. Drainage can reach skin that looks intact, so bare hands are not safe.

options.text: Stand back so that only the nurse touches the patient
options.rationale: Limiting contact sounds protective, but the leg still needs to be steadied. Gloves let the assistive personnel help safely.

questions.takeaway: Wash hands and use Standard Precautions for any care of a patient with impaired tissue integrity, including during cultures.
questions.strategy: Touching only intact skin sounds safe. Standard Precautions apply to the whole care episode, not only to the lesion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hand hygiene and Standard Precautions with impaired tissue integrity.
Bare hands fail; a dressing blocks the culture.
Hand hygiene and gloves.

elimination.verdict: Hand hygiene and gloves before touching the leg.

questions.objective: Plan evidence based care and support for patients undergoing diagnostic testing of the skin or nails.

questions.stem: Before a punch biopsy of a lesion on the right forearm, a patient who has signed the consent says as the nurse sets up, "Nothing is going to be cut, right?" What does the nurse do?

options.text: Explain how a punch biopsy is done, then continue the setup
options.rationale: Teaching the patient is part of the nurse's role, so this sounds helpful. Explaining the procedure for consent is the provider's job, and continuing assumes consent is valid.

options.text: Say a light examination is painless, then continue the setup
options.rationale: A light examination describes a Wood lamp test, not a biopsy. This reply confirms the patient's mistaken belief and continues without understanding.

options.text: Point to the signed form and reassure the patient it is minor
options.rationale: The signature is on file, which makes the form look complete. A form does not replace understanding, and calling the procedure minor ignores the question.

options.text: Stop and ask the provider to explain the procedure again
options.rationale: A punch biopsy removes a small piece of skin, and the patient believes nothing will be cut. A signed form without understanding is not informed consent, and the provider who does the procedure explains it.

questions.takeaway: If a patient's words show they do not understand a procedure they consented to, stop and have the provider explain it again.
questions.strategy: The signed form makes it feel safe to continue. The patient's question shows the consent is not informed.

steps.detail: The patient expects nothing to be cut.
A punch biopsy removes skin.
Stop and involve the provider.

elimination.verdict: Stop and have the provider explain again.

questions.objective: Plan evidence based care and support for patients undergoing diagnostic testing of the skin or nails.
questions.concept: Patient understanding before a skin biopsy

questions.stem: The provider schedules a Wood lamp examination of a pale patch on a patient's left arm. The patient asks whether anything will be cut. Which reply by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "No. A special light is shined on the skin, and nothing is removed."
options.rationale: A Wood lamp examination uses a special light to look at the skin. No tissue is taken, so nothing is cut.

options.text: "Yes. The top of the patch is shaved off with a blade."
options.rationale: Shaving off the surface describes a shave biopsy, which removes a layer of tissue. A Wood lamp examination removes nothing and involves no blade.

options.text: "Yes. The whole patch is cut out and the skin is closed with stitches."
options.rationale: Cutting out the whole area describes an excisional biopsy. It is the most invasive choice and does not match a light examination.

options.text: "Yes. A small round plug of skin is removed after numbing."
options.rationale: A small round plug of skin describes a punch biopsy. That is a different test from the light examination this patient is scheduled for.

questions.takeaway: A Wood lamp examination is a light examination with nothing removed; punch, shave, scissor, curette and excisional biopsies remove tissue.
questions.strategy: Three replies describe real skin biopsies, which makes each sound plausible. Only one of these tests is a light examination.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Wood lamp examination.
Lamp is light; punch, shave and excisional are biopsies.
Nothing is removed.

elimination.verdict: Nothing is cut in a Wood lamp examination.

questions.objective: Plan evidence based care and support for patients undergoing diagnostic testing of the skin or nails.
questions.concept: Diagnostic tests: Wood lamp versus biopsy

questions.stem: During a home health visit, a patient's wife says she first saw raised, itchy red patches on his back and legs yesterday evening. Which history finding does the nurse explore first?

options.text: Has used the same aftershave for 3 years
options.rationale: A product used without problems for years is unlikely to trigger a sudden new rash. The finding that changed shortly before the rash appeared deserves attention before this one.

options.text: Has a brother with eczema
options.rationale: Family history matters for genetic skin risk, but it does not explain a rash that appeared suddenly yesterday. An exposure that came shortly before the rash is the stronger lead.

options.text: Began a prescribed drug 10 days ago
options.rationale: Drug rashes can appear days to weeks after the first dose, and this drug was started before the rash appeared. A skin change that follows a new drug makes the drug the strongest lead.

options.text: Switched to a new body wash this morning
options.rationale: A new product applied to the skin is a reasonable allergen to ask about. The rash appeared yesterday evening, before the body wash was first used, so it cannot have started the rash.

questions.takeaway: A new drug is a likely cause of a new rash even days to weeks after it was started, but only an exposure that came before the rash can explain it.
questions.strategy: The new body wash is the most recent change and feels like the answer. It started after the rash appeared, so the drug begun 10 days earlier is the only exposure that fits the timing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The rash appeared yesterday evening.
The body wash started this morning, after the rash.
The aftershave and the family history are long standing.

elimination.verdict: Began a prescribed drug 10 days ago.

questions.objective: Use knowledge of anatomy and physiology to perform a focused assessment of the skin, hair, and nails.
questions.concept: Skin history: new drugs and allergens

questions.stem: At an outpatient dialysis center, a patient with brown skin looks more yellow brown today than at her visits last month, and she reports feeling tired. A student says the color change means jaundice. The nurse inspected her hard palate and the sclera next to each cornea an hour ago and found no yellowing. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Compare the color of her palms with her soles
options.rationale: Palms and soles can look yellow from calluses even without jaundice, so they mislead. They also do not show pallor as reliably as the mucous membranes do.

options.text: Recheck her hard palate and sclera for yellowing
options.rationale: These are the right sites for jaundice in dark skin, and checking them was a sound first step. They were inspected an hour ago and were clear, so repeating them adds nothing new.

options.text: Report new jaundice to the provider
options.rationale: Reporting would fit if jaundice were present, but the most accurate sites showed no yellowing. Calling the change jaundice would send the team after the wrong problem.

options.text: Inspect mucous membranes for an ash gray tone
options.rationale: In brown skin, pallor can look yellow brown rather than pale. With no yellowing at the palate or sclera, checking the mucous membranes for an ash gray tone tests the likelier problem.

questions.takeaway: In brown skin, pallor can appear yellow brown; confirm it in the mucous membranes, and confirm jaundice in the palate and the sclera next to the cornea.
questions.strategy: Rechecking the jaundice sites looks careful, but they were clear an hour ago. A yellow brown cast on brown skin is how pallor shows, so the mucous membranes are next.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The palate and sclera were clear an hour ago.
Pallor looks yellow brown on brown skin.
Mucous membranes show an ash gray tone.

elimination.verdict: Inspect mucous membranes for an ash gray tone.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect health equity for patients with skin, hair, or nail health problems.

questions.stem: On a surgical unit, a patient with very dark brown skin has a gallstone blocking the bile duct. The nurse checks him for yellowing from the blocked duct. Which assessments give reliable information? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect the sclera closest to the cornea
options.rationale: The sclera right next to the cornea gives the most accurate view of yellowing in dark skin. Checking it confirms what the mouth suggests.

options.text: Inspect the oral mucosa
options.rationale: The oral mucosa has less pigment than the outer skin, so yellowing can be seen there. It is one of the recommended sites, together with the hard palate.

options.text: Inspect the sclera near the outer corner of the eye
options.rationale: The sclera is the right structure, which makes this option tempting. Near the outer corner it can hold yellowish fatty deposits in dark skin, so only the part closest to the cornea is reliable.

options.text: Inspect the nail beds for a bluish tinge
options.rationale: A bluish tinge in the nail beds is a cue for cyanosis in dark skin, not for yellowing. It answers an oxygenation question rather than the one the nurse is asking.

options.text: Inspect the hard palate
options.rationale: The hard palate is a recommended site for yellowing in dark skin, because it shows color that the outer skin hides. Its finding is then confirmed at the sclera.

options.text: Inspect the skin of the face for a yellow tone
options.rationale: Dark pigment in the outer skin hides yellowing, so the face is one of the least reliable places to look. A normal looking face would not rule out jaundice in this patient.

questions.takeaway: Check jaundice in dark skin at the oral mucosa, the hard palate and the sclera closest to the cornea, where pigment does not hide yellowing.
questions.strategy: The outer sclera sounds right because the sclera is the correct structure. The deciding detail is the location: only the sclera closest to the cornea is accurate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Oral mucosa and hard palate both show yellowing.
Closest to the cornea, not the outer corner.
