Facial skin hides yellowing; nail beds show cyanosis.

elimination.verdict: Hard palate, oral mucosa and the sclera closest to the cornea.

questions.objective: Identify factors that affect health equity for patients with skin, hair, or nail health problems.

questions.stem: During an employee health visit, a woman who feels well has a horizontal groove about 1 mm wide across every fingernail. Each groove sits about halfway between the nail base and the tip. Which question helps the nurse interpret the finding?

options.text: Were you very ill or unable to eat months ago?
options.rationale: Beau's lines form when nail growth stops during acute severe illness, prolonged fever or severe malnutrition. A groove halfway up the nail formed at the base months ago and has grown out since.

options.text: Has a provider ever told you that you have psoriasis?
options.rationale: Psoriasis causes pitting, which is many small pits rather than one horizontal groove. Asking about it fits a pitted nail, not the single line across each nail seen here.

options.text: Have you injured your fingers at work recently?
options.rationale: Local injury can change a single nail, so asking about it fits one damaged nail. A groove across every fingernail points to an event affecting the whole body rather than an injury.

options.text: Have you had a fever or felt sick this week?
options.rationale: Fever and acute illness do cause these grooves, so the question targets the right causes. A groove halfway up the nail formed months ago, and she feels well now, so this week is the wrong time frame.

questions.takeaway: Beau's lines record a past growth arrest; a groove partway up the nail points to a severe illness, fever or malnutrition weeks to months earlier.
questions.strategy: Asking about a fever this week names the right cause at the wrong time. The groove has grown halfway out and she feels well, so the event was months ago.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A 1 mm horizontal groove on every nail is Beau's lines.
Halfway up the nail means it formed months ago.
Every nail is affected, so injury does not fit.

elimination.verdict: Were you very ill or unable to eat months ago?

questions.objective: Interpret assessment findings for patients with a suspected or actual skin, hair, or nail problem.

questions.stem: On an orthopedic unit, the nurse supervises a nursing student who collects a swab culture from a lesion on a patient's right foot. The lesion has a small amount of drainage, and no splashing is expected. Which action by the student needs correction?

options.text: Seals the swab in its container before removing gloves
options.rationale: Closing the specimen container while still gloved keeps drainage off clean surfaces and protects the specimen. This order of steps is correct and needs no change.

options.text: Wears clean gloves without a gown for the swab
options.rationale: A gown is added under Standard Precautions when drainage could soil clothing, which makes this look unsafe. The drainage is small and no splashing is expected, so gloves alone are appropriate.

options.text: Skips hand hygiene after removing intact gloves
options.rationale: Hands can be contaminated during glove removal and through tiny defects that cannot be seen. Standard Precautions require hand hygiene after every glove removal, whether or not the gloves tore.

options.text: Performs hand hygiene before putting on gloves
options.rationale: Hand hygiene before gloving protects the patient and the specimen from organisms on the student's hands. This step is correct and needs no change.

questions.takeaway: Gloves never replace hand hygiene: wash hands before gloving and again after every glove removal when caring for impaired skin.
questions.strategy: Gloves without a gown looks like the missing protection. No splashing is expected, so the gown is not needed, while skipping hand hygiene after gloves is always wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the one unsafe action.
Small drainage and no splashing need gloves, not a gown.
Hand hygiene follows every glove removal.

elimination.verdict: Skips hand hygiene after removing intact gloves.

questions.objective: Plan evidence based care and support for patients undergoing diagnostic testing of the skin or nails.

chapters.title: Care of Clients with Conditions of the Skin, Hair, and Nails

questions.stem: An 94 year old in assisted living bumped her forearm on a doorframe this morning, leaving a 1 cm skin tear. She says, "It is tiny, so just leave it alone." What does the nurse do?

options.text: Respect her wish and record that she declined wound care
options.rationale: Her wishes matter, but she has not refused care; she has underestimated the wound. Explaining why older skin needs prompt care comes before charting a refusal.

options.text: Clean and cover the tear today and check it every shift
options.rationale: In older adults any wound can become chronic, so even a small tear is treated right away. Cleaning, covering and checking it often gives it the best chance to close.

options.text: Leave it open to air and look at it again in one week
options.rationale: Leaving a small tear alone might suit young, healthy skin. At 88 her skin heals slowly, and a week of waiting lets a minor wound become a chronic one.

options.text: Ask the provider for an antibiotic to prevent infection
options.rationale: An antibiotic is not routine for a clean, minor tear with no signs of infection. The first step is local wound care and close monitoring.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, act on even a minor wound right away, because any wound can become chronic.
questions.strategy: Her comment invites a wait and see plan. Her age is the deciding fact: older skin heals slowly, so prompt local care wins.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: At 88, a small tear can turn into a chronic wound.
A week without care loses the window for easy healing.
No infection signs are present, so an antibiotic is not the first step.

elimination.verdict: Clean and cover the tear today and check it every shift.

questions.objective: Analyze factors that influence wound healing and tissue integrity
questions.concept: Older adults: act on minor wounds

questions.stem: The nurse is planning skin assessments on a medical unit. Which patient does the nurse identify as having the highest risk for a pressure injury?

options.text: A patient after an appendectomy who is alert and eating well
options.rationale: Recent surgery adds some risk, but this patient is alert and well nourished. Neither immobility nor undernutrition is present to drive breakdown.

options.text: A patient with heart failure who walks to the bathroom with a walker
options.rationale: Heart failure makes this patient ill, but walking to the bathroom shifts weight off any one area. Regular movement protects the skin, so the risk stays lower.

options.text: A patient with a casted wrist who walks the hall several times a day
options.rationale: A cast can press on the skin beneath it, so that skin needs checking. This patient is up and moving, and one local risk does not match whole body immobility with poor perfusion.

options.text: A patient with peripheral vascular disease on prolonged bed rest
options.rationale: Peripheral vascular disease already starves tissue of blood, and bed rest keeps the same areas compressed for hours. Two risk factors that both cut perfusion make this the highest risk patient.

questions.takeaway: Immobility combined with poor circulation, such as peripheral vascular disease, creates the highest pressure injury risk.
questions.strategy: Each distractor has a diagnosis that sounds serious. Ask who cannot relieve pressure and whose tissue already gets too little blood.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only the patient on prolonged bed rest cannot shift weight.
Peripheral vascular disease reduces blood flow to tissue under pressure.
Walking, eating well and alertness all protect the skin.

elimination.verdict: A patient with peripheral vascular disease on prolonged bed rest.

questions.objective: Analyze factors that influence wound healing and tissue integrity

questions.stem: After assistive personnel move a patient with Parkinson disease up in bed by sliding him across the sheet, the nurse finds torn, scraped skin on both of his elbows. Which change prevents this injury?

options.text: Lower the head of the bed to 30 degrees or less
options.rationale: A low head of bed prevents shear, which kinks vessels beneath intact skin. This injury is torn surface skin from dragging, which is friction.

options.text: Lift him with a lift sheet and a second staff member
options.rationale: Torn, scraped skin after dragging is friction, the surface rubbing against fragile skin. Lifting him instead of sliding him removes the rubbing.

options.text: Turn and reposition him every hour instead of every 2 hours
options.rationale: More turns means more moves, and dragging him each time causes more friction. The way he is moved is the problem, not the schedule.

options.text: Apply a barrier cream to both elbows before each move
options.rationale: Barrier creams protect skin from moisture such as urine and stool. They do not stop a sheet from scraping skin during a drag.

questions.takeaway: Friction is surface rubbing from dragging a patient across linens; lifting with a lift sheet prevents it.
questions.strategy: Lowering the head of the bed is a correct prevention step, but for shear. Match the mechanism: torn surface skin after sliding points to friction.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Skin scraped during a drag is friction.
Only lifting rather than sliding removes the rubbing.
Head of bed height prevents deep tissue sliding, not surface scraping.

elimination.verdict: Lift him with a lift sheet and a second staff member.

questions.objective: Analyze factors that influence wound healing and tissue integrity

questions.stem: In the clinic, a patient reports that a lower leg laceration has not closed after 4 weeks. Which findings in the patient's history does the nurse identify as factors that slow wound healing? Select all that apply.

options.text: A high dose corticosteroid taken daily for lupus
options.rationale: High dose steroids blunt the inflammatory response that starts the healing process. This drug alone can keep a wound open for weeks.

options.text: A 30 minute walk on most days
options.rationale: Regular walking improves circulation to the legs, which helps a leg wound. Activity is not one of the factors that delay closure.

options.text: A wood splinter still lodged in the wound
options.rationale: A foreign body keeps the wound inflamed and gives bacteria a place to grow. Healing cannot finish until the object is removed.

options.text: Protein at every meal and a stable weight
options.rationale: Adequate protein and a steady weight support healing rather than slowing it. Poor nutrition delays healing, and this history shows the opposite.

options.text: Moist, beefy red tissue in the wound bed
options.rationale: Beefy red, moist tissue is healthy granulation, the tissue a healing wound should have. It describes the wound itself, not a cause of delay.

options.text: Peripheral arteriosclerosis
options.rationale: Arteriosclerosis narrows the arteries, so less blood, oxygen and nutrients reach the wound. Poor circulation is one of the most common reasons a wound stalls.

questions.takeaway: Poor circulation, high dose steroids and foreign bodies slow healing, while good nutrition and activity support it.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are healthy habits and one describes healthy tissue. Sort each item by whether it harms blood flow, inflammation or the wound bed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what each item does to the wound
steps.detail: Arteriosclerosis, steroids and a splinter all work against healing.
Protein and walking support healing, so they are not factors that slow it.
Beefy red, moist tissue is healthy granulation, not a cause of delay.

elimination.verdict: Arteriosclerosis, the daily high dose corticosteroid and the retained splinter.

questions.objective: Analyze factors that influence wound healing and tissue integrity

questions.stem: On a surgical unit, a patient recovering from bowel surgery keeps the head of his bed at 60 degrees for hours to watch television and slowly slips toward the foot of the bed. His sacral skin is intact, but the nurse is concerned about damage beneath it. Which action addresses the mechanism?

options.text: Keep the head of the bed no higher than 30 degrees
options.rationale: As he slips down, his skin stays on the sheet while the deeper tissue moves, kinking blood vessels. That is shear, and a head of bed at 30 degrees or less prevents it.

options.text: Use a lift sheet each time he is moved up in bed
options.rationale: A lift sheet prevents friction during repositioning. The damage here happens while he sits and slips down, which is shear, so lifting him later does not stop it.

options.text: Apply a moisturizer to the sacrum twice a day
options.rationale: Moisturizer protects dry skin on the surface. Shear injures tissue deep under intact skin, where a cream has no effect.

options.text: Turn him from side to side every 2 hours
options.rationale: Turning every 2 hours relieves pressure on any one spot. With the head of the bed still at 60 degrees, he keeps sliding on each side, so the shear continues.

questions.takeaway: Shear happens when skin stays still while deeper tissue moves; a head of bed at 30 degrees or less prevents it.
questions.strategy: The lift sheet answer is the right fix for friction. The cue here is sliding while sitting with intact skin, which is shear.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Intact skin while he slips down a high bed means deep tissue is moving under it.
That is shear, which kinks vessels and leads to ischemia.
Only lowering the head of the bed stops the sliding; turning and lifting leave it in place.

elimination.verdict: Keep the head of the bed no higher than 30 degrees.

questions.objective: Analyze factors that influence wound healing and tissue integrity

questions.stem: On the second day after an open gallbladder removal, a woman's stapled incision is red, warm, slightly swollen and tender. The edges are together, there is no drainage and her temperature is 37.1 C. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: These are signs of infection; report them to the surgeon now
options.rationale: The same signs could mean infection later in healing. On day 2, with no drainage and no fever, they are the normal inflammatory response.

options.text: Healing is delayed; the incision should be pale and flat by now
options.rationale: A pale, flat scar belongs to the maturation phase, which begins around 3 weeks. Expecting it on day 2 misreads the healing timeline.

options.text: These are expected findings; continue routine incision checks
options.rationale: Redness, warmth, swelling and pain are expected in the inflammatory phase, days 1 to 5. Closed edges, no drainage and a normal temperature support normal healing.

options.text: New granulation tissue is causing the swelling
options.rationale: Granulation forms in the proliferative phase, starting around day 4, and fills open wounds. A closed incision on day 2 is still in the inflammatory phase.

questions.takeaway: Redness, warmth, swelling and pain in the first 5 days are the expected inflammatory phase, not infection.
questions.strategy: The infection answer feels safe, but every cue fits the timeline. Day 2, closed edges, no drainage and no fever tip it to expected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Place the day on the timeline
steps.detail: Day 2 falls in the inflammatory phase, days 1 to 5.
There is no drainage and no fever.
Granulation starts around day 4 and a pale scar comes weeks later.

elimination.verdict: These are expected findings; continue routine incision checks.

questions.objective: Differentiate wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: Seven months after a knee replacement, a man notices that his scar is still pink and slightly raised and asks whether something is wrong. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Your scar should have stopped changing at 3 months, so it needs a look."
options.rationale: Three months is too early to expect a final scar. Maturation can take a year or longer, so this reply would alarm him without cause.

options.text: "Scars remodel for a year or longer and usually turn thinner and paler."
options.rationale: The maturation phase runs from about 3 weeks to a year or longer while collagen remodels. A pink scar at 7 months is still within that window.

options.text: "A pink scar at this point means the wound never fully closed."
options.rationale: Closure happened months ago when new tissue covered the incision. The color comes from collagen that is still remodeling, not from an open wound.

options.text: "The redness shows that the inflammatory phase is still going on."
options.rationale: Inflammation lasts about the first 5 days after injury. Pinkness months later belongs to maturation, not to active inflammation.

questions.takeaway: During maturation, from about 3 weeks to a year or longer, a scar becomes thinner, paler and firmer.
questions.strategy: Two distractors place him in the wrong phase. Seven months after surgery is still maturation, so a pink scar is expected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Maturation lasts from 3 weeks to a year or longer.
That phase ends around day 5.
Three months is too soon for a final scar.

elimination.verdict: Scars remodel for a year or longer and usually turn thinner and paler.

questions.objective: Differentiate wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: The surgeon decides to leave a patient's abdominal incision, which separated after surgery, open to heal without closing it. Which statement shows she understands how the wound will heal?

options.text: "It will fill in from the bottom and scar more."
options.rationale: An open wound heals by second intention, filling with granulation tissue from the inside out. It takes longer and leaves more scarring than a closed incision.

options.text: "It will heal faster now because air will dry it."
options.rationale: Open wounds heal more slowly, not faster. Healthy granulation tissue is moist, so drying the wound would slow healing further.

options.text: "It will be stitched closed when the infection clears."
options.rationale: Waiting for infection to clear and then closing the wound is third intention. Her plan is to let the wound heal open with no later closure.

options.text: "It will heal quickly with a thin line scar."
options.rationale: A thin line scar comes from first intention, when the edges are held together. Her edges are apart, so healing will be slower and the scar wider.

questions.takeaway: A wound left open heals by second intention: it fills with granulation from the inside out, slowly, with more scarring.
questions.strategy: The stitched closed statement describes a real healing pattern, but not hers. No later closure is planned, so it is second intention.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Left open with no planned closure is second intention.
Second intention means slower healing and more scarring.
A thin line scar is first intention and planned closure is third.

elimination.verdict: It will fill in from the bottom and scar more.

questions.objective: Differentiate wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with dark brown skin who has been immobile since a stroke. Over his sacrum the intact skin is darker than the surrounding skin, warmer and firmer. There is no purple or maroon color. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injury; apply a moist dressing to the wound
options.rationale: Stage 2 is partial thickness loss with exposed dermis. His skin is intact, so there is no wound bed to dress.

options.text: Normal pigment variation; recheck at the next skin assessment
options.rationale: Pigment does vary, but this area is also warmer and firmer than nearby skin. Over a bony prominence in dark skin, those changes mark early damage.

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury; request a surgical consult
options.rationale: Deep tissue injury shows persistent deep red, maroon or purple color. This area has no purple or maroon, so stage 1 fits better.

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury; take all pressure off the sacrum
options.rationale: Intact skin whose color differs from the surrounding tissue, with warmth and firmness, is stage 1 in dark skin. Offloading now can stop the damage from progressing.

questions.takeaway: In dark skin, stage 1 shows as intact skin whose color differs from the surrounding tissue, often with warmth or firmness.
questions.strategy: No visible redness tempts a normal reading. Warmth and firmness over the sacrum, with color that differs from nearby skin, tip it to stage 1.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Intact skin rules out stage 2.
No purple or maroon rules out deep tissue injury.
Warmth and firmness make normal pigment unlikely.

elimination.verdict: Stage 1 pressure injury; take all pressure off the sacrum.

questions.objective: Differentiate wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.scenario: The nurse on a surgical unit reviews how several patients' wounds are being managed.
questions.stem: For each wound, indicate the type of healing intention.

rows.text: Laparoscopic incisions closed with sutures
rows.rationale: Sutures bring the edges together, and there is little tissue loss or dead space. Approximated edges heal by first intention with a thin scar.

rows.text: A contaminated abdominal wound left open 4 days, then closed once free of infection
rows.rationale: The wound stays open until the infection risk clears and is closed surgically afterward. That delayed primary closure is third intention.

rows.text: A drained abscess packed open, with surgery booked to close it next week
rows.rationale: A planned closure after the infected area is clean means the wound is not left to fill in on its own. A late surgical closure is third intention.

rows.text: A venous leg ulcer filling in from its base
rows.rationale: Venous ulcers are open wounds that fill with granulation and contract over time. Nobody brings the edges together, so they heal by second intention.

rows.text: A stage 3 sacral pressure injury left open under a foam dressing
rows.rationale: An open cavity fills from the inside out with granulation tissue. Pressure injuries heal by second intention, slowly and with more scarring.

questions.takeaway: First intention closes the edges, second fills an open cavity with granulation, and third closes the wound only after the infection risk clears.
questions.strategy: Wounds that are open now can be second or third intention. Look for a planned later closure, which makes it third.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask whether the edges are closed now
steps.detail: Sutured or stapled edges are first intention.
Open now with a later closure is third intention.
Open wounds left to fill in are second intention.

elimination.verdict: Sutured incisions are first; the pressure injury and venous ulcer are second; the contaminated wound and drained abscess are third.

questions.objective: Differentiate wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: A patient with multiple sclerosis who uses a wheelchair has a shallow open area over her right ischium where a blister broke yesterday. The wound bed is pink, moist and shiny, and no yellow fat or dead tissue is seen. How does the nurse document the finding?

options.text: Unstageable pressure injury
options.rationale: Unstageable means slough or eschar hides the wound bed so depth cannot be confirmed. This bed is fully visible and pink, so it can be staged.

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury
options.rationale: Stage 1 is nonblanchable redness of intact skin. Once a blister has broken and the dermis shows, the skin is no longer intact, so the injury is past stage 1.

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injury
options.rationale: A ruptured blister with a pink, moist, viable bed is partial thickness loss with exposed dermis. Fat, granulation, slough and eschar are not visible, which fits stage 2.

options.text: Stage 3 pressure injury
options.rationale: An open wound can look deep, but stage 3 is full thickness loss with fat visible in the ulcer. No fat is seen here, so the loss is only partial thickness.

questions.takeaway: A pink, moist, shiny bed from a ruptured blister with no fat, slough or eschar is a stage 2 pressure injury.
questions.strategy: An open wound tempts a stage 3 label. Stage 3 needs visible fat; a pink, moist bed with nothing deeper showing stays stage 2.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Check whether the skin is intact
steps.detail: The blister broke, so it is not stage 1.
No fat is seen, which rules out stage 3.
Nothing hides the base, so it is not unstageable.

elimination.verdict: Stage 2 pressure injury.

questions.objective: Differentiate wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: In intensive care, a patient has been sedated on a ventilator for 4 days with his ankles resting on the mattress. Over the outer bone of his left ankle is an intact area of persistent maroon discoloration that does not blanch. Before sedation he had said the ankle ached. What does the nurse document?

options.text: Unstageable pressure injury
options.rationale: Unstageable means full thickness skin and tissue loss hidden by slough or eschar. This skin is intact and its discoloration is fully visible, so nothing obscures the extent of damage.

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury
options.rationale: Stage 1 is nonblanchable discoloration of intact skin, and this skin is intact and nonblanchable. Stage 1 color is not purple or maroon, so persistent maroon points to deeper damage.

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injury
options.rationale: Stage 2 is partial thickness loss with exposed dermis or a serum filled blister. This skin is intact with no blister, so there is no partial thickness loss to stage.

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury
options.rationale: Persistent nonblanchable deep red, maroon or purple discoloration of intact or nonintact skin defines a deep tissue pressure injury. Damage starts at the muscle and bone, so the surface can stay intact.

questions.takeaway: Persistent nonblanchable maroon or purple discoloration over a bony area is a deep tissue pressure injury, even when the skin is intact.
questions.strategy: Intact, nonblanchable skin pulls toward stage 1. The maroon color rules stage 1 out and points to damage that started deep.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Intact, so not stage 2, and nothing is obscured.
Maroon is excluded from stage 1 and defines deep tissue injury.

elimination.verdict: Deep tissue pressure injury.

questions.objective: Differentiate wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: After an 8 hour cardiac surgery, a woman has an area on her left heel that is intact, deep purple and nonblanchable. By the next day a blood filled blister has formed over it. What does the nurse document?

options.text: Unstageable pressure injury
options.rationale: Unstageable means slough or eschar obscures the base. A blood blister over purple skin has its own category, deep tissue pressure injury.

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury
options.rationale: Persistent purple, nonblanchable color and a blood filled blister define deep tissue injury, which begins at the muscle and bone interface. Long immobility during surgery is a common cause.

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injury
options.rationale: Stage 2 blisters are filled with clear serum. A blood filled blister over purple skin signals damage that started deep and is moving outward.

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury
options.rationale: Deep tissue injury can first look like stage 1, but stage 1 is never purple or maroon. Persistent purple color and a blood filled blister point deeper.

questions.takeaway: Persistent deep red, maroon or purple discoloration or a blood filled blister is a deep tissue pressure injury, which develops from the inside out.
questions.strategy: Each distractor has a true piece: the skin was intact, and there is a blister. The purple color and blood in the blister decide it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Purple or maroon is never stage 1.
Blood, not serum, rules out stage 2.
No slough or eschar, so it is not unstageable.

elimination.verdict: Deep tissue pressure injury.

questions.objective: Differentiate wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: A man admitted with pneumonia has intact skin and a Braden Scale total of 17. The facility guideline flags a total of 18 or less as increased risk. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Record low risk, because only totals of 16 or less show risk
options.rationale: Some facilities use 16 as the cutoff, but this one uses 18. The nurse follows the facility guideline, which places a total of 17 at increased risk.

options.text: Ask the wound care nurse to stage the skin over the sacrum
options.rationale: Staging applies to an existing pressure injury. His skin is intact, so there is nothing to stage yet.

options.text: Start the skin care bundle and pressure prevention measures today
options.rationale: Under this facility's guideline, 17 falls in the at risk range. Lower Braden scores mean higher risk, so prevention starts now while the skin is still intact.

options.text: Wait to start prevention until redness appears over a bony area
options.rationale: Redness means tissue damage has already begun. The Braden Scale exists to start prevention before the skin breaks down.

questions.takeaway: On the Braden Scale lower is worse, and a total at or below the facility cutoff of 16 or 18 starts prevention now.
questions.strategy: The 16 cutoff is a real number, which makes that distractor tempting. The facility guideline in the stem sets the cutoff the nurse uses.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lower totals mean higher risk.
17 is at or below 18, so he is at risk.
Prevention starts before redness, not after it.

elimination.verdict: Start the skin care bundle and pressure prevention measures today.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions to prevent pressure injuries and promote skin integrity
questions.concept: Braden Scale scoring direction and cutoff

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the Braden Scale scores of a patient with frequent liquid stools from antibiotic associated diarrhea. Her total is 15, and her subscores are sensory perception 3, moisture 1, activity 3, mobility 3, nutrition 3, and friction and shear 2. Which intervention targets her greatest risk?

options.text: Clean her skin after each stool and apply barrier cream
options.rationale: Moisture scored 1, constantly moist, which is her lowest subscore and greatest risk. Cleaning promptly after soiling and applying a barrier cream protects her skin from stool.

options.text: Request an air fluidized bed for her room
options.rationale: Specialty beds redistribute pressure for patients who cannot move. Her activity and mobility subscores are 3, so pressure from immobility is not her main problem.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at or below 30 degrees
options.rationale: A low head of bed prevents shear, and her friction and shear score of 2 shows some risk. Her moisture score of 1 is lower, so it comes first.

options.text: Consult the dietitian to raise her protein and calorie intake
options.rationale: Nutrition matters for healing, but her nutrition subscore is 3. The lowest subscore, and so the largest risk, is moisture.

questions.takeaway: Each Braden subscore points to a target; the lowest subscore is the greatest risk and gets the first intervention.
questions.strategy: Every option prevents pressure injury in someone. Find her lowest subscore, because that is the risk to treat first.

steps.detail: Moisture is 1, the lowest number.
Lower means worse on every subscale.
Cleaning and barrier cream answer a moisture problem.

elimination.verdict: Clean her skin after each stool and apply barrier cream.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions to prevent pressure injuries and promote skin integrity
questions.concept: Braden Scale scoring direction and cutoff

questions.scenario: During wound rounds on a rehabilitation unit, the nurse assesses pressure injuries on several patients.
questions.stem: For each wound description, indicate the stage the nurse documents.

rows.text: Bone felt with an applicator but not seen; fat visible
rows.rationale: Stage 4 includes exposed or palpable bone. Bone that can be felt counts even when it cannot be seen.

rows.text: Tendon visible at the base of the wound
rows.rationale: Exposed tendon, muscle, fascia, ligament, cartilage or bone means stage 4. Fat alone would only make it stage 3.

rows.text: Black eschar covering the entire wound bed
rows.rationale: When eschar covers the whole bed, the depth cannot be confirmed. Dark color does not prove that bone is involved, so the wound is unstageable.

rows.text: Yellow slough filling the entire wound bed
rows.rationale: Slough covering the whole bed hides the base, so the true depth is unknown. The wound stays unstageable until the base can be seen.

rows.text: Fat visible; slough over one third of the bed, base visible elsewhere
rows.rationale: Visible fat means full thickness skin loss, and slough may be present in stage 3. Most of the base can be seen, so the wound can be staged.

rows.text: Fat visible with rolled edges and undermining; no deeper tissue seen or felt
rows.rationale: Rolled edges and undermining often appear in stage 3 wounds. With fat showing and no deeper structure seen or felt, it stays stage 3.

questions.takeaway: Fat means stage 3, exposed or palpable bone, tendon or muscle means stage 4, and a base fully hidden by slough or eschar is unstageable.
questions.strategy: Slough or eschar can appear in stages 3 and 4. It makes a wound unstageable only when it covers the whole base.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask whether the base can be seen
steps.detail: A fully covered base is unstageable.
Fat is stage 3; bone, tendon or muscle seen or felt is stage 4.
Rolled edges and undermining occur in stage 3 and stage 4.

elimination.verdict: Partial slough and rolled edges with fat are stage 3; tendon and palpable bone are stage 4; full eschar and full slough are unstageable.

questions.objective: Differentiate wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: During rounds, the nurse finds a patient who is in a coma after a head injury lying directly on his right hip at a 90 degree side lying angle, with the head of the bed at 30 degrees. Which correction does the nurse make?

options.text: Lower the head of the bed until it is flat
options.rationale: A head of bed at 30 degrees already meets the guideline for preventing shear. Lowering it further does not take weight off his hip.

options.text: Tilt him to a 30 degree side lying angle
options.rationale: Lying at 90 degrees puts full body weight on the bony trochanter. A 30 degree tilt spreads the load across the buttock and keeps it off the bone.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Raising the head of the bed above 30 degrees lets him slip down and adds shear. It also leaves his full weight on the hip at 90 degrees.

options.text: Keep him on the right side and turn him hourly
options.rationale: More frequent turning helps, but every hour at 90 degrees still loads the hip bone. The angle itself must change.

questions.takeaway: Side lying positions use a 30 degree tilt, not 90 degrees, to keep weight off the trochanter.
questions.strategy: The head of bed is a distractor because it is already correct. The angle of the side lying position is what needs to change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Check each setting against the guideline
steps.detail: Head of bed 30 degrees is correct; 90 degree side lying is not.
A 30 degree tilt takes weight off the trochanter.

steps.action: Rule out head of bed changes
steps.detail: The head of the bed is already correct, so raising or lowering it misses the problem.

elimination.verdict: Tilt him to a 30 degree side lying angle.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions to prevent pressure injuries and promote skin integrity

questions.stem: Assistive personnel tell the nurse that a woman with end stage kidney disease has a red area over her sacrum and offer to massage it with lotion to bring back circulation. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Rub around the red area but not on top of it."
options.rationale: Rubbing near the area still stresses fragile capillaries that may already be damaged. Reddened areas are never massaged, either on them or around them.

options.text: "Rub it gently with a barrier cream instead of lotion."
options.rationale: A barrier cream protects skin from moisture, but the problem here is the rubbing. Massaging a reddened area damages capillaries no matter what product is used.

options.text: "Go ahead, then place a donut cushion under her."
options.rationale: Both actions damage capillaries. Massage rubs fragile vessels, and a donut cushion compresses the ring of tissue around the red area.

options.text: "Don't rub it; I'll check it and keep her off it."
options.rationale: Massage damages capillaries in an area that may already be injured. The nurse assesses the area for blanching and takes pressure off it.

questions.takeaway: Never massage a reddened area or use a donut cushion; assess for blanching and take the pressure off.
questions.strategy: The gentler massage options sound like compromises. Any rubbing of a reddened area damages capillaries, so only the response that stops it works.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three responses still involve rubbing or a donut.
The nurse checks the area for blanching.
Keeping her off the area restores blood flow.

elimination.verdict: Don't rub it; I'll check it and keep her off it.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions to prevent pressure injuries and promote skin integrity

questions.stem: On a cardiac unit, a patient recovering from a myocardial infarction sits in a recliner for most of the day. He can stand and walk short distances with help. Which plan reduces pressure while he is in the chair?

options.text: Have him shift his weight once every 4 hours
options.rationale: Shifting weight helps, but every 4 hours leaves tissue compressed far too long. Chair patients who can stand should do so every hour.

options.text: Return him to bed once a shift so he can rest
options.rationale: Bed rest trades one set of pressure points for another and lowers his mobility. Hourly standing works better while he is up.

options.text: Help him stand and march in place 5 steps every hour
options.rationale: Standing and marching in place 5 steps every hour relieves pressure on the sacrum and ischia for patients who are able. It also keeps him moving.

options.text: Place a donut cushion on the seat of the recliner
options.rationale: A donut cushion presses on a ring of tissue and damages capillaries. It is never used to relieve pressure.

questions.takeaway: A patient in a chair who is able should stand and march in place 5 steps every hour.
questions.strategy: Shifting weight is a reasonable idea at the wrong interval. Check the timing in each option against the hourly standard.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every 4 hours or once a shift is too long.
Donut cushions damage capillaries.
He can stand, so standing every hour fits.

elimination.verdict: Help him stand and march in place 5 steps every hour.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions to prevent pressure injuries and promote skin integrity

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient recovering from a hip replacement who has urinary incontinence and wears incontinence briefs. Her plan already includes a zinc oxide barrier cream and checks under the brief at least every 2 hours. Which cleaning routine does the nurse add?

options.text: Clean after each episode with mild soap and warm water, then pat dry
options.rationale: Prompt cleaning with mild soap and warm water removes urine before it breaks down the skin. Patting dries the skin without the friction that rubbing causes, which protects fragile tissue.

options.text: Clean once the brief is saturated, with mild soap and warm water, then pat dry
options.rationale: The products and the drying method are correct. Waiting until the brief is saturated holds urine against the skin for hours, and moisture is a major pressure injury risk.

options.text: Clean after each episode with hot water and strong soap, then pat dry
options.rationale: Cleaning after each episode and patting dry are correct. Hot water and strong soap strip and irritate the skin, so the routine calls for mild soap and warm water.

options.text: Clean after each episode with mild soap and warm water, then rub dry
options.rationale: The timing and the products are correct, so most of this routine is right. Rubbing wet, fragile skin adds friction that can tear the surface, so the skin is patted dry.

questions.takeaway: Clean skin promptly after each soiling with mild soap and warm water, pat it dry without scrubbing, and protect it with a barrier cream.
questions.strategy: Each wrong routine changes one detail: timing, drying or products. Check all three in every option before choosing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: After each episode, not once the brief is saturated.
Mild soap and warm water, not hot water and strong soap.
Pat, never rub.

elimination.verdict: Clean after each episode with mild soap and warm water, then pat dry.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions to prevent pressure injuries and promote skin integrity

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy for lymphoma has a Braden nutrition subscore of 2. He drinks about 1000 mL of fluid a day and has no fluid restriction. Which plan does the nurse put in place?

options.text: Encourage 2000 to 3000 mL a day and consult the dietitian
options.rationale: Fluids of 2000 to 3000 mL a day keep the skin hydrated and support healing when no restriction applies. The dietitian sets his protein and calorie goals.

options.text: Offer a vitamin supplement and leave meals up to him
options.rationale: Vitamins alone do not meet protein and calorie needs. A low nutrition subscore calls for a dietitian plan, not a single supplement.

options.text: Keep intake at 1000 mL and recheck his Braden score weekly
options.rationale: His intake is well below the 2000 to 3000 mL goal. Waiting a week leaves dry, poorly nourished skin at risk.

options.text: Limit his fluids so that his skin gets wet less often
options.rationale: Limiting fluids reduces urine but dehydrates and weakens the skin. Moisture is managed with prompt cleaning and barrier creams, not by withholding fluids.

questions.takeaway: Unless restricted, fluids of 2000 to 3000 mL a day and a dietitian plan for protein and calories support skin integrity.
questions.strategy: Limiting fluids sounds like a moisture fix. Skin needs hydration from within, so the 2000 to 3000 mL goal wins.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Compare his intake with the goal
steps.detail: 1000 mL is far below 2000 to 3000 mL.
No restriction is ordered, and limiting fluids weakens skin.
A low nutrition subscore needs the dietitian.

elimination.verdict: Encourage 2000 to 3000 mL a day and consult the dietitian.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions to prevent pressure injuries and promote skin integrity

questions.nursesNote: 0800 Admitted from home after a fall. Alert and oriented to person only. Skin warm and dry. Incontinent of urine twice since arrival. Lungs clear bilaterally. Weight down 7% from usual in one month. Radial pulse 78/min and regular. Lies in one position unless helped to turn.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that increase this patient's risk for a pressure injury.

segments.text: Admitted from home after a fall
segments.rationale: A fall explains the admission but is not itself a pressure injury risk factor. What matters is how the patient moves, eats and stays dry now.

segments.text: Alert and oriented to person only
segments.rationale: Orientation to person only shows cognitive impairment. A patient who is confused may not sense pressure or ask to be turned.

segments.text: Skin warm and dry
segments.rationale: Warm, dry skin is a normal finding. Dry here means not moist from sweat or urine, which protects the skin.

segments.text: Incontinent of urine twice since arrival
segments.rationale: Incontinence keeps the skin moist, and moist skin breaks down faster. Moisture is one of the main risk factors for pressure injury.

segments.text: Lungs clear bilaterally
segments.rationale: Clear lungs support good oxygenation, which helps tissue rather than harming it. This finding does not add to the risk.

segments.text: Weight down 7% from usual in one month
segments.rationale: A weight loss over 5% is a nutrition cue. Undernutrition leaves the skin with less protein and fat to withstand pressure.

segments.text: Radial pulse 78/min and regular
segments.rationale: A regular pulse of 78/min is within normal limits. It suggests adequate perfusion and does not raise the risk.

segments.text: Lies in one position unless helped to turn
segments.rationale: Immobility is the leading cause of pressure injury, because tissue stays compressed between bone and the mattress. This patient cannot relieve pressure alone.

questions.takeaway: Cognitive impairment, moisture, weight loss over 5% and immobility each raise pressure injury risk.
questions.strategy: Several normal findings sit between the risk factors. Ask of each finding whether it affects pressure, moisture, nutrition or sensation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cognition, moisture, nutrition and mobility.
More than 5% loss is a nutrition cue.
Warm dry skin, clear lungs and a normal pulse do not add risk.

elimination.verdict: Oriented to person only, incontinent of urine, weight down 7% and lies in one position.

questions.objective: Evaluate wound and skin assessment findings to determine appropriate nursing actions

questions.stem: While caring for a patient admitted with a urinary tract infection, the nurse notes a red area over her left hip after she has been lying on that side. When the nurse presses on it, the area turns white, and the red color returns once pressure is released. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Massage the area to restore circulation to the hip
options.rationale: Reddened areas are never massaged, because rubbing damages capillaries that may already be injured. Offloading restores blood flow without that harm.

options.text: Document a stage 1 pressure injury on the left hip
options.rationale: Stage 1 is nonblanchable. This area blanched, which shows the capillaries are still filling, so it is not a stage 1 injury.

options.text: Turn her off the hip and recheck the area later
options.rationale: Blanching shows blood flow is intact, so tissue damage has not set in. Taking pressure off the hip and rechecking keeps it that way.

options.text: Report a deep tissue injury to the provider now
options.rationale: Deep tissue injury is persistent, nonblanchable maroon or purple color. Red skin that blanches shows perfusion is intact.

questions.takeaway: Redness that blanches means perfusion is intact; offload and recheck. Nonblanchable redness signals tissue damage.
questions.strategy: Any redness over a bony area tempts a stage 1 label. The blanch test result decides it: this skin blanched.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The area whitened and color returned.
Blanching means blood flow is intact, so it is not stage 1.
Offload the hip and recheck.

elimination.verdict: Turn her off the hip and recheck the area later.

questions.objective: Evaluate wound and skin assessment findings to determine appropriate nursing actions

questions.stem: After spinal fusion surgery, a patient with deeply pigmented skin has been lying on her back in intensive care. The nurse sees no redness over her heels or buttocks. Which assessment best detects early pressure damage?

options.text: Measure each heel with a cotton tipped applicator
options.rationale: An applicator measures the depth of an open wound. Her skin is intact, so there is nothing to measure.

options.text: Compare each area with nearby skin for warmth, edema, pain and induration
options.rationale: On darker skin, temperature, edema, pain and induration reveal early damage that color can hide. Comparing with nearby skin makes small differences easier to find.

options.text: Photograph the heels and look for redness on tomorrow's photo
options.rationale: Serial photographs track a known wound over time. A photo shows only color, the least reliable cue on darker skin, and it delays the assessment.

options.text: Press and release the skin and record it intact if no redness appears
options.rationale: The blanch test works well on lighter skin, but redness may not be visible on darker skin. No visible redness does not rule out early damage.

questions.takeaway: On darker skin, assess temperature, edema, pain and induration, because redness may not be visible.
questions.strategy: The blanch test is correct technique for lighter skin. On darker skin, color is unreliable, so the nurse adds touch and the patient's report.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Redness may not show on deeply pigmented skin.

steps.action: Choose cues that do not rely on color
steps.detail: Warmth, edema, pain and induration.

steps.action: Rule out tools for open wounds
steps.detail: An applicator measures depth, and her skin is intact.

elimination.verdict: Compare each area with nearby skin for warmth, edema, pain and induration.

questions.objective: Evaluate wound and skin assessment findings to determine appropriate nursing actions

questions.stem: A patient admitted after a car crash wears a cervical collar and has a nasogastric tube taped at her nose. The nurse inspects her sacrum, hips and heels and finds intact skin. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Document that her skin is intact and recheck in 24 hours
options.rationale: The sacrum, hips and heels are common sites, but devices cause pressure injuries too. Charting intact skin now skips the areas under her devices.

options.text: Ask the provider to remove the collar so the skin can rest
options.rationale: A cervical collar protects the spine and stays on as ordered. The skin under it is checked regularly instead of removing the device.

options.text: Pad the collar with folded gauze so it presses less
options.rationale: Padding a collar without looking underneath hides any damage that has started. The nurse inspects first, then decides what the skin needs.

options.text: Inspect under the collar, at the nostril and at the occiput
options.rationale: Collars and tubes press on skin and can cause pressure injuries. The back of the head is also easy to miss in a patient lying on her back.

questions.takeaway: Inspect the entire body, including the occiput and the skin under every medical device.
questions.strategy: The common sites look complete, which makes charting tempting. Her collar and tube are the cue that the assessment is not finished.

steps.detail: A collar and a nasogastric tube both press on skin.
Skin under the devices and the back of the head.
Padding or removing the collar comes after looking.

elimination.verdict: Inspect under the collar, at the nostril and at the occiput.

questions.objective: Evaluate wound and skin assessment findings to determine appropriate nursing actions

questions.stem: The day nurse documented a woman's sacral wound with "tunneling at 6:00, 3 cm deep." Before the dressing change, in which direction does the evening nurse expect the tunnel to run?

options.text: Toward the patient's feet
options.rationale: In the clock method the patient's head is 12:00 and the feet are 6:00. A tunnel at 6:00 runs toward her feet.

options.text: Toward the patient's left side
options.rationale: Side directions fall at 3:00 and 9:00, not 6:00. Only the head and feet anchor 12:00 and 6:00.

options.text: Straight down from the center of the wound
options.rationale: Depth at the center is measured with an applicator and recorded as the third number. A clock position describes a tunnel running away from the wound.

options.text: Toward the patient's head
options.rationale: The head is 12:00 on the wound clock. Reading 6:00 as the head reverses the method and would send the probe the wrong way.

questions.takeaway: In the clock method the head is 12:00 and the feet are 6:00.
questions.strategy: Head and feet are an opposite pair. Anchor 12:00 at the head, and 6:00 falls at the feet.

steps.detail: Head is 12:00.
Directly opposite, toward the feet.
Depth is recorded separately, not by clock position.

elimination.verdict: Toward the patient's feet.

questions.objective: Interpret wound characteristics and documentation findings to monitor healing or deterioration

questions.stem: While assessing a pressure injury on a man's right buttock, the nurse finds that an applicator passes about 1 cm under the intact skin rim all along the edge from 2:00 to 5:00. How does the nurse document this finding?

options.text: Tunneling at 2:00
options.rationale: Tunneling is also probed and described by clock position, but it is a single channel at one point. Separation along a whole stretch of the edge from 2:00 to 5:00 is undermining.

options.text: Undermining from 2:00 to 5:00
options.rationale: Skin that has separated from the tissue beneath it along the wound edge is undermining. Recording the clock positions shows where the separation runs.

options.text: Cellulitis along the wound edge
options.rationale: Cellulitis is inflammation spreading into the skin beyond the wound, seen as redness and warmth. An applicator sliding under the rim describes tissue separation, not inflammation.

options.text: Eschar at the wound edge
options.rationale: Eschar is black, brown or gray dead tissue that the nurse can see. The finding here is a space under the skin, found only by probing.

questions.takeaway: Undermining is skin separating from the tissue beneath it at the wound edges, documented by clock positions.
questions.strategy: Tunneling and undermining are both found by probing and both use the clock. A stretch along the edge, rather than one channel, makes it undermining.

steps.detail: Probing found a space under the rim.
It runs along the edge from 2:00 to 5:00, not at one point.
Skin separating along the edge is undermining.

elimination.verdict: Undermining from 2:00 to 5:00.

questions.objective: Interpret wound characteristics and documentation findings to monitor healing or deterioration

questions.stem: The nurse measures the depth of a pressure injury on a man's left trochanter. Place the steps in the order the nurse performs them.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene and put on clean gloves
options.rationale: Hand hygiene and gloves come before touching any wound. They protect both the patient's open tissue and the nurse.

options.text: Gently insert a cotton tipped applicator into the deepest part of the wound
options.rationale: Depth is measured at the deepest point of the wound bed. The applicator goes in gently so it does not injure fragile tissue.

options.text: Record the depth in cm with the length and width
options.rationale: Wounds are documented as length by width by depth in cm or mm. Recording all three lets the team track healing over time.

options.text: Remove the applicator and hold it against a centimeter guide
options.rationale: The distance from the tip to the mark is the depth. Reading it against a centimeter guide gives a number that others can compare.

options.text: Mark the applicator where it meets skin level
options.rationale: The mark shows how far the applicator went below the skin surface. Without it, the depth cannot be read once the applicator is removed.

questions.takeaway: Depth is measured by inserting a cotton tipped applicator, marking it at skin level and reading it against a centimeter guide.
questions.strategy: The steps follow the applicator from the wound to the chart. The mark at skin level must come before removal, or the measurement is lost.

steps.detail: Hand hygiene and gloves come first.
In, mark, out, measure.
Depth is charted with length and width.

elimination.verdict: Hand hygiene and gloves, insert, mark at skin level, measure against a guide, record.

questions.objective: Interpret wound characteristics and documentation findings to monitor healing or deterioration

questions.stem: A patient with paraplegia has a stage 3 pressure injury over his left ischium. Three weeks ago it measured 5 x 4 x 1.5 cm; today it measures 3.5 x 3 x 1 cm, and the bed is beefy red, moist and slightly spongy. How does the nurse evaluate the wound?

options.text: It is too moist; switch to a dressing that dries the bed
options.rationale: Healthy granulation is moist, and drying it would slow healing. Moisture in the bed is expected, not a problem.

options.text: It is infected; report the red color to the provider today
options.rationale: Redness spreading beyond the wound would suggest infection. A beefy red wound bed is healthy granulation, the expected color of healing.

options.text: It is healing; continue the plan and keep measuring
options.rationale: Every measurement is smaller, and beefy red, moist, slightly spongy tissue is healthy granulation. Both show the plan is working.

options.text: It is necrotic; request debridement before the next dressing
options.rationale: Necrotic tissue is black, brown or gray eschar, or slough. Spongy red tissue is healthy granulation that should be protected.

questions.takeaway: Shrinking measurements and beefy red, moist granulation show a wound is healing.
questions.strategy: Beefy red sounds alarming, which makes the infection answer tempting. In the wound bed it is the color of healthy granulation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Length, width and depth all decreased.
Beefy red, moist and spongy is granulation.
No eschar, and no redness beyond the wound.

elimination.verdict: It is healing; continue the plan and keep measuring.

questions.objective: Interpret wound characteristics and documentation findings to monitor healing or deterioration

questions.stem: During a dressing change, the nurse finds that a patient's stage 3 pressure injury on her right trochanter is unchanged at 4 x 3 x 1 cm with red granulation tissue. Today redness and warmth extend 3 cm onto the surrounding skin, and her pain has risen from 3 to 6 on a 0 to 10 scale. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Give pain medicine before dressing changes and keep the plan
options.rationale: Pain relief is reasonable, but treating pain alone ignores its cause. Spreading redness and warmth point to infection that needs a report.

options.text: Turn her every hour to keep pressure off the trochanter
options.rationale: Offloading prevents more pressure damage. It does nothing about an infection spreading into the skin around the wound.

options.text: Remeasure the wound in one week, since its size is the same
options.rationale: Stable size is reassuring, but size is not the only sign to watch. The surrounding skin now shows infection, which cannot wait a week.

options.text: Report the spreading redness and new pain to the provider
options.rationale: Redness and warmth spreading beyond the wound is cellulitis, a sign of infection. Changes like these are reported to the provider so treatment can begin.

questions.takeaway: Redness and warmth spreading beyond the wound edge is cellulitis; report it to the provider.
questions.strategy: The unchanged size is the distractor. Look past the wound bed to the surrounding skin, where the deterioration is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Redness and warmth now extend 3 cm onto the skin.
Spreading inflammation is cellulitis.
Report the change so infection can be treated.

elimination.verdict: Report the spreading redness and new pain to the provider.

questions.objective: Interpret wound characteristics and documentation findings to monitor healing or deterioration

questions.stem: A student documents a new pressure injury as "Coccyx wound, 3 x 2 x 0.5 cm, stage 3." Which addition does the nurse tell the student to make so that the team can track healing?

options.text: A note that the wound looks fairly small and is draining only a little
options.rationale: This mentions size and drainage, two things that are documented. The vague wording cannot be compared from one nurse to the next, so it does not track healing.

options.text: The Braden Scale total from admission and the current turning schedule
options.rationale: Both belong in the record, so they look like useful additions. The Braden total predicts risk and the schedule describes care; neither describes this wound or tracks its healing.

options.text: The stage the team expects the wound to reach by the time of discharge
options.rationale: Wound records describe what the nurse sees now so later findings can be compared. A predicted stage is not an observation, so it cannot be used to track healing.

options.text: Tissue type in the wound bed, the exudate and the surrounding skin
options.rationale: Tissue type, exudate and the skin around the wound show whether the wound is healing or declining. Size alone cannot show that, and these details give the next nurse something to compare.

questions.takeaway: Wound documentation includes location, size, color, tissue type, exudate, surrounding skin and any foreign bodies.
questions.strategy: The vague note is the near miss because it names size and drainage. Choose the details that describe this wound objectively, so another nurse can compare them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask whether it describes the wound
steps.detail: Risk scores, schedules and predictions do not.

steps.action: Ask whether another nurse can compare it
steps.detail: Vague phrases such as fairly small cannot be compared.

elimination.verdict: Tissue type in the wound bed, the exudate and the surrounding skin.

questions.objective: Interpret wound characteristics and documentation findings to monitor healing or deterioration

questions.stem: Ten days after negative pressure wound therapy is started for a stage 4 pressure injury over a patient's right ischium, the nurse evaluates the wound. Which finding shows the therapy is achieving its purpose?

options.text: A dry wound bed and an empty canister for 2 days
options.rationale: The therapy draws fluid out of the wound, but an empty canister and a dry bed are not its goal. Healthy granulation tissue stays moist.

options.text: Wider separation of the skin at the wound edges
options.rationale: Skin separating from tissue at the edges is undermining. Wider separation means the wound is getting worse, not better.

options.text: More granulation tissue and less edema in the wound
options.rationale: Negative pressure wound therapy increases blood flow, reduces edema and promotes granulation tissue. More granulation and less swelling show it is working.

options.text: Firmer, more swollen skin around the wound
options.rationale: Reducing edema is one purpose of the therapy. More swelling around the wound points to a problem, possibly infection.

questions.takeaway: Negative pressure wound therapy works by increasing blood flow, reducing edema and building granulation tissue.
questions.strategy: A dry bed sounds like the vacuum is doing its job. Its purpose is healing, so look for more granulation and less swelling.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blood flow up, edema down, granulation up.
Only more granulation with less edema fits.
Wider separation and more swelling mean worsening.

elimination.verdict: More granulation tissue and less edema in the wound.

questions.objective: Apply evidence based nursing care to patients with impaired skin integrity

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with a stage 4 pressure injury on her left heel with exposed bone. She has a new temperature of 38.6 C, a heart rate of 116/min and new confusion. The wound itself looks unchanged. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Report the changes to the provider
options.rationale: Fever, a fast heart rate and new confusion in a patient with exposed bone suggest sepsis or osteomyelitis, both complications of pressure injury. These changes are reported right away.

options.text: Change the dressing using sterile technique
options.rationale: Careful dressing technique helps prevent infection, but these signs are already systemic. Reporting comes first so treatment can start.

options.text: Recheck the temperature in 4 hours
options.rationale: Waiting 4 hours with fever, tachycardia and confusion delays treatment of a possible life threatening infection. These findings need action now.

options.text: Increase turning to every hour
options.rationale: Offloading protects the wound, but it does not treat a systemic infection. Her new findings point beyond the wound.

questions.takeaway: Fever, tachycardia and new confusion in a patient with a pressure injury suggest sepsis or osteomyelitis; report them now.
questions.strategy: The unchanged wound makes local care look like enough. The new findings are systemic, so the provider needs to know now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The changes are in her temperature, pulse and mental status.
Sepsis and osteomyelitis are complications of deep pressure injuries.
Report the changes rather than wait or treat locally.

elimination.verdict: Report the changes to the provider.

questions.objective: Apply evidence based nursing care to patients with impaired skin integrity

questions.nursesNote: 1400 Sacral pressure injury, stage 3. Measures 6 x 5 x 2 cm; last week 4 x 3 x 1 cm. Wound bed pale pink to beefy red and moist in the center. New black eschar along the upper edge. Exudate moderate, same as last week. Surrounding skin red and warm 4 cm beyond the wound margin. Undermining from 9:00 to 12:00, new since last week. Patient rates pain 3 of 10, unchanged. Foam dressing applied.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate the wound is deteriorating.

segments.text: Measures 6 x 5 x 2 cm; last week 4 x 3 x 1 cm
segments.rationale: Every dimension has grown in one week. A wound that is getting bigger is deteriorating, no matter how the bed looks.

segments.text: Wound bed pale pink to beefy red and moist in the center
segments.rationale: Pale pink to beefy red, moist tissue is healthy granulation. This part of the wound bed shows healing, not decline.

segments.text: New black eschar along the upper edge
segments.rationale: Eschar is black, brown or gray dead tissue. New necrotic tissue means part of the wound is getting worse.

segments.text: Exudate moderate, same as last week
segments.rationale: Exudate is fluid that leaks from a wound as it heals. An amount that has not changed since last week is not a sign of decline.

segments.text: Surrounding skin red and warm 4 cm beyond the wound margin
segments.rationale: Redness and warmth spreading beyond the wound edge is cellulitis. It signals that infection is moving out of the wound and into the surrounding skin.

segments.text: Undermining from 9:00 to 12:00, new since last week
segments.rationale: New undermining means more skin has separated from the tissue at the edge. The wound is extending under the surface.

segments.text: Patient rates pain 3 of 10, unchanged
segments.rationale: Pain that has stayed the same is not new evidence of decline. A rise in pain would raise concern, but this is stable.

segments.text: Foam dressing applied
segments.rationale: Applying a dressing is a nursing action, not an assessment finding. It does not show whether the wound is better or worse.

questions.takeaway: Larger measurements, new eschar, spreading redness and new undermining signal a deteriorating wound.
questions.strategy: Healthy granulation in the center can make the whole wound seem fine. Compare each finding with last week and with the surrounding skin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Size and undermining are worse; exudate and pain are the same.
Beefy red is healthy; new black eschar is not.
Redness 4 cm out is cellulitis.

elimination.verdict: The larger measurements, new eschar, spreading redness and new undermining.

questions.objective: Interpret wound characteristics and documentation findings to monitor healing or deterioration

questions.stem: At a clinic visit, a patient with diabetes has dry, itchy skin with scratch marks on his shins. His nails are long, and he says he plans to trim both his fingernails and his toenails himself tonight. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Leave your nails long and wear cotton gloves at night instead."
options.rationale: Gloves can limit scratching at night, but long nails keep damaging his skin during the day. Keeping fingernails short and filed is part of itch care.

options.text: "Trim your fingernails short and file them; a podiatrist should do your toenails."
options.rationale: Short, filed fingernails limit skin damage from scratching. Patients with diabetes should avoid cutting their own toenails, so the nurse refers him to podiatry.

options.text: "Trim all of your nails straight across tonight, then file the edges."
options.rationale: Short nails do reduce scratch damage, but cutting his own toenails puts a patient with diabetes at risk of foot injury. Toenail care goes to podiatry.

options.text: "Soak your feet in hot water first so the toenails cut more easily."
options.rationale: Softening the nails does not change who should cut them. With diabetes, cutting his own toenails risks injury, so podiatry does it.

questions.takeaway: With pruritus, keep fingernails short and filed; a patient with diabetes should not cut his own toenails and is referred to podiatry.
questions.strategy: Trimming nails short is the right itch measure, which makes the first distractor tempting. The diabetes in the stem changes who cares for the toenails.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fingernails are kept short and filed.
He should not cut his own toenails.
Gloves and soaking do not fix either problem.

elimination.verdict: Trim your fingernails short and file them; a podiatrist should do your toenails.

questions.objective: Differentiate common skin disorders based on clinical presentation and nursing priorities

questions.stem: A graduate student tells the nurse that chronic itching with no rash flares every exam week, when the student sleeps little and feels tense; the soap, lotion and diet have not changed. Which response by the nurse explains the pattern?

options.text: Itching this regular suggests infection, so the skin needs a culture
options.rationale: Infection is a real cause of skin trouble, but it brings a rash, redness or drainage. This skin has no rash, and the flares follow a calendar pattern rather than a wound.

options.text: Short sleep dries the skin, so heavier lotion should stop the flares
options.rationale: Dry skin does worsen itching, and preventing dryness is part of pruritus care. The lotion routine has not changed, though, so dryness does not explain why flares come only in tense weeks.

options.text: A new allergen is likely, so check the products you use daily
options.rationale: A new allergen does set off itching and hives, so asking about products is reasonable. The soap, lotion and diet have not changed, which leaves no new exposure to explain the flares.

options.text: Stress can make itching worse, so tension may be driving these flares
options.rationale: Itching is worsened by dry skin, sweat, stress and changes in blood flow. With the products unchanged and the flares tied to tense, sleepless weeks, stress is the trigger that fits.

questions.takeaway: Itching is worsened by dry skin, sweat, stress and changes in blood flow, so a flare that tracks tense periods points to stress.
questions.strategy: Dry skin is the most familiar itch trigger and pulls students toward more lotion; the unchanged routine and the timing tie the flares to stress instead.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only the stress and short sleep of exam weeks changed; products and diet stayed the same.

steps.action: Test each trigger against the stem
steps.detail: No new product rules out an allergen, and no rash rules out infection.
The lotion routine is unchanged, so dryness cannot explain flares limited to tense weeks.

elimination.verdict: Stress is worsening the itching.

questions.stem: A woman who takes insulin for diabetes has dry, itchy shins with scratch marks and two small open scratches. Her fingernails are long and sharp. She says, "Since I have diabetes, I am not supposed to cut any of my nails, so I wait for the foot doctor to do them all." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "That is right; ask the foot doctor to see you sooner."
options.rationale: Seeing podiatry for her toenails is correct and worth keeping. Agreeing that she cannot trim her fingernails leaves long, sharp nails breaking her itchy skin until that visit.

options.text: "Keep your fingernails short and filed; podiatry still does your toenails."
options.rationale: Short, filed fingernails cause less skin damage when she scratches, and the podiatry rule covers only toenails. Keeping both parts of the advice protects her skin and her feet.

options.text: "Moisturize your shins daily, and the scratching will stop."
options.rationale: Preventing dry skin is part of pruritus care and will help her. It does not address the long, sharp nails that are already opening her skin.

options.text: "You may trim all of your nails yourself if you are careful."
options.rationale: Trimming her own fingernails is safe and helps. Patients with diabetes should not cut their own toenails, however careful they are, so toenails stay with podiatry.

questions.takeaway: In pruritus, fingernails are kept short and filed; a patient with diabetes refers toenail care to podiatry, and that rule does not extend to fingernails.
questions.strategy: Her belief sounds like the diabetes rule, so agreeing feels correct. The rule covers only toenails, and her fingernails still need trimming to protect her itchy skin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She applies the toenail rule to every nail.
Fingernails short and filed; toenails to podiatry.
Agreeing, trimming everything and moisturizing alone each miss one part.

elimination.verdict: Fingernails short and filed; podiatry for toenails.

questions.stem: An hour after eating shellfish for the first time, a woman has raised, red, swollen plaques on her trunk. Her breathing is unlabored, and her lips and tongue are not swollen. An antihistamine is ordered. Besides removing the trigger, which plan fits?

options.text: Encourage a brisk walk to take her mind off the itch
options.rationale: Distraction can help itching in general, but overexertion dilates vessels and worsens hives. She should rest until the hives fade.

options.text: Apply a moisturizer to the plaques for dry skin
options.rationale: Moisturizers treat dry skin, which is not the cause here. These plaques come from an allergen, so the antihistamine is the treatment.

options.text: Give the antihistamine and keep the room cool
options.rationale: Treatment for hives is removing the trigger and giving antihistamines. Heat dilates blood vessels and worsens hives, so a cool room helps.

options.text: Offer a warm bath to soothe the itching
options.rationale: Warmth feels soothing, but heat dilates blood vessels and makes hives worse. A warm bath would spread the swelling.

questions.takeaway: For urticaria, remove the trigger, give antihistamines and avoid heat, alcohol and overexertion, which dilate vessels.
questions.strategy: The warm bath and walk both sound like comfort measures. Anything that dilates blood vessels makes hives worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Breathing is unlabored and her lips and tongue are normal.
Heat, alcohol and overexertion dilate vessels.

steps.action: Pick the plan that avoids them
steps.detail: Antihistamine and a cool room.

elimination.verdict: Give the antihistamine and keep the room cool.

questions.stem: A resident of a long term care facility is diagnosed with scabies after several weeks of itching. She shares a room with another resident. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Place her on contact precautions
options.rationale: Scabies is a contagious skin infection caused by mites that spreads through skin contact. Contact precautions protect staff and her roommate while treatment begins.

options.text: Apply a moisturizer to her itchy skin
options.rationale: A moisturizer may ease dry skin, but it does not stop the mites from spreading. Preventing transmission comes first with a contagious infestation.

options.text: Give an antihistamine at bedtime for itching
options.rationale: An antihistamine may help her sleep, but it is a comfort measure. It does nothing to keep the mites from reaching her roommate.

options.text: Check her roommate's skin at the next weekly review
options.rationale: The roommate does need assessment, but waiting a week allows more spread. Precautions for the patient with scabies come first.

questions.takeaway: Scabies is a contagious mite infestation, so contact precautions start as soon as it is diagnosed.
questions.strategy: The comfort measures treat her itch, not the risk to others. A contagious diagnosis makes preventing spread the first action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Scabies is contagious.
Itch relief can follow; spread to others cannot wait.
A weekly check lets mites spread.

elimination.verdict: Place her on contact precautions.
