questions.scenario: An interdisciplinary team meets about a man with a stage 4 sacral pressure injury with tunneling that has not healed in 2 months. He has urinary incontinence, has lost 10% of his weight and is too weak to get out of bed.
questions.stem: For each need, indicate the team member best suited to address it.

rows.text: Set protein, calorie and fluid goals for healing
rows.rationale: The registered dietitian nutritionist plans protein, calories, vitamins and fluids. Severe protein deficiency stops healing, so these goals come from the dietitian.

rows.text: Advise on managing incontinence near the wound
rows.rationale: This nurse is trained in elimination needs as well as wounds. Keeping urine away from the wound protects it.

rows.text: Recommend a treatment plan for the tunneling wound that has not healed
rows.rationale: This RN has advanced training in complex and hard to heal wounds. A stalled stage 4 wound with tunneling calls for those recommendations.

rows.text: Address his 10% weight loss
rows.rationale: Weight loss over 5% is a nutrition cue that slows healing. Planning intake to reverse it belongs to the dietitian.

rows.text: Help him regain function so he can get out of bed
rows.rationale: Improving overall function and quality of life is a physical therapy goal. Getting him out of bed also takes pressure off the sacrum.

rows.text: Plan ways to offload pressure and build his strength
rows.rationale: Physical therapists plan strategies to redistribute and offload pressure and to maximize function. His weakness keeps him in one position, which they address.

questions.takeaway: The wound, ostomy and continence nurse handles complex wounds and continence, the dietitian handles nutrition, and the physical therapist handles offloading and function.
questions.strategy: Offloading can sound like a nursing or wound care task. Strategies to redistribute pressure and build function belong to physical therapy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Wound and continence, nutrition, or movement and function.
Protein goals and weight loss go to the dietitian.
Offloading and function go to physical therapy.

elimination.verdict: Wound plan and incontinence to the wound nurse; nutrition goals and weight loss to the dietitian; offloading and function to the physical therapist.

questions.objective: Apply evidence based nursing care to patients with impaired skin integrity

questions.stem: Ten days after starting allopurinol for gout, a patient is admitted with painful red skin, blisters over less than 10% of his body and mouth sores. His next allopurinol dose is due now. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Hold the dose and report the likely drug trigger
options.rationale: Stevens Johnson syndrome is usually triggered by a drug, and allopurinol is a high risk one. The first step is to stop the drug, so the nurse holds it and reports.

options.text: Apply moisturizer to the blisters, then give the dose
options.rationale: Skin care is part of supportive care later, but giving the dose continues the trigger. Stopping the drug comes first.

options.text: Give the dose and report the rash on provider rounds
options.rationale: Continuing the drug keeps feeding the reaction. Allopurinol is a high risk trigger, and waiting for rounds delays stopping it.

options.text: Give the dose with food to lessen the reaction
options.rationale: Food can ease stomach upset from a drug, but it does not stop an immune skin reaction. The drug itself must be stopped.

questions.takeaway: In Stevens Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, the first step is to stop the suspected drug.
questions.strategy: A rash may seem minor next to a scheduled dose. A new drug, blisters and mouth sores point to a drug reaction, so the dose is held.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Allopurinol started 10 days ago, then blisters and mouth sores.
Allopurinol is a high risk drug for Stevens Johnson syndrome.
Stop the drug.

elimination.verdict: Hold the dose and report the likely drug trigger.

questions.stem: A patient with Stevens Johnson syndrome had the causative drug stopped yesterday and is receiving IV fluids. This morning the patient has new hoarseness, is drooling because swallowing hurts, and speaks in short phrases. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply ordered lubricating drops to both eyes
options.rationale: Eye care is part of supportive care in this syndrome, because the eyes can be damaged too. Nothing in the stem shows eye trouble, and the voice change and drooling point to the airway.

options.text: Cover open blisters with nonadherent dressings
options.rationale: Protecting open skin from infection is part of supportive care. The skin can wait a few minutes, while new hoarseness and drooling can signal an airway that is closing.

options.text: Give the ordered pain medicine before meals
options.rationale: Pain control is part of supportive care, and swallowing does hurt this patient. Pain does not threaten life the way a narrowing airway does, so it follows the airway check.

options.text: Assess the airway and get urgent help
options.rationale: Hoarseness, drooling and short phrases suggest swelling or sloughing in the mouth and throat. Airway comes first in supportive care, so the nurse assesses it now and calls for help before it closes.

questions.takeaway: In SJS and TEN, supportive care starts with the airway; hoarseness or drooling from mouth and throat involvement comes before pain, eye and skin care.
questions.strategy: Every option is correct supportive care, so the choice rests on priority; the new voice change and drooling make this an airway problem.

steps.action: Notice that every option is appropriate
steps.detail: Pain, eye and skin care are all part of supportive care, so priority decides.
Hoarseness and drooling mean the mouth and throat are involved, which threatens the airway.

elimination.verdict: Assess the airway and get urgent help.

questions.objective: Differentiate common skin disorders based on clinical presentation and nursing priorities
questions.concept: SJS and TEN: supportive care priorities

questions.stem: Three weeks after starting a new anticonvulsant for seizures, a patient has painful red skin with blisters on her trunk and sores on her lips. She breathes comfortably and speaks clearly. Her next anticonvulsant dose is due now, and she asks for something for pain. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give this dose to prevent a seizure, then report the rash
options.rationale: Stopping an anticonvulsant does raise seizure risk, which the provider manages with a substitute. Another dose keeps feeding a reaction that can become life threatening, so the drug is held and reported now.

options.text: Give the analgesic she asked for, then reassess
options.rationale: Pain control is part of supportive care, and her pain is real. Stopping the likely drug comes first, because comfort measures do not halt the reaction.

options.text: Hold the anticonvulsant and notify the provider now
options.rationale: Anticonvulsants are high risk drugs for this reaction, and the first step is to stop the drug. Notifying the provider now ends the exposure and lets a safer seizure drug be chosen.

options.text: Apply nonadherent dressings to the blistered areas
options.rationale: Protecting blistered skin helps prevent infection and is part of supportive care. It does nothing about the drug still driving the reaction, so stopping the drug comes first.

questions.takeaway: When a recently started high risk drug is followed by painful blistering skin and mucosal sores, stopping the drug comes before supportive care.
questions.strategy: Seizure prevention, pain relief and wound care all sound responsible. The first step is stopping the likely trigger and reporting it, because the provider can cover seizures with another drug.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An anticonvulsant started 3 weeks ago is a high risk drug.
She breathes and speaks normally, so airway does not outrank stopping the drug.
Stop the drug first; pain and skin care follow.

elimination.verdict: Hold the anticonvulsant and notify the provider now.

questions.stem: At a community health fair, a woman who coaches outdoor soccer practices from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. asks how to lower her risk of skin cancer. Which plan does the nurse recommend?

options.text: Keep the schedule and rely on sunscreen alone each morning
options.rationale: Sunscreen helps, but it does not replace avoiding midday sun. Her practices fall during the strongest hours of the day.

options.text: Shift practices away from midday and wear a hat and sunscreen
options.rationale: Avoiding midday sun cuts the strongest exposure, and a hat and sunscreen protect what remains. Prevention combines all three.

options.text: Build a base tan in a tanning bed before the season
options.rationale: Tanning beds add ultraviolet exposure rather than protecting against it. Avoiding them is part of skin cancer prevention.

options.text: Wear sunglasses and a cap and keep her arms uncovered
options.rationale: Sunglasses and a cap help, but uncovered arms still take hours of sun. Protective clothing means covering the skin.

questions.takeaway: Prevent skin cancer by avoiding midday sun and tanning beds and using sunscreen and protective clothing.
questions.strategy: Sunscreen appears in more than one option. The plan that also moves her out of the midday sun is the complete one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Practices run through midday.
Tanning beds increase risk.
Avoid midday sun and add a hat and sunscreen.

elimination.verdict: Shift practices away from midday and wear a hat and sunscreen.

questions.objective: Evaluate skin cancer risk factors and assessment findings to support prevention and early detection

questions.stem: During a skin cancer screening, a patient with many moles on his back and arms asks how he can find a skin cancer early. Which plan does the nurse teach?

options.text: Check all of your skin monthly and photograph the moles to compare
options.rationale: A monthly self exam of the whole body finds changes early. Photos or a body map let him compare each mole against its earlier appearance.

options.text: Check your face, neck and arms monthly, since they get the most sun
options.rationale: Sun exposed areas carry risk, but skin cancer can appear anywhere, including his back. The self exam covers all of the skin.

options.text: See a provider yearly and skip the checks between visits
options.rationale: Provider exams help, but a year is a long gap for a changing lesion. Monthly self exams catch changes between visits.

options.text: Report a mole only if it becomes painful or starts to bleed
options.rationale: Bleeding is a warning sign, but waiting for it misses earlier changes in color, size or shape. Any new or changing lesion is reported.

questions.takeaway: Teach a monthly self exam of all the skin, tracking moles with a body map or photos.
questions.strategy: Each distractor narrows the check by time, area or sign. The plan that covers all skin every month with a way to compare wins.

steps.detail: Monthly, not yearly.
All of the skin, including his back.
Any change, not only pain or bleeding.

elimination.verdict: Check all of your skin monthly and photograph the moles to compare.

questions.objective: Evaluate skin cancer risk factors and assessment findings to support prevention and early detection

questions.scenario: The nurse admits a patient who has taken a sulfonamide antibiotic for 2 weeks. She has a temperature of 38.9 C, sheets of peeling skin over about 40% of her body surface, mouth sores and red, irritated eyes. Her blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg and her urine output has dropped.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Begin ordered fluid and electrolyte replacement
options.rationale: Losing skin over 40% of the body loses large amounts of fluid and electrolytes. Low blood pressure and falling urine output show she needs replacement now.

options.text: Apply a barrier cream to the peeling skin
options.rationale: Barrier creams protect intact skin from urine and stool. On peeling, open skin they add a contamination risk and do nothing for fluid loss.

options.text: Stop the sulfonamide antibiotic
options.rationale: A sulfonamide is a high risk trigger, and stopping the drug is the first step. Every hour it continues adds to the skin loss.

options.text: Give the next antibiotic dose to treat the fever
options.rationale: The fever comes from the skin reaction, and this antibiotic is the likely trigger. Giving it again would worsen the reaction.

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injuries
options.rationale: Stage 2 injuries form over bony areas from pressure. Skin peeling over 40% of the body after a new drug is a drug reaction, not pressure damage.

options.text: Toxic epidermal necrolysis
options.rationale: A drug triggered reaction covering more than 30% of the body surface is toxic epidermal necrolysis. Her 40% skin loss after a sulfonamide fits.

options.text: Stevens Johnson syndrome
options.rationale: Stevens Johnson syndrome is the same kind of reaction, but it covers less than 10% of the body surface. At 40%, she is past that range.

options.text: Urticaria
options.rationale: Hives are raised, swollen plaques from an allergen, and the skin stays intact. Sheets of peeling skin and mouth sores point to a far more serious reaction.

options.text: Braden Scale total
options.rationale: The Braden Scale predicts pressure injury risk. Her skin is failing from a drug reaction, so it does not guide her urgent care.

options.text: Intake, output and electrolytes
options.rationale: Large skin loss drains fluid and electrolytes, and her urine output has already dropped. Tracking them shows whether replacement is keeping up.

options.text: Wound depth with a cotton tipped applicator
options.rationale: Applicator depth suits a single open cavity such as a pressure injury. Her skin loss is spread over her body, and fluids and temperature are the urgent measures.

options.text: Body temperature
options.rationale: Without intact skin she cannot hold heat or keep out microbes. Temperature tracks both heat loss and infection.

questions.takeaway: Toxic epidermal necrolysis covers more than 30% of the body surface; stop the drug and support airway, fluids, temperature, pain, eyes and infection prevention.
questions.strategy: Stevens Johnson syndrome is the same reaction at a smaller size. The 40% body surface sets the condition, and the low blood pressure and urine output set the priorities.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Over 30% is toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Stop the sulfonamide.
Replace fluids and monitor intake, output, electrolytes and temperature.

elimination.verdict: Stop the sulfonamide and replace fluids; toxic epidermal necrolysis; monitor intake, output, electrolytes and temperature.

questions.objective: Differentiate common skin disorders based on clinical presentation and nursing priorities

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse that she photographs a mole on her left shoulder each month. Its size, shape and color match last month's photo, but it has become itchy and tender. What does the nurse advise?

options.text: Take an antihistamine for the itch and keep the shoulder covered
options.rationale: An antihistamine may calm the itch, but it hides a warning sign rather than evaluating it. The change still needs to be checked.

options.text: Keep taking monthly photos and report it if size, shape or color change
options.rationale: Size, shape and color changes are reportable, but they are not the only ones. New itching or tenderness is also a reportable change.

options.text: Apply moisturizer and sunscreen to it and recheck in a month
options.rationale: Sunscreen helps prevent new damage, and moisturizer eases dry skin. Neither evaluates a mole that has changed, and a month delays detection.

options.text: Have a provider examine the mole now rather than wait
options.rationale: New itching or tenderness in a lesion is a reportable change, even when size, shape and color are stable. Prompt evaluation supports early detection.

questions.takeaway: Report any new or changing lesion, including new itching, tenderness, redness, bleeding, oozing, crusting or scaling.
questions.strategy: Unchanged size, shape and color make the mole look stable. New itching and tenderness are reportable changes too.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Itching and tenderness are new.
Itching or tenderness count, not only size, shape and color.
Treating the itch delays evaluation.

elimination.verdict: Have a provider examine the mole now rather than wait.

questions.objective: Evaluate skin cancer risk factors and assessment findings to support prevention and early detection

questions.stem: During a home health visit, the nurse reassesses a sacral pressure injury that was documented as unstageable last week because black eschar covered the wound bed. The provider debrided the eschar 2 days ago. Today yellow fat is visible, and the nurse can feel bone at the base with a cotton tipped applicator, although no bone is seen. How does the nurse document the wound now?

options.text: Stage 3 pressure injury
options.rationale: Visible fat fits stage 3, and no bone is seen, which makes this choice tempting. Bone that can be felt counts the same as exposed bone, so the wound is deeper than stage 3.

options.text: Stage 4 pressure injury
options.rationale: Palpable bone means the loss reaches through skin and fat into deep structures, which meets stage 4. With the eschar removed, the base can be assessed and the wound is staged by its depth.

options.text: Unstageable pressure injury
options.rationale: Unstageable was the right label while eschar hid the wound bed. The eschar was debrided 2 days ago, so the depth can now be confirmed and the label no longer fits.

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury
options.rationale: A deep tissue injury shows persistent deep red, maroon or purple color, often over skin that is still intact. This open wound with visible fat and palpable bone is a full thickness injury that can be staged.

questions.takeaway: Unstageable applies only while slough or eschar hides the base; once it is removed, stage by depth, and palpable bone means stage 4.
questions.strategy: Unstageable is last week's correct answer, and stage 3 fits the visible fat. The removed eschar and the bone felt with the applicator make it stage 4 today.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The eschar is gone, so the base can be assessed.
Bone is felt, even though it is not seen.
Palpable bone meets stage 4.

elimination.verdict: Stage 4 pressure injury.

questions.objective: Differentiate wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

questions.stem: On a step down unit, a patient recovering from a pulmonary embolism receives oxygen by nasal cannula, and her oxygen saturation drops whenever the cannula is off. Her sacrum and heels are intact. Over the top of each ear, where the tubing rests, the intact skin is red and does not blanch. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Massage the reddened ears to restore blood flow
options.rationale: Massaging reddened areas damages the small capillaries that are already injured. Rubbing the ears would worsen the injury rather than restore blood flow to the skin.

options.text: Document intact skin and continue routine checks
options.rationale: Intact skin can still hold a stage 1 injury when the redness does not blanch. Documenting the skin as intact misses the ear damage and leaves the tubing pressing on it.

options.text: Pad the tubing over the ears and recheck them
options.rationale: Nonblanchable redness of intact skin under tubing is a stage 1 injury from the device, and padding spreads the pressure while oxygen continues. Rechecking the ears shows whether the damage resolves or progresses.

options.text: Remove the cannula for an hour to rest the ears
options.rationale: Taking pressure off injured skin is the right goal, which makes this tempting. Her saturation drops whenever the cannula is off, so removing it trades a skin problem for an oxygenation problem.

questions.takeaway: Oxygen tubing can cause a pressure injury on the ears; protect the skin under the device while keeping the needed therapy in place.
questions.strategy: Removing the cannula relieves pressure, the usual fix for nonblanchable redness. Her saturation drops without it, so the pressure is spread with padding instead.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nonblanchable redness of intact skin under a device.
Her saturation drops off oxygen, so the cannula stays.
Pad the tubing and reassess.

elimination.verdict: Pad the tubing over the ears and recheck them.

questions.objective: Evaluate wound and skin assessment findings to determine appropriate nursing actions

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with cirrhosis who has a provider ordered fluid restriction of 1500 mL a day for low blood sodium. Her Braden nutrition subscore is 2, and she has lost weight since admission. Assistive personnel ask whether to keep offering extra fluids to protect her skin. What does the nurse direct?

options.text: Offer fluids freely but limit sodium in her meals
options.rationale: Cutting sodium does not make extra fluid safe for a patient whose sodium is already low. Offering fluids freely breaks the ordered restriction and can lower her sodium further.

options.text: Encourage 2000 to 3000 mL a day and consult the dietitian
options.rationale: Fluids of 2000 to 3000 mL a day support skin health for most patients at risk. This patient has an ordered 1500 mL restriction, so the nurse does not override it.

options.text: Keep her current fluid limit and consult the dietitian
options.rationale: The ordered restriction treats her low sodium and stays in place unless the provider changes it. The dietitian can still raise protein and calories within the limit, which addresses her nutrition risk.

options.text: Hold fluids until her Braden score improves
options.rationale: Withholding fluids would leave her dehydrated and raise her skin risk. The order sets a limit rather than stopping fluids, and the Braden score does not decide fluid intake.

questions.takeaway: The skin bundle's fluid goal gives way to an ordered fluid restriction; meet nutrition needs through the dietitian within the limit.
questions.strategy: The 2000 to 3000 mL goal and the dietitian consult are the textbook bundle. The ordered restriction in the stem makes the fluid half wrong for this patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A 1500 mL restriction is in place for low sodium.
Both consult the dietitian; only one keeps the limit.
Free fluids and no fluids both break the order.

elimination.verdict: Keep her current fluid limit and consult the dietitian.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions to prevent pressure injuries and promote skin integrity

questions.stem: The day after fire ant bites at a picnic, a man has itchy red welts on both legs. He is taking the prescribed antihistamine, and the nurse teaches him how to care for the rash at home. Which statement by the patient shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: With the antihistamine on board, I'll go to spin class tonight.
options.rationale: Overexertion dilates blood vessels and can worsen hives even while an antihistamine is working. Hard exercise should wait until the welts clear, so this statement needs correction.

options.text: I'll stay away from the anthill at the park.
options.rationale: Removing the trigger is the first step in treating hives. Avoiding the ant mound keeps him from new bites, so this statement is correct.

options.text: I'll take cool showers instead of hot ones until the welts fade.
options.rationale: Heat dilates blood vessels and worsens hives, so cool showers are the right choice. This statement shows he understood the teaching and needs no correction.

options.text: I'll skip my evening beer until the welts are gone.
options.rationale: Alcohol dilates blood vessels and can make hives worse. Avoiding it until the welts clear is correct, so this statement shows the teaching worked.

questions.takeaway: Hives worsen with anything that dilates vessels: heat, alcohol and overexertion; an antihistamine does not make them safe.
questions.strategy: The antihistamine makes the spin class sound safe. Overexertion dilates vessels whatever drug is on board, while skipping beer and choosing cool showers are both correct.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the one wrong statement.
Heat, alcohol and overexertion worsen hives.
The antihistamine does not cancel the exercise risk.

elimination.verdict: With the antihistamine on board, I'll go to spin class tonight.

questions.objective: Differentiate common skin disorders based on clinical presentation and nursing priorities

questions.stem: During a routine clinic visit, the nurse takes a skin cancer history from a woman. Which findings increase her risk of skin cancer? Select all that apply.

options.text: She used tanning beds often in her twenties
options.rationale: Tanning beds deliver concentrated ultraviolet exposure, which damages skin the same way the sun does. Past use still adds to her lifetime risk.

options.text: Her mother had melanoma
options.rationale: Genetic predisposition is a risk factor for melanoma and basal cell carcinoma. Family history of skin cancer is a key assessment question.

options.text: She has had seasonal allergies since childhood
options.rationale: Seasonal allergies are not linked to skin cancer. They affect the immune response to pollen, not damage from ultraviolet light.

options.text: She had a skin growth removed from her back 3 years ago
options.rationale: Past surgery to remove skin growths is part of the skin cancer history. It suggests earlier skin damage or a precursor lesion.

options.text: She has worked as a roofer for 20 years
options.rationale: Years of outdoor work mean long sun exposure, and sun overexposure is the major cause of skin cancer. Occupation is part of the skin cancer history.

options.text: She now works night shifts in a warehouse
options.rationale: Indoor night work limits her current sun exposure. It does not add to her risk, though her years of roofing still count.

questions.takeaway: Skin cancer risk includes sun exposure at work or play, tanning beds, family history and past removal of skin growths.
questions.strategy: Her current indoor job can make her seem low risk. Past sun exposure, past tanning and past lesions still count.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Roofing and tanning beds.

steps.action: Look for genetic and past lesion history
steps.detail: Her mother's melanoma and the removed growth.
Night work indoors and allergies add no risk.

elimination.verdict: Roofing, her mother's melanoma, tanning beds and the removed skin growth.

questions.objective: Evaluate skin cancer risk factors and assessment findings to support prevention and early detection

questions.stem: In the burn unit, a patient whose skin began peeling after she took an NSAID has had the drug stopped. Large sheets of skin are gone from her trunk and legs. She breathes easily and speaks in full sentences. Her urine output has fallen over the past 4 hours, and she is dizzy when the head of the bed is raised. Her eyes are crusted and burning, and she rates her pain 8 of 10 and asks for pain medicine. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the ordered pain medicine she requested
options.rationale: Severe pain needs treatment, and she has asked for relief. Pain comes after circulation, and her dizziness and dropping urine output show a circulation problem that is more urgent.

options.text: Apply the ordered lubricant to both eyes
options.rationale: Eye care protects her vision and is part of supportive care. Her eyes are uncomfortable but not a threat to life, so this follows the fluid problem.

options.text: Cover the open areas with nonadherent dressings
options.rationale: Covering open areas helps prevent infection and further fluid loss. It does not correct the volume she has already lost, so reporting the circulation change comes first.

options.text: Report signs of fluid volume loss
options.rationale: Losing large areas of skin lets fluid escape, and less urine with dizziness points to low volume. With the airway clear, circulation comes next, so the provider needs to adjust fluids now.

questions.takeaway: After the drug is stopped, supportive care follows the ABCs: with the airway clear, fluid loss through the lost skin comes before pain and eye care.
questions.strategy: She is asking for pain medicine and rates her pain 8, which pulls hard. Her easy breathing clears the airway, and the dizziness and falling output make circulation the priority.

steps.detail: She breathes easily and speaks in full sentences.
Less urine and dizziness point to fluid loss.
Pain, eyes and dressings follow circulation.

elimination.verdict: Report signs of fluid volume loss.

questions.objective: Differentiate common skin disorders based on clinical presentation and nursing priorities
questions.concept: SJS and TEN: supportive care priorities

questions.stem: At the start of a night shift, the nurse finds a woman with advanced dementia lying on her back with both heels resting on the mattress. She rarely moves her legs, and the skin over her heels is intact and blanches when pressed. Which plan does the nurse put in place?

options.text: Apply foam dressings and rest her heels on the bed
options.rationale: Foam dressings do help protect bony prominences, so this plan sounds complete. Her heels would still bear weight on the mattress, and a dressing cushions pressure without removing it.

options.text: Raise her calves on a pillow so her heels float
options.rationale: Supporting the calves lifts the heels off the mattress, so no pressure reaches them at all. Floating the heels protects a small bony area that breaks down quickly when it bears weight.

options.text: Place a pillow under her knees
options.rationale: A pillow under the knees bends the legs, but the heels stay pressed against the mattress. It also presses on the vessels behind the knee and slows blood flow to the lower legs.

options.text: Set each heel on a donut shaped cushion
options.rationale: A donut cushion presses on the ring of tissue around the heel and damages the capillaries there. It concentrates pressure rather than relieving it, so it is never used for prevention.

questions.takeaway: Float the heels by supporting the calves so the heels touch nothing; dressings and cushions under the heel do not remove the pressure.
questions.strategy: Foam dressings are a real prevention measure and make the second plan look right. Only lifting the calves takes the heels off the mattress, which is the goal for a patient who does not move her legs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both heels rest on the mattress and she rarely moves.
Only lifting the calves leaves the heels touching nothing.
Donut cushions damage capillaries; a pillow under the knees leaves the heels down.

elimination.verdict: Raise her calves on a pillow so her heels float.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions to prevent pressure injuries and promote skin integrity

questions.stem: Two weeks after a dog bite on her right calf was cleaned and left open to heal, a patient's wound is smaller than it was last week. The base is filled with moist, red, slightly bumpy tissue, and the skin around it is not warm or swollen. How does the nurse interpret this finding?

options.text: Early wound infection
options.rationale: Infection brings redness, warmth or swelling that spreads into the skin around the wound. The surrounding skin here is not warm or swollen and the wound is shrinking, which points to healing.

options.text: Maturation phase scar formation
options.rationale: Maturation remodels collagen into a thinner, paler, firmer scar from about 3 weeks to a year or longer. This wound is still open and filling with new tissue, so it has not reached that phase.

options.text: Expected proliferative phase healing
options.rationale: From about day 4 to 2 to 4 weeks, new capillaries and collagen build red granulation tissue while the wound contracts. A shrinking wound with moist red tissue at two weeks fits this phase.

options.text: Inflammatory phase that has not resolved
options.rationale: Redness does belong to the inflammatory phase, which makes this choice tempting. That phase lasts about days 1 to 5 and brings warmth and swelling, and this wound at two weeks has neither.

questions.takeaway: In the proliferative phase, from about day 4 to 2 to 4 weeks, granulation tissue fills the wound and the wound contracts.
questions.strategy: Red tissue pulls students toward inflammation or infection. The two week timing, the shrinking size and the cool, flat skin around the wound tip it to expected new tissue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Place two weeks on the timeline
steps.detail: Day 4 to 2 to 4 weeks is the proliferative phase.
The surrounding skin is not warm or swollen, and the wound is shrinking.
Maturation needs a closed wound and starts around 3 weeks.

elimination.verdict: Expected proliferative phase healing.

questions.objective: Differentiate wound healing patterns and pressure injury stages

skills.title: FSBS/Insulin Administration Check-Off
skills.subtitle: Interpreting the value, recognizing hypoglycemia, insulin types and timing, and injection technique

questions.stem: A 67-year-old on sliding scale NovoLog has a prelunch fingerstick of 92 mg/dL after readings of 210 and 198 mg/dL this morning. The assistive personnel says the finger was still wet and was squeezed hard. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Chart 92 mg/dL and give the meal insulin with no correction dose
options.rationale: Correct handling of a trusted 92 mg/dL. This value came from a wet, squeezed finger, so it cannot be trusted yet.

options.text: Repeat the fingerstick on a dry finger without squeezing
options.rationale: Water and squeezing both dilute the sample and can give a false low. A clean, dry finger gives a value the dose can rest on.

options.text: Give a snack now, since the glucose fell more than 100 mg/dL
options.rationale: Food for a falling glucose is reasonable when the fall is real. Here the fall may be a diluted sample.

options.text: Report the drop from 198 mg/dL to 92 mg/dL to the provider
options.rationale: Reporting a sudden change is sound once the value is confirmed. The nurse confirms it first.

questions.takeaway: A reading that does not fit the trend and came from a wet or squeezed finger is repeated before any dose is based on it.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The stem gives a number and two reasons to doubt it. Settle the doubt before charting, feeding or calling.

steps.action: Compare the value with the morning
steps.detail: 92 mg/dL after 210 and 198 mg/dL does not fit.
A wet finger and hard squeezing dilute the drop.

steps.action: Cut the options that trust the number
steps.detail: Charting, feeding and reporting all act on 92 mg/dL.

elimination.verdict: Repeat the fingerstick on a dry finger without squeezing.

questions.objective: perform and interpret a fingerstick blood glucose

questions.stem: At 1130 a 67-year-old has a fingerstick of 224 mg/dL. NovoLog 5 units and a NovoLog correction scale are both ordered with meals. The kitchen says the lunch tray will arrive at 1300. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give both doses now so they are working when the tray comes
options.rationale: Giving ahead of the meal fits regular insulin. Rapid-acting insulin starts in 10 to 30 minutes, long before a 1300 tray.

options.text: Give the correction dose now and the meal dose at 1300
options.rationale: Treating the high sounds prompt. The correction is ordered with meals, and rapid-acting insulin with no food for 90 minutes sets up a low.

options.text: Wait for the tray, then repeat the fingerstick and dose from it
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin follows the food, and a value 90 minutes old no longer describes the client. A fresh fingerstick at 1300 sets the dose.

options.text: Wait for the tray, then give the doses the scale lists for 224 mg/dL
options.rationale: Right time, wrong number. By 1300 the 1130 value is 90 minutes old.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting insulin is given when the food is present, and a sliding scale dose is based on the glucose at the time it is given.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two questions decide it: when is the food here, and how old will the number be by then.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rapid-acting insulin starts in 10 to 30 minutes. The tray is 90 minutes away.

steps.action: Cut the options that give insulin now
steps.detail: Both put rapid-acting insulin in with no food.
One doses from a current value, one from a 90 minute old value.

elimination.verdict: Wait for the tray, repeat the fingerstick and dose from the new value.

questions.objective: insulin timing and peak time risk

questions.stem: A 67-year-old received NovoLog with lunch at 1300 for a glucose of 224 mg/dL and ate the whole meal. At 1500 the fingerstick is 171 mg/dL with no symptoms. The correction scale starts at 151 mg/dL, with meals only. Which conclusion does the nurse reach?

options.text: The value is in the 70 to 180 mg/dL target, so the dose worked
options.rationale: 171 mg/dL sits inside the inpatient target and the client has no symptoms. That is the expected response.

options.text: The value is on the correction scale, so another dose is due now
options.rationale: 171 mg/dL is above 151 mg/dL, but the scale is ordered with meals only. No meal is present at 1500.

options.text: The value is hyperglycemia and is reported to the provider now
options.rationale: Reporting fits a value above 180 mg/dL. This one is below that line.

options.text: The value fell quickly, so fast-acting carbohydrate is given now
options.rationale: Carbohydrate treats a value under 70 mg/dL. A fall from 224 to 171 mg/dL is the insulin doing its job.

questions.takeaway: Effective glucose treatment lands between 70 and 180 mg/dL. A correction scale ordered with meals is not used between meals.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Check the number against the target range first, then read exactly when the scale applies.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 171 mg/dL is between 70 and 180 mg/dL.
The scale applies only with meals.

steps.action: Cut the options built on a wrong line
steps.detail: 180 mg/dL for a high and 70 mg/dL for a low are not crossed.

elimination.verdict: The value is in the target range, so the dose worked.

questions.objective: perform and interpret a fingerstick blood glucose

questions.stem: At 0730 a 67-year-old with NovoLog 5 units ordered with meals has a fingerstick of 68 mg/dL. The client is alert, swallows safely and reports no symptoms. The breakfast tray has arrived. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the NovoLog now, since the tray is here and the client will eat
options.rationale: Food present is the usual signal for rapid-acting insulin. Insulin is never given while the glucose is under 70 mg/dL.

options.text: Let the client eat breakfast, hold the NovoLog and recheck before lunch
options.rationale: Holding the insulin is right and food will help. A meal with fat and protein raises glucose slowly, and a low is rechecked in 15 minutes, not hours later.

options.text: Let the client eat half the tray, then give the NovoLog as ordered
options.rationale: Waiting for intake is sound for a normal value. This still puts insulin into a client whose glucose has not been shown to be over 70 mg/dL.

options.text: Give fast-acting carbohydrate, hold the NovoLog, recheck in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Under 70 mg/dL is treated with or without symptoms. 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and a 15 minute recheck come first, and insulin waits.

questions.takeaway: A value under 70 mg/dL is a low even with no symptoms. Treat it, recheck in 15 minutes and do not give insulin to a client who is low.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two options hold the insulin. The one stated cue is 68 mg/dL, which is under 70 mg/dL, so the low itself needs treatment and a timed recheck.

steps.detail: 68 mg/dL is under 70 mg/dL.

steps.action: Cut the options that give NovoLog
steps.detail: Now or after half the tray, it is insulin during a low.

steps.action: Compare the two that hold it
steps.detail: Breakfast alone is slow and has no 15 minute recheck.

elimination.verdict: Give fast-acting carbohydrate, hold the NovoLog and recheck in 15 minutes.

questions.objective: hold, question or report

questions.stem: A 71-year-old is ordered Novolin R 6 units and Novolin N 14 units in one syringe before breakfast. The nurse rolls the Novolin N vial, then sees that the unrolled Novolin R vial also looks cloudy. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Discard the cloudy Novolin R vial and obtain a clear one
options.rationale: Regular insulin is a clear solution. A cloudy vial of it is not used, and the dose still has to be prepared.

options.text: Roll the Novolin R vial gently until the cloudiness is even
options.rationale: Rolling is correct for NPH, a suspension. Regular insulin should never look cloudy, so rolling fixes nothing.

options.text: Draw the Novolin N first so the cloudy R vial matters less
options.rationale: The order of drawing is clear before cloudy. Reversing it does not make a spoiled vial usable.

options.text: Mix the dose as planned, since the final syringe looks cloudy
options.rationale: The mixed syringe does look cloudy because of the NPH. That does not excuse a regular vial that has changed.

questions.takeaway: Regular insulin is clear and NPH is cloudy. A cloudy vial of regular insulin is discarded and replaced before mixing.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Ask which vial is supposed to be cloudy. Only one of the two is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Novolin R is clear. Novolin N is cloudy.
Rolling belongs to the suspension.

steps.action: Cut the options that use the vial
steps.detail: Drawing order and the look of the final mix do not make it safe.

elimination.verdict: Discard the cloudy Novolin R vial and get a clear one.

questions.objective: prepare and give subcutaneous insulin

questions.stem: A nurse prepares regular insulin 6 units and NPH insulin 14 units in one syringe for a 71-year-old before breakfast. Place the steps in order.

options.text: Roll the NPH vial gently between the palms
options.rationale: The cloudy suspension is mixed first so the NPH dose is even.

options.text: Inject air into the NPH vial
options.rationale: Air goes into the cloudy vial first, with nothing drawn out yet.

options.text: Inject air into the regular insulin vial
options.rationale: Air goes into the clear vial second, and the needle stays in for the draw.

options.text: Withdraw regular insulin to the 6 unit mark
options.rationale: Clear is drawn first so the regular vial is never contaminated with suspension.

options.text: Withdraw NPH insulin until the plunger is at the 20 unit mark
options.rationale: The syringe already holds 6 units, so 14 units of NPH brings the total to 20.

questions.takeaway: Roll the NPH, air into cloudy, air into clear, draw clear, then draw cloudy to the total of both doses.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Fix two anchors: the clear insulin is drawn before the cloudy, and the last mark is the sum.

steps.detail: NPH is rolled so the dose is even.
Air goes into the NPH vial first, then the regular vial.
Regular to 6 units, then NPH to 6 plus 14, the 20 unit mark.

elimination.verdict: Roll NPH, air into NPH, air into regular, draw regular to 6, draw NPH to 20.

questions.objective: prepare and give subcutaneous insulin

questions.stem: A 71-year-old received regular and NPH insulin in one syringe at 0730 and ate a quarter of the breakfast tray at 0800. The client is alert with no symptoms. Which plan addresses the earliest risk?

options.text: Check the glucose at 0745, since regular insulin starts in 10 minutes
options.rationale: A 15 minute interval belongs to the recheck after treating a low. Regular insulin starts in 30 to 60 minutes.

options.text: Check the glucose at 1530, when the NPH is working hardest
options.rationale: The NPH peak, 1130 to 1930, is a real risk for this client. It is the later risk, not the earliest.

options.text: Check the glucose between 0930 and 1130 and offer carbohydrate
options.rationale: Regular insulin peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose. With a quarter of breakfast eaten, that window is the first setup for a low.

options.text: Check the glucose before lunch as scheduled and chart the intake
options.rationale: Charting intake is needed. A routine prelunch check may come after the regular insulin peak has already caused a low.

questions.takeaway: Reduced intake at an insulin's peak is the setup for a low. Regular insulin peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose, NPH at 4 to 12 hours.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Count the hours from 0730 for each insulin and pick the window that opens first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Regular peaks 0930 to 1130. NPH peaks 1130 to 1930.
Earliest means the regular insulin window.
Regular insulin does not start in 10 minutes.

elimination.verdict: Check between 0930 and 1130 and offer carbohydrate.

questions.objective: insulin timing and peak time risk

questions.stem: At 1545 an assistive personnel reports that a 71-year-old who received NPH insulin before breakfast at 0730 slept through the 1500 snack, has damp skin and is hard to wake. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Have the assistive personnel wake the client and give 4 ounces of juice
options.rationale: A low is likely, and juice treats one. Oral treatment is for a client who is alert and can swallow, and this client is hard to wake.

options.text: Go to the client, check responsiveness and get a fingerstick
options.rationale: A missed snack, damp skin and poor arousal at the NPH peak point to a low. The nurse assesses a changed client in person, and the value and swallowing ability decide the route of treatment.

options.text: Have the assistive personnel obtain a fingerstick and report the value
options.rationale: An assistive personnel can obtain a routine fingerstick. A client whose condition has changed is assessed by the nurse, and this adds a delay.

options.text: Let the client sleep and check the glucose before the dinner tray
options.rationale: Sleep is a reasonable guess for a tired client. Damp skin and a missed snack 8 hours after NPH make a low more likely than sleep.

questions.takeaway: New drowsiness and sweating in a client on insulin is a low until a fingerstick says otherwise. The nurse assesses the unstable client, and the mouth is used only if the client is alert and can swallow.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Juice and a delegated fingerstick are both defensible. The cue that tips it is hard to wake: that rules out the mouth and makes this the nurse's assessment.

steps.detail: 0730 to 1545 is just over 8 hours, inside the NPH peak.
Waiting for dinner ignores the cues.
Hard to wake means swallowing is not safe to assume.
Routine checks are delegated. A changed client is not.

elimination.verdict: Go to the client, check responsiveness and obtain a fingerstick now.

questions.objective: recognize and treat hypoglycemia

questions.stem: At 1045 a 76-year-old who received regular insulin before breakfast at 0700 and ate half of breakfast is being helped with a bath. Which findings point to a low blood glucose? Select all that apply.

options.text: Snaps at the nurse, which is new behavior
options.rationale: A behavior change in a client on insulin is a warning sign of a low.

options.text: Reports strong thirst
options.rationale: Thirst goes with a high glucose, not a low one.

options.text: Says twice that the hunger is hard to ignore
options.rationale: Hunger is a warning sign of a low, so the glucose is checked before it is treated as a food request.

options.text: Is sweating while sitting still
options.rationale: Sweating without exertion is a sign of a low.

options.text: Has deep, rapid breathing with abdominal pain
options.rationale: That pattern goes with a very high glucose and ketoacidosis.

questions.takeaway: Irritability, hunger and sweating in a client on insulin are warning signs of a low, most of all at the insulin's peak with reduced intake.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding as a sign of too little glucose or too much. Thirst and deep rapid breathing belong to a high.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 1045 is inside the 2 to 4 hour peak of regular insulin given at 0700.

steps.action: Keep the signs of a low
steps.detail: New irritability, hunger and sweating.

steps.action: Cut the signs of a high
steps.detail: Thirst, and deep rapid breathing with abdominal pain.

elimination.verdict: A, C and D.

questions.objective: recognize and treat hypoglycemia

questions.stem: At 1050 a 76-year-old who received regular insulin before breakfast at 0700 has a fingerstick glucose of 58 mg/dL. The client is alert, shaky and able to swallow. The lunch tray is due at 1200. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Send for an early lunch tray and use the meal as the treatment
options.rationale: Food is the right idea. A meal with fat and protein raises the glucose slowly, and the tray is not at the bedside.

options.text: Repeat the fingerstick on the other hand before treating
options.rationale: Confirming a doubtful value is sound. Nothing in the stem makes this value doubtful, and the symptoms match it.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck when shakiness eases
options.rationale: Right treatment, wrong endpoint. Symptoms easing does not show the glucose is back over 70 mg/dL.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The client is alert and can swallow, so the low is treated by mouth with simple sugar and rechecked on the clock.

questions.takeaway: Alert and able to swallow with a glucose under 70 mg/dL: 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, then a fingerstick recheck in 15 minutes.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The assessment is complete in the stem, so act. Then check each option for the amount, the type of food and the recheck time.

steps.detail: 58 mg/dL, alert, able to swallow.
The value fits the symptoms.
A meal is not fast-acting.
One rechecks by the clock, one by symptoms.

elimination.verdict: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes.

questions.objective: recognize and treat hypoglycemia

questions.stem: At 1050 a 76-year-old on insulin with a fingerstick glucose of 58 mg/dL was given 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate. Lunch is due at 1200. Which finding shows the treatment was effective?

options.text: Fingerstick glucose of 76 mg/dL at 1105
options.rationale: The 15 minute recheck is at least 70 mg/dL. The number is what shows the low has resolved.

options.text: Client says the shakiness is gone at 1055
options.rationale: Feeling better is encouraging. Symptoms can ease while the glucose is still under 70 mg/dL.

options.text: Fingerstick glucose of 67 mg/dL at 1105 with no symptoms
options.rationale: The recheck was done on time, but 67 mg/dL is still a low and the treatment is repeated.

options.text: Client eats the whole lunch tray at 1200
options.rationale: Good intake helps later. It does not show what the glucose was 15 minutes after treatment.

questions.takeaway: A treated low has resolved when the 15 minute recheck is 70 mg/dL or higher. Symptoms do not decide it.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Evaluate with the measure the treatment was aimed at: a number, at 15 minutes, at or above 70 mg/dL.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fingerstick at 15 minutes.

steps.action: Cut the options with no number
steps.detail: A symptom report and a meal.
67 mg/dL is under 70 mg/dL. 76 mg/dL is not.

elimination.verdict: Fingerstick glucose of 76 mg/dL at 1105.

questions.objective: recognize and treat hypoglycemia

questions.stem: A 76-year-old on insulin with a fingerstick glucose of 55 mg/dL was alert 10 minutes ago and was given juice. The client now slurs words and coughs with each sip. There is no IV access. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and continue the juice in small sips
options.rationale: Juice was right while the client swallowed safely. Coughing with each sip means oral treatment now risks aspiration.

options.text: Stop the juice and start an IV line so dextrose can be given
options.rationale: IV dextrose is the route when access is already in place. With no access, starting a line delays treatment of a worsening low.

options.text: Stop the juice, give glucagon by injection, turn client to the side
options.rationale: The client can no longer swallow safely and has no IV access. Glucagon by injection treats the low without the mouth, and side positioning protects the airway.

options.text: Stop the juice, keep the head raised and repeat the fingerstick in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Stopping the juice is right. Waiting 15 minutes leaves a low untreated while the client is getting worse.

questions.takeaway: When a client with a low can no longer swallow safely, stop oral treatment. IV access present means IV dextrose. No IV access means glucagon by injection and side positioning.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Three options stop the juice. The stated cue, no IV access, picks the route that works right now.

steps.detail: Slurred words and coughing with sips mean the mouth is no longer safe.
More juice risks the airway.
The low is still untreated.
Dextrose needs a line that is not there.

elimination.verdict: Stop the juice, give glucagon by injection and turn the client to the side.

questions.objective: recognize and treat hypoglycemia

questions.stem: A 62-year-old has Humalog 6 units ordered with meals. At 0750 the fingerstick is 162 mg/dL, and the kitchen says the breakfast tray will come at 0820. When does the nurse give the Humalog?

options.text: At 0750, so the insulin is working when the tray arrives
options.rationale: Thirty minutes ahead is the timing for regular insulin. Humalog starts in 10 to 30 minutes and could act before any food is present.

options.text: At 0820, when the tray is in front of the client
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin is given with the food. The glucose is above 70 mg/dL, so the dose is safe once the meal is present.

options.text: At 0920, one hour after the client begins eating
options.rationale: Waiting for intake sounds careful. An hour later the meal has already raised the glucose with no insulin to cover it.

options.text: Not at breakfast, because the tray is running late
options.rationale: A late tray moves the dose. It does not cancel it, since the client will still eat.

questions.takeaway: Insulin timing follows the food: rapid-acting as the tray arrives, regular about 30 minutes before, basal on the clock.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Name the insulin type before you look at the clock. One option is the correct timing for a different insulin.

steps.detail: Humalog is rapid-acting, onset 10 to 30 minutes.
30 minutes ahead leaves it acting before the tray.

steps.action: Cut the late and the omitted dose
steps.detail: Both leave the meal uncovered.

elimination.verdict: At 0820, when the tray is in front of the client.

questions.objective: insulin timing and peak time risk

questions.stem: A 62-year-old takes Lantus 22 units at 2100 and Humalog with meals. The client vomited and ate no dinner, so the Humalog was held. At 2100 the fingerstick is 148 mg/dL and the client asks to skip the Lantus. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hold the Lantus tonight, because the client ate no dinner at all
options.rationale: That reasoning is correct for mealtime Humalog. Lantus is basal insulin with no pronounced peak and is not timed to food.

options.text: Give half of the Lantus dose to match the missed meal
options.rationale: Lantus is not matched to meals, and a changed dose needs an order.

options.text: Hold the Lantus and recheck the fingerstick at 0200
options.rationale: Checking overnight is cautious. Without basal insulin the glucose climbs, and illness raises it further.

options.text: Give the Lantus as ordered and explain it is not tied to meals
options.rationale: Basal insulin continues through a missed meal and through illness. At 148 mg/dL there is no low to stop it.

questions.takeaway: Mealtime insulin follows the meal the client actually eats. Basal insulin is given on the clock and continues through illness.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The same missed meal has opposite effects on the two insulins. Decide which kind Lantus is.

steps.detail: Humalog is mealtime. Lantus is basal.
Three options tie the Lantus to the missed dinner.
148 mg/dL is above 70 mg/dL.

elimination.verdict: Give the Lantus as ordered and explain why.

questions.objective: hold, question or report

questions.stem: At 2100 a nurse preparing Lantus 22 units for a 62-year-old takes a vial from the client's bin. The solution is clear, and the label reads Humalog. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Return it and obtain the vial labeled Lantus
options.rationale: Both insulins are clear, so only the label separates them. The nurse gives the insulin that was ordered.

options.text: Draw up 22 units, because a clear solution matches Lantus
options.rationale: Checking appearance is a real step. It cannot tell two clear insulins apart.

options.text: Give the Humalog 22 units with a bedtime snack to cover it
options.rationale: Food does make rapid-acting insulin safer. It does not turn the wrong insulin into the ordered one.

options.text: Ask the provider to change the bedtime order to Humalog
options.rationale: Calling the provider fits a questionable order. The order is correct here. The vial is wrong.

questions.takeaway: Read the label against the order every time. Appearance separates clear from cloudy insulin, not one clear insulin from another.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Ask what is actually wrong: the order, or the vial in the hand.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Order says Lantus. Label says Humalog.

steps.action: Cut the options that give Humalog
steps.detail: With or without a snack it is the wrong insulin.
The order needs no change.

elimination.verdict: Return it, obtain the Lantus vial and read its label against the order.

questions.objective: prepare and give subcutaneous insulin

questions.stem: A 62-year-old takes Lantus at 2100 and Humalog with meals. Over 4 days the fasting readings were 104 to 126 mg/dL with no overnight lows, and readings after meals were 232 to 258 mg/dL. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: The Lantus is not holding the glucose through the night
options.rationale: That would show as high fasting readings. The fasting values are in range.

options.text: An overnight low is rebounding into high readings
options.rationale: A rebound follows an overnight low and shows in the morning. No overnight lows were found.

options.text: The mealtime Humalog is not covering the meals
options.rationale: Glucose after meals reflects the rapid-acting insulin. Those are the only readings above range.

options.text: The Lantus should be moved from bedtime to mealtimes
options.rationale: Long-acting insulin is given on the clock, not with meals. The fasting readings show it is working.

questions.takeaway: Fasting glucose reflects the long-acting insulin. Glucose after meals reflects the rapid-acting insulin.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Match each set of readings to the insulin that is responsible for it, then see which set is out of range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fasting goes with Lantus. After meals goes with Humalog.

steps.action: Find the set out of range
steps.detail: 232 to 258 mg/dL after meals.

steps.action: Cut the options that blame Lantus
steps.detail: Fasting values of 104 to 126 mg/dL are in range.

elimination.verdict: The mealtime Humalog is not covering the meals.

questions.objective: insulin timing and peak time risk

questions.stem: For each action by the student, indicate whether it is correct technique or needs correction.
questions.scenario: A student gives a 62-year-old Humalog 6 units at 1700 as the dinner tray arrives while the nurse observes. The client's injections are given in the abdomen. Lantus is due at 2100.

rows.text: Draws the dose in an insulin syringe marked in units
rows.rationale: Insulin is drawn up only in an insulin syringe marked in units.

rows.text: Chooses a spot on the abdomen away from the lunch injection
rows.rationale: One region is kept and the spot within it changes each time.

rows.text: Pinches up the skin and inserts the needle at 90 degrees
rows.rationale: This keeps the dose in the subcutaneous tissue.

rows.text: Pulls back on the plunger to look for blood
rows.rationale: Aspiration is not required for subcutaneous insulin.

rows.text: Rubs the site firmly after withdrawing the needle
rows.rationale: Massage speeds absorption and makes the dose act unpredictably.

rows.text: Offers to add the 2100 Lantus to this syringe to save an injection
rows.rationale: Long-acting insulin is never mixed with another insulin, and it is given on its own schedule.

questions.takeaway: Insulin syringe in units, one region with a new spot, pinch and 90 degrees. No aspiration, no rubbing, and long-acting insulin is never mixed.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Judge each action alone. Three of them are habits that sound careful or kind and are still wrong for subcutaneous insulin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Check the equipment and the spot
steps.detail: Unit syringe, same region, new spot.
Pinch and 90 degrees, no aspiration, no rubbing.
Lantus goes in its own syringe.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1, 2 and 3 are correct technique. Rows 4, 5 and 6 need correction.

questions.objective: prepare and give subcutaneous insulin

questions.stem: A 49-year-old injects NPH insulin before breakfast each day into the same firm, raised area on the left abdomen because it does not hurt there. Readings before lunch are near 240 mg/dL. Which instruction does the nurse give?

options.text: Keep using that spot and massage it after each injection
options.rationale: Massage does speed absorption. It is not a taught fix, and the thickened tissue stays in use.

options.text: Use the thigh on one day and the upper arm on the next
options.rationale: Leaving the damaged area is right. Moving between regions changes absorption from dose to dose.

options.text: Keep using that spot until the provider raises the NPH dose
options.rationale: A higher dose answers the high readings. The cause is poor absorption, and a larger dose becomes dangerous once healthy tissue is used.

options.text: Use intact abdominal spots and check the glucose more often
options.rationale: Thickened tissue absorbs insulin poorly. In healthy tissue the same dose works harder, so the client rotates within the region and watches for lows.

questions.takeaway: Avoid damaged or thickened areas and rotate within one region. When a client moves to healthy tissue the same dose absorbs better, so watch for lows.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The high readings have a cause in the stem. Fix the site, keep the region and plan for what better absorption does.

steps.detail: A firm, raised area absorbs poorly.

steps.action: Cut the options that keep the spot
steps.detail: Two of them stay in damaged tissue.
Thigh and arm absorb at different rates.

elimination.verdict: Use intact abdominal spots and check the glucose more often.

questions.objective: prepare and give subcutaneous insulin

questions.stem: A 49-year-old injects regular insulin into the abdomen before breakfast and asks to move that dose to the buttock because it would hurt less there. Which response does the nurse give?

options.text: "The buttock absorbs fastest, so you would need to eat much sooner."
options.rationale: This reverses the order. The abdomen is fastest and the buttock is slowest.

options.text: "The buttock absorbs slowest, so the dose may lag behind the meal."
options.rationale: Absorption runs abdomen, upper arm, thigh, then buttock. A slower site can leave a mealtime dose acting after the food.

options.text: "All sites absorb alike, so choose whichever one hurts the least."
options.rationale: Comfort matters to the client. Sites do not absorb alike, so the choice changes how the dose acts.

options.text: "Alternate the abdomen and the buttock so each area can rest."
options.rationale: Resting tissue is a kind thought. Switching regions makes each dose absorb at a different rate.

questions.takeaway: Absorption is fastest from the abdomen, then the upper arm, then the thigh, then the buttock. Changing the region changes when the dose acts.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Two responses state an absorption speed for the buttock and they are opposites. Settle that pair first.

steps.detail: Abdomen, upper arm, thigh, buttock.
Slowest is true of the buttock.
Alternating regions varies absorption.

elimination.verdict: The buttock absorbs slowest, so the dose may lag behind the meal.

questions.objective: prepare and give subcutaneous insulin

questions.stem: A 49-year-old injects regular insulin at 0700, drives 50 minutes to work and eats breakfast there at 0815. The client reports feeling shaky during the drive on most days. Which change does the nurse suggest?

options.text: Inject at home and eat about 30 minutes later, before driving
options.rationale: Regular insulin starts in 30 to 60 minutes. Eating about 30 minutes after the dose puts food in before the insulin acts on the road.

options.text: Keep the routine, since regular insulin takes 2 hours to start working
options.rationale: Two hours is where the peak begins. The onset is 30 to 60 minutes, which matches the shakiness on the drive.

options.text: Eat breakfast at work first, then inject once the meal is finished
options.rationale: Tying insulin to food is right. Regular insulin given after a meal acts too late to cover it.

options.text: Leave out the morning dose on the days the client drives to work
options.rationale: This stops the shakiness by removing a prescribed dose, which is not the nurse's or the client's decision.

questions.takeaway: Regular insulin is given about 30 minutes before the meal because its onset is 30 to 60 minutes. Food that comes later than that leaves the insulin working alone.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Line up the injection, the onset and the meal on the clock. The gap between them is the problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Onset 0730 to 0800. Breakfast at 0815.
Regular insulin does not wait 2 hours.
Skipping or moving the dose after the meal is not the fix.

elimination.verdict: Inject at home and eat breakfast about 30 minutes later, before driving.

questions.objective: insulin timing and peak time risk

questions.stem: A 49-year-old injects regular and NPH insulin into the abdomen before breakfast at 0700. The client began a 40 minute walk at 1430 this week, with fingersticks of 58 and 62 mg/dL at 1500 twice. Meals are unchanged. Which plan does the nurse suggest?

options.text: Stop the afternoon walks for now and restart once the lows have ended
options.rationale: This would stop the lows. It gives up the client's exercise when the timing, not the walking, is the problem.

options.text: Move the morning injection to the thigh for slower absorption
options.rationale: The thigh is slower than the abdomen at rest. It is the working limb on a walk, and exercise speeds absorption from it.

options.text: Check the glucose before each walk and eat a carbohydrate snack first
options.rationale: The walk lands in the NPH peak, 1100 to 1900, and meals have not changed. A check and a snack before activity cover the peak and keep the client walking.

options.text: Take 2 units less NPH on the days a walk is planned
options.rationale: Too much insulin for the activity is one cause of a low. A dose change is the provider's decision, not the client's or the nurse's.

questions.takeaway: Exercise lowers glucose most when it lands on an insulin's peak. Check before activity and put food ahead of it. Do not inject a limb that is about to work.
questions.coverage: Not in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Stopping the walk and covering the walk both end the lows. The stated cue is the time: 1430 sits inside the NPH peak, so cover that window and keep the activity.

steps.detail: NPH at 0700 peaks 1100 to 1900. The walk is at 1430.
That needs an order.
A working limb absorbs faster.
Covering keeps the client active and safe.

elimination.verdict: Check the glucose before each walk and eat a carbohydrate snack first.

questions.objective: insulin timing and peak time risk

questions.stem: A nurse watches an assistive personnel check an 80-year-old's fingerstick with a shared meter: two identifiers, clean dry hands, new lancet, side of the fingertip. The assistive personnel then carries the meter toward the next room. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Let the morning checks continue, since each step was correct
options.rationale: Every step at this bedside was correct. The problem is the one that comes next.

options.text: Remind the assistive personnel to use the center of the finger pad
options.rationale: The side of the fingertip is the taught site. The center pad hurts more.

options.text: Take over the remaining fingersticks for the rest of the shift
options.rationale: Stepping in is right. A routine fingerstick stays a task the assistive personnel can do once the error is corrected.

options.text: Stop the assistive personnel and have the meter disinfected first
options.rationale: A meter used on more than one client is cleaned and disinfected between clients. This is the step about to be missed.

questions.takeaway: A glucose meter used on more than one client is cleaned and disinfected between clients. Lancets are single use.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Check off what the stem says was done. The answer is the step that is missing, not a step that was done well.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Identifiers, clean dry hands, new lancet, side of the fingertip.
Nothing was done to the shared meter.
Correct the step. Do not remove the task.

elimination.verdict: Stop the assistive personnel and have the meter disinfected first.

questions.objective: perform and interpret a fingerstick blood glucose

questions.stem: At 0730 an 80-year-old has regular insulin 10 units ordered before breakfast, and the tray comes at 0800. The fingerstick is 112 mg/dL. The client has been nauseated since 0500 and says no breakfast will be eaten. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose now, because 30 minutes before the tray is correct
options.rationale: The timing is correct for regular insulin. The client has said no food will follow it.

options.text: Hold the dose and report the nausea and lack of intake
options.rationale: Insulin is held and clarified when the client will not be eating. Reduced intake is a key cause of inpatient lows.

options.text: Give 5 units now and 5 more if the client eats
options.rationale: Matching insulin to intake is the right instinct. A split dose is a dose nobody ordered.

options.text: Give the dose now and add juice to the breakfast tray
options.rationale: Carbohydrate behind the insulin is sensible. A nauseated client who refuses breakfast may not take the juice.

questions.takeaway: Hold mealtime insulin and clarify it when the glucose is under 70 mg/dL or the client will not be eating.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: The number is fine and the timing is fine. The cue that decides it is what the client says about eating.

steps.detail: 112 mg/dL is not the problem.
Nausea and no plan to eat.

steps.action: Cut the options that give insulin
steps.detail: Full dose, half dose or dose with juice all go in without a meal.

elimination.verdict: Hold the dose and report the nausea and lack of intake.

questions.objective: hold, question or report

questions.stem: An 80-year-old on scheduled insulin with meals and no correction scale has prelunch fingersticks of 176, 184 and 192 mg/dL on three days. The client is alert with no symptoms. Each value was charted without action. Which action does the nurse take today?

options.text: Chart today's value, because the client has no symptoms
options.rationale: Charting is required. A value above 180 mg/dL that keeps rising is not left at charting.

options.text: Give 2 extra units of the scheduled insulin with lunch
options.rationale: More insulin may be what is needed. Units added without an order are outside the nurse's scope.

options.text: Assess the client and review the orders against the trend
options.rationale: Above 180 mg/dL is hyperglycemia that calls for assessment and a review of orders. The three day climb makes it worth acting on.

options.text: Repeat the fingerstick on the other hand to confirm the value
options.rationale: A repeat is for a reading that does not fit the trend or came from poor technique. Three days of rising values fit each other, so this adds a puncture and no answer.

questions.takeaway: Above 180 mg/dL is hyperglycemia. Read the trend, assess the client and review the orders. Do not ignore it, recheck it away or treat it without an order.
questions.coverage: Covered in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Know the top of the range and read the three values as a line. Two options assess: one gathers what the provider needs, one only repeats a number that already fits.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 184 and 192 mg/dL are above 180 mg/dL.
Each day is higher than the last.

steps.action: Cut the unordered fix and the repeat
steps.detail: Extra units need an order. A repeat fingerstick only confirms a value that fits the trend.

elimination.verdict: Assess the client and review the orders against the rising trend.

questions.objective: perform and interpret a fingerstick blood glucose

questions.stem: At 2100 an 80-year-old has NPH insulin 12 units ordered at bedtime. The fingerstick is 72 mg/dL, down from 140 mg/dL before dinner at 1700, and the client ate half of dinner. The client has no symptoms. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Call the provider with the value and intake before giving it
options.rationale: The value is barely above 70 mg/dL and falling after a half eaten dinner, and NPH would peak from 0100 to 0900 while the client sleeps. The dose is questioned before it is given.

options.text: Give the NPH as ordered, since 72 mg/dL is inside the target range
options.rationale: 72 mg/dL is inside 70 to 180 mg/dL, and that is why this is tempting. The falling trend and reduced intake point to a low once the NPH peaks.

options.text: Give fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, then give the NPH
options.rationale: This is the treatment for a value under 70 mg/dL, and 72 mg/dL is not under it. It also gives the full 12 units without anyone weighing the fall and the half eaten dinner.

options.text: Hold the NPH tonight and recheck the fingerstick at 0700
options.rationale: Caution is right. Leaving out a dose without telling the provider is not the nurse's decision.

questions.takeaway: Read the trend, not only the number. A glucose falling toward 70 mg/dL with reduced intake, ahead of an insulin's peak, is a reason to question the dose before giving it.
questions.coverage: Not in skills lab material. There is no Lecture PPT for this skill.
questions.strategy: Giving it and questioning it are both defensible at 72 mg/dL. The cues that tip it are the fall from 140 mg/dL and the half eaten dinner.

steps.detail: 72 mg/dL is in range by 2 points.
Down 68 mg/dL in 4 hours, half of dinner eaten.
NPH at 2100 peaks 0100 to 0900.
Holding without reporting is not within scope.

elimination.verdict: Call the provider with the value, intake and trend before giving it.
